source every `pollSeconds`:

1. `discover()` → for each item whose `key` has no job, or whose newest job is re-runnable
   (see **Re-run** below): create one via the host's
   `ingest(item)` — spec `{ executor: item.executor, payload: { prompt, cwd, model?, env },
   priority, goal: title, submittedBy: "<source>:<author>", kind: "coding" }`; `item.invalid`
   or a payload the executor rejects → job created and failed in one tx (`job.queued` +
   `job.failed`); for items that already have a job: `host.refresh(jobId, item, source)`
   (re-sort and respecify; applies only to queued/held — see **Waiting jobs take the config as
   it is now** below),
   `source: JobSourceRef`, with `payload.prompt = item.prompt`, `payload.env = item.env` —
   then `report({kind:'claimed'})`, merge the returned patch into
   `sourceState`. A key whose newest job is not re-runnable → skip (the host's `ingest` guard).
2. `check(active)` for this source's non-terminal jobs → `cancel` signal → engine cancel
   (reason recorded); `answer` signal → `QuestionService.answerByHuman(questionId, answer)`
   (ignored if not open).
3. **Outbound reports** are event-driven and retried: on `job.progressed` (throttled to one
   per `progressCommentSeconds` per job), the **first** `question.escalated {target: human}`
   of a question (re-notifies are ignored — one question comment per question),
   `question.answered`, `job.finished`, `job.failed`, `job.cancelled` for a job with a
   `source`, call `report(...)`. Reports for one job are serialized (a per-job promise
   chain). The returned `source` state replaces `sourceState.source` via
   `host.setSourceState` in a tx that re-reads the job. `sourceState.sync` (owned here)
   records `claimReported`, `reportedQuestions: string[]`, `finalReported`, `cancelReason`.
   **Retry scan** each sync: claim not reported; open human-tier questions not reported;
   terminal jobs (finished/failed/cancelled) whose final report did not go out — so a crash
   right after a job ends still reports. A `SourceError` with `permanent: true` marks the
   report done-with-error (status `detail.permanentErrors`) and is never retried.
4. Status → `SourceStatus` (state, last sync, last error, counts, detail) → `/api/sources`,
   SSE `source.updated`.
5. **A failing source is never silent** (issue #358): its error is logged once when it changes, and
   once when the source is ok again; a source in error longer than the **stall threshold**
   (`STALL_AFTER_MS`, 30 min) records `source.stalled { source, kind, error, since }` once per run of
   failures, which the notifiers send.

**Waiting jobs take the config as it is now** (issue #375). Each sync offers every item that already
has a waiting (`queued`/`held`) job to `host.refresh(jobId, item, source)`, one tx that re-reads the
job (`src/engine/source-host.ts`):

- **Priority:** the routing rule's, else the item's, as now; a change → `job.reprioritized`. A job
  that ran before (requeued) is re-sorted too.
- **Spec, only while the job has never started** (`attempts` 0, no pending answer): routing is run
  again and the parts the source and routing rules give the spec — executor, model, work tree,
  default work tree, machine pin, routing rule (`SpecFromConfig`) — are worked out again. The job
  keeps what they gave it last as `fromConfig` (absent on a job from before: its spec as it is). A
  part whose value on the job differs from `fromConfig` was changed by hand and is kept; the others
  take the new value. When the config's answer changed, the spec is replaced
  (`JobRepository.respecify`), `fromConfig` updated and `job.respecified { from, to }` recorded; a
  Decision follows, since the pin may have moved. A new spec its executor rejects is not applied
  (logged); the job keeps the old one.
- **A started job keeps its spec.** A job waiting on an answer resumes in the pane, agent session
  and work tree it ran in, so neither its machine nor its work tree can change under it. To run it on
  the new config, cancel it and run it again.

**Re-run.** A source key may have many jobs; `jobs.source_key` is an index, not unique, and
`getBySourceKey` returns the **newest** (`created_at`, then `seq`, descending). An item whose
newest job ended — `finished`, `failed` or `cancelled` — **and** whose end was reported
(`sourceState.sync.finalReported`, so the source's marker — `hopper:done` or `hopper:failed` on
GitHub — was written at least once) gets a new job when the source offers it again. The GitHub
source stops offering an issue while `hopper:failed` or `hopper:done` is present (and a finished
job's issue is closed), so removing that label — after reopening, for a finished one — is the
re-run gesture, and a leftover `hopper:claimed` does not block it (the old job makes the key known).
Unreported, the item stays one attempt, so a failing label write cannot loop. Predicate:
`isRerunnable` in `src/domain/types.ts`. The key spans sources: an old `github` job and a
`github-app` re-run share it. Before issue #186 a finished job was never re-run, so an issue reopened
after a job that finished without shipping stayed stuck, skipped without a word.

**Run again** (issues #313, #354). An ended job need not wait for a human to clear its marker at the
source, nor for a sync to offer its item again: `POST /ui/api/jobs/:id/rerun` (operator; the Ended
panel's Run again button) asks the sync loop (`SourceRegistry.rerun`) to queue the item again now. Only
the newest job of its key, status `failed`, `finished` (a result that is not wanted), `rejected` or `cancelled`
(issue #1352), whose end was reported (`finalReported`), of a running source that implements `JobSource.rerun` —
else 409; unknown → 404. **An item belongs to its repository and issue, not to the source that first saw it**
(issue #1352): when a job's own source no longer runs (its instance was removed, as the polling `github-account`
was), a running source that **adopts** it (`JobSource.adopts`: the job's repository is one of its job repositories)
takes the item back in its place, and the new job is that source's. Its end need not be reported: the removed source
is told nothing more. Retry, Continue and Push it ask the same (`takesBack`). On the job's report chain the source gives the item back (`JobSource.rerun`) — on GitHub
(`takeBack`) a closed issue is **reopened** (the new job is cancelled while its issue is closed, and its
own pull request's merge closes it again), `hopper:failed`, `hopper:done`, `hopper:rejected` and
`hopper:claimed` go, and the source label comes back if it was taken off — and answers the item as it
stands now. `SourceHost.rerun` then, in one tx, creates the new job as `ingest` does (routing rules, the
queue gate; priority and lane caps apply as to any job), with `rerunOf` the ended job, and appends
`job.rerun { by: "user" }` on the ended job; the route answers the new job, and the UI's toast says where
it is (waiting for acceptance, held and why, queued, or failed at intake with its reason). A sync that
offered the item in between already made the job: that one is answered. The ended job is kept as it
ended. A source that cannot give the item back → 502 with its error, and nothing is recorded. **An issue no
longer assigned to the connected account is assigned to it first** (issue #1010): its new job was cancelled
`unassigned` at once while Run again answered success (issue #527, 22 such jobs in one day), and from then until
issue #1010 `takeBack` refused it (409, "assign it (Sources, Assign to me) and run it again") — a step the hopper
can take itself, as Assign to me does, so Run again, Continue, Rework and tending stopped on it with no way out
in their own view. `takeBack` now adds the connected account to the issue's assignees before any other write;
other assignees stay. Before
issue #354 Run again only cleared the labels and waited for a sync, and a closed issue was refused (409,
issue #348); neither is so now. Any job made for a key that already had one carries `rerunOf`, whether
Run again or a human clearing the marker made it.

**Locked entries** (issue #355). A failed job does not drop out of the queue: a failed job whose failure is
still its work item's — the work-item ledger has the item `failed` on it, or handed to a person on it (issue #1067:
not run again, not dismissed, its issue not closed) — is a **locked entry** (`isLocked`, `src/domain/locked.ts`), listed in
`/api/queue` `locked`, highest priority first, then oldest — under the Dashboard's Waiting jobs and in the
Queue view's Locked panel, with its failure, the job it runs again (`rerunOf`), Run again and Dismiss.
Its status stays `failed`: the decider never sees it, so it takes no lane and no budget, and nothing
else that reads `failed` (the Ended list, the cards, the webhooks, the source's `hopper:failed`)
changes. The queue is the truth; the issue's labels mirror it. Run again (above) unlocks it: its new
job is the item's newest, so the failed one leaves `locked`, and a new failure is the locked entry in its
place. **Dismiss** (`POST /ui/api/jobs/:id/dismiss`, operator) sets `dismissedAt` and appends
`job.dismissed { by: "user" }`: the job leaves the locked entries, stays failed, keeps its issue's
`hopper:failed`, and can still be run again. A job that is not failed, or already dismissed → 409. A job
of no source (from before phase 3) is never a locked entry: it cannot run again. The UI keeps the locked
entries apart from its other jobs (`locked` in the store), since they are of any age while the rest
reach back 24 hours.

**Stale failures dismiss themselves** (issue #1123). A failed job that nothing waits on any more stayed undismissed
for ever: a store held 163 such rows, 162 of them with a newer job of the same item, and the failures they left in
the Failures view hid the one live one. Now the hopper dismisses a failed job by itself when a newer job of its item
exists (`job.dismissed { by: "superseded" }`), or when its work item is closed at its source, done or dropped
(`by: "item_closed"`): at each `job.queued` and `work_item.issue_closed`, at each failure sweep, and at start
(`Handoffs.dismissStale`, `src/failures/handoffs.ts`). An open hand-off of the job closes the same way (`end`
`superseded` or `item_closed`), its record settled; one a person is resolving now is left to that person. Only a
person's dismissal (`by: "user"`) opens a hand-off when nothing else ends it: a dismissal by itself waits on nobody.
A failure whose job is dismissed with no hand-off has ended (`endedAt`): it leaves the open failures. The failure
count was already the ledger's (`failed` work items, issue #1067), which counts one item once, on its newest job.
For what the automatic path has not reached yet, **Dismiss many** (`POST /ui/api/jobs/dismiss`, operator):
`{ jobIds }` dismisses each as one Dismiss does and answers each refusal with why, or `{ superseded: true }` runs
the automatic pass now; the CLI's `hopper job dismiss <id>...` and `hopper job dismiss --superseded` (`src/cli-operator-dismiss.ts`).

**A failure ends when its item's work ends** (issue #1461). An operator cleared failures by hand for hours: items whose
work had landed, or whose pull request was closed, kept a hand-off open, because an item a person holds is `needs_you`
and a merge or a close only marked its pull request. Now the item waits on no failure also when its pull request merged
as the whole item (`mergedWhole`: not a part, not a culprit reverted from the landing branch) or closed without a merge
(`itemEnded`, `src/failures/stale.ts`). The automatic pass also runs at each `job.pull_request_merged`,
`job.pull_request_closed`, `job.pull_request_abandoned` and `landing_batch.promoted`: the hand-off closes
(`item_closed`), its record settles, and the job is dismissed `by: "item_closed"`. The ledger then has the item `done`
(merged) or `dropped` (closed). The sidebar's counts are issue #1457's.

**Run again offered only where it is taken** (issues #362, #354). The UI never offers an action the
daemon refuses: the Ended panel's Run again (`canRerun`) needs a failed or finished job, the newest of its
item, its end reported. A closed issue no longer blocks it (Run again reopens it), so the per-sync
`JobSource.closedItems` check and its `sourceState.sync.itemClosed` mark that #362 added are gone; rows
that still carry `itemClosed` keep it, and nothing reads it.

**Not run again, said out loud** (issue #186). An offered item whose newest job ended but cannot
re-run yet (its end is not reported to the source) is not dropped silently: it is listed in the
source status `detail.notRerun` (`{ key, job, status, reason }`, shown on the Sources view) and
logged once per key, `hopper: <key> not run again: job <id> <status>, <reason>`. An item whose job is
still live is only re-sorted, as before. Residual: gh mode's search can lag about a minute, so a
just-reported issue may be offered once more with its old labels and re-run; the app source never
searches.

A source error never stops the daemon or other sources; it is shown in status and retried.

## GitHub source

> **Since issue #359** the gh CLI adapter is gone, and with it `owners`, `whoami()`,
> `searchOpenIssues` and every search: discovery lists the app's installed repos or a connected
> account's job repositories, repo by repo. The GitHub sources are `github-account` and `github-app`
> ("One way to GitHub as the user", at the end). The rest of this section is the phase-3 design.

Config `~/.config/hopper/sources.yaml` (`HOPPER_SOURCES_FILE`), validated with zod;
invalid → the source is `error` with the message, nothing is pulled.

```yaml
version: 1
github:
  enabled: true
  pollSeconds: 60
  owners: []            # discover across repos owned by these; empty → the `gh` user
  repos: []             # allowlist: when non-empty, ONLY these owner/repo are acted on
  authors: [owner]      # required, at least one login: no default allowlist
  label: hopper
  priorityLabels: { "hopper:high": 75, "hopper:low": 25 }
  defaultPriority: 50
  repoPaths: {}         # owner/repo → local path (cwd); default defaultCwd
  defaultCwd: ~/workbench/app-workflows
  executor: herdr-claude
  model: null           # optional claude model for jobs
  progressCommentSeconds: 300
  recentComments: 10    # comments passed into the job's context
  projects: {}          # per repo, optional — see "Priority"
  # projects:
  #   owner/hopper-sandbox:
  #     owner: owner
  #     number: 3
  #     mode: field         # field | rank
  #     field: Priority     # field mode: single-select or number field name
  #     map: { P0: 100, P1: 75, P2: 50, P3: 25 }   # single-select option → priority
```

**Priority** (owner request, phase 3 addition). Both sources are supported, configurable per repo;
**when both are present, the project wins**:

1. Project (repos listed under `projects`): the issue's item in that Projects (v2) board.
   - `mode: field` — a single-select value mapped through `map`, or a number field used
     directly (clamped 0..100).
   - `mode: rank` — the item's position in the project's item order:
     `priority = max(0, 100 − index)`, so the top item is 100.
   - Read with `gh project item-list <number> --owner <owner> --format json --limit 1000
     --query "is:issue is:open"`; field keys come back lowercased, so the configured field
     name matches case-insensitively; rank counts only eligible items. That needs
     the `read:project` token scope. Without it, or on any project error, the source falls
     back to labels and shows the error in status `detail.projectErrors`. It never blocks.
2. Labels: the highest matching `priorityLabels` value.
3. `defaultPriority`.

**Filing labels** (issue #31). Filing a job needs only `label` (`hopper`); every job then runs
at `defaultPriority` (50). Optional, set by a person on the issue:

| label | effect |
|-------|--------|
| `hopper:high` | priority 75: runs before default jobs |
| `hopper:low` | priority 25: runs after default jobs |
| `hopper:backburner` | never picked up while set (not a priority: discovery skips the issue); a waiting job whose issue gets it is cancelled, a running job finishes. Removing the label takes the issue in again on the next poll |

The `hopper:p0`..`hopper:p3` labels are gone: removed from the issues and the watched repos.

`priorityReason` records which one applied, e.g. `project:Priority=P1`, `project:rank=2`,
`label:hopper:high` or `default`. **Re-sorted on every poll:** discovery recomputes the
priority of every eligible item. When a waiting (`queued`/`held`) job's priority changed,
the sync loop updates it and emits `job.reprioritized { from, to, reason }`, then
triggers a decision. A started job's priority follows too, since issue #535 ("High priority everywhere"): the live priority.

**Full issue context into the job** (owner request, phase 3 addition). The prompt is the issue
body, then a block:

```
[hopper issue context]
repo: owner/repo · issue: #N · url: …
title: …
labels: a, b · author: owner
priority: 75 (label:hopper:high) · project item: <project title> · Priority=P1 (or "none")
windows: …: only with a Windows label: the Windows work runs as Windows sandbox steps ("Windows sandbox steps")
checks: …: not for an artifact deliverable: run the type check, lint, build and the affected test files here; the pull request's checks run the full suite; list environment skips apart (issue #1038, `CHECKS_LINE`)
done: …: done is the job's pull request, ready for review; with yolo mode on for the repo, it may also merge it ("Done is a pull request" below)
recent comments (oldest first, up to recentComments; only the assignee's, no hopper-marked comments — anyone else's text never reaches the job; issue #387):
- <author> at <ISO>: <body, ≤ 1000 chars>
...
```

The block ends at the comments list: no footer (write criteria below).

Size caps: body ≤ 64 000 chars, context block ≤ 16 000 chars (comments truncated to fit).

Job environment, set on the job's herdr tab with `herdr tab create --env`:
- `HOPPER_ISSUE_URL`, `HOPPER_REPO`, `HOPPER_ISSUE_NUMBER`, `HOPPER_ISSUE_TITLE`
- `HOPPER_COMMENT_MARKER` = `<!-- hopper v1 kind=job-comment -->`
- `HOPPER_JOB_ID`, added by the herdr-claude executor from `ctx.job.id`

The herdr-claude payload gains `env?: Record<string, string>`: keys must match
`^[A-Z_][A-Z0-9_]*$`, values contain no newline. The marker matters because the job
comments as the owner: the answer detector skips marked comments, and a job is paused (Claude
idle) while it waits for an answer anyway.

**GitHubApi port** (`src/sources/github/api.ts`) — the adapter's seam: `whoami()`,
`projectItems(owner, number)` → `{ url (issue url), index, fields: Record<string, string |
number> }[]` (throws `missing read:project scope` distinctly),
`searchOpenIssues({ owners, label })`, `listOpenIssues(repo, label)`, `getIssue(repo,
number)` → `{ state, labels, author, title, body, url, updatedAt }`,
`listComments(repo, number)` → `{ id, author, body, createdAt, url }[]`,
`ensureLabel(repo, name, color, description)`, `addLabels`, `removeLabels`,
No comment write: the port has none.
Real adapter: `gh` CLI via `execFile` (no shell), JSON output, `gh api` for comments/labels,
timeouts, typed errors; env passes through (gh's keyring auth). Fake: an in-memory GitHub
(issues, labels, comments, authors) used by unit and integration tests.

**Discovery:** `repos` non-empty → `listOpenIssues` per repo (no search lag). Else
`searchOpenIssues` over `owners` (or `whoami()`), restricted to repos owned by them —
GitHub search can lag new issues by up to about a minute. Eligible: open, has `label`,
author in `authors` (issue #387: assigned to the user's connected account instead), no `hopper:done` / `hopper:failed` / `hopper:rejected` / `hopper:backburner`, repo allowed,
not addressed to another hopper (`hopper@<name>`, "Queue gate"). Already-claimed
issues with no job here (another machine, a wiped database) are **not** re-run: an issue
labelled `hopper:claimed` with no local job is skipped and shown in status detail.

**Item → job:** key = issue URL; title → goal; prompt = body + issue context (above); env as
above; empty body → claimed, then failed with error "empty issue body"; priority per
"Priority"; cwd = `repoPaths[repo]` (expanded) else `defaultCwd`.

**Write criteria.** The hopper's only issue writes are labels (state); it posts no comments at all
(owner decision, 2026-10-04: a finished issue needs no comment). It never closes an issue (issue
#187): the merge of the job's own pull request does — a person's, the job's own with yolo mode on (issue #579), or the
hopper's own with yolo mode on (issue #637, "PR waiting" below) —;
until then the issue stays open, labelled `hopper:done`. (Issue #38 had the hopper close a finished job's issue; once
done meant merged, that close only ever met a closed issue.) A failed or cancelled job's issue stays open.
The one write that is not a label: the user's **Run again** reopens the job's closed issue (issue #354, above). One more
(issue #677, "Closing finishes the loop" under "No checks means ready"): after the hopper's own merge — yolo mode or Merge
now — of a pull request that did not close its issue and is no part, the hopper closes the issue as completed, with one
comment that links the pull request. No claim, progress,
question, answered, failure, cancel or completion comment; no reactions, other issue edits, or PR
comments — except a question asked on the issue thread under the thread policy (issue #435, "The hopper label means
full automation" below), which supersedes "a reply on the issue is not an answer" for those questions. Jobs get no way to write to their issue (no token, no helper), and their prompt says
nothing about commenting (owner decision, 2026-10-04: a job has no reason to talk on its issue): the
issue context block ends at the comments list, with no footer. A question goes to the owner through
the UI and the Grok Bot routine webhook, never onto the issue; a reply on the issue is not an
answer.

Comments the hopper posted before this rule start with a hidden marker line (`<!-- hopper v1
kind=… -->`). They remain on issues, so the context filter still drops any comment carrying the
`<!-- hopper v1 ` prefix (and, in app mode, any by the bot).

**Done is a pull request** (issues #171, #187, #579, #637). A job that ends done (`HOPPER_DONE`, or any
executor's `finished` outcome) is not recorded finished until its source has said its work is **complete**
(`JobSource.notComplete(job)`, asked by the engine's runner before `recordOutcome`). **What GitHub shows decides, not
what the job did** (issue #637): before it the rule asked "did this job make the pull request?", and a run again that
pushed to an older pull request, one whose older pull request merged before the check, or a maintenance job with nothing
left to push all ended failed. For the GitHub sources (`src/sources/github/completion.ts`) complete is one of:

1. The issue is **closed as completed** — by any pull request, commit or person, at any time (`isClosedAsCompleted`: its
   `state_reason` is completed, or its last close event's closer is a merged pull request and it is not closed as not
   planned). Closed as not planned is not done.
2. A pull request **of the issue's repo that closes or references it** — `closedByPullRequestsReferences` (a closing
   keyword, to the default branch), or a cross-reference (`Refs #N`, any mention) — is open, not a draft, has no merge
   conflicts (GraphQL `mergeable` is not `CONFLICTING`; `UNKNOWN`, not yet computed, does not count against it) and no
   failing checks (issue #736: its head commit's status check rollup is not `FAILURE`/`ERROR`; checks still running, or
   none, do not count against it — the hopper merges only once they pass), or is
   merged at or after the job's `createdAt`. Whoever opened it, whenever. One that says `Part of #N` ships a part, not the
   whole (partly done, below). A merge before the job, on an issue still open, is work the job was asked to redo: not done.
   An open pull request of the repo that names the issue **only on its branch** (`namesIssue`: `issue-N`, `issue_N`,
   `issueN` anywhere, or `N-…` at the start or after a slash; not `fix-N`), ready for review, counts the same
   (`GitHubApi.openPullRequests`, the newest 100 open; asked only on a miss): no cross-reference shows it. A pull request
   on such a branch whose body says `Part of #N` is still a part, never the whole (issue #721: a part on `issue-N-…`
   ended the job as the whole issue, and its merge put `hopper:done` on an issue with work left).
   The job's own pull request **in another repository** (issue #2004: the issue's change lands there, as infrastructure
   code does) counts the same: opened at or after the job's `createdAt`, or with a push from the job since. There a bare
   `#N` names that repository's issue, so it names the issue by its full name (`owner/name#N`) or its URL, and
   `Part of owner/name#N` is a part. Another repository's pull request the job did not open or push to never counts.
3. The issue **asks to update the pull requests it names** (`asksToUpdate`: its title, or a line of its body, starts with
   bring / rebase / update / refresh / fix the conflicts and names a pull request): each pull request it names in its own
   repo (`#N` or its URL, at most 10 asked, `GitHubApi.pullRequest`; a number that is an issue counts for nothing) is
   merged, at any time, or open with no merge conflicts. The job need not have pushed: one already current has nothing to push.
4. The issue's **deliverable is an artifact** (issue #673: `isArtifactDeliverable`, a line of its body that says
   `Deliverable: artifact`, any case): the job made at least one artifact linked to the issue (its `issue` is the job's
   issue URL; `JobSourceContext.jobArtifacts`), and a comment on the issue names one — its link or its id. `share ID
   --owner` posts that comment ("Artifacts": share with the owner). A pull request still counts too. The job's `done` line
   says so (`artifactDoneLine`). The line sits in the issue's text, which anyone who may edit the issue can change: the
   most it can do is end a job done with an artifact and no pull request, the same reach as asking for no code change.

**A merge is never needed:** a pull request is done; a merge is only allowed (owner decision, issue #579). A miss names
what was looked at (issue #637): `not complete: the issue <url> is open, and no pull request in <repo> that closes or
references it is ready for review or merged since the job began: #12 (open, draft), #13 (open, merge conflicts)` — plus,
for an update, the named pull requests and their state. **A miss is asked again** once after `HOPPER_DONE_RECHECK_MS`
(default 60 s): GitHub may list a new pull request, or a new head commit, only some seconds after the push. The failure
assessor looks a third time before it assesses the failure ("Failure assessment": a done-check miss).

**A read error is no miss** (issue #2235). When the source cannot be read to check the work (a connect timeout, a busy
service, a rate limit), nothing shows the work incomplete. The runner reads it again after `HOPPER_DONE_READ_RETRY_MS`
(default 5 s), then after twice as long. When the last read fails too, the job fails with `could not confirm the work is
complete: <the read error>`. The built-in cause **Done check unread** (`done-check-unread`, transient, decision `retry`)
matches that text ahead of every other cause, because the read is the hopper's own, not the machine's or the agent's. The
run again asks the source first whether the work is done there (`DoneAtSource.beforeRun`): then the job ends finished.

**A pull request left in conflict, with failing checks or as a draft** (issues #626, #736) is not done, but the next
step is fixed, so no person is asked. When a done job is neither complete nor partly done, the runner asks its source for
the job's own open pull request that one step finishes (`JobSource.unfinishedPullRequest`; for GitHub one that closes the
issue or ships part of it): with merge conflicts, `rebase` it onto its base branch (conflicts come first: a draft with
them is rebased); with failing checks, `fix_checks`; a draft free of both, `mark_ready` it for review. The job then goes
on in its own session (`Executor.resume`, in the same pane and work tree) told that step's **finish brief**
(`finishBrief`, `src/domain/pull-requests.ts`): fixed text, no model call, recorded as `job.finish_briefed`. Its next end
is judged again. At most `MAX_FINISH_BRIEFS` (3) per run; after them, or with no such pull request, an executor that
cannot resume, or any other state, the job fails `not complete:` and is handed to a person as before — except a job whose
own pull request is there with red checks (issue #1230): its miss names that pull request and its failed checks
(`PR #N: checks failed: <names>`), and the hopper finishes it ("Own PR checks red"), and a job whose own pull request is
there with merge conflicts or as a draft (issue #1265): its miss names that pull request and its step, and the hopper
finishes it ("Own PR unfinished").

**Tending a waiting pull request** (issue #736: conflicts must not pile up for a person). A PR waiting job's pull request
can go bad after its job ended: its base branch moves and it has merge conflicts with it, or a check fails. Each sync
— on its round of the **in-motion cycle** (issue #985, "The in-motion cycle"), and at once after a merge or close (issue
#967) — follows it (`follow.ts`) and keeps what it saw (`seen`); after that follow, off the job's report chain, the sync loop's
after-done half (`src/sources/after-done.ts`) asks `tendStep(seen)`: merge conflicts → `rebase`, else failing checks →
`fix_checks`; a draft is a person's and is never tended. A step due, the job's item **runs again** on Run again's own path
(`job.rerun`, `by: "tending"`), its prompt followed by the **tend brief** (`tendBrief`: work on that pull request's
branch, the step's lines, open no new pull request, and fail saying which files or checks and why when it cannot). The
tended job follows it no more (`follow: tended`, `tended` names the pull request, the step and the new job) and
`job.pull_request_tended` records it. The new job is a **tend job** (`spec.tend`, issue #967): when every lane is in use it
elbows in past a lane cap ("Specialty jobs elbow in"), so it never waits behind feature work. It is judged as any other: done once the same pull request is ready again
(an older pull request counts, rule 2 above; a part counts when the job pushed to it, `isUpdatedBy`), and it then waits
and is followed in its turn; a job that cannot ends failed, and its hand-off in Needs a person says why — the problem card.
At most `MAX_TENDS` (3) `fix_checks` tends in a row of one pull request (`tendsInRow`, along `rerunOf`): then it waits on a
person, as before tending, its card on the Pull requests list saying `checks failing`. A `rebase` is never capped (issue
#786): each is made needed by a new merge on the base, not by the tend before it, and a rebase that fails ends the row by
itself — the tend job ends failed and waits on a person. With a cap, a busy base left pull requests conflicting after
three good rebases, and nothing tended them again. **A tend starts only on an open pull request** (issue #1456): a tend
works from what was last seen, and the tended job follows its pull request no more, so a pull request closed or merged
on GitHub after its tend job failed was rebased again at each move of its base, and shown open. Before each tend the
source reads whether it ended (`JobSource.endedPullRequests`); ended, no tend starts, the job follows it again at once, and
that follow records its end (`job.pull_request_closed` or `job.pull_request_merged`) and its labels, as any follow does. A
read that fails tends it as before. **A closed work item is tended no more after a tend job** (issue #2127): a tend job that finds the pull
request has nothing left to merge (its base already holds the same change) closes the work item's issue, or the pull
request; a rebase is never capped, and a done tend job follows the pull request, so the same tend job started again and
again, and each tend's Run again reopened the issue. Before each tend of a tend job's pull request the source reads the
item's issue when the ledger does not hold it closed (`JobSource.issueState`, recorded as `work_item.issue_closed` with
`via: read`); closed, no tend starts, and the card says why. A closed item's first tend still runs (issue #927: a merge
recorded that GitHub contradicts leaves the issue closed and the pull request open). A read that fails tends it as before. A refusal because a newer job of
the item exists is no failure; any other refusal is kept as the source's retry and asked again next sync. No setting turns
it off: a job repository whose pull requests the hopper follows is one whose jobs it runs.

**The tending queue** (issue #796, `src/domain/tending-queue.ts`). Each merge moves its base, so tending every conflicting
pull request of a repository at once made each merge break the other rebases again (one merge re-conflicted six pull
requests). The tends of one job repository are a queue: after all the follows of a sync, a tend starts only when no
**head** that conflicts with it holds it (`queueHeads`; one queue per set of pull requests that conflict, below): a tend job at work on a pull request (not ended, or finished
and not following it again yet), or a pull request on its way to the hopper's merge — followed, yolo mode on for its
repository (`JobSource.mergesOnReady`), of a trusted or approved origin, and as last seen no draft, no merge conflicts, no
failing checks and no refused merge, and its checks passed, or it has none, or they run within `PENDING_HOLD_MS` (30
minutes) of its last push (issue #927). Nothing holds the queue for good: checks that stay pending (a required check that
never reports), checks the hopper cannot read, or a pull request not seen yet hold nothing, so the conflicted or failing
pull requests behind it are tended. Before, any of them held the queue, and one pull request with stuck checks stopped every
tend of its repository for a day. Once the head is merged, closed, or waits on
a person (yolo mode off, a failed tend, failing checks past the cap, a refused merge), the next is tended against the new
base: one rebase per merge. The next is the rules' first (`tendOrder`: the highest priority, then the oldest pull request,
then the job), or Jev's applied pick at the `merge-order` decision point ("Decider calls"). Yolo mode off, nothing is merged
by the hopper, so a tend holds the queue only while its job works. Each repository has its own queue.

**One queue per set of pull requests that conflict** (issue #939). One tend at a time per repository was the bottleneck:
pull requests that touch different code waited for each other's rebase, checks and merge. Now a head holds only the due
pull requests that conflict with it, and two due ones that do not conflict are tended at the same time. Whether two
conflict is the **hopper's mirror**'s answer (`JobSource.conflictBetween`, `GitMirrors.conflictBetween`): `git merge-tree
--write-tree` of their two heads as the sync pass fetched them — clean, their own changes do not touch the same lines, so
merging one does not give the other merge conflicts. Two pull requests that both change `docs/design.md` in different
places do not conflict; a file-name overlap would have put nearly every pull request of this repository in one queue. Where
the mirror cannot say (no mirror, outside a pass, a head not fetched), they conflict: one tend at a time, as before. Each
sync, after the follows: the due pull requests no head conflicts with, Jev's pick first (`merge-order`, asked only when two
or more are free), then the rules' order, each tended unless it conflicts with one tended before it in the same sync. What
holds each other one is kept on its job (`heldBehind`, `Holds`) and shown on its card.

**No hold lasts for ever** (issue #1143). A head holds a due rebase at most `MAX_HELD_MS` (one hour): since when it is held
is kept on its job (`heldSince`, cleared when nothing holds it), and a rebase held that long is tended whatever holds it
(`heldTooLong`). On a busy repository new pull requests reach their checks all the time, each a new head, and each
conflicts with the same old pull request: it was held behind one head after another, conflicted, with no job on it and no
signal on GitHub. At worst the late rebase needs one more rebase after the head's merge. The tend job it starts is said on
the pull request ("Pull request housekeeping"). The log says each such release: the pull request, its head, and since when.

**A merged pull request holds nothing** (issue #1162). A tend job holds its queue only while it works on the pull request:
queued, held, claimed, running, or in its own wait on the outside world, or finished with its end still to report to its source
(`queueHeads`' `reported`). Once that end is reported, the finished tend job follows the pull request, which holds the
queue only on its way to the merge, or the pull request was merged or closed first and there is nothing to follow; either
way the tend job holds nothing. Before, a tend job whose pull request a person merged while it worked finished following
nothing, and held every conflicted pull request of its repository until the hour above ran out, again and again. A tend job
that waits on a person (a question, parked, worked by hand) holds nothing either, nor one whose pull request any job saw
merged or closed. A held card says since when (`heldSince`) and the tend job that holds it with its status now
(`heldBehind.jobId`).

**A tend job on its own command holds nothing** (issue #1210). A tend job on its own wait for its own background command
(`ownCommand`, "A wait on its own command") works on nothing meanwhile, as one that waits on a person, so it holds nothing
(`ownWaitOf` in `tending`). One tend job ran a `sleep` loop that read another pull request, and named it as its own command:
four conflicted pull requests waited behind it with every lane free until `MAX_HELD_MS` ran out. Once its wait ends and it
pushes, it is a head again. The protocol's wait line also says that a poll is never a command of the job's own, and that a job
never waits in a loop for the hopper to tend, rebase or merge a pull request. The rest of issue #1210 (a wait on mergeability,
polls flagged, the one-hour cap, the wait's words): "Polls of hopper state".

**Rework goes back at once** (issue #938). The queue holds only a `rebase`: a rebase onto a base that a head is about to
move is made again after that merge. A `fix_checks` is rework, and no head holds it: every pull request with failed checks
goes back to its job in the same sync, all at the same time, limited only by free lanes (a tend job elbows in, above). A
pull request that waits for its checks holds no rework. A started `fix_checks` tend job is still a head for the rebases
that conflict with it, as any tend job at work: its push moves the pull request. A merge conflict comes before failing
checks (`tendStep`), and `pr / test` runs on `pull_request` only, which GitHub does not run on a head with merge conflicts:
no check runs on a conflicted head, only on the head the rebase or the base merge pushes.

**The merge gate** (issue #939, `src/sources/github/merge-gate.ts`). The hopper's own merges (yolo mode) of one repository
in one sync pass are made one at a time. A ready pull request that conflicts with one the hopper merged before it in the
same pass is not merged: GitHub would refuse that merge (`mergeError`) once it saw the new base. Its follow keeps
`seen.mergeHeldBehind`, its card waits `merge held` and says behind which, and the next sync sees it conflict with the new
base and tends it. Where the mirror cannot say, the merge is made, as before. A person's Merge now is not gated.

**The base merge** (issue #967, `src/git-mirror/mirrors.ts` `baseMerge`, `JobSource.baseMerge`). A tend is a job, and a
job waits for a lane: with every lane busy (the Claude usage cap held the hopper to two lanes), pull requests with only a
simple conflict waited for hours. So a `rebase` tend the queue starts is first asked of the source. The **hopper's mirror**
merges the base branch, as the sync pass fetched it, into the pull request's head (`git merge-tree --write-tree`), with no
job and no lane. A conflict is resolved only in a Markdown file (`*.md`), or an **additions file** ("PR tending without lanes, part 3"),
where both sides only added lines at the same
place — no line of the merge base is in the conflict (`git merge-file --diff3`, `keepBothAdditions`): both additions are
kept, the base branch's first. That is a `WHATS-NEW.md` line, or two design sections added at the end of
`docs/design.md`. Any other conflict — a code file, a line one side changed or removed, a file not on all three sides —
is a real one: nothing is pushed, and the tend job runs as before. So is a merge git fails to make, and a resolution the
shrink guard refuses (issue #1218, "The shrink guard"). Clean, the hopper makes the merge commit (parents: the
head, then the base; author `hopper`, no person) and pushes it to the pull request's branch with
`--force-with-lease=refs/heads/<branch>:<head as fetched>`: a branch that moved since the fetch, or a fork's branch that
is not in the repository, is never written, and the refusal is logged. Pushed, `job.pull_request_base_merged` records the
commit and the files resolved, and what the job saw of its pull request says no merge conflicts and its checks pending from
now, so with yolo mode on it heads its queue at once and the pull requests that conflict with it wait for its merge. The
checks run on the merge commit as on any push, and yolo mode merges only once they pass. The push uses the source's own
credential, as the mirror's fetch does (an App installation token, or the connected account's): a push the token may not
make (one that changes a workflow file, without that permission) is refused and goes to a tend job. Where the source has no
mirror, or outside a sync pass, there is no base merge.

What issue #939 did not do, by the path a person selected: a batch of ready pull requests merged into one trial branch with
one run of the checks, and a bisect of a batch that fails. The tree with every ready pull request merged is still not
tested before the merges: two pull requests with green checks that break each other, without a merge conflict, can still
break the base branch, as before. Checks run on each pull request against the base it was rebased onto; the merge gate and
the tending queue only stop merge conflicts.

What the hopper does about each pull request that needs tending shows on its card in Pull requests (issue #927,
`PullRequestCard.queue`, `gaveUp`): "the hopper rebases it onto dev on its next sync" or "the hopper fixes its failed
checks on its next sync" (issue #938: the step, not only "tends it"), "the hopper cannot tend it" with the source's
refusal (issue #967: `tendRefused`, kept on the job until a tend starts; before, a refused tend left the card at "the hopper
tends it next" for hours), "held behind #N" with why (a job works on it, or it waits
for its checks to merge), or "the hopper gave up" with why (its checks still fail after `MAX_TENDS` fixes, or its tend job
failed: then why is that job's own reason, `Job.error`, on one line, at most 300 characters). A stall is never silent.
Every other open card says what the hopper does now, too (`doingText`, `ui/src/model/pull-requests.ts`): its tend job's step
("the hopper rebases it onto dev: job N works on it now", `PullRequestCard.tendStep`; a tend job queued or held: "job N
waits to start:" and the lane cap that binds or its hold, `tendWaits`, issue #967), the merge it waits to make ("merges
it when its checks pass", "on its next sync", "tries the merge again on each sync"), or nothing, and who acts then (yolo mode
off, checks it may not read, a draft). A card with merge conflicts and pending checks says "checks run after the rebase"
(`checksText`, issue #938), never "checks pending": no check runs on its head until it is rebased.

**Conflicts a rebase sends to a person** (issue #927, `tendBrief`). A rebase tend resolves the small conflicts itself:
imports, call sites, type updates, and lines both sides added to a list (a `WHATS-NEW.md` line). Only when both sides change
the design of the same thing, and it cannot keep the intent of both, does it fail, naming the files, what each side does,
and the choice a person must make. That reason is the card's "gave up" line and its Needs you line.

**Tend attempts on the job graph** (issue #927, `JobGraphNode.tends`). A pull request's node lists each tend of it, oldest
first: the step, its job, that job's status, and when it started and ended, read from the jobs on each read of the graph,
so it is live. The node details of the Jobs view show them, each linked to its job. A pull request handed to a tend or a
rework (`follow: tended`, `reworked`) stays open on the graph. A pull request the hopper gave up on is also a row line in Needs you, with why (`gaveUpLines`,
`ui/src/model/pull-requests.ts`): the Pull requests row and its nav badge count those, not the ones with merge conflicts,
which the hopper rebases itself.

**What a check fix is told** (issue #927, `tendBrief`, `TendChecks`). The follow keeps the checks that failed, by name and
link, on what it saw (`PullRequestSeen.failedChecks`, at most `MAX_FAILED_CHECKS`), and a `fix_checks` brief lists them,
each with what it reported (`FailedCheck.reported`), and, since issue #993, its job log's excerpt ("Failed checks' logs").
It reads each failed check run's annotations (`annotations` on the `CheckRun`, in the one
pull request a follow reads), which carry a test's failure (vitest's GitHub Actions reporter, on by itself in Actions) and
typecheck and lint errors (setup-node's problem matchers). It keeps the `FAILURE` ones, `path:line: title: message`, not
the runner's "Process completed with exit code N." line, at most `MAX_CHECK_REPORTED` (5) of a check, each cut to
`MAX_CHECK_REPORTED_CHARS` (500). The brief quotes them as the check's output, data, not instructions. A check with no such
annotation is named with its link, and its log's excerpt when it is a GitHub Actions job (issue #993). The
first fix of a row may run the checks again once — a flaky check, not related to the change (a test that fails by chance, a
runner or network failure) —: it pushes an empty commit and changes no code. A later fix of the row is told to fix the cause.
The rerun is a push, not GitHub's "re-run failed jobs": the hopper's GitHub App has no Actions write, and a push needs no new
permission. It counts as one of the row's `MAX_TENDS`.

**Checks as seen** (issue #927, `src/sources/github/closer.ts`). GitHub keeps a pull request's check rollup pending while any
check still runs, so a failed shard stayed "pending" until every other shard ended. The one pull request a follow reads
also reads each check's end (`statusCheckRollup.contexts`): a check run that ended `FAILURE`, `TIMED_OUT` or
`STARTUP_FAILURE`, or a commit status `ERROR` or `FAILURE`, makes the checks failing at once. It keeps the name and link of each
(`CheckRun.name`, `detailsUrl`; `StatusContext.context`, `targetUrl`). The lists read the rollup
only: 100 checks of each of 100 pull requests would cost too much of the rate limit.

**The newest run of each check** (issue #2129, `src/sources/github/newest-runs.ts`). A check can run again on the same head
commit: a re-run, or a new workflow run that another event starts (an edit of the pull request's body re-plans an
infrastructure pull request). GitHub's rollup then fails on the older failed run, but GitHub's required checks read only
the newest run of each check name. So every read of a head commit's checks counts the newest run of each check only
(newest: the greater id): the read by number and the follow's batched read (`statusCheckRollup.contexts`, with
`totalCount`, and in the batch only each check's id, name, status and end), the checks fallback and the done criteria's
check runs over REST, and the GitHub proxy's own read of a pull request the hopper does not follow. A rollup that fails
with no newest run failed is pending while one runs, else passing. When GitHub gives only some of the contexts (more
than 100), a newer run can be among the others, so the rollup's state stands. `pr checks` still lists every run.

**Rework** (issue #724, `src/sources/rerun.ts`, `src/sources/github/rework.ts`) sends a done job's open pull request back
to be reworked, in place of the manual draft, comment and label edits. A person asks from the card in Pull requests
(Send back for rework), the operator CLI (`hopper job rework <id> --notes <text>`) or `POST /ui/api/jobs/:id/rework`
(least role operator), always with notes. It is open only for a finished job that follows an open pull request (**PR
waiting**), the newest job of its item, its end reported. On the job's report chain, its source (`JobSource.rework`)
makes the pull request a draft — it stays open on its branch, never merged or closed — and gives the item back as Run
again does (on GitHub the end labels go, `hopper:pr-ready` with them). Then, in one tx (`SourceHost.rework`), the ended
job's source state stops following the pull request (`follow: reworked`: no card, no yolo merge), and a new job of the
item is queued, its `rerunOf` the ended job and its `rework` the pull request, the notes and who asked, told the
**rework brief** (`reworkBrief`) after its prompt: check out that branch, make the changes, push, mark it ready, open no
new pull request. `job.rework_requested` on the ended job. A draft is not done, so the pull request never counts as done
while it is in rework. The new job's done-check counts the reworked pull request as its own (a part, a finish step) but
counts it done only once the job pushed to it after the job began (`isUpdatedBy`): marking it ready again with no push is
`not complete: … the pull request sent back for rework, #N, has no push since the rework`. Once done, the new job follows
the pull request as any other. The notes go to the job only, never to GitHub.

**Yolo mode** (issue #579, `src/domain/yolo-mode.ts`) is whether a job may merge its own pull request once the
repo's checks pass. Off unless a person turns it on: an admin's setting of the user's (`yoloMode` in the user's
settings; `GET /api/yolo-mode`, `POST /ui/api/yolo-mode`, `yolo_mode.changed`; Settings → Yolo mode), `on` for every
job repository, and per repository (`repos`, `owner/repo` lowercased), which wins. The source reads it each time it
builds a job's prompt (`JobSourceContext.yoloMode(repo)`), so a change applies to the next job without a restart; a
running job keeps what it was told. It never changes what done is. Off by default because a merge with nobody
reviewing it is a merge nothing else stops where a repository has no branch protection, and a merge to the default
branch runs what it triggers there (here: the `dev` image is published from it) — the UI says so beside the switch.
**Direct push** (issue #1806, "Direct push" at the end) is set with it, and is no part of the merge: the repositories
where a job may push straight to the target branch, off unless a person names one, whatever `on` says.
Not *Yolo*, the herdr-claude executor's choice that Claude runs with every permission ("Yolo" above). Since issue #637
yolo mode also has the **hopper** merge: following a PR waiting job's pull request (below), it merges one that is ready —
not a draft, no merge conflicts, its checks passed, or it has none and none started within two minutes of its last push (issue #677, "No checks means ready" below; on this repository the check is `pr / test`, issue #672, `docs/deploy.md` "Local development and tests") — with a merge commit (`GitHubApi.merge`, `PUT
/pulls/{n}/merge`, through the job's source's own connection). One definition of done; the merge is an extra step after
it.

| yolo mode | the job's prompt says |
|-----------|-----------------------|
| off (default) | `done:` checks pass, pushed, a pull request with `Closes #N` open, not a draft, no merge conflicts; an issue that needs no code change: closed as completed. Do not merge it: a person reviews and merges it |
| on for the repo | the same, then: the hopper merges the pull request once its checks pass, or, when the repo has no checks, a short time after the last push. Do not merge it yourself (issue #652: the job holds no token to merge with; before it, the job merged) |

Both say, before the yolo part: an issue that asks to update an existing pull request is done by pushing to its branch,
no new pull request, once it has no merge conflicts with its base (issue #618).

The prompt's `done:` line carries the parts the hopper cannot see — the repo's own checks, verifying where the
product runs — so a job is told everything done means, and the gate holds it to the part GitHub can show. Anything
short of it — a local commit, a branch, a draft, a pull request with merge conflicts, the issue closed as not
planned — fails the job with `not complete: <what was looked at>` after the re-check; an error asking GitHub
(transient or not) fails it with `could not confirm the work is complete: <error>`. Fail closed: a failed job's issue
stays open with `hopper:failed`, never `hopper:done`, and removing that label re-runs it. A source without `notComplete`, and a job
of no source, take every done job as complete. Before issue #171, a job that said it was done was closed as
completed with nothing on the default branch.

**Partly done** (issue #579). A job that ships part of its issue opens its pull request with `Part of #N` in its body
in place of `Closes #N`, lists in it what is left, and ends done; its prompt's `done:` line says so. Not complete by
the rule above, it is asked once more before it would fail (`JobSource.partlyDone`; the engine's verdict,
`src/domain/pull-requests.ts` `judge`): the job's own pull request that mentions the issue (the issue's
`CROSS_REFERENCED_EVENT` timeline, `GitHubApi.referencingPullRequests`), in the issue's repository, whose body says
`Part of #N`, open and ready for review — not a draft, no merge conflicts — or merged already. Found, the job ends
`finished` with `partlyDone` (its URL; on the job and on `job.finished`), never failed; the issue gets
`hopper:partly-done`. The next part runs once that pull request is merged (below): the hopper does not split the issue
and does not ask; a person who wants it split splits it.

**After done** (issue #579, `src/sources/after-done.ts`, `src/sources/github/follow.ts`). A finished job's report
keeps its pull request in the job's source state (`pullRequest`, `follow: open`, `part` for a part), and each sync of
its source asks again where it is (`JobSource.follow`), on the job's report chain:

| the pull request | then |
|------------------|------|
| still open | what is seen of it — a draft, merge conflicts, its checks, when it opened — kept in its source state (`seen`), no event (issue #637); with yolo mode on for its repository and it ready, the hopper merges it: then as merged, `byHopper: true` on the event. A refused merge (405, 409, no access) is kept on it (`mergeError`) and asked again next sync; a transient error is a report retry. Neither fails the job nor makes a failure record |
| merged, and it closed the issue — the issue closed as completed, or its body closes the issue with a closing keyword (`closesByKeyword`: close/closes/closed, fix/fixes/fixed, resolve/resolves/resolved, then `#N`, `owner/repo#N` or the issue's URL) and does not say `Part of #N` | `job.pull_request_merged`; `hopper:pr-ready` → `hopper:done`; `mergeChecked: true` in its source state |
| merged, and it did not close the issue — a part, a mention (`Refs #N`), a pull request named for the issue only on its branch | a part (issue #721), whatever the report took it for: `job.pull_request_merged` with `part: true`; `hopper:partly-done` and `hopper:pr-ready` only come off, so the next sync offers the issue again and a new job takes the next part. Only a merge that closes the issue, or the last part's — the part that makes every declared part done ("Declared parts" below) —, puts `hopper:done` on it, with `parts` in its source state |
| closed without a merge | `job.pull_request_closed`; → `hopper:pr-closed`, which keeps the issue out until a person removes it (then it runs again). Closed on GitHub (no person's Close PR, not superseded), its item is blocked (`pr_closed`, issue #1891): the first time in a row the item reconciler runs it again by itself, which takes the label off; a second time a person decides: Run again or Won't do on its row in Intake ("The item lifecycle") |
| none named, none open, and a pull request of the issue's repository that mentions it merged since the job began (issue #1891) | named, and ended as a merged part: the job's own "Part of #N" first (issue #1231), else one that only mentions the issue (`mention: true`), such as a pull request of several issues. The next part is taken, or the issue is done when every declared part is done |
| none named, one found open (issue #1891) | named from now on (`pullRequest`, `part` for a part); an issue the report left `hopper:blocked` gets `hopper:pr-ready`, or `hopper:partly-done` for a part, in its place |
| still open, or none found yet, and the issue closed as not planned (issue #428) | abandoned: `job.pull_request_abandoned`; `follow: abandoned`, followed no more and never merged, yolo mode or not; the pull request is left as it is; `hopper:pr-ready`, `hopper:partly-done` and `hopper:failed` come off and no end label goes on. A person's Merge now or Close PR still goes through. Reopened with the pull request still open, reconciling (issue #763) follows it again |

**Pull-based completion** (issue #428). The item is resolved upstream; the hopper only follows. Closed as completed — by
a person, a commit, or a pull request — the follow ends merged (first row above, `hopper:done`) with no hopper action,
within one sync of the job's source. But a followed pull request still open on GitHub is open, whatever its issue (issue
#927): it is followed to its end as "still open" says, and the follow ends merged once it is merged or closed. Before, the
follow ended merged under an open pull request, and reconciling (issue #763) followed it again at each sync: a re-follow
loop, and a conflicted pull request never tended. Closed as not planned, it ends abandoned (last row). It is the same for every job
repository, owned or not. The `hopper:complete-at-merge` and `hopper:complete-at-pr` labels went with issue #579: done is
always a pull request, and the follow decides the rest.

**The merge re-check** (issue #721). Before it, a merged part on a branch named for its issue was recorded as the whole
issue (`follow: merged`, no `part`), and `hopper:done` stopped the hopper from working the rest. Each sync, the newest job
of its item whose merge is so recorded and not checked yet (`rechecksMerge`: `follow: merged`, no `part`, no
`mergeChecked`) is asked once by the same rule. Closed by it: `mergeChecked: true`, nothing else (`FollowUp` outcome
`checked`, no event). Not: it was a part — `hopper:done` comes off, `part: true`, `job.pull_request_merged` with
`part: true` — and the next sync offers the issue again. An older job of the item is never asked: its merge must not
take off a `hopper:done` that a later job, or a person, set.

**Declared parts** (issue #729, `src/sources/github/parts.ts`). An issue declares its parts as a checklist under a heading
`Parts` (any level), up to the next heading of that level or higher; a checklist in a code block, or anywhere else in the
issue, is not parts (an acceptance checklist must not count as work). A part is done when its box is ticked, and each
merged pull request of the issue's repo that says `Part of #N` counts as one more: the parts done are the larger of the
two, never more than the parts. The hopper never ticks a box: it never edits an issue's text, so it counts. At each sync
the source reads the parts of each issue it offers (one `referencingPullRequests` per issue that declares parts; a read
that fails counts the ticked boxes only) and gives them with the item (`SourceItem.parts`); the job keeps them in its
source ref (`JobSourceRef.parts`), and its prompt says `parts: x of y done`, to ship the next part with `Part of #N` and to
use `Closes #N` only for the last. When a part merges, following it reads the parts again, counting that merge even when
GitHub does not list it yet, and keeps them in the job's source state (`parts`); when every part is done, the issue gets
`hopper:done` in place of being offered again. It stays open: the hopper closes no issue for a part (issue #677). The job card shows
`parts x/y`, as followed, else as offered.

A part whose text starts with an issue — `#N`, `owner/repo#N` or the issue's URL — is a **required child**: it is done only
when that issue is closed (as completed or not planned: a person closed it), whatever its box says, and no merged pull
request counts for it; the merged `Part of #N` pull requests count only for the parts that name no issue. Each required
child is read once per parts read (`getIssue`); one that cannot be read counts by its box, read again next time. An issue's
**GitHub sub-issues** are parts too: a closed sub-issue is a done part. With no checklist under `Parts` they are its only
parts, as GitHub counts them in the issue (`sub_issues_summary`, read with the issue: no extra call). Beside a checklist
(issue #729 part 3), the sub-issues are listed (`subIssues`, one more call, only for an issue that has both), and each one no
checklist item names is one more part; a sub-issue an item names counts once, as that item. A list that cannot be read
adds them as GitHub sums them up (a named one may then count twice; done still waits for it). This is what makes a job's
**required child** ("Issue lineage" below) hold its parent whatever the parent declares. So a parent is not done while a
child it named in `Parts`, or a sub-issue, is open. When every part is done, the prompt says so and tells the job to check
the issue and close it as completed when nothing is left.

**Issue lineage** (issue #729 part 3, `src/github-proxy/broker.ts`, `ui/src/model/lineage.ts`). An issue a job files through
the hopper (`issue.create`) is a **child** of the job's own issue — its source's, a fork's parent's —, recorded both ways:

- **On GitHub, child → parent.** The hopper's note at the issue's end names the parent: `Follow-up of owner/repo#N.`, or
  `Required child of owner/repo#N: that issue is not done while this one is open.` GitHub shows the mention on the
  parent's timeline too, so the parent links back.
- **In the hopper, both ways.** `job.child_issue_filed` on the job's timeline: `parent`, `child` (with its URL),
  `required`. The job card (`LineageChips`) reads these events (`GET /api/events?types=job.child_issue_filed`, again
  on each new one) and shows `child of #N` (`required by #N`) on a child's card, and `children n, m required` on a
  parent's, with every child and the count of all descendants on hover.

A child is a **follow-up** unless the job marks it **required** (`hopper-gh issue create … --required`): then the hopper
also links it as a **GitHub sub-issue** of the job's issue (`POST …/issues/{n}/sub_issues`, with the new issue's id), and
so it is a part the parent waits on (above). The question left by part 2 — a sub-issue is a required part, so linking
every filed issue would let a nice-to-have follow-up block its parent — is answered so: only a child the job marks
required is linked; any other is lineage only. A link GitHub refuses leaves the issue filed: the answer and the event
carry `subIssue: false` and `subIssueError`, and the job can say so. The link is kept (issue #1607): the answer adds
`subIssueLater`, and the user's link pass (`src/github-proxy/sub-issue-links.ts`, at start and every 5 minutes) tries each
such link again until it is made, then records `job.sub_issue_linked`. A link GitHub already holds counts as made. Only the hopper's own job marks a required child, and
only of an issue it has: another user's job (untrusted) does not change the hopper's issues' parts.

The issue closes when the pull request merges, by whoever merges it, as GitHub does; the hopper closes one only after its
own merge of a pull request with no closing keyword that is no part (issue #677, "Closing finishes the loop").
A pull request the report could not name is followed only to its merge; with none open, the job's own part merged since
it began is named, so its merge ends as a part's ("A merged part moves its item on", issue #1231). A throw is a report retry, asked again next
sync. **A job that failed only for want of a merge** — its error `not complete: …`, from before a pull request was
done — and still waiting on a person in Needs a person is judged again at each sync of its source: done or partly done
now, it is finished (`SourceHost.finishComplete`), its hand-off closes on `job.finished`, and its end is reported again,
so its issue loses `hopper:failed`. The failure assessor's `not-complete` cause says so: a pull request waiting for its
merge is never a failure.

**PR waiting and the Pull requests list** (issue #637, `src/domain/pull-request-list.ts`). A finished job whose pull
request is open and followed is **PR waiting**: done, not failed, using no lane, and kept in sight until its pull request
merges (it drops off) or closes without a merge (it shows `closed` and waits on a person: `hopper:pr-closed`). It is not a
job status: the job is `finished`, its source state `follow: open`. The report names the newest ready pull request that
closes the issue, else one that references it, else one on a branch named for it, so the list can link it; one it cannot
name is followed only to its merge. `GET /api/pull-requests` (`PullRequestsView`), the UI's Pull requests view and `hopper
prs` give the same: per job repository (and any other a card is in), its yolo mode and its cards, oldest first — the
issue, the pull request, `state` (`open`, `closed`), `checks` (`passing`, `pending`, `failing`, `none`, `unknown` until
seen), `mergeable` (`mergeable`, `conflicts`, `unknown`), `draft`, `openedAt`, `yolo`, and for an open one why its merge
`waits`: the first of `no pull request`, `tending`, `tend failed` (issue #763, below), `not checked yet`, `draft`, `conflicts`, `checks failing`, `yolo off`, `checks pending`, `checks
not started`, `merge refused` (`mergeError` says what GitHub said), `ready` (issue #677); `base`, the branch it merges into. At the top, `yolo: { on, total }` over those repositories, and `waiting`:
per repository and reason, how many, the most first. All of it is what the last sync saw (`seen`), never asked of GitHub
at read time. Only the newest job of an item counts. Each repository's yolo switch is `POST /ui/api/yolo-mode` with
`repos`; `hopper yolo <owner/repo> on|off|default`. An open card has Merge now and Close PR (issue #677, "No checks means
ready").

**A pull request in another repository** (issue #1778). A job may open its pull request in another repository than its
issue's (an infrastructure change for a workflow issue). The pull request's own repository comes from its URL, never from
the job's: the follow reads, merges, moves and closes it there; its card is in that repository's group; its yolo mode,
change rule, landing branch and tending queue are that repository's (`jobPullRequestRepo`, `src/domain/pull-requests.ts`).
On a repository the hopper does not work on, yolo mode is on only when a person named it on (issue #1806, "Yolo mode on a
repository the hopper does not work on").
Only its issue — labels, the close after a merge — stays in the job's repository.

**A pull request stays in sight while it is open** (issue #763: open pull requests a job opened were on GitHub and not on
the list, and nothing tended them). Two ways it fell out, each closed:
- *Its tend job works on it.* A tended job follows its pull request no more (`follow: tended`), and its new job is not
  finished yet. The list keeps the tended job's card while that job — `tended.nextJobId` — is the newest of the item and
  has not finished: `state` `open`, `waits` `tending`, or `tend failed` once it ended failed (it waits on a person, its
  hand-off says why), and `tendJobId` names it. A tend job **cancelled by no person and no source** (issue #1010: the
  sweep, a restart — any reason but `DELIBERATE_CANCELS`: `cancelled in UI`, `question dismissed`, and the source's
  `issue gone`, `issue closed`, `label removed`, `backburner`, `unassigned`) is no reason to give up: its report puts
  `hopper:pr-ready` back, so the issue is not taken again as a new job, and `tendRetryAt` makes the same step due again
  5, 10, then 20 minutes after each cancel in a row (`tended.retries`, at most `MAX_TEND_RETRIES`, 3). Meanwhile the
  card waits `tending`, `tendWaits` saying when. Run again by `tending` may pass the cancelled tend job, the newest of
  the item; the new tend job's `rerunOf` is that cancelled one. A fourth cancel in a row gives up, saying so. The card has no Merge now or Close PR meanwhile: no job follows it. Once
  the tend job finishes, its own card follows the pull request, or there is none.
  **Tend again** (issue #1010): a card the hopper gave up on — `waits` `tend failed`: its tend job ended failed,
  cancelled or rejected, and no retry is due — had no action, so the pull request sat. Now it has one, for an operator:
  Tend again (`POST /ui/api/pull-requests/tend` with the card's `jobId`, a box action; `hopper pr tend <n>`). It marks
  the tend (`tended.again`, the time; `tendRetryAt` answers it for any of those ends, so Run again by `tending` may pass
  the ended tend job) and tends at once: the same step, its tend brief, a new row of retries (`retries` 0), and
  `job.pull_request_tended` with `person` and `via`. Refused with why (`tendAgainRefusal`, 409) when the hopper did not
  give up, a newer job of the item exists, its source is not running, the tend job's end is not reported yet, or the
  source refuses the tend. A tend that cannot start now keeps the mark: the next sync starts it, and the card waits
  `tending` ("a person asked to tend it again"). A failed tend job's hand-off closes when the new tend job is queued, as
  for any run again. Why no Merge now or Close PR beside it: the card's job does not follow the pull request while it is
  tended; Tend again is the one action that moves it, and a person who wants to merge or close it does so on GitHub.
- *Its job follows none.* A done job that ended before the hopper followed pull requests, or whose follow ended, is
  **reconciled** with its source at each sync, before the follows (`src/sources/after-done.ts`, `JobSource.unfollowedPullRequests`,
  on GitHub `src/sources/github/reconcile.ts`). A candidate is `reconcilable`: finished, its end reported, the newest job
  of its item, and following nothing (`follow` absent, `merged` or `closed`; not `open`, `tended`, `reworked`, nor a merge
  still to check again). Finished or failed (issue #786): a pull request is followed to its end, whatever its job's end —
  but not a failed tend job's (`failedTend`), which waits on a person. Per repository one listing of its open pull requests (newest 100, each with its branch and body);
  per candidate the newest that closes its issue by a closing keyword, else the newest that ships part of it ("Part of
  #N"), else the newest on a branch named for it; the issue is read only for a match. An issue closed as completed still
  has its open pull request taken when that one closes it by keyword or ships a part of it, never one named for it only on
  its branch (issue #786: issues were closed from under their open parts, and the parts were left); an issue closed as not
  planned has none taken. A match is followed from then on, on the job's report chain (`follow: open`, `pullRequest`, `part`; `seen`
  starts again) and `job.pull_request_followed` records it: it shows on the list, yolo mode merges it, tending tends it,
  as any PR waiting job's. A paused source is not reconciled; a throw is logged and asked again next sync. A failed job that
  follows its pull request is followed and tended as a finished one (`followsWhenEnded`), and shows on the list; its
  pull request's merge or close takes off `hopper:failed`. The judge-again path above still finishes one whose pull
  request is done.
- *Another issue's pull request was taken for it* (issue #786). A pull request that only mentions the issue ("depends on
  #N") and closes or ships part of another issue (`worksOnAnotherIssue`) is that issue's work: it never makes this issue
  done, the report never follows it, and the hopper's merge of it never closes this issue. Before, such a mention counted
  as done, its merge closed the issue as completed, and the issue's own open part was left.
- *A promotion was taken for it* (issue #876). A pull request from a **release branch** (`fromReleaseBranch`: its head
  is one of `RELEASE_BRANCHES`, `src/domain/landing-batches.ts`) is no issue's work, whatever its body says: a promotion
  of `dev` into `beta` lists in its body the issues it carries. It never makes an issue done, is never a part, is never
  followed for it, and the hopper's merge of it never closes it. A job branch never is a release branch: no job pushes
  to one. Before, a job on an issue that a promotion mentioned ended done with no pull request of its own, and in yolo
  mode the promotion's merge closed the issue.
  A batch run's branch (`hopper-batch/…`, a batch run, a bisect run or a back-merge) counts as a release branch here
  (issue #2132, "A batch run is no member's pull request").

**The done-check backfill** (issue #637, `src/failures/backfill.ts`). Failures an earlier done rule left — `not complete:`,
waiting on a person (its hand-off open, or its record neither run again nor settled), the newest job of its item — are
judged once by today's rule (`doneAtSource`). Done: in one transaction its hand-off closes (`finished`), its record turns
`resolved`, and its job ends finished with one event, `job.finished` with `result.backfill: "done-check"`; its end is told
to its source again, so the issue gets `hopper:done`, or `hopper:pr-ready` and is followed (PR waiting) when a pull request
of it is still open. Its issue is never reopened and nothing runs again. Not done: it stays in Failures; the answer gives
its card's plain sentence. It runs once per store at the first start of a build that has it, before the sync and the
assessor start (`backfills` in the user's settings, set once every job's source could tell; a GitHub error leaves it for
the next start), and again whenever asked: `POST /ui/api/backfill/done-check` (operator), `hopper backfill done-check`,
answering `{ backfill, changed: [{ jobId, state: finished | pr-waiting }], unchanged, failures: [{ jobId, reason }] }`. A
job it changed is no longer failed, so a second run changes nothing and writes no event.

**A failed job whose issue is closed as complete is finished** (issue #350). A job can end failed
after its work landed: its pane ends on a restart after its own pull request merged, a credential
expires while it waits on a question, or it closes its issue with a commit and then trips. Before
the sync loop reports a failed job, the work-item ledger decides (issue #1067, part 4,
`src/sources/closed-as-complete.ts`): when the ledger does not hold the item's issue closed, the source reads it
(`issueState(job)`; GitHub: closed as complete, above, `src/sources/github/completion.ts`) and the read is recorded first
as `work_item.issue_closed` (`via: read`); the ledger's item closed as complete (`issueClosedAsComplete`) →
`SourceHost.finishShipped` ends the job `finished` (its `error` cleared; `job.finished` with result `issue closed as complete`,
after the `job.failed` already logged), and the report labels the issue `hopper:done`, never
`hopper:failed`. Any failure path is covered — the runner's outcome, restart recovery, an expired
question — because the report is the one place every failure passes. A transient error asking is a
report retry; a permanent one reports the failure. A source without `issueState` leaves every
failed job failed unless the ledger holds its issue closed as complete (a GitHub delivery, the fallback read).

| report | on GitHub |
|--------|-----------|
| claimed | ensure labels `hopper:claimed`, `hopper:done`, `hopper:failed` exist (`gh label create --force`, once per repo per process); add `hopper:claimed`. **No comment** |
| finished | **no comment**; remove `hopper:claimed` (and `hopper:failed`, for a failed job found done later), add `hopper:pr-ready` while the issue is open — its pull request waits for review —, `hopper:partly-done` for a part, `hopper:done` when the issue is closed as complete already (only a job whose work is done or partly done is finished, above); never a close. The pull request is then followed ("After done"). Removing the end label from the open issue — reopened, when a merge closed it — is the re-run gesture |
| failed | **no comment**; remove `hopper:claimed`, add `hopper:failed` (removing it is the re-run gesture) |
| cancelled | **no comment**; remove `hopper:claimed` |
| rejected | **no comment**; remove `hopper:claimed`, add `hopper:rejected`; the issue stays open (removing the label is the re-run gesture) |

Progress and questions are not reported to the source at all (`SourceReport` has no such kinds).
Stored `sourceState.source` keys from before this rule (`claimCommentId`, `progressCommentId`,
`questionComments`, `answeredComments`, `finalCommentId`) and `sourceState.sync` keys (`reportedQuestions`,
`answeredQuestions`, `lastProgressAt`) stay in the JSON and are never read; no column changed, no
migration. `progressCommentSeconds` left `sources.yaml`: `migrate-sources-yaml.ts` (install) dropped
its lines; since phase 5 slice 4 the daemon's plugins-file migration drops the key instead (that
script is gone).

A failure never goes to the issue as text. It is one stderr line in the daemon log
(`hopper: job <id> failed (<issue url>): <error>`, `src/engine/failure-log.ts`), the job's
`error` in `/api/jobs`, and the `job.failed` row (with its error) in the UI event feed.

**Signals (check):** per active job, `getIssue`:
- issue `closed`, or `label` removed → `cancel` (reason `issue closed` / `label removed`);
  issue 404/410 → `cancel` (`issue gone`).
- **Except the job's own pull request** (issue #38): a closed issue whose last close event's closer
  is a merged pull request opened at or after the job's `createdAt` gives no signal — that is the
  job's work landing, and the job still has to install and verify. It runs on and ends as it
  reports (`finished` on `HOPPER_DONE`). `closingPullRequest` asks GraphQL
  (`src/sources/github/closer.ts`); a pull request opened before the job closing the issue cancels
  as above; a permanent error asking counts as "not its own".
- **And a started job's issue closed as complete with no pull request** (issue #350): closed as
  completed (`state_reason`) at or after the job's `createdAt` — a commit's `Closes #N`, or a close
  with no code — gives a job that has started (not `queued`/`held`) no signal: a job may end its
  issue itself. A waiting job is cancelled; a close as not planned, or before the job, cancels.
