**Reject.** `POST /ui/api/jobs/:id/reject` takes an optional `{ reason }` (≤ 500 characters): the job ends
`rejected` with it as its error and in `job.rejected` (none: `rejected by the user`). Offered on every
waiting job in the Queue view and in the Dashboard's Waiting list, in a dialog with the reason field. On
GitHub the rejection writes nothing: the claim label goes, no `hopper:rejected`, no comment, never a close
and no unassignment (D1 and D9 of `docs/assignment.md` are open). A shared label would turn the issue away
for every user and every hopper on the repo. Instead the source asks the host which items' newest job was
rejected (`JobSourceContext.rejections`: when, and for which assignee) and skips such an issue until its
newest `assigned` event for that login is later than the rejection (`GitHubApi.assignedAt`, one events
read per rejected issue per sync); such an issue shows `rejected by you: not taken until assigned to you again` in the source's intake outcomes (issue #440).
**Run again** now takes a rejected job too: the issue is queued at once. A rejection recorded before this
change (no assignee) leaves the issue to its `hopper:rejected` label, as before: removing it offers the
issue again.

**Unassignment** (`check()`, `assignmentDrift`), for jobs with an assignee only:

| the issue is no longer assigned to the job's account | |
|---|---|
| job waiting (queued, held, awaiting acceptance) | cancelled, reason `unassigned`: it leaves the queue |
| job started (claimed, running, on a question, operator-led) | runs on, **flagged**: signal `unassigned` → `sourceState.sync.unassignedAt`, `job.unassigned { assignee }` once. The UI shows "No longer assigned to you on GitHub. Stop it, or let it finish." on the job's lane or row, beside its stop button |
| a flagged job's issue assigned to it again | signal `reassigned` → the flag is cleared, `job.reassigned { assignee }` |

A job taken before this change (no assignee) is never cancelled or flagged for having none: in-flight
work survives the update. The label rules are unchanged (label removed still cancels, D3 open).

**Not built here** (follow-ups of `docs/assignment.md`): the author trust gate, comment context by repo
permission, one claim per issue across users of one hopper, unassign on reject, dismissing a locked entry on
unassignment, intake reasons for every skipped issue, `job.needs_decision`.

**Verification:** `test/integration/github-assignment.test.ts` (the acceptance: any author, assigned →
a job on the next sync; unassigned or unlabelled → none; reject with and without a reason, not taken again
until reassigned, Run again; unassigned while waiting and while running), `test/sources/github-discover.test.ts`,
`test/sources/github-check.test.ts`, `test/sources/github-context.test.ts`, `test/sources/github-app.test.ts`,
`test/sources/config.test.ts`, `test/store/tenant-migration-16.test.ts`, `test/ui/assignment.test.ts`,
`test/ui/ended-rerun.test.ts`.

## Operator actions from the CLI (issue #374, 2026-10-07)

A script or assistant acting for the user read everything through `GET /api/*`, but every operator action
needed a UI session, so it either scripted a human sign-in or wrote rows behind the daemon's back. The
issue offered two ways: a scoped API token that may mutate, or CLI commands. The CLI is taken. A
mutating token would be a second door beside the UI session, against the rule that every mutation is
`POST /ui/api/*` behind one (AGENTS.md); the API door stays reads only ("The API door"). Superseded in
part by issue #718 (owner decision): an **API token** is a session at that same door ("API tokens"). The CLI already
holds the database's credentials, the daemon's own trust, so acting from it widens nothing.

- **Commands** (`src/cli-operator.ts`): `hopper job accept|reject|rerun <id>` (`reject --reason <text>`),
  `hopper job show <id>` and `hopper queue list` (issue #874: reads, a viewer's; a held job with its `holdReason`, a job
  waiting for a lane with its `waitReason`; issue #1780: a job on its **own wait** with what it waits on, `waitsOn` and
  `waitsFor`, `queue list` after the jobs that wait to run; `job show` by a job's id or its **short id**, a start of
  the id more than one job has refused with 409), `hopper queue order <id>...`, `hopper queue gate <auto-accept|review> [--per-hour <n>|none]` (without
  `--per-hour` the throttle stays), `hopper question list [--reason <reason>]` (issue #679: the open questions, each with why it came to a person), `hopper question answer <id> <text>`, `hopper question close|dismiss <id>`.
  `--user <id>` as on `config` (default the one user). Each prints the daemon's answer as JSON.
- **Through the daemon, never around it.** Each command is the UI's own route on the running daemon, so its
  checks, its events (`job.accepted` by `user`, `queue.gate_changed`, `question.answered` by `human`, …) and
  its runtime (the source told; an answer typed into a waiting pane) are the click's. Accept is the Queue
  view's Accept: the accepted waiting jobs in queue order, then the job, posted as the user order.
- **The session.** The CLI mints a UI session in the database (`ui_sessions`, only the token's hash stored)
  for the one call, with the least role the route names (operator; admin for the queue gate), and drops it
  after, whatever the answer. It lives five minutes at most. Its identity's realm is `cli`, which no sign-in
  config names, so a reconcile drops a leftover.
- **Where.** `--url`, else `HOPPER_URL`, else `http://127.0.0.1:<HOPPER_PORT, default 4790>`; the `Origin` sent
  is the URL's own, so it passes the guard as the UI on that origin does. Inside the container the default
  reaches the daemon.
- **Answers.** The daemon's 4xx is a refusal: its message, exit 2. No daemon at the URL, or a 5xx: exit 1.

**Residual risk, stated.** Whoever can run the CLI with the database's credentials can act as any user; that
was already true of `config set` and of the database itself.

**Not built.** Cancel, approve and operator-led from the CLI — no caller yet. Dismiss of locked entries is built
(issue #1123): `hopper job dismiss <id>...` and `hopper job dismiss --superseded` ("Locked entries").

## Failures from the operator CLI (issue #623, 2026-10-10)

A false recurring problem held new jobs, and only a signed-in UI session could release it or close a hand-off.
An operator or an assistant on the host could not unblock the queue. The Failures actions are now operator CLI
commands, on the same footing as issue #374's.

- **Commands** (`src/cli-operator.ts`):
  - `hopper problem list` (the open problems), `release <id>`, `resolve <id> [--note <text>]`;
  - `hopper handoff list` (the open hand-offs), `continue <id> [--note]`, `fixed <id> [--note]`,
    `done-by-hand <id> [--note] [--link <url>]`, `wont-do <id> --note <why>`;
  - `hopper failure list` (the open failures), `retry <id>`;
  - issue #637: `hopper prs` (the Pull requests list, `GET /api/pull-requests`), `hopper yolo <owner/repo> on|off|default`
    (admin; `POST /ui/api/yolo-mode` with `repos`) and `hopper backfill done-check` (`POST /ui/api/backfill/done-check`);
  - issue #677: `hopper pr merge <n>` and `hopper pr close <n>` (`POST /ui/api/pull-requests/merge|close`, "No checks
    means ready").
    `--json` is taken by every command and changes nothing: the answer is JSON.
  A list is `GET /api/failures`, narrowed; each other command is the UI's own `POST /ui/api/failures/*`. The
  verbs are the glossary's words: the issue asked for `settle`, `done`, `run-again` and `clear`, but `settle` would
  be a second word for resolve and `clear` already names the `cleared` end of a hand-off.
- **One path.** The UI and the CLI call the same route and the same `Failures` method, so the events, the
  write-back to the source (the one comment and the end label on GitHub) and the runs again are the same.
- **No new door.** The API keeps one way to mutate: a UI session. The CLI mints one in the database for the call
  (issue #374), so the operator's credential is the database's. A mutating operator token or an operator socket
  would be a second door; neither is built.
- **Who acted** (the **acting person**). Each person's action on Failures keeps who and the way in its event:
  `person` (the session's identity name; `operator CLI` for the CLI) and `via` (`ui`, or `cli` when the session's
  realm is `cli`). On `failure.resolved` (with the `note`), the new `failure.released`, `handoff.closed` (and
  `via` on the hand-off's resolution) and `job.rerun` (a failure's Retry, a hand-off's Run again or Continue in a
  new job). Additive fields: the event versions stay. The check's resolution and the assessor's runs again carry
  none.
- **A note on a problem.** `POST /ui/api/failures/problems/:id/resolve` takes an optional `{ note }`, kept in
  `failure.resolved`; the UI sends none.

**Not built.** A `failure dismiss`: the UI has no such action on a failure record. A failure ends when its job
runs again, its hand-off is resolved (`handoff wont-do` ends it with no more work), or its job finishes.

Tests: `test/integration/operator-cli.test.ts`.

## Request cards from the operator CLI (issue #2220, 2026-10-20)

A script or an assistant that takes in safe work at night could not approve a **request card**: Approve and Decline
were only the Intake page's, `POST /ui/api/sources/:name/intake` with the text's hash. A card a job filed waits for a
person even with **auto-approval** on, so it waited all night. They are now operator CLI commands, on the same footing
as issue #374's.

- **Commands** (`src/cli-operator-intake.ts`):
  - `hopper intake list` (a viewer's): the open request cards of each source's last sync (`GET /api/sources`,
    narrowed): `source`, `key`, `title`, `repo`, `hash`, `author`, `why` (why it is a request), and `reopened` for a
    **reopened card**.
  - `hopper intake approve <key>` and `hopper intake decline <key> --close|--open` (an operator's): the card is found by
    its key in that list (`--source <name>` picks one when two sources list it), and the UI's own route is posted
    with the hash of the text the last sync read, or the hash `--hash` names (the one a script read with `list`).
    Decline names its **decline choice** always: a script says which.
- **One path.** The route, its hash check, Access (`item#can_accept_text`), the box action check and the events
  (`source.request_approved`, `source.request_declined`, `via: cli`; `via: api` for a grant) are the click's. A key
  the daemon did not do (the text changed, or it is no card now) is in the answer's `failed`, and the exit code is 2.
- **`--as <person>`** names who decided, as the CLI session's identity name, so the event's `person` is theirs. It is
  a name only: the session's role and user stay the CLI's. With `HOPPER_REFRESH_TOKEN_FILE` it is refused: the grant
  already names who acts. A grant needs `sources:intake` (the presets `agent-intake` and `agent-approvals`), else 403.

**Not built.** An auto-approval rule for cards a job of a trusted item filed: a follow-up, off by default when built.

Tests: `test/integration/operator-cli-intake.test.ts`.

## The vault and sandbox boxes from the operator CLI (issue #716, part 1, 2026-10-10)

**Superseded (issue #1349, "Sandboxes are burned after each step").** The hopper launches no box that joins as a machine: Add machine → A sandbox box, `POST /ui/api/machines/sandbox`, `hopper sandbox launch`, the reconcile pass, the start check and the launch scope are removed. Kept as the record of what was built.

An agent that needs a template for its job could not make one: templates, vault secrets and sandbox launches were
only `POST /ui/api/vault` and `POST /ui/api/machines/sandbox` behind an admin UI session, and the operator CLI had no
command for them. They are now operator CLI commands, on the same footing as issue #374's: the UI's own routes on the
running daemon, under a session the CLI mints for the one call and drops after it.

- **Commands** (`src/cli-operator-vault.ts`):
  - `hopper vault` (the vault's view: secrets and templates, never a value), `vault set <name> [--scope <text>]` with
    the value on stdin only (never an argument: it would be in the shell history and the process list), `vault remove <name>`;
    `vault set <name> --mints aws-account/<id>|cluster/<name>` marks a minting credential as Vault does
    (issues #791, #872: the same `mints` field, checked before the call and again by the vault), `--mints none` makes it a
    plain secret again, and a set without `--mints` keeps what it was; a shared secret takes no `--mints`;
  - `hopper template list`, `template save <name> --image <image> [--secret <name>]... [--profile <operation>/<kind>/<asset>]...
    [--cpus <d>:<max>] [--memory-mb <d>:<max>]` (issue #1349 removed `--ttl-minutes` and `--keep-home`), `template approve <name>`,
    `template approve-profile <name> <operation>/<kind>/<asset>`, `template revoke <name>`, `template remove <name>`;
  - `hopper sandbox list` (the user's boxes, as `GET /api/sandboxes`), `sandbox launch [--template <name>] [--secret <name>]...
    [--cpus <n>] [--memory-mb <n>] [--ttl-minutes <n>] [--profile <p>]`.
- **A save keeps what it leaves out.** As the vault keeps profiles and limits a save omits, `template save` without
  `--secret` keeps the template's secrets (it reads them first; a new template has none). A profile is written as a launch
  names it, `<operation>/<kind>/<asset>`; the asset may hold `/`. A malformed profile or number is refused before any call.
- **The gate is the vault's, unchanged.** A new scope, image or read profile waits for `template approve`; a write, sync
  or apply profile waits for `template approve-profile`. The CLI approves only what its operator runs: an agent with the
  database's credentials can approve, as it could already through `config set` and the database itself.
- **Roles.** The reads are `viewer`; every change is `admin`, the least role its route names.

**Built since (issue #718).** The read-only negative suite run before a requested template's first box ("The read-only
check", issue #716, item 4). The
token-scoped API for agents is built, after the owner's decision: "API tokens" (issue #718). Shared secrets (issue #718, item 3) are
built: `vault set <name> --shared` ("Shared secrets"). A template made on request, with read approved inside the read
policy, is built ("Templates on request"); so is `template read-policy`. Tools assembled per run are built, with
`template save --tool` and `sandbox launch --tool` ("Tools assembled per run"). An agent with an API token, or the CLI, asks for a
template as a job does: `request-template`, `hopper template request` ("Template requests over the API").

## Templates on request (issue #716, item 1, 2026-10-10)

Owner's model (issue #716): you ask the hopper to make the template a job needs, and the hopper makes it. Before it, a
template was only what a person saved on Vault, or with `hopper template save`. Owner, issue #718: jobs do
not get write access over the API; they still ask the hopper. So a job asks through the skill request it already has
(`POST /job/skill`, "Skills: what the hopper can set up for a box"), and the hopper decides.

- **The ask.** `sh "$HOPPER_SKILL" sandbox-template --needs "read/cluster/lab read/aws-account/123456789012" [--wait]`.
  Each **need** is an operation profile, written as the CLI writes one, `<operation>/<kind>/<asset>`; split by spaces,
  commas or lines; at most 16; each once. A line can also be plain words ("Needs in words"). A need the hopper cannot
  read is a 400 that says how to write it.
- **The template** (`requestTemplate`, `src/skills/template-request.ts`). Its name is `asked-` and 12 hex of a SHA-256
  over the sorted needs: the same needs, in any order and from any job, get the same template, so a later job with the
  same needs makes no second one. It runs the hopper's box image (`ghcr.io/henningfutrell/hopper:box-claude`), holds no
  vault secret, and declares one operation profile per need. It is saved through the vault's own `saveTemplate`, by
  `job <id>`: the same checks and the same `template.saved` event as a person's save. No secret goes in its scope: when a
  job on its box loads a skill, the dynamic vault asks a person for that credential ("The dynamic vault"), and a person's
  giving it approves only that one secret.
- **The read policy** (`ReadPolicy`, `src/domain/read-policy.ts`; the user's settings, key `readPolicy`, no migration).
  The assets the hopper approves read on with no person. Each entry is an asset as Access names it (`cluster/lab`), or
  one that ends in `*` (`aws-account/*`, `namespace/lab/*`): every asset of that kind whose name starts with what is before
  it. At most 64 entries. An admin sets it on Vault (panel **Read policy**), with `POST /ui/api/vault`
  `set-read-policy` (`assets`; replaces it; empty clears it), or `hopper template read-policy set <entry>...`; each set is
  `vault.read_policy_set`. `GET /api/vault` answers it as `readPolicy`. Empty, or never set: the hopper approves nothing.
- **The approval.** The hopper approves the template with no person only when it makes it now and every need is a
  `read` on an asset the policy holds: the vault's own `approveTemplate`, `by` **the read policy** (`vault.approved`,
  `template.profile_approved` with that `by`). All or nothing: one need outside the policy, or one write, sync or apply
  need, and the whole template waits for a person on Vault, as a template a person saved does. The policy
  never approves a template again: one a person revoked waits for a person.
- **A job never widens a template.** A template of that name whose profiles differ from the needs — a person changed it —
  is a 409: the job is told to ask a person. A job never approves, revokes or removes one.
  Issue #1468: the 409 names the needs the template holds now (`--needs "<them>"`), so a job can ask for those, and
  where a person changed it: through the operator CLI (`savedBy` is `operator CLI`) or in Vault.
- **A read the check cannot mint for is refused at the ask** (issue #1468). A template of read needs only takes the
  read-only check, and the vault mints the check's read credentials for an `aws-role`, a `cluster` or a `namespace` only
  (a `terraform-workspace` takes the aws-role's). A read need on any other kind (`aws-account`, `argocd-app`) in such a
  request failed the check at every run, after the template was saved and approved. Now the request (and its preview)
  is a 400 that names the need to ask for in its place: `read/aws-role/<account>/<role>` for an `aws-account`. A request
  with a write, sync or apply need takes no check, so its `aws-account` read is asked for as before.
- **The answer.** 200 when the template is approved, its image the approved one, every profile approved in Access, and
  (a template of read needs only) its read-only check passed ("The read-only check"):
  its name, who approved it, how a person starts a box of it (Machines → Add machine, or `hopper sandbox launch
  --template <name>`), and the skill each need's asset loads on that box. Else 202 `waiting: template <name> waits for a
  person in Vault: …`, with what waits and why the policy did not approve it; `--wait` opens a watch, and the
  job stream ends it when a person approves (`vault.approved`, `template.profile_approved` ask it again). While the
  check waits: 202 `waiting: template <name> is approved; waiting for the read-only check …`; `template.checked` asks again.

**Built since (issue #991).** A job gets the box too: `sandbox` in place of `sandbox-template` ("Sandboxes jobs start").
With skip template approval on, the hopper approves a template it makes now that the read policy does not.
**Not built.** (Tools assembled per
run, item 2, and the read-only check, item 4, are built: "Tools assembled per run", "The read-only check".) A need's credential is asked of a person when a job on the box first loads the skill;
the template does not name a vault secret the user already has. Templates made on request are not removed when no job
uses them.

**Residual risk, stated.** Any job at work may make a template, one per distinct set of needs; it holds no secret and,
outside the read policy, gives nothing until a person approves it. Inside the policy, a new template's boxes may read the
assets the policy names: the policy is the admin's statement that this is fine, and it is empty by default.

Tests: `test/integration/template-requests.test.ts` (the real daemon, the real `hopper-skill`, OpenFGA as a double: read
needs inside the policy approved with no person and allowed by Access; the same needs again, the same template; a write
need waits, and the job's `--wait` ends when a person approves; no policy, a read waits; a person's change is never
widened back and a revoke is not approved again; needs it cannot read refused; the policy set, shown, an event, and an
entry it cannot read refused), `test/skills/template-request.test.ts`, `test/integration/operator-cli-vault.test.ts`
(`template read-policy`), `test/ui/vault-read-policy.test.ts`.

## Sandboxes jobs start (issue #991, 2026-10-13)

Since issue #1349 ("Sandboxes are burned after each step"), an approved request starts no box: each box step runs in a
sandbox of its own. What follows is the model before it, where it says the box starts.

Owner's model (issue #991): sandboxes are started by jobs, not created by hand. A user never creates a sandbox, and
approves sandbox runs only if they choose to. Before it, a job could ask for a template ("Templates on request"), but a
person or the CLI started the box (issue #769).

- **The ask.** `sh "$HOPPER_SKILL" sandbox --needs "write/aws-account/123456789012" [--wait]`, the needs as for
  `sandbox-template`. The broker (`src/skills/broker.ts`) first asks for the template, through the same `requestTemplate`:
  the same needs reuse the same template, and a missing one is made. A template that waits for a person or for its
  read-only check answers 202, as before.
- **Skip template approval** (`SandboxApprovals.skipTemplateApproval`, `src/domain/sandbox-approvals.ts`). With it on, a
  template the hopper makes now, and the read policy does not approve, is approved at once: `approveTemplate`, then
  `approveProfile` for each write, sync or apply profile, each `by` **skip template approval** (`vault.approved`,
  `template.profile_approved`). The read policy approves first when it holds every need. As with the read policy, a
  template that is there already — one a person revoked among them — is never approved by it.
- **The sandbox request** (`createSandboxRequests`, `src/sandbox/requests.ts`; per user, `src/users/sandbox-requests.ts`).
  With the template ready, the job asks for a box of it: one request per job and template, kept in memory, as credential
  requests are ("The dynamic vault"). `vault.sandbox_requested`. It waits for a person on Access requests, panel
  **Sandbox runs**, unless **skip sandbox approval** is on: then it is approved at once, `by` that toggle, a template of a
  high blast radius too. A person approves (`POST /ui/api/sandbox-requests` `approve`) or declines with a reason the job
  is told (`decline`, `vault.sandbox_declined`). Approved (`vault.sandbox_approved`), the hopper starts the box through
  the sandbox module, `launch` with the template and its defaults (`params: {}`), beside the hopper:
  `vault.sandbox_started` with the box's name, or `vault.sandbox_failed` with the reason. Each event is on the job's
  timeline. The job's `--wait` ends on them (`src/skills/waits.ts`).
- **The answers.** 202 while the request waits for a person or the box starts; 200 when it runs: the box's name, who
  approved it, and the skills it loads for each asset — and, for a job that does not run on a box of that template,
  that it runs elsewhere (issue #1009), and how it runs each command in the box as a **box step** (`sh "$HOPPER_STEP"
  box <box>`, issue #1004, "Box steps"); a single command run by its needs, with no box asked for first, is a **need
  step** (`sh "$HOPPER_STEP" need …`, issue #1007, "Need steps"); 403 when declined; 503 when the start failed. Asked again, the
  job gets the same request and the same box. A box that went makes the next ask a new request. A start that failed
  stays failed: a new one on each event would start the box again and again. A person starts one by hand instead.
- **YOLO** (`sandboxYolo`). Both toggles on. A job that needs AWS gets a running box with no human step. Off by
  default. The toggles are the user's settings (key `sandboxApprovals`, no migration): `POST /ui/api/sandbox-approvals`
  with `yolo`, `skipTemplateApproval`, `skipSandboxApproval` (absent keeps; a toggle named with `yolo` wins),
  `vault.sandbox_approvals_set`; the vault's view answers them (`sandboxApprovals`) and the requests of jobs at work
  (`sandboxRequests`). Vault, panel **Sandbox approvals**.
- **Roles.** Both routes are `admin`, and both are box actions (`src/http/ui/box-actions.ts`): approving a request
  starts a box; the toggles approve work with no person. An API token needs a box grant for either.
- **Manual creation is no longer the main path.** Machines → Add machine → A sandbox box stays, for a test; its hint says
  that jobs start their own boxes.

**Decided here, from issue #769's open questions** (as issue #1349 changed it, "Sandboxes are burned after each step").
The owner's decision on issue #769: a sandbox is only for a short-lived, ephemeral action. A job never runs in a
sandbox; it runs on a machine (a job box). What the job does with the sandbox: it runs each command that needs the
template's assets as a box step (issue #1004, "Box steps"): the hopper makes a new sandbox of the template for that
step, and burns it with its home when the step ends; the job stays where it runs. No sandbox joins as a machine, and a
person moves no work. Who pays: the template's limits (`cpus`, `memoryMb`) for each step; a request names none. When it
ends: with its step, never at a time limit (a template has none since issue #1349 part 4) and never with the job; the
check pass's sweep burns a sandbox that no step holds. A request of a job no longer at work is forgotten.

**Residual risk, stated.** With skip template approval on, any job at work may get a template with write, sync or apply
on any asset it names, approved with no person; with skip sandbox approval on too, a box of it starts. Every such
approval is an event that names its toggle. Both are off by default, and only an admin turns them on.

Tests: `test/sandbox/requests.test.ts`, `test/skills/template-skip-approval.test.ts`,
`test/integration/job-sandboxes.test.ts` (the real daemon, the real `hopper-skill`, OpenFGA and the container runtime as
doubles: YOLO, a running box with no human step, each approval an event naming its toggle, the same box asked again;
both off, a person approves the template and the run and the job's wait ends; a decline; the toggles, a box action),
`test/ui/sandbox-runs-view.test.ts`.

## An answer ends the job's own wait (issue #998, 2026-10-13)

Seen on a hopper: a job asked for a sandbox, its template waited for a person, and the job ended its turn with
HOPPER_WAITING. A person approved the template, and the job still waited: nothing woke it. The job's own wait ("A job's
own wait") ends only when its agent goes on by itself or a person ends it, and the job had asked without `--wait`, so no
background command was there to end. Its next ask for the same read need then made a second template, though a person
had approved one with the same profile under another name.

- **Every 202 opens a watch** (`src/skills/waits.ts`). With `--wait`, as before: a new watch, which the job's command
  reads on its stream. With no `--wait`, the hopper opens one too, so it hears the answer: one per job and request (the
  same fields asked again keep the watch it has, with no second one). The answer says so: `watch: <id>: when the answer
  is ready, the hopper ends this job's own wait (HOPPER_WAITING) with it.` The watch's deadline is the default hour.
- **The hopper ends the job's wait.** When a watch ends with an answer — the skill (200) or a no — and its job is
  `waiting_on`, the hopper ends that wait as a person's end-wait does (`Engine.endWait`, `by: hopper`): the job is queued
  again, pinned to its machine, and told in its pane `[hopper] The hopper ended your wait (<what it waited for>): the
  answer to a request you made is ready. The answer: <the answer> …`. `job.wait_ended` with `by: hopper`. A job not on its
  own wait is not touched; one whose agent went on meanwhile is left as it is. A watch that expires ends no wait.
- **A template approved for the same needs is used** (`requestTemplate`, `previewTemplate`). Before the hopper makes
  `asked-<hash>`, it looks for a template with exactly the needs as its profiles, no vault secret and nothing waiting for
  a person (`approvedFor`): one whose read-only check passed first. Found, the request answers with it and saves nothing;
  `sandbox` starts a box of it. The template the needs name still wins when it is approved for them. A template with a
  secret, a wider set of profiles, or anything waiting is never used for a job's needs: it would give the box more than
  the job asked for, or skip a person's approval.

**Not changed.** A template still waits for its read-only check after its approval, and the check runs on the sandbox
module's pass; a check that failed still waits for a person to run it again. A sandbox run still waits for a person
unless skip sandbox approval is on (since issue #1001, also the auto-approve policy or the template's approval: "Fewer
sandbox approvals").

Tests: `test/integration/skill-wait-wakes-job.test.ts` (the real daemon over the fake herdr, the real `hopper-skill`: a
job on its own wait asked for a sandbox without `--wait`; a person approves the template and its profile; the box starts
and the hopper ends the job's wait with its name; asked again, one watch), `test/skills/template-reuse.test.ts`.

## Fewer sandbox approvals (issue #1001, part 1, 2026-10-13)

Seen on a hopper: an admin was asked to approve too much. Each job ask made a template approval, then a sandbox run
approval, then one explicit approval per write profile; a read-only dig waited on all of it. While one approval was
pending, every other approval button on the page was disabled.

- **The auto-approve policy** (`SandboxApprovals.autoApprove`, `src/domain/sandbox-approvals.ts`; the user's settings,
  key `sandboxApprovals`, no migration: a value saved before it reads as the default). For each blast radius level
  (`low`, `medium`, `high`), whether a template the hopper makes for a job, and a sandbox run of a template, of that level
  is approved with no person. **Default: low on, medium and high off.** A template a job asks for holds no vault secret,
  so it is low when every need is a read and high when one is a write, sync or apply ("A template's blast radius").
  - A template: after the read policy, which still approves first what it holds, the policy approves a template the
    hopper makes now whose level it holds (`requestTemplate`, `automaticApprover`), its write, sync and apply profiles
    with it: `vault.approved`, `template.profile_approved`, each `by` **the auto-approve policy**. Then skip template
    approval, as before. A template that is there already is never approved by it. A template of read needs only still
    takes its read-only check before its first box.
  - A run (`createSandboxRequests`): approved at once when the template's level is one the policy holds,
    `vault.sandbox_approved` `by` **the auto-approve policy** with `radius`.
  - Set on Vault, panel **Sandbox approvals** (`Auto-approve low radius`, …), or `POST
    /ui/api/sandbox-approvals` with `autoApprove` (each level named sets itself). `vault.sandbox_approvals_set` carries
    the whole policy; the vault's view answers it in full. Sandbox YOLO stays the override.
- **A template's approval covers its job's run.** A person who approves a template a job asked for (its `askedBy`), or one
  the job's `sandbox` ask waited on (`SandboxRequests.waited`, kept in memory while the job is at work), approved the
  run for that job: the job's run starts with no second approval, `by` **the template's approval by <person>**. Another
  job's run of the same template still waits for a person, unless the policy or skip sandbox approval approves it. An
  approval given by the read policy, the auto-approve policy or skip template approval covers no run: those toggles
  keep their own meaning.
- **Approve all listed.** A template card on Access requests with a write, sync or apply profile shows one action, in one
  confirm, that approves the template (when it waits) and each listed profile, in place of one button per profile. They
  are sent side by side, not one after another (issue #1018, "Approve several at once").
- **Approvals do not block each other.** A template card and a sandbox run card each keep their own pending state: while
  one approval is pending, only that card says `Approving…`, and every other card stays clickable. The route returns once
  the decision is recorded; the box starts in the background, and its card shows `starts now`, then `runs`.

**Residual risk, stated.** By default, any job at work may get a box that reads any asset it names, approved with no
person. It holds no vault secret: each credential a skill on it needs is still asked of a person, or minted after
Access. An admin turns low off on Vault to have a person approve each read again; the read policy then
decides as before.

**Built since: part 2** below (remembered write approvals; cards that say what the sandbox is for).

Tests: `test/skills/template-auto-approve.test.ts`, `test/sandbox/requests.test.ts`, `test/store/sandbox-settings.test.ts`,
`test/integration/job-sandboxes.test.ts` (a person approves the template a job asked for, and its run starts; the policy
set over the API), `test/ui/sandbox-runs-view.test.ts` (two cards approved in a row, each its own progress; Approve all
listed; the policy's switches).

## Fewer sandbox approvals, part 2 (issue #1001, 2026-10-13)

Issue #1001's done line: a repeat write ask on an approved account and namespace runs with zero clicks, and an admin
approves or declines from the card alone, without opening the job.

- **Remembered write approvals** (`src/domain/remembered-writes.ts`, pure; the user's settings, key `rememberedWrites`, no
  migration: absent reads as none). A person's approval of a write, sync or apply profile (`POST /ui/api/vault`
  `approve-profile`, which Approve all listed sends too) is remembered for that asset and access, `by` and `at`; a later
  approval of the same replaces it. An approval no person gave (`NO_PERSON`: the read policy, the auto-approve policy,
  skip template or sandbox approval, a remembered approval itself) is never remembered, so nothing extends itself.
  - A template the hopper makes now (`automaticApprover`, after the read policy and the auto-approve policy, before skip
    template approval) and a sandbox run (`createSandboxRequests`, after the auto-approve policy) are approved `by` **a
    remembered write approval** when the remembered approvals cover it (`rememberedCovers`): no vault secret, at least one
    change, every change remembered, and every read approved with no person (the read policy holds it, or the
    auto-approve policy holds low). Reads only are never covered here: they stay the two policies'.
  - The repeat ask: a second job's same needs reuse the approved template (issue #998), and its run is covered. Zero clicks.
  - **The time limit** (`SandboxApprovals.rememberWritesHours`): an admin's, in hours, 0 to 8760; 0 keeps each approval
    until forgotten; absent, 168. It counts from each approval's `at` at the moment of use, so a shorter limit takes effect
    at once. An approval that ended is left out of every use and of the view, and dropped at the next remember.
  - **Forget**: an admin, on Vault, panel **Sandbox approvals**, or `POST /ui/api/sandbox-approvals`
    `forgetWrite` (`operation`, `asset`): `vault.write_forgotten`. `rememberWritesHours` on the same route; both are box
    actions, as the route is. The vault's view answers `rememberedWrites`, each with `expiresAt` when it ends, and
    `sandboxApprovals.rememberWritesHours` in full.
- **The job says why, and its plan** (`src/skills/broker.ts`). `sandbox` and `sandbox-template` take `--why` (required, at
  most 300 characters) and `--plan` (at most 2000; required when a need changes an asset: the commands, and for each
  change what it changes and whether it can be undone). Missing: a 400 that says how. A template made by the ask keeps
  them (`Template.purpose`, `plan`, kept through every save as `askedBy` is); the sandbox request keeps the asking job's,
  with its issue or pull request (`jobUrl`). A watch asks again with them (`waits.ts`). An API caller's `request-template`
  needs none: the caller is a person.
- **The cards** (`ui/src/views/sandbox-ask.tsx`). Each template card and sandbox run card shows, before its buttons: a
  readable name (`TemplateView.label`, the purpose's first words, at most 48 characters) with `asked-<hash>` beside it;
  **Why**; **Job**, its title and a link to its issue or pull request (`TemplateView.askedByJob`, from the job the hopper
  knows); **Plan**; and each need in plain words: the operation, the asset, the name and scope of the minting credential
  the vault holds for it (a namespace's cluster's, an AWS role's account's), and whether it reads or changes the asset.

**Decided here.** The template's name stays `asked-<hash>` of the needs: it is how the same needs find the same template,
and a name from the purpose would make a second template for the same needs. The label is shown, not stored. The asset's
plain words come from the vault's minting credentials, which a person named, never from the job: a job could call a
production account a test one.

**Residual risk, stated.** A person's one approval of a change on an asset now lets any later job make that change there,
until the time limit (a week by default) or a forget. Each such approval is an event that names a remembered write
approval, on the job's timeline. An admin sets the limit to 1 hour to have a person decide almost each time.

Tests: `test/domain/remembered-writes.test.ts`, `test/skills/template-remembered.test.ts`, `test/sandbox/requests.test.ts`,
`test/store/sandbox-settings.test.ts`, `test/integration/job-sandboxes.test.ts` (a repeat write ask runs with zero clicks,
until forgotten; an ask with no `--why`, or a change with no `--plan`, refused; the template and the run keep them; the
time limit over the API), `test/ui/sandbox-runs-view.test.ts` (the cards; the remembered list, Forget, the time limit).

## Template requests over the API (issue #718, 2026-10-11)

Issue #718's acceptance: an agent with no UI session asks the hopper for a read-only diagnostics template, launches a
box of it, all over the API. Before it, only a running job could ask ("Templates on request"); an API caller had to
write the template itself with `save-template` and approve it as an admin, so the read policy did not decide.

- **The ask.** `POST /ui/api/vault` `request-template` with `needs`, written as a job writes them
  (`"read/cluster/lab read/aws-account/123456789012"`), or `hopper template request --needs "…"`. Like every vault edit
  it is the `admin` role's, and an API token reaches it ("API tokens"). It is not a second path: the route calls the same
  `requestTemplate` with the same user side (`templateRequestUser`, `src/http/vault.ts`), which `POST /job/skill` uses
  too. So the name, the image, the tools, the profiles, the read policy's approval and the refusals are the job's, and a
  template of read needs only takes the read-only check before its first box ("The read-only check"), as a job's does.
- **Who asked.** The template's `savedBy`, and `template.saved`, name the token's or the session's person, not a job.
  An approval the read policy gives is still `by` **the read policy**: the admin's own role does not approve it. A person
  who wants more approves it after, as for any template.
- **The answer.** The vault's view, as every vault edit answers, plus `request`: `template` (its name), `ready` (true
  when a job would get 200; false when it waits for a person) and `text`, what a job would be told. 400 for needs it
  cannot read, 409 when a person changed the template since it was asked for. The CLI prints `request` only.

Tests: `test/integration/template-request-api.test.ts` (the real daemon, an API token, OpenFGA and the container runtime as
doubles, the check box running the check's real script with fake cloud tools: read needs inside the policy approved by
the policy; a box refused until the read-only check passed; the same needs again, the same template, ready; a box of it
launched with the same token; a write need waits and no box launches; needs it cannot read refused; a viewer's token
refused; the CLI). This is the acceptance of issue #718, over an API token from end to end.

## Template requests on the page (issue #708, part 9, 2026-10-11)

Owner's model (issue #708): a person writes what a box must do, and the hopper builds the box's template from it; the
secret scope is derived and shown for approval, never typed by hand. Before it, a template request was a job's
(`sandbox-template`), an API caller's (`request-template`) or the CLI's (`hopper template request`); on the page, a
person could only write a whole template by hand.

- **The panel** (Vault, **Template request**, `ui/src/views/vault-template-request.tsx`). An admin writes the
  needs, one per line, as a job writes them (`read/cluster/lab`). Other roles do not see the panel.
- **Shown before it is made** (`POST /ui/api/vault` `preview-template`, `previewTemplate`, `src/skills/template-request.ts`).
  The answer is `preview`: the template's name, its image, the tools its needs use, the needs in words, `readOnly`, who
  approves it (`the read policy`, or `a person` with `waits`: why the read policy does not), and `exists` when a template
  of that name is there (`same`; or `changed` by a person, when asking again is refused). It saves nothing and sends no
  event. It is the same derivation as a request: `requestTemplate` uses the same `outsidePolicy` reasons.
- **Ask for it** sends `request-template` with the same needs and shows its `text`. A change to the needs hides what was
  shown, so a person asks only for what they saw. The new template is then in Templates, where a person approves what
  waits, as for any template.

Needs in plain words: "Needs in words".

Tests: `test/skills/template-preview.test.ts`, `test/ui/vault-template-request.test.ts`,
`test/integration/template-request-api.test.ts` (the preview over an API token: what it shows, nothing saved, `exists`
after a request, 400 for needs it cannot read, 403 for a viewer).

## Needs in words (issue #708, part 11, 2026-10-12)

Owner's model (issue #708): a person writes what a box must do, and the hopper works out the needs; the secret scope is
derived and shown for approval, never typed by hand. Before it, every template request (a job's, the API's, the CLI's,
the page's) took only needs written out, `read/cluster/lab`.

- **The reader** (`needsFromWords`, `src/skills/needs-in-words.ts`, pure). One line of plain words gives needs:
  - **Assets** are a kind word, then the name: `cluster NAME`, `namespace NAME`, `workspace NAME` (a terraform
    workspace), `account ID` (an AWS account), `role NAME` (an AWS role), `Argo CD app NAME` (also `argocd app`). `named`,
    `called` or `is` may stand between them. A namespace takes the one cluster the line names (`namespace web on cluster
    lab` is `namespace lab/web`), a role the one account (`role ReadOnly in account 1234…` is `aws-role 1234…/ReadOnly`);
    that cluster or account is then no need of its own. `namespace lab/web` and `role 1234…/ReadOnly` are read as they are.
  - **Operations** are the words for them, each with its -s, -ed and -ing forms, and each part of a command such as
    `get-caller-identity`: read words (`get`, `list`, `describe`, `plan`, `logs`, `show`, …), `apply` and `deploy`
    (apply), `sync` (sync), and change words (`delete`, `restart`, `install`, `upgrade`, `scale`, `exec`, …: write). Each
    asset of the line gets each operation the line says. A change word just after `not`, `never`, `no` or `don't` says
    no change.
  - **Refused, with what to write:** a line that names no asset, a kind word with no name, a name an asset may not have,
    a namespace or role with no single cluster or account to go in, and a line that says no operation. The reader never
    makes a need the words did not name: no read is guessed when no read word is there.
- **Where it applies** (`needsOf`, `src/skills/template-request.ts`). Each line of a request is either needs written out
  (every word holds a `/`; the refusals of "Templates on request" are unchanged) or plain words. Both kinds mix in one
  request; the needs merge, each once, at most 16. So a job's `sandbox-template --needs`, `request-template`,
  `preview-template` and `hopper template request` all take words, and the same needs in words or written out make the
  same template.
- **Why a fixed set of words, and no model.** The needs decide what a box may be given. A model's reading can change from
  one call to the next, and text in the request could steer it. A fixed reader is the same each time, and nothing in the
  words can make it give more than the words name. The cost: words it does not know are refused, and a person writes
  those as needs. The preview on the page shows the needs it read before anything is made ("Template requests on the
  page"), and a change still waits for a person, so a reading that goes wide is caught before it gives anything.

**Not built.** A tool name alone names no asset (`kubectl get pods` needs `on cluster NAME`). A word the reader does not
know is not suggested.

Tests: `test/skills/needs-in-words.test.ts` (the reader: assets, a namespace in its cluster, a role in its account,
operations, `not`, the refusals; mixed lines; the preview), `test/integration/template-request-api.test.ts` (words over
an API token: the same template as the needs written out; words that name no asset, 400),
`test/integration/template-requests.test.ts` (a job's `--needs` in words gets the same template; unreadable words
refused).

## Tools assembled per run (issue #716, item 2, 2026-10-10)

Owner's model (issue #716): the hopper picks or composes the image with the tools a job asks for, instead of one fixed
image per template. Before it, a box ran its template's image as it was, and every template made on request ran the one
box image, with no `aws`, `kubectl`, `helm` or `terraform` in it.

- **The catalog** (`BOX_TOOLS`, `src/domain/sandboxes.ts`; the recipes in `src/sandbox/tools.ts`): `aws`, `helm`,
  `jq`, `kubectl`, `logcli`, `promtool`, `terraform` (`jq`, `logcli` and `promtool` since issue #2146, "Observability
  sandboxes"). Each is one version, pinned, from the tool's own release (AWS CLI v2 from awscli.amazonaws.com,
  Helm from get.helm.sh, kubectl from dl.k8s.io, Terraform from releases.hashicorp.com; jq, logcli and promtool from
  their projects' GitHub releases), with its SHA-256 for `amd64` and
  `arm64`. The sums were taken from each project's published sums; the AWS CLI's from the archives, whose signatures were
  checked against the AWS CLI team's key. A new version is a change to that file, reviewed like any other. A tool outside
  the catalog is refused (400) with the ones the hopper adds.
- **The image.** `toolsImage` writes a Containerfile: a fetch stage from Debian bookworm-slim, pinned by its index digest,
  that downloads each tool, checks it with `sha256sum -c` and installs it under `/opt/hopper-tools` (one `RUN` per tool,
  so a tool fetched for one image is a cached layer for the next); then the box's own image, with only `/opt/hopper-tools`
  copied in and put first on `PATH`. Nothing else of the base changes: its user, its entrypoint, its labels; it adds the
  label `io.hopper.tools`. A sum that does not match fails the build, and nothing starts.
  Each download tries again on a network error (issue #1737): `curl --retry 4 --retry-delay 3 --retry-all-errors`, and
  `apt-get -o Acquire::Retries=4`, so one lost DNS answer or reset does not fail the build. A build that fails all the same
  is said to the job as the hopper's failure, not the command's (`boxImage`, `src/sandbox/box-image.ts`): the step's
  problem says the tools image did not build, so the command did not run, and to run the step again.
- **Built once.** Its tag is `localhost/hopper-box-tools:<16 hex>`, a SHA-256 of the Containerfile and the base image's
  id: the same tools on the same base build once. The runtime port has `build(tag, containerfile)` (Podman's
  `/libpod/build`, Docker's `/build`; the context is a tar of the one Containerfile, `containerfileTar`). It builds only
  when no image of that tag is there. The image stays local: it is never pushed.
- **Built ahead of the first step** (issue #1737). The first need step of a template paid the build, 10 to 60 s, and a
  download error in it failed the step. The **warm pass** (`createWarmPass`, `src/sandbox/warm.ts`) runs with the check
  pass, every 10 s and at start. For each template with tools whose image (and tools) are approved, it runs `boxImage`
  where the user's steps run (`forCheck`: beside the hopper, else a client target that is dialled in): the base image is
  pulled and the tools image built when they are not there. A template a read-only check is due for is left to the check,
  which builds the same image. It looks at each image again `WARM_EVERY_MS` (an hour) after, so one the leftover-builds pass
  removed is built again; a build that fails is logged and tried again `WARM_RETRY_MS` (5 minutes) after. The memory of
  what it built is in memory only: a hopper that starts looks at each image once more, which costs an exists call.
- **Each pass on its own** (issue #1965). The sweep, the read-only check pass and the warm pass each have their own
  guard: a tick starts each one that is not in flight, and joins one that is. Before, one guard held all three, so a warm
  pass build (up to 30 minutes, `BUILD_MS`) held every check that `check-template` queued, and nothing in the log said
  why. A tick that finds a pass in flight `PASS_STALL_MS` (5 minutes) after it started logs it once: `hopper: the <pass>
  has run for <n> min and has not ended; the next <pass> waits for it`. A pass that fails logs `hopper: the <pass> failed:
  <reason>` (`src/sandbox/service.ts`).
- **The time of each part of a step** (issue #1737). `runNeedBox` gives the time of its image (pull and build), the box's
  start (volume, create, start, copy in) and its run (`NeedBoxPhases`), and the line `need box … ended with <exit>` in the
  hopper's log carries them: `(image 0.2 s, start 1.1 s, run 9.8 s)`. A slow step then says which part was slow. The
  credential mint before the box is not in it.
- **A template's tools** (`Template.tools`). Saved with the template (`POST /ui/api/vault` `save-template` `tools`, Settings
  → Vault **Tools**, `hopper template save --tool <name>`); a save that names none keeps the ones it has. They are part of
  what its boxes run, so they are approved with its image (`approval.tools`, `imageApproved`): a change of tools waits for
  a person as a new image does, and `template.saved` and `vault.approved` carry `tools`. Templates are a JSON body: an old
  one has no `tools`, which is none. No migration.
- **A box's tools** (`boxImage`, `src/sandbox/box-image.ts`). A need box and a check box of a template run its image
  with all the template's tools. Before issue #1349 a launch could name fewer (`params.tools`, the tool toggles on the
  Add machine form, `hopper sandbox launch --tool <name>`), and the sandbox record kept the tools and the built image.
  Since issue #1349 there is no launch: Add machine adds a computer only, and a template's tools are set on its form
  (Vault) or with `hopper template save --tool <name>`.
- **A template made on request** gets the tools its needs use (`toolsForNeeds`): `cluster` and `namespace` → `kubectl`,
  `helm`; `argocd-app` → `kubectl`; `aws-account` and `aws-role` → `aws`; `terraform-workspace` → `terraform`, `aws`. The
  read policy approves them with the template, as it approves the box image: they are the hopper's own pinned software.
  A template a job asked for before this has no tools, and a job does not add them (a job never widens a template).

**Not built.** Removing old tools images: each new base or tool set leaves one in the runtime's storage, as pulled images
do. A tool outside the four; a version per template. A step gets all its template's tools, never fewer.

**Residual risk, stated.** The build fetches from the four release hosts and Debian's mirrors with the runtime's network.
A compromised release host cannot change what is installed (the sums are pinned here), but it can make the build fail.
The tools run as the box's user, under the sandbox flags; what they can reach is what the box's credentials and network
allow, unchanged.

Tests: `test/sandbox/tools.test.ts` (the Containerfile, the tag, the catalog, the tools of each asset kind),
`test/sandbox/warm.test.ts` (the warm pass: built once, which templates, a failed build tried again later, an image
looked at again), `test/sandbox/need-box.test.ts` (the time of each part),
`test/sandbox/params.test.ts`, `test/integration/sandbox-tools.test.ts` (the real daemon, the runtime as a double: a box of
a template with tools runs the built image, built once; a change of tools waits for approval; tools outside refused; a box
of no template; a build that fails leaves nothing), `test/adapters/podman-runtime.test.ts` and `docker-runtime.test.ts`
(the build call), `test/integration/template-requests.test.ts`, `test/integration/operator-cli-vault.test.ts`,
`test/ui/vault.test.ts`. Checked by hand against rootless Podman 6.1: the image of the box image with all four built in
about 20 s, a second build was skipped, the four tools ran as `agent` on a read-only root with every capability dropped,
and a wrong sum failed the build with no image left.

## The read-only check (issue #716, item 4, 2026-10-10)

Owner's model (issue #716): a template made on request runs a negative suite before its first use: each write is
refused. Owner's decision on the job's question: build the hook now, in a box of the template, with write probes per asset
kind after #715, the result recorded and launch blocked while it is red; keep the probes pluggable so #715 adds or
replaces them; test with doubles, and state the gap to a real environment.

- **Which templates.** One a job asked for with read needs only (`Template.readOnly`, set by `requestTemplate`, kept
  through every save); since issue #2146 part 5, with read and observe needs only ("Bastions"). A template with a write, sync or apply need takes none: a person approves those profiles one by
  one, and a check that writes are refused would fail by design. A template a person saved takes none.
- **The gate.** Until the check of its current version (`check.version` = its `savedAt`) passed (`checkWait`,
  `src/domain/read-only-check.ts`): a launch of it is a 409 that says why; a box of it that is attached takes no new job
  (`approvalWait`, as for an approval); a job's template request answers 202. A save makes the check stale, so a changed
  image, tool or profile is checked again.
- **When it runs.** The check pass (`createCheckPass`, `src/sandbox/check.ts`) runs with the reconcile pass, every 10 s
  and at start, up to `CHECKS_AT_ONCE` (3) checks at once (issue #2236). A template is due when it takes a check, its image (and tools) are approved, and its
  version has no check, or one still `running` (a hopper stopped mid-check). A failed check is not run again by itself
  (issue #1468: but one that failed only on a network error — each mint refusal, or the check box's start, said
  `ECONNRESET`, `ETIMEDOUT`, a timeout and the like — is `transient`, says so, and runs again `CHECK_RETRY_MS`, 5 minutes,
  after it ended, with no person; issue #1736: one that failed only on probes the catalog passes now, from what each did —
  `helm.list` refused on secrets, judged before a right refusal passed it — runs again at the next pass, `judgedAgain`,
  so the jobs that wait on it go on): a
  person runs it again (`POST /ui/api/vault` `check-template`, Vault **Run the check again**, `hopper template
  check <name>`), which drops the check (`template.check_requested`) so the next pass runs one. The command says when
  that is, or why it is not yet: a template whose image is not approved waits for the approval (issue #2226).
- **A check that does not end** (issue #2226). The pass runs one check at a time, so one check that hangs (a pull, a
  build or a mint that never answers) held every later check, for hours, and the jobs that waited on them. A whole check
  may take `CHECK_DEADLINE_MS`, 45 minutes (the check box's 30 minutes, and its image and its mints). Then it fails as
  `transient`, its problem names the step it stopped at (`CheckContext.stepped`), the check box's mints are released, and
  the pass goes on to the next template; it runs again `CHECK_RETRY_MS` after, with no person. A run that ends late
  records nothing, and its check box, if any, is no run's: the next pass removes it. A check a stopped hopper left
  `running` runs again, after the templates with no check, so a check that hangs again holds none of them.
- **A check holds only its own template** (issue #2236). A template the read policy approved got no check for hours, as
  the pass waited for a check that did not end. Now each tick runs a pass of its own, which starts the check of each due
  template that is not checked now, up to `CHECKS_AT_ONCE` at once; a pass ends when every check that runs now has, and
  no tick waits for it. A due check that cannot start now is held, with the reason, in the hopper's memory
  (`CheckTemplates.held`, the vault's `holdCheck`; never stored): as many checks run, or no place can run it (no runtime
  beside the hopper, and no machine of the user dialled in with one). The template's view carries it (`checkHeld`), so
  its wait says why (`checkWait`: "it has not run on this version yet: <reason>"), and a check that runs says since
  when. `sandbox --needs`, `sandbox-template`, `hopper-step need` and `hopper-step box` give that text; a box step of a
  template not ready says what it waits for (`templateWait`, `src/domain/sandboxes-before-start.ts`).
- **The check box.** A one-shot container of the template's image with its tools (`boxImage`, as a box gets them), under
  the sandbox flags (`ContainerSpec.script`: `sh -c` in place of the entrypoint, on a terminal, never restarted), on the
  hopper's network, as the image's own non-root user, with a home volume made for it. It carries the label
  `io.hopper.check`, not `io.hopper.box`: the reconcile pass leaves it, and the check pass removes one no run holds. It
  is removed, with its volume, when the check ends. The runtime port has `wait(id, timeoutMs)` and `logs(id)` for it
  (libpod frames its logs even on a terminal: `logText` takes the frames off). A check may run 30 minutes.
- **The probes** (`PROBES`, `src/sandbox/probes.ts`), for each read need, by its asset's kind. A write must fail and say
  it was refused in the tool's own words (`DENIAL`: `AccessDenied`, `UnauthorizedOperation`, `is forbidden`, …); a read
  must exit 0. Each write leaves nothing when refused, and is a dry run where the service has one; a write that went
  through runs its `cleanup`, and the check fails.
  - `aws-account`, `aws-role`: read `aws sts get-caller-identity`; writes `ec2 create-vpc --dry-run` (probe id
    `aws.ec2-create-tags`, kept so probe marks still name it: EC2 looks up each resource a write names before the dry
    run asks the authorization, so a VPC or instance the account does not hold answers NotFound or InvalidID, never a
    refusal, issues #882, #1903; create-vpc names none), `ssm
    put-parameter`, `iam create-user`, `sts assume-role` to another role of the account.
  - `cluster`, `namespace` (`<cluster>/<ns>`): read `kubectl get ns` (or pods in the namespace), `helm list`; writes
    `kubectl create namespace --dry-run=server`, `kubectl delete pod --dry-run=server`, and the install of a chart `helm
    create` makes: `helm template` renders it and `kubectl create --dry-run=server` creates its objects. A server dry run
    still asks the API's authorization. `helm install --dry-run=server` does not (issue #869): it renders the chart and
    creates nothing, so it ended 0 on a view role and the probe passed falsely. One object created fails the probe, even
    when the others are refused.
  - `helm list` reads the Secrets helm keeps its releases in. The built-in `view` role (EKS `AmazonEKSViewPolicy`)
    cannot read Secrets, so on a view role `helm list` is Forbidden on secrets: that is right for a read credential.
    A probe can carry a **right refusal** (`Probe.rightRefusal`, issue #1736): the words of a refusal a right read
    credential gives. An `allowed` probe with no mark that is refused in those words passes; `helm.list`'s are
    `secrets is forbidden: … cannot list resource "secrets"` (`HELM_LIST_REFUSAL`), so a refusal of anything else, or an
    error, still fails it. A probe can carry a `note` for such a case; a result that did not pass carries it, and so does
    a read that passed refused, and the report shows it under the output (issue #869). The report's summary names each
    read that passed refused. A person can still mark it `expect-denied` or `skip` (issue #916, "Probe marks").
  - `argocd-app`: read the Application; write a label patch with `--dry-run=server`.
  - `terraform-workspace`: read `terraform plan` of a one-resource stack (an SSM parameter); write `terraform apply` of it,
    once with `terraform` on `PATH` (a read-only wrapper there, when #715 adds one) and once with the real binary in
    `$HOPPER_TOOLS` (`/opt/hopper-tools/bin`), past any wrapper.
- **Pluggable.** A probe is data (`Probe`: id, kinds, tool, expect, a shell snippet with `$ASSET`, its own `denial`
  words, a `cleanup`). A catalog (`ProbeCatalog`, `probeCatalog(probes)`) picks the probes for a template's needs;
  `createSandboxes` takes `probes`, the hopper's catalog by default. #715 adds probes to `PROBES` or passes its own.
- **The result** (`ReadOnlyCheck` on the template; a JSON body, no migration): `running`, then `passed` or `failed`, each
  probe's outcome (`allowed`, `denied`, or `error`: it failed some other way, or did not run), its exit code and the last
  500 characters of its output, and a `problem` when the box did not run. `template.checked` records each end, with the
  probes that failed. Vault shows it on the template (**Read-only check**). A check that ran no probe fails.
- **The script** (`checkScript`, `src/sandbox/check-script.ts`) writes each snippet to a file under `/tmp` (the box's only
  writable place) and runs it alone under `timeout` (300 s), with its asset in `$ASSET`. It prints one line per probe,
  `HOPPER-PROBE <n> <exit> <output in base64>`; `readResults` reads them, and a probe with no line did not run.

**The check box's read credentials (issue #797, 2026-10-11).** Reported from a real run: a template of read on an
`aws-role` failed its check, every read `NoCredentials` and every write probe an `error`, while `hopper vault mint-test`
on the same role passed. The check box got no credential at all, so no read could work and no write could be refused
by the account. Now, before the check box starts, the vault mints the read credential of each read need, as for a job:

- **What is minted** (`mintKindFor`, `src/domain/minting.ts`): for read on an `aws-role`, an AWS read session (900 s,
  the `ReadOnlyAccess` session policy, named `hopper-read-only-check` or as the minting credential says: `CHECK_MINT_ID`
  in place of the job id); for read on a `cluster` or a `namespace`, a TokenRequest token for `hopper-read` (600 s).
  `mintTarget` decides, as for a job. A need of another kind (`aws-account`, `argocd-app`, `terraform-workspace`) has no
  minter: the check fails, saying so.
- **Under Access** (`decideCheckMint`, `src/authz/service.ts`). The check runs no job, so Access is asked as for a live
  job of the template — a made-up job `running` the template, told as a contextual tuple, as a trial is — and the
  decision is recorded with `check: {box}`; Users & access → Access names it *read-only check <box>*. A deny (the template's
  read revoked) mints nothing.
- **Where** (`src/vault/checks.ts`, `VaultService.mintForCheck`). In the hopper, or with the vault in a container of
  its own (#586) through the same `MintFrom` as a job's mint: the minting credential never leaves it. `MintFrom` now also
  answers `reach`: the minting credential's region and STS endpoint, or its API server and CA — not secrets, what the box
  needs to reach the account or cluster. `vault.check_minted` records each mint, `vault.check_mint_refused` each refusal;
  never a credential. The minting credential's `lastUsed` stays a job's.
- **Fails closed, per need** (issue #873). A need that gets no credential — no minter for its kind, Access denied it, no
  minting credential for the account or cluster, STS or the Kubernetes API refused — fails the check. Each of its probes
  is `not-run`, with its reason (`not run: the check box gets no credential for read on cluster lab: …`). The probes of
  the other needs still run in the check box, so a person sees all that is wrong in one check. With no probe left to
  run, no check box runs. A need with no credential and no probe gives its reason as the check's `problem`.
- **Into the box** (`checkEnv`, `checkScript`, `src/sandbox/check-script.ts`). The credentials are in the check box's
  environment, `HOPPER_CHECK_<n>_<NAME>`, never in its script. The script takes each into a shell variable and out of the
  environment at its start, and writes each kubeconfig (the server, its CA, the token; JSON) under the box's `/tmp`
  (mode 600). Each probe runs with the credential of its own asset only (`ProbeRun.kind` and `asset` pick it): the AWS
  CLI's `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, `AWS_SESSION_TOKEN`, `AWS_REGION` (the minting credential's
  `Region`, else `us-east-1`, the region the hopper asks STS in: `awsRegionOf`) and `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_STS` when its STS
  is not AWS's; `KUBECONFIG` for kubectl and helm.
- **Kubernetes minting, decided.** The kube minter is built (issue #580): it needs, in the cluster, the service account
  `hopper-read` (bound to `view`) in each namespace a template reads, or in `hopper` for a whole cluster, and a minting
  credential for `cluster/<name>` whose token may only `create` `serviceaccounts/token`. `docs/deploy.md` "Minting
  short-lived credentials" has the manifest. No kubeconfig in the template is needed: the hopper writes the check box's.

**Residual risk, stated (issue #797).** The minted read credentials are in the check box's container spec until it is
removed, at most the check's 30 minutes: anyone who can inspect the hopper's containers (the hopper's own user) can read
them, and they stay valid until they expire (15 and 10 minutes). They are read credentials of the template's own read
needs, which Access allowed. A check that outlasts them (a slow terraform init) sees later probes refused for an expired
credential: an `error`, and the check fails closed.

**Minted once the image is ready (issue #2112, 2026-10-19).** Reported from a real run: the check of read on an EKS
cluster failed on `kube.get`, and each write probe was an `error`, not a refusal, while the mint test of the same
cluster passed. An EKS token works for 15 minutes from its signing, and the check minted it before it pulled the box's
image and built its tools image, which can take longer: the box then signed in with a token EKS no longer takes
(`Unauthorized`). `runCheck` (`src/sandbox/check.ts`) now has the image (`boxImage`) first, then mints, then makes the
box. An image it cannot have fails the check with nothing minted. When each probe is marked `skip` or cannot run (no
state backend), it has no image. When the vault mints for no need, it has the image but makes no box, as before.

**What stays #715's.** The terraform wrapper, a read-only state backend, `terraform destroy` and `state rm` against the
workspace's real state, a credential for an `aws-account`, an Argo CD app or a Terraform workspace, and the check on a
schedule. (Built since, as "A read-only infra box" parts 1 to 6; egress moved to #849.) A test stack of its own and a scratch bucket are not assumed: the probes use fixed names under
`hopper-read-only-check`.

**Not built.** The check on an attached machine's runtime (it runs on the hopper's own); the check
of a template with secrets a person gave (#583): a secret given later does not make the check stale. (The check on a
schedule, the terraform wrapper and its probes are built since: "A read-only infra box", issue #715.)

**A check that failed on a mint (issue #1779, 2026-10-17).** Reported from a real run: a check failed as STS refused the
minting credential's AssumeRole; a person fixed the credential, and `hopper vault mint-test` passed, but the failed check
stayed until a person ran `hopper template check`. Two jobs waited on a template whose role the new minting credential
may not assume, with nothing to tell them.
- **Kept.** A failed check keeps the read needs the vault minted nothing for, each with the vault's reason
  (`ReadOnlyCheck.unminted`, `unmintedNeeds`): a refusal that is not a network error (one is **transient**, issue #1468).
- **Run again when the credential is set.** The vault's set of a minting credential (`recheckUnminted`,
  `src/vault/checks.ts`, in the set's transaction) drops the failed check of each template with an unminted need minted
  from that account or cluster, and records `template.check_requested` `by` `minting credential <name>`. The next check
  pass runs it. A credential for another account or cluster changes nothing, but one for an AWS account runs again a
  check with an unminted cluster need too, as cluster discovery looks in every account (issue #1845).
- **Run again in an hour** (issue #1845). What the vault can mint also changes outside the hopper: a cluster made, a
  trust policy fixed, a new build that looks in more places. A check failed so is due again `CHECK_UNMINTED_MS` (an
  hour) after it ended (`dueForCheck`), and its wait says so.
- **The job is told.** A template request for such a template is a 409, not a 202 wait (`requestTemplate`,
  `src/skills/template-request.ts`): it names each unminted need and the vault's reason, and the read needs on the same
  account or cluster that a check of another template passed with, to ask for in its place. `template.checked` asks a
  waiting request again, so a job on its own wait is woken with that refusal.
- **A stranded wait (part 2).** A job on a wait the hopper watches whose agent session ended — its pane a bare shell —
  is marked stranded and counted as stuck work (`stranded`, Wake all): "Stuck work" and "Watched items" below.

Tests: `test/integration/read-only-check-unminted.test.ts` (the real daemon and `hopper-skill`: the check fails on a
cluster with no minting credential, the job's wait ends with the refusal, a credential for another cluster keeps the
check, one for that cluster drops it and the next pass passes), `test/skills/template-request-unminted.test.ts`,
`test/sandbox/check-transient.test.ts`.

**Unknown assets (issue #2067, 2026-10-19).** Reported from a real run: jobs asked for `read/cluster/staging`,
`read/cluster/central` and `read/cluster/pipeline`, while EKS names those clusters `staging-eks`,
`central-eks` and `pipeline-eks`. The templates were approved by the read policy, their checks marked
every probe `not-run`, and the jobs waited for days on a name that never resolves, until a person ended each wait.
- **What is unknown** (`unknownAssets`, `src/domain/unknown-assets.ts`, pure). A need on a cluster (`cluster/<name>`, or
  the cluster part of a `namespace` or an `argocd-app`) that **cluster discovery** would look for — no minting credential
  mints for that cluster, and no cluster override names it — and that no AWS source of the user's **infrastructure
  topology** lists in its last good snapshot (`knownClusters`). While the topology lists no cluster, no asset is unknown.
- **The job is told at once.** A template request (and its preview) with an unknown asset is a 400 before anything is
  saved, so no template waits and no wait is recorded: `no cluster staging; known: staging-eks, …` — the known clusters
  nearest first (a name that holds the asked name, then by edit distance, `fastest-levenshtein`), at most ten — and the
  needs to ask for with the nearest name in place. A template saved before is refused the same way, so a job that asks
  again (its `--wait` too) ends its wait with the refusal.
- **Shown, not counted as an approval.** The vault's read (`GET /api/vault`, `vaultAnswer`) gives each template its
  `unknownAssets`; `hopper template list` adds `unknownAsset` in words; the template's card says `unknown asset: …` in
  place of its approval; Needs you counts it, one line each (in its own row since issue #2168).
- **Residual risk, stated.** The topology is read every 6 hours and on Discover now: a cluster made since is refused
  until the next read. The refusal says so, and a cluster override for the name (Settings → Clusters) lets it through at
  once. The names it gives a job are the ones `GET /job/topology` already serves it.

Tests: `test/domain/unknown-assets.test.ts`, `test/skills/template-request-unknown.test.ts`,
`test/ui/unknown-assets.test.ts`, `test/integration/unknown-assets.test.ts` (the real daemon and the operator CLI).

**Short cluster names (issue #2168, 2026-10-19).** Reported from an install: the Access requests badge showed 29 with no
approval open. Templates named clusters by short names (`utility` for `utility-eks`), each an unknown asset, and the badge added
the unknown assets to the approvals.
- **A short name resolves** (`matchCluster`, `src/domain/unknown-assets.ts`, pure). A need's cluster with no minting
  credential and no cluster override is matched against the clusters the topology lists: its full name first; else the
  one cluster whose name it starts (`utility` → `utility-eks`); else, when it starts several, it is **ambiguous** — an unknown
  asset with its `candidates`, never a guess; else no match. A cluster override (the configured alias) wins over it.
- **Discovery finds it so.** `mintSourceFor` takes the clusters the topology lists (`readKnownClusters`, read at each
  mint, as the overrides are) and looks for a short name by the full name it resolves to; an ambiguous one is refused
  with its candidates. A short name only ever finds a cluster for a read: a write needs a minting credential or an
  override, which names it exactly.
- **Shown, never counted as an approval.** `GET /api/vault` gives each template its `shortClusters` (`{ cluster, to }`)
  beside its `unknownAssets`. The Access requests badge and its Needs you row count only what waits for approval
  (`accessRequestsWaiting`); the templates with an unknown asset have their own Needs you row, **Unknown clusters**.
- **One click fixes it.** **Point at** (an admin's, on the template card for a resolved short name and on Access
  requests for each candidate of an ambiguous one) saves the template through `save-template` with each need on that
  cluster renamed; a changed profile waits for approval again, as any edit of its needs does.
- **Residual risk, stated.** A short name follows the topology: when a second cluster that it starts appears, it turns
  ambiguous and its mints are refused until a person points the template at one. A read approved for `cluster/utility` reads
  the cluster the topology resolves it to; **Point at** writes that name into the template, so the approval names it.

Tests: `test/domain/unknown-assets.test.ts` (no match, ambiguous, a cluster renamed after the template was saved),
`test/vault/cluster-discovery.test.ts`, `test/ui/unknown-assets.test.ts`, `test/ui/unknown-assets-panel.test.ts`,
`test/integration/unknown-assets.test.ts`.

**Residual risk, stated.** A probe that writes runs the write for real when the credential allows it (the dry runs do
not): with a writable credential, `ssm put-parameter` and `iam create-user` make their resource and the cleanup deletes
it. That is what the check exists to find, and it fails then. Every probe runs under the sandbox flags, as the box's user.

Tests: `test/integration/read-only-check.test.ts` (the real daemon, the real `hopper-skill`, the runtime as a double whose
one-shot containers run the real check script under `sh` with fake `aws`, `kubectl`, `helm` and `terraform`, which answer
only with the minted credentials (issue #797) — minted by the real minting adapters against an STS and a Kubernetes API
faked on loopback —, OpenFGA as a double: the check box gets a read session and a token, each after an allowing decision
recorded as the check's, and no minting credential; a need with no minter or no minting credential, and a read Access
denies, fail the check with the reason and run no box; the same through the vault's own container; a read-only credential passes and the job's wait ends with the template ready, a box of it then starts; a writable
one fails, launch 409, until a person runs it again and it passes; a save makes it stale; a template with a write need, and
one a person saved, take none; a check box no run holds is removed and its check runs again),
`test/sandbox/check-script.test.ts` (the script under `sh`: every probe of every kind, the cleanup of a write that went
through, terraform on `PATH` and past it, a probe with no line, a catalog of its own, each probe with its own asset's
credential and none in the script or left in the environment), `test/adapters/podman-runtime.test.ts`
and `docker-runtime.test.ts` (the one-shot create body, `wait`, `logs` with and without frames),
`test/integration/template-requests.test.ts`, `test/integration/operator-cli-vault.test.ts` (`template check`),
`test/ui/vault.test.ts`. Against real rootless Podman, `test/adapters/podman-check.test.ts` (runs where
`HOPPER_TEST_PODMAN_SOCKET` is set): a check box of the box image with `kubectl` added ran its probes as `agent` and was
removed with its volume; with a token minted for a cluster no server answers at, the hopper's own cluster probes were
all `error`, kubectl asked the server its kubeconfig names, and the check failed.

## The cloud acceptance run (issue #866, 2026-10-17)

The sandbox module (issues #708 to #864) was shown against doubles for the cloud side; no run used real cloud tools.
Owner's decision on issue #866: no outside credentials are used, and nothing goes into the hopper's vault from the
maintainers. Make the real-cloud acceptance easy for outside testers to run in their own environment with their own
credentials: a runbook, one command, results in a form they report back, and a way to collect them.
