- **The runbook.** `docs/cloud-acceptance.md`: what the run proves, what a tester needs (a hopper with sandbox boxes, a
  minting credential for an AWS account and a cluster), the command, the client-machine variant, how to read and file
  the report, and how maintainers collect the reports.
- **The command.** `node scripts/cloud-acceptance.ts run --aws-role <account>/<role> --cluster <name> [--namespace
  <cluster>/<ns>] [--terraform-workspace <name>] [--hopper "<cli>"]`. It adds no path into the hopper: each step is an
  operator CLI command, so the vault's checks, the approval gate and the read-only check apply as for a person. The steps:
  `hopper vault` (the hopper answers, and a minting credential mints for each asset); `hopper vault mint-test` for the
  role and the cluster; `hopper template request --needs` with the needs in plain words ("Needs in words"), reads only;
  the template approved, by the read policy or by a person while the command waits; then its read-only check, which is
  dropped first when one ended before the run, so the report is of this run. The check is the box run with real tools:
  one read per tool and the write probes ("The read-only check"), beside the hopper, or on a client machine when the
  hopper has no runtime ("The read-only check on a client target").
- **The report.** `report.json` and `report.md`: each step `passed`, `failed` or `skipped` with a short output, and each
  tool (`aws`, `kubectl`, `helm`, `terraform`) `passed` (its read worked and each write was refused), `failed` or `skipped`
  (no probe of it ran, with what to name to cover it). Masked before it is written: the tester's account id, role,
  cluster, namespace and workspace become `<account>`, `<role>`, `<cluster>`, `<namespace>`, `<workspace>`; any other
  12-digit number, email address, key, token, IP address, private host name and the host name are masked too
  (`src/secrets/mask.ts`). `report.md` ends with the report as a `json hopper-cloud-acceptance` block.
- **Collecting.** A tester files `report.md` with the issue form `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/cloud-acceptance.yml` (label
  `cloud-acceptance`). `node scripts/cloud-acceptance.ts collect <file>...` reads the reports from `report.json` files and
  from `gh issue list --label cloud-acceptance --json number,url,body` output, and prints a sum per tool and one row per
  report; it names each issue with no report. It reaches no network itself.

**Not built.** The secret scope of a launch (a box gets only the secrets its launch named) and a launch of a box for a
job are not in the command: the CLI launches no box, and the integration tests already prove both against the real
daemon (`test/integration/job-sandboxes.test.ts`, `test/integration/template-request-api.test.ts`). No run of the command
against a real cloud is recorded here: that is the testers' reports.

Tests: `test/scripts/cloud-acceptance.test.ts` (the hopper CLI as a double: a passing run with each tool's reads and
writes; the plain-words needs; a template waiting for a person; a check that ended before the run, run again; a write
that went through fails the run and names the tool; a hopper out of reach; a tool no asset covers; the masking;
`collect` over report files and an issue list; the command's files and exit codes).

## Probe marks (issue #916, 2026-10-12)

Reported from a real run: a template of read on a cluster, with a view role, failed its read-only check on `helm.list`
alone. The view role correctly cannot read Secrets, so `helm list` is Forbidden: that refusal is right for the
credential, but every probe failure failed the whole set, and the template took no box.

- **The mark** (`Template.probeMarks`, `ProbeMark`, `src/domain/read-only-check.ts`). A template keeps a person's mark on
  each of its read probes, by probe id: `expect-denied` (the read must be refused) or `skip` (the check does not run it).
  One mark applies to the probe on every asset of the template.
- **Only read probes.** A write probe takes no mark (`probeMarksProblem`, 400): each write must be refused, always. A mark
  can only make the check ask for less access, never let a write through. `markRuns` also ignores a mark on a write probe,
  so a mark that a later catalog makes a write probe changes nothing.
- **What the check does** (`readResults`, `src/sandbox/check-script.ts`). A probe marked `expect-denied` expects
  `denied`: it passes only when it fails with a refusal (`DENIAL`). It fails when the read works (`allowed`) or fails for
  another reason (`error`). A probe marked `skip` is not in the check box's script; its result is `skipped` and passed.
  Every write probe runs as before, so a write that goes through still fails the check. The result carries the `mark`;
  the check report and Vault name each marked probe.
- **How a person marks a probe.** Only a person, through a save of the template (`POST /ui/api/vault` `save-template`,
  admin role): `probeMarks`, an object of probe id → mark, replaces the marks; absent keeps them; `{}` drops them all. In
  Vault, edit the template: each read probe its last check ran has a mark (**must work**, **expect-denied**,
  **skip**). On the operator CLI: `hopper template save <name> --image <image> --mark helm.list=expect-denied`; each
  `--mark` changes one probe, `<probe>=none` drops its mark, and the other marks stay. A job's template request never
  sets or changes a mark.
- **A save makes the check stale.** The mark is part of the template's version, so the check runs again. The save keeps
  the approval, as the image and tools are the same. `template.saved` records the marks.
- **Kept in the template's JSON.** A new optional field: no migration. A template saved before has no marks.

**Residual risk, stated.** `skip` leaves a read unproven. A read probe only proves the credential works, so a skipped
read never lets a write through; the box can still fail at that read in its job.

**Verification.** `test/domain/probe-marks.test.ts` (which marks a template keeps; a mark on a write probe changes
nothing), `test/sandbox/check-script.test.ts` (under `sh`: `helm.list` marked `expect-denied` and refused passes and the
set passes; it fails when the read works or fails for another reason; `skip` runs no `helm list`; a writable credential
still fails the writes), `test/integration/read-only-check.test.ts` (the real daemon: a view role fails the check on
`helm.list`, a mark on a write probe is a 400, the mark makes the next check pass, a later save and the job's request keep
it, and a writable credential still fails the check), `test/integration/operator-cli-vault.test.ts` (`--mark`),
`test/sandbox/check-report.test.ts`, `test/ui/vault.test.ts`.

## A read-only infra box (issue #715, part 1, 2026-10-11)

Issue #715 asks for a box for diagnostics that **cannot** change infrastructure, in layers, and a negative suite that
proves each write fails. "The read-only check" (issue #716, item 4) and its read credentials (issue #797) built the suite,
the gate and the minting. This part adds the layers the suite was waiting for, and runs the suite again on a schedule.
A template that a job (or an API token) asks for with read needs only is that box: there is no fixed `infra-read`
template, since the needs decide the assets and the read policy decides the approval ("Templates on request").

- **The deny policy** (`awsReadDenyPolicy`, `src/domain/minting.ts`). Every read session the vault mints from STS — for a
  job, a check box, or a mint test — carries an inline session policy beside the managed `ReadOnlyAccess`: explicit
  denies of the `Create*`, `Delete*`, `Put*`, `Update*` and `Modify*` actions of twelve services (`iam`, `s3`,
  `dynamodb`, `ec2`, `ssm`, `rds`, `lambda`, `ecs`, `eks`, `kms`, `secretsmanager`, `cloudformation`), IAM's other writes
  (`iam:Attach*`, `iam:PassRole`, `iam:Tag*`, …), and `sts:AssumeRole` (and its SAML and web-identity forms) on any role
  but its own. Only denies: a session policy's allow could add to what `ReadOnlyAccess` gives. An explicit deny wins over
  every allow, so a role whose own policy can write still gives a read session none of those writes. Each service is
  named (issue #853): IAM takes no wildcard in a service prefix, and the first form, `*:Create*`, made STS refuse every
  read mint (`Invalid service prefix for action '*:Create*'`). A session gets only what both the role and its session
  policies allow, so `ReadOnlyAccess` is the cap on every other service; the 2048-character limit keeps the list short. `AssumeRole` sends it as `Policy`; with the
  vault in a container of its own it crosses in the mint target (`policy`, at most 2048 characters, STS's limit). A write
  session carries neither policy.
- **The read-only wrapper** (`TERRAFORM_WRAPPER`, `src/sandbox/terraform-wrapper.ts`). A read-only template's image
  (`toolsImage(…, { readOnly: true })`, from `Template.readOnly`, for a box and for its check box) puts a `terraform`
  first on `PATH`, in `/opt/hopper-tools/read-only`, in front of the real binary in `/opt/hopper-tools/bin`
  (`$HOPPER_TOOLS`). An allow-list: `init`, `plan`, `show`, `validate`, `output`, `providers`, `version`, `state list` and
  `show`, `workspace list` and `show`, with any `-chdir`; every other command is refused before the real binary runs,
  with `terraform <command>: refused by the read-only wrapper` and exit 1 — `apply`, `destroy`, `import`, `refresh`,
  `taint`, `force-unlock`, `state rm`/`mv`/`push`, `workspace new`/`delete`/`select`, and any command terraform adds later.
  `plan` takes no state lock (`-lock=false` is added; `-lock=true` is refused), as a lock is a write to the lock table.
  `init -upgrade`, `-migrate-state` and `-force-copy` are refused; with a `.terraform.lock.hcl` present, `init` gets
  `-lockfile=readonly`. `TF_CLI_ARGS*` are cleared, so no flag slips past it. It is written into the image in base64 by
  one `RUN` of the fetch stage: the Containerfile needs no build context and no heredoc. The image's tag hashes the
  Containerfile, so a read-only image is a different image from the plain one.
- **Its probes** (`src/sandbox/probes.ts`). For a `terraform-workspace` need, beside `plan`, `apply` on `PATH` and `apply`
  past the wrapper: `destroy`, `import`, `state rm`, `state mv`, `state push`, `taint`, `force-unlock`, `workspace new` and
  `workspace delete`, each on `PATH`, each must be refused. `apply` past the wrapper (`$HOPPER_TOOLS/terraform`) shows the
  account refuses on its own: the IAM layer holds with the wrapper bypassed. A box with no wrapper fails those probes:
  that layer is missing.
- **The check on a schedule** (`CHECK_EVERY_MS`, `dueForCheck(t, now)`, `src/sandbox/check.ts`). A passed check runs again
  when it is a day old: an account or a cluster can change under a template (a role gets a write policy, a binding
  widens). While it runs, the template keeps the check that passed, so its boxes and jobs go on. A pass replaces it with
  the new time; a failure replaces it, and the template takes no box and no job until a person runs it again, as for any
  failed check. A failed check is not run again by the schedule.

**Part 2: a terraform workspace's credential (2026-10-11).** Part 1 left a `terraform-workspace` need's check failing,
as it got no credential: the hopper did not know which AWS account and role a workspace's provider and state live in.

- **The mapping is the template's own** (`workspaceRole`, `src/domain/read-only-check.ts`). A workspace is minted nothing
  of its own. Its probes run with the AWS read session of the template's one `aws-role` read need — the session Access
  allowed and the vault minted for that role, under the deny policy (`credentialsFor`, `src/sandbox/check.ts`). No new
  record, no new setting: the template that asks to read a workspace says which role reads it. A template with no
  `aws-role` read need, or with more than one, fails the check, saying so on each workspace probe, which is not run
  (issue #873: the probes of its other needs still run): the hopper does not guess which role a workspace uses. Considered and not built: an `aws-role` in the workspace's name (it changes the
  name of an asset that Access tuples and saved templates hold) and a mapping record (state a person keeps beside the
  template, for no case the template's own needs do not cover).
- **The state backend is read-only under the read session already.** The deny policy matches the S3 backend's writes
  (`s3:PutObject`, `s3:DeleteObject`) and its DynamoDB lock's (`PutItem`, `DeleteItem`, `UpdateItem`) by name, and leaves
  what `plan`, `show`, `output` and `state list` read (`s3:GetObject`, `s3:ListBucket`, `dynamodb:GetItem`). No backend
  policy of its own is needed. `ViewOnlyAccess` does not read S3 objects: a workspace's role takes `ReadOnlyAccess`
  (`docs/deploy.md`).

Tests: `test/integration/read-only-check-terraform.test.ts` (the real daemon and check: a workspace and a role, one read
session minted for the role, the terraform probes run with it — `plan` allowed, `apply` past the wrapper reaches the fake
real binary with the session and is refused by the account —, and the check passes; a workspace with no role, and one
with two, fail with the reason and run no box), `test/vault/read-session-policy.test.ts` (the deny policy matched as IAM
matches it: each state and lock write denied, each read left). The fake terraform answers only with the minted session
now, as the real AWS provider does.

**Part 3: providers from the image's mirror (2026-10-11).** Issue #715 asks for a plugin cache that is pre-baked or
read-only, with no arbitrary provider downloads. Before, `init` in a read-only box downloaded any provider from the
registry.

- **The mirror** (`PROVIDER_MIRROR`, `/opt/hopper-tools/providers`). A read-only image with terraform holds the AWS
  provider (`AWS_PROVIDER`, `src/sandbox/tools.ts`) in a filesystem mirror, in its packed layout: the release's zip under
  `registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws/`. It is pinned and checked by its SHA-256 in the fetch stage, as each tool is, and
  a new release is a change there. The box's user cannot write the mirror (it is root's, from the image).
- **The CLI config** (`TERRAFORM_CLI_CONFIG`, `src/sandbox/terraform-wrapper.ts`, at `/opt/hopper-tools/terraform.rc`).
  Its `provider_installation` has the mirror and nothing else: no `direct` block, no network mirror. So terraform asks no
  registry, and `init` of a provider the image does not hold fails with `was not found in any of the search locations`.
  The image sets `TF_CLI_CONFIG_FILE` to it, so the real binary in `$HOPPER_TOOLS` reads it too, and the wrapper sets it
  again before each command, so a caller cannot name another one through the wrapper.
- **The wrapper refuses `providers lock` and `providers mirror`**: both ask the registry past the CLI config (`lock`
  rewrites the lock file too). `providers` and `providers schema` still run.
- **Its probe** (`terraform.provider-download`, `src/sandbox/probes.ts`). `init` of a stack that needs `hashicorp/null`,
  terraform on PATH, must fail. `hashicorp/null` is small and real: with the registry in reach and no mirror, `init`
  installs it, and the probe fails. A box with no mirror config fails it, unless the egress proxy filters the registry:
  `init` then fails with `could not connect to registry.terraform.io: … Filtered`, and that is a refusal too (issue
  #2107). A registry out of reach for another reason (no DNS, no route) is an error. Off a terminal terraform wraps its
  error at 78 columns, so the probe reads these words across a line break (issue #2564).

Considered and not built: a read-only plugin cache (`TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR` on a directory the box cannot write) — a cache
does not stop a download, it only keeps one; more providers or more versions of the AWS provider — no case asks for one
yet, and each one is a large download in every read-only image.

Friction, stated: a workspace whose configuration needs another provider, or whose `.terraform.lock.hcl` or version
constraint asks for another version of the AWS provider, cannot `init` in a read-only box. Its `plan` fails with the
error above, and the person adds that provider to the image (a reviewed change in `src/sandbox/tools.ts`).

Tests: `test/sandbox/tools.test.ts` (a read-only image fetches the provider, checks its sum, keeps it in the mirror, writes
the CLI config and sets `TF_CLI_CONFIG_FILE`; a plain one does none of it), `test/sandbox/terraform-wrapper.test.ts` (each
command runs with the image's CLI config, whatever the caller set; `providers lock` and `mirror` refused),
`test/sandbox/check-script.test.ts` (the new probe passes with the mirror, and fails with none). The fake terraform finds
only the providers its mirror holds when `TF_CLI_CONFIG_FILE` names one. Checked by hand: the read-only image of a Debian
base with `terraform` built with rootless Podman, its network open; as the box's user, `init` installed `hashicorp/aws`
6.68.0 from the mirror; `hashicorp/null` was not found, through the wrapper with `TF_CLI_CONFIG_FILE=/dev/null` given and
past it; `providers lock` and `mirror` were refused; the mirror could not be written.

**Part 4: the suite's result as a job artifact (2026-10-11).** Issue #715 asks for the results to be recorded as a job
artifact. Before, a check's result was on the template (the last one only) and in `template.checked` (the failed probes
only): no page showed each probe's output, and a person could not share it.

- **The job that asked** (`Template.askedBy`). A job's template request (`requestTemplate`, `POST /job/skill`) saves the
  template with its job's id. The vault keeps the first one through every save, as it keeps `readOnly`: a person's
  later save does not move the report. A template a person or an API caller asked for (`request-template`) has none.
- **The check report** (`checkReport`, `src/sandbox/check-report.ts`). An HTML page: the template, its needs, a bar of the
  probes that passed and failed (an inline SVG, so the artifact is a visual), and a table of each probe — its id, asset,
  what it expected, its outcome, its exit code and the end of its output. Every text is escaped; the page runs no script.
  Its summary is the one line the check ended with (`passed: 10 probes, every write refused, every read worked`, or
  `failed: 3 of 10 probes failed (…)` and the problem).
- **One artifact per template, a revision per check** (`keepReport`). After each check ends, the check pass
  (`CheckTemplates.report`) puts the report as an artifact of the asking job, `read-only-check-<template>.html`, made by
  `read-only check` (`UserArtifacts.put`'s new `by`). The next check — the daily one, or one a person asks for — finds
  that job's artifact of that name and adds a revision, with the check's state and time as the note ("One piece of work,
  one artifact"). A person who removed it gets a new one at the next check. The artifact's limits, retention, shares and
  Access are an artifact's: a revision past the retention goes, the latest stays.
- **Named on the check.** `ReadOnlyCheck.artifact` and `template.checked`'s `artifact` carry its id; Vault
  links **Check report** (`#artifacts/<id>`) in the template's **Read-only check** row.
- **It never changes the check.** A report that cannot be kept (the job is gone, the user's artifacts are full) is logged
  (`… passed, but its report was not kept: …`), and the check is kept with no artifact: the gate reads the check, never
  the report. A template no job asked for keeps its check on the template only.

Considered and not built: an artifact with no job (the `artifacts.job_id` column is `NOT NULL`, and every view of an
artifact names its job; a migration for one case the template itself already covers), the report on every job that waits
on the template (one shared template, many copies of one result), and a JSON artifact (a person reads the report; the
check on the template is the machine-readable form, in `GET /api/vault`).

Tests: `test/sandbox/check-report.test.ts` (the page: each probe, escaped output, the bar, the summary; the pass keeps each
ended check's report and names it on the check; a report that fails or has no job leaves the check as it is),
`test/integration/read-only-check-report.test.ts` (the real daemon: a job asks, the check passes, the artifact is the
job's with the summary and each probe, `template.checked` and the template name it; the account turns writable, a person
runs the check again: the same artifact, revision 2, the failure in its summary; a template a person asked for keeps no
artifact), `test/ui/vault.test.ts` (the link only for the current version's check).

**Part 5: `destroy` past the wrapper (2026-10-11).** Issue #715 asks for `destroy` to be refused by the wrapper and,
with the wrapper bypassed, by IAM. Part 1 proved the IAM layer for `apply` only: past the wrapper, a `destroy` of the
probe stack found nothing in its state to delete, so it asked the account nothing.

- **The probe** (`terraform.destroy-direct`, `src/sandbox/probes.ts`). The probe stack again, in a directory of its own
  (`$HOME/tf-held`), with a local state the probe writes that holds the stack's SSM parameter. Then
  `"$HOPPER_TOOLS/terraform" destroy -refresh=false`. With no refresh, terraform does not first read the parameter, so
  it sends `ssm:DeleteParameter` whether or not the parameter exists, and the account must refuse it (the deny policy's
  `ssm:Delete*`). Allowed, the provider deletes the parameter, or gets `ParameterNotFound` and ends with no error: in
  both cases the probe fails. With a refresh, a missing parameter leaves the state empty and nothing is asked: the
  probe would pass with a writable credential.
- **No cleanup.** A delete that went through removed only the check's own parameter, which nothing else uses.

Checked by hand: the probe's script, under Terraform 1.13 with the AWS provider 6.68.0, its SSM endpoint a local fake:
the hand-written state was taken and the destroy sent `DeleteParameter`; an `AccessDeniedException` answer failed it in
words the check reads as a refusal; a `ParameterNotFound` answer ended `Destroy complete! Resources: 1 destroyed.`, exit 0.

Tests: `test/sandbox/check-script.test.ts` (refused under a read-only credential with the wrapper and with none; allowed
under a writable one; the fake terraform deletes what a state holds only with no refresh),
`test/integration/read-only-check-terraform.test.ts` (the probe with the workspace's read session, refused).

**Part 6: a state write past the wrapper, refused by the account (2026-10-11).** Issue #715 asks for `state rm` to be
refused by the wrapper and, with the wrapper bypassed, by IAM. With the probe stack's local state, a state write past the
wrapper is a file write that no IAM policy sees: the account is asked only when the state is in its backend. The hopper
did not know a workspace's backend.

- **The backend is on the need** (`OperationProfile.backend`, `StateBackend`, `src/domain/state-backend.ts`): the S3
  bucket, its region, and the key prefix the workspace's states are under. A person sets it on the template's
  `terraform-workspace` profile — Vault (the template's form, **State backend**), `save-template`'s
  `profiles[].backend`, or `hopper template save --backend <workspace>=<bucket>[/<key prefix>]@<region>`. It is no part
  of what is approved: Access tuples, `sameProfile` and a job's request (`sameNeeds`) read the operation and the asset
  only, so a backend set on a template the read policy approved leaves it approved. A save is a new version, so the check
  runs again. `profileProblem` refuses a backend on another kind and a bucket, region or key prefix it cannot use (400).
  The template keeps it as it keeps its profiles: no migration (a template's profiles are its JSON).
- **The probe** (`terraform.state-push-direct`, `src/sandbox/probes.ts`). Past the wrapper, `init` with an S3 backend
  configured only by `-backend-config`: the bucket, the region, and the key `stateProbeKey(backend)` —
  `<key prefix>/hopper-read-only-check/terraform.tfstate`, the check's own key. Then `state push -lock=false` of a state
  of its own (no resources, lineage `hopper-read-only-check`). `init` only reads (`ListObjectsV2`, `HeadObject`); the push
  is the one write, `s3:PutObject`, and the deny policy's `s3:Put*` must refuse it. The probe never names the workspace's
  own state key. Under the key prefix, not at the bucket's top: a role or bucket policy that allows writes under the prefix
  where the workspace's states are is the case to find, and a key elsewhere would miss it. Its `denial` is a refused
  `PutObject` only, so a read that `init` is refused (a role that cannot read the bucket) is an `error`, not a pass.
- **Allowed, it is undone and fails.** The push exits 0; the cleanup deletes that key (`aws s3api delete-object`, with
  the probe's credential), and the probe fails. Nothing else is in that key.
- **No backend: not run, not passed** (`ProbeRun.notRun`, outcome `not-run`). The catalog gives a probe that needs the
  backend (`Probe.backend`) its variables (`HOPPER_STATE_BUCKET`, `HOPPER_STATE_REGION`, `HOPPER_STATE_KEY`), or, for a
  need with none, the reason it is not run. The script writes no step for it; `readResults` keeps it with `passed: false`
  and `not run: no backend configured. …`. So the check fails: a state write past the wrapper is unproven, and an
  unproven write is not a pass. The check report says **NOT RUN** on its row; Vault shows each workspace's
  backend, or that it has none, in the template's facts.

Considered and not built: `state rm` against the workspace's real state (with a writable credential it removes a resource
from that state: the check would break what it guards); a backend taken from the repository's configuration (the hopper
does not read a workspace's repository, "Discovery"); a job naming the backend in its request (a person sets it: a job's
request names needs only, and a backend changes no need). DynamoDB locking is not probed: the wrapper adds `-lock=false`,
and the deny policy's `PutItem` deny is checked in `test/vault/read-session-policy.test.ts`.

Checked by hand: the probe's script under Terraform 1.16.5 (the read-only box-tools image), its S3 and STS endpoints a
local fake. `init` asked only `GET ?list-type=2` and `HEAD` of the probe key; the push sent one `PUT` of the probe key.
A 403 `AccessDenied` answer ended `Failed to persist state: failed to upload state: operation error S3: PutObject, …
api error AccessDenied: …`, exit 1, which the probe reads as refused; a 200 answer ended exit 0.

Tests: `test/sandbox/check-script.test.ts` (refused under a read-only credential, with the wrapper and with none; allowed,
failed and cleaned up under a writable one; the only backend key named is the probe key; no key prefix: the bucket's
top; no backend: not run, not passed, nothing pushed), `test/integration/read-only-check-terraform.test.ts` (the real
daemon: a job's template fails its check with the probe not run; a person sets the backend, nothing waits for approval,
and the next check passes with the push refused; a backend it cannot use is refused at save),
`test/integration/operator-cli-vault.test.ts` (`--backend`, kept by a later save), `test/ui/vault-state-backend.test.ts`,
`test/sandbox/check-report.test.ts` (NOT RUN).

**What stays of #715.** Nothing. Egress limited to the AWS, Kubernetes and GitHub endpoints moved out of #715 to its
own issue (#849, after #315's open question): read-only boxes and the check box on an internal Podman network with an
allowlisting HTTPS proxy. Built since: "A read-only box's egress" (issue #849).

**Residual risk, stated.** The wrapper is one layer: anything in the box can run `$HOPPER_TOOLS/terraform` past it, by
design, and the deny policy is what refuses then. Past the wrapper, a process can also unset `TF_CLI_CONFIG_FILE` and
download a provider: the mirror stops the downloads terraform makes through the wrapper and by default, not every
download a box can make, until egress is limited (#849; built since: such a download finds no route and no proxy that
allows the registry). `ec2:Create*` and its kind match by the action's name: a write whose name
starts with another word (`s3:Restore*`, `ec2:Run*`, `lambda:Invoke*`) is not in the deny policy, and neither is a write of a service the deny
policy does not name; each is refused only when `ReadOnlyAccess` does not allow it — which it does not, as it allows only reads. The deny policy is a guard against
a role whose own policy and a later change to `ReadOnlyAccess` could otherwise widen a session. It is checked in tests
against IAM's policy grammar and AWS's list of services and actions (`@cloud-copilot/iam-policy`,
`@cloud-copilot/iam-data`, issue #853: a fake STS took `*:Create*`, AWS did not), not against AWS itself:
`hopper vault mint-test` mints one with it, so a person sees STS take it.

Tests: `test/vault/read-session-policy.test.ts` (the policy: denies only, each write, every other role, within 2048
characters; none on a write session), `test/integration/vault-mint.test.ts` (the policy reaches STS as `Policy`, through the
hopper and through the vault's own container), `test/sandbox/terraform-wrapper.test.ts` (the real wrapper under `sh`
with a fake real binary: each read passes as given, `plan` without a lock, `init` with a lock file, each write and each
`init` flag refused in the check's words, the real binary never run), `test/sandbox/tools.test.ts` (a read-only image has
the wrapper first on `PATH`; a plain one, or one with no terraform, has none), `test/sandbox/check-script.test.ts` (the
wrapper's probes with the wrapper on `PATH`: refused there, `apply` past it refused by the account; with no wrapper they
fail), `test/sandbox/check-schedule.test.ts` (a day later the check runs again with the template open; a pass replaces
the old one; a failure blocks it). Checked by hand: the Containerfile of a read-only `terraform` image built with rootless
Podman; in it, `terraform` is the wrapper, `apply`, `state rm` and `destroy` are refused, `init` and `plan` of a small
stack run with the real Terraform 1.16.5, and the real binary in `$HOPPER_TOOLS` runs past it.

## Reserved lanes (issue #372, 2026-10-07)

Reported: every lane of a machine was taken by jobs that could run on any machine, while a job a
routing rule had pinned to it (work only that machine can do) waited for one to free. With long jobs it
would wait hours while other machines had free lanes. Nothing in placement kept room for the jobs that
can only run there.

Three ways were offered: a per-machine count of reserved lanes, a placement rule that sends unpinned
jobs elsewhere while pinned demand exists, or requeueing an unpinned job off the machine. Built the
first: it is the smallest, it is per machine, and it needs no job moved once placed. The second would
make one job's placement read every other job's pin; the third would stop work already begun.

**As built:**
- **`reservedLanes`**, an optional option of every machine-source plugin (`local`, `ssh`, `docker`,
  `client`; a whole number ≥ 0, not command-bearing), reaches the decider on
  `MachineSnapshot.reservedLanes`. Edited in the Plugins view's options form like any machine option;
  the machine's card in the Machines view says how many it keeps.
- **The decider (step 7).** A job is pinned to a machine when `pinOf(job)` names it (its
  `spec.machineId`, or for a resuming job the machine holding its pane). A job not pinned to `m` may
  take a lane there only while `unpinned(m) < max(0, cap(m) - reservedLanes(m))`, where `unpinned(m)`
  counts the lanes busy or draining with jobs not pinned to `m` — a lane whose job is not among the
  inputs counts as unpinned, so the reserve stays free — plus this Decision's starts of such jobs.
  Pinned jobs may use every lane. The room an unpinned job sees on `m` is that smaller figure, so it
  goes to a machine with more room for it first. It counts against the **lane cap**, not `maxLanes`:
  past a usage soft limit the reserve stays whole and unpinned jobs give way first.
- **At or above the cap**, only jobs pinned to the machine run there.
- **Wait reason.** An unpinned job with room on its machine save the reserved lanes waits with
  `waiting for a lane: machine m keeps R of its N lanes for jobs pinned to it, the other K are in use`.
- A running job is never moved: the reserve applies to new starts. Absent or 0, placement is as before.

**Verification:** `test/decider/reserved.test.ts` (cap less the reserve, the wait reason, a pinned job
takes a reserved lane, pinned jobs use every lane, pinned lanes do not count against unpinned ones,
unpinned jobs go elsewhere first, a reserve at the cap), `test/plugins/machine-targets.test.ts`,
`test/plugins/host-sources.test.ts`, `test/adapters/ssh-machine.test.ts`,
`test/adapters/machine-usage.test.ts`, `test/ui/machines.test.ts` (`reservedText`).

## Leak prevention: scope, sweep, shared dependencies (issue #410, 2026-10-08)

Follow-up to issue #401. Owner request: reap a job by its process scope, not only by its environment;
reap after a crash; give job worktrees shared dependencies; reap print-agent jobs; hold new claims on a
low disk; every threshold a setting that applies without a restart.

**As built** (each part in "Work tree" and "A machine's disk"):
- **The job's scope**: a herdr-claude pane shell, and each print-agent turn, runs in the transient systemd
  user scope `hopper-job-<job id>` where the machine has a user manager; the reap stops it.
- **The reap through the machine's connection**: this machine, ssh, or a client target's `POST /reap`;
  never keys to a pane. A job whose pane is gone is still reaped.
- **The sweep**: at startup after recovery, then on each machine every `reapEveryMinutes` (default 10), the
  scopes and processes of known jobs that are not live (nor queued or held with an answer pending, issue #2707) are
  stopped, and an ended job's scratch dir is
  removed once `scratchMaxAgeHours` old (default 24), or at once while its work was kept and is now pushed
  (`job.work_removed`).
- **Shared dependencies**: a job worktree's `node_modules` links to the dependencies installed once per
  lockfile in `<work tree>/.worktrees/@deps/<hash>` (herdr-claude option `sharedDependencies`, issue #1188).
- **Print agents**: their own scratch dir, a scope per turn, the reap at the end.
- **A low disk holds new claims** on that machine, by its `diskLowBelowGiB` / `diskLowBelowPercent`.

**Settings, live**: `reapEveryMinutes`, `scratchMaxAgeHours`, `diskLowBelowGiB`, `diskLowBelowPercent` are
plain options of the `local`, `ssh` and `client` machine sources, read at every list or sweep;
`sharedDependencies` an option of herdr-claude, read when a job starts. Machines and executors follow the
plugins config live ("Every setting applies without a restart").

**Not done, by choice**: a worktree per issue reused across runs (branch
`hopper/<issue>`), as the issue sketched: issue #379 (merged first) gives each job its own worktree in its
scratch dir, which the reap and the sweep already own; reuse across runs would need a second lifetime for
it. A Windows client has no `sh`: its reap and survey answer an error and the job is left to its pane's
close, as before.

**Verification:** `test/client/reap.test.ts` (the reap and the survey for real: a scope stopped with a
process that cleared its environment and left its session, where systemd runs; a `node_modules` link no
work of the job's), `test/client/machine-shell.test.ts` (this machine and a real client target's `/reap` and
`/survey`, refusals, 401), `test/herdr/executor-scope.test.ts`, `test/herdr/executor-resume.test.ts`
(the reap never through the pane; a pane gone), `test/herdr/shared-deps.test.ts` (for real with a stand-in
npm: four jobs at once, one install), `test/herdr/executor-job-worktree.test.ts`,
`test/adapters/print-agent-executors.test.ts` (a print-agent job leaves nothing behind),
`test/engine/sweep.test.ts`, `test/integration/sweep-restart.test.ts` (a hopper stopped mid-job and
started again: the job's leftover process stopped, a stranger's not), `test/decider/disk-low.test.ts`,
`test/plugins/machine-targets.test.ts`.

## Intake outcomes, claim holders and the intake migration (issue #440, 2026-10-08)

Owner report: one job ran where a full queue was expected. Dispatch was not the cause: of 16 open labelled
issues, 14 were on the backburner and one had a stale claim and no assignee — and intake said nothing about
any of them. Owner decisions (2026-10-08): M1 (c), M2 holder label + own stale claims released + legacy
claims released once by the migration + one-click release, M3 leave the labels and show the reason, M4 keep
the job repositories and suggest the others, M5 nothing to do (tenant migration 16 already removed
`authors`, so no trusted accounts can be seeded from it).

**As built:**
- **Intake outcomes.** `discoverIssues` gives every open labelled issue it lists one outcome (`IntakeOutcome`,
  `src/domain/intake.ts`): taken, or one reason — `done, but the issue is still open`, `failed: …`,
  `rejected: …`, `on the backburner`, `addressed to another hopper`, `not assigned to you` (action `assign`),
  `claimed by another hopper` / `… (no holder recorded)` (action `release`), `claimed by another user of this
  hopper`, `claimed with no job here (stale); releasing it failed: …`, `rejected by you: …`. The first
  matching reason wins, in that order. `JobSource.intake()` answers them; the sync loop adds each taken
  issue's `jobId` and puts the list in `SourceStatus.detail.intake` (none while paused). Sources lists them,
  not-taken first, with **Assign to me**, **Assign all to me** and **Release claim**
  (`POST /ui/api/sources/:name/intake { kind, keys }`, operator; only on items the last sync offered that
  action for; the source syncs at once, after the answer: issue #1194).
- **Claim holders.** A claim adds `hopper:held-by:<id>` beside `hopper:claimed`; the end of the job, a
  cancel, a rejection and Run again remove both. The id is the user's **claim holder** id: 12 random hex
  characters made on first use (`UserSettingsRepository.claimHolder`), naming no person or machine. A claimed
  issue with no local job: this user's own holder label → stale, released (`source.claim_released`,
  `by: hopper`) and taken in the same sync; another holder → respected (or, when another user of this hopper
  has a job for it — `UserRuntimeOptions.otherUsersKnow` — `claimed by another user of this hopper`, no
  release offered). A new install has a new id, so its predecessor's claims read as another hopper's: the
  user releases them in Sources.
- **The intake migration.** Once per source (`intakeMigration:<source>` in the user's settings), on the first
  sync that lists every repo of its scope: a claim with no holder label and no job in any user of this hopper
  is released (`by: migration`); labelled issues not assigned to the user are listed. The record
  (`detail.intakeMigration`) and `source.intake_migrated { changes }` say what it did; a second run is a
  no-op, across restarts. Nothing to restart: it runs on the first sync of the updated daemon.
- **Repos outside the job repositories.** A connected account's source lists `GET /issues?filter=assigned`
  (one listing, not a search, at most every 10 minutes, `OUTSIDE_EVERY_MS`) and shows the repos outside its
  job repositories with issues it would take there (`detail.outsideRepos`). Sources offers **Add to job
  repositories** (the existing `choose`, admin). Never added by itself; the no-search rule of issue #321
  stands for intake. The app source has no user to list for, so it shows none.
- **Why a lane is idle.** Each Decision's lane plan carries `idle` when the machine leaves lanes unused
  (`idleReason`, `src/decider/lanes.ts`): its lane count is 0, offline, home not known, disk low, usage pacing
  (lane cap below its lanes), reserved lanes, waiting jobs that cannot run there, every waiting job held (the
  queue gate is `awaiting acceptance`), or no job waiting. The Dashboard's idle lanes and empty lane slots show
  it. A waiting job already said why (`holdReason`, `waitReason`). `decision.made` v3 gains the optional
  field; v1 and v2 keep their old lane plan (`legacyLanePlan`).
- **GitHub writes.** Assign to me is the second kind of issue write besides labels and Run again's reopen; it
  is the user's act from Sources, never the hopper's own.

## Issues not taken, surfaced (issue #798, 2026-10-11)

Owner report: a source said "26 open labelled issues: 8 taken, 18 not taken", and on a phone the 18 looked gone. Nothing
was dropped, but the intake list sat in an inner scroll box (`max-h-[32rem] overflow-y-auto`) inside the scrolling page,
with no groups or counts; request cards lived only inside the source's card in Sources, with no badge and no event; the
backburner issues had no action; and "taken" showed for an issue whose job had already ended, until the next sync.

**As built:**
- **Not-taken groups.** Each outcome not taken carries `group` (`NotTakenGroup`, `src/domain/intake.ts`): `request`,
  `not-assigned`, `backburner`, `pr-waiting` (`hopper:pr-ready`), `partly-done`, `other`. `discoverIssues` sets it from
  the reason; `source.ts` sets `request` where it makes the request card. The UI groups by it (`ui/src/model/intake.ts`,
  `IntakeGroups`), in that order, a count per group, and never in an inner scroll region: the page scrolls. Each row's
  link to its issue says `owner/repo#number` with the title (issue #1463: `intakeRef`, from the outcome's `repo`); a source
  whose waiting issues are of more than one repository filters them by repository (`reposOf`; the page's own state, the
  counts then of that repository, Assign all of the issues shown); `not-assigned` says under its heading that intake takes
  only a labelled issue assigned to the user.
- **Not taken, a view.** `#not-taken`, after Queue: per source, the issues not taken, grouped, with every action Sources
  has. Its nav badge counts the request cards (`requestsWaiting`). Sources keeps the full intake, grouped the same way,
  taken last. A request card has no job, so the Queue (which lists jobs) does not show it.
- **Declined requests** (issue #1035): group `declined`, after `partly-done`. Intake lists none of them, and counts them in
  one line (*1 request declined*); "Trusted origin and request cards" says what Decline does.
- **Take off the backburner.** `unbackburner` on `POST /ui/api/sources/:name/intake` (operator; only on an outcome the last
  sync offered it for): the `hopper:backburner` label goes, `source.backburner_lifted { source, key }`, and the source
  syncs at once. A label write, like Release claim.
- **`source.request_opened`.** A new request card records `{ source, key, hash, author, why }`, once per item and text
  hash: `IntakeContext.requestOpened` reads the events, and the source keeps the ids it saw, so a restart or a second
  sync records nothing new, and an edit to the title or body records it again. Never the text. The Grok Bot routine
  notifier posts it (`sourceName`, `issueUrl`, `author`, `why`); webhook subscribers get it like any event.
- **Live job status.** `SourceStatus.detail.intake` is the list as of the last sync, but each taken outcome's `jobId` and
  `jobStatus` are read when the status is (`liveIntake`, `src/sources/intake-live.ts`, for `/api/sources` and each SSE emit). The UI
  prefers the job as its store knows it. An ended job's issue shows "its job ended: <status>" in place of "taken" until
  the next sync says what became of it.

## The backburner, always visible (issue #808, 2026-10-11)

Owner report: 15 of 21 open labelled issues were on the backburner, and from the board they looked gone: a kept-out issue
and a dropped one looked the same. Built on Not taken (issue #798), which lists them and has Take off the backburner.

**As built:**
- **Since when, and by whom.** An intake outcome on the backburner carries `backburner { since, by }`: the newest
  `labeled` event of `hopper:backburner` (`src/sources/github/backburner.ts`). Each source reads an issue's events once
  while the label stays, and forgets the issue when it leaves the backburner, so a sync reads only the issues new to it.
  Events it cannot read leave the outcome without `backburner` (logged), and are read on the next sync. The label is a
  person's (`labels.ts`); the hopper keeps no reason of its own, so "why" is the label, who set it and when.
- **Counted where people look.** The Not taken nav entry has a second badge, dashed and muted, for the issues on the
  backburner, apart from the request badge (`onTheBackburner`, `ui/src/model/intake.ts`). The Queue, which lists jobs,
  links to Not taken with the same count.
- **Distinct rows.** Every intake row shows its issue number. A backburner row has a dashed left edge and says
  "on the backburner <age>, by <login>"; its group heading has the backburner icon. Never the word *parked*: that is a
  job a person took out of its lane.

## When each card arrived in Intake (issue #2228, 2026-10-20)

Owner request: Intake showed no time, so a card that waited overnight looked the same as one that arrived a minute ago.

**As built:**
- **The arrival is kept.** After each sync the sync loop (`keepArrivals`, `src/sources/sync-slots.ts`) gives each item the
  source lists its **arrival**: the time of the sync that first listed it, kept in `intake_arrivals` (tenant migration 87,
  `src/store/intake-arrivals.ts`), one row per source and item key. A row is never changed or removed: a later sync, a
  restart and a second hopper on the same store read the same arrival. A paused source keeps the arrivals it had.
- **One field for every reader.** Each `detail.intake[]` entry of `GET /api/sources` carries `arrivedAt` (ISO 8601, UTC),
  for every source kind, so automations and the operator CLI read the card's age from it and compute none of their own.
- **Shown on each row.** Intake says "arrived <age>" on each row, with the date and time in the viewer's time zone, the zone
  named, on hover (`zonedTime`, `ui/src/model/format.ts`).

**Decisions.** The arrival is the hopper's own first listing, not the issue's creation time on GitHub: the store always keeps
it, so no fallback to the creation time is needed. A row is never removed, so an issue that leaves Intake and comes back
(closed and reopened, or taken and back as a reopened card) keeps its first arrival; one row per item is small. An item
listed before this change arrives at the first sync after the update. Intake keeps its order: the issue's optional sort by
age is not built.

Tests: `test/integration/intake-arrival.test.ts` (the real daemon and store: the arrival is kept at the next sync and across
a restart, and a later item arrives later), `test/ui/intake-view.test.ts` (the age on the row and the time on hover).

## Per-machine work trees (issue #361, 2026-10-08)

Owner request: jobs failed when routed to a machine that did not have the configured work tree — four
jobs went to an agent box while the host's lanes were full, carried the host-only path the GitHub source
set, and failed the scratch check within seconds. Each machine has its own work tree, set in the UI; the
hopper provisions it on the machine itself (directory, the job's repository, scratch, trust) with no
manual setup; a path valid on one machine never reaches another; the router never picks a machine whose
work tree cannot be made usable — the job stays queued, with why, never failed; ephemeral agent boxes
work the same way. Configured on the machine, as the issue recommended: the work tree belongs to the
machine; a routing rule may still override it per repository, on the machine it names. The issue's word
"workspace" is the glossary's **machine work tree** (herdr's own workspaces are something else).

**As built:**
- **The work tree is the machine's.** `resolvePayload` (`src/executors/herdr/payload.ts`, herdr-claude
  and the print agents): the job's own `cwd` — only a routing rule's, which pins the job to the rule's
  machine — applies only on the machine the job is pinned to (`spec.machineId`); anywhere else the
  lane's machine's `workTree`; absent, the jobs directory. No other path exists: the GitHub sources'
  `repoPaths` and `defaultCwd` and the herdr-claude and print agent executors' `cwd` are gone
  (`SourceItem.cwd`/`defaultCwd` and `SpecFromConfig.defaultCwd` too), because none of them names a
  machine. A routing rule's `workTree` without `machine` is refused (`src/routing/`, and the Routing view
  says so first).
- **Set in the Machines view.** An attached machine's Edit form has a `work tree` field (ssh and client
  targets; a container target runs commands only and has none), this machine's Edit form too; empty
  removes the option. The machine panel shows the work tree (the jobs directory when none is set) and
  its work tree problem.
- **Made on the machine when it is probed.** The probe that finds a machine online (at attach, then
  every 30 s) makes its work tree there and says what is wrong — `MachineSnapshot.workTreeProblem`:
  - this machine: `createLocalMachineSource` makes it in the background (`src/client/work-tree.ts`
    `makeWorkTree`: `mkdir -p`, writable, never the home or above it), at most once per 30 s;
  - an ssh target (an agent box is one): in the same ssh call that asks its home and its disk
    (`probeSsh`), a shell `mkdir -p` and a write check, `~` as `"$HOME"` there; the answer's last line
    says made or not. A box made again from its image, with an empty home, has its work tree again at
    the first probe after attach;
  - a client target running the hopper's client release: `POST /work-tree {workTree}` on its link
    (`src/client/server.ts`, signed like every call), answered `{workTreeProblem?}`. The call is in a new
    client file (`work-tree.ts`), so the release id changes and the release keeper loads it onto every
    client first; a client on another release is not asked.
  A probe that cannot run the check (the client call fails) reports that as the problem.
- **Never routed there.** The decider (`src/decider/assign.ts`, `workTreeHolds`) takes a machine with a
  work tree problem for no new job, as a machine whose disk is low. A job no other machine can take is
  held — `no machine running executor <x> has a usable work tree: <m>: <problem>`, or `pinned machine
  <m>: <problem>` — and starts once a probe finds the work tree usable or another machine has room; a job
  that waits for the other machines' lanes says that. A job already running there keeps its lane, and a
  job resuming there returns to its pane. The hold reason is the job's `holdReason`, shown in the UI;
  the attached machine's log line says it takes no new job and why.
- **The repository, at each start** (`src/executors/herdr/job-worktree.ts`). Since issue #431 only when that repository is
  the job's ("Repository-agnostic lanes"): a work tree that is the top
  of a git repository — a checkout the owner keeps, as before — is used as it is: no clone is put in it,
  and each job gets its own worktree of it ("Each job its own git worktree"). Any other work tree (the
  jobs directory, a fresh box's) gets the job's repository when the job has one (a GitHub issue's,
  `job.source.repo`): the job worktree command fetches the **checkout** `<work tree>/workspace/<name>` (issue #1103), whose
  `origin` must be that repository, or clones it there from `https://github.com/<owner/name>.git` the
  first time (into `<name>.hopper-clone-<pid>`, then moved in, so two jobs cloning at once leave one),
  and makes the job's worktree of it, `<work tree>/.worktrees/<name>/<job id>` (issue #1188). Git takes github.com
  credentials from `GH_TOKEN` when the pane has it, else from `gh auth git-credential` (the job's
  credentials dir, issue #441), through `GIT_CONFIG_*` variables naming a helper: the token is never on
  a command line. `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0`: git never waits for a person. A checkout of another
  repository under that name, or a refused clone, fails the job at once with what git said. With
  `jobWorktrees` off, the checkout is fetched or cloned and the job runs in the work tree. The print
  agents run the same command, worktrees off, before their first turn, its output on stderr.
- **Scratch and trust.** The scratch dir is made first, as before; the machine's work tree is made by the
  scratch command too (`mkdir -p`), a routing rule's never. Claude's folder-trust dialog for the job
  worktree is accepted at startup (`trustWorkdir`, default on) — on a fresh box too; no trust is written
  into any file of Claude's, which running Claude processes also write.
- **Migration.** Tenant migration 18 (`src/store/migration-machine-work-trees.ts`): the path jobs fell
  back to (the first job source's `defaultCwd`, else the first work tree executor's `cwd`) becomes the
  `workTree` of each `local`, `ssh` and `client` machine that has none — not when it is the jobs
  directory, the default — so every job runs where it ran before; a `repoPaths` entry that is not that
  path becomes a routing rule `{ name: '<source> <repo>', match: { source, repo }, set: { machine,
  workTree } }` after the existing rules when there is exactly one such machine, else it is dropped; a
  routing rule's `workTree` without a machine gets the one machine there is, else loses the work tree (a
  rule left setting nothing goes); every executor `cwd` and source `repoPaths`/`defaultCwd` goes. Stored
  jobs lose `defaultCwd`, and `cwd` unless a rule set it with the machine the job is pinned to; their
  `fromConfig` follows. A machine that got a path it does not have is then held off by its probe, with
  why, instead of failing jobs: fix its work tree in Machines. The build before runs on the migrated
  store: it reads a machine's `workTree` (issue #324) and defaults the gone options.

**Residual.** A failure at start (a clone refused for credentials, a disk filled since the probe) still
fails that job with what the shell said: the probe checks that the work tree can be made and written,
not that every repository can be cloned there. A work tree a routing rule names is not probed (only the
machine's own is); a missing one fails the job at start, as a misconfigured path should (issue #324).

**Verification:** `test/herdr/machine-work-tree.test.ts` (the machine's work tree, the jobs directory,
a job's own path only on its pinned machine, made wherever it is, the job's repository named to the job
worktree command), `test/herdr/job-worktree.test.ts` (against real git: a clone into a plain work tree
and its job worktree, a fetch of an existing checkout, a checkout of another repository refused, a work
tree that is a repository left without a clone), `test/decider/work-tree.test.ts`,
`test/adapters/ssh-machine.test.ts` (`probeSsh` makes the work tree, the jobs directory by default,
one that cannot be made, the home), `test/adapters/machine-usage.test.ts` (this machine),
`test/adapters/client-transport.test.ts` (the client's `/work-tree`), `test/store/tenant-migration-18.test.ts`,
`test/integration/attached-machines.test.ts` (held with why through the real composition root, then run
once the probe finds it usable), `test/routing/rules.test.ts`, `test/ui/machines.test.ts`,
`test/ui/routing.test.ts`, `test/sources/config.test.ts`.

## Webhook signing secrets (issue #451, 2026-10-08)

Owner request: a webhook subscription's signing secret is made by the hopper's operator for the hopper,
so the hopper stores and manages it, instead of the form naming a runtime variable. Held to current
practice for secrets at rest: a key per value (salted), a master key outside the database (the pepper),
authenticated encryption bound to the value's place, and a key id for rotation.

- **Entered in the UI.** `add` takes `secret` (typed in: 32 to 4096 printable ASCII characters, no
  spaces) or none, and then the hopper makes one (32 random bytes, 64 hex digits). `add` no longer takes
  `secretEnv`, from the UI or anywhere: no route names a variable for a subscription.
- **Encrypted at rest** under the master key ("Sealed in the database"): the subscription id is the
  context. Stored in `webhooks.secret_sealed` with `secret_changed_at` (tenant migration 19). Never in
  clear, never logged (an audit line names the subscription and how it changed: typed in, made by the
  hopper, replaced, rotated), never in an event, never answered.
- **Write-only.** `GET /api/webhooks` and every answer carry `secretChangedAt` only. The actions are
  `replace` (`{ action, name, secret }`) and `rotate` (`{ action, name }`: the hopper makes one).
  A secret the hopper made is answered once, as `generatedSecret`, in the answer to the edit that made
  it; the UI shows it in a box to copy and never puts it in its store. Every answer of the route is
  `cache-control: no-store`. `remove` deletes the row, and the sealed secret with it.
- **Applies without a restart.** The dispatcher opens the stored secret at each delivery (and each test
  event), so a new, replaced or rotated secret signs from the next one (issue #356).
- **Subscriptions from before (M1).** A row with `secret_env` and no stored secret keeps reading that
  variable under the user's secret prefix, exactly as before; its card says "secret from runtime variable
  X: replace to store it in hopper". Storing a secret (replace or rotate) clears `secret_env`: it is no
  longer read, and the variable can be removed from the runtime. Nothing is imported from the runtime on
  its own (M2 not taken): the operator decides when each moves.
- **The key.** The master key of issue #441, not a second one: one runtime value to keep, which the
  compose install and `install.sh` already make. Its derivations are separated by context, so the
  connected account's tokens and the webhook secrets never share a key. Rotation, missing and wrong keys:
  "Sealed in the database".
- **Messages.** `secretProblem` (on `GET /api/webhooks`), a test event's `detail` and a delivery's
  `lastError` say: a runtime variable not set (`WEBHOOK_SECRET_X is not set`), no secret set (`replace
  or rotate it`), or the stored secret cannot be opened (no key: `HOPPER_MASTER_KEY is not set`; another
  key: the key id it was sealed under; altered or moved).
- **One key for every user.** Each user's secrets are in their own schema; the per-user secret prefix is
  no longer needed for a stored secret (it stays for a subscription from before).

Carried, not in this change (the issue's audit, rows 2–10): the Grok Bot routine's URL and key, the
anthropic-api and TypeSafe API keys, the GitHub App's private key, the realms' secrets (sealed and
write-only), client machine keys, the hopper's ssh and link keys, and moving the connected account's
tokens onto the sealer (a key id, so its key can rotate; and never kept in clear without a key).

## Logins (issue #476, 2026-10-08)

A machine or agent that waits on a sign-in — a CLI printing a device code to enter at a URL — is handled
apart from the questions. The action is always the same (open the URL, enter the code before it expires),
so no escalation level can act on it, and a question about it either climbed to nobody or stalled the job
until its timeout. A **login** (glossary) goes to its **login kind**; `device_code` is the first.

- **Raised.** A herdr-claude job ends its turn with `HOPPER_AUTH_PENDING` and the field lines (the
  protocol line in "Phase 2"; marker table there) while the command waits in the background. A print-mode
  run — an agent CLI under the codex, opencode, omp or cursor-agent executor, or an escalation level's
  `claude -p` — is watched as its output comes (`run-output.ts`): a device code a CLI the hopper knows
  prints (`recognise.ts`: gh, codex; each tested on its real output) is reported while the run waits.
  A client target's herdr job is a herdr job; there is no client-to-hopper message of its own yet.
- **Seen on screen** (issue #698). A herdr job that ends its turn with no marker while its turn shows a device code
  — a CLI's output, or the job's own words about it — has it reported all the same, before any nudge or wait: the
  recognisers read the turn after its anchor (`turnText`), never the prompt above it. Besides gh and codex, **any**
  CLI's prompt is read by its shape (`recognise.ts` `any`): a code the words call one (`code`, `code:`, six or more
  letters and digits, with or without dashes) and, within 400 characters, a URL whose host or path names a device page
  (`device`, `activate`, `verif`, `pair`, `/link`, `/login`, `/auth`); its tool is the page's host, its expiry the
  "expires in N minutes" near it, else 900 s. The job is then told (`loginSeenNote`) that the user was shown it and to
  report it with the protocol lines — the same code, so the same login —, so a login signal can end it. A GitHub code
  is steered to the hopper's GitHub proxy, as a reported one is. The executor keeps each job's codes, reported or seen,
  in memory (never written) until the job ends: a code still on screen is a new login once. Not while the job already
  waits on a login. A CLI whose words fit neither is missed, never misread; a print-mode run's output is read the same
  way.
- **Never a question.** A login opens no question and reaches no escalation level. An escalation level's
  run that waits on one reports it with the question (`questionId`, the level as `run`); the run ending
  in an error still climbs the question, as any error does.
- **The logins** (`src/logins/service.ts`, the `RunLogins` port). One open login per job (or question)
  and prompt: a report with the same tool, the same code, or (no code) the same URL is that login (issue
  #567). The same code again changes nothing — no event, its expiry kept from when it was first shown —, so
  a device-flow script that polls, or a job that reports its login again each time it checks on it, is one
  login however often; a new code updates it (`auth.pending` again, same `loginId`, `renewed: true`), never
  a duplicate. The run asks `check` on each poll for what the user did: wait, a new code, cancelled, fail,
  or `ended` (it ended with nothing to tell: the run stops waiting on it).
- **Login signals** (issue #567, `src/logins/signals.ts`). A herdr job's login ends only on a **login
  signal** the turn shows after its `HOPPER_AUTH_PENDING`: a token obtained, the CLI or Claude saying it is
  logged in, authenticated or signed in as or to an account (issue #2144), or the authentication went through (`completed`); the code expired (`expired`, at once, as at
  `expiresAt`, `onExpiry` applies); the user denied it at the provider (`failed`). The protocol line asks the
  job to report a login once per code and, when it goes through, to say so in a line `Logged in.`. Polling output
  (`authorization_pending`, `slow_down`, "waiting for authorization", the same code printed again), Claude
  going on by itself, and the screen changing are no signal: before issue #567 Claude going on completed the
  login, and the same report still on screen made a new one on the next poll, every few seconds. A line
  that says not, never, yet, still, waiting or pending is no signal either. A job that ends with no signal
  leaves its login to the sweep (`failed`, `the job ended`), never `completed`. A print-mode run's login
  is `completed` when the run succeeds; `failed` when the run ends first. Tenant migration 27 collapsed the
  logins the flood made: one of a job's (or question's) tool reported before the kept one's `expiresAt` is
  that login again, and the kept one took its last status. The tick
  sweeps: an open login whose job no longer runs fails (`the job ended`), an expired one too (issue #529: nothing
  waits on it, so no Cancel or New code is offered that does nothing), and so does an escalation level's login
  whose question is no longer open (`the question ended`); a pending one past `expiresAt` expires, with or without
  word from the machine.
- **Login outcome** (issue #1110). Only the requester — the job that asked for the login — knows whether it worked: a
  signal on screen is a guess, a print-mode run's success is a proxy, and nothing at all reached the hopper from a job
  whose output differed, so its login stayed pending, then renewed, with no way to clear it. So the job says what came of
  it: `sh "$HOPPER_LOGIN" completed <tool>`, or `failed <tool> --reason "<why>"` (`hopper-login`,
  `src/logins/script.ts`, beside `hopper-gh` in the job's credentials dir), which is `POST /job/login`
  (`src/http/job-login.ts`) with the job's proxy token, while the job is at work. It names the login by its tool (left
  out: the job's latest login). `completed` ends it `completed` (`auth.completed`, `by: requester`), a login that failed
  or was cancelled too: the requester's word is the last. `failed` fails an open one (`auth.failed`, `by: requester`,
  the reason with any code it holds hidden); on a completed or dismissed one — a later check found it does not work — it
  **reopens** it: `pending` again with the `reason`, a fresh `expiresAt` (`REOPENED_SEC`, 900 s), no code
  (`auth.reopened`), until the job reports a new code, which the same login takes (`auth.pending`, `renewed: true`,
  its reason cleared). A failed or cancelled login stays as it is. The protocol line asks for it beside `Logged in.`;
  the login signals stay, so a job that does not report still ends its login as before. The route changes no job,
  question, webhook or setting. No polling: the job reports once, when it knows.
  The tool is named as the job likes (issue #2144): `hopper-login` takes a command of many words quoted or not (a
  word that starts with `-` too, but `--reason`), and the route finds the login of that tool with its words spaced
  any way, else the newest whose words hold every word named, a path by its last part (`mcp_auth.py` names
  `python3 …/mcp_auth.py login`). Before, a helper's command named unquoted was a bad call (exit 2), so the sign-in a
  person finished never reached the hopper and the card waited until its code expired.
- **Dismiss** (issue #1110, `POST /ui/api/logins/:id/dismiss`, operator). The fallback when the requester never says:
  a person puts an open login away, whatever its job does. `dismissed` (`auth.dismissed`, `by: user`), its code
  dropped; the run that waited on it reads `ended` and stops waiting, and nothing is typed into a pane (Cancel does
  that). A login ended otherwise cannot be dismissed (409).
- **The active list.** The Logins section counts `pending` logins (`GET /api/sections`); the Logins view's cards are
  the pending ones, the expired ones a job still waits to renew, and, for a short while, the failed, cancelled and
  expired ones. A resolved login — completed or dismissed — leaves the cards at once (issue #1110) for Earlier logins.
- **Browser profile** (issue #1249, `ui/src/model/browser-profile.ts`, `ui/src/components/browser-profile.tsx`). Signing two
  machines in one after the other in the browser's default profile let the first sign-in's cookies sign the second machine's
  tool in as the wrong account. So each card that shows a page to open names a **browser profile**: `hopper-<machine id>-<account>`,
  lower case letters, digits and dashes, each part at most 40 characters. The account is the one the login names (the Claude
  sign-in for pods names it), else the machine's last account (issue #1269); with none known, `hopper-<machine id>`; with no
  machine, `self`. The name comes from nothing else, so a sign-in again on the same machine and account opens the same profile,
  with its cookies. A web page cannot pick the browser's profile, so the card gives the ways to open the page in it: a command,
  copied, that starts Chrome or Edge with the profile's own data dir (`--user-data-dir`; PowerShell on Windows, the dir under
  `%LOCALAPPDATA%\hopper\browser-profiles\`; a shell on macOS and Linux), made at its first use; and a Firefox container
  link (`ext+container:name=<profile>&url=<page>`), which the add-on Open external links in a container opens in the container of
  that name. The page's own Open button is unchanged: a new tab of the browser's current profile, `noopener`. Nothing of the
  profile is kept by the hopper or sent to it; the command carries the page's URL, as the Open button does.
- **Expiry.** The logins setting `onExpiry` (`POST /ui/api/logins/settings`, admin; the user's settings,
  read at each expiry, so a change applies without a restart): `renew` (the default since issue #1016: two codes of a
  job expired before a person saw them, and the job stalled) — at each expiry the hopper asks the job for a new code
  by itself (`check` answers `new-code` with `expired`; the job is told its code expired and, first, to say so with
  `hopper-login` when the login went through after all — the code expires on the hopper's clock, and a sign-in done is
  never followed by a new code (issue #2144) —, else to start the login again and report the new code,
  `loginExpiredNewCodeNote`; a login completed before its run read the ask is not asked again), `auth.expired` carries `renewing: true`, and the new code is the
  same login (`auth.pending`, `renewed: true`, so the notifiers post it again), until the login is completed or
  cancelled, or the job's own timeout; a run that cannot ask its tool again (a print-mode run) holds; `hold` (the
  default from issue #698 to #1016) — the job keeps waiting until its own timeout, the card says Expired and offers
  Request a new code, and the notifier says it expired; `fail` (the default before) — the job fails, its error
  `the <tool> login expired at <time> before it was completed`. A user who saved `hold` or `fail` keeps it; a build
  before issue #1016 reads a saved `renew` as unset, its default.
- **Acting** (`POST /ui/api/logins/:id/cancel`, `…/new-code`, operator). Cancel ends the login and types
  into a herdr job's pane that the user cancelled it: stop the command, go on without it or fail. A new
  code types in: stop the command, start the login again, report the new code. A print-mode run takes no
  input, so it cannot be asked for a new code (409); cancel only ends the login there.
- **Who completes it.** Always the user, at the provider. No agent or other machine completes a login; the job that
  asked for it only says that it went through (issue #1110).
- **Sensitive data.** The URL and the code are credentials in flight. Never stored: the `logins` table
  and every `auth.*` event carry the login's id, kind, tool, status, times and what waits on it (`auth.pending` also
  the URL's host, issue #698), never them, nor the account or scopes; they live in the daemon's memory while the login is open and are dropped when it ends (a restart
  drops them: `codeKept: false`; a herdr job still waiting is read back from its screen). Only a UI session
  of the user whose role may act on a login (operator or admin, issue #477) reads them, from `GET /api/logins`
  and `/api/logins/:id`: never a viewer's, never the API door's token, never a loopback read without a session. Wherever a run's output goes on — a job's progress, a question's text
  and recent output, a job's result or error, a login's failure reason — a code its screen or output shows
  is replaced with `[code hidden]`. Webhooks deliver `auth.*` events as any other, without the URL or code.
- **What asks** (issue #698). A login report may name the `account` (or host) the tool signs in to and the `scopes` it
  asks for (the protocol's optional field lines `account:`, `scopes:`). An account may name a person, so both are kept
  as the code is: in memory, answered only with it. The **host** of the URL to open (its host name, never its path or
  query, which may carry the code) is answered to anyone who reads the login while the code is kept, and is in
  `auth.pending`. The Logins card lists them, and the lane, under what waits.
- **Notifiers** (issue #698). The Grok Bot routine notifier posts `auth.pending` (a new code too) and `auth.expired`
  ("Grok Bot routine webhook"): what asks, what waits — the job, its issue, the machine and lane —, the time left and a
  link to the Logins view (`NotifierEvents.loginsUrl`, `#logins`). Never the URL to open or the code: a phone or a
  routine is outside the hopper, and the code is a credential in flight; the person opens the Logins view, signed in,
  for them. Before issue #698 no `auth.*` event went to a notifier. Webhook subscribers may subscribe to `auth.*`. The
  Logins UI is issue #477.
- **Naming.** "Login lane" in the issue is a login kind here: a **lane** is a job slot (`lane.opened`).
- **The Logins view** (issue #477, `ui/src/views/logins.tsx`, its model `ui/src/model/logins.ts`). A view of its
  own (`#logins`), apart from Questions: no login is ever a question card. One card per login, open ones first
  with the least time left on top: the machine, the tool, what waits on it (the job, or the escalation run),
  the code with copy and open (`DeviceCode`), a countdown, and Request a new code (a run that can ask) and
  Cancel (asks first). **Phases**, from the server's status and the clock: `pending`; `expiring` under the
  **warning** — the setting `warnSec` (default 60 s; `POST /ui/api/logins/settings`, admin; 10 to 3600) or a
  fifth of the code's life from its last report, whichever is longer — the card and the badge amber, the
  countdown larger, and a polite live region says it once; `expired` at `expiresAt` by the browser's clock,
  before the server's `auth.expired` arrives (the code no longer shown, the card says what happens to the
  job by `onExpiry`); then the server's status is final: `completed` (Signed in, the time, the job goes on: a login signal said so),
  `cancelled`, `failed` with its reason. **Server time:** `GET /api/logins` answers `now`; the UI keeps
  server time less its own clock and counts down on the shared 1 s clock plus that offset, so a skewed
  browser clock does not move the countdown. **Live:** each `auth.*` event refreshes the logins, as each
  `question.*` refreshes the questions. **Badge:** the nav entry and a header link count the open logins
  (pending, not past `expiresAt`), and, since issue #1016, an expired code its job waits to renew (`onExpiry` renew
  or hold, a run that can ask, `awaitsNewCode`: amber, as one about to expire), on every view until none is left —
  so Needs you counts it too —, never cleared by being seen
  (issue #499's rule for Questions). An ended login stays on its card 5 minutes (`ENDED_ON_CARD_MS`), an
  expired one held for a new code until it changes; then it goes to Earlier logins, under the cards, a
  compact list that never had the code. A viewer's card shows the countdown and a notice instead of the
  code and the actions. The logins settings are a panel there for an admin.
  Taken conservatively, each one place to change: a top-level nav entry, not a tab beside Questions; the
  warning one setting per user (the logins settings are the user's); 5 minutes on a card; no browser
  notification (the notifiers carry logins since issue #698, above).

Open decisions taken conservatively, each one entry to change: the kinds after `device_code`
(`LOGIN_KINDS`, `kinds.ts`); who completes a login (the user only); on expiry (`onExpiry`, default
`renew` since issue #1016, no limit on renewals but the job's timeout); notifiers (the Grok Bot routine since issue #698, never with the URL or code).

## Failure assessment (issue #509, 2026-10-08)

A failed job stayed failed until someone looked at it, and a cause that hit many jobs showed as many failures.
The **failure assessor** (`src/failures/`, one per user runtime) judges every failed job once, from its
`job.failed` — whatever failed it: an executor's outcome, restart recovery, a question's end, an invalid item at
intake. A failed job left unassessed (no `assessment`) — by a restart, or by a build before the assessor — is
assessed at start and by the sweep, whatever its age (issue #517); the sweep leaves a job that failed in the last
minute to its own `job.failed`.

**Rules first, no model.** The error is normalised and hashed to a **signature**; a **known cause** is matched —
a cause a person named for that signature first, then the built-in ones by their text (`causes.ts`). In order
(`assess.ts`, pure):

0. A job that **timed out** (the built-in cause `timed-out`) is decided by its **liveness** alone (issue #630,
   "A timed-out job" below): never grouped into a problem, nor joined to one.
   A job whose own pull request's checks are red (the built-in cause `own-pr-checks-red`, issue #1230, "Own PR checks
   red" below) goes on to fix them while under `maxAttempts`, then a person: never grouped, nor joined to a problem.
1. The open **problem** of the signature whose scope covers the job's machine takes it: held, or redirected. Not a
   `job` cause's failure (issue #637): a done-check miss is its own job's, even when an older build grouped its
   signature into a problem.
2. A known `shared` cause opens a problem, scoped by the cause to the job's machine (`machine`), its executor on
   that machine (`executor`: an expired login), or every machine.
3. The signature failed on `groupThreshold` items (default 3, counting this one; a retry chain is one item)
   within `groupWindowMin` minutes (default 60): a **general** cause, grouped and held, scoped to the machine
   and executor every failure of it shares. Only when they share a machine or an executor, and only when its cause
   is absent or `transient`: a `job` cause (`not-complete`, `invalid-spec`, `question-unanswered`, or a cause a
   person named with the decision "a person") belongs to its one job and never groups (issue #625).
4. A `transient` cause runs again while its retries are under `maxAttempts` (default 3): after
   `backoffSec × backoffFactor^(attempt−1)`, at most `backoffMaxSec` (defaults 60 s, 2, 1800 s). At the limit:
   a person, saying so.
5. Anything else: a person, with a summary — what was tried (runs, machine, how long), what failed (the error's
   first line), the last line of output.

Two cases come before the rules and act on nothing (issue #517):

- **Superseded.** A failed job that is not its item's newest job — a person ran it again, or anything else did —
  is recorded `superseded`, `nextJobId` the newer job: its class and decision kept for the profile, no problem
  opened or joined, no retry, not for a person. The sweep does the same to a record that was `surfaced`,
  `not_retried` or `held` once its item runs again, so it leaves the person's list.
- **Older than a day** (`STALE_AFTER_MS`) when assessed — an upgraded install's backlog. Its decision stands, as a
  recommendation (`auto: false`, `Retry recommended`, `Redirect recommended: <cause>`), and it waits on a person:
  its work may be stale, and a failure that old neither retries by itself nor opens or joins a problem that would
  hold other jobs.

**The same failure twice in a row** (issue #1461). The record of its item's run before it — the same job's, when it
was continued, else that of the job it ran again (`rerunOf`), by whatever ran it again — has the same signature
(`repeatedOf`, `chain.ts`). A run again did not help, so the item stops: `person`, `repeated`, and no Jev pick (issue #550) runs it
again. One the rules would run again gets the summary "Stopped: the same failure twice in a row"; one they give to a
person already keeps its summary, with the repeat in its reasons. It is raised once, as one
hand-off (`retry_limit` for a `transient` class, else `person`). Not a daemon restart, a timeout (its liveness
