proposed in one job; `GET /api/sections`), `test/ui/research-view.test.ts`, and the proposal tests on the shared contract.

## Decider calls (issue #550, 2026-10-09)

Hopper and its jobs make many small decisions. A **decider call** is a bounded choice with a known option set and a
low blast radius. Jev picks it first — before an escalation level, a model or a person — and the decision goes on as
before when Jev's pick is not applied. Jev is not the router (that is the gate router, "Gate router"): it is asked
before anything else at each **decision point**.

**Jev at its seam** (`src/minor-decisions/jev.ts`, `jev_pick.py`): one TypeSafe `Choice` named `decision` over the
point's options (`criteria`: option id → what it means), with the point's instructions and the facts as `state`, model
`jev-latest` (grok-bot-jev's own default) — the call grok-bot-jev's `jev_client` makes, through the `typesafe_sdk` the
image installs (0.7.4). The key is the user's **TypeSafe API key**, kept in the vault's system scope and opened on every
call ("The TypeSafe API key in the vault's system scope", issue #657). No key: Jev is off, nothing is asked and nothing recorded, and every point decides as it did before (an
escalation level, the rules, a person). Every failure — no SDK, TypeSafe refusing, 30 s without a pick, a pick outside
the options — is no pick, never a throw. Not a plugin and not a setting: no option of it is something a person setting
up the hopper knows (issue #217). Tests put a double at the seam (`UserSeams.jev`).

**Decision points.** Each declares its options; the settings are per point, in the database (`minorDecisions`, a user
setting), edited in Settings → Decider (admin), read at every decision:

| point | asked | options | applied |
|---|---|---|---|
| `question-answer` | a question whose text lists at least two numbered options (`1. …`, `2) …`, a dialog's cursor and border aside; the last run of them, numbered from 1), before the first escalation level | each listed option, by its number | the number is the answer (`answeredBy: jev`), typed as a level's answer is |
| `failure-assessment` | a failure the rules hand to a person with no known cause, not superseded, not stale, within the retry limit — after the rules | `retry`, `person` | `retry`: the job runs again by the assessor (`job.rerun`, `by: assessor`; its record `retried`, note `run again: Jev picked it`); its hand-off, opened by the rules, closes as for any run again |
| `lane-count` | a machine's lane recommendation by the rules changed, when it is recorded (issue #688, "Lane tuning") | the lanes the rules allow (`laneCountOptions`) | the machine's lane recommendation, `decidedBy: jev`; an admin still applies it |
| `job-machine` | a waiting job that two or more machines online, with its executor and not kept by the blast-radius gate, can take; once per waiting spell (issue #688) | those machines | a placement pick: in step 7 the job goes there first |
| `intake-order` | one sync of a job source finds two or more new items — no job follows them — (issue #796, `src/sources/intake-order.ts`) | the first 10 new items, in the source's order | the picked item is offered first: its job is queued first, and goes first among jobs of its priority; the rest follow in the source's order |
| `merge-order` | a repository's tending queue is free and two or more of its waiting pull requests need tending (issue #796, "The tending queue", `src/sources/tend-order.ts`) | the first 10, in the rules' order | the picked pull request is tended next |
| `intake-trust` | a waiting job whose trust stamp is due for Jev's trust check: `approved` or `trusted`, no person stamped it, no check on it (issue #655 part 4, "Trust stamps", `src/engine/trust-checks.ts`) | `keep`, and each lower level but `quarantined` with each reason (`lower:untrusted:touches_ci`) | the job's stamp is signed at the picked level; active, the job waits for the check, and a check with no sure pick gives `untrusted` (fail closed) |
| `intake-kind` | a waiting work job from a job source that never started and has no kind check: no research or proposal asked, no fork, follow-on or tend job, on an executor that writes reviews (issue #655, "Trust stamps", `src/engine/kind-checks.ts`) | `keep`, `research`, `proposal` | research or a proposal asks the job for it (`research.asked`, `proposal.asked`, `by: jev`); active, the job waits for the check, and a check with no sure pick keeps the work |
| `sandbox-request` | a job's sandbox request that the sandbox approvals would approve with no person, under sandbox strictness `standard`, of a template not of low blast radius (issue #655 part 13, "Trust stamps", `src/sandbox/requests.ts`) | `allow`, and `hold` or `deny` with each reason (`deny:out_of_scope`) | allow approves the run by `Jev`; hold leaves it for a person; deny declines it and lowers the job's trust; active, the request waits for Jev, and a check with no sure pick holds it (fail closed) |

A `failure-assessment` ask is kept on its failure record (`jev { error, attempt, ranMs?, machineId?, doneCheck? }`, issue
#1608) until Jev answers: a daemon that stopped first asks it again at its start, for a job still failed whose newest
record it is, within a day of the record; any other is cleared.

Grouping stays the rules' own (a problem needs failures on several items), so it is not an option. The other decider
calls the issue names — the queue gate and pre-sort, priority, phase shifts, stale cleanup, client repair — are not
decision points yet; each one is a new row here. Lane choice is two rows (`lane-count`, `job-machine`, issue #688).
Ordering is two (`intake-order`, `merge-order`, issue #796): each picks the first of a set, never a whole order, so each
is one bounded choice; the rest keep the rules' order. Neither deletes, sends or publishes anything: never consequential.
Each gives the rules' own pick (`MinorDecisionInput.rules`), so a pick not applied is compared with it at once
(`decidedBy: rules`). Only facts go to Jev: an item's title, priority, labels, repository and number, never its author
or its text; a pull request's number, step, title, priority, when it was opened, its base and checks.

**Modes.** `off`: Jev is not asked. `shadow` (the default for every point): Jev's pick is recorded next to what was
decided, and nothing else changes. `active`: a pick whose confidence is at or above the point's `threshold` (default
0.85) is applied; below it, the decision goes on as before. A point whose decision does not wait for Jev (`job-machine`:
a free lane claims the job at once) gives a `settled` check: when it was decided while Jev was asked, the pick is
`too_late`, never applied, and compared at once with what was decided.

**Never for consequential actions** (`guard.ts`). A decision is consequential when its text matches the question
pipeline's risk rules (delete, deploy and publish, force-push, spend, credentials, sending a message) or names a
permission change (permissions, chmod, chown, grant, revoke, sudo, access to), or when its job's machine is one the
blast-radius gate keeps (`BlastRadius.gates`, issue #542). For a question the text is the question with its options;
for a failure, the job's goal. A consequential pick is recorded (`notApplied: consequential`, with what made it so) and
never applied, whatever its confidence.

**Visible.** Every pick is a `minor_decision.picked` event on its job (and its question): the options, the pick and its
confidence or the error, the mode and threshold, whether it was applied, and why not (`shadow`, `below_threshold`,
`consequential`, `no_pick`). A question's pick is also the first entry of its trail (`role: jev`, outcome `accepted`
when applied). The event stream shows it as one line.

**Agreement.** What is decided after a pick that was not applied is compared with it (`minor_decision.compared`): a
question's accepted answer — a level's or a person's —, read as the option it names (its number or its words; a typed
answer naming none is a disagreement), and a person's end of a failure's hand-off — Run again is `retry`, Clear is
`person` (a hand-off closed by anything else is not compared), the machine a job was claimed on (`job-machine`), and an
admin's act on a machine's lane recommendation (`lane-count`): the lanes applied, or, dismissed, the configured lanes. A person may override any pick, applied or not
(`POST /ui/api/minor-decisions/picks/:id/override`, operator; `minor_decision.overridden`): what it should have been,
one of its options. It changes nothing already done; it replaces the comparison in the agreement rate. An applied pick
is compared only through an override: what follows it is its own doing. `GET /api/minor-decisions` gives, per point
over the last 30 days, how often Jev was asked, picked, applied, compared, agreed, the agreement rate and the overrides,
and the newest 50 picks; the figures are read from the events, so no table and no migration. An admin flips a point to
active once its rate holds; `minor_decision.settings_changed` records each change.

Open decisions taken as defaults, each one entry to change: every point starts in shadow; threshold 0.85; the
consequential rules are the question risk rules plus permissions; an active failure pick opens the hand-off first and
closes it when it runs the job again (a webhook told of the hand-off sees it close).

Tests: `test/minor-decisions/` (options, the guard, the view from events, Jev through the fake `typesafe_sdk`),
`test/integration/minor-decisions.test.ts` (shadow, active, below the threshold, consequential, Jev failing, a failure
in shadow and active, a known cause, overrides, settings, off, no key), `test/ui/minor-decisions.test.ts`.
## Phase shifts (issue #548, 2026-10-09)

Owner requirement: when a job asks a question, the right response is sometimes "go research this aspect" or "write a
proposal for this first". The question card says so directly, as a **phase shift**: **Research this** and **Propose
this**, next to Send answer, Park, Close and Dismiss, each with an optional note scoping the aspect, in one of two modes.

**Phase** (`src/domain/phase.ts`): a job is in one — `work`, `research` or `proposal` (`JOB_PHASES`). `Job.phase` is set
by a shift; absent, `phaseOf` derives it from the spec (a job asked for research is in research; one asked for a
proposal, or that reached its proposal, in proposal; else work). Every route that answers a job names it (`withPhase`:
`/api/queue`, `/api/jobs`, the shift routes), and the UI shows it wherever a job is named (`JobTitle`: Dashboard, Queue,
Questions, the sections), unless it is `work`.

**Fork** (`mode: fork`): a separate job asked for research or a proposal about the aspect — the parent's spec with that
one special job's flag, its priority, its payload and work tree, accepted at once (a person or an allowed level asked
for it) — the orchestration loop of #537 / #538. It has **no source of its own**: the sync never reports it to the
parent's item (labels, completion), and `getBySourceKey` never takes it for the item's job. `forkOf` carries the parent
job and question, the kind, the note, the question's text (it is told it, after its job rules: `forkBrief`) and the
parent's source (where it came from in the sections, the repository its work tree holds, the connection it acts through).
The parent records it (`forks`) and is parked where its executor can park (issue #2335; else it keeps waiting on its question
— which holds no lane and does not expire while a fork of it runs). Its priority follows the parent's while it runs
(`job.reprioritized`), and the usage limits apply to it as to any job. Accepted, its document answers the parent's
question while that is open (`settleWith`, answered by `fork:<id>`, `forkAnswer`: the document and the notes, "use it
as the answer, or as context"); rejected, the question stays open and waits on a person again, its timeout from now.
`job.forked` on the parent, `job.queued { forkOf }` on the fork, `job.fork_resolved { decision, delivered }`.

**Switch** (`mode: switch`): the question is answered with what the job is to do now (`switchBrief`: research or write
a proposal first, the aspect, the section's ask) and the same job and session move into the phase (`phase`, `shift`:
the question, the note, who, when; `job.phase_changed { from, to, mode: switch, questionId, note, by, reason }`). Its
document is a review item like any (`switchedFrom` names the question). At Accept the person picks what the job does
next (`then`, offered only while the job is in a switched phase of the item's kind — `ReviewItemView.then` lists the
choices — and refused otherwise, 409): `work` — back to the work in the same session with the document as context
(`backToWorkBrief`), the default —, `end` — it ends finished with its decisions as its result —, or, from research,
`proposal` — it writes a proposal next, in the same session, still switched. A rejected proposal of a switched job sends
it back to work, told so. Each move is `job.phase_changed`; `<prefix>.accepted` carries `then`.

**Suggestions.** A job suggests a shift in its question (`Suggest: research — <aspect>` on a line of its own; the
protocol tells every job, `SUGGEST_PROTOCOL`); an escalation level in its reply (`suggest: { to, note }`, the claude-cli
level's schema and prompt). The question carries the first one (`suggestion`, `by` `job` or the level), and the card
offers it as one click in the default mode. Only a person shifts — or a level the settings name (`levels`), which then
shifts the job itself in the default mode (its reply's attempt `accepted`); a level's fork moves the question to a person,
who may still answer it first.

**Rules as everywhere else.** Only a job whose executor runs the research and proposal loop may shift (`Executor.reviews`:
the test executor, herdr-claude, the print-mode agents; `GET /api/health` `reviewingExecutors`); the question's
`shifts` (`QuestionView`) lists the modes the server takes now, or none with the refusal, and the card offers exactly
those. The settings (`GET /api/phase-shifts`, `POST /ui/api/phase-shifts`, admin; settings row `phaseShifts`, read at
each shift; `phase_shifts.settings_changed`): `defaultMode` (`fork`), `levels` (none); `forkParent` is gone (issue #2335). No schema
change: the job's new fields are in its body, the settings a settings row.

**Open decisions, as taken** (defaults, all live settings or per-decision choices): D1 the default mode is Fork — it
leaves the original job as it was; D2 under Fork the parent waits on its question (no lane is held while it waits), Park
a setting; D3 under Switch the person picks at each Accept, back to work preselected; D4 a research phase may go on to a
proposal in the same job, and each step is the person's pick at Accept.

**A fork on its question** (issue #570). Owner report: a fork made from a question showed nowhere on it, so it looked as
if nothing happened; the question was reminded "still unanswered", answered directly, and the same feedback given again in
the fork's review, whose acceptance then delivered nothing. The fork and its question are now linked both ways.
`QuestionView.forks` lists the jobs forked from the question (`forksOf`, `src/questions/stale.ts`): each one's kind, note,
job status, `running`, and its review item and status once written; the card shows each as a line ("Proposal in
progress: <note>", its status, a link to its section or, before it wrote one, to the queue). While a fork of a kind runs,
a second fork of that kind is refused (`refusal(q, to, mode)`, 409) and not offered; a switch, or a fork of the other
kind, still is. While any fork of it runs, the question is not reminded (`renotify` checks `forkRuns`, as `expire` does,
and looks again a period later, so a fork that ended without a decision lets the reminders resume). The question can still
be answered directly: inside the settling tx (`forksOnAnswered`, called by the engine's `onAnswered`) each running fork
keeps the answer (`forkOf.answered { answer, by, at }`), and the parent's answer carries `forkRunningBrief` — the fork
still runs, its result no longer comes to it, and its reviewer is told so. The fork is told the answer once
(`forkResume`, at its next start: a fresh start by `forkBrief`, a resume before what it resumes with; `answered.told`). A
fork's review item carries `forkQuestion` (the question's status now, and who answered it), and the item says that
accepting it delivers nothing; `job.fork_resolved` carries `question`, the question's status at the decision. A fork made
from the card toasts "Proposal forked" or "Research forked" with a link, and the jobs and the review section are read
again. No schema change: `answered` is in the fork's body.

Tests: `test/integration/phase-shifts.test.ts` (switch and back to work; research then proposal then end; `then` only in
a switched phase; fork, its link, priority and accepted result answering the parent; a rejected forked proposal; the
settings live; refusals; suggestions by a job and by levels, allowed and not; issue #570: the fork on its question and a
second one refused, no reminders while it runs, a direct answer told to the parent, the fork and the reviewer),
`test/ui/phase-shifts.test.ts`, `test/job-rules/job-rules.test.ts` (a fork's brief with the answer),
`test/plugins/claude-cli-prompt.test.ts` (the level may suggest).

## The TypeSafe API key in the vault's system scope (issue #657, 2026-10-10)

The Jev page said "Jev is off until HOPPER_USER_<ID>_TYPESAFE_API_KEY is set", and nobody could turn Jev on from the
UI. The owner's rule: the hopper keeps its own secrets, entered in the UI and kept in its database, never read from a
variable or a mounted file. The owner's direction on the issue: keep the key in the vault, in a **system scope** that no
job, worker or sandbox can mint, ask for or read, enforced through OpenFGA; the vault's sealer and master key, not a
table or column of its own. Moving the hopper's other secrets into the system scope is issue #658, not this one.

- **The system scope** (`src/domain/vault.ts` `SYSTEM_SECRETS`, `src/vault/system.ts`). A **system secret** is a row of
  `vault_secrets` named `system/<name>` (`system/typesafe-api-key`; since issue #673 `system/artifact-content-key`), a name no vault secret can take (the
  name rule has no `/`). It is sealed by the hopper's sealer under `HOPPER_MASTER_KEY`, bound to `vault:<id>/value`, as
  a vault secret is — under the master key even when the vault's own secrets are under a KMS's data key or in a vault
  container, so only the hopper opens one, in its own process, when it uses it. It is none of the vault's own
  secrets: `GET /api/vault` lists none, `remove` there does not find one, a template that names one is refused (400),
  the rating and a box's scope leave one out, the vault's reseal skips one (the system scope reseals its own), and a
  job's ask for one (`POST /client/vault`) is refused and recorded (`vault.refused`). No schema change: a new row
  name in an existing table. The build before lists such a row in the vault as a plain secret; it gives it to no job,
  since no template holds it.
- **Access** (`src/authz/model.ts`, `Access.decideSystemSecret`). The default model gains `type system_secret` with
  `owner: [user]`, `admin: [user]`, `can_change: owner or admin` and `can_read: owner`. At each ask the hopper tells
  OpenFGA, as contextual tuples for that check only, the user the secret is kept for (`owner`) and, for an admin's UI
  session, that user as `admin`: no stored tuple says either. A change asks `can_change` of `user:<id>`; a job's ask
  asks `can_read` of `job:<user>/<id>`, which the default model never allows. A job's ask is refused even when an
  edited model allows it. OpenFGA not set up, not reached, or a model without these relations: every change is
  denied (403), never a mint. A model the hopper wrote and nobody edited is upgraded to this build's default.
- **The key** (`src/minor-decisions/typesafe-key.ts`). `set` trims the value, checks it once against TypeSafe — one
  Choice over two options through `jev_pick.py`, the call Jev makes, with the key offered (`JevChooser.check`) —, then
  keeps it in place of any key kept. A key the check fails is not kept: 400, TypeSafe's error with the key masked
  (`maskSecret`, `src/secrets/mask.ts`). `remove` deletes it. Jev's readers ask for the key at each decision: the
  decider calls (`createJev({ key })`) and the gate router (the user's runtime secrets answer `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`
  with the key kept, never the variable), so a set, a replace or a removal applies from the next decision, without a
  restart. Events: `vault.secret_set` and `vault.secret_removed`, name `system/typesafe-api-key`, with who; never the
  key. A failed pick's error (`minor_decision.picked`) masks the key too.
- **The view** (`TypesafeKeyView`, `typesafeKey` in `GET /api/minor-decisions`): `set`, the key's last 4 characters
  (`last4`, read from the key at each view), `setAt` and `setBy`; `environment.variable` while the runtime still
  gives the variable; `problem` when no key can be kept or opened (no `HOPPER_MASTER_KEY`). Never the key.
- **The edit** (`POST /ui/api/typesafe-key`, `{ action: 'set', value }` or `{ action: 'remove' }`; least role
  operator, then Access; not cached): answers the view. The Jev page (Settings → Decider) has the field right
  under "Jev is off until a TypeSafe API key is set": a password field the browser does not fill in, Save or Replace,
  and Remove; it shows only "Set — ends in wxyz — set <when> by <who>" or "Not set".
- **The operator CLI** (`hopper typesafe-key`, `set`, `remove`; issue #623's JSON answers): `set` reads the key from
  stdin, never from an argument, so it is in no shell history or process list; an argument is refused.
- **The variable, once.** At each start, while no import is recorded (the user's backfills, `typesafe-key-import`):
  a key the runtime gives as `<secret prefix>TYPESAFE_API_KEY` (or `_FILE`) is kept when none is, unchecked (TypeSafe
  may not be reachable at start), and the log says "imported from the environment into the vault; remove it from the
  environment". Then the import is recorded, and the variable is never read again: a key removed later stays removed.
  While the variable is still set, the Jev page says so.

**Residual risk, stated.** The last 4 characters of the key are shown, as the issue asks. Whoever holds the database
and the master key holds the key, as for every sealed secret.

Tests: `test/integration/typesafe-key.test.ts` (the real daemon and the real Jev with a fake `typesafe_sdk`: save turns
Jev on without a restart; no answer, event, log line or row carries the key; a bad key is not kept and its error is
masked; the one-time import and its note; remove turns Jev off; Access decides; the CLI from stdin),
`test/vault/system-scope.test.ts` (the vault lists none, puts none in a template, gives none to a job, whatever Access
says), `test/authz/model.test.ts`, `test/minor-decisions/jev.test.ts`, `test/ui/minor-decisions.test.ts`.

## The vault's system scope: the hopper's own secrets (issue #658, 2026-10-10)

Before this change the hopper kept its own secrets in four places with four sets of rules: the GitHub connection's
tokens in `connected_accounts` (the token box of issue #441), the webhook signing secrets in `webhooks.secret_sealed`
(the sealer, issue #451), the sign-in realms' secrets in clear in the `sign-in` record (issue #216), and the TypeSafe
API key in the vault's system scope (issue #657). There was no one page, no one audit trail and no one way to replace
one. Now each is a **system secret**, kept, changed, read and audited one way. Owner decision on the issue (the jobs'
hand-off): move all four kinds, including the access token, into the system scope, and make OpenFGA deny any job,
worker or sandbox that asks the vault for one. Since issue #652 no job holds a GitHub token at all: a job's GitHub
goes through the hopper, which reads the token through the vault at each call.

- **Where.** A user's in that user's vault (`vault_secrets`): `typesafe-api-key`, `connected-account.github.access-token`,
  `connected-account.github.refresh-token`, `webhook.<subscription id>.signing-secret`. The whole hopper's in the
  **instance's vault**, a `vault_secrets` table in the instance schema (instance migration 33, a table only):
  `sign-in.<realm>.clientSecret` (oidc, gateway) and `sign-in.<realm>.bindPassword` (ldap). Each a row `system/<name>`,
  sealed by the hopper's sealer under the master key `HOPPER_MASTER_KEY` (issue #659), bound to `vault:<id>/value`, its
  metadata (who, when, its last 4 characters) in the row's body. Never in clear: without the master key (the hopper
  limited) none is kept (503, naming `HOPPER_MASTER_KEY`) or opened, and no old copy is moved; a realm's secret given
  meanwhile stays in the `sign-in` record, as before #658, and a realm whose secret cannot be opened is read as off.
- **One way in** (`src/vault/system.ts`, `SystemSecrets`). `keep` is the only code that writes a value: a set, a
  replace, a GitHub renewal and a webhook rotation; `drop` removes one (a subscription removed, a connection
  disconnected, a realm's secret left out); `migrate` keeps one moved from its old place. `open` is the hopper's read.
  Every part writes through it: `src/connected-accounts/at-rest.ts` (the connection), `src/webhooks/secrets.ts`,
  `src/auth/sealed-secrets.ts` (the sign-in config), `src/minor-decisions/typesafe-key.ts`.
- **Renewals write through the vault with the lock** (`AtRest.swap`). In one transaction: the `connected_accounts` row
  locked (`FOR UPDATE`), the stored refresh token compared with the one the renewal used, then the new pair kept. The
  advisory lock per account (issue #441) still parts processes. So two renewals at once call GitHub once, and the vault
  holds exactly one refresh token, the newest.
- **The sign-in config over the vault** (`sealedSignIn`). Every part reads and writes the sign-in config as before:
  `read` gives each realm its secrets, opened; `write` keeps each secret given (a secret the same as the one kept writes
  nothing), removes each one left out, and stores the record without them, all in one transaction. Its `version` also
  covers when each realm secret last changed, so a secret replaced alone is applied at once and an edit against the
  older version is refused (409). The operator CLI opens the same way with the runtime's key; `config get sign-in` no
  longer prints a secret, and `config set sign-in` checks a record without them as having those the vault holds.
- **The move, once, at start** (`src/users/system-secrets.ts`, `src/users/instance-secrets.ts`). Each old copy is read,
  kept in the vault, opened again and compared, and only then removed: `webhooks.secret_sealed` emptied,
  `connected_accounts` without its tokens (under the account's renewal lock), the `sign-in` record without its secrets
  (before the sign-in config is read). One `vault.secret_migrated` per secret (`name`, `from`), never a value. A start
  with nothing left to move changes nothing. An old copy that cannot be opened (its key is missing) stays where it is,
  said in the log; a connection whose old tokens stay reads unreadable, as before.
- **One audit trail.** `vault.secret_set` (`replaced`; `rotated` when the hopper made or renewed it), `vault.secret_removed`,
  `vault.secret_migrated`, `vault.secret_read` (`by: hopper`, `purpose`: at most once an hour per secret and process,
  `READ_EVENT_EVERY_MS`: the hopper reads the GitHub token at every source poll) and `vault.refused` (a job's ask). The
  instance's events go to every user's log once the runtimes exist, as the update events do. Vault, panel
  **Hopper's own secrets** (`ui/src/views/vault-system.tsx`): each system secret, the user's and the whole hopper's,
  with what it is for, its last 4 characters, who set it and when, where it is changed, and why it
  cannot be opened; then the newest 50 audit entries (`GET /api/vault` `system`: `secrets`, `audit`). Never a value.
  Each keeps its own page for changes: Sources (the connection), Webhooks (replace, rotate), Sign-in (the realm's
  form), Decider (the TypeSafe key).
- **No job, worker or sandbox reads one.** A job's ask (`POST /client/vault`) for any `system/` name asks Access
  `decideSystemSecret` (`system_secret#can_read` of the job), which the default model never allows, and is refused
  (`vault.refused`) whatever it answers; no template may name one and none is minted from. `test/authz/system-secrets.test.ts`
  asks for every kind as a job, as its machine and as a box of an approved template: each denied.
- **The start check** (issue #647, requirement 8 of this issue). Each system secret that cannot be opened logs
  `start check: system secret <name> cannot be opened: …`, naming `HOPPER_MASTER_KEY` when the launch gives none, else
  the key id it was sealed under; the panel says it too. It never asks for a new value.
- **The key stays outside.** The master key comes from the launch (issue #659), never from a vault. With
  `HOPPER_KMS_URL` or `HOPPER_VAULT_URL` the vault's own secrets are under the KMS's data key or in the vault container;
  the system scope stays in the hopper under the master key. The master key's start check counts the system secrets
  of every user's vault and of the instance's (`keptSecrets`).

**A system secret in a vault backend** (requirement 6): "System secrets in a vault backend" below.

**A build before this one on a moved store** (`docs/deploy.md` "Update channels and promotion"): it finds no GitHub
tokens in `connected_accounts` (the connection reads unreadable: reconnect), no webhook secret (replace it), and no
realm secret (a realm that is on and needs one stops that build at start). Builds since issue #527 refuse a store a
newer build migrated anyway.

Tests: `test/integration/system-scope.test.ts` (the real daemon on a store from before: each secret moved, sealed, its
old copy gone, one event each, GitHub, the webhook's signature and the realm still working; a second start changes
nothing; the view and its audit, no value), `test/vault/system-secrets.test.ts` (keep, rotate, the read event once an
hour, nothing kept without the master key, a new key sealing again, the start check, the move), `test/authz/system-secrets.test.ts` (OpenFGA
denies a job, its machine and its box every kind), `test/vault/system-scope.test.ts` (every kind refused to a job),
`test/connected-accounts/rotation.test.ts` (a renewal through the vault keeps exactly one refresh token),
`test/auth/sealed-secrets.test.ts` (the sign-in config over the vault), `test/ui/vault-system.test.ts`.

### System secrets in a vault backend (issue #658, part 2, 2026-10-10)

Requirement 6: the vault backends (issue #585) cover system secrets too, when the owner turns that on; the default stays
the hopper's own vault, with no outside system. Two facts shape it. A backend only reads, and reads asynchronously. The
hopper reads its own secrets synchronously (`SystemSecrets.open`: the webhook signature, Jev, the sign-in config).

**Owner decision on the issue (option 1), with its reasons.**

- **Which.** Only a secret a person gives, of one user: the **TypeSafe API key** and a **webhook's signing secret**
  (`systemBackendRefusal`, `src/domain/vault.ts`). These stay in the hopper's own vault, each refused (400) with why:
  - the GitHub connection's access and refresh tokens: the hopper writes them at each renewal, and a backend only reads;
  - the artifact content key (issue #673): the hopper makes it;
  - each sign-in realm's secret: it is the whole hopper's (the instance's vault), and a vault backend is one user's
    plugin, so the instance has none.
- **Held in memory: the keeps-no-copy rule, relaxed for the hopper's own use.** "Vault backends" says the hopper reads a
  backend's value at the moment of use and keeps no copy, not even in a cache. That stays true for a vault secret
  delivered to a box. For a system secret kept in a backend, the hopper reads the value at start, when a person sets it,
  and every 5 minutes (`BACKEND_READ_EVERY_MS`), and holds it in its own process memory, so each synchronous read finds
  it. Never in the database, an event, a log line or an answer: the row keeps only `backend: { name, reference }` and an
  empty sealed value. The process already holds the master key, which opens every sealed secret, so the copy in memory
  adds no reach. A value changed in the backend applies within 5 minutes; a restart reads it at once.
- **No stale or local copy.** A read that fails (the backend gone from the plugins config, unable to run, unreachable, or
  without the reference) drops the value held: the secret cannot be opened until a read succeeds. A webhook then has no
  secret to sign with (`secretProblem`), Jev is off. One warning per new reason, naming the secret, the backend and the
  reference; Vault shows the same as its `problem`. Before its first read (the start), it cannot be opened
  either: "not read from vault backend … yet".
- **The start check** (requirement 7's shape). Once the plugin host runs, each one kept in a backend is read; each that
  cannot be read logs `start check: system secret <name> cannot be read from vault backend <backend> at <reference>:
  <why>`. A sealed one's start check (`check`) passes over it, and so does the reseal: there is nothing sealed.
- **Set** (`POST /ui/api/vault` `system-in-backend`: `name`, `backend`, `reference`; admin, then Access
  `system_secret#can_change`). Refused (400) for another system secret, a backend the plugins config does not name, a
  reference its `check` refuses, or a value the backend cannot read now; 404 for a webhook that is not there. It is read
  once, and only then kept: `vault.secret_set` with `backend`, never a value. Vault, panel **Hopper's own
  secrets**: such a secret shows "kept in vault backend X at R, held in memory only" and its last 4 characters (from the
  value held), and a person changes or sets it with **Keep in a vault backend**.
- **Rotation.** The hopper cannot rotate one a backend keeps: Webhooks → Rotate answers 409, "the signing secret is
  kept in vault backend X at R: rotate it there, or replace it here to keep it in the hopper again"; `keep` with
  `rotated` refuses it the same way. A value a person gives on its own page (Webhooks → Replace, the Jev page) keeps it
  in the hopper again, sealed, as `set` does for a vault secret.
- **Persisted state.** No migration: a row with an empty sealed value and `backend` is the shape tenant migration 31
  already allows. The build before reads such a row as a system secret it cannot open: the webhook has no secret to sign
  with, and Jev is off, until it is replaced or this build runs.

**Not built:** a backend that writes (it would let the GitHub tokens and the artifact key go there); vault backends of the
whole hopper (for the sign-in realms' secrets); a TypeSafe check of a key kept in a backend (the Jev page's check runs on
a key typed in; a wrong key in the backend shows at Jev's next pick).

Tests: `test/vault/system-backends.test.ts` (with a fake at the `VaultBackend` port: set, the read once, no value in the
store, an event or a log line; a refresh reads the new value and a failed read drops the held one; a fresh start before
its read and a backend gone: none can be opened; rotation refused, a value given keeps it in the hopper again; the
refusals; the reseal and the start check pass over it), `test/integration/system-backends.test.ts` (the real daemon and a
real HashiCorp Vault: a webhook signed with the value Vault holds, no value in the database; rotate refused; a start
that cannot read names the secret and the backend; a GitHub token refused), `test/ui/vault-system.test.ts`.

## Shared secrets (issue #718, part 1, 2026-10-10)

Owner request (issue #718, item 3): besides each user's own vault secrets, a scope any agent can read under OpenFGA, so
a credential many users' jobs need has no copy per user. It extends #658's instance's vault, but it is not the system
scope: a system secret is the hopper's own and never given to a job; a **shared secret** exists to be given to jobs.
Per-user stays the default; sharing is the hopper's admin's explicit act.

- **Where.** A row `shared/<name>` of the instance's vault (`vault_secrets` in the instance schema, instance migration
  33: no migration), sealed by the hopper's sealer under the master key, bound to `vault:<id>/value`; its metadata — the
  scope line, the **readers**, who set it and when — in the row's body. Under the master key always: never in a vault
  container or under a KMS's data key, which are per user. Without the master key none is kept (503) or opened.
  `src/vault/shared.ts` (`SharedSecrets`) is the only code that writes or opens one; its events are the instance's
  (`vault.secret_set`, `vault.secret_removed`, the row name, who; never a value), which reach every user's log.
- **Who changes one.** Only the instance admin: `POST /ui/api/vault/shared` (`set` — name, value, optional `scope`,
  optional `readers`; `remove`) behind the `instance` guard, and `hopper vault set <name> --shared [--reader <user id>]...`
  / `hopper vault remove <name> --shared` from the operator CLI (its session's realm `cli` is an instance admin's). Access
  is asked too (`shared_secret#can_change`, the admin told as a contextual tuple): a model edit can take the right away.
- **Who reads one.** A job, through the box client's helper, as any vault secret: `$HOPPER_SECRET get shared/<name>`
  (the client takes the `shared/` form). The hopper answers it in its own process, in front of the user's vault wherever
  that runs (`withSharedSecrets`, `src/vault/shared-delivery.ts`): the same box checks as a delivery (`boxAsk`), then the
  box's template must give it — the template names `shared/<name>` in its scope and a person approved that, as for any
  secret (`save-template` refuses one the hopper does not hold) —, then Access: `shared_secret#can_read` of
  `user:<the job's user>`, the readers told at each ask as contextual tuples — `user:*` when the admin named none, else
  each user named. Delivered: `vault.delivered` in the job's user's log; refused: `vault.refused` with why. Never minted
  from: a minting credential stays a user's own.
- **The model** gains `type shared_secret` (`admin: [user]`, `reader: [user, user:*]`, `can_change: admin`,
  `can_read: reader`). Its relations are checked apart (`sharedSecretGaps`): a model edited before them denies every
  shared secret, naming the gap, and still decides mints; a model the hopper wrote is replaced by this build's default.
- **Seen by everyone.** `GET /api/vault` carries `shared` (each one's row name, scope, readers, who and when) for every
  user, so a template can name one; Vault shows the panel **Shared secrets**, with **Share secret** and
  **Remove** for the instance admin, and the template form offers the shared names beside the user's own secrets.
- **One reseal.** `resealRows` (`src/vault/reseal.ts`) seals again, on a key rotation, the user vault's own rows, the
  system scope's and the shared secrets' (at start, with the instance's system secrets).

**Residual risk, stated.** With no readers named, every user's job on an approved template that names it may read it:
each user's own template approval is the gate, as for that user's own secrets. The readers are user ids, not checked
against the users the hopper has: an id of no user matches no one.

**Built since (issue #718).** The read-only check before a requested template's first box (item 5): "The read-only
check". The token-scoped API (item 4): "API tokens". A template request over the API: "Template requests over the API".

Tests: `test/integration/shared-secrets.test.ts` (the real daemon, a real joined box and the real CLI: shared and listed
for every user, sealed in the instance's vault, refused to an admin of their own user only; given to a job only once the
template naming it is approved; refused when the readers leave the job's user out, and after removal; the CLI's
`--shared`), `test/authz/shared-secrets.test.ts` (every user reads with no readers named, only the named ones else, only
an admin changes; a model without the type denies and names the gap), `test/ui/vault-shared.test.ts`.

## API tokens (issue #718, part 2, 2026-10-11)

Owner decision on the issue (item 4), which replaces the narrower one before it: **everything an admin can do is available
over the API**, guarded by tokens. A user acts through the API with a short-lived token scoped to what they may do, and
OpenFGA decides; no action is UI-only. An agent acting for a user (Grok Bot) is one caller of this same API. Jobs keep no
write door of their own: a job asks the hopper (no `/job/vault` or `/job/sandbox` routes under a job's proxy token).
This supersedes "a mutating API token is a second door" (issue #374, "Operator actions from the CLI"): the door is the
same one, `POST /ui/api/*`; the token is one more kind of session at it.

- **What it is.** An **API token** is a UI session row (`ui_sessions`, instance migration 35: `kind` `api`, `label`) —
  so its identity, user, role, hashed storage, ends and reconcile are the session's. Its token is `hopper_at_` and 64 hex
  digits; only its SHA-256 is kept. It lives the admin's **API-token lifetime** (issue #881: 5–15 minutes, default 10), or
  `minutes` less, a fixed end; the sign-in config's idle timeout applies too. Its id, as listed and revoked, is the start
  of the hash; a grant's token is known to Access by its grant's id.
- **How it is sent.** `Authorization: Bearer hopper_at_…`, on every `GET /api/*` and `POST /ui/api/*`. An API token is
  accepted only there and a UI session only in `x-hopper-session` (`sessionIn`, `src/http/ui/guard.ts`): neither stands in
  for the other. A mutation with an API token needs no Origin and no `Sec-Fetch-Site`: those defend the UI session, a
  credential a page can make the browser send; no browser sends `Authorization` by itself, and a cross-site page may set it
  only through a CORS preflight the hopper never allows. The JSON body is still required. The `hopper_at_` prefix keeps
  the API door from taking one for a GitHub token and asking GitHub about it: one that names no live session is 401
  (`the API token is unknown, revoked or expired`), on loopback too.
- **What it may do.** What a UI session of its user with its role may do: the route's least role (`allow`, the
  `instance` guard) as for any session, then Access (`decideApiToken`): `user:<id>` must have, on `api_token:<user>/<id>`
  (the user told as its `owner` at each ask), the relation of the role the request needs — a read `can_view`, an
  operator's route `can_operate`, an admin's `can_administer`. The default gives each to the owner; a user narrows what
  their tokens may do by editing the model in Users & access → Access. OpenFGA out of reach: 503, never a 401 or 403. The
  relations are checked apart (`apiTokenGaps`): a model edited before them denies every API token, naming the gap, and
  still decides mints; a model the hopper wrote is replaced by this build's default. A UI session is not asked of Access.
- **Its role.** At most its minter's: the mint takes `role` (default the minter's) and refuses one above. A reconcile
  (start, a sign-in change) lowers it with its identity's role, never raises it, and ends it when its realm is gone or
  grants no role: turning a realm off closes every door at once.
- **Who mints one.**
  - Refreshed from a **grant** a person minted (issue #881, "Grants and refresh tokens" below): from their UI session
    (Settings → **API tokens**, `POST /ui/api/api-tokens` `mint`) or the operator CLI (`hopper token mint`). This replaces
    the one-hour token a person minted directly: a person now mints once, and the agent refreshes.
  - An agent with no UI session, by exchange: `POST /ui/auth/api-token` with `Authorization: Bearer` a sign-in the API
    door accepts (a gateway realm's JWT; a GitHub token of a user's connected account), checked as the door checks it
    (`createApiDoor`, `src/http/tenants.ts`): the token is minted for the user that identity is linked to, as that
    identity, its role at most the one the sign-in config grants. The door signs nobody new in (401). This is how an agent
    authenticates as the user it acts for and keeps acting unattended: a new short-lived token per need, from a credential
    the user's identity provider issues, never a long-lived hopper secret.
  - Never another API token (403): an API token cannot outlive the sign-in behind it by chaining.
  Every mint asks Access for the role it gives, and drops the token again when refused (403; 503 out of reach). Each
  mint is a log line (id, label, user, role, minutes), never the token.
- **Who acted.** A person's action records `via` `api` (`ActingPerson`, issue #623) beside `ui` and `cli`, with the
  minter's identity as the person.
- **Parity, kept.** Every mutation is a `POST /ui/api/*` route behind `allow` or `instance` (AGENTS.md), so a new UI
  action is an API action the day it lands. `test/integration/api-tokens.test.ts` walks every `POST /ui/api/*` path the
  API reference names (which must match the routes, or the daemon does not start) with a viewer's token: each refusal is
  the role's, never the session's or the Origin's.
- **Not given to a token.** A login's device code (`GET /api/logins`): answered only to a UI session, as before.

**Residual risk, stated.** Whoever holds a token acts as its user, with its role, until it ends, it is revoked, or Access
says no: the API-token lifetime at most (15 minutes). Whoever holds a grant's refresh token acts as long as the grant
lives ("Grants and refresh tokens"). A token handed to an agent is a bearer credential like any other; the label and the log line say
whose. A GitHub token on the exchange is any token of the account (as on the API door): GitHub says whose it is, not
which app it is for. The build before this one reads `Authorization` only as the API door, so on a downgrade it would ask
GitHub about an API token sent to it (a token it then refuses); the token is useless there and ends within the hour.

**Box actions** (issue #795): a box action needs a box token too ("Box tokens" below).

**Scopes.** A grant's token uses only the routes its scopes cover (issue #881, "Grants and refresh tokens"); an exchanged
token has no scopes: its role and Access bound it, as before. (The rest of issue #718 is built under issue #716: "Templates
on request", "Tools assembled per run", "The read-only check"; its real-environment part is carried on #715.)

Tests: `test/integration/api-tokens.test.ts` (a person mints, an agent sets a secret, saves and approves a template and
launches a box with the token alone; every route takes a token; the role cap, the hour, no chained mint; revoke; an unknown
token never reaches GitHub; Access denying `can_administer`; no OpenFGA, no mint; the gateway exchange; the CLI),
`test/http/ui-sessions.test.ts` (the token's own end, its list and revoke, a reconcile never raises its role, renewal
without a gateway check), `test/authz/model.test.ts` (the gaps), `test/ui/api-tokens.test.ts`.

## Box tokens: the auth boundary for box actions (issue #795, 2026-10-11)

Owner decision on the issue: the API token alone may read, hold and cancel; an action that runs on a box needs a **box
token** — a separate capability, off by default, minted only by a person from a UI session, never by the sign-in exchange.
So the token Grok Bot exchanges its own sign-in for, the one it keeps through the tunnel, cannot start work on a box.
When it must, a person gives it a short-lived box token.

- **What a box action is.** A route that starts a job, runs a command, approves or merges work, updates the hopper or a
  client, or changes the work on a machine. The list is `BOX_ACTIONS` (`src/http/ui/box-actions.ts`), each with its kind;
  a route not on it is no box action. Reads (every `GET /api/*`), holds (park, keep a job from its lane, mark a question
  seen, close or dismiss it), cancels, rejects and settings are not box actions.

  | Kind | Routes (`POST`) |
  |------|-----------------|
  | start a job | `/ui/api/jobs/:id/approve`, `rerun`, `rework`, `requeue`, `gate-pass`, `research`, `propose`; `/ui/api/sources/:name/intake`; `/ui/api/repo-checks/queue`; `/ui/api/failures/:id/retry`; `/ui/api/failures/problems/:id/release`; `/ui/api/questions/:id/research`, `propose`; each review decision but Reject all (`/ui/api/research/:id/accept`, `dig-deeper`, `steer`; `/ui/api/proposals/:id/accept`, `more-paths`, `steer`) |
  | run a command | `/ui/api/blast-radius/discover`; `/ui/api/plugins` (an instance's options may hold a command) |
  | approve or merge work | `/ui/api/pull-requests/merge` (Close PR is not: it runs nothing) |
  | update the hopper or a client | `/ui/api/update` (a client updates with the hopper); `/ui/api/plugin-store` |
  | change work on a machine | `/ui/api/questions/:id/answer`, `correct` (typed into the job's pane); `/ui/api/jobs/:id/end-wait`, `notes` (typed into the job's session, issue #997), `keep-original`, `accept-new-text`; `/ui/api/logins/:id/new-code`; `/ui/api/machines`, `machines/join`, `machines/sandbox`; `/ui/api/windows-hosts` (issue #731); `/ui/api/lanes/apply`, `lanes/undo` |

  A new route that does any of these goes on the list in the same change. `test/integration/box-tokens.test.ts` walks
  every `POST /ui/api/*` path with a token that is no box token: each listed one is refused for want of a box token, and
  no other is.
- **What a box token is.** An API token whose session row has `box` (`ui_sessions.box`, instance migration 36; every
  token from before is no box token). Minted with `{ action: 'mint', label, role?, minutes?, box: true }` at
  `POST /ui/api/api-tokens`, from a UI session only (an API token never mints one), or with the Box token box in
  Users & access → API tokens. The exchange (`POST /ui/auth/api-token`) refuses `box` (400): a sign-in the hopper only checks is
  not a person at the UI. Listed with `box` (`GET /api/api-tokens`); the card says "box token". Its role, end and revoke
  are those of any API token.
- **How it is decided.** At a box action with an API token, after the role (`apiTokenAnswer`,
  `src/http/ui/api-tokens.ts`): a token that is no box token is refused (403, `this is a box action: it needs a box
  token…`) without asking OpenFGA; a box token is asked `api_token#can_run_on_box` (`decideBoxAction`), with its owner
  told as `owner` and as `box_runner` — the hopper tells `box_runner` for a box token only. The default model:
  `define box_runner: [user]`, `define can_run_on_box: box_runner and owner`. A user narrows it further in Settings →
  Access. A mint with `box` asks it too, and drops the token when refused. The relations are checked apart
  (`apiTokenBoxGaps`): a model edited before them refuses every box action, naming the gap, and decides everything else; a
  model the hopper wrote is replaced by this build's default. A UI session is never asked: the person is there.
- **Why not per-action confirmation.** A held action waiting on a person in the UI (path 3 on the issue) was not chosen:
  the box token keeps an agent able to act unattended for as long as a person allows. Since issue #881 a box token is
  the API token of a box grant, so that is as long as the grant lives, within its scopes.

**Residual risk, stated.** A box token in an agent's hands does every box action its role and its grant's scopes allow
until it ends or is revoked. The boundary is the route list together with the scopes: a route that runs work on a box but
is missing from the list is open to an exchanged token of the role, and to a grant's token only when its scopes name it
(issue #881: a scope is named from the route, so a new route is in no existing grant's scopes but `*` and its area's `*`). A downgrade to the build before reads no `box` column, so there every API token may again do
what its role allows.

Tests: `test/integration/box-tokens.test.ts` (no box token: reads, holds and cancels pass, every box action is refused; a
box token launches a sandbox box; the exchange never mints one; every listed route exists and only those ask; a model
without the relations refuses box actions only), `test/http/ui-sessions.test.ts` (the flag is kept and listed),
`test/authz/model.test.ts` (the gaps), `test/ui/api-tokens.test.ts` (the card's line).

## Grants and refresh tokens (issue #881, 2026-10-12)

Owner decision on the issue, which supersedes the one-hour, no-refresh limit of "Box tokens": a person mints a scoped
**grant** once, and the agent (Grok Bot) keeps acting unattended with no new mint. Modelled on OAuth 2.0 refresh-token
rotation (RFC 6749, OAuth 2.0 Security BCP RFC 9700). UI sessions are unchanged.

- **A grant.** Minted only by a person: `POST /ui/api/api-tokens` `{ action: 'mint', label, holder?, role?, scopes,
  box?, days?, minutes? }` from a UI session (Users & access → API tokens), or `hopper token mint` (the operator CLI's session).
  Never by an API token (403). Its role is at most its minter's; Access is asked for it (and for `can_run_on_box` when
  `box`) at the mint, which ends it again when refused. It lives `days` (1–365, default 90) at most, or with
  `days: null` has no fixed end — an admin's only, answered with a `warning` —, and dies `GRANT_IDLE_DAYS` (30) after its
  last refresh. A row of `api_grants` (instance migration 37: its body as JSON), its refresh tokens rows of
  `api_grant_tokens` (only their SHA-256, a rotated one kept for reuse detection until its grant goes), and each API
  token a `ui_sessions` row with its `grant_id`. The mint answers the grant (`view`), its first API token and its refresh
  token, once, `cache-control: no-store`.
- **The refresh token.** `hopper_rt_` and 64 hex digits. Its one use: `POST /ui/auth/token/refresh` `{ refresh }`,
  which answers a new API token and a new refresh token, and spends the one sent. Under `/ui/auth/`, beside the
  exchange, and not `/api/token/refresh` as the issue wrote: `/api/` is the read door (GET, a session across the LAN,
  the API door's `Authorization`), and the refresh carries its credential in its body; it has the sign-in limit per
  caller, as the exchange, and passes the tunnel's edge with the same limit.
  - **Rotation.** Each refresh is one transaction: the sent token marked rotated, its successor stored.
  - **Grace.** A refresh token sent again within `REFRESH_GRACE_MS` (30 s) of its rotation is answered the same pair,
    kept in memory, so a refresh retried after a network blip loses nothing. After a restart within those 30 s the pair
    is gone: the retry is refused (401) and the grant stands.
  - **Reuse detection.** A spent refresh token sent after the grace ends the whole grant at once, with every API token
    of it: `api_grant.reuse_detected` (with who sent it), then `api_grant.revoked` reason `reuse-detected`, and a log
    line. A notifier or webhook subscribed to the event tells the owner.
  - **Rights, live.** Each refresh asks the sign-in config for the minter's role now: none ends the grant
    (`realm-changed`), a lower one lowers it, a higher one never raises it. A sign-in change applies to grants as to
    sessions (`reconcile`, at start and after Settings → Sign-in). Access is asked at every use of its tokens, as of any
    API token. The CLI's identity is no realm's, so a grant the CLI minted keeps the role it was minted with.
  - **Not peppered.** The issue allowed a hash with a pepper from the vault. The refresh token is 32 random bytes, kept
    as its SHA-256 as every token the hopper mints; a pepper adds nothing a guess could use against 256 random bits, and
    would tie every refresh to the master key.
- **API tokens of a grant.** Opaque, a session row as any API token (the issue's "opaque with a hashed lookup"): no
  signing key, no `kid`, no denylist; revoking a grant drops its rows, so it stops at once, not after the lifetime.
  They live the **API-token lifetime**: the instance admin's setting, `POST /ui/api/api-tokens/settings
  { tokenMinutes }` or Users & access → API tokens, 5–15 minutes, default 10, a key of the instance settings; a change applies
  to the tokens issued after it (`api_tokens.settings_changed`). A grant may ask for less at its mint (`minutes`,
  5–15, never above the setting); the setting lowered below it wins. They are not listed apart: the grant is.
- **Scopes** (`src/domain/token-scopes.ts`). Named from the route, so no route is left without one: `GET
  /api/<area>/…` needs `<area>:read`, `POST /ui/api/<area>/…/<act>` needs `<area>:<act>` (its last fixed segment),
  `POST /ui/api/<area>` needs `<area>:edit`. A grant holds `<area>:<act>`, `<area>:*`, `*:<act>` or `*`; a mint refuses
  a pattern that is malformed or covers no route (400). Checked at every use of a grant's token, before Access: a read in
  the tenancy hook, a mutation in its guard. Deny by default: a route its scopes do not cover, or one that names no scope,
  is 403 naming the scope it needs. `GET /api/api-tokens` lists every scope the routes need, from the API reference.
  - **Not OpenFGA relations.** The issue asked for scopes as OpenFGA relations. A relation per scope would grow the model
    with every route, and a model edited before a route would deny it with a gap. The scope list is the grant's, checked
    by the hopper; OpenFGA keeps deciding the role (`can_view|can_operate|can_administer`) and the box
    (`can_run_on_box`) at each use, with the grant's id as the token's id — so a user still narrows one grant in Settings
    → Access. A route outside a grant's scopes never reaches OpenFGA.
- **Box.** A box grant's tokens are box tokens: a box action needs the box flag, the scope, and `can_run_on_box`.
- **Revoke.** `{ action: 'revoke', id }` ends a grant (or an exchanged token) with its API tokens at once;
  `{ action: 'revoke-all' }` ends every grant and token of the user. Settings lists each grant: holder, role, scopes, when
  it was made, last used (its last refresh, and from where, as the sign-in limit counts callers), its end, Revoke,
  Revoke all.
- **Events.** Each mint, refresh, reuse and end is an event of the user's: `api_grant.minted`, `api_grant.refreshed`,
  `api_grant.reuse_detected`, `api_grant.revoked` (reasons `revoked`, `revoked-all`, `reuse-detected`, `expired-idle`,
  `expired-absolute`, `realm-changed`, `refused`). Never a token. "Notified" is the notifiers' and webhooks' that
  subscribe to them; nothing else is sent.
- **The exchange stays.** An agent with no grant may still exchange its sign-in for one API token (`POST
  /ui/auth/api-token`): no refresh token, no scopes, no box, the API-token lifetime at most.
- **Migration.** Tables and a column (instance migration 37). Every API token there is runs to its own end, an hour at
  most; nothing is migrated, and none was a grant. The build before reads a grant's API token as an API token of its own
  (it has no scope check) until it ends, 15 minutes at most, and never reads a grant.

**Residual risk, stated.** A refresh token is a long-lived bearer credential: whoever holds it acts as the grant, within
its scopes and its minter's live rights, until the grant ends, it is revoked, or the holder's next refresh finds it spent
(then the grant ends). The agent keeps it in its own secret store and must replace it at each refresh. Reuse detection
needs the legitimate holder to refresh after a thief: a thief who refreshes first and keeps refreshing holds the grant
until the holder's next refresh ends it. The scope names a route's area and act, not an object: `questions:answer` answers
any question of the user. A grant bound to its agent's key ("Sender binding" below) closes the theft of a token alone;
a limited grant ("Grant limits" below) acts only on the repositories and job sources it names.

The follow-ups of issue #892 are built: "Grants by device approval", "Sender binding" and "Grant limits" below.

Tests: `test/http/api-grants.test.ts` (mint, rotation, grace, reuse detection, a restart within the grace, idle and fixed
ends, no fixed end, the lifetime and its setting, rights at each refresh, a sign-in change, revoke and revoke all),
`test/integration/token-grants.test.ts` (the issue's flow over HTTP: a box grant for Grok Bot refreshed again and again,
in scope and out, the retry, the events; no box flag; revoke and revoke all; the mint's checks; the setting's bounds),
`test/domain/token-scopes.test.ts`, `test/integration/api-tokens.test.ts`, `test/integration/box-tokens.test.ts`,
`test/ui/api-tokens.test.ts`.

### Grants by device approval (issue #892, 2026-10-16)

The first part of issue #892, a follow-up of #881: an agent gets a grant with no token pasted into it. On the model of the
OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant (RFC 8628). Sender binding is the second part ("Sender binding" below); per-grant
repository and job source limits the third ("Grant limits" below).

- **The ask.** `POST /ui/auth/device-grant`, with no credential: the grant the agent wants, in a mint's fields (`label`,
  `holder`, `role`, `scopes`, `preset`, `box`, `days`, `minutes`, `deny`). It answers a **device code** (`hopper_dc_` and
  64 hex digits, which the agent keeps) and a **user code** (`BCDF-GHJK`: eight letters of twenty, no vowels, so no word is
  spelled and none reads as a digit), `verificationPath` (`/#users-access/api-tokens`) and `verificationPathComplete` (with
  the code), `expiresAt` (`DEVICE_GRANT.minutes`, 10) and `interval` (5 s). Only the device code's SHA-256 is kept.
  The paths are the hopper's own: the agent knows the URL it called, and the hopper builds no URL from a Host header.
- **The approval.** A signed-in person enters the user code in Users & access → API tokens (Approve a device; case, spaces and
  dashes do not count), or opens the link, which looks it up at once: `GET /api/api-tokens/device/:code` shows the ask and
  who sent it (as the sign-in limit counts callers), never the device code. Approve is `POST /ui/api/api-tokens`
  `{ action: 'approve-device', code }`: the ask is checked as that person's own mint (`checked`, the role at most theirs,
  the scopes, the preset, `days: null` an admin's only, a delegate's `deny`), so a refusal is the person's to read (400,
  403). Deny is `deny-device`. An API token may approve none (403, as a mint): an agent never approves a grant. The CLI:
  `hopper token device|approve|deny <code>`.
- **The poll.** `POST /ui/auth/device-grant/poll` `{ deviceCode }`: `{ state: 'waiting', interval, expiresAt }` until a
  person answers; then once, and the request ends — approved: the grant is minted now (`granted`), Access asked for its
  role and box flag as at a mint, and the answer is a mint's (`ApiGrantMinted`) with `state: 'granted'`; denied: 403.
  After that, or when it ended, the device code is unknown (401). The grant is minted at the poll, not at the approval,
  so an approval nobody collects leaves no grant behind.
- **Kept in memory.** `src/http/ui/device-grants.ts`: requests by the device code's hash, each ends `DEVICE_GRANT.minutes`
  after it was made, approved or not; at most `DEVICE_GRANT.most` (50) wait at once (429 beyond). A restart drops them
  all, and the agent asks again: an ask is cheap, and a stored one would be a credential in the database for nothing.
- **Limits.** The ask and the poll share the sign-in limit per caller (20 a minute): a poll each interval keeps under it.
  Through the tunnel both pass (`throughTheTunnel`); the ask counts as a token route (5 a minute), the poll does not.
- **No slow-down answer.** RFC 8628 answers `slow_down` to a poll faster than the interval. The sign-in limit already
  answers 429 to a caller that polls too fast, so there is no second rule.
- **Events.** None new: the grant's mint is `api_grant.minted`, as any mint. Each ask, approval and denial is a log line,
  never a code but the user code.

**Residual risk, stated.** Anyone who reaches the hopper may ask; the ask holds nothing until a person approves it. The
risk of a device flow is phishing: someone asks, then gets a person to approve their code as if it were the person's
own agent's. The form says to approve only a code from the agent the person runs, and shows who asked and what for. Whoever
holds the device code when the request is approved takes the grant; it is shown to nobody but the agent that asked.

Tests: `test/http/device-grants.test.ts` (the codes, waiting, approve once, deny, the end, the cap),
`test/integration/device-grants.test.ts` (the flow over HTTP and its refresh; deny; the mint's checks at the approval;
no approval by an API token; the CLI), `test/http/tunnel.test.ts`, `test/ui/api-tokens.test.ts`.

### Sender binding (issue #892, part 2, 2026-10-17)

The second part of issue #892: a stolen refresh token, API token or device code alone is not enough. A grant may be
**bound** to a key its agent holds, on the model of DPoP (RFC 9449): then each request that uses the grant carries a
**DPoP proof**, a short JWT the agent signs with that key for that one request, in the `DPoP` header. The hopper keeps
only the key's JWK SHA-256 thumbprint (RFC 7638, `jkt`) in the grant's body; the private key never leaves the agent.

- **Binding.** A grant is bound at its birth or at its first refresh with a proof; once bound it stays bound.
  - A device grant request with a proof on the ask (`POST /ui/auth/device-grant`) binds its grant to the proof's key.
    The person sees "bound to the asking agent's key" before they approve. The poll then needs a proof of that key: a
    device code alone, or with another key's proof, takes nothing (401) and the request stands.
  - A mint names `jkt` (`POST /ui/api/api-tokens` `mint`, `hopper token mint --jkt=<thumbprint>`; a thumbprint can start with `-`, so the CLI takes it after `=`): the thumbprint the agent shows. A
    `jkt` on an ask with a proof must be the proof's (400).
  - An unbound grant's refresh with a proof binds it to the proof's key. The refresh token a person copied to the agent
    is then worth nothing to anyone without the key, from the agent's first refresh on.
- **A refresh** of a bound grant needs a proof of its key (`htm` `POST`, `htu` the refresh URL), else 401 with
  `WWW-Authenticate: DPoP error="invalid_dpop_proof"`. This is checked before reuse detection: a spent refresh token sent
  without the key does not end the grant, so a thief cannot end it either. The answer has `tokenType: 'DPoP'`.
- **Each use of a bound grant's API token**, read or mutation, is `Authorization: DPoP <token>` (a `Bearer` one is
  refused, RFC 9449 §7.1) with a proof of the grant's key whose `ath` is the token's SHA-256. Checked in the tenancy hook
  (`src/http/tenants.ts`), before the scopes and Access; the grant's API tokens made before its binding need the proof too.
- **The proof** (`src/http/ui/dpop.ts`). jose checks the signature with the key in the proof's own header
  (`EmbeddedJWK`: a public key only), `typ` `dpop+jwt`, and an asymmetric algorithm (`DPOP.algorithms`: ES256, ES384,
  EdDSA, Ed25519, RS256, PS256; never `none` or HMAC). The hopper checks the rest of RFC 9449 §4.3: `htm` is the method;
  `htu` names this request's Host and path (a query does not count; `http` or `https`, since behind a proxy or the tunnel
  the hopper sees `http`); `iat` is at most `DPOP.maxAgeS` (60) seconds off the hopper's clock; `jti` was not seen with
  that key while a proof with it is fresh (kept in memory, `DPOP.jtiMost` (10 000) at once; beyond, 401 until one is
  forgotten); `ath` for an API token. A proof that fails is refused even on a route or grant that needs none: it is no
  proof of the request.
- **Not built: the server nonce** (`DPoP-Nonce`, RFC 9449 §8). The 60-second `iat` window and the `jti` cache stand for
  it; a nonce would add a round trip to each refresh and a state the agent must keep.
- **Why jose and not a library of its own.** No maintained Node library checks a DPoP proof as a resource server; jose
  (already the hopper's, by the same author as openid-client) does the JWS part, and the claim checks are a few lines.
- **Migration.** None: `jkt` is a field of the grant's JSON body (`api_grants.body`). The build before reads it as no field:
  there a bound grant's tokens work as bearer tokens again, until the grant ends.
- **Events.** None new: the mint and the refresh are `api_grant.minted` and `api_grant.refreshed`, as before. A refused
  proof is a log line.

**Residual risk, stated.** Binding is optional: an agent that sends no proof keeps a bearer grant, as before. A refresh
token taken before the agent's first refresh can be bound to the thief's key instead; the agent's next refresh then fails,
and the person revokes the grant. To close that gap, bind at the birth (a device grant request with a proof, or `jkt` at
the mint). The key is the agent's to keep safe: whoever holds the key and a token acts as the grant. The `jti` cache is
in memory: a proof seen before a restart can be sent again after it, within its 60 seconds, to the same URL.

Tests: `test/http/dpop.test.ts` (the proof: the key, htm, htu, iat, jti, ath, no proof, a private key, `none`, HMAC, two
headers, the cap), `test/integration/sender-binding.test.ts` (a device grant bound by its ask's proof; a mint with
`jkt`; binding at the first refresh; an unbound grant as before; a mutation; the CLI), `test/http/device-grants.test.ts`,
`test/ui/api-tokens.test.ts`.

### Grant limits (issue #892, part 3, 2026-10-17)

The third part of issue #892: beside its scopes, a grant may name what its tokens act on. The scopes say which routes; the
**limits** say on what: the repositories (`owner/name`) and the job sources (their names) of the work it touches.

- **The mint.** `limits: { repos?, sources? }` on `POST /ui/api/api-tokens` `mint` and on a device grant request (`POST
  /ui/auth/device-grant`), at most `GRANT_LIMITS_MAX` (50) of each; `hopper token mint --repo <owner/name>... --source
  <name>...`; in Users & access → API tokens, two fields under the role. Kept in one form (`normalLimits`): repositories lower
  case (GitHub's names do not care for case), each list sorted and once; two empty lists are no limits. A repository that
  is not `owner/name`, or a source name that is not letters, digits, `. _ : -`, is 400. The person who approves a device
  grant request sees its limits ("only acme/app") before they approve; the grant list shows them too.
- **The targets.** A limited grant's mutation names its **limit targets**: the repository and job source of what it acts
  on, found once the body is read (`src/http/ui/grant-limits.ts`, a table by route):
  - `/ui/api/jobs/:id/…` and `/ui/api/failures/:id/retry`: the job's source and its repository (`job.source`).
  - `/ui/api/questions/:id/…`: the question's job's; `/ui/api/<review section>/:id/…`: the review item's job's.
  - `/ui/api/pull-requests/merge|close|tend`: the job its `jobId` names; `diff`: its `repo`.
  - `/ui/api/sources/:name/intake`: each item named, of that source, with the repository of its key when the key is a
    GitHub issue or pull request URL (`repoOfItemKey`).
  - `/ui/api/direct-jobs`: the source `direct` and its `repo`; `/ui/api/repo-checks/queue`: its `repo`.
- **The check** (`limitRefusal`, `src/domain/grant-limits.ts`, pure). Each target must be in every list the grant names:
  with `repos`, its repository is one of them; with `sources`, its source is. A target with no repository (a job of no
  repository) while the grant names repositories is refused; so is one with no source while it names sources. An act
  that names no target — a route not on the table, such as a setting, or an id that names nothing — is refused too: deny
  by default, as for scopes. Refused is 403 naming the limits and what the act acts on, and a log line. It runs in the
  tenancy hook's `preHandler` (`src/http/tenants.ts`), after the role, the scopes, the box flag and Access, and after the
  action scope (issue #909).
- **Reads are not limited.** A limited grant's `GET /api/…` reads as its scopes allow, all of its user's work: the lists
  (the queue, the sources, Needs you) would each need a filter of their own, and the limit is on what an agent changes.
- **Migration.** None: `limits` is a field of the grant's JSON body (`api_grants.body`). The build before reads it as no
  field: there a limited grant acts on anything its scopes allow, until the grant ends.
- **Events.** None new, and no change to `api_grant.minted`: older builds read the events strictly. The grant list and
  `GET /api/api-tokens` show the limits.

**Residual risk, stated.** The limits hold what an agent changes, not what it reads: a limited grant with `*:read` still
reads every job of its user. A route a later change adds is refused to a limited grant until the table names its targets.
A route on the table finds its job by id at the check: an act whose handler then acts on another object than the one its
path or body names would pass with the named one's targets; the table names only routes whose handler acts on what they
name.

Tests: `test/domain/grant-limits.test.ts` (the one form, the checks of the mint, the targets, item keys),
`test/integration/grant-limits.test.ts` (a grant limited to a repository on a job of it and of another; a route that
names no target; a job source limit on jobs and on intake; a device grant request's limits; the mint's checks; the CLI),
`test/ui/api-tokens.test.ts`.

### The scope registry and presets (issue #909, 2026-10-12)

Owner direction on the issue: an agent must do approvals over the API with a grant, and nobody types scope strings: the
form offers presets as one click, and lays out every permission as a box, in sections by area of work, always open, each
with its plain description and the routes it covers, generated from the registry so a new capability shows up by itself.

- **Every approval already has a scope.** Scopes are named from the routes (above), so intake (`sources:intake`), a held
  job (`jobs:approve`), a job's vault grant ask (`jobs:grant-vault`), an infra plan (`infra-plans:edit`), a vault template
  or credential request (`vault:edit`), a question (`questions:answer`) and a pull request (`pull-requests:merge`) each have
  one. The 403 the issue saw was a grant whose scopes did not name the route, and a token with no box flag at a box
  action. No route is left unscoped: `test/domain/scope-registry.test.ts` holds every route of the API reference to a
  scope in a named section.
- **The registry** (`src/domain/scope-registry.ts`, pure; `src/http/scopes.ts` gives it the API reference's operations
  and `isBoxAction`). One permission per scope: `description` (its routes' summaries), `routes`, `role` (the least of
  theirs), `box`. Sections by area (`SCOPE_SECTIONS`); a job's vault grant is shown under the vault; an area no section
  names goes under **Other**, so it is still listed. `GET /api/scopes` answers it, `scopes:read` for a grant's token;
  `hopper token scopes` prints it.
- **Presets.** `read-only` (`*:read`), `agent-intake` (`*:read sources:intake`, a box grant), `agent-approvals` (`*:read
  sources:intake jobs:approve jobs:grant-vault`, a box grant: infra plans and vault templates stay a person's unless
  ticked), `full-admin` (`*`). A preset is a box grant when its scopes cover a box action. `*:read` covers every read the
  Needs you list makes (`sources`, `vault`, `queue`, `sections`).
- **The mint.** `POST /ui/api/api-tokens` `mint` takes `preset` beside `scopes`: the grant holds both; `box` named wins
  over the preset's. An unknown preset, no scope at all, or a scope that covers no route is 400. `hopper token mint
  --preset <id>`.
- **The form** (`ui/src/views/scope-checklist.tsx`). The presets, each with what it does in plain words; then every
  section with every scope as a box: its description, scope, routes, a "box action" mark and a "needs <role>" mark when
  the grant's role is lower. A preset ticks its boxes and stays a wildcard (`*:read`) until a box it covers is cleared;
  then it gives way to the scopes it covered, less that one. A grant is a box grant when a ticked scope is a box action:
  the form says which; the box flag is no longer a box of its own.
- **Risk guards kept.** A box action still needs the box flag, its scope and `api_token#can_run_on_box`; Access decides
  each use by role. The `agent-approvals` preset leaves infra plans and vault templates out. A high-risk plan and a write
  profile a person confirms ("A person confirms what an agent asks", below).

**Action scopes** (part 2 of #909). A route whose body names one of several actions — a discriminated union, or an
object whose `action` or `kind` is one of a set (`bodyActions`, `src/http/scopes.ts`, read from the operation's zod body)
— has a scope for each action, `<route scope>.<action>` (`vault:edit.approve-template`, `sources:intake.approve`; the
action lower case, any other character a hyphen). The route's scope covers them all, so a grant made before holds what it
held. The registry lists each action's scope right under its route's, with `parent`, its routes as `POST <path>
(<field>: <action>)`, and a description from the action's words and the route's summary; the form indents them, and a
tick of the route's box takes the place of its actions' boxes. Two checks: the door (`grantScopeRefusal`, before the body
is read) lets a grant through when it holds the route's scope or one of its actions'; once the body is read, a
`preHandler` of `installTenancy` (`grantActionRefusal`) needs the scope of the action the body names, or the route's own
when it names none, and refuses with 403 naming that scope. A route with one action (`infra-plans`: approve) has only its
route's scope.

Tests: `test/domain/scope-registry.test.ts`, `test/domain/token-scopes.test.ts`, `test/integration/token-grants.test.ts`
(a grant from a preset; a grant that holds one action of a route), `test/ui/api-tokens.test.ts`,
`test/ui/scope-checklist.test.ts`.

### A person confirms what an agent asks (issue #909, part 3, 2026-10-12)

The issue keeps risk guards: a high-risk or production plan and a write credential need a person's confirmation of the
item, by a tap, not a token the operator mints. So an API token's approval of such an item is never done; it is a
**confirmation ask**, and a person's approval of the item is the confirmation.

- **What needs a person** (`src/domain/confirmation-asks.ts`, pure). An infra plan whose summary is not `low`
  (`planNeedsPerson`: it destroys, touches IAM, prod or data, or has no summary), and a template's profile that does more
  than read (`profileNeedsPerson`: write, sync, apply). A low-risk plan, a read profile, a template's own approval (it
  approves its read profiles only) and every other approval stay the agent's, within its scopes.
- **The ask.** `POST /ui/api/infra-plans` `approve` of such a plan that waits (not approved, no failed check), and `POST
  /ui/api/vault` `approve-profile` of such a profile that waits, from an API token (`kind: api`, a grant's or not): nothing
  is approved. The route answers 202 `{ waiting }`, which says what to approve and that a person does it in the UI. It
  appends `approval.confirmation_asked` (`kind`, `ref`, `words`, `asker` — the API token's label —, and the plan or the
  template and profile; on the plan's job's timeline), unless the item was asked for in the last hour
