Settled without asking, each one place to change: content in Postgres, not a volume (no config file, nothing on the
machine); a content URL's key is a system secret of its owner's, kept across restarts (issue #673); a public link is on by default and expires in a day, at most a
week; views are not recorded in Access's decisions (they would drown the mint decisions); a job lists its own artifacts
unless `--all`, and may get, share or remove any of its user's (the same person's work); SVG is neutralised by the
policy rather than rewritten.

Tests: `test/integration/artifacts.test.ts` (the real daemon, a joined machine, the real `hopper-artifact`: put an HTML
chart and get a URL, recorded with its job, issue and hash, on the timeline and the job stream, served under the
sandbox; a share with another user that works and stops after a revoke; a public link without a session, its most
hours, public links off and on, revoked; the size limit, a PNG byte for byte, a GitHub token masked, list and markdown,
rm, a token that is no job's, a bad call; the retention sweep), `test/integration/artifact-revisions.test.ts` (issue #675: a
put to an artifact is revision 2 under the same id, revision 1 readable, the API and the events; restore as a new revision;
the quota counts revisions; pin and the sweep; a public link follows the latest or pins one; the CLI),
`test/integration/artifact-pages.test.ts` (issue #675: the libraries copied and served to an opaque origin, a missing one
refused at start; an HTML page's script source is `/artifact-lib/` at the address used; the warnings; the share page;
the skill help), `test/integration/artifact-merge.test.ts` (issue #687: owner revise by file and by `from`; merge order,
content, the job of each revision, the latest, the events, the quota, a merge that does not fit leaves the source; the
duplicate warning and `--new`; the help; the CLI's revise, merge and links), `test/ui/artifacts.test.ts` (the UI's model).

## A connection's health (issue #647, 2026-10-10)

On one evening a GitHub connection stopped for 45 minutes and the owner was not told. A sign-in replaced the stored
grant; GitHub then refused the new token; the renewer read GitHub's `incorrect_client_credentials` as a setup problem
and tried again about 52 times without saying "reconnect needed". A second sign-in fixed the connection, but jobs
already running kept the dead token until the next renewal, 7 hours later. #597 removed the revoke and the wrong
reading. This change closes the gaps that remained.

**Every new token reaches running jobs at once.** The connected accounts call `onToken` after every new token they
keep — a renewal, a connect from Sources, a sign-in (taken at once or from a held grant) — and the user runtime runs
`engine.renewCredentials` on it: each job at work with a **credentials dir** has its files (`gh/hosts.yml`) rewritten
through its machine's own connection, as after a renewal (#441). A job whose files cannot be rewritten gets a progress
line and `Job.credentialsWarning` (the job card shows it, `CredentialsFlag`); a later rewrite clears it.

**GitHub refusing the connection reads "reconnect needed".** The connection ends (`state: 'expired'`,
`connected_account.expired`, the header's "GitHub: reconnect needed") when GitHub refuses the refresh token
(`bad_refresh_token`), when it answers `incorrect_client_credentials` to a renewal sent with no client secret (#597),
and now also when GitHub answers 401 to a token the renewer renewed less than `FRESH_REFUSED_MS` (5 min) before: a
second renewal would not help. A source or proxy call that gets a 401 on the token it was just given reports it to
the renewer the same way. The header banner follows the source's status, pushed at the end, so it shows within the
renewer's minute.

**Renewals are recorded.** `connected_account.renewed { provider, account, expiresAt? }` for each renewal kept, and
`connected_account.renewal_failed { provider, account, code }` for each failed try: GitHub's OAuth error, else
`http_<status>`, `renewal_blocked` or `no_answer`. Never a token. The stored account keeps `renewedAt` and
`connectedBy` (`sources` or `sign-in`); the status adds them, `grantedBy`, `nextRenewalAt` (an hour before expiry, or
the retry of a failed renewal) and `lastError` (`{ at, error }`, kept after later renewals succeed, cleared by a new
grant). Sources shows them under the account (`ConnectionHealth`).

**A 401 skips the backoff at most once a minute** (`SKIP_BACKOFF_EVERY_MS`, per account). Before, every 401 asked
GitHub again during a failed renewal's backoff; a busy source made the backoff void.

**A sign-in never quietly replaces a healthy connection** (`src/connected-accounts/held.ts`). A GitHub sign-in made
while the connection is connected, readable, not ended and with no failed renewal waiting is checked at GitHub and then
**held** in memory, one per provider: the status shows `held { account, at }`, Sources asks Use this sign-in
(`take-held`: it replaces the connection, and running jobs get its token) or Keep this connection (`drop-held`: its
token is deleted at GitHub, best effort). Nobody acting within `HELD_MS` (15 min) drops it. A restart drops it
without deleting it; it then expires at GitHub on its own. A sign-in over a connection that is not healthy replaces
it at once, as before. Connect in Sources is the person's own act and replaces at once.

**Why a UI session is unknown is logged.** A request whose session token names no live session logs why: `expired:
<reason>` (it expired on this request), `ended: <reason>` (it ended earlier in this process: logout, connection-ended,
…), or `not found` (before this process started, a database reset, another hopper's). The cause of the session loss
on that evening is still unknown; this is what finds it the next time.

**The start check says which key is missing.** At start each connection the runtime cannot open logs `start check:`
with what is missing: `HOPPER_MASTER_KEY` (the runtime gives none), or the key it was sealed under (neither
`HOPPER_MASTER_KEY` nor `HOPPER_MASTER_KEY_PREVIOUS` opens it). It never asks for a new sign-in: that would mint another
grant toward GitHub's ten.

Tests: `test/connected-accounts/connection-health.test.ts` (renewed and failed renewals told, no token; a 401 on a
fresh token ends it; the backoff skipped once a minute; the status facts; a held sign-in taken, dropped, refused; a
sign-in over an ended connection replaces it and hands the token on; the start check), `test/integration/
connected-account-renewal.test.ts` (connecting again and a held sign-in taken reach a running job's `hosts.yml` within
10 s; one `connected_account.renewed` event with no token; `connected_account.renewal_failed` with its code; a job
whose files cannot be rewritten gets a progress line and a warning, cleared by the next rewrite),
`test/http/ui-sessions.test.ts` (why a session is unknown), `test/ui/sources-view.test.ts`,
`test/ui/credentials-warning.test.ts`.

## Agent text as Markdown (issue #569, 2026-10-10)

Owner requirement: questions, proposals, research reports and the like are long, and hard to read as plain text. The
UI renders them as Markdown, and the agents are told to write Markdown. Part 1 of the issue; the model-written summary
(below, "Not built") is carried.

**Where.** Every place the UI shows **agent text**: the question card (the question, each level's answer and reason),
the question history (the question and its answer), a parked job's question (Parked, issue #565), a proposal's or a
research report's parts and the review trail's notes, earlier versions too, Needs a person's assessment summary and a
resolution's note (issue #551), a recent failure's summary, and a phase shift's note — a fork's and a suggestion's
(issue #548). A line that is cut short (the question line of a parked row, a history row, an earlier review item's
headline, a note) renders its inline Markdown only. The raw error and the recent output stay as written: they are a
program's output, not agent text.

**Safe, two layers, each enough alone** (`ui/src/lib/markdown.ts`). The text comes from agents and, through issues, from
people the hopper does not know. The renderer (marked, already the artifacts' Markdown preview) makes only safe HTML: raw
HTML in the text is escaped and shows as text, block or inline; an image is never loaded — it is a link to its URL, named
by its alt text; a link goes only to `http:`, `https:`, `mailto:` or `#` (a view of the UI), with `target="_blank"` and
`rel="noopener noreferrer"`, and any other link is its text alone; a task list's box is a character, no form input.
DOMPurify then keeps only the tags a card needs (paragraphs, breaks, emphasis, code, blocks, lists, headings, rules,
links, tables) and the attributes `href`, `title`, `start`, `align`, `target`, `rel`, with the same link rule, and
sets the new-tab attributes on every link it keeps. The renderer is tested on its own: DOMPurify needs a browser's DOM,
and in happy-dom (the UI tests' DOM) it lets HTML through unchecked; the live check runs it in Chromium. `.md` in
`ui/src/index.css` keeps rendered text compact: the card's text size, small headings, tight lists, scrolled code
blocks and tables.

**Compact cards** (`ui/src/model/card-text.ts`, `CardText`). A text of at most 600 characters and 8 lines shows whole.
A longer one shows its **summary** — its first paragraph that is not a heading, a leading code block skipped, cut at
400 characters — and **Show all** opens the whole text (**Show less** folds it again). A review item's newest version
shows its first part (a proposal's Goal, a report's Question: the summary the pre-check asks for, issue #631), at its
summary, and Show all opens every part; an earlier version, already behind its own fold, shows whole. A question's
compact line (`firstLine`) is the first line of its summary, so a heading never stands in for the question.

**Agents write Markdown.** The default job rules carry one more line, `MARKDOWN_RULE` (`src/job-rules/`): "[hopper
formatting] Format the text you write for a person in the hopper (a question, a research report, a proposal, a note)
in Markdown: a short summary first, then sections and lists. Put names, paths and commands in code spans. Do not use
raw HTML or images." Saved job rules are the owner's: they carry it only if the owner adds it. The fixed protocol lines
say it whatever the saved rules say: the question line asks for one short sentence that says what is needed first, then
the context, with the options as a numbered list (the list Jev's `question-answer` point reads, issue #550); the
research and proposal lines ask for each part in Markdown, with a short summary first. A part's label may be a
Markdown heading or bold: `reviewSections` reads it either way (issue #537).

**Notifications and webhooks** carry the Markdown source as written, so a receiver can render it as the UI does: the
Grok Bot routine's question body has `question` (the text) and `questionFormat: 'markdown'`; the events keep `text`
(`question.asked`), `goal` (`proposal.submitted`) and `question` (`research.submitted`) as the agent wrote them.

The TL;DR on top of a long card is the next section's.

Tests: `test/ui/markdown.test.ts` (the renderer: every element kind, line breaks, raw HTML and script escaped, no image,
new-tab links, refused link schemes, inline lines; the summary and the long-text rule), `test/ui/markdown-cards.test.ts`
(a long question folded and opened, its HTML and script shown as text; a short one whole; a long proposal's Goal first
and the rest behind Show all; reviewer notes), `test/job-rules/markdown-format.test.ts`, `test/herdr/screen.test.ts` (the
footer verbatim), `test/plugins/grokbot-payload.test.ts`.


## TL;DR (issue #569, 2026-10-10)

Owner requirement: agents are long-winded, so every long card — a question, a proposal, a research report, a Needs a
person hand-off — leads with a **TL;DR**: one or two plain sentences, what is asked or proposed and what the person must
decide (for a question, its options in a few words each). The agent's Markdown is behind Show all.

- **Which cards** (`src/tldr/text.ts`). A card whose text is long by the card's own rule (more than 600 characters or
  8 lines, "Agent text as Markdown"): a question's text, a research report's newest round, a hand-off's summary and
  reasons. A short card is whole already and gets none. **A proposal is not one of them:** since issue #651 its agent
  writes a `TL;DR:` part first, the pre-check asks for it, and the proposal card shows it on top ("Proposals as paths");
  a second TL;DR from a model would say the same thing twice. Its notifications carry that part. The UI keeps its copy of the long-text and summary rules
  (`ui/src/model/card-text.ts`): it may not import `src/` at run time.
- **The model** (`src/tldr/haiku.ts`). Claude Haiku (the `haiku` alias) through the `claude` CLI in print mode, locked
  down as an escalation level's run is (no tools, MCP, settings or session; the answer bound to a JSON Schema; the prompt
  on stdin), with the user's CLI config dirs, in the user's work dir; 60 s at most. Jev (issue #550) is not asked: it
  picks one of a decision's options and writes no text. Tests put a double at the seam (`UserSeams.tldrWriter`); the
  test app's default fails, so no test starts `claude`. Checked once against the real CLI (`claude-haiku-4-5`): a long
  question with an injected instruction gave a plain two-sentence TL;DR with its options, the instruction ignored.
- **The prompt.** One or two plain sentences, at most 300 characters, in Simplified Technical English (one clause, as
  the protocol lines name it, issue #571), plain text only. The agent's text is fenced as data — it may hold whatever an
  issue's author wrote — and the model is told it is not instructions; a closing fence marker inside it is broken.
- **Plain text, whatever the model says** (`plainText`). Control characters, HTML tags, `<` and `>`, Markdown marks
  are taken out; an image or a link is its words; one line, cut at a word. The UI shows it as text (React escapes it),
  never as HTML; a receiver that renders Markdown finds none in it.
- **Written once, stored with the card** (`src/tldr/service.ts`). A sweep, every tick, over the open questions, research
  reports and hand-offs asks the model, one card at a time, for each long card whose stored TL;DR (`tldr: { text, of,
  model?, at }` in its body; no migration) was not written from its text as it is now — `of` is the SHA-256 of that
  text. So a research report's next round gets a new one, and nothing is written again on a render or a restart. A text
  the model failed on is not asked again for the same text: the card keeps its hash (`tldrFailedOf`, issue #1608), so a
  restart does not ask again either, and a TL;DR written later clears it. A card is never
  waited on; a text that changed while the model wrote is left for the next sweep. Each one written is
  `tldr.written { kind, id, text, model? }` on the card's job.
- **Shown while it matches** (`withShownTldr`). The question, research and hand-off routes answer a card's `tldr`
  only while it was written from the card's text as it is now and the setting is on.
- **The card** (`CardText`, `TldrLine`). A long text with a TL;DR shows the TL;DR, marked TL;DR, and Show all opens the
  whole text below it; without one, the summary as before. A research report's newest round: the TL;DR alone, every
  part behind Show all. A hand-off: the TL;DR under what happened.
- **Notifications and webhooks lead with it.** The human-stage events — `question.escalated` with target `human`,
  `question.escalated_to_human`, `proposal.escalated_to_human`, `research.escalated_to_human` — carry `tldr` for a long
  card: its TL;DR when written, else the agent's own summary (`summaryOf`: a review item's first part — a proposal's
  TL;DR part, a report's Question —, else the first paragraph that is not a heading; as plain text).
  The Grok Bot routine's question body has `tldr` first, after the sender and the job. A card that reaches a person
  before the model answers carries the agent's summary: the notification never waits.
- **The setting** (`tldr`, a user setting: `GET /api/tldr`, `POST /ui/api/tldr { enabled }`, admin,
  `tldr.settings_changed`; Settings → TL;DR). On by default. Off: nothing is written, the routes answer none, the
  events carry none; turned on again, the open cards get theirs at once. Read on every sweep and read, so no restart.

Tests: `test/tldr/text.test.ts` (the rules), `test/integration/tldr.test.ts` (written once, stored and shown; a short
question; the answer made plain; the model failing and the agent's summary in the event; a research report's next
round; a proposal led by its own TL;DR part, no model asked; the setting), `test/plugins/grokbot-payload.test.ts` (the body leads with it), `test/ui/markdown-cards.test.ts` (the
card, HTML in the TL;DR as text, the setting).
## A job's own wait (issue #483, 2026-10-10)

A job blocked on something only a person or the outside world can do (write access to be granted, a review, a release)
had no way to say so. The protocol had three end markers: a question, done and failed. A message with none was a status
note, nudged again and again; so a job that waited sent status notes, opened a question only to park itself (a wait on a
person's question list as if it needed an answer), or ended failed though it was not.

- **The marker.** A protocol line (`WAIT_LINE`, `src/job-rules/index.ts`): end the message with a line `HOPPER_WAITING`, then
  `for: <what you wait for>` and, if it can, `until: <how it will know>`. To be woken, the job first starts a command in the
  background that ends when the thing happens (a poll), and names it in `until:`. Never a question only to wait. The status
  note nudge names the marker too. A `HOPPER_WAITING` without a `for:` line is no wait: a status note.
- **Read.** herdr-claude: `readTurn` (`screen.ts`) reads the marker and its fields (`waitFields`); the monitor returns the
  outcome `{ kind: 'wait', wait: { for, until? } }` at once, with no nudge, and saves the turn with `parkedSeq` and
  `markersAfter` (the turn's output lines then). A print-mode agent: the marker, then its fields to the end of the answer
  (`outcomeOf`); its session id is saved, as on a question.
- **Recorded** (`src/engine/outcome.ts`): status `waiting_on`, `wait: { for, until?, since }` on the job, its lane freed,
  `resumeOn` its lane's machine, `job.waiting { for, until? }`. No question opens and none is counted; nothing is cleaned up:
  its pane and agent stay. (Issue #2303: while a job waits for memory on its machine, a wait the hopper ends by itself has its agent ended,
  "Wait release".) It is not in the decider's inputs (it is neither queued nor running), and holds no lane.
- **It goes on by itself** (`src/engine/pane-answers.ts`). On every tick the engine probes each `waiting_on` job's pane, as a
  job on a question's (`answeredInPane`): Claude past the wait — working again, text typed in the pane, or new output past
  `markersAfter` (a short turn may be over by the time it is looked at) — ends it. The job runs again on a lane of its machine
  (one more over the cap when none is idle), `wait` cleared, `job.reattached { reason: 'the wait ended in the pane' }`, and the
  runner watches the turn with the wait already taken left out. Its own background poll ending is what wakes Claude: the
  hopper runs no check of its own.
- **A comment ends it** (issue #2159, "A comment ends the job's own wait"). A trusted account's new comment on its issue or
  its own pull request, seen by a GitHub watch while it waits, ends the wait; the job is told the comment as untrusted text.
- **The hopper ends it** (issue #998, "An answer ends the job's own wait"). When an answer the job asked the hopper for
  (a skill request that answered 202) is ready, the hopper ends the wait with it, as a person does below, `by: hopper`.
- **A person ends it.** `POST /ui/api/jobs/:id/end-wait { note? }` (least role `operator`; 409 unless `waiting_on`): queued
  again with `waitEndedNote` pending, which pins it to `resumeOn` as an answer does; its claim types it into the pane (`[hopper] A
  person ended your wait: what you waited for (<for>) has happened. The person's note: <note> Check it, then go on with the
  job.`). `job.wait_ended { by: 'person', note? }`. A print-mode job resumes its session with it.
- **Cancel** works as for any job: the pane closes through the normal reap. A person gives a reason if they like (issue #1460):
  `POST /ui/api/jobs/:id/cancel { reason? }` or `hopper job cancel <id> [--reason <text>]`, for any job that has not ended;
  `job.cancelled { reason: 'cancelled in UI', note }` keeps it, and the source is told only the cancel (the claim labels go).
- **Its item closes** (issue #1460). A job on its own wait never runs on to its own end, so the source's check ends it: its
  issue closed by its own work — the merge of its own pull request, or closed as completed after it started, the done-check —
  gives the `finish` signal, and it ends `finished` (`job.finished { result: 'issue closed as complete' }`, its wait dropped,
  `hopper:done`); closed any other way cancels it (`issue closed`). Either way its claim labels come off, and its pane closes
  through the normal reap. Before, both kinds of close gave it no signal, and it waited for ever.
- **Live job.** A `waiting_on` job's processes still run on its machine (its background poll): it is in every "at work" list —
  credentials renewed, the GitHub proxy, skills, the vault, the job stream, artifacts, Access, the sweep and the rename guard
  keep it as live — and in `jobsOnMachine`.
- **UI.** The Dashboard's Waiting panel lists the jobs on their own wait in their own group ("On its own wait"), and the Queue
  view in its own panel (`WaitingOnRows`, `ui/src/views/dashboard/queue.tsx`): what it waits for, how it will know, its machine,
  since when; **End the wait** (operators) and Cancel. It is no question: not in Questions, its badge or Attention. The Waiting
  card counts it in its line. The lane timeline ends a span at `job.waiting`.
- **Not built.** Parking a job on its own wait; a check the hopper runs itself (the job's own background poll covers it); a
  note field for End the wait in the UI (the route takes one).
- **Persisted state.** No schema change: the status and `wait` are in the job's JSON. A build before this one, on a store
  holding a `waiting_on` job, shows it in no group and never runs it; its pane stays until it is cancelled.

## A wait on its own command (issue #1037, 2026-10-13)

A job that started a long local test run in the background ended its turn with `HOPPER_WAITING` and `until: background
command <id> ends`. It went to `waiting_on`, and the Jobs graph showed it as waiting on the outside world, as a job blocked
on a person. Nothing outside the job was involved: the command ends by itself, and the agent goes on.

- **Read.** `namesOwnCommand` (`src/domain/own-command.ts`): the wait's `until:` names its own background command and its
  end — `own command <id> ends`, `background command|shell|task|process … ends|exits|finishes|completes|stops`. A poll is
  the outside world. The protocol's wait line tells the job to write `until: own command <its id> ends` for such a wait.
  Recorded (`src/engine/outcome.ts`): `ownCommand: true` on the wait and on `job.waiting`. The status stays `waiting_on`:
  its lane is free and its pane stays, as for any own wait.
- **Shown as running.** `stageOf` gives stage *running* while it is not stuck: "Running: waiting on its own command", its
  stage since the wait began (the command's runtime as near as the hopper knows it), next "It goes on when its own command
  ends." The Dashboard and the Queue view list it under On its own wait with a running badge and "running for"; the
  Waiting card does not count it, the Running card says how many run so. It was never in Needs you, and is not now.
- **The harness's running shell is not the test.** Every outside wait also runs a background poll (the wait line asks for
  one), so Claude Code's footer ("1 shell") cannot tell the two apart. The footer is the liveness check below only.
- **Its command gone** (`src/engine/pane-answers.ts` `watchOwnCommand`). On every tick, a job on its own command that has
  not gone on is asked `ownCommandRuns` (herdr-claude: its agent and pane alive and the footer naming background work,
  `backgroundWork`). No background work, or its pane or agent gone: `goneSince` on the wait. After the own command grace
  (`HOPPER_OWN_COMMAND_GRACE_MS`, default 5 min) the hopper types one nudge into its pane (`nudgeInPane`, `ownCommandNudge`:
  check the command, read its output or start it again, then go on), `nudgedAt`, `job.own_command_nudged { delivered }`.
  Its agent going on ends the wait in the pane as before. A grace after the nudge, still not gone on: before issue #1694,
  `stuckAt`, `job.own_command_stuck`, and the job waited on a person; now its wait check ends the wait ("Wait checks"
  below). A wait flagged stuck before is shown as before until its check ends it. Background work seen again clears
  `goneSince`.
- **Not built.** A stuck job in Needs you (it shows in Waiting and on the Jobs graph as waiting on you); the command's own
  start time (the wait's start stands in); a check of the command by the hopper itself.
- **Persisted state.** No schema change: the new fields are optional in the job's `wait` JSON. A build before this one
  reads such a job as any own wait. A wait recorded before this build has no `ownCommand` and shows as before.

## Item snapshots (issue #662, 2026-10-10)

Run again, the assessor's reruns, a problem's release and an item offered again by hand used to read the issue's live
title, body and comments. An issue edited after its first run then ran with text nobody approved: a way around every
check at intake. Now the text a job runs is the item's **snapshot**, and a live text that differs **holds** the job.

- **Recorded at intake** (`src/engine/item-snapshots.ts` `gateItem`, from `ingest` in `source-host.ts`): the first job of
  an item that can run records its **item text** — title, body and the assignee comments the job sees (`SourceItem.text`)
  — and its SHA-256 (`textHash`), in the user's `item_snapshots` table, one row per item key. `item.snapshot_recorded
  { key, hash, reason: 'intake' }`. A job that is invalid (an empty body) ran nothing and records none.
- **Every later job runs the snapshot.** Run again (`sources/rerun.ts`), the failure assessor's rerun and a problem's
  release (both `rerun(jobId, 'assessor')`), a failure's Retry and a hand-off's Run again, and an item offered again
  because a person removed its end label: each goes through `ingest`. Its item is rendered from the snapshot's text
  (`JobSource.withText`; GitHub: `promptWithText`, the untrusted block of issue #652 made from the snapshot's title, body
  and comments, the context block — priority, yolo mode, done line — as read now). A brief is appended after.
- **Changed → held.** When the live title or body differs from the snapshot's, the new job is created with the snapshot's text and a
  **text change** (`Job.textChange`: both texts, who edited it, and the job's text with the new text). The decider holds
  it before every other judgement (`TEXT_CHANGED`): no approval, acceptance or queue order starts it.
  `item.changed_since_snapshot { key, snapshotHash, liveHash, editors, newComments }` — never the text.
- **A comment is no change** (issue #747, 2026-10-10). The hash still covers the comments, but only the title and body
  are compared (`sameAsk`): with the same title and body the job runs the snapshot's text at once, however many comments
  came since. A status note, design notes or a bot's update re-held approved jobs before: seven at once, each with no
  editor and only new comments, the queue idle with every lane free. Tenant migration 37
  (`store/migration-comment-holds.ts`) drops the text change of each job held only for new comments; the decider then
  judges it as any other waiting job. A held change with an edited title or body still lists its new comments on the card.
- **Edits while queued.** Each sync offers an item whose job has not ended again (`refresh`); a job not started whose
  item's text changed is held the same way (`refreshText`). Its comments are not read then (no extra call per poll), so
  only an edit of the title or body is a change; the comments it last saw stand in. The refresh never changes a job's
  task text: only its priority, and the config parts of its spec (executor, model, work tree, machine, issue #375).
- **Who edited it.** When the text changed, the sync loop asks the source's timeline (`JobSource.editsSince`, GitHub:
  GraphQL `userContentEdits` for the body and `RenamedTitleEvent` for the title, the newest 50 of each) for the edits since
  the snapshot (`sources/item-text.ts` `withEdits`). A timeline that cannot be read leaves them empty; the job still holds.
- **The card** (`ui/src/components/text-change.tsx`, in the Dashboard's Waiting panel and the Queue view): the title
  change, the body's lines removed and added (the `diff` library), the new assignee comments — not in the prompt unless
  accepted —, who edited it, and three ways on:
  - **Rerun the original** — `POST /ui/api/jobs/:id/keep-original` (operator; `hopper job keep-original <id>`): the hold
    ends, the job runs the snapshot's text, and that live text (`Job.originalKept`) holds it no more. `item.original_kept`.
  - **Accept the new text** — `POST /ui/api/jobs/:id/accept-new-text` (operator, and the owner only; `hopper job
    accept-new-text <id>`): Access asks OpenFGA `item#can_accept_text` for the signed-in user, telling at the check that the
    user whose hopper takes the item is its `owner` (`itemObject`: the owner and the key's SHA-256). Denied — OpenFGA not set
    up or not reached, or a model without `item` (`itemGaps`) — it answers 403 and nothing changes. Allowed, the job's spec
    takes the new text, it is the item's new snapshot, and the job runs it. `item.new_text_accepted { key, fromHash, toHash,
    editors, person, via }`, then `item.snapshot_recorded { reason: 'accepted' }`.
  - **Cancel** — the job's Cancel, as for any job.
- **Agents cannot accept.** A job reaches no `/ui/api/*` route (its proxy token opens only `/job/*`), and the operator CLI's
  call is the UI's route, under Access like a click.
- **Backfill** (tenant migration 35, `store/migration-item-snapshots.ts`): each item's first job gives its snapshot — the
  spec's goal as the title, its body, and the comments its prompt carried, read back (`commentsInPrompt`: from the
  untrusted block, or from the end of the context block for a prompt from before it). A comment cut
  short in the prompt reads back short, so that item's next job holds once: safe, never a run of unapproved text.
- **A started job's item edited** (issue #655 part 7): the job goes on with its text, and its trust stamp drops to
  `untrusted` (`refreshEdit`, `Job.editSeen`); "Trust stamps" holds the rule.
- **Not built.** A gate re-entry for the card once the intake gate (issue #655) ships; until then the card stands alone.
  A history of every snapshot (the events keep each hash). A snapshot for a source with no `withText` (the GitHub sources
  are the only ones with item text).
- **Persisted state.** A table only (`item_snapshots`); `textChange` and `originalKept` live in the job's JSON. A build
  before this one runs on the migrated store and ignores both fields: it would start a held job, with the snapshot's
  text, the approved one, never the edited text.

## No checks means ready (issue #677, 2026-10-10)

Issue #652 had yolo mode merge only a pull request with a check that passed. A repository with no checks then never
merged anything: its pull requests waited in the Pull requests list with `no checks`, and yolo mode did nothing there.

**The rule** (`src/domain/pull-requests.ts` `readyToMerge`, `noChecksSettled`, `NO_CHECKS_GRACE_MS`). Ready for the
hopper's merge: not a draft, no merge conflicts, and its checks passed — or it has none, and none started within the
grace window, two minutes after its last push (`pushedAt`: the later of when it was opened and its head commit). The
window keeps a check that starts late from being missed: a check that starts holds the merge until it passes, as
before. A repository's required checks are GitHub's: a merge without them is refused, and the refusal is kept on the
card (`merge refused`), as any refused merge. Yolo mode off: nothing changes, a person merges.

**Card states.** The follow keeps `pushedAt` and `base` (`baseRefName`) on what it saw (`PullRequestSeen`); the list,
given the time now, says why each card waits: `no pull request`, `not checked yet`, `draft`, `conflicts`, `checks
failing`, `yolo off`, `checks pending`, `checks unknown`, `checks not started`, `merge refused`, `ready`. The UI says each in plain words
(`ui/src/model/pull-requests.ts` `waitsText`): `waiting for a person to merge`, `waiting for checks`, `waiting for checks
to start`, `conflicts with <base>`, `ready, merging`, and so on.

**Checks the hopper may not read** (issue #855). The pull request queries read each head commit's `statusCheckRollup`,
which needs the app's Checks and Commit statuses read. An app without them gets the data and a `FORBIDDEN` error on
that field. The hopper keeps the answer and takes those checks as `unknown` (`src/sources/github/closer.ts`): the
done-check, the follow and the reconcile go on, and yolo mode never merges a pull request whose checks are `unknown`
(card `checks unknown`). Any other GraphQL error still fails the call.

**Checks fallback** (issue #1244, `src/sources/github/checks-fallback.ts`). A pull request whose checks are `unknown`
has them read again over REST, with the same connection: its head commit's check runs
(`GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/commits/{ref}/check-runs`, Checks read) and its combined status
(`GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/commits/{ref}/status`, Commit statuses read), one state as the rollup says it — one failed
fails it, one still running keeps it pending, all passed is passing, none is no checks (`src/sources/github/app/rest-checks.ts`).
Every read of the port that tells a pull request's checks goes through it (the follow's batch and its read by number, the
reconcile), in both GitHub sources, inside the pass reads. Yolo mode then merges on passing checks as on any other.
Nothing falls back to another credential: a source reads only with its own connection.
When GitHub refuses the REST read too (403, 404), the checks stay `unknown` and say why (`checksWhy` on what the follow
sees and on the card): the connection (the GitHub App, or the connected GitHub account), the permissions it lacks, and
the fix. The card says `checks unknown: <why>`. Which read works is kept per repository in memory: a refused repository is
not asked again for ten minutes (`UNREADABLE_KEEP_MS`), so a sync over many of its pull requests asks GitHub once, and a
permission added is seen within ten minutes. A REST read that fails otherwise (a timeout, 5xx) keeps the checks `unknown`
with GitHub's error, and is asked again at the next read.

**A refusal says what the app lacks** (issue #1351, `src/sources/github/app/refusal.ts`). GitHub refuses a GitHub App's
token — the hopper's app for a connected account, an admin's app for the app source — with "Resource not accessible by
integration" and names neither the permission nor the install. Every refusal the hopper passes on (the App adapter, the
connected account's adapter, the GraphQL reads of pull requests, a repository's checks read) adds what the app needs and the
fix: the permission GitHub asks for — REST's `x-accepted-github-permissions` header, or the GraphQL field it refused, by the
permission the hopper knows that field needs — or, when neither names one, that the app lacks a permission or is not
installed there; then install it on the repository's owner with that repository, at the app's install link
(`<app>/installations/new`: the app source's own app, or the hopper's app from its slug, `ConnectedAccountTokens.endpoints`,
for a connected account and its repository checks), and accept its new permissions. A connected
account reaches only the repositories where the hopper's app is installed, so its checks fix says that too. A paused source
says why in the log, once when the pause starts or changes and once when it ends (`pauseTold`, `src/sources/sync-setup.ts`):
its pass asks GitHub nothing new, and its traffic line alone reads as a healthy zero. So the traffic line of every pass that
takes nothing new says why too — `sync pass <name> (nothing new taken: <the setup problem, else the pause>): REST 0, …`
(`JobSource.pass`'s `idle`, `trafficLine`). A source not configured that still runs its pass for its own jobs is
`needs-setup`, never ok. The GitHub sign-in, and the hopper's app installed on every repository, do not configure the app
source: it is an admin's own app, with its own id, slug and key (`help/github-app-setup.md`); without them, take the issues
through the GitHub account source.

**A job is told why too** (issue #1279, `src/github-proxy/api.ts`). A job's `pr status` and `pr wait` read on GitHub
take a refused check-runs read (403, 404, not a rate limit) as `unknown` with `checksWhy` — the connected GitHub account,
the permission it lacks, and the fix (`checksLack`, the fallback's own words) —; one answered from the hopper's records
carries the card's `checksWhy`. `pr checks` reads the check runs and the statuses side by side: one refused, it answers the
other with `unreadable` and `checksWhy`; both refused, it fails with GitHub's message and `checksWhy`. Every other
"Resource not accessible by integration" a job's request gets says what the app needs and the fix (`explained`, as below).
A `pr wait` cannot wait on checks it may not read: it answers at once, and the help says to pass `checksWhy` to a person.

**Checks read problem** (issue #1244, part 2). A refusal marks the checks `checksRefused` (on `OpenPullRequest`,
`PullRequestState` and `PullRequestSeen`); a read that failed otherwise does not. The Pull requests list
(`src/domain/pull-request-list.ts`) makes one **checks read problem** per repository of its open cards that wait on
`checks unknown` with that mark — `checksProblems: { repo, why, pullRequests }[]` on `GET /api/pull-requests`, never one
per pull request. Its `why` is the newest refusal's: the connection, the permissions it lacks, and the fix. The Pull
requests view says it once at the top of the repository's group (`repo-checks-unread`, `checksProblemText`); each card
still says `checks unknown: <why>`. Needs you has a **Checks** row (`checksProblemLines`), one line per repository with the
fix, linked to Pull requests; the Pull requests nav badge adds it. Pure, from what the follow last saw: no new route, table
or event. It is gone at the first sync after a permission is added (the fallback's cache keeps a refusal ten minutes). It
is not a failure **problem** (`src/failures/`): those group failed jobs and hold new ones, and here no job failed and no
job need wait — only the merge does.

**A pull request the report could not name** (the report names only a ready one) is looked for again at each follow: the
newest open one that closes the issue, else one in its repository that mentions it — a part when it says `Part of #N` —,
else one on a branch named for the issue. Found, it is named in the job's source state and followed as any other, so a
card never stays `not checked yet` or without its pull request for more than one sync.

**Persisted state.** `pushedAt` and `base` are new, optional fields in a job's source state. A build before this one
ignores them; a `seen` without `pushedAt` counts as pushed long ago.

Tests: `test/sources/pull-request-list.test.ts` (each card state, the grace window), `test/sources/github-follow.test.ts`
(no checks merges after the window, waits inside it; a pull request the report missed is found and named, a part as a
part), `test/integration/pull-requests.test.ts` (the real daemon: waits for checks to start, a late check holds it, an old
one with no checks merges), `test/ui/pull-requests-view.test.ts` (the plain words).

**Merge now and Close PR** (the second part of issue #677, `src/http/ui/pull-request-acts.ts`). An open card with a pull
request has two actions for an operator, each confirmed once in a dialog: **Merge now** and **Close PR**. Both take the
yolo path: `POST /ui/api/pull-requests/merge` or `/close` with the card's `jobId` →
`SourceRegistry.pullRequestAct` → answered at once (issue #1194, "Actions answer at once"), then on the job's report
chain, `JobSource.follow(job, act)`. With `merge`, the follow merges
the open pull request (`GitHubApi.merge`, a merge commit) whatever yolo mode and its checks say; with `close`, it closes it
without a merge (`GitHubApi.closeWithoutMerge`, `PATCH /pulls/{n}` `state: closed`). The rest is the follow's own: the
merge closes the issue through the pull request's closing keyword and the item gets `hopper:done` (a part: the next part
is offered), a close flags the item `hopper:pr-closed`, and `job.pull_request_merged` or `job.pull_request_closed` is
recorded with `person` and `via` (`ui`, `cli`): who pressed it. GitHub still refuses a draft, merge conflicts or a required
check: `job.pull_request_act_failed` records what GitHub said, nothing else is kept, and the card stays; so does GitHub
out of reach. A job with no open pull request (merged, closed, none found yet) is 409. Least role: operator, as for a job's other actions.
`hopper pr merge <n>` and `hopper pr close <n>` (`src/cli-operator-pr.ts`) find the open card of pull request `<n>` on
the Pull requests list and post the same route; `--repo <owner/repo>` picks one when two repositories have that number.

Tests: `test/integration/pull-requests.test.ts` (Merge now with yolo off and checks pending; a refused merge; Close PR;
the CLI), `test/ui/pull-requests-view.test.ts` (the buttons, the confirmation, none for a viewer).

**Closing finishes the loop** (the third part of issue #677, `src/sources/github/own-merge.ts` `closeAfterMerge`). A merge
by the hopper — yolo mode, or a person's Merge now — of a pull request that did not close its issue (no closing keyword:
one that only mentions the issue, or one named for it only on its branch) left the issue open, and issue #721 took that
merge for a part, so the issue was offered again. Now, when the hopper made the merge and the pull request is no part
(its body does not say `Part of #N`), the hopper closes the issue as completed (`GitHubApi.closeAsCompleted`,
`PATCH /issues/{n}` `state: closed`, `state_reason: completed`) and posts one comment that links the pull request
(`closedAfterMergeComment`: neutral, the link only). The item then is done: `hopper:done`, `mergeChecked`. The issue is
closed before the comment, so a sync after a failed comment finds it closed as completed and the item done. A part
merged by the hopper stays a part: the issue stays open and its next part runs. A merge a person made on GitHub stays as
issue #721 has it: the hopper did not merge it, so it does not close the issue. This is the seventh exception to "GitHub
text is neutral" in `AGENTS.md`: the user's setting (yolo mode) or act (Merge now) merged it.

**The merge marker** (issue #1588). "The hopper made the merge" was known only in the follow that made the merge call. A
stop after the call and before the record (or a lost answer, then the Merge now row sent again) left the pull request
merged on GitHub and read as a person's merge: no close, the merge taken for a part, the issue offered again, and
`byHopper` and who pressed Merge now lost. Now, just before the merge call, the follow keeps a **merge marker** in the
job's source state (`merging`: the pull request, its head commit, `byHopper` or the acting person), through
`FollowAt.keep` (`JobSource.follow`'s third argument; the sync loop and the Merge now row pass it). A later follow that
reads the pull request merged, with the marker on it and the same head (or a head not known), takes it as the hopper's
merge: the issue is closed with its one comment as above, and `job.pull_request_merged` says `byHopper` or the person.
Another head is a person's merge on GitHub after the hopper's call was refused. The marker goes with the next state the
follow keeps. A Merge now row sent again after a sync recorded the merge is answered done. Not for a direct job's pull
request (`direct-follow.ts`): it has no issue to close.

Tests: `test/integration/merge-marker.test.ts` (yolo mode and Merge now, the merge's answer lost and the daemon stopped:
after the start the issue is closed once, with one comment, and who merged it is recorded).

Tests: `test/sources/github-follow.test.ts` (yolo merges a pull request that only mentions the issue: closed with one
comment; Merge now on one named only on its branch; a closing pull request gets no extra close or comment; a part stays
open; a person's merge on GitHub stays a part), `test/integration/pull-requests.test.ts` (the real daemon: Merge now of a
pull request with no closing keyword closes the issue with the comment).

**Not built yet** (carried in issue #677): spotting repositories with no checks and recommending a job that adds them
(`hopper repo checks`).

## Lane tuning (issue #688, 2026-10-10)

Owner request: the hopper records machine resources over time (issue #560) and plan usage over time (issue #385), but
each machine's lane count is fixed, and the usage limits scale every machine's lanes the same way. Combine the two
histories so that the hopper sets lanes per machine. The hopper shows and records a **lane recommendation** per machine,
next to its configured lanes. It **recommends and applies nothing by itself** (owner's scope change on the issue): an
admin applies a recommendation, dismisses it, or undoes the last one applied. Applying sets the machine's configured
lanes on the path an edit of the machine takes. A second part had built an **active mode** that applied the
recommendation by itself; the third part took it out (tenant migration 38 below).

**Lane load** (`MachineHistoryRepository.laneLoad`, `src/store/machine-history.ts`). In SQL, over the machine samples of
the last 7 days (`LANE_TUNING_WINDOW_DAYS`): per machine and lanes in use, how many samples, how many at or above each
**resource pressure** (`RESOURCE_PRESSURE`: CPU busy 95%, memory used 90%, disk used 95%), the average CPU busy and the
average memory used. No new table: `machine_samples` already keeps the lanes in use of each sample.

**Lane headroom** (`laneHeadroom`, `src/decider/lane-tuning.ts`, pure). Only lane counts with 10 samples or more (ten
minutes) count. A lane count shows pressure when more than 5% of its samples do; the headroom is one less than the
first such count of 1 or more, and the reason names the resource with the most pressured samples. With no pressure,
it is the most lanes seen, plus what each lane's measured cost leaves room for: the cost is the difference in average
memory used and CPU busy between the fewest and the most lanes seen, per lane; the room is to 85% memory and 90% CPU
(`LANE_TARGET`); at most 2 more (`MAX_LANE_STEP`), so the hopper learns a step at a time. A lane whose cost reads as
nothing leaves room for the 2. With one lane count only, no cost is known, and the headroom is that count.

**Lane progress and slow progress** (`laneProgress`, `src/decider/lane-tuning.ts`, pure; part 5 of the issue). The job
runs of the lane tuning window (`jobRuns`, as for the job cost profiles) that ended `finished` or `failed`, per machine and
lane count: a run's average lanes in use, rounded, at least 1; a run with no sample has none. A cancelled, re-queued or
parked run is a person's act or a recovery, not the machine's, and does not count. A lane count shows **slow progress**
when 4 runs or more ended there (`MIN_PROGRESS_RUNS`), 4 or more ended at fewer lanes (1 or more), and the share that
failed is more than 25 points above the share at fewer lanes (`FAILURE_RISE`). The comparison is what makes it the load's
and not the jobs': a job that fails at one lane fails for its own reasons. The headroom is then one less than the first
lane count with resource pressure or slow progress; at the same count, slow progress is the reason given
(`slow progress at 3 lanes in use (3 of 4 runs failed; 0 of 6 at fewer lanes): 2 lanes run without it`). Its confidence
stands on the samples of the highest lane count below it. The issue names stalls, timeouts and out-of-memory kills: the
hopper keeps no event or field for any of them on its own (a job's own timeout, the agent's death and a kill all end the
run as `job.failed`), so each counts as the failed run it ends in. The engine reads the runs once per plan, beside the
lane load.

**Lane recommendation** (`recommendLanes`). Usage is the machine's own used fraction, as the decider reads it (its
least limited executor, `laneEffect`, `src/decider/usage.ts`, so a week window in its burn window does not count), against
the usage limits the decider uses (`policyOf`).
Below the soft limit by more than 10% (`free`), the recommendation is the headroom. Within 10% of the soft limit
(`near`), past it (`soft`) or at the hard limit (`hard`), it is never more than the configured lanes: the decider's
lane cap already scales the lanes down from there, so the recommendation adds none, and high-priority work keeps its
lanes (issue #535). It is never more than the machine's **memory lanes** (issue #2499, `memoryLaneCaps` in
`src/decider/memory-floor.ts`): its memory total less its memory floor ("The memory floor"), divided by a job's memory;
on a host pool, the lower of that and the kernel's memory less the pool's floor and a job's memory for each configured
lane of the pool's other machines. 9 lanes of 2 GiB each did not fit a 14 GiB VM, and a lane count that history showed
free of pressure said nothing of it. The reason then ends `; its memory holds 3 jobs: 8 GiB less its floor of 1 GiB, at
2 GiB a job: no more than 3 lanes`, or `; its host (shared with b) holds 4 jobs: 14 GiB less its floor of 1.4 GiB and
4 GiB for the 2 lanes of b, at 2 GiB a job: …`. It reads the memory total, not the memory available, so the
recommendation does not move with each reading; a machine with no memory reading, or a floor of 0, has none. Then it is
kept within the machine's bounds. Auto-tune off, the machine offline, or no headroom yet
(not enough history): the configured lanes, confidence 0. **Confidence** is the samples the headroom stands on per hour
(60 samples: 1).

**Settings** (`laneTuning` in the user's settings, `LaneTuningSettings`: per machine id, `{ autoTune, minLanes,
maxLanes }`; a machine absent has the defaults: on, 1, 8). In the database, edited on Machines (admin) and by the CLI.
`POST /ui/api/lanes/tuning { machineId, autoTune?, minLanes?, maxLanes? }`: a field left out keeps its value;
bounds are whole numbers from 0 to 64 (`MAX_TUNED_LANES`), the least at most the most (else 400); an unknown machine is
404. Each change is one `lanes.tuning_changed { machineId, from, to, by }`. The answer is the plan.

**The plan** (`GET /api/lanes/plan`, `LaneTuningPlan`: `at`, `windowDays`, per machine its `LaneRecommendation` —
`configured`, `lanes`, `headroom`, `reason`, `confidence`, `usedFrac`, `usage`, `tuning`, `apply`, `dismissed`, `undo`
—, and `changes`, the latest 20 `lanes.applied` and `lanes.undone`, newest first). One code path
(`engine.laneTuning.plan`, `src/engine/lane-tuning.ts`): the Machines view and `hopper lanes plan` (JSON) read the same
route, as issue #623 asks. `hopper lanes tune <machine> [--auto on|off] [--min <n>] [--max <n>]` and `hopper lanes
apply|dismiss|undo <machine>` make the UI's POSTs (`src/cli-operator-lanes.ts`).

**Record.** After each resource record that kept new samples (every minute, `createHistoryRecorders`'
`afterMachineRecord`), the plan is computed again, and for each tuned online machine with a known headroom whose
recommended or configured lanes changed since its last record, one `lanes.recommended { machineId, lanes, configured,
headroom, reason, confidence, usage }`. A change in the reason alone records nothing, so the log is not a
minute-by-minute copy. The last recorded per machine is read from the event log once, so a restart records no
duplicate. The record changes no lanes.

**What an admin can do** (`laneActions`, `src/decider/lane-tuning.ts`, pure). `apply: { to }` when the recommendation
differs from the configured lanes, stands on a known headroom, with auto-tune on and the machine online, and is not
dismissed. `dismissed: { at, by }` when an admin dismissed these lanes at these configured lanes. `undo: { to }` when
the machine's last lane change is an applied recommendation and its configured lanes are still that change's lanes; a
hand edit since stands, and leaves nothing to undo.

**Apply.** `POST /ui/api/lanes/apply { machineId, lanes? }` (admin). `lanes` is the recommendation the admin saw: when
the recommendation moved since, 409 names the new one. Nothing to apply is 409 with the reason; an unknown machine 404.
The machine's configured lanes become the recommended lanes through the engine's `machineLanes`
(`src/users/machine-lanes.ts`): the plugins config edit of its machine-source instance's options (`POST
/ui/api/plugins`, `action: 'options'`), `lanes` changed and every other option kept, against the config's version
read now — the path an edit of the machine on Machines takes. So the decider, its lane cap, priority lanes, the
Machines view and the usage report read the new lanes as they read any lanes edited by hand, and the machine's edit
form shows them. Then one `lanes.applied { machineId, from, to, reason, confidence, by }`, and the machine's dismissal
goes. `lanes.applied` and `lanes.undone` are triggers: the next Decision opens or drains lanes to the new count.

**Dismiss.** `POST /ui/api/lanes/dismiss { machineId }` (admin) keeps `{ lanes, configured, at, by }` per machine
(`laneDismissals` in the user's settings, `LaneDismissals`) and records one `lanes.dismissed { machineId, lanes,
configured, reason, by }`. The recommendation is not offered again until the recommended or the configured lanes move.
Nothing to dismiss is 409.

**Undo.** `POST /ui/api/lanes/undo { machineId }` (admin) sets the configured lanes back to the lanes before the last
applied recommendation, on the same path as Apply, with one `lanes.undone { machineId, from, to, by }`. Nothing to undo
(none applied, an undo already, a hand edit since) is 409; an unknown machine 404.

**Tenant migration 38** (`src/store/migration-lane-recommendations.ts`). A machine in active mode with auto-tune on ran
on its applied lanes, kept within its bounds: those lanes become its configured lanes in the plugins config, so no
machine changes its lanes on the upgrade. The `appliedLanes` setting and each machine's `mode` go. The build before
runs on the migrated store: it reads a setting with no mode as shadow, and the configured lanes. Events recorded
before keep their shape: `lanes.recommended` and `lanes.tuning_changed` may carry `mode`; a `lanes.applied` without
`by` (with `configured`) is one the hopper applied by itself, and the history shows it without a name.

**UI.** Machines has a *Lane tuning* panel under the machine cards (`ui/src/views/lane-tuning.tsx`): per machine the
recommended lanes against the configured lanes (`Recommends 4 lanes; configured 2: 2 more`), the reason, the
confidence, who dismissed it, its last 5 changes with who and why, and for an admin *Apply: 4 lanes*, *Dismiss*, the
undo of the last one applied (`Undo: back to 2`), auto-tune and the bounds, saved per machine; read again on
`machine.recorded`.

**Job cost profiles** (part 4 of the issue). What a finished job costs its machine, so the next parts can place a job by
its expected cost. Read on demand; nothing new is kept and no migration: the runs are the job's own events, the costs
the machine and usage samples (both kept for the history retention).
- **Job run** (`MachineHistoryRepository.jobRuns`, `src/store/machine-history.ts`, SQL). A `job.claimed` on a machine
  and the job's next event of `job.finished`, `job.failed`, `job.cancelled`, `job.requeued` or `job.parked` (by event
  order), that ended in the last 30 days (`JOB_COST_WINDOW_DAYS`). A claim followed by another claim (no end recorded)
  is no run.
- **Machine baseline**: the average CPU busy, memory used and disk used of the machine's samples with no lane in use over
  the same 30 days. A machine with no such sample has no baseline, and its runs no resource cost (absent, never read as
  0: no implicit fallback).
- **One lane's share**, per sample in the run (`at` in `[claim, end)`): the sample's use less the baseline, never below
  0, divided by the lanes in use (at least 1). Per run, the average and the peak (`ResourceCost`) of CPU busy (a share of
  the machine), memory and disk (bytes), and the average lanes in use.
- **Usage burned**: per usage window (its name, else the source's) of the machine's own usage samples (a budget for every
  machine is shared by all of them and left out; informational readings too), the rise in the share of the limit from
  the run's first sample to its last; a reset in the run reads as no rise. Divided by the run's average lanes in use.
- **Job cost profile** (`jobCostProfiles`, `src/decider/job-costs.ts`, pure): one per job whose last run in the window
  ended `finished` or `failed`, over all its runs there: durations add up, averages are weighted by samples, the peak is
  the highest, usage adds up. `repo`: the job's source repository; `kind` (**job cost kind**): `research`, `proposal`,
  else `code`; `template`: the template of its last run's machine, when that machine is a sandbox box listed now.
- **Groups** (`jobCostGroups`): per repository, job cost kind and template, the jobs, the failed, and the mean of each
  figure over the profiles that have it, most jobs first. A profile with no repository or template is in no group of it.
- `GET /api/lanes/costs` (`JobCosts`: `at`, `windowDays`, the latest 100 profiles newest first, and `groups` over every
  profile), and `hopper lanes costs` (JSON, the same route). Machines shows a *Job costs* panel
  (`ui/src/views/job-costs.tsx`): the groups by kind, repository or template, read again on `machine.recorded`.
- Not in the issue's list and not known to the hopper: an `artifact` or `maintenance` job kind. The hopper keeps no field
  that says so (an artifact deliverable is a line of the issue's text), so those jobs count as `code` until one exists.

**The graph** (part 6 of the issue). One machine's resource graph (`GET /api/machines/:id/history`, "Machine resources
over time") overlays what lane tuning reads. Beside its resource lines and its lanes in use (a share of its lane cap,
dashed), it carries:
- `usage`: the usage that limits the machine, at the resource step — the lines of its own usage samples and of a
  budget every machine shares (machine id `''`), as the usage graph draws them (`UsageHistoryQuery.limiting`,
  `src/store/usage-history.ts`). Another machine's readings are not in it.
- `laneChanges`: its `lanes.applied` and `lanes.undone` in the range, oldest first, as the plan's `changes` reads them
  (`laneChangeOf`, `src/domain/lane-tuning.ts`). A hand edit of the lanes is no event: the lanes in use line shows its new
  cap only.
`GET /api/machines/history` (every machine) carries neither. On Machines, the card's *Resources, lanes and usage* opens
it (`machineLines`, `ui/src/model/machine-history.ts`): the usage lines in one colour of their own after the resources,
a week dashed and an informational one dotted and hidden, as on the usage graph; each lane change a dotted line down
the graph in the lanes colour (`GraphLine.marks`), named in the hover box when the pointer is within half a step of it
(`marksAt`): `Applied: 2 → 4 lanes, by <who>. <reason>`, `Undone: 4 → 2 lanes, by <who>`.

**Placement by expected cost** (part 7 of the issue; `src/decider/placement-cost.ts`, pure). A waiting job's **expected
cost** (`ExpectedCost`) is the job cost group it falls in: its repository's group, else its job cost kind's, with 3 jobs or
more (`MIN_EXPECTED_COST_JOBS`) and a CPU or memory figure; else it has none. The engine reads the groups again with
each lane recommendation record (every minute) and at `GET /api/lanes/costs`, and keeps them in memory
(`engine.laneTuning.expected`); a Decision never reads the runs. `DecisionInputs.expectedCosts` holds each waiting job's
expected cost (none for a job resuming in its pane), so a stored Decision shows what it read. In step 7 ("The decider"),
of the machines a job may go to, the ones where its expected cost **fits** go first: the machine's last resource reading
plus the expected costs this Decision placed there before, plus the job's own — its memory peak and its average CPU —,
stays below resource pressure (memory 90%, CPU 95%, `RESOURCE_PRESSURE`). A machine with no reading, or a figure it does
not read, fits. When it fits nowhere, every machine stays: the cost is a preference, never a hold, and the job is placed
as before. The start reason names it: `expected cost (repo o/r, 4 jobs): memory peak 3 GiB, CPU 12%`, with `, fits no
machine` when so. A priority lane, placement pressure and the most room still choose among the machines where it fits.

**The Decider** (part 8 of the issue; "Decider calls", `src/engine/lane-calls.ts`, `src/decider/lane-calls.ts`). Two
decision points, Jev first, these rules the fallback and the envelope: Jev never picks outside what the rules allow.
- `lane-count`. When `record` finds a machine's recommendation by the rules changed (its lanes or its configured lanes),
  Jev is asked before `lanes.recommended` is recorded. Options (`laneCountOptions`): from one fewer than the lower of the
  configured and the recommended lanes to the higher of them, within the bounds — never past the headroom, as the rules
  recommend no more; fewer than two, Jev is not asked. Jev reads the rules' recommendation and reason, the headroom, the
  usage band and the limits, the bounds, the lane load and lane progress per lane count, and each of the machine's lanes'
  reliability (issue #535, the priority lanes' figures). A machine the blast-radius gate keeps is consequential: its
  lanes are never Jev's. Applied (active, sure), the pick is the machine's recommendation (`withJevLanes`): `lanes`,
  `confidence` Jev's, `reason` `Jev picked 3 lanes at 90%; the rules: 4 lanes, <their reason>`, `decidedBy: jev`, and
  `rules` the rules' own; `lanes.recommended` carries the same. It stands until the rules' recommendation or the
  configured lanes move (a change of the point's mode does not take it back), and survives a restart (read from the
  last `lanes.recommended`). An admin applies, dismisses and undoes it as any. In shadow the rules' recommendation stands,
  and Jev's pick is compared with the admin's act. One record runs at a time, so a change asks Jev once.
- `job-machine`. A waiting job that is not pinned and not resuming in its pane, when two or more machines online can
  take it (its executor, a usable work tree, not kept by the gate), asks Jev once per waiting spell: at `job.queued`, and
  on each tick for any not asked yet (after a restart), 4 at most at once. Options: those machines. Jev reads the job (its
  executor, priority, job cost kind, repository, expected cost) and each machine's lanes, lanes in use, last resource
  reading and lanes' reliability. Applied, it is a **placement pick** (`DecisionInputs.placementPicks`): in step 7, of the
  machines where the job may go and its expected cost fits, the picked one goes first (`jevPicked`), and the start reason
  says `Jev picked laptop at 95%`; when the picked machine is not among them, the job is placed as before. A free lane
  claims a job before Jev answers, so most picks are `too_late` and compared at once with the machine the job got; the
  rest are compared at its claim (`decidedBy: placement`). A claim or a cancel forgets the pick.

Tests: `test/decider/lane-calls.test.ts` (the lanes Jev may pick, its applied lanes, a placement pick first or passed over),
`test/integration/decider-lanes.test.ts` (the real daemon, Jev as a double: `lane-count` in shadow compared with an
Apply, active as the recommendation and applied, below the threshold; `job-machine` in shadow compared with the machine
the job got, active where the held job goes, one machine not asked), `test/decider/lane-tuning.test.ts` (headroom: none without history, pressure and its resource, a few pressured
samples, the room past the most seen, one lane count; the recommendation: free, near, soft, hard, bounds, off, offline,
no history; slow progress: lane progress per machine and lane count, the failure rise over fewer lanes, too few runs or
too small a rise, resource pressure first at fewer lanes, only the machine's own runs; what an admin can do: apply, nothing to apply, dismissed until it moves, undo while the lanes are its
lanes), `test/integration/lane-tuning.test.ts` (the real daemon: the plan from samples, slow progress from seeded runs, near the soft limit, settings
and refusals, the record once per change after a resource record and no lanes changed by it, Apply as the machine's
lanes in the plugins config, the decider and the usage report, its refusals, Dismiss until the recommendation moves,
Undo and its refusals after a hand edit, `hopper lanes plan`, `tune`, `apply`, `dismiss`, `undo`),
`test/store/tenant-migration-38.test.ts` (the applied lanes become configured lanes; the mode goes),
`test/decider/placement-cost.test.ts` (the expected cost: the repository's group, else the kind's, too few jobs; a
machine passed over for memory or CPU, one with no reading kept, the jobs placed before in the Decision counted, fits no
machine), `test/integration/placement-cost.test.ts` (the real daemon: with no history the old order; with seeded runs
the job goes where its memory peak fits, and says so), `test/decider/job-costs.test.ts` (job cost kind, a profile per finished or failed job, runs added up, groups),
`test/integration/job-costs.test.ts` (the real daemon: a run's share net of the baseline, its usage burned, a parked job
left out, `hopper lanes costs`), `test/integration/machine-history.test.ts` (one machine's graph: the usage that limits it, its lane changes in
range; every machine's graph carries neither), `test/ui/machine-history.test.ts` (the usage lines and the lane change marks),
`test/ui/usage-history.test.ts` (a mark named under the pointer), `test/ui/job-costs.test.ts`, `test/ui/job-costs-view.test.ts` (the panel and its groupings),
`test/ui/lane-tuning.test.ts` (the model), `test/ui/lane-tuning-view.test.ts` (the panel: the line, Save sends what
changed, crossing bounds refused, Apply and Dismiss, a dismissed one, the history, undo, a viewer reads only).

## Repositories with no checks (issue #677, 2026-10-10)

In a job repository with no checks, yolo mode merges a ready pull request that nothing verified (the grace window above
lets it). The last part of issue #677 finds those repositories, warns of them, and recommends the job that adds checks.

**Has checks** (`src/domain/repo-checks.ts` `repoChecksState`, pure). A repository has checks when its default branch
requires a status check — its branch protection (`GET /repos/{r}/branches/{b}`, `protection.required_status_checks`) or a
ruleset (`GET /repos/{r}/rules/branches/{b}`) —, when a file in `.github/workflows` runs on pull requests (its `on:` names
`pull_request` or `pull_request_target`, `runsOnPullRequests`, parsed with `yaml`), or when one of its five newest pull
requests had checks (GraphQL `statusCheckRollup`, as the GitHub source reads it). With none of the three: `no checks`.
GitHub out of reach, no connection, or not read yet: `unknown`, with the reason, never `no checks`. The workflow files
are read through the contents API, a permission the hopper's GitHub App has; the Actions API needs one it does not ask
for. All of it is read with the person's own GitHub connection (`src/repo-checks/github.ts`, the same binding and token
renewal as Report a bug; `UserGitHubProxy.repoChecks`).

**Never at read time** (issue #1250, 2026-10-15). Each job repository's last read is kept in the user's database
(`repo_checks`, tenant migration 64, `RepoChecksRead`: when, what was found, the reason a read failed, the queued job,
when it is read again, and the answers' ETags), so a restart reads nothing again. `GET /api/repo-checks`
(`src/repo-checks/service.ts`) answers only from it and never reads GitHub: a repository never read is `unknown` with no
`checkedAt`; one read now has `reading`. GitHub is read in the background, one read per repository at a time, a second
ask joining the read under way:

- **Refresh** (`POST /ui/api/repo-checks/refresh`, operator; `repo` for one): Sources' Repository setup has the button.
  It answers at once with the list, `reading` on each repository it reads.
- **The schedule** (`tick`, every minute, with the user's runtime): each repository whose `nextAt` passed. That is 30
  minutes after a read (`FRESH_MS`); after a failure, 1 minute (`RETRY_MS`), doubled with each failure in a row, at most
  30 (`MAX_RETRY_MS`), and never before GitHub's rate limit lets it (`retryAt`). A failure keeps what was read before,
  as of when it was read, with the reason.
- `?repo=owner/name` reads that one repository now, which is what `hopper repo checks <repo>`
  (`src/cli-operator-repo.ts`) asks.

**Conditional reads** (`src/repo-checks/conditional.ts`). Every GET of a read is sent with the ETag of the answer kept
from the read before (`If-None-Match`); GitHub's 304, which costs no call, is answered with what was kept. Answers are
kept by route and parameters, not by token, so a renewed token keeps them. A 404 or 403 has no ETag — a release branch
the repository does not have, branch protection only an admin sees —: it is kept as refused, and answered again with no
call while the repository's own answer (read first, the anchor) is unchanged; a new branch or permission changes that
answer, and each refusal is asked again. GraphQL has no conditional request, so the newest pull requests' check rollups
are read only when they decide the state: no required check and no workflow on pull requests found (else `pullRequests`
is `{ read: 0, withChecks: 0 }`). An unchanged repository with checks is all 304s. All calls go through the shared rate
limiter (issue #436), as before. Where the app is installed, which Sources shows beside them, is kept the same way
(issue #1250 part 2, "Sign in with GitHub, and work through that connection": **Install status**).

**The recommendation.** A repository with no checks, not dismissed, recommends the job "Add PR checks to <repo>"
(`addChecksJob`: find the stack; add a GitHub Actions workflow on pull requests for the typecheck, the lint, the tests and
the build; make them pass; make them required status checks where the token allows, else say how a person sets them).
**Queue job** (`POST /ui/api/repo-checks/queue`, operator) files it as the person's own issue with the hopper label,
assigned to their connected account, so a job source takes it as any other job. An open issue with the hopper label and
that title is answered instead (`kind: exists`), and is shown as `queued as #N` in place of the button. One
`repo_checks.job_queued`. A repository that has checks, or whose checks are unknown, is refused (409). The label is the
job sources' default `hopper`; a source with another `label` option does not take it. **Dismiss**
(`POST /ui/api/repo-checks/dismiss`) hides the recommendation for one repository and keeps the warning; `dismissed: false`
brings it back. Dismissals are the user's setting (`repoChecksDismissed`, `owner/repo` lowercased; absent: none), one
`repo_checks.dismissed` per change. The recommendation goes away by itself once checks run: the next read finds them.

**The UI** (`ui/src/views/pull-requests.tsx`). The header names every repository with no checks, and says yolo merges
unverified code there when yolo mode is on for any of them. A repository's group has a `no checks` badge and a warning,
with the recommended job, Queue job and Dismiss for an operator.

**GitHub text.** The job's issue is the person's own act, through their own connection: the eighth exception to the
"GitHub text is neutral" rule (AGENTS.md). Its text is fixed and names no person.

**Persisted state.** One new settings record, `repoChecksDismissed`; a build before this one ignores it. The table
`repo_checks` (issue #1250): derived data, a table only; the build before runs on it.

Tests: `test/repo-checks/checks.test.ts` (the triggers, the state, the job's text), `test/repo-checks/service.test.ts`
(a list reads nothing; Refresh is coalesced; the schedule and its backoff), `test/repo-checks/conditional.test.ts` (304s
and kept refusals), `test/integration/repo-checks-local.test.ts` (loads make no GitHub call; an unchanged repository is
all 304s; a restart keeps the reads and their ETags), `test/integration/repo-checks.test.ts`
(the real daemon and CLI, GitHub a fake on loopback: each of the three makes checks, none makes no checks with the
recommendation; Queue job files the issue once; a job queued by hand is found; Dismiss and back; checks added drop the
recommendation; GitHub down and no connection say unknown; `hopper repo checks`), `test/ui/pull-requests-view.test.ts`
(the header, the warning, Queue job and Dismiss post the repository, a queued job's link, a viewer has no buttons).

## Repository setup (issue #652, 2026-10-11)

Requirement 8 of issue #652. A job pushes only to a branch of its own work (part 1), and yolo mode merges a job's pull request
only once a check passed (parts 1 and 2; since issue #805 whatever the job's origin). Nothing in the hopper keeps anyone else off a release branch: GitHub
does. So the hopper checks each job repository's setup, and Sources warns when it is not as asked. The owner's steps
are in deploy.md "Repository setup".

**What is asked** (`src/domain/repo-setup.ts`, pure). Each **guarded branch** — the default branch, and each release
branch (`RELEASE_BRANCHES`: `main`, `master`, `dev`, `beta`, `stable`) the repository has — needs a pull request, requires
a status check, and takes no force push. Secret scanning and push protection are on. "No direct push except by the
owner" is the pull request rule: GitHub lets a repository admin bypass it, and nobody else.

**How it is read** (`src/repo-checks/setup.ts`), with the person's own GitHub connection, beside the checks above and
in the same read: `GET /repos/{r}` (the default branch, `security_and_analysis`), and per guarded branch
`GET /repos/{r}/branches/{b}` (`protected`, its required checks; 404: the repository has no such branch, skipped),
`GET /repos/{r}/rules/branches/{b}` (the rulesets' rules: `pull_request`, `non_fast_forward`, `required_status_checks`)
and, for a protected branch, `GET /repos/{r}/branches/{b}/protection` (`required_pull_request_reviews`,
`allow_force_pushes`). A ruleset's rule counts by itself. A branch that is not `protected` has no branch protection.

**Unread is not off.** GitHub shows the branch protection and `security_and_analysis` only to a repository admin. A 403
or 404 on the protection, or no `security_and_analysis`, makes that point **unread** (`null`), never "off": a
connection that is no admin must not make a protected branch look open. The state (`repoSetup`): `not set up` when any
point is off, with each problem in words; else `unknown` when any point is unread, with each one; else `set up`. Not read,
or GitHub out of reach: `unknown`. The hopper's GitHub App asks for no administration permission for this: a person who
wants every point read connects as a repository admin, or checks the settings by hand.

**Where it shows.** `GET /api/repo-checks` answers `setup: { state, problems, unread }` for each job repository, and
`found.setup` holds what was read (`{ branches: [{ branch, pullRequest, statusCheck, forcePushBlocked }], secretScanning,
pushProtection }`); `hopper repo checks <repo>` prints the same. Sources (`ui/src/views/repo-setup.tsx`) shows a
"Repository setup" section under GitHub: a line naming the repositories not set up and those not known, then each job
repository with its state, its problems, what GitHub did not show, and when it was read (`read 5m ago`, `reading
GitHub…`, `not read yet`), with **Refresh**. It is read when the repository's checks are: on Refresh or on the schedule,
never at a page load (issue #1250, "Repositories with no checks"). No event: a read is GitHub's state, not an act.

**Persisted state.** The read is kept with the checks, in `repo_checks` (issue #1250).

Tests: `test/repo-checks/setup.test.ts` (each point from what GitHub shows, the state and the words),
`test/integration/repo-setup.test.ts` (the real daemon and CLI, GitHub a fake on loopback that shows the branch protection
and the security settings only to an admin: set up, not set up with each problem, a ruleset read without admin, a
protected branch read without admin is unread, GitHub down, `hopper repo checks`), `test/ui/repo-setup-view.test.ts` (the
section, the line, the problems, the unread note; no section with no job repository or no answer).

## Updates only to a merged pull request with passing checks (issue #652, 2026-10-11)

Requirement 9 of issue #652. A branch protection (part 4) keeps a direct push off `dev`, `beta` and `stable` only when it
is set up, and an admin can bypass it. So the updater checks the commit itself before it offers it.

**The release check** (`src/update/release-check.ts`, the `ReleaseCheck` port). When the channel's head is newer than the
install, the updater asks whether it is the merge of a pull request whose checks passed, before it says anything:

1. `GET /repos/{r}/commits/{sha}/pulls`: a pull request with `merged_at` whose `merge_commit_sha` is the head. This
   answer lags a merge (it can be empty for a minute or more), and it can name only a later pull request that holds the
   commit (a promotion from `dev` to `beta`). So when it names none (issue #913): `GET /repos/{r}/commits/{sha}`, and a
   head with two parents whose message starts "Merge pull request #N " is checked against `GET /repos/{r}/pulls/N`, the
   same way. Still none: the head is a direct push, or a pull request's own commit, and it is **held**.
2. `GET /repos/{r}/commits/{head of that pull request}/check-runs`: every check run completed, each `success`, `neutral`
   or `skipped`, at least one `success`. No check runs: held ("no checks is not passing", as for yolo mode). A check that
   failed or has not finished: held, with its name.

Asked of `https://api.github.com` with a token, never with none (issue #822): github.com gives a request with no token
60 calls an hour per address, shared with everything else on that address, and an update was held on "API rate limit
exceeded for <address>". The token is the GitHub connection of the oldest user who has one on github.com
(`releaseAccount`; a GitHub Enterprise connection's token is no good there), asked at each check, and renewed once when
GitHub refuses it (`tokenCaller`, as the GitHub proxy). The calls go through the shared rate limiter ("The shared rate
