limiter"), so they are conditional and paced like every other call. No such connection: the update is held with why, and
GitHub is not asked. An update repository not on github.com, or GitHub not answering, holds the update: it is not offered
when it cannot be checked. A passed answer is kept for the commit; any other, "not the merge of a pull request" too (issue
#913), is asked again after five minutes. GitHub refusing for the rate (403 or 429 with no calls left, or `retry-after`) holds
the update until GitHub's reset time, with "GitHub rate-limited the hopper: it asks about <commit> again at HH:MM UTC" as
the reason, and GitHub is not asked again before then.

**Held** (`UpdateState` `held`). The status carries the target and `reason`; no `update.available`, no auto-update, and
`apply` answers 409 "no update available". The daemon logs `hopper: update held: …` once per target and reason. The update
notice shows "Update held: <reason>" with the commit, and nothing to apply or run. A passing target carries
`target.pullRequest` (`{ number, url }`); `update.available` records its number (`pullRequest`, an additive field). The
notice names the commit and links the pull request: `stable 1a2b3c4 · pull request #775, checks passed`.

**An image.** The notice's commands pull the channel's tag, which the image workflow builds from the branch head the
updater checked. A tag moved by a newer push after the check is not checked again by the commands: the next check holds
or offers that newer commit, and the notice changes with it.

**Persisted state.** None: the verdicts are kept in memory.

Tests: `test/update/release-check.test.ts` (GitHub a fake on loopback: passed, a direct push, no checks, failed, still
running, not on GitHub, GitHub down, what is asked again and when), `test/update/updater.test.ts` (offered with its pull
request; held: no announcement, no apply, auto-update on; nothing asked at the head), `test/integration/update.test.ts`
(the daemon: held over `GET /api/update`, apply 409), `test/ui/update.test.ts` and `test/ui/update-notice.test.ts` (the
words, the commit line and the link).

**Left of issue #652:** the vault helper only by a per-job grant (requirement 5), and the issue's open points.

## Report a bug (issue #694, 2026-10-10)

Owner request: people who use any hopper need a way to report a hopper bug. Every hopper is connected to GitHub, so it
files the issue itself, with that connection. A job on a beta install that wanted to file a hopper issue had no way to,
and tried a `gh` device sign-in instead.

**Where a report goes.** Every **bug report** goes to the hopper's own repository, `henningfutrell/hopper`
(`REPORT_REPO`), filed through the person's **own** GitHub connected account (`UserGitHubProxy.reports`,
`src/users/github-proxy.ts`), so GitHub shows it as filed by that person — not the hopper's oldest user's connection, as
the GitHub proxy's is. It gets the label `user-report` (`REPORT_LABEL`), no `hopper` label and no assignee: intake takes
only `hopper`-labelled issues assigned to the connected account (issue #387), so a report never starts a job, and a
person who wants one labels it after triage, through the intake gate (issue #655). GitHub keeps a label only from a
person who may triage the repository: a report by anyone else arrives with no label, which changes nothing above.
Filing needs the hopper's app installed on the repository with issues write (the app reaches only the repositories it is
installed on); without that, GitHub refuses it, and the person reads why.

**The report context** (`reportContext`, `src/bug-reports/context.ts`, pure). What the form fills in: the System line
only (issue #2478) — the platform, its release, the architecture and the Node version. Never the hopper's version or
revision, its install type, a job, its failure or its log: a report is a public issue, and none of them belongs there.
The generator makes no other line, so nothing else can reach GitHub; the person adds what they want to say in their own
sections. Masked before the person sees it (`maskReportText`): the host name by value, GitHub tokens, keys (as the log
mask, issue #685), and `maskAddresses` (`src/secrets/mask.ts`): IPv4, IPv6 (full or with `::`, so a time is none), host
names under a private suffix (`.local`, `.lan`, `.home`, `.internal`, `.corp`, `.ts.net`) and the user name in a home
directory. The person reads and edits it; what they leave in is sent.

**Filing** (`createBugReports`, `src/bug-reports/service.ts`). `POST /ui/api/bug-reports { title, happened, expected?,
context?, jobId?, commentOn?, force? }`, operator. First the **duplicate search**: the title's words (three letters or
more, common words out, at most six, `searchTerms`) against the open `user-report` issues' titles (`GET /search/issues`,
`in:title`, the words joined by OR); a title with half of them or more is similar (`similarityOf`), at most five, best
first. When there are some, nothing is filed and they are answered (`kind: similar`); the person adds the report to one
(`commentOn`: a comment with the title in bold and the same sections, `kind: commented`) or files a new one anyway
(`force`). A failed search files as if there were none. The body is the person's sections with text — What happened,
What I expected, Context — and the note "Filed with Report a bug in a hopper."; GitHub tokens and keys are always
masked in the title and body. Each outcome is one event on the person's log, never with the text:
`bug_report.filed { repo, kind: issue | comment, number, url, jobId?, by }`, or `bug_report.failed { repo, error, jobId?,
by }` — 503 with no GitHub connection, 502 when GitHub refuses. `POST /ui/api/bug-reports/context {}` answers
`{ context, repo }` and changes nothing. A report's `jobId` stays on the hopper: its row and its events name the job
(issue #1147 reads it), the text sent to GitHub does not.

**Jobs report too** (`fileForJob`). A running job files a hopper bug with `sh "$HOPPER_GH" report bug --title T (--body
TEXT | --body-file F) [--comment-on N] [--force]` — a subcommand of `hopper-gh` ("GitHub through the hopper"), not a
second script: one script, one token, one place a job looks for anything GitHub. The proxy checks the job's token and
the limits (3 per job, 10 per machine, in any day), then files it by the person's path, with the **job's own user's**
connection, so the job never signs in to GitHub. No person reads a job's text before it is sent, so its title and body
pass through the whole report mask (`maskReportText`), not only the token mask; its context is the hopper's System line;
the body ends "Filed by a job with Report a bug in a hopper." (no job id, issue #2478); `bug_report.filed` and `.failed` carry
`fromJob: true` and `by: job <id>`. Similar open reports are answered **409** with the list and what to do next
(`--comment-on N`, or `--force`): nothing is filed until the job chooses. The label is still `user-report`, so a job's
report never starts a job either.

**UI.** The user menu (issue #666) has *Report a bug* for an operator or admin (`ui/src/app/bug-report.tsx`): a form
with a title, what happened, what you expected, and the context, editable, under a line that says what was masked and
to remove anything private. Send is off until there is a title and what happened. Similar open reports are listed with
*Add to #N* each and *File a new report*; after filing, the line names the issue and links it. Every hand-off card,
failure row and question card has *Report a bug* too (`ReportBugButton`), for an operator or admin: the same form and
context; the report's row names that job, the text does not. A problem card has none: it is many jobs, and each of its failures has its own row.

**Kept and sent later.** With no GitHub connection, or when GitHub cannot take the report now — no answer, 401 (the
connection refused or ended), 403 or 404 (no access to the repository: the app is not installed there), 429, or a 5xx
(`sendLater`) — the report is not refused: it is a **kept report**. Its row in the person's store (`bug_reports`, tenant
migration 37, `src/store/bug-reports.ts`) holds the title, the body as it would have been filed, and a comment's target;
the answer is `{ kind: kept, id, problem }` and `bug_report.kept` records it. GitHub refusing the report itself (a 422)
still fails it (502, `bug_report.failed`): sending it again would fail the same way. The form says the hopper keeps it
and sends it later, and links Your reports. A job's report is kept the same way (`hopper-gh report bug` prints `kind:
kept`; its help says not to send it again). The duplicate search ran before it was kept, or was skipped: a kept report
is sent as it was, a new issue or a comment on the report the person chose.

**Your reports** (`src/bug-reports/later.ts`, `ui/src/views/bug-reports.tsx`). Every report filed or kept is a row:
title, state (`waiting`, `open`, `closed`), kind (`issue`, or `comment` on the open report `number`), number and URL
once on GitHub, who filed it (`by`, `jobId`, `fromJob`), the tries and the last check. The body is dropped once sent: the
issue on GitHub is the record. The send pass (`createReportSender`, one per user, started and stopped with the user's
runtime through `UserGitHubProxy.bugReports`) runs at start and every 10 minutes (`REPORT_SEND_MS`): it sends each
kept report, oldest first, with the person's own connection — `bug_report.filed` with `later: true` and the report's
`id` — or keeps the reason for the next try; then it reads the state of each filed report on GitHub (`GET
/repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{n}`, closed ones too: an issue can be opened again). One pass at a time, so a report is
never sent twice. `GET /api/bug-reports` (never the text) and `POST /ui/api/bug-reports/refresh` (operator: one pass
now) serve Settings → Your reports, which lists them newest first with a Refresh button.

**From the CLI** (`src/cli-operator-report.ts`, issue #623): `hopper report context` prints the context,
masked, to read first; `hopper report bug --title <t> (--happened <text> | --happened-file <f>) [--expected <text>]
[--job <id>] [--context-file <f>] [--comment-on <n>] [--force]` files it by the UI's path — the hopper's context unless
`--context-file` gives the person's own —; `hopper report list` and `hopper report refresh` are Your reports. Each is
the UI's own call under a session minted for it; the answer is JSON.

Tests: `test/integration/bug-reports-jobs.test.ts` (a job's report through the real `hopper-gh`: filed with its user's
connection, masked, marked; similar first, `--comment-on`, `--force`; the daily limit),
`test/bug-reports/context.test.ts` (the context, what it never carries, the masks, the body, the search terms),
`test/integration/bug-reports.test.ts` (the real daemon over the fake GitHub: the context the System line only, also on a job's report, filing as the person
with the label and no assignee, a similar report offered, a comment, filing anyway, kept with no connection, a refused
draft), `test/integration/bug-reports-later.test.ts` (kept with no connection and sent once connected; kept while GitHub
refuses access, a comment too; Your reports' states refreshed; a 422 not kept), `test/integration/bug-reports-cli.test.ts`
(`hopper report context|bug|list|refresh`), `test/ui/bug-reports-view.test.ts` (Your reports),
`test/ui/bug-report-view.test.ts` (the form), `test/ui/user-menu.test.ts` (the item, not for a viewer).

## Work trees per repository (issue #691, 2026-10-10)

Owner request: a machine had one work tree, so a job for one repository ran inside another repository's
work tree. The rule: a job works in its own repository's tree, never another's; a repository with no tree
of its own keeps the machine's work tree; a mapped tree that is missing is made (or fails clearly), never
replaced by the machine's.

**As built:**
- **A machine option, `workTrees`** (`local`, `ssh`, `client`; `workTreesOption`,
  `src/plugins/machine-source/attached.ts`): `{"owner/name": "<path>"}`, each path absolute or under `~`,
  each key a repository (`owner/name`), else the instance is refused. Command-bearing, as `workTree` is.
  Carried to `MachineSnapshot.workTrees`. Edited in Plugins (a JSON field); the Machines Edit
  forms keep it; the machine panel shows it (`work trees per repository`).
- **Resolved per job** (`resolvePayload`, `src/executors/herdr/payload.ts`, herdr-claude and the print agents):
  the job's own `cwd` on the machine it is pinned to (a routing rule's) first; then the tree the machine maps the
  job's GitHub repository to, matched in any case (`mappedWorkTree`); then the machine's `workTree`; then the
  jobs directory. A fork uses its parent's repository.
- **Made and cloned when missing**, as the machine's own work tree is: the pane's shell runs `mkdir -p`, then the
  job worktree command fetches or clones the repository in it (issue #361). It is not probed ahead: a mapped tree
  that cannot be used (the home or above it, not writable) fails that job with what the shell said, and the
  machine still takes jobs of other repositories. The issue's other way — a routing rule that sets `workTree`
  without a machine — is not built: a path is one machine's (issue #361), and the map is per machine already.

**Windows clients, the same issue** (dropped by #691 when native Windows was refused, brought back by issue #1348).
Two failures stopped every job on a Windows client:
- **The temp link.** Under Git for Windows (MSYS), `ln -s` copies the directory, or names it `/c/…` where the work
  tree said `C:/…`, so the link check failed and the job ended `hopper-scratch-unusable` in seconds. The scratch
  command runs `tmpCommand` (`src/executors/herdr/start.ts`): when `uname -s` is `MINGW*`, `MSYS*` or `CYGWIN*`
  it makes no temp link and exports `TMPDIR` and `CLAUDE_CODE_TMPDIR` as the scratch dir itself, in the pane's shell,
  where Claude then starts; elsewhere the temp link as before (issue #506).
- **`spawn env ENOENT`.** The client ran each fixed script (discovery, a reap, a survey) as `env -u HOPPER_JOB_ID sh …`,
  and a Windows client has no `env` on its PATH. The client removes the variables itself (`spawnOf`,
  `src/client/spawn.ts`, used by `runArgv` in `src/client/run.ts`) and runs `sh` directly.

Tests: `test/herdr/machine-work-tree.test.ts` (mapped, any case, made when missing, other repository, pinned path wins,
the home refused), `test/plugins/machine-targets.test.ts` (the option, its refusals, command-bearing),
`test/herdr/job-tmp.test.ts` (a Windows shell: no link, TMPDIR is the scratch dir), `test/client/spawn.test.ts`
(no `env` program, the variable removed), `test/ui/machine-work-tree.test.ts` (the panel line).

## The client door and the reach check (issue #695, 2026-10-10)

The case: a job on an attached machine could not push or ask the hopper for GitHub: "Could not resolve host: hopper".
The hopper had given it `HOPPER_URL` with its bare container name, which resolves only inside the hopper's compose
network. The job held no GitHub token (#652), so it was stuck, and it asked the owner for a DNS fix or a `gh` device
sign-in. The same cause as the artifact links of #673. Requirement: every URL the hopper gives a job is one the job's
machine reaches; a client target's jobs need no name resolved; a machine that cannot reach the hopper fails at the job's
start, plainly; a job never falls back to a GitHub sign-in.

**Which URL** (`jobHopperUrl`, `src/github-proxy/reach.ts`, pure). This machine: loopback. A client target: its client
door (below); a client older than it, the URL it dialled in at. An ssh or container target, and a client not dialled
in yet: `reachBase` (`src/artifacts/links.ts`; a person's links use `personBase` there, issue #712): the user's link base (Settings →
Artifacts), else the public URL's origin, else the first LAN name that is an IPv4 address or ends in `.local`, else the
first LAN name. A bare name is given only when the hopper knows no other: an agent box in the hopper's own network
reaches it; any other machine fails the reach check, which names the setting that fixes it. None at all: the job gets no
way to the hopper, as before.

**The client door** (`src/client/door.ts`). The hopper client listens on `127.0.0.1`, on a port the OS picks, and passes
each `/job/` request on to the hopper's URL as the client reaches it: the URL it joined at and dials in to, which works
by definition. It says the door's URL in `/release` (`door`); the hopper keeps it on the machine snapshot
(`client.door`, only a loopback URL is taken) and gives it to each job there as `HOPPER_URL`. So hopper-gh, git,
hopper-skill, hopper-artifact and the job stream reach the hopper with no DNS and no address of the hopper's. The door
is not a tunnel down the link: the link is HTTP/2 with the client as its server, so the client opens a request of its
own per job request, as the vault's ask does (`askHopper`). It adds no right: every `/job/` route still asks for the job's
proxy token, and the hopper's Host guard sees the Host the client joined with. It takes only `/job/` paths (else 404) and
only its own Host, `127.0.0.1:<port>` or `localhost:<port>` (else 421), so a web page that rebinds a name to loopback
reaches nothing through it. Answers stream through (the job stream, git). A hopper it cannot reach is held, below.

**The door waits instead of failing** (issue #752, path 2 of the field-survival kit). A request whose connection to the
hopper cannot be made (refused, no route, a name not resolved, no connection within 10 s) is held: the door notes when
the hopper went **out of reach** and tries again with backoff (0.25 s, doubling, at most 5 s) until `DOOR_HOLD_MS` (120 s,
the reconnect grace's default) from that time. The hopper back → the request goes on, and the door logs how long it was
away. The hold over → 503, `Retry-After: 30`, `the hopper is out of reach since <ISO time>; wait, do not sign in another
way.` and the URL; while it stays away, a later request gets that answer after one try. The door sends a request again
only when no connection was made, so the hopper never got it: each connection is fresh (no keep-alive socket that could
have carried it), and the body goes on only once connected. A connection that breaks after that is a 502, as before: the
hopper may have done the write. So no write needs a de-duplication key — the audit of `/job/` writes the proposal asked
for comes out empty — and a lost answer stays the job's to read (`pr view`, `issue view`). Nothing is cached: no token, no
text, no buffered write; every write still goes through the hopper with the job's proxy token, so no owner escalation,
mint, push or grant can happen while it is away. Out of scope: a proxy in front of the hopper that answers 502 itself
(the door passes that answer on), and a hopper that takes the connection and then hangs.

**The scripts obey Retry-After** (`hcurl`, `src/github-proxy/retry-after.ts`). hopper-gh, hopper-skill and
hopper-artifact send each request through one shell function: a 503 with `Retry-After` is waited out (at most 60 s) and
sent again, `RETRY_AFTER_TRIES` (4) tries in all; then the script prints the door's reason and exits as for a no
(hopper-artifact: 3, cannot reach). Not curl's own `--retry`: it sends a 500 or a 502 again too. git has no Retry-After:
the door's hold is all it gets, and after it git fails with the 503. The protocol line `OUT_OF_REACH_LINE` tells the job:
on that answer, keep the local work going (edit, build, test, commit), wait to push and to ask the hopper, then try
again; never sign in another way. Path 1 (the hopper holds the job through a link outage, "Link-lost hold") and path 3
(a box-side watchdog with a time limit) are their own changes.

**The reach check** (`src/client/reach.ts`). At each start, resume and turn, before the job's files are kept,
`placeCredentials` asks the machine's shell `reach(url)` for the URL the job is given: the fixed script, through the
machine's own connection — this machine, ssh, or the client's `POST /reach {url}` (signed like every client call). It is
curl, which the job's tools use too, at `<url>/job/stream` without a token: any answer of the hopper's (401 included) is a
reach; no answer, a name that does not resolve, a refused address (421) or a 5xx (a proxy whose hopper does not answer)
is not, and curl missing is said. Not reached: the reason is `this machine cannot reach the hopper at <url>: <why>` and
the action (`REACH_ACTION`: set an address this machine reaches as the link base, or join the machine as a client
target), never a mid-job question. A resuming job fails at once with it: it returns to the pane it holds there.

**A job keeps its way to the hopper** (issue #2040). A reach check or a file write that cannot run (the machine's
connection failed at that moment) is no answer that the machine is out of reach. A fresh job then runs without the
proxy, and its progress says why. A job that ran there before (`job.agentSession` known: a resume or a turn) keeps the
variables its start gave it — `HOPPER_GH`, `HOPPER_URL`, git's way to GitHub —, which point at the files its start
placed, and its progress says that they were not placed again. Before, it ran on with none: a lane pod's job that had
opened its pull requests found `HOPPER_GH` empty at its last step and ended failed. A failed job is also looked at once
more at its source before it is assessed, whatever its failure says ("Failure assessment", `lookedAgain`): one that
delivered ends finished.

**A resumed session never goes on with no way to the hopper** (issue #2233, a regression of #1465). A placement that
fails is tried once more first. A job that reopens in a new pane after the end of its run (a continued job, a parked job)
has no files of its start left: that end's reap removed its credentials dir. Its start's variables would point at
nothing, so it fails with `this machine cannot reach the hopper: its way to the hopper was not placed again for the
resume (<why>)`, never resumed without it. That failure, and a job's own report that `HOPPER_URL` or `HOPPER_GH` is
missing or that it cannot reach the hopper, is the known cause `no-way-to-hopper` (transient, retry): it runs again as a
new job, placed afresh. Continue on its hand-off runs a new job too (`continueResumes` false): the session's history
keeps telling its agent the hopper is out of reach, whatever its new pane holds. The reach check's own text (`cannot
reach the hopper at <url>`) is not this cause: it is the machine's. A checkpoint restore's own line (issue #2316, `hopper: the job has no way to
the hopper`) is this cause too, never the restore script's text that the pane's screen echoes.

**A machine out of reach takes no new job** (issue #1920, `src/engine/reach-holds.ts`). A job must not fail for the
machine it was placed on. The case: a long-lived sandbox box, a registered machine no probe reads, was offered ordinary
jobs, and its jobs were given a loopback URL it does not reach: each failed at once. Now a fresh start that the reach check
finds out of reach holds that machine: for ten minutes (`REACH_HOLD_MS`) it carries the reason as its **address
problem**, so the decider holds a new job there (`addressHolds`) and the Machines view shows it off-network. The job is
queued again (`job.requeued`, the reason), never failed, and is placed on a machine that reaches the hopper, or waits,
held with the reason. After the ten minutes the next job placed there checks again. The hold is in the memory of the
hopper whose start found it: a restart forgets it, and the next start there finds it again. A probe's own address
problem (an ssh target's) wins over it. A client older than the check has no `/reach`: its jobs start unchecked, and
the hopper loads its release there as for any client.

**A check in a stall is no proof** (issue #2427, `src/domain/loop-held.ts`). The machine's check waits for the
hopper's own answer, so a stall of the hopper's event loop makes every machine fail at the same moment: once a ten-second
stall held every ssh seat for ten minutes, and the jobs waited on the one not-ready client left. The event loop watchdog
("The event loop watchdog") gives each process one reading: how long the loop was held since a moment
(`loopHeldSince`). A reach check that fails after the loop was held 2 s or more (`LOOP_HELD_DOUBT_MS`) since it began
is checked again, once the loop is free. When that check fails in a stall too, the job is queued again, but its machine
is not held (`Unreached.loopHeld`). An ssh target's probe whose address check fails in such a stall keeps the address
state it had, and is probed again at the next read of the machines. A hold's reason says when it began and when the next
job placed there checks again. A job's hold or lane wait that names other machines also names the machines held off as not
reaching the hopper (`heldOff`, src/decider/machine-holds.ts), so a hold of every seat does not read as a placement that
targets only the machine left.

**A resumed session never runs with no way to the hopper** (issue #2427). A parked job picked up on its seat in such a
stall reopened its session in a new pane with no `HOPPER_URL`: the seat's probe had found no URL, and `placeCredentials`
gave the pane no variables. The job could not push, ended failed, and its five commits stayed in its worktree on that seat.
Now three things stop that:
- A job that reopens its session in a new pane (parked, continued, or released from its own wait: `reopensPane`,
  src/domain/checkpoints.ts) is held off a machine with an address problem as a new job is (`addressHolds`). It waits for the
  problem to end, its work kept there, or the busy-machine move takes it elsewhere.
- A job placed meanwhile on a machine with an address problem and no URL for its jobs gets `Unreached`, never an empty
  environment. A job that reopens in a new pane goes back to the queue with its session and answer (the no-way move,
  `noWayMove`), as one that resumes elsewhere does. The machine's hold is not made longer for it.
- A run that ends failed with the cause no-way-to-hopper (its session found no `HOPPER_URL` or `hopper-gh`, for any other
  reason) does not fail when it can resume: the hopper takes its checkpoint once more, through the machine's own
  connection, with the commits of its last turn, and the job resumes on another machine from it, as the lost-machine move
  takes a job (`moveNoWay`, src/engine/no-way-move.ts; its `job.parked` is `move: lost_machine`, its `why` says the
  session had no way to the hopper). A job with no checkpoint that holds its agent session, an executor that cannot move
  it, or three such moves already fails as before.

**The reap on a native Windows client** (issue #2427). Node gives a Windows program its argv as one command line, and
writes a `\"` of an argument as `\\\"` there. The sh of Git for Windows (MSYS) reads a backslash as an escape only before a
quote, so it read `\\"` back, and the reap script closed a quote early: `sh: -c: line 1: unexpected EOF while looking for
matching '"'`, and every job there failed after it ran. Only the reap held a `\"`: the runtime config it writes again
before a reset (`CONF_SH`, `src/client/job-runtime.ts`). Its printf formats are now in single quotes. Every fixed script
a client runs is held to the round trip (`test/client/windows-command-line.test.ts`).

**A job's end acts only on its own pane** (issue #2676). A job's executor state names its pane by herdr's id, and herdr
gives ids again once its server starts again (a lane's machine, or a lane box, that started again): the next job on the
lane had the pane whose id an ended job's state still named. That job's cleanup (a cancel while it waited, a deferred
cleanup tried again) sent ctrl+c to that pane and closed it, and the next job's Claude ended with exit code 143. Now the
end of a pane — at a cleanup, a park, a run's end, or the end of the pane a moved job left — first asks whose the pane
is (`ownPane`, `src/executors/herdr/pane-ends.ts`): the job's while its agent runs in it or its tab's label names the job
(the pane key). Another job's pane, or none, gets no key and stays open; the reap, which acts by the job's id, runs all
the same. A pane whose herdr is not reached gets no key either, and the cleanup is tried again. A cancel of a job no
runner holds also clears the lane id an earlier attempt left on it.

**A Windows client's script is not on its command line** (issue #2676). The sh of Git for Windows cut the reap script
near 8 KiB on a native Windows client's command line: `sh: -c: line 2: syntax error: unexpected end of file` (the error
of issue #2427 was the same cut, at another place in the script of that time). There the client puts a `sh -c` script in
the variable `HOPPER_CLIENT_SCRIPT` and gives sh only a short `-c` that takes it out of the environment and runs it
(`CLIENT_SCRIPT_SH`, `src/client/spawn.ts`); the script's arguments stay on the command line.

**Never a GitHub sign-in.** The protocol line on GitHub (`GITHUB_PROXY_LINE`) says: when the hopper cannot be reached,
never start or ask for a GitHub sign-in to get around it; end failed with the reason. A herdr-claude job that reports a
GitHub login again right after it was steered fails (`GITHUB_LOGIN_AGAIN`); before, that login went to the Logins.

**The vault's socket** needs nothing new: the helper asks the client over its socket, and the client asks the hopper at
the URL it joined at.

**Not built.** An ssh target gets no door: its jobs reach the hopper at `reachBase`, and the reach check says when they
cannot. An ssh reverse tunnel would give it one; build it when an ssh target needs it.

Tests: `test/github-proxy/reach.test.ts` (the URL per machine), `test/client/door.test.ts` (a request and a streamed
answer through the door, the refusals, an unreachable hopper: held and sent once when it is back, 503 with Retry-After
after the hold, never sent again once connected), `test/github-proxy/retry-after.test.ts` (each script waits out a 503
with Retry-After, stops after its tries, and never sends a 500 or a plain 503 again), `test/client/reach.test.ts` (the check on this machine and
on a client: reached, a name not resolved, 421, 502, no curl), `test/integration/client-door.test.ts` (a real joined
client: the job is given the door, checked first, and `hopper-skill` works through it),
`test/integration/github-proxy.test.ts` (a job whose machine cannot reach the hopper is queued again at its start, and
the machine holds it, with the action), `test/engine/reach-holds.test.ts` (the hold and its end), `test/herdr/executor-login.test.ts` (a GitHub login reported again fails the job).

## herdr client and server on an ssh target (issue #741, 2026-10-10)

Two seats each had two herdrs: an old one an image baked into `/usr/local/bin` (protocol 17) and herdr's own install in
`~/.local/bin` (protocol 22), which ran the session server. The hopper's ssh calls put `~/.local/bin` after the PATH, so
the old client won, and every job start failed with `client protocol 17 is older than server protocol 22`. The machines
still answered `status: running`, so they showed online and took jobs, and nothing named the cause.

**`~/.local/bin` first.** `REMOTE_PATH` is `PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"`: the herdr that installs and updates itself
there, and that `systemd/hopper-herdr.service` runs the session server from, is the one every call finds. A machine
whose only herdr is on its PATH (an agent box's `/usr/local/bin/herdr`) still finds it. `scripts/attach-machine.sh` and
the Add machine check look it up the same way.

**The probe reads both versions** (`probeHerdrOverSsh`, `src/machines/herdr-version.ts`): after `status server`, it asks
`status client` over the same connection, and keeps `version`, `protocol` and the client's `binary` in
`MachineSnapshot.herdr` (`{ session, client?, server? }`). A **herdr problem** (`MachineSnapshot.herdrProblem`) is named
when the server says `compatible: no`, or (a herdr that does not say) the client's protocol is older than the server's,
or `status server` itself fails with herdr's protocol error: then the machine is online, not offline. A `status client`
that fails says no client version, nothing more.

**A machine with a herdr problem takes no new job** (`herdrHolds`, `src/decider/assign.ts`), as with a work tree or an
address problem: its jobs go to another machine or are held with the reason (`no machine running executor <x> has a
working herdr: <m>: …`, `pinned machine <m>: …`); a job resuming there returns to its pane. The log says it once
(`… online (ssh <m>), takes no new job: <problem>`); Machines shows a `herdr outdated` badge, the versions, and the
problem.

**A job start that fails on the protocol** is the known cause `herdr-outdated` (shared, redirect, scoped to the machine):
its first failure opens the problem `Herdr outdated on <m>`, not a recurrence later. Its check is the machine's herdr
problem: once a probe finds it gone, the problem resolves by itself (`causePresent`, `src/failures/causes.ts`).

**The hopper owns the herdr there** (part 2 of the issue; `src/machines/herdr-owned.ts`, the decision and the commands,
pure; `src/machines/herdr-owned-ssh.ts`, the keeper over ssh). Each probe of an ssh target that runs herdr first runs the
keeper (`probeOwnedHerdr`), then `probeHerdrOverSsh` as above:

- **The hopper's herdr** is the one on the daemon's PATH (`/usr/local/bin/herdr` in the image), its version from
  `herdr --version`, read again every 5 minutes: an update of the hopper brings a new one. The hopper has none, or it
  says no version: nothing is installed, and Machines says why.
- **Installed per version.** When `~/.local/share/hopper/herdr/<version>/herdr` is missing there, the keeper copies the
  hopper's herdr there over the same ssh connection (stdin to a `.part` file, then a rename; the copy must say its
  version). Only to a machine whose `uname -sm` is the hopper's: another platform keeps the lookup by name, and the probe
  says why. The installer at herdr.dev installs only the latest release, so the hopper's own binary is the only herdr
  of a known version.
- **`current` while the server takes it.** The keeper asks the session server through the owned herdr. Compatible, or no
  server running: it links `~/.local/share/hopper/herdr/current` to that version. Every herdr call there starts with
  `REMOTE_HERDR` (`src/executors/ssh.ts`): `current/herdr` when it is executable, else herdr by name from
  `~/.local/bin` and the PATH. Not compatible: the keeper removes the link, so the calls go on through the herdr the
  server takes.
- **The switch** (`decideHerdrSwitch`): restarting the session server from the owned herdr closes every pane there, and
  stopping a container's main process stops the container (and its image starts its own herdr again: a loop). So the
  keeper switches only when all hold: no job of the hopper runs there; no pane is open in the session (counted with
  `pane list`, and counted again just before the stop); the server is not the container's main process — in a
  container (`/run/.containerenv`, `/.dockerenv`) a server with PID 1, or whose parent is PID 1, is; and no switch to
  this version was tried there before (`<version>/switch-tried`, written before the stop, and kept in memory too).
  The switch stops the server (`server stop`), links `current`, and starts it again: by `systemctl --user restart
  hopper-herdr` when the unit there starts from `current` (the session `hopper` only), else as a process of its own
  (`setsid`, else `nohup`). Then it waits up to 10 s for the server. The log says it once.
- **What waits, what holds.** A job or a pane: the switch waits for a later probe, and Machines says so. A server that
  is a container's main process: a **herdr problem** — the machine takes no new job — saying the herdr its image puts in
  place must be updated to the hopper's version. A switch already tried: never again for that version; the note says to
  restart the server by hand. When the probe finds a herdr problem, the keeper's note follows it.
- **Machines** shows the hopper's herdr per ssh target (`MachineSnapshot.herdr.owned`): its version, `in use`, or `not in
  use` and why.
- **`scripts/attach-machine.sh`** copies this machine's herdr to the same versioned path there and links `current`
  (same platform only, else a warning); `systemd/hopper-herdr.service` starts the session server from `current/herdr`,
  else `~/.local/bin/herdr`.

**Not built (carried in the issue).** Seat images: they must not put herdr in `/usr/local/bin`. That change is in the
images, not in this repository. Until it is made, a seat whose session server is the container's main process and
runs another protocol than the hopper's herdr shows the herdr problem above.

Tests: `test/machines/herdr-version.test.ts` (the parse), `test/adapters/ssh-machine-herdr.test.ts` (the probe over the
fake ssh, the snapshot and the log), `test/machines/herdr-owned.test.ts` (the switch decision and the facts),
`test/adapters/ssh-machine-owned-herdr.test.ts` (install, link, switch, once per version, over the fake ssh),
`test/scripts/attach-machine.test.ts` (the install there), `test/herdr/cli-client-ssh.test.ts` (`~/.local/bin` wins over the PATH),
`test/decider/herdr-problem.test.ts` (the hold), `test/failures/signature.test.ts`, `test/failures/assess.test.ts` and
`test/failures/cause-check.test.ts` (the cause, its problem, its check), `test/ui/machine-herdr.test.ts` (the versions on
Machines).

## Trusted origin and request cards (issue #652, 2026-10-10)

Owner requirement (the 2026-10-10 intake security review, paths A + C; path F was the first part, "Git through the
hopper"): the hopper took an open issue with the source label assigned to the user, whoever wrote it, labelled it or
assigned it. The repository is public, so a stranger's text — or an issue a job filed — could become a job. Now **an issue
is a job only from a trusted origin, or from a request card a person approved**, and the job runs the approved text.

**Trusted origin** (`src/domain/intake-origin.ts`, `src/sources/github/origin.ts`). At each sync, for each issue the
source would take and that has no job that has not ended, the source reads the issue's events (`GitHubApi.issueEvents`,
REST `GET /repos/{o}/{r}/issues/{n}/events`, `labeled` and `assigned` only) and names three acts: who wrote it, who added
the source label (the newest `labeled` event of that label), and who assigned it to the user (the newest `assigned`
event of the connected login). Since issue #655 part 17 it also reads who edited the issue's title or body
(`GitHubApi.issueEdits`, GraphQL `userContentEdits` and `RenamedTitleEvent`, the newest 50 of each; `editActs`), as GitLab's
origin does (issue #1642): one `edited` act per editor. Edits that cannot be read are one edit by nobody known. Each counts
only when a **trusted actor** did it:

- an app or a bot never is one: an actor of GitHub type `Bot`, a `name[bot]` login, or an act `performed_via_github_app`;
- this hopper's own **Assign to me** (issue #440) goes through the hopper's app as the user: it is the user's act when the
  user's event log holds `source.issues_assigned` for the item (`IntakeTrust.assignedHere`);
- a login is asked of **Access**: OpenFGA `intake#can_start_jobs` for `github_login:<login>`, the user's trusted actors
  told at the check as `trusted_actor` tuples (`intakeActorCheck`) — those named in **Settings → Intake**, else the
  user's connected login only. One check per distinct login per sync. No OpenFGA, OpenFGA not reached, or a model without
  `intake` (`intakeGaps`; the hopper's own unedited model is upgraded) trusts nobody: every issue is then a request card,
  and its card says why.

An issue whose body carries the hopper's note under an issue a job filed (`FILED_BY_JOB`, the proxy's `filedNote`) is
never of a trusted origin, though the hopper's connection wrote it: a job cannot make work for itself (requirement 6;
the proxy already adds no label or assignee).

**Request cards.** An issue not of a trusted origin is no item: its intake outcome is the request (`IntakeOutcome`
`action: 'approve'`, `request`: the SHA-256 of its title and body, both as read, its author, the three acts and whether
each is trusted, and why). Sources shows it first, as a card (`ui/src/components/request-card.tsx`): the reasons, who
wrote, labelled and assigned it, the title and the body as plain text, and **Approve**. Approve —
`POST /ui/api/sources/:name/intake` `{ kind: 'approve', keys: [key], hash }` — is a person's act: a UI session signed in
(a job's routes reach no `/ui/api/`), the operator role, and Access's `item#can_accept_text` for the signed-in user (as
for accepting new text, issue #662; 403 denied, 503 when OpenFGA cannot be asked). Only when `hash` is the hash of the
title and body the last sync showed is that text — with the assignee's comments the job would see — recorded as the
item's snapshot, reason `approved` (`IntakeTrust.approve`), with `source.request_approved` (the hash, the actors, who;
never the text). The issue is not read again (issue #1194): the person approves the text they read, and an edit since
makes the next sync show the card again (**Approved** below). The answer comes once the approval is recorded; the
source syncs after it, not awaited, and the stream shows the issue taken (see "Actions answer at once").

**Approve again** (issue #1045). The source checks Approve against its last sync, so a page that still shows a card the
sync since took (another tab, an API client, an earlier click) sends Approve on an item no longer offered it. When the
text a person approved for the item hashes as `hash`, the answer is `done`, and nothing more is recorded: one approval,
one job. Else, on a taken item, `failed` says `already approved` (a person approved another text) or `already taken, no
approval needed` (a trusted origin), and the sync loop adds `: its job is <status>` when it has one. The UI reads either
as taken, not as a refusal: the card shows approved once the sync lists the issue taken.

**Approve takes at the first click** (issue #1316). The card leaves Intake in Approve's answer: the source lists the
item taken at once (`createApprovals` `on`), as the next sync will. A sync that read the item before the approval, and
lists the card again with the same hash, does not bring it back; the first sync that lists the item otherwise — taken,
or a card of new text — ends that (`listed`). So an approved item comes back to Intake only with new text, or reopened
(issue #1126). When the last sync does not list the item as a card of `hash` — no sync since a restart, or its read was
older than the page — Approve is **resolved again** (`resolve`): the issue is read now, and approved only while it is
open, labelled, assigned to the user, not claimed, not `hopper:done`, has no job here, is not declined, is not of a trusted
origin, and its title and body hash as `hash`. For an item the ledger holds (issue #1892), its work item's state says
whether it is a card, in place of `hopper:done`: an item waiting for approval is one, also with `hopper:done` left on (the
label mirror takes that off); an item in any other state is not, whatever its labels. `hopper:done` decides only for an
item the hopper does not know. Else `failed` says why, and the card keeps the refusal on the page, also
when the next list shows the new text.

**Approved.** At a later sync, an issue not of a trusted origin whose title and body hash as the text a person approved
— a snapshot of reason `approved`, or `accepted` (Accept the new text) — is taken, origin `approved`. Its first job runs
the snapshot (issue #662 `gateItem`), and a change since holds it as a text change. An edit after the approval and before
its job is made shows the card again, with the approved text and the change line by line.

**Declined (issue #1035).** A card also has **Decline** —
`POST /ui/api/sources/:name/intake` `{ kind: 'decline', keys: [key], hash }`, offered where Approve is and checked the same
way (a person signed in, operator, Access's `item#can_accept_text`). Only when `hash` is the hash the last sync showed is
the text declined: `source.request_declined` (the hash, the author, who; never the text), kept by `IntakeTrust.decline`.
Nothing is written to GitHub: no label, no comment, no close; an issue a person declines stays open, like a rejected job's
(issue #387). At each sync a request whose hash a person declined (`IntakeTrust.declined`) is the outcome
`a request you declined: …`, group `declined`, with no action: no job, and not waiting in Intake, which counts it in one
line. An edit to its title or body makes a new hash, so it is a request card again. A declined text cannot be approved
later; the request's author edits it, or a trusted actor files the work again. (Issue #1710 changed this for GitHub
cards: see "Decline" below. A GitLab card, and a decline recorded before issue #1710, still work this way.)

#### Decline (issue #1710, 2026-10-17)

The decline above left the issue open with its labels, its assignee and no comment: from GitHub it looked queued, and
nothing ran. It was also kept only in this hopper's events, so another hopper on the repository, or one rebuilt, offered
the card again. Now the person picks what happens to the issue, the page says it before the click, and GitHub keeps the
record.

- **The choice.** `{ kind: 'decline', keys: [key], hash, choice }`, `choice` `close` or `open`
  (`src/domain/intake-decline.ts`). `close`: the hopper takes off the source's label, the priority labels and `hopper:done`
  the last listing showed, and closes the issue as not planned. `open`: the hopper takes off the source's label only; the
  issue stays open. Either way it posts one comment (`declineNote`): what the hopper did, and how to queue it again. The
  comment names no person and never quotes the issue. A reopened card's comment says it was declined after a reopen.
- **The default.** Settings → Intake, Decline (`GET /api/intake-decline`, `POST /ui/api/intake-decline`, admin,
  `intake.decline_changed`): the choice the confirm step offers first, for a request card (`open` by default) and for a
  reopened card (`close` by default). A decline with no `choice` takes it.
- **The outbox.** The writes are rows in the GitHub outbox (act `decline`, tagged with the hash), kept in the transaction of
  `source.request_declined` (now with `choice`): remove the labels, the comment, and, for `close`, the new change
  `close_not_planned` (`GitHubApi.closeAsNotPlanned`), sent last. Each is safe to send again: a label already gone is no
  error, the comment carries its hidden key (issue #1590), and a closed issue stays closed. `source.request_decline_written`
  is recorded once GitHub took the last row. A failed row shows on the item with Retry, as every outbox row.
- **The record.** `IntakeTrust.declined` holds a decline with a choice only until its written event: until then the item is
  in group `declined` with no action. After it, the issue has no source label, so no listing of any hopper has it. It comes
  back only when a person adds the label again (and reopens it, when it was closed); an edit to its title or body does
  nothing. Its card is then judged as any new card.
- **Neutral text.** This is one of the exceptions of the rule "GitHub text is neutral" (`AGENTS.md`): the person's own act,
  a fixed comment.

**Reopened (issue #1126, 2026-10-14).** An issue whose job was done keeps `hopper:done`, so when a person reopened it —
the merged pull request did not fix it all — intake said `done, but the issue is still open` and offered nothing: no job
could start. Now an open issue with `hopper:done` whose job here ended (`rerunnable`: its end reported to the source) is a
request card again, the **reopened card** (`reopenedRequest`, `src/sources/github/origin.ts`): reason
`reopened after its job was done: approve it to run it again`, group `request`, its title and body as read, no acts, and
the item's history (`IntakeRequest.reopened`, `itemHistory`, `src/domain/intake.ts`): the newest job and the jobs it ran
again (`rerunOf`), newest first, at most ten, and the item's pull request from the work-item ledger. It is a card whatever
the issue's origin: a person decides whether the item runs again. It records `source.request_opened` as any card, so the
item's ledger row moves from `done` to `waiting_for_approval` and the Intake badge counts it. A card opens again after an
approval of the same text (`requestOpenedSince`: since the last `source.request_withdrawn` or `source.request_approved`).
Approve is the card's Approve, checked the same way; it also takes `hopper:done` off the issue (a label, the hopper's own
write) before it records the text. The next sync — at once, as for every Approve — lists the issue with no end label, judges
its origin as any issue's (a trusted origin, or the text just approved), and makes a new job of the item, which runs again
from its ended job (`rerunOf`). Decline makes no job; the item is `done` again (a dropped item whose pull
request merged is done). By default it closes the issue as not planned and takes off `hopper:done` (issue #1710,
"Decline" above). An issue with `hopper:done` and no job here, another hopper's, stays `done, but the issue is still
open`.

No GitHub delivery is needed: the source lists every open labelled issue of its job repositories at each intake sync
(the listing cache, "Repository listings": one batched read per due repository at the intake sync interval), and a
reopened issue is one of them. A delivery of `reopened` (issue #1079, off by default) only makes its repository due at
once.

**The job's origin.** `SourceItem.origin` → `JobSourceRef.origin`: `trusted` or `approved`. Run again and Rework keep the
origin of the job they follow. A job of a source that does not judge origins has none; one taken before this change has
none until the backfill below judges it.

**Yolo mode** merges a job's ready pull request whatever its origin (issue #805, the owner's later decision over
requirement 7, which held a job with none for a person as `untrusted origin` on the Pull requests card). The origin is a
decision about running the work: the job ran, and its checks judge its pull request. A job with no origin is one taken
before origins were judged, or one of a source that judges none; such a pull request merges as any other, and the card
has no `untrusted origin` state. Its checks rule stays as issue #677 set it: no checks, settled, is ready — the owner's
later decision over the issue's "no checks does not count".

**Settings → Intake** (`/api/intake-actors`, `POST /ui/api/intake-actors`, admin): the whole list of trusted actors,
by GitHub user id (issue #930); empty: the connected login only, shown as trusted by default. Nobody types a login: the
picker offers **actor candidates** (`GET /api/intake-actors/candidates`) — the connected account, each job repository's
collaborators (GitHub shows them only to who can push), the members of the organizations that own them, the authors of
their 50 newest issues and pull requests, and every hopper user and API token holder by their connected GitHub account —,
and looks one up by login (`GET /api/intake-actors/lookup?login=`, 404 when GitHub knows none). All read now with the
user's own GitHub connection (`src/intake-actors/`), one page of each; what could not be read is listed in `problems`,
never an error. The save takes ids and reads each from GitHub first: an id GitHub does not know, or an account that is no
person's (`type` not `User`: an app, a bot, an organization), refuses the whole save (400), so no login that does not
exist is kept. Each account is kept with its login, type and avatar as GitHub answered (`accounts`), beside its login
lowercased (`actors`), which the build before reads. `intake.actors_changed { from, to, by }` names the logins. The same
reads and the save are the API's, so an agent picks as a person does.

At each check the hopper tells OpenFGA each account by the login it has now: an act's GitHub user id (the issue's
`user.id`, the event's `actor.id`) that matches a trusted actor tells that actor by the act's login, so a renamed account
stays trusted; a trusted actor's old login that an account of another id now holds is not told, so it gets no trust. An
act whose id GitHub did not give compares by login. A list kept before ids has logins only (`unresolved` in the view):
they count by login until an admin saves the list again; the picker looks each up and has it ready to save. The role lives
in the model (`intake#trusted_actor`, by `github_login`), so an edited model can widen or narrow who it admits.

**Residual risk** (issue #930). The candidates are read with the user's own connection: what that account cannot see is
not offered, but can be looked up. Avatars are GitHub's images, loaded by the person's browser from GitHub.

**The backfill** (requirement 10). A job queued before this change has no origin, and its issue was never judged.
Tenant migration 39 (`store/migration-origin-pending.ts`), at the first start of the build that has it, marks every
queued or held job of a GitHub source (`kind` `github`, `github-account`, `github-app`) with no origin **origin pending**
(`Job.originPending`). The decider holds such a job before every other judgement (`ORIGIN_PENDING`), and Waiting offers no
Approve for it, only a link to Sources: approving the job is not approving its issue. At each sync the source judges the
issue of a job whose origin is pending (`IntakeTrust.originPending`), though it has a job that has not ended. Of a trusted
origin, or approved, the item is offered; the host's refresh sets the job's `source.origin`, drops the flag
(`job.origin_judged { key, origin }`), and the job runs as any other. Any other issue is a request card in Intake, and
its job stays held until a person approves the card or cancels the job. Approving a card whose job already exists makes
no second job: the next sync gives the job its origin. A running job keeps running; only queued and held jobs wait. A
job whose source is gone stays held: cancel it. The build before ignores the flag and runs such a job.

**Not in this part** (later parts of #652): the repository setup check in Sources ("Repository setup"), updating only to
a merged and checked commit ("Updates only to a merged pull request with passing checks"), and the vault helper only by
a per-job grant ("Vault grants").

**Residual risk.** Events GitHub cannot be asked for count as done by nobody known: the issue is a request card. An
`assigned` event through the hopper's app is the user's while the user's log says this hopper assigned the item, even
when a later bot assigned it again. A person with write access to the repository who removes the hopper's note from a
job-filed issue makes it read as the author's.

### Auto-approval (issue #1268, 2026-10-15)

Owner requirement: an issue the user opened or reopened, or that an app acting for the user filed, waited in Intake for
the user's own approval. The user was the bottleneck for work they already asked for. Now **the hopper approves a
request card itself when the user's own act already asks for it**, and records that approval as a person's is recorded.

**The rules** (`src/domain/intake-auto-approve.ts`, `src/sources/github/auto-approve.ts`), in this order. An act
counts when a trusted actor did it, or a **listed app**: an app or bot named in the setting, by its slug (`helper` for
`helper[bot]` or an act `performed_via_github_app` `helper`).

- `reopened`: a reopened card (an open issue with `hopper:done` whose job here ended, issue #1126) whose newest
  `reopened` event is an act that counts. Approval takes `hopper:done` off, as Approve does, and the next sync runs it.
- `author`: a trusted actor wrote the issue, whoever labelled or assigned it.
- `app`: a listed app wrote the issue.
- `high-label`: the issue has `hopper:high`, and the newest `labeled` event of `hopper:high` is an act that counts. The
  author may be anyone: the label is the approval.

**Guards.** A card waits for a person whatever the rules say when a job filed it (`FILED_BY_JOB`), the trusted actors
cannot be checked (no OpenFGA), its text changed since a person approved it, a person took it into Intake (issue #1176:
Take into Intake asks for a card, not a job), or someone whose act does not count edited its title or body
(`GitHubApi.issueEdits`) — unless a person approved this same text before. A card whose events or edits cannot be read
waits too.

**Recording.** The approval is `IntakeTrust.autoApprove`: the item's snapshot is the text as read, reason `approved`,
as for Approve, and `source.request_auto_approved` names the rule, the actor, the hash and the three acts — never the
text. Its GitHub work is Approve's rows in the GitHub outbox, kept in the same transaction: the comments the job would
see, and `hopper:done` off a reopened card. The card opens no `source.request_opened`; its outcome says `approved by the
hopper: <rule> <actor>; taken at the next sync`, and a sync after the rows are sent takes the item with origin `approved`. The work-item ledger moves a waiting item to queued on it, as on
`source.request_approved`.

**The setting** is the user's, in Settings → Intake below the trusted actors: `GET /api/intake-auto-approval`,
`POST /ui/api/intake-auto-approval` (admin) `{ on, apps }`, kept as `intakeAutoApproval`, recorded as
`intake.auto_approval_changed`. On by default, with no app listed. Read at each sync. Off, the source reads and asks
nothing more, and every card is as before.

**Residual risk.** A trusted actor's old issue that someone else labels and assigns to the user runs: its text is the
trusted actor's, and an edit by anyone else keeps it waiting. Listing an app trusts every act through it: listing the
hopper's own app makes this hopper's writes count, though a job-filed issue still waits by its note. A person with write
access who removes that note, or who adds `hopper:high` while being a trusted actor, approves as the user.

## Trust stamps (issue #655, parts 1 to 21, 2026-10-17)

Owner decision on the issue: build trust stamps. A stamp is not only an author rule: when something warrants it, the stamp
can lead to a deeper trust analysis, up to a fuller review before the job runs. The author-based passes stay as the simple
first tier. This part builds that first tier: **each job carries a trust level from where its work came, signed, and a job
starts only with a stamp that verifies, at the dispatch minimum or above.**

**The trust level** (`src/domain/trust-stamp.ts`), lowest first: `quarantined`, `untrusted`, `screened`, `approved`,
`trusted`, `owner`. The rules (`ruleCeiling`) read the job's source and its job origin (issue #652):

| the job's source | level | reasons |
|---|---|---|
| GitHub, a trusted origin, its author is the login it was taken for | `owner` | `origin:trusted`, `author:assignee` |
| GitHub, a trusted origin, another trusted actor wrote it | `trusted` | `origin:trusted` |
| GitHub, a request card a person approved (or auto-approval approved) | `approved` | `origin:approved` |
| GitHub, no job origin | `untrusted` | `origin:none` |
| a direct job (a signed-in person submitted it, issue #901) | `approved` | `source:direct` |
| another job source, which an admin configured and which judges no origin | `approved` | `source:configured` |
| no source | `untrusted` | `source:none` |

A job a job made — a follow-on of an accepted proposal (issue #651), a fork of a phase shift (issue #548) — gets at most
its parent's level as it verifies then, and never `owner` (`childLevel`); a parent whose stamp does not verify gives none.
`quarantined` and `screened` are no rule's: a person's quarantine (part 2) gives the first, and Jev's trust check (part 4)
can lower a job to the second.

**The stamp** (`Job.stamp`): `{ v: 1, level, reasons, by, at, mac }`. `by`: `intake` (the store made the job), `job` (a job
made it), `respecify` (its spec changed), `backfill` (made before stamps), `person`, `jev`, `edit` (an edit of its item after the start, part 7). `mac` is HMAC-SHA256 under the user's **stamp
key** over the other fields, the job's id and the SHA-256 of its spec as canonical JSON (keys sorted). The stamp key is
HKDF of the hopper's link key for the user (issue #308), label `hopper-job-stamp/1`, as the proxy token's key is (issue
#563): never stored, never sent. So a stamp of another job, a raised level or a changed prompt does not verify.

**Where it is made.** In the job store (`src/store/jobs.ts`), the one code path every job is made by: the runtime gives the
store the key at its start (`useStampKey`), and from then `create` stamps each job by the rules, or by its parent
(`create(spec, priority, source, parent)`). `respecify` — a routing rule's re-sort (issue #375), Accept the new text
(issue #662), a review kind set — stamps the new spec again at the level the old stamp verified at, never higher; a stamp
that does not verify stays as it is. A job whose origin a sync judges after it was made (issue #652, the backfill) is
stamped again by the rules (`restamp`), as intake would stamp it now. `update` cannot set a stamp. A row a writer changes outside the store has no stamp,
or one that does not verify.

**The dispatch check.** At each Decision the engine asks the store why each waiting job's stamp holds it
(`stampHold`), and gives the decider `stampHeld`. The decider holds such a job before every other judgement but its
origin pending (issue #652), a job resuming after a question too:

- no stamp: `no trust stamp: held — …` (`STAMP_MISSING`);
- a stamp that does not verify: `its trust stamp does not match the job: held — …` (`STAMP_MISMATCH`);
- a level below the **dispatch minimum** `approved`: `trust stamp <level> is below approved: held — …`.

Cancel and Run again are the ways out: Run again makes a new job, which intake stamps again from its item.

**The backfill** (requirement 10). At each start, the store stamps every job that has not ended and has none, by the rules
(`by: backfill`; a fork or a follow-on at most its parent's rule level; a job with no source `approved`, reason
`source:none`, since only the hopper's own code or an older build made it), and the runtime logs how many. A job queued before
this build, and one a steadier channel's older build made on the same store (`docs/deploy.md` "Update channels and
promotion"), so runs as before. No migration: `stamp` is one more field in the job's body, which the build before ignores.

**Quarantine and the doors** (part 2). A person can **quarantine** a job that has not ended (`POST
/ui/api/jobs/:id/quarantine`, the job view's Quarantine, `hopper job quarantine <id>`; least role operator). The store signs
its stamp `quarantined` (`by: person`), and keeps the level it had as `was`, which the MAC covers; a job whose stamp did not
verify keeps none. Then:

- the decider holds it, a job about to resume too: `quarantined by a person: held — …` (`QUARANTINED_HOLD`);
- its **proxy token opens no door** of the hopper (gate 2's first step). The one check is in the user's `holds`
  (`src/users/github-proxy.ts`), which every door that takes a proxy token asks — the GitHub proxy, git and GitLab git,
  the vault's ask, skills, Windows and box steps, logins, artifacts, infra plans, checkpoints and the job stream: the token
  opens a door only while the job's stamp verifies and is not `quarantined` (`opensDoors`). A door answers such a job as a
  token that is no job's (401), so it learns nothing of why. A stamp that does not verify — a row changed outside the
  hopper — closes the doors too, not only the start;
- a running job keeps its pane and its work on its machine: a person cancels or parks it as any job. Since part 6, its
  steps stop and its item's vault grant is revoked (below, "What a quarantine takes back").

A new spec keeps the quarantine (`respecify` signs the level it verified at). An origin judged later (the #652 backfill,
`restamp`) keeps it too, and the level the rules give then is the one its lift gives back. **Lift quarantine** (`POST
/ui/api/jobs/:id/unquarantine`, a box action of kind `start a job`: the job may start and reach the hopper again) signs the
level the job had before, never higher, and with none kept, the rules' level now. Each act is one event with who acted and
how: `job.quarantined` (`was`), `job.unquarantined` (`level`). 409: the job ended, is quarantined already, is not
quarantined, or has no stamp (no stamp key).

What part 2 does not do: a deny at gate 2 that lowers the level, and a second that quarantines (part 5); stopping a
quarantined job's steps and revoking its vault grant (part 6); Jev's decisions (part 4).

**Intake strictness: brake 1** (part 3). The dispatch minimum is no longer fixed: an admin sets the **intake strictness**
(`src/domain/intake-strictness.ts`), the level a job's stamp needs before the job starts, in Settings → Intake (`GET
/api/intake-strictness`, `POST /ui/api/intake-strictness`, least role admin, `intake.strictness_changed` with `from`, `to`
and who):

| strictness | the stamp needs | so runs |
|---|---|---|
| `open` | `screened` | also a job Jev's trust check lowered to `screened` (part 4; no rule gives it) |
| `standard` (the default) | `approved` | a trusted origin, a request card a person approved, a direct job, a configured source's job |
| `strict` | `trusted` | only a trusted origin: a person's approval is not enough |
| `closed` | `owner` | only an item the user wrote and was assigned |

It is set by default, per job source (its configured name) and per job repository (`owner/name`, lowercased). The most
specific wins: the job's repository, else its source, else the default (`brakeOf`), so an admin can also loosen one
repository below a strict default. The engine reads the setting at each Decision and gives the store's `stampHold` the
brake of each waiting job; a change applies at the next Decision with no restart. A job held by the brake says which
(`trust stamp approved is below trusted (intake strictness strict for octo/tools): held — an admin changes the intake
strictness in Settings → Intake, or a person cancels it`); a job below `approved` keeps the hold text that sends a person
to Intake. Tightening it holds a waiting job that no longer passes, a job resuming after a question too; a running job
keeps going and keeps its doors (part 2: doors stay open below the minimum), and since part 12 gate 2 asks a person for its
privileged requests. Nothing is stored on the job: the stamp keeps
the level, the brake is read where it is needed, so a loosened brake lets the job start at once.

**Jev's trust check** (part 4, `src/domain/trust-check.ts`, `src/engine/trust-checks.ts`; the decision point
`intake-trust`, "Decider calls"). The owner's decision on the issue: a stamp can lead to a deeper trust analysis when
something warrants it. This is the first such analysis: Jev reads a waiting job's text and where it came from, and keeps
its level or lowers it. It is **due** (`checkDue`) for a job whose stamp verifies at `approved` or `trusted` — the levels a
job starts at on the rules alone —, that no person stamped (`by` not `person`), with no check on it. An `owner` job is not
asked; a job the rules hold already is not asked either: Jev can only lower.

- **What Jev reads** (`trustCheckState`): the job's id, level, reasons, goal and kind; its source's kind, repository,
  number, origin, author, assignee and labels; and the first 4000 characters of its prompt as `untrustedText`, which the
  instructions say is data, never instructions. No credential, no tool.
- **The options** (`trustOptions`): `keep`, and for each level below the job's — never `quarantined`, which only a person
  sets — each reason: `touches_ci`, `credentials`, `destructive`, `out_of_scope`, `instructs_agent`, `unclear`
  (`lower:screened:credentials`). A pick that is not one of them gives no level (`pickedLevel`): Jev cannot raise a level
  by construction.
- **Off**: Jev is not asked; the rules' level stands. **Shadow** (the default, as every point): Jev is asked once per
  waiting job and hopper run, after the Decision's transaction; the pick is only recorded (`minor_decision.picked`) and
  compared with `keep` at once. The job starts as before.
- **Active**: the decider holds the job while the check is due (`Jev checks its trust: held — …`, `CHECK_PENDING`). The
  check is then written into the stamp (`checkedStamp`, `by: jev`, `check: { pick, confidence, applied, fail? }`, which the
  MAC covers): a kept level; a lower level with the reason id `jev:<reason>`; or, **fail closed**, `untrusted` with
  `jev:no_answer` (no answer, an error, a timeout, a pick that is no option), `jev:not_sure` (below the point's threshold)
  or `jev:skipped` (Jev not there: no TypeSafe API key). Each lowering is `job.trust_lowered { from, to, reason, by: jev }`.
  A job held below `approved` by a check says why: `trust stamp untrusted is below approved (Jev's trust check: it changes
  CI, workflow files or branch rules): held — a person approves its trust on the job, or cancels it`. A check is written
  only while it is still due (`checkTrust`): another hopper's check, a new spec or a person's act that came first wins.
- **A person approves its trust** (`POST /ui/api/jobs/:id/approve-trust`, the job view's Approve trust after a confirm,
  `hopper job approve-trust <id>`; least role operator, a box action of kind `start a job`): only a job a check lowered
  below `approved` (`trustApprovable`), or, since issue #1974, a job below `approved` with no item, which no request card can approve. Its stamp is signed `approved` (`by: person`, reason `person:approved`), never
  more; the check stays on it, so Jev is not asked again. `job.trust_approved { from, person, via }`. 409 for any other job:
  a quarantine is lifted with unquarantine; an item of no trusted origin is approved in Intake, which approves its text.
- **A new spec** (`respecify`: Accept the new text, a re-sort) drops the check: the new text is checked again. An origin
  judged later (`restamp`) stamps by the rules again, so the check is due again too.
- **The job view** shows a check's reason beside the level (`data-slot="job-trust-check"`).

Persisted state: `check` is one more field in the stamp. The build before verifies such a stamp (its MAC covers every
field but `mac`), and does not read `check`; a job it made has none, and a build with this part asks for it.

**A person's deny at gate 2** (part 5, `deniedStamp`, `recordDeny` in `src/engine/quarantine.ts`). The issue: "deny by Jev
or a person: the job stamp drops one level, and a second deny in the job sets it to `quarantined`". A person's deny is a
**declined sandbox request** (`POST /ui/api/sandbox-requests`, `decline`; a delegate approver's too, issue #1138), the
one request a job makes that a person answers no to now. After the decline, in its own transaction:

- the job's stamp is signed one level lower, `by: person`, with the reason id `deny:sandbox`
  (`job.trust_lowered { from, to, reason, by: person, person, via }`);
- the **second** deny in the job — two `deny:sandbox` on its stamp —, or a deny of a job at `untrusted`, signs it
  `quarantined`, its level then kept as `was` (`job.quarantined { was, reason: deny:sandbox, person, via }`): it is held,
  and its proxy token opens no door of the hopper, as for a person's quarantine (part 2);
- nothing changes for a job that ended, is quarantined already, or whose stamp does not verify: the decline itself
  stands, and the job is told no as before.

A running job lowered below the dispatch minimum keeps running and keeps its doors (part 2): the level holds only a start.
A job held before it starts (issue #1471, "Sandboxes before the start") and lowered below its brake waits again; below
`approved` it says why (`trust stamp screened is below approved (a person declined its sandbox request): held — a person
approves its trust on the job, or cancels it`) and **Approve trust** takes it (`trustApprovable`, as for a check). The job
view shows `A person declined its sandbox request` beside the level. The denies stay on the stamp: a lift of the
quarantine and a person's approval keep them, so the next deny quarantines the job again. A new spec (`respecify`) keeps
its reasons too. Jev's trust check is not asked for a job a person stamped, a deny's included.

What is not a deny: an approval; a decline of a request that no longer waits (409, nothing changes); a person's decline
of a **credential request** (the dynamic vault, issue #583), which often says only that no such credential exists, and
which answers every job that waited on it at once. No migration: `deny:sandbox` is one more reason id, which the build
before verifies (its MAC covers the reasons) and reads as any other.

**What a quarantine takes back** (part 6, `src/users/quarantine.ts`). The issue: "`quarantined`: hopper parks the job,
revokes its proxy token and live sandbox credentials, stops its sandboxes". Part 2 closed the doors; this part ends what the
job still holds behind them. Each `job.quarantined` — a person's quarantine, or the second deny at gate 2 (part 5) — does:

- **its steps stop** (`stepsMayRun`): a need, box or Windows step runs only while its job is at work **and** its proxy
  token opens the hopper's doors. A step that runs looks every 5 s ("Need steps kept as sagas") and stops; its need box's
  minted credentials end with it, as at any stop. A step that has not started ends `cancelled: job <id> is not at work`.
  Since issue #1349 a sandbox lives only as long as its step, so no other sandbox of the job is left to stop;
- **its item's vault grant is revoked** (`revokeOnQuarantine`): after the append, the user's runtime takes the grant of the
  job's item back, as a person's Revoke does: `vault.grant_revoked { job, key, by: "quarantine by <person>" }`. An item with
  no grant: nothing. The standing read grant (issue #1472) needs no revoke: the vault's ask goes through the closed doors;
- **its grant ask is not open** (`withVaultGrants`): the Vault page does not show the ask of a quarantined job, and it cannot
  be denied, so no person grants its item while it is quarantined. The ask goes; after a lift, the job's next ask opens a
  new one.

The **lift** lets the steps run again (the job opens the doors again). The grant **stays revoked**: a person grants the
item again, after they looked at why the job was quarantined. A stamp that does not verify (a row changed outside the
hopper) stops steps too, as it closes the doors; it revokes no grant, since no `job.quarantined` is recorded. Its sandbox
requests are not dropped: approving one of a quarantined job runs nothing, as each step is refused at the door.

**An edit after the start, and gate 2 below `approved`** (part 7, `editedStamp`, `autoApprovable`; `refreshEdit` in
`src/engine/item-snapshots.ts`). The issue: "An edit (a new hash on a sync): a job that is queued is held [...]. A running
job continues, but gate 2 drops it to `untrusted` for new requests until a person approves the new snapshot." A queued job
is held already: its item snapshot holds it with a text change ("Item snapshots", issue #662), and Accept the new text makes a
new spec, which Jev's check reads again (part 4). This part does the rest:

- **A started job** — one that is not waiting with no attempt: running, waiting on a question or a wait, parked, or back in
  the queue after a run — whose item's title or body a sync sees changed since the snapshot goes on with the text it
  started with. Its stamp is signed `untrusted`, `by: edit`, with the reason id `edit:text`; Jev's check stays on it
  (`job.trust_lowered { from, to: untrusted, reason: edit:text, by: edit }`). The live text is kept as the job's
  `editSeen`, so the same text lowers it once; a later, other edit lowers it again. Comments are no edit (issue #747). A job
  at `untrusted` or lower, quarantined, or whose stamp does not verify keeps its stamp; the text is still seen.
- **Below `approved`, gate 2 gives the job nothing with no person** (`autoApprovable`: the stamp verifies at `approved` or
  above). Whatever lowered it — an edit, Jev's check, a deny:
  - its **sandbox request** waits for a person: skip sandbox approval, the auto-approve policy, a remembered write approval
    and a person's approval of its template do not approve it (`src/sandbox/requests.ts`);
  - a **box step** runs only from a request a person approved (`approvedBy` not one of the approvers that are no person);
  - a **need step** is refused (403): `its trust stamp untrusted is below approved: a need step runs only for a job at approved
    or above. Ask for a sandbox a person approves: sh "$HOPPER_SKILL" sandbox --needs "…" --why "…"`;
  - the **standing read grant** grants it nothing, one it granted before too: a person grants the item.
- **A person approves its trust** (part 4's Approve trust, `trustApprovable`, now for an edit too): `approved`, never more.
  The job view shows `Its item was edited after it started` beside the level. A job lowered by an edit that waits again (a
  question) says why: `trust stamp untrusted is below approved (its item was edited after it started): held — a person
  approves its trust on the job, or cancels it`.

What gate 2 keeps: the job's doors stay open below `approved` (part 2; only a quarantine closes them), so the job still
pushes to its own branch, opens its pull request and reads through the GitHub proxy. A vault grant a person made stays, and a
template's approval stays: a template is not a job's. Persisted state: `edit` is one more value of `by` and `edit:text` one
more reason id, which the build before verifies (its MAC covers every field but `mac`); `editSeen` is one more field in the
job's body, which it ignores, so it may lower the same edit once more.

**Sandbox strictness: brake 2** (part 8, `src/domain/sandbox-strictness.ts`). The issue: "Brake 2, sandbox strictness,
per template and per blast-radius level". An admin sets which sandbox runs gate 2 may approve with no person, in Settings →
Vault (`GET /api/sandbox-strictness`, `POST /ui/api/sandbox-strictness`, least role admin, a box action of kind `approve or
merge work`; `sandbox.strictness_changed` with `from`, `to` and who):

| strictness | a person approves each run of |
|---|---|
| `relaxed` | nothing more: the toggles and the auto-approve policy decide (issues #991, #1001) |
| `standard` (the default) | the same as `relaxed`, but Jev's sandbox check first for a medium, high or unrated template (part 13) |
| `strict` | a template of medium or high blast radius, or one with no rating (fail closed) |
| `locked` | every template |

It is set by default, per blast radius level (`radius`) and per template (`templates`, by name). The most specific wins:
the template, else its radius level, else the default (`sandboxBrakeOf`). Where it asks a person (`personBrake`), it acts
as part 7 does below `approved`, for that template only:

- a **sandbox request** waits for a person: skip sandbox approval, the auto-approve policy, a remembered write approval and a
  person's approval of the template do not approve it (`src/sandbox/requests.ts`);
- a **box step** runs only from a request a person approved (`runnable`, which also holds part 7's rule);
- a **need step** of that template is refused (403): `sandbox strictness locked for the template dig: a person approves each
  run of the template dig, and a need step has no approval of its own. Ask for a sandbox a person approves: …`;
