- the **standing read grant** grants nothing on a box of that template, one it granted before too.

It is read at each ask and each step, so a change applies at once, with no restart. **Tightened, it re-checks**: a run
that a toggle or a policy approved before no longer lets a box step run, and the standing read grant it gave no longer
counts; a run a person approved still counts. Loosened, those runs count again. It only takes approvals away: no strictness
approves a run that the toggles and policies would not. A template's own approval (issues #716, #1001) is not a run, and
the brake does not change it.

In the issue, `standard` asks Jev's `sandbox-request` point for medium and high; part 13 built it (below), and `relaxed`
keeps the toggles alone. With the point off or in shadow, `standard` is the same as `relaxed`: the issue's fail-closed table
says gate 2 is then "policy plus a person", which is what the toggles and policies give.
Persisted state: one more key in the user's settings, `sandboxStrictness`; the build before does not read it.

**A held request that times out** (part 9, `expire` in `src/sandbox/requests.ts`; `holdSweep` in
`src/users/sandbox-requests.ts`). The issue: "`hold` timed out with no answer: treated as deny for this request only". A
sandbox request that waits 24 hours (`SANDBOX_HOLD_MS`) with no person's answer is declined by the hopper: its state
`declined`, `declinedBy` the **hold timeout** (`HOLD_TIMEOUT`), the reason `no person answered it within 24 hours`, and
`vault.sandbox_declined { by: the hold timeout }` on the job's timeline, which wakes a job that waits on it (`--wait`). The
job is told `the hopper declined the sandbox runs of template <name>: no person answered it within 24 hours. Find another
way.` — not that a person declined. It is a deny **for this request only**: no person said no, so it is no deny of part 5,
and the job's trust stamp stays. A person's approve or decline after it is 409, as for any request that no longer waits.
The hopper looks for overdue requests at each ask and list, and once a minute (`HOLD_SWEEP_MS`), so a job is told even when
nobody opens the Vault page. A request held before the start (issue #1471) times out the same way: declined, it holds the
job no more, and the job is told no when it asks. Requests are kept in memory, as before: a restart forgets them, and
the job asks again. 24 hours is fixed, not a setting: the issue names no default, and a person's working day with a night
between fits in it.

**The stamp view** (part 10, `src/domain/stamp-view.ts`). The issue: "`GET /api/jobs/<id>/stamp`; the CLI with
`--json`". `GET /api/jobs/:id/stamp` (by its id or its short id, issue #1780; least role viewer) and `hopper job stamp
<id>` answer one **stamp view** (`stampView`), read only:

- `stamp`: the stamp as kept — `level`, `reasons`, `by`, `at`, `was`, `check` —, each field named, so the MAC never
  leaves the hopper; null: none;
- `verifies`: `yes`; `no` (the job or its stamp changed outside the hopper); `missing`; `unknown` (no stamp key: the
  hopper holds nothing on a stamp, as the store does); and `level`, the level as verified, else null;
- `brake`: the intake strictness on the job (`strictness`, the level it `needs`, where it was set `at`), as the engine
  reads it at each Decision, and `startHold`, why the stamp holds the job's start (`stampHold`), else null. A job Jev's
  active check holds says `checkDue: true`; the hold text for that is the engine's, not the stamp's;
- `gate2`: `auto` (`autoApprovable`, under the job's brake since part 12) or `person`; `doorsOpen` (`opensDoors`).

The job view keeps reading the stamp from the job itself. No migration: nothing is stored.

**The stamp as an event** (part 11, `intake.stamped`). The issue: "It goes in the event log (`intake.stamped`). The job
row keeps only the record id." Each stamp the job store signs **from where the job came** is one event on the job's
timeline, so the log shows the level the job got, why, and for which text:

- at its making: `by` `intake`, or `job` for a job a job made (a follow-on, a fork). The engine appends it right after the
  job's `job.queued` (`appendStamped`, `src/engine/quarantine.ts`), so a job's timeline still starts with `job.queued`;
- for a new spec (`respecify`), at the backfill (`backfill`), and when a sync judges the job's origin later (`restamp`,
  `by` `intake`; `by` `person` when a quarantine stays on it): the store tells it after the write (`onStamped`, which the
  user store wires to the event log, in the same transaction).

The data (`stampedEvent`, `src/domain/trust-stamp.ts`): `level`, `reasons`, `by`, `was` (a quarantined job's level
before), `from` (the level the stamp verified at before, when it had one), and `spec`: the SHA-256 of the spec as
canonical JSON, the hash the MAC covers (`specHashOf`). The MAC is never in it. A job with no stamp — no stamp key, or a
parent whose stamp does not verify — gets no event. A person's act, Jev's check, a deny and an edit keep their own events
(`job.quarantined`, `job.trust_lowered`, …), so they are not told twice.

The stamp stays on the job row, signed, as before: the event is the audit trail, not the source of truth. The issue's S2
keeps the record in the log and only its id on the row; that moves the check at each Decision from one row to the log,
for no gain in security, since the MAC already shows a changed row. One event, not two: the issue also names
`intake.restamped`; `by` and `from` say which stamp it is. No migration: nothing new is stored on the job.

**A tightened intake strictness re-checks started jobs at gate 2** (part 12, `gate2Hold`, `gate2Min`, `jobBrake`). The
issue: "Tightening a brake re-checks live stamps and live sandboxes." Brake 1 holds only a start (part 3), so a job that
runs when an admin tightens it keeps running and keeps its doors. But gate 2 now reads the brake on the job at each ask:
it approves the job's privileged requests with no person only while its stamp is at `approved` **and** at the level the
brake needs (`gate2Min`: the higher of the two). Below it, gate 2 acts as part 7 does below `approved`:

- its **sandbox request** waits for a person: skip sandbox approval, the auto-approve policy, a remembered write approval
  and a person's approval of its template do not approve it, and a box step runs only from a request a person approved;
- a **need step** is refused (403): `its trust stamp approved is below trusted (intake strictness strict for the source
  manual): a need step runs only for a job at trusted or above. Ask for a sandbox a person approves: …`;
- the **standing read grant** grants it nothing, one it granted before too.

The stamp view says `gate2: person` for such a job, waiting or running. Loosened, the brake lets the toggles and policies
approve again at once, with no restart. Approve trust does not help here (it gives `approved`, never more): a person
approves each request, or an admin loosens the brake. Why only gate 2, not a park or a stop: the issue keeps a running
job going on an edit (part 7) and at the migration, and lets gate 2 treat it lower; a stop on a settings change would
lose a person's work for a choice that is about new jobs. No migration: nothing is stored.

**Jev's sandbox check** (part 13, `src/domain/sandbox-check.ts`, `src/sandbox/requests.ts`; the decision point
`sandbox-request`, "Decider calls"). The issue's gate 2 order: policy first, then Jev, then a person. Part 7, part 8 and part
12 are the policy; this is the Jev stage. It is asked only for a run the sandbox approvals — skip sandbox approval, the
auto-approve policy, a remembered write approval, a person's approval of the template the job asked for — would approve with
no person, and only where sandbox strictness is `standard` for a template of medium or high blast radius, or none rated
(`jevChecks`). A run a person must approve anyway (below `approved`, under the intake strictness, under `strict` or `locked`)
goes to the person, not to Jev; a `low` template and `relaxed` keep the approvals alone.

- **What Jev reads** (`sandboxCheckState`): the request (its id, template, when, and the approver it would have), the
  template's profiles (`write aws-role/…`), how many vault secrets it gives (never their names) and its blast radius with
  its reasons, the job's id, trust level, reasons, goal and source, and the job's other requests with their state and who
  decided them. The job's purpose and plan, its own words, go as `untrustedText`, which the instructions say is data, never
  instructions. No credential, no tool.
- **The options** (`sandboxCheckOptions`): `allow`, and `hold:<reason>` and `deny:<reason>` for each reason:
  `out_of_scope`, `novel_target`, `rate_spike`, `high_blast_radius`, `capability_mismatch`, `pattern_suspicious`,
  `history_denied`. A pick that is not one of them gives no verdict (`pickedVerdict`). Jev only sees what the approvals
  would approve, so it cannot approve more, and no option widens a request.
- **Off**: Jev is not asked. **Shadow** (the default): the approvals approve the run at once, as before; Jev is asked after,
  and the pick is only recorded and compared with `allow`.
- **Active**: the request waits for Jev (`jev: { state: checking }` on the request; the job is told `Jev checks the sandbox
  runs …`, and a job held before its start says so). Then (`checkedVerdict`):
  - `allow` approves the run, `by` `Jev` (`JEV_APPROVER`, one of the approvers that are no person: a tightened brake stops
    it counting, as for the toggles, part 8), if the approvals still would;
  - `hold` leaves it for a person, with why (`jev: { state: held, reason }`, on the Vault page card and in the job's answer);
  - `deny` declines it, `by` `Jev`, with the reason as the text the job is told (`Jev declined the sandbox runs of template
    … Find another way.`), and is a **deny at gate 2**: the job's stamp is signed one level lower, `by: jev`, with the
    reason id `deny:jev` (`job.trust_lowered { from, to, reason: deny:jev, by: jev }`); it counts with a person's
    `deny:sandbox`, so the second deny in the job, either way, quarantines it (`job.quarantined { was, reason, by: jev }`
    when Jev's was the second), and part 6 takes back what a quarantine takes back;
  - **fail closed**: no answer, an error, a pick that is no option, one below the point's threshold, or Jev not there (no
    TypeSafe API key) holds the request for a person, with why (`Jev gave no answer`, `Jev was not sure enough`, `Jev could
    not be asked`). It never allows.
  A person's approve or decline while Jev reads it wins: Jev's later answer changes nothing. A held request times out as
  any other (part 9).

A job a Jev deny lowered below `approved` gets no run with no person (part 7), so Jev is not asked for its next request: a
person approves or declines it. The job view shows `Jev denied its sandbox request` beside the level, and Approve trust
takes it (`trustApprovable`). Why not `allow_narrowed`, which the issue also names: a narrower run is a narrower template,
which only a template request makes (issue #716), and the hopper never narrows one for the job; a person can decline with
a reason that says what to ask for. Persisted state: none — requests are kept in memory, and `deny:jev` is one more reason
id, which the build before verifies (its MAC covers the reasons) and reads as any other.

**Origin acts kept with the job** (part 14, `JobSourceRef.originActs`). The issue: "Provenance (captured at intake, stored
with the snapshot)": the author, the nominator, and the timeline events that matter, each with its actor and `via_app`. The
hopper already reads these to judge a job's origin (issue #652, "Trusted origin and request cards": the issue's author, and
the newest `labeled` and `assigned` events from its events; on GitLab also who edited it), and before this part it kept only
the verdict. Now a job of a trusted origin or of an approved request card keeps its item's **origin acts** as read then: each
act's `role` (`author`, `labelled`, `assigned`, `edited`), `login` and GitHub or GitLab user `id` when known, `app` (an app or
bot it was done through, `performed_via_github_app`), and `trusted` (a trusted actor did it, not through an app). A job of an
approved card keeps the acts no trusted actor did too, so a person sees why it needed an approval.

- Run again and Rework keep the acts of the job they follow, as they keep its origin; a job queued before origins were
  judged gets them with its origin (`job.origin_judged`).
- **Shown**: the stamp view (`originActs`, null when none is kept; `hopper job stamp`), the job view (a line `origin`,
  each act not a trusted actor's marked), and `job.queued`'s `source`.
- **Jev reads them**: Jev's trust check (part 4) gets them in `source.originActs`, as the issue's "plus the provenance facts".
- **No rule reads them**: the stamp's level still comes from the job origin and the author (`ruleCeiling`). The acts are a
  record of what the origin was judged from, not a second judge.
- Persisted state: one optional field on the job's source. A job made before this part has none, and the build before reads
  a job with them as before. No migration.

**The stamp in OpenFGA, and a minimum trust** (part 15, `src/authz/trust.ts`, `src/authz/trust-model.ts`). The issue:
"OpenFGA gets `trust:<level>#holder@job:<id>`. Template approvals can then require a minimum trust"; "an
`operation_profile` has `min_trust`, and the requester must hold `trust:<level>` at or above it". So:

- **Each live job holds its trust** in OpenFGA: the runtime gives Access the level each live job's stamp verifies at
  (`trustLevel`), and the hopper writes `trust:<level>#holder@job:<user>/<job>` for that level **and each level below
  it** (`holderTuples`), so `trust:approved#holder` is every live job at `approved` or above. A quarantined job, a job
  whose stamp does not verify, and every job while there is no stamp key hold none. A level that changes (a deny, an edit,
  a quarantine) is pushed with the next change of who is live, within 2 s (`REQUESTERS_CHECK_MS`); a job that is no longer
  live loses them, as its other tuples.
- **A minimum trust** on an operation profile (Users & access → Access, panel **Minimum trust**; `POST /ui/api/access`
  `{ action: "min-trust", operation, asset, level }`, `level: null` clears it; least role admin, the instance admin's, as
  every edit of Access): the hopper keeps `trust:<level>#min_trust@operation_profile:<profile>` with who set it and when,
  one per profile, and writes `job:*#trust_gated` on that profile with it (`gateTuples`, never stored). The default model
  (`TRUST_MODEL`): `below_trust: trust_gated but not trust_met`, `trust_met: holder from min_trust`, and the profile's
  `requester` is `requester from approved_for but not below_trust`. So a job below the minimum is no requester of the
  profile, whatever its template's approvals say, and its mint is denied: `job <id> is at trust approved, below the
  minimum trust trusted to read on cluster prod` (`belowMinimum`). A profile with no minimum is as before.
- **Only a job is gated.** A box (`machine`) and a person (`user`) have no stamp: the minimum does not apply to them. The
  vault asks each mint as the job (`src/vault/mint.ts`), so a box job is gated by its own level.
- **A trial** (Try a check) is told a level for its made-up job (`level`, `owner` when none), and records it
  (`trial.level`). A read-only check's mint (issue #797) is told `owner`: it tests a template, not a job's work.
- **The permission matrix** shows each job's trust (`RequesterRow.trust`), and a path through a minimum names it and the
  job's holder tuple (`trustedPath`); a job below it reaches no grant of that profile.
- **A model without the trust relations** (`trustGaps`: `trust#holder`, `operation_profile#min_trust`,
  `operation_profile#trust_gated`) writes no trust tuple and still decides mints; a minimum trust is refused (400). A model
  that drops them is refused while a profile has a minimum (400: clear them first), so no minimum stops counting by an
  edit. The hopper's own older default is upgraded at the start, as for every relation it writes.

Persisted state: one more relation in the access tuples (`min_trust`), and the new default model as a new version. The
build before pushes a stored minimum with the model it finds (this build's, which it keeps, since it lacks nothing that
build needs) but writes no `trust_gated` and no holder: there, no job is below a minimum, so mints are decided as before
this part. No migration.

**The request's capabilities against the stamp's** (part 16, `src/domain/stamp-capabilities.ts`; `outsideStamp` in
`src/sandbox/requests.ts`). The issue's gate 2, policy first: "A request outside the stamp's capabilities is denied", and
the test "denied by policy, with no Jev call". A stamp's capabilities are the operation profiles whose minimum trust (part
15) its level meets, as it verifies now; a profile with no minimum is in every stamp. A need above it is **outside the
stamp** (`outsideStamp`: `the job's trust stamp is approved, below the minimum trust owner to write on aws-account …`; a
quarantined job meets no minimum, and a job whose stamp does not verify meets none either, as in OpenFGA):

- **At the skill broker**, `sandbox --needs` and `sandbox-template --needs` are refused (403) before a template is made:
  `the minimum trust refuses these needs: … Asking again does not change it: an admin sets the minimum trust in Settings →
  Access. Find another way.` A need step (`/job/step?needs=`) is refused the same way, before its template request.
- **A sandbox request** of a template with such a profile (`sandbox --template NAME`, a template named in the brief before
  the start, or a template a person approved meanwhile) is declined at once, before the approvals, Jev and a person, by
  **the minimum trust** (`MIN_TRUST_DECLINER`): `vault.sandbox_declined { by: the minimum trust }`, with the reason the job
  is told.
- **Set later**, the minimum stops a run approved before: a box step of that template does not run while the job is below
  it (`runnable`), whoever approved it; cleared, it runs again. The mint is denied as well (part 15).

A deny by policy is no deny of part 5: the job's trust stays, and Jev's sandbox check is not asked. Access reads the minima
as kept (`minTrusts`), so a change applies at the next ask, with no restart. Persisted state: none.

**Edits in the origin** (part 17, `editActs`, `originsOf` in `src/sources/github/origin.ts`). The issue's rule: "Any actor
on the timeline who is not trusted, and who edited the body or set a nominating event: at most `untrusted`". Before this
part a GitHub issue's origin read only who wrote, labelled and assigned it (issue #652), so a collaborator who is no trusted
actor could rewrite the body of the user's own issue before a sync took it, and the job ran that text at `owner`. Now the
origin reads who edited its title or body too, as on GitLab (issue #1642):

- **An edit by someone who is no trusted actor**, or by an app or a bot (a `name[bot]` login), makes the issue a **request
  card**: `edited by <login>, not a trusted actor`, `edited by an app or a bot (<login>)`. A job made from it is
  `untrusted` by the rules (no job origin) until a person approves its text; then it is `approved`, as for any card.
- **Edits that cannot be read** are one edit by nobody known (`who edited it is not known`): the issue is a card. A GitHub
  API with no edit read (`issueEdits` absent) reads none, as before.
- **The job keeps its editors** in its origin acts (part 14): one `edited` act per editor, in the order of their first edit,
  each with whether a trusted actor did it. The stamp view, the job view and Jev's trust check show them; the request card
  shows them with the other acts.
- **Only an issue the source judges** is read: one with no job that has not ended, one to run again, or one waiting for its
  origin. A job that started keeps its origin; an edit after its start lowers it at gate 2 (part 7).

Cost: one more GraphQL read per judged issue per sync, as the events read is one REST read. Persisted state: none new —
`edited` is a role the job's origin acts and `job.queued`'s schema already take (GitLab). No migration. An issue a build
before this part took keeps its job; an issue it judges again (Run again) is judged with its edits.

**Jev's kind check** (part 18, `src/domain/kind-check.ts`, `src/engine/kind-checks.ts`; the decision point `intake-kind`,
"Decider calls"). The issue: "A second point, `intake-kind`, picks job, question, proposal, research, permission or status".
The hopper has three kinds of job a source item can start: the work, research and a proposal (issues #537, #543). So Jev picks
from `keep` (the work), `research` and `proposal`. It is **due** (`kindCheckDue`) for a waiting work job from a job source
that never started (no attempt, no answer waiting), with no check on it: no research or proposal asked already (a label, a
heading or a person), no fork, follow-on or tend job, on an executor that writes reviews.

- **What Jev reads** (`kindCheckState`): the job's id and goal; its source's kind, repository, number and labels; and the
  first 4000 characters of its prompt as `untrustedText`, which the instructions say is data, never instructions.
- **Only less, never more.** Research and a proposal change nothing and open no pull request. Jev can ask a work job for
  one of them, as a person's ask does (`askFor`), and never turns research or a proposal into work.
- **Off**: Jev is not asked; the job does the work. **Shadow** (the default): Jev is asked once per waiting job and hopper
  run; the pick is only recorded and compared with `keep` at once.
- **Active**: the decider holds the job while the check is due (`Jev checks what kind of job it is: held — …`). The check is
  then kept on the job (`kindCheck { pick, confidence, applied, kind?, fail? }`). A pick of research or a proposal sets that
  flag on its spec (`respecify`, so its stamp is signed for the new spec and the trust check is asked again) and appends
  `research.asked` or `proposal.asked` with `by: jev`. A check is written only while it is still due: a start or a person's
  ask that came first wins.
- **No gate.** The kind is not trust: a check with no sure pick — no answer, not sure (`fail: not_sure`), Jev not there
  (`fail: skipped`), a pick that is no option — keeps the work. Trust stays the job of the stamp and Jev's trust check.

Persisted state: `kindCheck` is one more optional field in the job's body; the build before keeps it as it is and does not
read it. No migration.

**Linked pull requests and the repository's visibility** (part 19, `src/domain/linked-pulls.ts`, `linksOf` in
`src/sources/github/origin.ts`). The issue's provenance fields `linked` ("the PRs and issues referenced, with their authors,
and whether a PR head is a fork") and `repo_visibility`. Fork code is the case to see: an issue of the user's own that says
"merge the change of #12" runs at `owner`, and #12 can be a stranger's pull request from a fork. So, for each GitHub issue
whose origin is trusted or approved (only its job keeps them):

- **The names in its text** (`linkedRefs`, its title and body, issue #2227): `#N`, `owner/name#N`, and the pull request and
  issue URLs of the issue's own GitHub host, each once, in their order, at most 10 (`LINKED_MAX`); never the issue itself,
  never a `#` joined to a word, never a bare `#N` in code (a log line or a snippet asks nothing of it).
- **One read per name** (`GitHubApi.linkedItem`, GraphQL `repository { visibility issueOrPullRequest(number) }`, in the
  batched reads of issue #822): its repository's visibility, and the pull request when the name is one — its URL, its
  author, `isCrossRepository` as `fork`. The issue's own read gives its repository's visibility.
- **Kept on the job** (`JobSourceRef.visibility`, `JobSourceRef.linkedPulls`): each pull request with `trusted` (its author
  is a trusted actor, asked of Access with the origin's logins; a bot never is). A name that is an issue, or that GitHub
  does not show (`NOT_FOUND`), is not kept. A read that fails is kept as `unread` (its URL from the name), so a person sees
  that something was not read. Run again, Rework and `job.origin_judged` keep them as they keep the origin acts.
- **Shown**: the stamp view (`visibility`, `linkedPulls`, null when none is kept), the job view (a line `links`, a pull
  request no trusted actor wrote marked), and `job.queued`'s `source`.
- **Jev reads them**: Jev's trust check gets them in `source`, and has one more reason, `fork_code` ("it brings in a pull
  request of a fork that no trusted actor wrote"), to lower the job.
- **No rule reads them**, as the origin acts: the stamp's level still comes from the origin. A rule would decide for every
  issue that names any pull request, and most do so for good reasons; Jev and a person read the text the name is in. A job's
  `pr edit` (issue #2151, "Jobs ask the hopper, not GitHub") reads the same names, but from the item's approved text at
  the edit, every one (issue #2227), not from these records; GitHub still decides whether its user may.

Also in this part: the GraphQL read of an issue's edits (issue #662, part 17) read the answer one level too high, so it
found no edits against GitHub; the fake GitHub hid it. It reads them under `data` now, and an answer with errors throws, so
the edits count as not known (a request card), as part 17 says.

Cost: one more GraphQL read per name and one for the issue, batched, only for an issue the source judges that may be taken.
Persisted state: two optional fields on the job's source; the build before reads a job with them as before. No migration.

**The Intake view of the stamp** (part 20, `ui/src/views/intake-trust.tsx`, `heldByTrust` in `ui/src/model/trust.ts`). The
issue's Intake section: "held candidates, history, provenance, grants and brake 1". A hold text sent a person "to Intake",
but Intake listed only a source's items, not the jobs a stamp holds. Now Intake shows **Held by trust** above the sources:

- **Which jobs**: each waiting job in status `held` whose hold reason is one `stampHold` or the trust check gives — no stamp,
  a stamp that does not verify, a quarantine, a level below the dispatch minimum or below the intake strictness, Jev's trust
  check due. The UI imports nothing of `src/` at run time, so it keeps the start of each text (`trustHold`);
  `test/ui/trust-held.test.ts` checks them against the daemon's. A job held for its origin (`ORIGIN_PENDING`) is not listed:
  its request card is.
- **Each row**: the job (a link to its view), the hold reason, and its trust as on the job view (`JobTrust`): the level, why
  it was lowered, its origin acts and links — the provenance —, with Approve trust and Lift quarantine for an operator. The
  history is the job's timeline (`intake.stamped`, `job.trust_lowered`), one click away.
- **Counted**: the jobs that wait on a person come first, and Intake's nav badge and Needs you count them; a job Jev still
  checks waits on Jev, and is listed last and not counted.
- **Grants and brake 1** stay where they are kept: the trusted actors (who may start jobs, the standing grant the hopper has)
  and the intake strictness, on Settings → Intake, which the panel links.

No route, no event, no persisted state: the daemon already sends each held job with its hold reason and stamp.

**A held job always has a way on** (issue #1974). A job of a GitHub source made before origins were judged, that had
started when migration 39 ran, kept no origin and no `originPending`. The stamps' backfill then stamped it `untrusted`
(`origin:none`), and when it waited again it was in Held by trust with only Quarantine: its hold text sent a person to
its item in Intake, but its issue had a job, so Intake listed no request card for it. Approvals keep one home (#896), so
the fix adds no second approval of an item:

- **It waits for its origin** (`awaitsOrigin` in `src/domain/trust-stamp.ts`): the backfill marks a job of a judging source
  with no origin, not a job a job made, `originPending`; tenant migration 85 marks those that have not ended. The next sync
  judges its issue as for any job that waits for its origin (`source-host.ts` `refresh`): of a trusted origin, it is stamped
  again by the rules (the owner's own issue at `owner`), and it goes on; else its request card opens in Intake, and Approve
  there approves it.
- **A job with no item** (no source: queued by hand, an older build) has no request card. Below `approved`, a person approves
  its trust on the job (`trustApprovable`), and its hold text says so.
- **Cancel in each row** of Held by trust, for an operator, after a confirm (`POST /ui/api/jobs/:id/cancel`).
- **A job made from an item offered with no origin** (issue #2113). The sync judges the origin only of an issue whose job
  has ended or that has none; an issue whose job was still live is offered with no origin, to refresh that job. When the
  job ended between the judgement and the offer, `ingest` made a new job of that item with no origin: stamped `untrusted`
  (`origin:none`), with no `originPending`, and so again in Held by trust with no request card and no approval. `ingest`
  now marks such a job (`awaitsOrigin`) `originPending`, as the backfill does: the next sync judges its issue, and it goes
  on, or its request card opens in Intake. An issue a job filed (a routed child) is no trusted origin, so a person approves
  its card. Tenant migration 86 marks the jobs made so since migration 85 that have not ended.

Persisted state: migrations 85 and 86 set `originPending` on rows only; the build before reads it as migration 39's. A job a job
made keeps the level its parent had at the backfill.

**The comment command** (part 21, `src/domain/comment-command.ts`; `nominated` in `src/sources/github/discover.ts`,
`nominatedAct` in `src/sources/github/origin.ts`). The issue's Decision N, recommended N1 + N3: the assignment, and "a comment
command `/hopper run|research|propose`". Before this part only the assignment nominated an issue. Now:

- **What a command is**: a comment whose first line that is not empty is `/hopper run`, `/hopper research` or `/hopper
  propose` (any case, nothing more on the line). A quote, a code span or words after the verb are no command.
- **Whose command counts**: only the source's connected account's, the login an issue must be assigned to, and only its
  newest command on the issue. A command whose comment was edited since it was written (`updated_at` is not `created_at`,
  or not known) is none: a collaborator who can edit a comment could have written it.
- **It nominates** a labelled issue not assigned to the account: discover reads the comments of each such issue (one read,
  kept with the listing as a job's reads are, issue #985) and takes it as an assigned one. Its origin has the act
  `nominated` (the command's writer, and the app it was written through) in place of `assigned`, judged as every act: through
  an app (`performed_via_github_app`, the Cursor case of the issue) it is no trusted act, and the issue is a request card
  (`nominated by an app or a bot (<app>)`). The author, the label and the edits are judged as before. After a rejection,
  only a command written since takes the issue again, as only an assignment since does.
- **It asks for the kind**, on an assigned issue too: `research` and `propose` set the job's research or proposal flag at
  its start, as the label `hopper:research` or a Research heading does (issue #543). `run` asks for the work.
- **No job writes one**: the GitHub proxy refuses a job's comment that is a command (`JOB_COMMAND`, `checkRequest`), so a
  job cannot nominate an issue in the user's name. A connection through the hopper's app marks a job's comment with the app
  anyway; a connection by token does not, so the refusal is the guard.
- The job keeps the act in its origin acts (part 14): the stamp view, the job view and Jev's trust check show it.

Cost: one comments read per labelled issue not assigned to the account, read again only when the listing shows the issue
changed. Persisted state: `nominated` is one more origin act role in the job's source and in `job.queued`,
`source.request_approved` and `source.request_auto_approved`; the build before reads a job with it and shows the role as it
is. No migration. Not in this part: N2 (watched repositories) and N4 (a Projects field), which the issue does not recommend.

Brake 1's `open` lets a `screened` job start; only Jev's check gives that level now.

**Residual risk.** The backfill trusts the row as it finds it at a start: a writer with database access who removes a
job's stamp and edits its source before a restart gets the stamp the rules give the edited row. Between starts, such a job
is held. The stamp key comes from the link key, which is kept in the user's schema: a writer who can read it can sign.

## Vault grants (issue #652, 2026-10-11)

Owner requirement (the 2026-10-10 intake security review, path F, requirement 5): "A job does not get the host's SSH
agent, the host's keys or the vault helper unless the user grants them to that job." Part 1 (#667) took the ssh agent
away. Before this part the vault gave a job on a box every secret its template's approved scope held: the template's
approval was a grant for every job any box of it ran. Owner decision on the issue (option 1): **a grant per job, asked
when it is needed**; the template's scope stays the upper bound; the grant is kept for the job across Run again; and no
`HOPPER_SECRET` on a machine that is not a box.

**No helper off a box.** A job gets `HOPPER_SECRET` only on a machine whose client serves the vault **and** that joined
as a box of a template (`MachineSnapshot.template`, `src/users/github-proxy.ts`). The vault gives nothing to any other
machine (`boxAsk`), so the path there was an invitation to ask, never an answer.

**The grant** (`src/vault/grants.ts`, `withVaultGrants`, outermost over the user's vault wherever it runs — in the hopper or
in its container — and over the shared secrets). A box's ask for a vault secret (`POST /client/vault`, a name) or a mint
(`kind operation asset`) passes the delivery checks first (`boxAsk`: the machine's link, the job's proxy token, the job at
work there, a box of a template the vault holds). A refusal there is the vault's own, with its reason. Then the job's
**item** must have a **vault grant**: a person's grant, kept for the job's source key (a job of no source: its id), in
the table `vault_grants` (tenant migration 40; the build before runs on it, and gives every box job the vault as it did).
Run again, Rework and Retry make jobs of the same item, so one grant covers them. With no grant the ask is refused
(`vault.refused` or `vault.mint_refused`, reason `job <id> has no vault grant: …`), and the hopper asks a person: a
**grant ask**, kept in the hopper's memory (dropped when the job is no longer at work or its item is granted),
`vault.grant_asked` once per job. A granted job's ask then goes on to the vault, which decides as before: the template's
approved scope, a launch's scope (issue #708), Access for a mint and for a shared secret. The grant widens nothing.
A Windows sandbox step's secret (issue #731, "Windows sandbox steps") passes the same grant: with none, the ask names the
Windows host (`windowsHost`) in place of a box and template.

**Granting** (Vault, panel **Vault grants**: each grant ask as a card — the job, its box and template, what it
asked for, the item — with **Grant**; each grant with who granted it and **Revoke**). `POST /ui/api/jobs/:id/grant-vault`
and `POST /ui/api/jobs/:id/revoke-vault`, operator: a person's act through the UI session — a job's routes reach no
`/ui/api/`, and its proxy token is no API token, so a job asks and never grants. **Access** decides first: OpenFGA
`vault_grant#can_grant` for the person signed in, the user whose jobs these are told as the grant's `owner`
(`vaultGrantObject`, the key hashed as an item's). 403 when denied; 503 when OpenFGA cannot be asked, and nothing is
granted. A model edited before this has `vault_grant` gaps apart (`vaultGrantGaps`): every grant is denied, mints are
not; the hopper's own unedited model is upgraded. `vault.granted { job, key, by }`; `vault.grant_revoked { job, key, by }`
(409 when there is none). Both answer the vault's view: `GET /api/vault` carries `grantAsks` and `grants`.

**What a grant covers** (issue #1124). A grant's key alone names no job a person can find: a direct job's is
`direct:<direct job id>`, not a job's id. So the view answers each grant and each grant ask with its **item**
(`grantView`, `grantItemOf`, `src/domain/vault-grants.ts`; read in `withVaultGrants`): its title (a direct job's own, else
the source's, else the job's goal), its repository, its issue or pull request link, the item's newest job
(`getBySourceKey`; a job of no source is its own key) and that job's status, and **stale** — no job of the item waits or is
at work, or none is kept. A stale grant gives nothing now; the panel flags it beside **Revoke**. Nothing revokes it by
itself: Run again makes a new job of the same item, and the grant is kept for it. Each grant also says how it was made:
`made: grant` (Grant, an API token, or `hopper vault grant`) or `made: submit` (a direct job's submission that authorized
`vault`, by its submitter); `via: cli` and `command` when the operator CLI made it — its session signs in no person, so
its grants are kept `by: operator CLI` (`OPERATOR_CLI_NAME`), whoever ran it on the hopper's host with the database's
credentials. `hopper vault` prints the same view. Tests: `test/domain/vault-grants.test.ts`,
`test/ui/vault-grants-view.test.ts`, `test/integration/operator-cli-vault.test.ts`.

**Granting with no browser** (issue #1089). `hopper vault grant <job>` and `hopper vault revoke <job>`
(`src/cli-operator-vault.ts`) are the same two routes, under the session the operator CLI mints for the one call (issue
#374), role operator. Access decides as for a click, for the hopper's user the CLI acts as; the answer is the vault's view.
An agent with an API token uses the routes themselves, with the scope `jobs:grant-vault` (in the preset "Agent: read
everything and approve what waits"). A job still never grants: its proxy token is no API token, and it runs no operator CLI
with the database's credentials. Tests: `test/integration/operator-cli-vault.test.ts`.

**Residual risk.** The grant is per item, not per secret: a granted item's jobs get the whole of their template's approved
scope, as every box job did before. A person who grants a job of a request card's approved text grants that text's work.
A job on a person's own account (no box) can still read that home's files (`~/.ssh`, a gh login): only a box keeps them
out ("Git through the hopper", residual risk).

### The standing read grant (issue #1472, 2026-10-16)

Owner decision on issue #1472 (part 4, a default read-only `cluster/utility-view` for every job): **a per-user setting, off
by default**, that grants with no person only what is read-only. It reverses issue #652 option 1 ("a grant per job, asked
when it is needed") for read-only grants only; every other grant is a person's, as above.

**What it covers** (`readsOnlyInPolicy`, `src/domain/vault-grants.ts`): a template that has needs, every one a `read`
the user's read policy holds ("Templates on request"), and no vault secret. A write, sync or apply, a read outside the
policy, a vault secret, or no needs at all: not covered, and the job's ask becomes a grant ask for a person as before.
`cluster/utility-view` is the first case: a template of `read cluster/utility` with `cluster/utility` in the read policy.

**The grant** (`withVaultGrants`, `src/vault/grants.ts`). The gate checks a person's grant first. With none, and the
toggle on, a box job whose box's template is covered passes, and `vault.granted { job, key, by: "standing read grant" }`
is recorded once for that job — the same event as a person's grant, with the setting as `by`, as skip template approval
names itself. The vault then decides as for any granted job: the template's approved scope, Access for a mint. The grant
widens nothing, and it covers only the box it was asked from: the same job on a box of a template with a write is refused
until a person grants it. No row is kept in `vault_grants`: the job is kept in the hopper's memory while it is at work, so
Run again and Rework do not inherit it — each new job is granted again only while the toggle is on. It does not show in
the **Vault grants** panel; the job's timeline shows the event.

**Turned off**, it grants no job that has not asked yet: a job already granted keeps it until it ends (its run had
started), and every other job's ask is a grant ask for a person. A hopper restart forgets the jobs it granted: with the
toggle off, such a job's next ask waits for a person — closed, never open.

**The toggle** is in Vault, panel **Sandbox approvals**: `standingReadGrant` on `POST /ui/api/sandbox-approvals`
(admin, a box action), kept in the user's `sandboxApprovals` setting (absent: off, so no migration), recorded in
`vault.sandbox_approvals_set`. YOLO does not set it. Tests: `test/integration/standing-read-grant.test.ts`,
`test/domain/standing-read-grant.test.ts`.

**Residual risk.** A read the policy holds is given to every job of the user while the toggle is on, whatever the job's
origin: a job of a request card a person approved reads what any trusted job reads. The read policy is the upper bound,
so an entry such as `cluster/*` gives every job a read of every cluster. Keep the policy narrow while the toggle is on.

## Delegate approvers (issue #1138, 2026-10-14)

Requirement: the owner hands approvals to an agent (Chief of Staff) without the agent touching the owner's browser session
or session token. A named, revocable credential with an end, scoped to approvals only; usable from the CLI headless; each
approval records the delegate, whom it acted for, and when; optional limits on what it may approve, prod staying the
owner's.

- **What it is.** A **delegate approver** is a **grant** ("Grants and refresh tokens") of the preset `delegate-approver`
  (`src/domain/delegates.ts` `DELEGATE_SCOPES`): `vault:read`, `jobs:grant-vault`, `jobs:deny-vault`,
  `vault:edit.approve-template`, `sandbox-requests:edit.approve`, `sandbox-requests:edit.decline` (and, since issue #2197,
  `sandbox-requests:edit.approve-run`, `sandbox-requests:edit.decline-run`: a run card). A box grant, as a
  sandbox request is a box action. A mint that names the preset and any other `scopes` is refused (400): it is approvals
  only, so settings, secrets, `revoke-vault`, the sandbox toggles and the master key are out of its scopes (403). Its name
  is the grant's label, its end the grant's `days`; its role is its minter's, at most. No new kind of token: the grant's
  refresh rotation, reuse detection, idle end and revoke all apply.
- **Minted and revoked on Access requests.** The panel **Delegate approvers** (`ui/src/views/delegate-approvers.tsx`, an
  admin's) mints one (`POST /ui/api/api-tokens` `{ action: 'mint', label, preset: 'delegate-approver', deny, days }`),
  shows its refresh token once with the command an agent runs, lists each delegate with its policy, and revokes it at
  once. `hopper token mint --preset delegate-approver --deny prod` mints one from the operator CLI.
- **The approver policy.** `deny` on the mint (at most 32 entries): each entry matches, in any case, any name an approval
  touches. A grant ask: its template, machine or Windows host, the names the job asked for, and the template's secrets and
  assets. A template: its name, secrets and profiles' assets, waiting ones too. A sandbox request: its template's. A match
  is 403 (`src/http/ui/delegates.ts` `refuseDenied`); the owner still approves it. Substring, not glob: `prod` keeps
  `shop-prod` and `prod/apps` the owner's. Kept on the grant's row (`api_grants` body `delegate`), so no migration; a build
  before this one reads the row and ignores the field, and its scopes still keep the token to the approval routes.
- **Only what waits.** A delegate grants or denies only a grant ask that waits (409 else): it never grants an item no job
  asked for. Its template approval and sandbox decisions are those of the routes, which approve only what waits already.
- **Deny.** `POST /ui/api/jobs/:id/deny-vault` (a person's too: Deny on the ask's card) drops the ask and records
  `vault.grant_denied`; that job, still with no grant, asks no more (kept in memory). Run again makes a new job, which may
  ask again.
- **Audit.** An approval by a delegate records `by` as `<label> (delegate of <person>)` in its event (`vault.granted`,
  `vault.grant_denied`, `vault.approved`, `vault.sandbox_approved`, `vault.sandbox_declined`), on the vault grant and on the
  template's approval, so Access requests shows it on the card, with the time. A notifier or webhook subscribed to those
  events tells the owner. An approval through another grant's API token (a `*` key, issue #2229) records `by` as
  `<label> (API token of <person>)` the same way, so a key's decisions are told apart from the person's own.
- **The CLI, headless.** `hopper grant [list] | approve <job> | deny <job>`, `hopper sandbox requests | approve <id> |
  decline <id> --reason <text>`, `hopper template approve <name>`. With `HOPPER_REFRESH_TOKEN_FILE` set the operator CLI
  opens no database (`runOperatorActionWithGrant`, `src/cli-operator.ts`): it trades the refresh token in that file at
  `POST /ui/auth/token/refresh`, writes the new one to the file (mode 600, by rename) before it acts, and sends the action
  with the API token. `HOPPER_URL` or `--url` names the hopper; `--user` is refused (the grant names its user). Any
  operator action works this way, within the grant's scopes.
- **Not built.** "Read-only approvals can be set to auto" is the read policy and the auto-approve policy already
  ("Templates on request", "Sandboxes jobs start"). A limit by role is not built: a delegate's role is its minter's, and its
  scopes already keep it to approvals.

**Residual risk.** Whoever holds the refresh-token file approves what waits, within the policy, until the grant ends or
is revoked. The policy is by name: an asset named with none of the deny entries is approved. A deny entry that is a
common word (`a`) denies nearly everything.

Tests: `test/integration/delegate-approver.test.ts`, `test/integration/job-sandboxes.test.ts` (a delegate's sandbox
approval), `test/domain/delegates.test.ts`, `test/ui/delegate-approvers-view.test.ts`.

## Repository-agnostic lanes (issue #431, 2026-10-11)

Job 7 of the pointed-job architecture (tracking issue #424). Requirement: a lane takes any job and gets a GitHub
client and a work tree scoped to that job's target repository, so one lane runs jobs of different repositories one
after another, each with the right clone, credentials and scope, and neither can touch the other's repository.

**What was already so.** A lane is a slot on a machine, never a repository's. Each job gets its own way to GitHub:
`hopper-gh` and git through the hopper's `/job/git/` proxy, both bound to the job's token and refused for any
repository but the job's own (issue #652, "Git through the hopper"; `test/integration/git-proxy.test.ts` "refuses a
push to another repository than the job's own"). The work tree follows the job's repository through the machine's
`workTrees` map (issue #691), and a plain work tree gets the job's repository cloned in it (issue #361).

**The gap, and the change.** A work tree that was the top of a git repository gave every job a worktree of that
repository, whatever the job's own: on a machine whose work tree is a checkout of repository A, a job of
repository B worked in A. Seen live: a job of one repository started in a worktree of another. Now the job
worktree command (`src/executors/herdr/job-worktree.ts`) compares the work tree's `origin` with the job's
repository (`owner/name`, in any case, as `mappedWorkTree` does):
- the job's own repository, or a job that names none: as before, a worktree of the work tree (`made`);
- another repository (or none at all): the job's repository is fetched, or cloned the first time, into the work
  tree's scratch dir, `repoCheckoutOf` = `<work tree>/.hopper-scratch/repos/<owner>/<name>` (since issue #858 the
  repository mirror `mirrorOf`, `<name>.git` there, outcome `mirror`: "Git efficiency"), and the job gets its
  worktree of that checkout, `<work tree>/.hopper-scratch/<job id>/<name>` (outcome `other`). The executor
  records the checkout (`PaneState.checkout`) and names it in the prompt, as for issue #361's checkout.
The checkout is under `.hopper-scratch`, which git ignores there, so the work tree's repository stays clean. The
reap removes the job's worktree with its scratch dir and keeps the checkout for the next job of that repository;
the sweep never touches it, as it touches only dirs named by a job id it knows (as `deps`). Owner and name both
name the path, so two repositories with one name do not meet.

**Not changed.** With job worktrees off, a repository work tree is used as it is (outcome `none`), as before: that
option says to share the work tree. The print agents (codex, cursor-agent, opencode, omp) run with job worktrees
off, so the same holds for them. The job record is still the queue's `Job`: the pointed-job record (#425) and the
tracking layer (#426) are not built yet; when they are, a lane takes that record the same way, through the
job's repository.

Tests: `test/herdr/job-worktree.test.ts` "a work tree that is another repository (issue #431)" (real git: the
clone in the scratch dir, the work tree untouched; one lane, two jobs of two repositories back to back, each in
its own; a later job fetches; a checkout of another repository there is refused; the reap keeps the checkout; the
job's own repository in any case as before), `test/herdr/executor-job-worktree.test.ts` (the executor's side over
the fake herdr: the checkout saved and named in the prompt; the job's own repository unchanged).

## Cross-references (issue #430, 2026-10-11)

Part 5 of the pointed-job architecture (tracking issue #424). A job keeps its issue's **cross-references**: each pull
request or commit, of its repository or another, that closes the issue on GitHub. They tie pull requests to jobs, the
input of pull-based completion (issue #428) and of the issue graph (issue #437).

**The text proposes, GitHub confirms.** `closingReferences` (`src/domain/cross-references.ts`, pure) reads the closing
references of a text: a closing keyword, then `#N`, `owner/repo#N` or the issue's URL; each issue needs its own keyword;
code spans, code blocks and HTML comments are left out. `confirmedCrossReferences` keeps only what GitHub links as
closing the issue, and adds the keyword the text used. So a text reference GitHub does not treat as closing is never
kept: a mention (`Refs #N`), a part (`Part of #N`), a closing keyword GitHub did not act on (a pull request to a branch
that is not the default one). A pull request GitHub links with no keyword in its text (by hand, in its Development box)
is kept, with no keyword. An issue's own text never closes anything on GitHub, so it gives no cross-references.

**One GraphQL call** (`GitHubApi.crossReferences`, `CROSS_REFERENCES_QUERY` in `src/sources/github/closer.ts`): the
issue's `closedByPullRequestsReferences` (any state, `includeClosedPrs`) with their bodies, and its newest 100 timeline
items of three kinds: `CrossReferencedEvent` (a pull request that mentions it, with its body), `ReferencedEvent` (a
commit, with its message) and `ClosedEvent` (a commit that closed it). The mentions are each text once, by URL; the
closing ones are the closing pull requests and the commit closers.

**When, and where it is kept.** At each sync, before the follow of a job that follows its pull request (`follow: open`,
`src/sources/after-done.ts`), `JobSource.crossReferences` is asked; a change replaces `crossReferences` in the job's
source state. The follow, a tend and a reconcile keep the field, as they keep every other one. A throw is only logged:
the follow goes on, and the next sync asks again. No event: the field is a view of GitHub, asked again each sync, as
`seen` is. A job of no GitHub issue has none and asks nothing.

**Pointed jobs.** A job of the hopper reads as a pointed job on its issue (issue #425, `pointedJobOf`), so its
cross-references are that pointed job's. A pointed job whose pointer is a pull request (the issues it closes,
`closingIssuesReferences`) is not read yet: nothing runs one until the tracking service (issue #426) does.

## The issue graph (issue #437, 2026-10-11)

Part of the pointed-job architecture (issue #424, job 13 of 13). Read by the job graph and by search (issue #945, "Search": an issue
and a pull request as search documents); nothing else depends on it.

**What it keeps** (`src/domain/issue-graph.ts`, glossary "Issue graph"). Nodes, each with the attributes the newest read
gave (merged, so a read that does not know a value leaves it): an **owner** (`owner:<login>`, a GitHub organization or user,
its `type` when GitHub said), a **repo** (`repo:<owner/name>`, lowercase), an **issue** and a **pull request** (their URLs:
repository, number, state; an issue read itself also its title and `updatedAt`), and a **project** (a Project (v2), its
URL). Edges: `owned_by` (a repository or a Project to its owner), `in_repo` (an issue or pull request to its repository),
`in_project` (an issue to a Project it is an item of), `closes` (a pull request to the issue its merge closes, any state),
`references` (an issue or pull request to an issue it mentions: the issue's timeline cross-references), `sub_issue_of` (a
sub-issue to its parent).

**Where** (tenant migration 42, `src/store/issue-graph.ts`): `graph_nodes` and `graph_edges`, in each user's schema. Every
edge is kept for the issue whose read gave it (`read_of`): a new read of an issue replaces only the edges its read before
gave, so another issue's read of the same link is left alone. Nodes are never removed. `read_at` is set on the node of an
issue read itself. Tables only: the build before runs on them.

**What feeds it** (`src/sources/github/graph.ts`). After each discover, a GitHub source (`github-account` or `github-app`)
reads the **place** of each open labelled issue it listed, taken or not (`GitHubApi.issuePlace`, one GraphQL query per issue,
`src/sources/github/issue-place.ts`: the repository's owner, `projectItems`, `closedByPullRequestsReferences` with closed
ones, the `CROSS_REFERENCED_EVENT` timeline items, `parent`, `subIssues`), and keeps it. An issue is read again when GitHub's
`updatedAt` changed since its last read, or when its last read is older than the source's option **`graphRefreshMinutes`**
(default 60; 0: at every sync). The option **`issueGraph`** (default on) turns the graph off for that source. Both are job
source options like the others: kept in the database, edited in Plugins, applied at the next build of the source, without a
restart. A token that cannot read a part (an
installation token and a user-owned Project) leaves that part out.

**Nothing depends on it.** A read or a write that fails is said per issue in the source's status (`graphErrors`, by issue
URL) and read again at the next sync; the discover, the items and the jobs go on as if there were no graph.

**Assumptions about the other jobs of #424.** The watches (job 3, #427) are not built. Until they are, the GitHub sources'
listing is what "sees" an issue. When the watches land, a watch feeds the same recorder (`recordIssueGraph`) for each issue
it watches. Cross-reference detection (job 6, #430, "Cross-references" above) is built and keeps its confirmed closing
references on the job, not in the graph. The graph does not read them: its `closes` edges come from the same GitHub
`closedByPullRequestsReferences` that #430 confirms against, so the two agree on closing pull requests. A commit that closed
an issue (#430 keeps it) is no node of the graph yet; a later change can add it through `recordIssueGraph`. An issue that
leaves the listing (closed, unlabelled) keeps the last state its read gave until something reads it again.

## The shared rate limiter (issue #436, 2026-10-11)

One limiter for every GitHub call and every GitHub watch (`src/github-limiter/`). Part of the pointed-job architecture (#424,
job 12); the GitHub watches themselves are job 3 (#427).

**Where it sits.** `makeRequest` (`src/sources/github/app/http.ts`) gives `@octokit/request` the limiter's `hook`. Every
GitHub adapter makes its calls through `makeRequest`: the job sources (App and connected account), the GitHub proxy, the
repository checks, bug reports, the release check. So does any GitHub watch. The sign-in and renewal calls of
`src/connected-accounts/` keep their own `@octokit/request`: they are few, and a person waits on them.

**Buckets.** GitHub keeps a rate limit per credential and resource (`core`, `graphql`, `search`, …). The limiter keeps
one bucket per credential (a hash of the `authorization` header, never shown) and resource, from GitHub's
`x-ratelimit-limit`, `-remaining`, `-reset` and `-resource` headers. Before GitHub has said, the resource is read from
the path (`/graphql`, `/search/`, else `core`).

**Pacing** (`waitBefore`, pure):
- A bucket not known yet, or past its reset: one call goes first (the probe) and learns it; the others wait for its answer.
- Above `slowBelowPercent` of the limit: no wait.
- Below it: the calls left above `reserve` are spread evenly over the time to the reset. Each call takes the next slot.
- At `reserve` or below: calls wait for the reset, then a probe learns the new window.
- A call counts against its bucket from when it is let go until GitHub answers, so a burst of GitHub watches cannot spend more
  than is left. An answer from an older window, or one that says more calls are left than a later one, changes nothing.
- After a 403 or 429 for the rate (`holdAfter`): `retry-after` when GitHub says it; no calls left, the reset; a 429 with
  neither, a minute. A 403 that is neither is no access: no hold.
- An answer with no rate-limit headers at all (a GitHub Enterprise Server with none) makes the bucket unlimited.

**Conditional requests.** A `GET` whose answer carried an ETag is kept (at most 2000 answers, the least recently used
out first), per credential and URL. The next `GET` of that URL sends `If-None-Match`. A 304 costs no call: the kept
answer is returned as a 200. `@octokit/request` throws on a 304; the hook catches it.

**The poll schedule** (`createPollSchedule`). GitHub watches register a poll; each round of the poll interval splits them into
batches of `batchSize`, the batches spread evenly across the round (`pollPlan`). The interval and the batch size are read
at each round. A GitHub watch still polling from an earlier round is skipped, never doubled. `stop` waits for the polls running.

**The intake reserve** (issue #983, 2026-10-12). Intake polls every selected repository; with many repositories it spent the
whole limit, and a job's end report and a rerun's read of its issue were then refused ("GitHub rate-limited the hopper"). So
the job sources' adapters (`src/sources/github/app/api.ts`, `account/api.ts`) make their **intake calls** — `listRepos`
(was `listOpenIssues`, issue #985), `listAssignedIssues`, `projectItems`, `listInstalledRepos` — through a `makeRequest` with `intake: true`. Such
a call, at `intakeReserve` calls left or below, waits for the reset; with `deferAfterMs` it is a **deferred call**, so the
sync pass ends and says when. Every other call — the job's own reads and writes, the report, the rerun — goes as before,
down to `reserve`. The pacing is the same for both: an intake call takes no longer slot. A 304 still costs no call, but an
intake call at the intake reserve is not asked at all: the limiter does not know beforehand that the answer is unchanged.
The other asks of the issue are already in place: conditional requests (above), and the buckets, calls left and reset time
on Settings → GitHub rate limit. (Syncs started by a followed repository's event feed, issue #967, are gone: issue #985's
in-motion cycle replaced them.)

**Settings.** `slowBelowPercent` (0–100, default 25), `reserve` (0–5000, default 50), `batchSize` (1–100, default 10),
`intakeReserve` (0–5000, default 1000; a record saved before it reads as the default), `intakeSyncMinutes` (1–1440,
default 15, issue #985: the **intake sync interval**, "Repository listings"; a record saved before it reads as the
default), `prCycleMinutes` (1–1440, default 3, issue #985: the **in-motion cycle**, "The in-motion cycle"; a record saved
before it reads as the default), whole numbers. The instance's (`githubRateLimiter` in the instance settings): one limiter serves every user. Changed only
by the hopper's admin, on Settings → GitHub rate limit (`POST /ui/api/github-rate-limiter`, the `instance` guard). The
change goes to the process's limiter at once: the next call and the next poll round use it, no restart; a pacing slot
kept from the old settings is dropped. A change is `github_rate_limiter.settings_changed`, an instance event.

**What it shows.** `GET /api/github-rate-limiter`: the settings, each bucket (fewest left first), the cache (answers
kept, hits, misses), the waits (count, total time) and `hourly`, the calls of the last hour by kind.

**Calls per hour by kind** (issue #985 part 4, 2026-10-13). `src/github-limiter/traffic.ts` keeps a rolling hour in memory:
60 one-minute buckets, the oldest dropped as the minutes pass; a restart starts at zero. A **call** is one GitHub charged:
an answer with data or a refusal (a 4xx or 5xx). A 304 is a cache hit, not a call; a call the limiter did not make (a
deferred call) or one with no answer is none. The **kind** (`callKindOf`) comes from the port read the call was made
under (`GitHubTraffic.read`, the pass reads' wrapper, now also outside a pass), so the adapters carry no flag:
- `intake`: `listRepos`, `listAssignedIssues`, `listInstalledRepos`, `projectItems`.
- `reconcile`: `openPullRequestsIn`. `pr_cycle`: `pullRequestStates`.
- `per_job_read`: any other `GET` or GraphQL query. `write`: any other REST call or a GraphQL mutation.
- `watch` and `job`: the GitHub watches' adapter (`src/github-watch/github.ts`) and the GitHub proxy's
  (`src/github-proxy/api.ts`: a running job's own requests) name their kind on
  `makeRequest` (`LimiterCall.kind`). A git fetch is no API call: it stays in the pass line only.

A call made inside a read counts under it, the installation token minted for it included. **GraphQL points**: the drop in
the `graphql` bucket's calls left since the last answer of the same window, for that credential; the whole window's use
at a new window; 1 when nothing was known. Calls that overlap make it approximate; summed over the hour it is good enough
for a dashboard. Settings → GitHub rate limit shows it as a table: one row a kind, then all. No repository, token or
credential is in it.

**The installed repositories** follow the intake sync interval too (issue #985 part 4). The app source's timed sync asked
for them at every sync (`GET /app/installations` and `GET /installation/repositories`, two calls a minute); it now asks
only when its last answer is older than `intakeSyncMinutes`, and at once on a sync a person asked for. An installation
change on GitHub is seen at most one interval later; Sync now sees it at once.

**Dependency.** This part does not wait for job 3 (#427). It assumes job 3's GitHub watches poll GitHub through `makeRequest`
and register with `createPollSchedule`, with the GitHub watch interval as `intervalMs` and the limiter's `batchSize`.

## One read per sync pass (issue #822, 2026-10-11)

Part 2 of issue #822 (GitHub API use). Part 1 (#825) gave the release check a token and a wait to GitHub's reset.

**Pass reads** (`src/sources/github/pass-reads.ts`). One **sync** of a GitHub source is one pass: the sync loop runs its
steps — discover, check, reports, write-backs, after done, thread asks — inside `JobSource.pass` (`RunsPasses`,
`src/domain/source-item.ts`; absent: the steps run as is). Inside a pass, a read of the `GitHubApi` with the same
arguments is asked of GitHub once, and two at the same time share one answer. Why: the check, the reports and the follow
of each job read the same issue and pull requests, and the GraphQL reads are POSTs, which the shared rate limiter's ETag
cache cannot answer. Measured on three followed pull requests of one repository: each issue was read twice per pass; now once.
- A write to a repository drops what the open passes read of that repository, and every read not of one repository
  (`projectItems`, `listAssignedIssues`, `listInstalledRepos`), when the write starts and again when it ends. A pass never acts
  on what it changed itself.
- A read that failed is not kept: the next one in the pass asks again.
- A read outside a pass goes to GitHub. The pass is an `AsyncLocalStorage` context, so only what the pass starts shares its
  reads; what is kept ends with the pass.
- Every `GitHubApi` method is sorted as a read or a write at compile time: a new method does not compile until it is.
- Wired in `src/sources/compose.ts`: the App source and a connected account's source each read through one `passReads`; the
  account's survives a rebuild of its source.

**Deferred calls** (`deferAfterMs`, `GitHubRateLimited`, `src/github-limiter/limiter.ts`). The job sources' adapters
(`src/sources/github/app/api.ts`, `account/api.ts`) make their calls with `deferAfterMs` = one minute
(`SOURCE_DEFER_AFTER_MS`). A call the limiter would hold longer — after GitHub refused one for its rate, or at the reserve —
is not made: it throws `GitHubRateLimited` with the time it may go. The pass ends at once instead of holding to the reset;
its work is kept, as for every transient error, and the next sync asks again. Shorter waits are waited, as before. Every
other caller (the GitHub watches, the proxy, the release check) waits as before.

**What a person sees.** A rate-limited call is a transient `GitHubApiError` with `retryAt` and the text
"<what>: GitHub rate-limited the hopper: next retry at HH:MM UTC" (`rateLimitedError`, `src/sources/github/app/http.ts`),
whether GitHub refused it (403 or 429, `holdAfter`) or the limiter deferred it. That text is what the source's status
(`lastError`, `detail.repoErrors`, `detail.checkErrors`) and a job's report retry (`detail.reportRetries`) show, in place of
GitHub's error.

**Left for a later part.** Fetching many issues or pull requests in one GraphQL request, and one combined status or
check-runs call per ref. Part 3 below does the first. The second needs nothing: the pull request reads carry their head
commit's checks (`statusCheckRollup`), so no status or check-runs call is made for a ref.

## Batched GraphQL reads (issue #822 part 3, 2026-10-11)

**Batched reads** (`src/sources/github/app/graphql-batch.ts`). The GraphQL reads of one issue or pull request —
`closingPullRequest`, `openClosingPullRequests`, `referencingPullRequests`, `crossReferences`, `pullRequest`, `issueEdits`,
`issuePlace` — go through `batchGraphQL`, one for each adapter (App and connected account). The reads asked with one token
in the same turn of the event loop (`setImmediate` from `node:timers`, so a test's fake timers do not hold it) go to GitHub
as one request: `q0: repository(owner: $o0, name: $n0) { … $k0 … }`, `q1: …`, at most `GRAPHQL_BATCH_MAX` = 20 to a
request. Why: the follows of one sync run side by side (`after-done.ts`, one job queue each), so each step of them asks
about every followed issue at about the same time. GitHub's GraphQL limit charges at least one point a request, and a
request of many small reads costs about what one does. Measured on three followed pull requests of one repository:
12 GraphQL requests per sync before, 4 now (`test/integration/github-graphql-batch.test.ts`).
- Each read gets the answer its own query would have had: its alias's data as `repository`, its alias's errors with the
  path under `repository`, and the errors that name no alias. So an issue GitHub does not know fails only its own read.
- A request that fails (a rate limit, a 5xx, the network) fails each read in it; each adapter maps the error for each
  read as before (its "what", a **deferred call**, a 401 renewal on the connected account).
- A read asked alone goes as its own query, as before.
- Pass reads (above) sit on top: a read asked twice in a pass is still asked once.
- A cold App adapter asks for a repository's installation, and for an installation's token, once for every read that waits
  on it (`installationFor`, `createAuth`): before, the reads of one sync each asked, and so went in separate requests.
- The node:http fake GitHub (`fake-graphql.ts`) answers the aliased form, each alias as its own query.

## Repository listings (issue #985 part 1, 2026-10-13)

**Repository listing** (`src/sources/github/app/graphql-listing.ts`, `listRepos` on the GitHubApi port, both adapters).
Intake lists each repository once per label per sync with REST (`listOpenIssues`): N repositories and L labels are at least
N×L calls a sync. A repository listing reads the same set with GraphQL, many repositories to a request:
`r0: repository(owner: $o0, name: $n0) { issues(states: OPEN, labels: $labels, first: 50, after: $ai0) { … }
pullRequests(states: OPEN, labels: $labels, …) { … } }`, `r1: …`, at most `LISTING_REPOS_MAX` = 25 to a request. So 60
repositories are 3 requests a sync, whatever the labels.
- GraphQL's `labels:` filter matches an item with any of the labels: the union of a listing of each label
  (`test/sources/github-graphql-listing.test.ts`).
- Each item: number, url, title, author, labels, assignees, `updatedAt`; a pull request also its head branch and commit,
  its base, `isDraft`, `mergeable` and its head commit's check rollup (`rollupChecks` of `closer.ts`; no rollup is `none`;
  a rollup the credential may not read is `unknown`).
- Paging: a repository whose issues or pull requests have a next page is asked again with only that connection and its
  cursor, beside the other repositories that have one. The rest are done after the first request.
- Errors: an error on a repository or its connection (path of one or two parts) fails that repository only
  (`repoErrors`); an error deeper, on one field of one item, leaves the item listed. A request that fails, or an error
  that names no alias, throws, and the sync asks again.
- By credential: an installation token reaches only its installation's repositories, so the App adapter groups the
  repositories by installation, one listing each. A repository the app is not installed on is a `repoErrors` entry. The
  connected account's adapter lists every repository with its one token.
- It goes through `makeRequest` and the shared rate limiter as an **intake call** (`intake: true`), and in a pass it is
  a pass read that any write drops.

**Listing cache** (tenant migration 52, `src/store/github-listings.ts`): `github_listings` (repository, when read) and
`github_listed_items` (one row per item: kind, `updatedAt`, a pull request's checks, the item as JSON). Recording a
repository's listing replaces its rows in one transaction. Derived data: the build before never reads the tables, and a
lost row is read again.

**Intake from the listing cache** (issue #985 part 2, 2026-10-13; `src/sources/github/listing.ts`). Intake never lists a
repository with REST: `listOpenIssues` is gone from the port. A discover takes the open labelled issues of its scope from
the listing cache, and lists again first the repositories that are due, all of them in one `listRepos`:
- Due: a repository with no listing, or one whose last listing — or this source's last failed ask (issue #1125) — is older
  than the **intake sync interval**, `intakeSyncMinutes` of the shared rate limiter (default 15; Settings → GitHub rate limit,
  `POST /ui/api/github-rate-limiter`, the admin's). Read at each discover, so a change applies at the next one.
- What asks: `JobSource.discover({ due: true })` is a timed sync (its timer, the sync watch, a rerun's sync). The first
  sync after start, a sync of a source new or changed in the plugins config, and a sync a person asked for — Sync now, an
  intake action, a new connection (`syncNow`, `intakeAction`) — call `discover()`, and every repository is listed at once.
- The listing cache follows the hopper's own acts between listings: a read of an issue from GitHub sets its row (a closed
  one goes), and the hopper's own label, assignee and close writes change its row. So a timed sync never takes an issue
  again on the labels from before its own claim.
- A repository GitHub does not answer for is a `repoErrors` entry until its next listing, and is asked again only then
  (in memory). Every repository failing fails the discover, as before.
- A listing has no body: each issue intake takes is read (`getIssue`), through the listed reads below.
- The outside-scope suggestions (`listAssignedIssues`, issue #440) are read with each listing, no longer every 10 minutes.
- The cache is the user's store (`githubListings`, in the job source context); with none (tests), in memory.

**Listed reads** (`src/sources/github/listed-reads.ts`). Inside a discover and a check, `getIssue` and `listComments` of
an issue are answered from what was kept while the listing cache still shows the `updatedAt` its listing or the read
showed. An issue the cache does not hold — closed, unlabelled, or its repository not listed — is read from GitHub each
time. A write to a repository drops what was kept of it. Outside a discover and a check — a report, a follow, a rerun,
where a write may come next — every read goes to GitHub. An issue with sub-issues is never kept, and `subIssues` is never
kept: a sub-issue that closes need not change its parent's `updatedAt`. Kept in memory: after a restart each issue is
read once again.

So between two listings a change on GitHub is seen late: a new labelled issue, an issue closed or unassigned, at most
one interval later; Sync now sees it at once. The pull requests the jobs follow are on the in-motion cycle (below).

## The in-motion cycle (issue #985 part 3, 2026-10-13)

Before it, each sync (every `pollSeconds`, default 60) followed every followed pull request with its own reads — the pull
request, its mentions, its closer, its issue, its cross-references — and the sync watch read each followed repository's
event feed every 15 seconds (issue #967). Both grew with the number of pull requests and repositories.

**Rounds** (`src/sources/follow-rounds.ts`, `followRound`; `src/sources/after-done.ts`, `FollowRound`). A sync follows pull
requests in rounds:
- `all`: every followed pull request, reconciling, the second judgement of a job that waits on a person, and the
  cross-references. Each **intake sync interval** (`intakeSyncMinutes`, default 15), and at once when forced: the first
  sync, a sync a person asked for (Sync now, an intake action, a new connection), and the sync after a merge or close.
- `in_motion`: only the pull requests **in motion** (`inMotion`, `src/domain/pull-requests.ts`): not seen yet, checks
  still running, no checks within the grace window after the last push, or ready while yolo mode merges it. Each
  `prCycleMinutes` (default 3, a setting of the shared rate limiter: Settings → GitHub rate limit,
  `POST /ui/api/github-rate-limiter`).
- `none`: between rounds. Tending still runs at each sync, from what was last seen.
- A round counts from when it starts, also when its read failed: a failing GitHub is asked again at the next round, not at
  each sync. The intervals are read at each sync. Without them (`SourceSyncOptions.followEvery` absent, tests), every sync
  is an `all` round.
- A merge or close recorded while a source syncs makes its next sync run at once (`Slot.again`) as an `all` round, so the
  hopper's own merges still cascade: the others are seen on the new base in seconds.

**The batch first** (`JobSource.readFollowed`, `src/sources/github/followed-batch.ts`). A round asks the source for every
pull request it follows in one batched read before its follows: `pullRequestStates` on the GitHub port
(`src/sources/github/app/graphql-pulls.ts`, both adapters): `p0: repository(owner: $o0, name: $n0) { pr: pullRequest(number:
7) { state isDraft mergeable createdAt body headRefName headRefOid baseRefName commits(last: 1) { … statusCheckRollup { state }
} } issue: issue(number: 3) { state stateReason updatedAt } }`, `p1: …`, at most `PULLS_MAX` = 50 to a request, one request
for each installation token. An error on one alias fails only that pull request; checks the credential may not read are
`unknown`. A failed request is logged, and the round follows nothing.

**Each follow reads the batch** (`seenFromBatch`, `src/sources/github/follow.ts`). The follow of an open pull request takes
its state from the batch, once, and keeps what it saw (`seen`) with no other read. It reads GitHub as before only when:
merged or closed; a new head commit, a new base, or merge conflicts that changed or are not computed yet (`UNKNOWN`);
checks that fail now (the read names the failed checks for the tend); its issue closed as not planned (abandoned); a part
whose body names the issue no more; or ready while yolo mode merges (a read before the write). The batch reads the newest
run of each check (issue #2129), so a failed check that runs again on the same head is pending, not failing, as GitHub's
required checks read it (issue #2230). A pull request the batch has no answer for is read as before. A person's Merge now and Close PR read and write
as before, at once.

**Reconciling** (`src/sources/github/reconcile.ts`) runs only in an `all` round, and reads the open pull requests of every
candidate repository in one batched read (`openPullRequestsIn`: `u0: repository(…) { pullRequests(states: OPEN, first: 100,
orderBy: { field: CREATED_AT, direction: DESC }) { … } }`, at most `OPEN_PULLS_REPOS_MAX` = 25 repositories to a request),
never one listing for each repository. A repository GitHub does not answer for is logged and asked again at the next
reconcile; none answering throws.

**Gone**: the sync watch (`src/sources/sync-watch.ts`, `WATCH_MS`), GitHub's event feed (`src/sources/github/moved.ts`,
`GitHubApi.repoEvents`, `JobSource.moved`) and the fake GitHub's feeds.

**Expected budget at 60 repositories** (one hour, the defaults): intake listings 3 requests × 4; reconciling 1–3 requests
× 4; the in-motion cycle 1 request × 20 (the 4 `all` rounds among them) — at most 44 calls an hour while the jobs follow at
most 50 pull requests. The budget test below holds it; the calls per hour by kind are on Settings → GitHub rate limit.

**Trade-off.** A change on GitHub to an idle pull request is seen late: one merged or closed by a person on GitHub, or a
new merge conflict after a merge that was not the hopper's, at most one intake sync interval (15 minutes) later. Sync now
sees it at once. A pull request in motion is seen at most one cycle (3 minutes) later; before, it took 15 seconds to a
minute.

**Webhooks: not part of issue #985** (decision recorded 2026-10-13). The issue's "webhook changes show up in hopper within
seconds" is declined: the proposal path accepted for the issue's job (pull-only in-motion cycle) was selected with its
