sign-off that webhooks are left out. The hopper takes no inbound webhooks and pulls by design ("Remote access"); the
in-motion cycle and Sync now are what make a change seen. Issue #1079 later added GitHub's `issues` webhook for intake, through a relay ("GitHub deliveries"); pull
requests are still seen by the in-motion cycle.

**The budget test** (issue #985 part 4, `test/integration/github-budget.test.ts`). The real app source and the real sync
loop run one hour on fake timers, at the defaults, against the node:http fake GitHub: 60 job repositories, ten jobs that
follow pull requests — two whose checks run and then pass, one ready while yolo mode merges it, one a person merges and
one a person closes on GitHub, five idle. From the fake's own log: intake, reconciling and the in-motion cycle make fewer
than 50 calls (34 when written); a merged or closed pull request has no read of its own after the round that saw it end;
an idle one has none after the first round, only its part of the batched reads; the hopper's count by kind is what the
fake saw. It found one cost the estimate above missed: the installed repositories, asked at every sync ("The shared rate
limiter").

**Declined** (decisions recorded 2026-10-13). Webhooks (above). A targeted read of one pull request when a person opens
its job's page: no new route; Sync now reads every followed pull request at once.

## The hopper label means full automation (issue #435, 2026-10-11)

Job 11 of the pointed-job architecture (tracking issue #424). A `hopper` job runs end to end with no person in the loop
until it is blocked; then it asks where the work lives — its issue thread — so the maintainers and contributors there
can answer as well as the owner. Supersedes, for these questions, the 2026-10-04 rule "a question goes to the owner
through the UI and the Grok Bot routine webhook, never onto the issue; a reply on the issue is not an answer" ("Write
criteria" above). Everything else in that rule stands.

- **The blocker.** A question of a GitHub-sourced job (`job.source.repo` and `number`) that reaches the human stage, open,
  and not kept for the owner (`Question.keptBy`: a risk rule or the consequential guard sent it — those are the owner's
  alone and never go on a thread). Its job waits on it (`waiting_answer`) or is parked.
- **The policy** (`ThreadAskSettings`, `src/domain/thread-ask.ts`): for repositories the connected account owns
  (`ownRepos`: the repo's owner is the job's `source.assignee`, case-insensitive) and for any other (`otherRepos`), one
  of `post` (post at once), `review` (hold the comment until a person approves it) or `off` (the question stays in the
  hopper only, as before). Default `post` and `review`: a post in someone else's repository goes out under the user's
  account, so it waits for the user unless they choose otherwise. The user's setting row `threadAsk`: `GET
  /api/thread-ask`, `POST /ui/api/thread-ask` (least role `admin`, `thread_ask.settings_changed`), Settings → Issue
  thread. Read at each pass, so a change applies without a restart.
- **The pass** (`src/sources/thread-asks.ts`), the sync loop's, on the job's report chain: at each sync of a source
  with a thread (`JobSource.thread`, `SourceThread`), and at once on `question.escalated_to_human` and
  `question.thread_approved`. No record yet: `post` posts and records `thread: { state: posted, commentId, url }`
  (`question.thread_posted`); `review` records `thread: { state: review }` (`question.thread_held`). `approved` posts
  it, keeping `approvedBy`. `posted`: the issue's comments are read and the reply below answers it. A throw is kept as
  the job's retry and asked again next sync.
- **The watch on the thread** (#427, "GitHub watches" below). While its question is posted and open
  (`watchesThread`), the job's issue has a GitHub watch, keyed by the job's id. It starts on `question.thread_posted`
  and polls at once; it ends when the question is answered, closed or gone, all followed through the question's events.
  A poll that sees a new comment records `github_watch.changed` with the job's `jobId`, and that event starts the job's
  pass at once: the replies are read and the first one that may answer settles the question. So a reply resumes the job
  within one watch interval, with no sync of its source. A sync reads the thread only when the watch cannot tell
  (`threadUnseen`): no watch snapshot, a problem on the watch (no GitHub connection of the user's own, a refusal), no
  poll since the post, or a comment after the question's in its snapshot. The last case is a comment that answered
  nothing (a stranger's), so such a thread is read at each sync, as before. The watch reads with the user's own
  connection, the post and the replies with the source's identity.
- **Approval.** `POST /ui/api/questions/:id/thread-approve` (least role `operator`): an open question held for review
  becomes `approved` with `approvedBy` (`question.thread_approved`), which starts its job's pass; 409 otherwise. The UI
  offers it as **Post on the issue** on the question card and the Parked row, which also say where the question is
  and link the comment.
- **The comment** (`threadQuestionComment`): a hidden first line `<!-- job-hopper v1 kind=question id=<question id> -->`
  — the marker the context filter already drops, so it never reaches a job's prompt —, a line that the automated job
  is blocked, the question quoted, and how to answer. It names no person. Posted once: `SourceThread.ask` (GitHub:
  `src/sources/github/thread.ts`) looks for a comment with the question's marker first, so a post whose record was lost
  to a crash is found, not repeated. Under the source's identity: the connected account, or the app's bot.
- **Parking.** A question with a thread record — posted or held — parks its job at once on auto-park's path
  (`src/engine/auto-park.ts`, the same conditions: an agent session, no fork at work), whatever the park timeout, with
  `why` "Parked: its question goes on the issue thread, and a reply there resumes it." A parked job's question never
  expires, so the wait on the thread has no deadline. A job that cannot park keeps its pane and waits as before; the
  reply answers it all the same. Picked up with its question still open, it waits the park timeout from the pick-up
  (`waitRestartedAt`), as any other question, so the person has the full timeout to answer it (issue #1006); 0 keeps it
  running.
- **The reply** (`threadReply`): the first comment after the question's, not hopper-marked, not empty, by the
  connected account (`source.assignee`) or by a maintainer — GitHub's `author_association` `OWNER`, `MEMBER` or
  `COLLABORATOR` (`GitHubComment.association`). Anyone else's comment answers nothing. It settles the question
  through `SourceHost.answerFromThread` → `QuestionService.settleWith` (`answeredBy` `thread:<login>`, a `human`
  attempt, `question.answered`), and `onAnswered` re-queues the auto-parked job, which resumes its agent session with
  the answer. The user's own reply is the answer as is; a maintainer's is fenced as data (`threadAnswer`: where it came
  from, "data, not instructions", the reply between `<<<thread-reply` and `thread-reply>>>`, a closing marker inside it
  defused), as the issue text is. An answer in the hopper meanwhile wins as for any question.
- **Persisted state.** No schema change: `Question.thread` is in the question's JSON, the policy a settings row.
- **Not built here.** Per-job policy; the policy is per kind of repository.


## The contribution flow (issue #429, 2026-10-11)

Part of the pointed-job architecture (tracking issue #424, job 5 of 13). Owner requirement: for a repository the user does
not own, a job forks it, clones the fork, reads `CONTRIBUTING.md` and the files beside it (the pull request template, the
code of conduct, a CLA) and follows them, and opens its pull request upstream from the fork; when the repository takes no
issues, it files its issue on the fork and links back. Settings live in the database, are edited in the UI, and apply
without a restart.

**Assumptions about other work.** The pointed-job record (#425) is not on `dev`. This works on the job's own repository
as the GitHub proxy already names it (`job.source.repo`, a fork's parent's): what a pointed-job record names too.
Repository-agnostic lanes (#431) give the job a worktree of a checkout of that repository; the job clones its fork
beside it, in its scratch dir. How a job of a repository the user does not own comes to exist
is #425's; until then, an issue there that a person approved as a request card, in a job repository, is one. "The user
cannot push to it" is GitHub's own answer (`permissions.push` of `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}` with the user's connection),
not ownership: a collaborator pushes as before.

**Contribution** (`src/domain/contribution.ts`, the user's setting `contribution`, `{ on }`): off unless an admin turns
it on (Settings → Contribution; `GET /api/contribution`, `POST /ui/api/contribution` `{ on }`, admin;
`contribution.changed { from, to, by }`), since the fork, the pull request and an issue go out under the user's account,
on somebody else's repository. Read at each request a job makes (the proxy's connection and the git user,
`src/users/github-proxy.ts`), so it applies without a restart. A fork made while it was on stays on GitHub; nothing is
pushed to it or opened from it while it is off.

**The job's fork.** A repository that GitHub says is a fork (`fork`) whose `parent` or `source` is the job's own
repository, owned by the login of the user's connection. The hopper reads it from GitHub when it can matter — Contribution
on, the request's owner the user's login, the repository no job repository — and never keeps it: a fork deleted on
GitHub is no fork at the next request.

**`hopper-gh` additions** (`src/github-proxy/policy.ts`, `api.ts`, `script.ts`):

| command | what | who |
|---------|------|-----|
| `repo view --repo R` | `canPush`, `hasIssues`, `defaultBranch`, `fork`, `parent`, and `contribution` (the setting) | the hopper's own job; on a job repository or the job's fork |
| `repo fork --repo R` | forks R into the user's account (`POST /repos/{o}/{r}/forks`, `default_branch_only`), or answers the fork the user has (GitHub makes one only once); when R takes no issues, turns the fork's issues on (`PATCH`, `has_issues`); answers `fork`, `url`, `defaultBranch`, `issues` (where an issue goes, or `issuesError`), and `next`: the steps | the hopper's own job; R its own repository; Contribution on; refused when the user can push to R |
| `pr create --head LOGIN:BRANCH` | a pull request on the job's own repository from a branch of the fork | the same; LOGIN the user's login, Contribution on |
| `issue create\|comment\|view`, `pr view` on the fork | as on a job repository; a filed issue names the job's issue as its parent (issue #729), the link back | the hopper's own job, Contribution on |

A pull request opened on the fork is refused, naming the command that opens it upstream. Rate limits: `repo.fork` 3 per job
and 20 per machine in an hour, `repo.view` as the other reads. Each is an event on the job's timeline as before
(`github_proxy.done` gains `op` `repo.view`, `repo.fork`, with `url` and, for a fork, `fork`; no `number`).

**`next`** (`contributionSteps`): clone the fork; before making a branch, read `CONTRIBUTING.md` (also under `.github/`
and `docs/`), the pull request template, `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md` and a CLA if named; follow the branch name, the commit style,
the tests and the template; when a CLA needs a person to sign it, ask; push to the fork; open the pull request upstream
with `--head <login>:<branch>`; and where an issue goes. The hopper reads none of these files itself: the job has the
clone, and a rule the hopper parsed would be a second, weaker reader of text the maintainers wrote for people.

**Git** (`src/github-proxy/git-broker.ts`): a push to the job's own repository first reads it (the read that already gave
the default branch): a user who cannot push is refused before GitHub refuses it — with Contribution on, `your user cannot
push to R: contribute through a fork: sh "$HOPPER_GH" repo fork --repo R, then push your branch to the fork`; off, the same
and that a person turns it on. A push to the job's fork goes with the user's connection under the same ref check
(`checkPush`, its own default branch and the release branches kept); a fetch of it goes with the connection too, so a fork
of a private repository clones. Any other repository is refused as before.

**The job is told** (`GITHUB_PROXY_LINE`, every job's protocol): when `repo view` says its user cannot push to the
repository, contribute through a fork; the help says how. One sentence, not the steps: a job of the user's own repository
pays nothing more, and the steps come with the fork.

**Not built** (each a later part of #424): a job record that points at an unowned repository's issue without a source
label (#425); following the upstream pull request to completion when no job repository holds it (#428); a per-repository
policy on what a job may post there without review (#435). Yolo mode is the user's per repository; on a repository the
user cannot push to, GitHub refuses the hopper's merge, which is kept on the pull request (`mergeError`) and never fails
the job: leave it off there.

**Residual risk.** A job with Contribution on can open pull requests and file issues on any job repository its user
cannot push to, under the user's account: the setting is the policy until #435. The fork is the user's own repository: a
job may push any branch of it but its default and the release branches, as on its own repository.

Tests: `test/integration/contribution.test.ts` (the real daemon, a fake GitHub with forks and git's own
`git-http-backend`, the real git and `hopper-gh`: off by default and refused saying so; on — a push upstream refused naming
the fork command, the fork made and answered again, the branch pushed to the fork, its default and `main` refused, the pull
request upstream from it, another login's head refused, a pull request on the fork refused; a repository with no issues —
the fork's issues on, the issue filed there with its parent; a repository that is no fork of the job's refused; a
repository the user can push to not forked; turned off after the fork — a push and a pull request refused; the setting's
guards), `test/github-proxy/contribution.test.ts` (the policy and the steps), `test/ui/contribution.test.ts` (the panel's
summary and note).


## Job tracking above lanes (issue #426, 2026-10-11)

Part 2 of the pointed-job work (tracking issue #424): "a service that owns the queue and the job pointers and hands
pointed jobs to lanes. Lanes ask it for work instead of sources creating lane work directly." The **job tracking** layer
already sits above the lanes. This section names its parts, so later parts (#427 watches, #431 repository-agnostic lanes)
build on them and do not make a second queue.

**What it is.** No new module and no new setting: the engine's job queue is the tracking layer.

| Part | Where | What it does |
|------|-------|--------------|
| The job queue | the `jobs` table, `JobRepository` (`src/store/jobs.ts`) | Every job, waiting or ended, in the database. A waiting job is `queued` or `held`. |
| The job pointer | `Job.source` (`JobSourceRef`: source, key, repo, number, url) | What a job points at. The source key is the item's identity in the queue. |
| Intake | `SourceHost.ingest` (`src/engine/source-host.ts`) | The only way a source's item becomes a job: one transaction that reads the key's newest job and makes a job only when there is none or that one may run again. |
| The queue gate | `src/engine/queue-gate.ts` | A new job waits unaccepted until the pre-sort or the user accepts it ("Queue gate"). |
| The order | the queue sorter, the user order, the effective priority (`src/engine/queue-order.ts`, `src/decider/assign.ts`) | Which admissible waiting job comes first. |
| The hand-off | `decide()`, then `apply` (`src/engine/decision-step.ts`) | Each Decision claims waiting jobs for the free lanes. |
| Restart | `recover` (`src/engine/recovery.ts`) | A claimed job, and a running job of an idempotent executor, goes back to the queue (`job.requeued`); a running job whose work is still alive is reattached on its lane; every other lane closes ("Recovery at startup"). |

**Source → queue → lane.** A source never touches a lane. A sync offers items to `ingest`; the job waits in the queue;
a Decision, not the source, gives it a lane. A lane holds only the job a Decision claimed for it ("The engine"). So lanes
already take their work from the queue. The issue's "lanes ask it for work" is the Decision's claim: the decider stays
the one place that matches waiting jobs to free lanes, because it alone sees every lane, machine and usage limit at once.
A lane that pulled for itself would need a second decider.

**Kept unchanged:** the queue order, the priority labels (`priorityOf`, `src/sources/github/priority.ts`, read at intake into the item's priority), and the queue gate. Nothing in
this part changes them.

**Survives a restart.** The queue is the database, so a restart loses no job. Intake reads the source key in the same
transaction that makes the job, so the next sync after a restart makes no second job of an item. The gate (a user
setting in the database), each job's acceptance, priority and user rank stay as they were.
`test/integration/job-tracking.test.ts` checks this through the real daemon: one lane, a running job, two accepted jobs
of priority 10 and 90 and one unaccepted job, then a restart over the same database. The interrupted job is requeued, the
90 runs before the requeued job and the 10, the unaccepted job stays held, and a sync after the restart makes no job.
`test/integration/restart.test.ts` and `test/integration/github.test.ts` ("a restart keeps sourced jobs deduped") check
the same for the manual and the GitHub source.

**The pointed-job record (#425) is not built yet.** When it is, its target repository and pointer are the job's
`source` fields named above, and its status follows the job's. This part adds no separate record, so #425 maps onto one
queue, not two.

## Pointed jobs (issue #425, 2026-10-11)

Part 1 of the pointed-job architecture (tracking issue #424). A **pointed job** is a record that points at work in any
GitHub repository, owned or not: `repo` (`owner/name`), a `pointer` (an issue or a pull request: `kind`, `number`, `url`),
the `directive` (what to do there), the `lane` that works it while it runs, a `status`, the `source` that made it, and
`createdAt`/`updatedAt`. A record only: nothing runs a pointed job yet. The tracking service above the lanes (issue #426)
and the watches (issue #427) build on it.

**Status and transitions** (`src/domain/pointed-jobs.ts`, pure). `queued` → `running` | `abandoned`; `running` →
`awaiting_review` | `queued` | `abandoned`; `awaiting_review` → `merged` | `running` | `abandoned`. `merged` and
`abandoned` are ends. A move outside `TRANSITIONS` is refused (409) and records nothing; each allowed move is one
`pointed_job.status_changed { id, from, to, lane?, by }`, in the same transaction as the write. The lane is kept while it
runs and dropped when it leaves running.

**Store.** Tenant migration 43: a `pointed_jobs` table (`id`, `status`, `created_at`, the body as JSON), as `bug_reports`.
A table only, so the build before runs on the migrated store.

**Existing jobs: an adapter, not a copy.** A job whose item names a repository, a number and a URL reads as a pointed job
on that issue (`pointedJobOf`, `jobId` set), its status from the job: its followed pull request first — merged →
`merged`, closed → `abandoned`, open, tended or reworked → `awaiting_review` —, else its job status: queued, held or
parked → `queued`; claimed, running, waiting on an answer or on its own wait, operator-led → `running`; finished →
`merged` (it ended done); failed, cancelled or rejected → `abandoned`. Its status follows its job, so the pointed job API
never moves it (409). A copy into `pointed_jobs` would drift from the job it copies; the adapter cannot, and the jobs
table is left as it was. A job of no repository (a manual item, a plain API job) is no pointed job.

**API** (`src/http/ui/pointed-jobs.ts`). `GET /api/pointed-jobs` (both kinds, newest first), `GET /api/pointed-jobs/:id`;
`POST /ui/api/pointed-jobs` (`pointed_job.created`, `source: api`) and `POST /ui/api/pointed-jobs/:id/transition`, operator,
through the UI session or an API token. Neither starts a job, so neither is a box action.


## GitHub watches (issue #427, 2026-10-11)

Job 3 of the pointed-job architecture (tracking issue #424). Requirement: a watch per pointed job polls GitHub on an
interval for its item — state, labels, comments, reviews, linked pull requests, merge —, compares it with the last
stored snapshot, and records a typed event only on a change. The interval is a setting in the database, changed in the
UI, applied without a restart.

**What is watched.** Each pointed job (issue #425) that has not ended (`watched`: not `merged`, not `abandoned`), on its
issue or pull request. The jobs the hopper already has, read as pointed jobs, are not: their pull request is followed
already (`src/sources/github/follow.ts`). One exception (issue #435): such a job while its question is posted on its issue
thread, read as a pointed job on that issue (`pointedJobOf`); its change event carries the job's `jobId`. The service
follows `pointed_job.created`, `pointed_job.status_changed` and every `question.*` event, so a new pointed job or a new
thread ask is watched at once and an ended one is dropped, with no restart. A job on its own wait is watched too (issue #2159, "A comment ends the job's own wait"): its issue and its own pull
request.

**A poll** (`src/github-watch/github.ts`). With the user's own GitHub connection (`githubProxy.watches`, as Report a bug
and the repository checks): `GET /repos/{repo}/issues/{n}` — it answers a pull request too, with its merge — and every
page of its timeline. Both through `makeRequest`, so the shared rate limiter (issue #436) paces them, and an unchanged
page is a 304 from its ETag cache that costs no call. One REST read and one timeline page per poll, where GraphQL would
be one call each time with no conditional request. The **watch snapshot** (`snapshotOf`): `state` `open`, `closed`
(with GitHub's `state_reason`) or `merged` (with `mergedAt`); the labels; the comments and reviews by id, author and time
— never their text —; the pull requests whose cross-reference is on the timeline, by URL.

**Change** (`src/domain/github-watch.ts`, pure). `githubWatchChanges(before, after)`: a state change, labels added and
removed, comments added and how many went, reviews added, linked pull requests added and removed — each part present only
when it changed; nothing changed is `undefined`. Labels and links compare as sets, so GitHub's order changes nothing. A
poll that found a change writes the new snapshot and one `github_watch.changed { pointedJob, repo, pointer, changes }` in
one transaction; every change of that poll is in the one event. A poll with no change writes its time only. The first
poll of a watch stores its snapshot and records nothing: there is nothing to compare. A failed poll keeps the snapshot,
stores the problem on the watch (`error`, logged once per new problem) and records nothing; the next good poll clears
it. No GitHub connection is such a problem.

**Schedule** (`src/github-watch/service.ts`). Every watch of the user is on one poll schedule (`createPollSchedule`, issue
#436): rounds of the interval, in batches of the shared limiter's `batchSize`, spread across the round. A new watch polls
at once for its first snapshot. One poll of a watch at a time: its first poll and its round never compare against one
snapshot twice. It starts and stops with the user's runtime.

**Interval.** `intervalSeconds`, 10 to 86400, default 60: the user's setting (`githubWatch` in the user's settings), an
admin's, Settings → GitHub watches (`POST /ui/api/github-watches`), `github_watch.settings_changed`. The schedule reads
it at each round; a change also stops the rounds and starts them again at once, so the watches poll now and then on the
new interval — a change from an hour to a minute does not wait out the hour. The same value records nothing.

**Store.** Tenant migration 44: `github_watches`, one row per pointed job, its watch as JSON (`repo`, `pointer`,
`snapshot`, `polledAt`, `changedAt`, `error`). A table only: the build before runs on it. The row stays after its
pointed job ends, with its last snapshot.

**API.** `GET /api/github-watches`: the settings and the watch of each pointed job that has not ended, and of each job on
its thread. Resuming a parked job on a reply (issue #435) acts on `github_watch.changed`: a new comment on a job's watch
starts its thread pass ("The hopper label means full automation").

**Dependency.** Built on the pointed job record (issue #425, PR #831) and the shared rate limiter's poll schedule (issue
#436, PR #817), whose commits this change carries: it depends on both, and neither on it.

## The Jobs view (issue #434, 2026-10-11)

Job 10 of the pointed-job architecture (tracking issue #424). Requirement: a board with a card per job — status,
repository, issue, lane and last event —, live, filterable by status and by repository, quick with 200 jobs and more.

**The record.** The pointed-job record (#425) is not built yet, so a card is the queue's `Job`, as for lanes (#431): its
issue is `source.repo` and `source.number`. When the record comes, the card reads it the same way.

**What it shows.** `#jobs` (`ui/src/views/jobs.tsx`): every job the job store holds — `/api/queue`'s jobs (not ended, or
ended in the last 24 hours) and the locked entries —, the latest change (`updatedAt`) first. The filters offer the
statuses and the repositories the jobs have; they are the viewer's, held in the page, not settings: nothing to keep in the
database. A job's **last event** comes from `GET /api/jobs/last-events`, read when the view opens: the newest event of
each job `/api/queue` holds (`EventLog.lastOfJobs`, one `DISTINCT ON (job_id)` query, on the index `events_job (job_id,
seq)`, tenant migration 45). The UI's own event list is capped at 500, so it alone could not name one for every job.
Each newer event the stream brings replaces it (`lastEvents` in `ui/src/model/jobs-view.ts`, by `seq`).

**Live, and quick.** Nothing new on the wire: the store already reads `/api/queue` again after each event, so a status
change reaches its card with no reload. Each refresh replaces every job object, so a card is memoised on what it shows
(id, `updatedAt`, status, lane, last event `seq`): one job's change renders one card again, not 200. A card shows times as
a clock, not a ticking age, so no card renders each second.

Tests: `test/integration/job-last-events.test.ts` (real database and HTTP: one event per job, the newest; none with no
job), `test/ui/jobs-view-model.test.ts` (filters, order, choices, last event), `test/ui/jobs-view.test.ts` (the whole app
over a fake daemon: the card's facts, both filters, a status change from the stream with 250 jobs; since issue #2353 a row
per job, 30 to a page).

### Long pages (issue #2353, 2026-10-21)

Requirement: the long pages show a first view under two viewport heights, with 200 jobs, 100 pull requests or 500 events.
One pattern for each page, in `ui/src/components/pager.tsx` and `panel.tsx`:

- **Rows or cards.** A page that shows cards has **Rows**: one line per item, its acts and details left to Cards. The Jobs
  view's List is rows only: a **job row** per job (`ui/src/views/job-row.tsx`), no card grid.
- **Groups fold.** A Panel with `onToggle` folds by its title (Pull requests' repository groups, Landing, Not tracked;
  Failures' sections; the Jobs view's trees).
- **Pages.** A list past one page shows a page of it with the **pager**: 30 rows or 6 cards, 8 trees in the graph.
  A filter starts again at the first page. Paging is in the page, not on the wire: every list here is already read whole.
- **The header stays.** A sticky Panel (`sticky`) keeps its header and its `toolbar` (the filters) under the app's header
  while its body scrolls with the page. A header sticks only inside its own card: a page whose header is a short card
  of its own (Pull requests' summary, Failures' counts) makes that whole card sticky. Its card clips with `overflow: clip`, not `hidden`: a hidden overflow makes the
  card its own scroll box, and the header would stick inside it.
- **One scroll box.** No list box (`list`) inside a page that scrolls: Failures' sections page in place of it. A log or a
  code view keeps its own.
- **Kept.** The mode and each fold are **page choices** (`jh_page_prefs`), as the nav groups are kept; which page shows is not.

Part 1: Jobs, Pull requests, Events, Failures, Search. Part 2:

- **Questions, Proposals, Research**: Cards or Rows (`ui/src/components/card-rows.tsx`), 6 cards or 30 rows to a page.
  A row opens its card in place, below it, so a person answers or decides with the same card; which rows are open is
  not kept. Questions' reason filter starts again at the first page.
- **Usage, Resources, Accounts**: each panel folds (Panel `fold`, its page choice key). A usage graph card folds too.
- **Sources**: the GitHub, GitLab and Repository setup sections fold by their heading (`FoldSection`), and each source.
- **Settings**: one section shows at a time already, so the long part was its strip of 35 links. The links are in six
  groups (General, Questions, Jobs, GitHub, Network, Access); each group folds by its title, and a folded group still
  shows the open section's link. A **jump list** above them names every section by its group. A section in no group
  fails the typecheck.

### Plain language in the UI (issue #2375, 2026-10-21)

Requirement: Decisions, Events and Questions read without the hopper's internals; labels a new reader does not know are
plain words. The terms stay in the glossary and the code; only the UI words change.

- **Decisions** is a table: time, the job it is about (its issue and title, `+N more` when it is about more), its kind
  (what woke the decider: `regular check` for a tick, else the trigger's words) and the **outcome** as a sentence
  (`ui/src/model/decisions.ts`: "started 1 job, held 3: awaiting acceptance"; the reason when the holds share one, else
  how many reasons). The raw ids, starts, holds, lane plans, divergences, reasons and raw inputs open below the row.
- **Events** is a table: time, job, event type and message (`detailOf`), 30 rows to a page. **Filter chips** by event
  type — its family, the part before the dot, each with its count (`ui/src/model/event-families.ts`) — beside the text
  filter. A row opens its detail: the ids and the data, in monospace. Copy takes every event the filters show.
- **Questions**: a card's escalation trail is folded behind "N model answers"; the reason banner, the question and the
  answer box stay in view.
- **Ask hopper** (`#ask`, `ui/src/views/ask.tsx`) is one nav entry in place of Direct jobs and Direct queries, a merged page (issue #2374) with two
  tabs: Run a job (`#ask/direct-jobs`) and Ask a question (`#ask/direct-queries`; `#ask/question` still opens it). `#direct-jobs` and `#direct-queries`, with or without an
  id after them, still open the matching tab (`MOVED` in `ui/src/app/routes.ts`), so links already sent keep working.
- **Waiting to be ordered** in place of the pre-sort: the Queue badge, the Queue column and its button (Accept this
  order), the Needs you row.
- **Later** in place of the backburner: the Intake group, its tooltip names the `hopper:backburner` label; the action
  is Take out of Later; the nav badge and the Queue link say "for later".

### The Jobs table (issue #2372, 2026-10-21)

Requirement: Jobs opens as a table, one row per job, at least 20 rows in view at 1440×900, the page at most 1.5 screens
tall with the demo data; the run graph on expand, no longer the default.

- **List is the default.** The `jobs.mode` page choice falls back to `list`; a browser that kept `graph` keeps it. Graph or
  List is the same `ModeToggle` and page choice as before (Machines' Cards / List toggle copied this control, #2352).
- **A table.** `JobTableHead` and `JobRow` (`ui/src/views/job-row.tsx`) share one column list: stage, issue, title and
  task count, lane, time in stage, pull request, last event. A row is 28 px. A narrow screen hides a column's cells and
  keeps its `col` at no width, so the table always has every column: a cell that spans them (the run graph's) then makes
  no extra column. The last event shows on a wide screen only, so the title keeps its room at 1440 px.
- **The run graph.** A click on a row, but on a link, opens a row under it with the **job tree** the job is in, drawn by
  the Graph mode's own `TreeGraph`, and a node's details on select. One row is open at a time; which one is not kept.
- **Measured** with the screenshot demo (`scripts/screenshots/demo.ts`) in Chromium at 1440×900: 25 rows in view, the
  page 1.22 screens tall with 30 rows, against 1.73 for Graph with its 8 trees.

Tests: `test/ui/jobs-table.test.ts` (the default mode, the columns, the toggle kept over a reload, a row's run graph).

### Settings' sub-nav and the views that left it (issue #2373, 2026-10-21)

Requirement: no horizontal strip of Settings links; every section in view at 1440x900; Settings keeps configuration only.

- **Sub-nav.** Settings is two columns from the `lg` width: a left **sub-nav**, sticky under the app's header and
  scrolling on its own, and the open section. The sub-nav has six groups: Jobs and agents, Intake, GitHub, Security and
  access, Integrations, System. Each group folds by its title and keeps the open section's link when folded (issue
  #2353). Below `lg` the jump list alone names the sections. A section in no group, or a group of one section, fails the
  typecheck, as a nav group of one entry does (`NAV_GROUPS`, `ui/src/app/nav.tsx`).
- **Views of their own.** Plugins (`#plugins`), Vault (`#vault`) and **Users & access** (`#users-access`, sections
  `users`, `access`, `permissions`, `api-tokens`; `ui/src/views/users-access.tsx`) are workflows a person acts in, not
  configuration. Each is an entry of its own, its one home: Vault in Infra, Plugins and Users & access in Admin (issue #2374). Webhooks and Sign-in stay in Settings.
- **Old hashes.** `#settings/plugins`, `#settings/vault`, `#settings/users`, `#settings/access`, `#settings/permissions`
  and `#settings/api-tokens` are replaced by their new hash; what follows the section (a device grant's user code)
  follows the new one. A device grant's `verificationPath` is `/#users-access/api-tokens`.
- **Cards that fold.** On Plugins and Access each block is a Panel with `fold` and a `summary`: one line beside its
  title, so a folded card still says what it holds (its instances, its approvals, its decisions denied). **Fold all**
  (`FoldAll`) folds every card of the page, or opens them all when none is open. Each fold is a page choice.

## The isolation stop (issue #752, 2026-10-11)

Issue #752 asks that a box cut off from the hopper degrade safely. This part is the box's own time limit: a client target
that cannot hear the hopper for long stops acting on the authority the hopper gave it, since the hopper can no longer
check it.

**Hearing the hopper** (`src/client/isolation.ts`). The client counts the hopper heard at each request the hopper signed
(verified, any route) and at each keepalive PING the hopper's end of the link answers ("Link-lost hold",
`src/client/keepalive.ts`: every 5 s, one PING out at a time). The watch sends no PING of its own; it checks every 15 s.
A half-open link, where the hopper is gone but the socket is not closed, answers no PING, so it is not heard; the
keepalive drops it within 10 s.

**Which jobs.** Each `/release` probe (every 30 s, and at once after a dial-in) carries `{ jobs }`: the ids of the jobs
the hopper has at work on that machine. The client keeps the last list. It stops only those: never a process of another
hopper's, or of a job the hopper did not name, on the same account. A client that restarts while cut off knows no jobs,
and stops none.

**The stop.** Not heard for the **max isolation** (`HOPPER_CLIENT_MAX_ISOLATION_MS` in the client's environment, default
30 min; `0` turns it off), the client runs the reap for each named job with no scratch dir: the job's scope and every
process carrying its `HOPPER_JOB_ID` stop; its scratch dir, its repositories and its credentials dir stay. It forgets
the list, so it stops each job once. It records `{ jobId, at, cutOffMs }`.

**The report.** The next `/release` answer carries `isolationStops`, each stop once. The client release keeper logs a
warning per stop: `client <machine>: stopped job <id> at <time>, cut off from the hopper for <n> s`. The job's end stays
the hopper's: its pane is gone, so a link-lost hold or a restart's reattach finds it not alive and fails it, or it has
failed already; its cleanup, deferred while the machine was out of reach, reaps it then.

**Why longer than the link grace.** A stop that comes too early loses the agent's session. The link grace
(`HOPPER_LINK_GRACE_MS`, 10 min by default) lets the hopper decide first in the normal case: it holds the job, then fails
it. The max isolation (30 min) is the box's own limit for when the hopper cannot. Set it longer than the link grace.

**Residual risk.** A box cut off for less than the max isolation goes on with what it holds: the job's short-lived
credentials, and its open session. A stop that fails (the reap times out) is logged and not tried again. Old clients
ignore `jobs` and say no stops.

## The job graph (issue #900, 2026-10-12)

Requirement (issue #900): the Jobs view is the at-a-glance tracker, apart from the Dashboard's health summary. Each job's
stage — partly done among them, which the status alone did not show —, its task progress, lane, time in stage, pull request
and checks; counts per stage; filters by repository and stage. Then the scope change on the issue: jobs form a graph
(parent and sub-issues, follow-ups, partly done remainders, plan to apply, forks from questions), so the primary mode is a
graph, with the tree by root issue, a node's details on select and what blocks a root marked; a list stays as the second
mode; the API gives the graph (issue #718's parity).

**The model** (`src/domain/job-graph.ts`, pure). `stageOf(job)` maps a status to a **job stage**; a finished job is
`partly_done` while its `partlyDone` pull request is not merged (its source's `follow` is not `merged`, `closed` or
`abandoned`), `pr_open` while its own pull request's `follow` is `open`, else `done`. `stageSinceOf` is the time in stage:
`createdAt` for queued, `startedAt` for running, `wait.since` or `parked.at` for waiting, `finishedAt` for the rest — what
the record holds, no new field. `jobGraph({ jobs, links, issueGraph })` makes the nodes (jobs, issues, pull requests) and
the typed edges (glossary "Job graph"), and `treesOf` the **job trees**: each connected group, rooted at a node no edge
leads into (an issue first); a node **blocks** the root when it is not `done` or `cancelled`, or leads to one that is not
(a depth-first walk that counts a cycle once). An issue takes the stage of its newest job. An issue no job here works
(issue #1895) takes its stage from its own state first: closed as completed is `done`; closed as not planned or as a
duplicate is `cancelled` with `closed` ("Closed"). The ledger's `issueState` comes before the issue graph's read, which can
be older than the close. An open issue then takes its work item's stage (`ITEM_STAGE`: its jobs may be gone from the
graph, so the route looks the item up by the issue's URL), and only an open issue with no item is `no_job` ("Not
started"). A tree's summary counts such an issue as shipped when `done`, and says how many are closed.

**Where the edges come from.** Nothing new is recorded: `rerunOf` (`next_part` when the job before is partly done, else
`rerun`), `forkOf` (`spawned`), `followOn` (`plan_apply`), the job's source state (`opened`, `waits_on_merge`), the
`job.child_issue_filed` events (`parent` for a required child, else `follow_up`), and the issue graph (issue #437:
`sub_issue_of` gives `parent`, `closes` gives `closes`) — read here for the first time, for the issues the graph already
has and nothing beyond them. GitHub's "blocked by" relation is not read: the hopper keeps no record of it (part 2 below
reads it).

**The route.** `GET /api/jobs/graph` (`src/http/jobs.ts`), the user's own: the jobs `/api/queue` holds, the followed jobs
whose pull request is open (at most 500, so a partly done job that ended days ago still shows), and the jobs these come
from, five steps back along `rerunOf`, `forkOf` and `followOn`; the newest 5000 lineage links; the whole issue graph. A
read, so an API token needs `jobs:read` (issue #881's scope rule). Made on each read, never kept.

**The view** (`ui/src/views/jobs.tsx`, `ui/src/model/jobs-view.ts`). It reads the graph when it opens and again,
debounced, each time the store's jobs change — the store already reads the queue after each event, so nothing new is on
the wire. A tree is laid out left to right with d3's tidy tree (`hierarchy`, `tree`; d3 is already the UI's chart
library): each node under the first node that reaches it along an edge either way, so every node has a place, and every
edge is drawn over it. A tree with nothing blocking it starts folded when other trees show. The list keeps #434's cards,
memoised on what they show, with the time in stage at minute resolution, so a card renders again at most once a minute.

**Dropped, and why.** A node per job only, with its issue on it, was simpler, but an issue with two jobs (a partly done
part and the next) and an issue no job works yet (a follow-up) then had no place. A force layout reads worse for trees
and moves on each read. Help: `help/jobs.md`.

Tests: `test/domain/job-graph.test.ts` (stages, each edge kind, trees, blocking, a cycle), `test/integration/job-graph.test.ts`
(real database and HTTP: a partly done job, the next part, a filed issue, the empty graph), `test/ui/jobs-view-model.test.ts`
(rows, trees, choices, counts, the layout, a pull request in words), `test/ui/jobs-view.test.ts` (the whole app over a fake
daemon: the graph mode, a node's details, the list's facts, partly done, counts and filters, a live stage change with 250
jobs, the empty states).

**Part 2: blocked by, stacks, questions and hand-offs (issue #900, 2026-10-12).** What part 1 left:

- **Blocked by.** The issue place's query (`src/sources/github/issue-place.ts`) reads `blockedBy` (GitHub's issue
  dependencies, first 50) beside the sub-issues; `placeGraph` keeps each as an issue graph edge `blocked_by` (the blocked
  issue to its blocker), and the job graph adds the blocker's issue node and a `blocked_by` edge in the same direction.
  The direction is the one `waits_on_merge` has: from what waits to what it waits on, so an open blocker blocks the root
  with no change to `treesOf`. A GitHub with no issue dependencies (an older GitHub Enterprise) refuses the whole query
  for the unknown field; `issuePlace` then asks once more without it (`noBlockedBy`), and the place has no `blockedBy`. No
  migration: the issue graph's edges are replaced at each read of an issue.
- **Stacks.** `headRefName` joins the pull request reads' shared fields (`HEAD_COMMIT`, `src/sources/github/closer.ts`),
  as `headRef` on the port's pull request, and following a pull request keeps it in `seen` beside `base`. In the job graph,
  an open pull request whose `base` is the `headRef` of another open one in the same repository gets a `stacked_on` edge
  to it. Only followed pull requests have branches, so a stack of pull requests no job opened is not seen. A pull request
  followed before this change has no `headRef` until its next follow writes it: no migration, the field is optional.
- **Questions and hand-offs.** The route reads the open questions (any tier: one a level holds waits too) and the open
  hand-offs, adds their jobs to the jobs it shows, and passes them in. Each is a node (`question:<id>`, `handoff:<id>`),
  at stage `waiting`, labelled with the question's text or the hand-off's TL;DR (else its summary), at most 120
  characters, its time in stage from when it was asked or opened, with an `asks` or `hands_off` edge from its job. A
  question or hand-off whose job is not in the graph is left out. The stage counts still count jobs only.

Dropped: a `blocks` edge from the blocker to the blocked issue, as the issue named it. It points against the direction
`treesOf` walks, so the blocker would become a root of its own and never mark the issue it blocks. A question node per
answered question: the graph shows what stands now, and the job view keeps the history.

Tests: `test/domain/issue-graph.test.ts`, `test/sources/issue-place.test.ts` (the `blockedBy` read, the second ask),
`test/sources/github-follow.test.ts` and `test/sources/github-checks-unreadable.test.ts` (`headRef`),
`test/domain/job-graph.test.ts` (each new edge and node), `test/integration/job-graph.test.ts` (an open question and
hand-off over the real database and HTTP server), `test/ui/jobs-view-model.test.ts` and `test/ui/jobs-view.test.ts` (the
question node, its edge and its details).

**Part 3: plain words (issue #935, 2026-10-12).** The graph read as technical and centred on pull requests: an issue node
led with `owner/name#n`, so a long title was cut; a stage read `PR open`; an edge read `job of`; and every node not
settled was said to **block** its root, also a job that only works on its issue.

- **Titles lead.** An issue node's `label` is its title alone (its `owner/name#n` when it has none); a pull request node's
  is the goal of the job that opened it. The repository and number stay in `repo` and `number`, and the view draws them
  in small type under the title.
- **Stage words** (`src/domain/job-words.ts`, pure). Each node carries `stageText`: Queued, Building it (attempt 2 of
  3), Plan, Research, Waiting on you: answer a question / approve the plan / accept the research / answer it / take it
  over, A person works on it, Parked, PR open: checks running / fixing checks / has merge conflicts / draft / waiting
  for the merge (issue #1067: never "Ready for review"), Part shipped, Merged, Done, Failed, Cancelled, Closed, Not started. An
  issue says what its item's job says. `waitsOnYou` marks a node that waits on
  the person. The attempt counts the failed runs a run again redoes (`attemptIn`), and its "of" is the failure settings'
  `maxAttempts` plus one, which the route passes in; a next part is no new attempt. The words are made on the server, as
  the UI imports nothing of `src/` at runtime, and so an agent over the API reads the same words.
- **A summary per tree.** `JobTree.summary` is one line: "3 of 4 pieces shipped, 1 being redone, nothing waiting on
  you." A piece is an issue of the tree (a job, when the tree has no issue); shipped is `done`; being redone, an issue
  whose newest job runs a failed one again; what waits on you counts the question and hand-off nodes, and the jobs that
  wait on a plan or report with no such node.
- **Edges as sentences** (`EDGE_TEXT`, the view's own copy): is being worked on by, produced, continues in, is being
  redone as, is waiting on the merge of, needs this first (blocked by), goes in after (stacked on), is waiting on your
  answer to. Only `blocked_by` says something must come first. The ring the view draws round a node not settled stays,
  but it reads "not settled yet", never "blocks".

**Part 4: finished work rolls up (issue #1036, 2026-10-13).** The graph made a finished queue look stuck: a pull request
merged after a tend or a rework took it over still showed its old checks and conflicts, and its job stayed partly done or
PR open; an issue a later job finished took the stage of an earlier cancelled job; a failure a rerun replaced, or a person
dismissed, still counted as Failed. The rollup reads only what the hopper keeps already. It adds no GitHub read and no
poll: the owner's constraint on the issue.

- **A pull request's state over every job that names it** (`src/domain/job-rollup.ts`, split from `job-graph.ts`). A
  tend or a rework hands the pull request to a newer job (issue #994: the old job is followed no more), and that job
  follows it to its end, so the link is the pull request URL both jobs name: nothing new is recorded. A final state — `merged`, `closed`, `abandoned` — that
  any job's follow saw wins for all of them, merged over the rest; so does `merged` in the issue graph (a closing pull
  request's state, from the issue place read). An ended pull request shows no checks, draft or conflicts. One still open
  shows what its newest follower saw of it.
- **An issue closed as completed is done.** The issue place query reads `stateReason` beside `state`, for the issue and
  for the issues it links (the field is on an issue only, so a pull request item does not ask it): no new query. An issue
  closed with no reason, or closed as completed, is done whatever its jobs did; `not_planned` and `duplicate` are not. A
  partly done job of a done issue waits on nothing: done.
- **Superseded** (a new job stage). A failed or cancelled job is `superseded` when a later job of its issue is in the
  graph, its issue is closed as completed, the pull request it was the tend of merged after all, or a person dismissed it
  (`dismissed`, its words "Dismissed", as the Failed jobs list drops it). It is settled: it blocks no root and counts as
  no failure in the stage counts or a tree's summary. A run again that failed after a finished job stays failed: nothing
  took its place. An issue reads its stage and words from its newest job that is not superseded. **Replaced by the
  work-item ledger (issue #1067):** an issue's stage is its item's state (`ITEM_STAGE`), and whether a failed or
  cancelled job is still a failure is the ledger's (`stageInItem`, `isFailureOf`): `failed` only while its item is
  failed on it, `waiting` (`handedOff`, "Waiting on you: take it over") while its item is handed to a person on it,
  else superseded. The rollup keeps only the pull request's state over the jobs that name it.
- **The route** adds the newest job of each issue it shows (`getBySourceKey`), so an issue whose last job ended before
  the queue's 24-hour window still takes its stage from it.

Left: an issue no job works, with no work item, closed after its last read, shows `no_job` until a read of it or of an
issue that links it (each discover reads the open issues of the hopper's label again). Reading closed issues again would be
a new poll. An issue with a work item reads the ledger, which a GitHub delivery moves at the close.

Tests: `test/domain/job-rollup.test.ts`, `test/domain/job-graph-issue-stage.test.ts`, `test/domain/issue-graph.test.ts` and
`test/sources/issue-place.test.ts` (`stateReason`), `test/integration/job-graph.test.ts` (the newest job of an issue).

## A job's parts list (issue #935, 2026-10-12)

Requirement (issue #935): for each job, everything it touched or made — a bill of materials —, grouped, each item with
its status and its own page, over the API too (issue #718's parity); and a drill-in job page: a plain-words header, the
job's own graph with each part as a node, a timeline newest first, and the parts as a filterable table; running parts
stay live, and what waits on the person is pinned at the top.

**The model** (`jobBom`, `src/domain/job-bom.ts`, pure; its types go out through `job-graph.ts`, as `types.ts` is at its
line limit). Nothing new is recorded for it: the parts are read from what the job's record, its events and its rows already say (since issue #2504 also its resource ledger's rows).

| Group | Parts, and where each comes from |
|---|---|
| What was asked (`asked`) | its issue (`source`); each issue it filed (`job.child_issue_filed`); rework asked (`job.rework_requested`); a changed spec (`job.respecified`) |
| Work (`work`) | each run (`job.started`); its task list (`tasks`); its lane; the time it took or runs so far; its usage (part 2, below); each job that ran it again, ran its next part, or forked from it |
| Code (`code`) | its pull request, checks and branch (its source state); its commits, oldest first — the pull request's (`seen.commits`, part 2), else the ones its latest checkpoint names (`checkpoint.commits`, issue #921) —; how many files it changes (`seen.files`); its place in the merge order (part 2); each push (`github_proxy.done`, `op: git.push`); its merge or close (`job.pull_request_merged`, `job.pull_request_closed`) |
| Outputs (`outputs`) | its artifacts and each revision (`artifact.revised`); its plan or research report (`proposalId`, `researchId`); the help pages and What's new lines among the files its pull request changes (part 2) |
| Infra (`infra`) | each plan and its approval (`infra.plan_recorded`, `infra.plan_approved`); each minted credential with its operation, asset and end (`vault.minted`); drift its check found (`infra.out_of_band_recorded`); a vault grant it asked for (`vault.grant_asked`, `vault.granted`) |
| Decisions (`decisions`) | each question, and who answered it — a person, or the level by name (rules, a model) —; each override of a Decider pick (`minor_decision.overridden`); its hand-off |
| Machines and sandboxes (`machines`) | each machine it was claimed on, with its runs (`job.claimed`); its latest checkpoint only, one part however many were taken (`job.checkpoint`, with how many `job.checkpointed` say were taken, issue #1975), with its commits and whether it holds the session; each Windows sandbox step (`step.started`); each container its reap removed, a database image's as a **test database** (`job.containers_removed`, issue #975, below); its cleanup status and each entry of its **resource ledger** (issue #2504, "The resource ledger") |

Each part's `status` is `waiting_on_you`, `running`, `open`, `done`, `failed`, `cancelled` or `recorded` (a fact, not a
piece of work: a lane, a branch, a credential); `href` is its page in the UI (`#questions`, `#artifacts/<id>/<n>`,
`#infra`, `#job/<id>`…) and `url` its place on GitHub. What waits on the person comes first, then the groups in order.
`header` says what was asked, where it stands (the stage words above) and what is next (`nextWords`: "You: answer the
question.", "Review and merge the pull request.", "The agent works on it: 1 of 3 tasks done."); `summary` counts the
parts that are work, not records. `events` is the job's events, newest first.

**Test databases** (issue #975). A job's tests start their own databases on its machine, and the hopper was told nothing
of them. Three decisions:

1. *What counts.* A container the job's tests start: in the job's own container runtime ("Each job its own container
   runtime"), or with its label (`hopper.job=<job id>`) in the machine's. A container of a database image (Postgres,
   MySQL, MariaDB, Mongo, Redis and the like, `DATABASE_IMAGE` in `job-bom.ts`) is a **test database**; any other is a
   container, listed the same way. A database a job copies for an ad-hoc daemon (`pg_dump` into a fresh database) does not
   count: it lives inside a Postgres the job did not start, and nothing on the machine tells it from any other database.
2. *How the hopper learns of one.* The machine says it, not the job: a job need not cooperate, and the reap already lists
   and removes each container (issue #1120). Before it removes one, the reap asks the runtime for its name, image, and
   when it started and stopped (`DETAILS_FORMAT`, `src/client/job-runtime.ts`), one line `hopper-container-details <id>
   …`; `readReap` reads it as `removed.details`, and `job.containers_removed` keeps it beside the ids. A client older
   than this says only the ids. Nothing new is kept but that optional field.
3. *What the part shows.* `container:<id>` in the machines group: "Test database <name>" (or "Container <name>"), its
   image and machine, when it started (`at`), how long it ran — until it stopped, or until the reap when it still ran —,
   and that its reap removed it. A recorded container is therefore never still there. A job whose reap has not run yet
   (it runs, or its cleanup is deferred, or it timed out and may go on) shows none: the hopper learns of its containers
   only at the reap.

**Resources used** (issue #2498). Lane machines ran out of memory, and nothing said which job held it. A job's processes
are already in its scope (`hopper-job-<job id>.scope`, "The job's scope"), so its cgroup counts them, whatever they did to
their environment. Three decisions:

1. *When it is read.* By the reap, before it stops the scope: once the scope stops, systemd removes its cgroup and the
   counts with it. The reap asks `systemctl --user show -p ControlGroup` for the scope's cgroup and reads three files
   there: `memory.peak` (Linux 5.19 and later), `cpu.stat` `usage_usec` and `memory.events` `oom_kill`. One line
   `hopper-used <bytes> <µs> <kills>`, `-` for a file it could not read; `readReap` reads it as `used`, and the cleanup
   records `job.resources_used` with the job's machine. A cgroup path with `..` is never read.
2. *What it misses.* A job with no scope there (no systemd user manager), a scope that ended before the reap (a parked
   job's pane closed at the park; a print-mode agent's turn ended), and a client older than this: the reap reads no peak.
   Then the cleanup records the job's **metered peak** in its place (issue #2737, `src/engine/job-peaks.ts`): the most
   memory its machine's meter said the job held (`jobUse.memoryPeakBytes`, of its scope or of its job processes), kept by
   the engine as it lists its machines, for 24 hours after the meter last named the job, and in memory only, so a restart
   forgets it. A peak the reap read wins. With neither, no peak. Disk per job is read by the same reap (part 4, below).
3. *What the part shows.* One part, `resources` in the machines group: "Peak memory <n>, CPU <time>", the OOM kills when
   there were any, and the machines. A job reaped on more than one machine (moved, resumed elsewhere) shows the highest
   peak, and the CPU time and OOM kills of all of them (`src/domain/job-resources.ts`).

**Disk used** (issue #2498 part 4). A job's build output, caches and test data are in its scratch dir and worktrees
("Work tree"), and nothing said how much a job left there. Three decisions:

1. *When it is read.* By the reap, after it stopped the job's processes and before it removes or keeps those dirs: one
   `du -skx` of each (cut off at 30 s where `timeout` is), added up, as one line `hopper-disk <KiB>`. `-x` keeps it on one
   file system, and du follows no link, so a worktree's `node_modules` link to the shared dependencies counts as a link
   only. `readReap` reads it as `used.diskBytes`, and `job.resources_used` records it with the scope's fields; with no
   scope there it is recorded alone. No scratch dir and no worktree there: none.
2. *What it is.* What the job held there at its end, not a peak over its life: the scratch dir only grows while the job
   runs, but a job that removed its own build output says less than it held. The sweep's survey still measures each work
   tree as a whole (issue #2494); it keeps nothing per job.
3. *What the part shows.* The `resources` part says "disk <n>" after the memory and the CPU time: the most one reap found
   (a job reaped on two machines held its dirs on each, and the highest says what one machine needed).

**Resources in use now** (issue #2498 part 3). The reap reads a job's use only at its end; a person who looks at a running
job, or at a machine that is full, could not see which job holds what. Three decisions:

1. *Who reads it.* The machine's resource meter (`src/client/resources.ts`), which already reads each job scope's memory
   in use for the memory floor (issue #2499, `jobMemoryBytes`). At each read it also reads the same three files as the
   reap (`memory.peak`, `cpu.stat` `usage_usec`, `memory.events` `oom_kill`) and says them as `jobUse`, per job id, with
   the CPU cores the scope kept busy since the read before (`cpuCores`; none at its first read, and a read sooner than a
   second after keeps the one before). A client's reading is checked field by field before it is believed
   (`src/machines/resources.ts`). No second reader and no new probe: an ssh target's probe prints the same files for each
   scope (issue #2499 part 13), with no cores busy, since it reads each scope once. A machine with no systemd user manager
   and an older client say none.
2. *Where it shows.* The job's parts list: one part `resources-now:<machine>` in the machines group, status `running`,
   "Memory <n> now, peak <n>, CPU <n> cores", and the CPU time so far, the OOM kills and the machine
   (`resourcesNow` in `src/domain/job-resources.ts`). `GET /api/jobs/:id/bom` reads the machines' last readings only for
   a job that has not ended (`liveUseOf`, `Queries.getLiveUse`). On Machines, each card says what its jobs use together:
   "<n> jobs use <memory> · <n> cores busy · <n> OOM kills" (`jobsUseText`). `GET /api/machines` has both fields in each
   machine's `resources`. On the lane board (Dashboard → Lanes, issue #2722), each lane with a job says the job's memory
   now and its peak: "memory <n> · peak <n>" (`laneMemoryText`, `ui/src/model/machine-history.ts`), from its machine's same
   reading; a lane whose job's scope the meter did not read says none. A lane's memory is its job's scope's: an agent's
   process tree has no reading of its own.
3. *What it is not.* No sample keeps it: the machine samples keep the waiting memory only (issue #2499), and the job's
   record at its end is still the reap's `job.resources_used`. A seat's total is its machines' totals: a seat's jobs run
   on its machines.

**Job limits and resource-limit failures** (issue #2498 part 2). A job that used all of a machine's memory stopped the
other jobs there too. Three decisions:

1. *Where the limit is.* On the job's scope, as it is made ("The job's scope"): `MemoryMax` from the machine's
   `jobMemoryMaxGiB`, `CPUQuota` from its `jobCpuPercent` (percent of one CPU), plain options of local, ssh and client
   machines (`src/plugins/machine-source/attached.ts` `jobLimitsShape`, `MachineSnapshot.jobLimits`), off by default.
   Past `MemoryMax`, the kernel's OOM killer stops a process of that scope only. No limit per seat: a seat's jobs are on
   its machines, and the memory floor (issue #2291) keeps the machine's own headroom. Issue #2622 made a memory limit the
   default: lanes admitted while light started four JVM builds at once on one WSL VM, and the VM ran out of memory. With
   no `jobMemoryMaxGiB`, each scope gets the machine's memory less its floor, shared by its lanes, with `MemoryHigh` at
   90% of it. A machine whose jobs get no scope and that has no cgroup memory limit of its own holds nothing: its meter
   says so (`ResourceReading.jobMemoryLimit` `none`: this machine's and a client's from their user manager's cgroup and
   their own cgroup's limit, an ssh target's from its probe's `um` line), and the Machines page shows the warning
   **no memory limit** with what to do. It still takes jobs: the memory floor and the host pool still admit them.
2. *How it is seen.* When Claude exits, the pane's shell, which runs in the job's scope, says its exit code and then the
   scope's `memory.events` `oom_kill` count (`src/executors/herdr/exited.ts` `oomKillsCommand`), read from its own cgroup
   and only when that is `hopper-job-<job id>.scope`. A count above 0 makes the failure `claude exited (…) at a resource
   limit: the kernel's OOM killer stopped <n> processes in the job's scope: …`. A machine OOM, with no job limit, counts
   too: the job's process was stopped for want of memory all the same.
3. *What happens.* The known cause **Resource limit** (`resource-limit`): transient, retry, first of the causes, so a
   text Claude printed as it died never names another. The job runs again with backoff, by the retry limit, and the
   memory floor decides where it starts. It is no lane fault: the lane is not wrong. An OOM kill of a build daemon that
   Claude lives through fails nothing; the parts list counts it ("Resources used").

**The route.** `GET /api/jobs/:id/bom` (`src/http/jobs.ts`), the user's own; 404 for a job it does not know. It reads the
job's newest 2000 events (`EventLog.recent` takes a job now, over the `events_job` index of tenant migration 45), its
questions, its newest hand-off, its artifacts, and the jobs among the newest 1000 that ran it again or forked from it.
A read, so an API token needs `jobs:read`.

**The page** (`ui/src/views/job.tsx`, `ui/src/views/job-bom.tsx`, `ui/src/model/job-bom.ts`). The job view at
`#job/<id>` keeps its facts and adds, in order: the header with what waits on the person pinned under it; the job's own
graph — the job, a node per group it has, a node per part, laid out with d3's tidy tree as the job trees are, a part
with a page a link to it —; the timeline, the parts list's events with the ones the UI holds, newest first; and the
parts table, filtered by group, status and text. The page reads the parts list again, debounced, each time an event of
the job arrives on the stream, so a running part changes with no reload. A daemon with no such route (a parts list that
cannot be read) leaves the page as it was: facts and timeline.

**The timeline as a Trace** (issue #1169, `ui/src/components/job-timeline.tsx`, `ui/src/model/timeline-steps.ts`). Each
event is a Trace line that opens to its data in a small code block (`JsonBlock`). What belongs together nests under one
line at the place of its newest event: a sandbox step's `step.started` and `step.finished` (one `step` id) — an error when
it ended with a non-zero exit or a problem, running while it has not ended and the job is at work —; a fork's `job.forked`
and `job.fork_resolved` (one `forkId`) — running while it is not decided and the fork job is at work, pending while that
job waits, an error when the fork job failed, with a link to the fork job; a **tend job**'s `job.pull_request_tended` and
a **rework** job's `job.rework_requested` (one `nextJobId` each) — one line that names the step and the pull request, or the
pull request and the notes, and that job's status: running while it is at work, pending while it waits, an error when it
failed. Opened, it links that job and reads that job's own events (`GET /api/jobs/:id/bom`, read again when that job's
status changes), each a line nested under it; all the job's `job.checkpointed` (issue #1975) — one line, the last
checkpoint and its machine, and how many were taken, each a line nested under it. An event with no such id stays a line of its own. Data shown as JSON elsewhere (a
decider decision's raw inputs, the built-in change rule) is the same `JsonBlock`; commands to copy, a direct job's result,
a failure's error, an out-of-band change's detail and an infra plan's text are `LogBlock`s (title, wrap toggle, copy).

**The job's transcript** (issue #1169 part 4, `src/domain/transcript.ts`, `src/http/ui/job-transcript.ts`,
`ui/src/views/job-transcript.tsx`). The agent session a job's latest checkpoint keeps ("Checkpoints and resume
elsewhere"; scrubbed when it was kept) is the transcript's one source: the hopper keeps no other copy of what the agent
said. `parseTranscript` (pure) reads Claude's session file, one JSON object a line: each prompt (a user line with text,
not `isMeta`) starts a **turn**; the agent's lines after it are the turn's parts, in order — `text`, `reasoning`
(thinking), `tool` (a tool call, its `title` from its description or the field that names its target, its `input`, the
command or the input as JSON, and its result and error from the tool result with its id), `plan` (`TodoWrite`) and
`subagent` (`Task`, `Agent`: what for, its kind, its prompt and what it gave back). A subagent's own lines (`isSidechain`),
a line that is no JSON and the session's bookkeeping lines are left out. A prompt, text or reasoning is cut at 20,000
characters, a tool call's input or result at 8,000, and says `truncated`. `POST /ui/api/jobs/:id/transcript` `{ before?,
limit? }` answers the newest `limit` turns (20 unless it says, at most 100) before turn `before`, with `start` and `total`.
Operator; Access decides as for the job's terminal (`terminal#can_attach`), because the transcript is what the job's pane
showed. A POST, as the terminal's screen, so it is behind the role guard; it changes and records nothing. 409: the
checkpoint keeps no session. The job view shows **Open transcript** to an operator when the job's checkpoint holds its
session: each turn is a prompt `Message` (end) and the agent's reply `Message` (start) in a `Message Scroller`, which
starts at the newest turn, keeps its place when **Load earlier turns** puts the turns before in front
(`preserveScrollOnPrepend`), and shows a button to the end. A reply's text is Markdown; each run of steps between texts is
a `Trace`, a line per step that opens to its input and result in small code blocks: a failed tool call is an error, and
the last tool call of the newest turn with no result runs while the job is at work. A new checkpoint (its `at` changes)
reads the newest turns again.

**The live transcript** (issue #1169 part 7, the same route and view). A read with `fresh: true`, for a job at work
(`running`, `waiting_answer`, `waiting_on`), takes the job's checkpoint first (`Checkpoints.take`, as the ten-minute pass:
read on the machine, scrubbed, kept, `job.checkpointed`) when the latest checkpoint, or the route's last fresh try of that
job, is `TRANSCRIPT_FRESH_MS` (a minute) old or more; else it answers the checkpoint kept. When the take says why it took
none (the machine cannot be reached, too large, one is being taken), the answer is the kept checkpoint's turns with
`stale` and why, or 409 and why when none is kept. The checkpoint is the one live source: the hopper reads the session
file only through it, never through the pane, so the scrub and the size limit stay one path. The view of a job at work
reads fresh when it opens and each `FOLLOW_MS` (a minute) while it is open, and says that it follows the job, or why the
last read took no new checkpoint; the checkpoint its own read took is no reason to read again at once. A newer read keeps
the earlier turns already loaded in front of its own (`newer`: a session only grows, so a turn keeps its index), so the
scroller neither jumps nor drops what the person loaded; at the end, the Message Scroller stays at the newest turn. A job
not at work is read as before, with no fresh checkpoint. The terminal still shows the pane second by second.

**Pull request diffs** (issue #1169 part 6, `src/http/ui/pull-request-acts.ts`, `ui/src/components/pull-request-diff.tsx`).
A card on the Pull requests page with a pull request, and each Landing card — a batch's **culprit** among them —, has
**Show diff** for an operator. `POST /ui/api/pull-requests/diff` `{ repo, number }` reads it on GitHub with the person's
own connection, as a job's `pr diff` (issue #1074) reads it: `files` and `diff`, each file's patch as `git diff` writes
it, cut at 200,000 characters (`truncated`). Only a job repository's (404 else); with no GitHub connection, 503. The read
counts as a job's other read (`per_job_read`) at the rate limiter. A POST, so it is behind the role guard; it changes and
records nothing, and nothing keeps it. The view shows it in a `CodeBlock` in diff mode (`LogBlock`: title, wrap toggle,
copy): a file's header lines and each hunk's `@@` line highlighted, added and removed lines as such
(`ui/src/model/pull-request-diff.ts`). Operator, not viewer: the person's connection may read a private repository the
viewer cannot.

**Part 2** (2026-10-12) adds the parts part 1 left, each from a record that exists, plus one fact the follow now keeps:

- **Usage.** The route reads the job's own job runs (`MachineHistoryRepository.jobRuns` takes a `jobId` now), from a day
  before its first event so the machine's baseline has samples with no lane in use. `usage` adds them up as a job cost
  profile does (issue #688): per usage window, each run's rise divided by its lanes in use; CPU weighted by samples; memory
  at its peak. One part, `usage`, `recorded`, linked to the job costs on Machines. No run ended: no part.
- **Commits and changed files.** The hopper's mirror says what a pull request changes (`GitMirrors.changes`): `git log
  base..head` (at most 100, `<short sha> <subject>`) and `git diff --name-only base...head` (at most 300 paths). Both read
  commits and trees, so no blob is fetched. `gitAnswers` adds them to a pull request read by its number in a pass — the
  follow's read —, and the follow keeps them on what it saw (`PullRequestSeen.commits`, `.files`; the last ones kept when
  git cannot say). A merged pull request keeps the last ones seen. So every commit shows, the ones after the latest
  checkpoint too; before git first says, the checkpoint's commits show as before. A field added to the source state's JSON:
  no migration, and an older build ignores it.
- **Pushes.** Each push through the hopper (`github_proxy.done` with `op: git.push`), with its branches, and whether it
  came after the latest checkpoint.
- **Help pages and What's new lines.** The changed files under a `help/` directory (`*.md`), the fragments under
  `whats-new/` (not its README), `WHATS-NEW.md` and `CHANGELOG.md`: `open` while the pull request is open, `done` once
  merged, linked to the pull request's files.
- **Merge order.** While the pull request waits: the pull request it goes in after, from what holds it in the tending
  queue (`heldBehind`, issue #939: a job fixes that one first, or the hopper merges it first) or from the merge gate
  (`seen.mergeHeldBehind`: the hopper merged a conflicting one first).

**Left for later** (issue #975): the test databases of a run. The hopper keeps no record of them: a job's tests start their own
databases on its machine, and nothing tells the hopper. Showing them needs a new record, which is a decision of its own.

Tests: `test/domain/job-bom.test.ts` (each group, the order, the header and summary, the timeline; part 2: usage, commits and
files, help pages and What's new lines, pushes, merge order), `test/git-mirror/mirrors.test.ts` and
`test/sources/github-git-answers.test.ts` (what a pull request changes, with no blob), `test/sources/github-follow.test.ts`
(the follow keeps it),
`test/domain/job-graph.test.ts` (titles, stage words, tree summaries), `test/integration/job-bom.test.ts` (a job that asked a
question and opened a pull request, over the real database and HTTP server; usage from its job runs; 404), `test/ui/job-bom-model.test.ts` (filters,
pinned parts, the layout, edge sentences), `test/ui/job-bom-view.test.ts` (the whole app over a fake daemon: header, pinned,
graph, table filters, timeline, a live read again), `test/ui/jobs-view.test.ts` (title, small reference and stage words on
a node, the tree summary).

## Infra plans: no apply without a plan (issue #870, part 1, 2026-10-12)

Owner's principle (issue #870): no apply without a plan. Plans and infrastructure changes never slide under the radar:
each one is surfaced to people. Before this, a box of a template with an approved `write`, `sync` or `apply` profile was
minted its credential at each ask, with nothing that tied the change to a reviewed plan.

- **A plan is a record of its own** (`InfraPlan`, `src/domain/infra-plans.ts`; tenant migration 46, `infra_plans`), apart
  from artifacts, and never changed once kept. It holds what made it (`tool`: `terraform`, `helm`, `gitops`), the raw
  plan (`text`: `terraform show` of the plan file, the `helm diff`, the GitOps diff; at most 1 MiB) and, for terraform,
  the saved plan file (`terraform plan -out`, at most 8 MiB, its size and SHA-256 beside it), the `asset` an apply of it is
  minted a credential for (an `aws-role`, a `cluster`, a `namespace`), the `target` (the workspace or app it changes), the
  `repo`, the branch (`ref`) and full `commit` it was made at, its `pullRequest`, the read profile it was made with
  (`read`, as the job says it), the job and its issue (who asked for it), `createdAt`, and `expiresAt` (60 minutes later).
- **A job records one**: `POST /job/infra-plans`, with its proxy token, JSON (`file` in base64): 201 with its id; a plan
  that is not whole is a 400 that says why. `GET /job/infra-plans/:id` answers it with its approval; `?file=1` gives the
  plan file back as it was put, so terraform applies only the saved plan. `infra.plan_recorded` on the job's timeline.
- **A person approves it**: Vault, panel **Infra changes** (every plan, newest first, with its state:
  waits for approval, approved, stale), or `POST /ui/api/infra-plans` `{ action: "approve", plan }` (admin, a box
  action). The approval is a row of its own (`infra_plan_approvals`), so the plan does not change; a second is a 409.
  `infra.plan_approved` on the timeline of the job that recorded it. A job never approves a plan.
- **The apply gate** (`applyRefusal`, `headRefusal`; `InfraPlans.gate`, `src/infra-plans/service.ts`). Before the vault
  mints a credential for any operation but `read` (`src/vault/mint.ts`, after Access allowed it), the ask must name a
  plan (`$HOPPER_SECRET aws apply aws-role/<account>/<role> --plan <id>`, the same for `kube`) that is kept, is a plan of
  that asset, is not stale, is approved, and was made at the commit its branch is at now: the hopper reads the branch's
  head on GitHub with the user's connection at each ask. Any other ask mints nothing (`vault.mint_refused`, with why),
  and the outside service is not asked. A head that cannot be read refuses too. A vault with no gate mints only reads.
  `vault.minted` names the plan. A renewal asks again, so a plan that went stale while it ran is not renewed.
- **The client** sends the plan in its ask (`VaultAsk.plan`), bound into the sealed answer's authenticated data only when
  it names one, so a client from before this opens its answers to a read as before; it sends no plan, so its applies are
  refused.

**Why every operation but read.** `write`, `sync` and `apply` each mint a credential that can change the asset; a gate on
`apply` alone would leave the same change one word away.

**Not built here (the next parts of #870).** The plain-language summary and explainer of each plan, with its risk
callouts (destroys, IAM, prod, data, network) and blast radius; notifications to environment watchers for every plan
and apply; approval by risk (a low-risk uat plan approved by its requester or automatically, still in the feed; prod,
IAM, destroys and identity by the owner through the blast-radius gate); the failing check for a new resource without
the MAP tag; a timeline of applies and drift, and the nightly drift plan; a terraform wrapper on write boxes that runs
`apply` only of the saved plan file; routing Argo CD syncs through the gate. The `read` a plan names is recorded as the
job says it, not checked against the job's mints.

**Residual risk, stated.** The gate binds a credential to a plan, not each command to the plan: within its 15 or 10
minutes, a minted credential can make any change its role or service account allows. The plan's commit is checked
