against its branch, not against the files the box applies from. The saved plan file, served back, is what makes the
apply the plan's; enforcing that on the box is the wrapper above.

Tests: `test/domain/infra-plans.test.ts` (the gate and the plan input, pure), `test/integration/infra-plans.test.ts` (the
real daemon, a joined box, STS and GitHub faked: an apply with no plan, an unapproved plan, a moved head and a plan of
another asset are refused and STS is not asked — the negative test of the issue's "Done when"; a current approved plan
mints, its audit naming it; the plan kept whole, listed, its file given back), `test/ui/infra-plans.test.ts`.

## Infra plans: the summary and the MAP tag check (issue #870, part 2, 2026-10-12)

Every plan gets a summary and an explainer in plain words, and a new AWS resource without the MAP tag fails the plan.
Before this, Infra changes showed only where a plan applies and from which commit; a person read the raw plan to learn
what it does.

- **The changes** (`changesOf`, `src/domain/infra-plan-changes.ts`, pure): what each resource of the plan has done to it
  (`create`, `update`, `replace`, `delete`). A terraform plan is read from `terraform show -json` of the plan file, which
  the job now sends as `json` (a string, at most 8 MiB) with `POST /job/infra-plans`: needed for terraform, refused for
  the others, read and not kept. A no-op, a read and a data source are not changes. A `helm diff` is read from its
  headers (`<namespace>, <name>, <Kind> (<group>) has changed:` / `has been added:` / `has been removed:`), an
  `argocd app diff` from its `===== <group>/<Kind> <namespace>/<name> ======` headers and its `<` (live) and `>`
  (desired) lines. Terraform JSON that is not a plan (no `planned_values`: the JSON of a state, say) is a 400.
- **The summary** (`summarize`, `src/domain/infra-plan-summary.ts`, pure; `InfraPlan.summary`), made once when the plan is
  kept and kept with it, so it never changes either:
  - `words`, one line: the changes by action and type, the environments, "changes nothing in prod" when the plan names
    environments and prod is not one, "destroys nothing" when nothing is deleted or replaced. For example "Adds 2
    security group rules in uat; changes nothing in prod; destroys nothing".
  - `environments`: `prod`, `uat`, `staging`, `dev`, `qa` as words of their own in the target, a resource's address or
    its `Environment` tag.
  - `risks`, the callouts, each with its resources: `destroy` (deleted or replaced), `iam` (IAM and identity: IAM, SSO,
    Identity Store, Organizations, Cognito, any `*_iam_*` type; Kubernetes roles, bindings, service accounts), `prod`
    (a resource in prod, or every one when the target is), `data` (a data store changed, replaced or deleted, not
    created: databases, buckets, volumes, KMS keys, secrets; Kubernetes volumes, stateful sets, secrets), `network`
    (VPCs, subnets, routes, security groups, load balancers, DNS, CDN; Kubernetes services, ingresses, network policies).
  - `blastRadius`: how many resources of how many kinds, where, applied as which asset to which target.
  - `checks`: the MAP tag check, for terraform.
  - `level`: `high` when the plan destroys, touches IAM, prod or data, fails a check, or is a diff with no change the
    hopper knows; else `low`. Network alone is `low`. Approval by risk (the next part) reads it.
- **The MAP tag check.** Each new AWS resource (action `create`, an `hashicorp/aws` provider) that takes tags (its plan
  has `tags` or `tags_all`) carries `map-migrated=migXWT2TUR4TJ` in either (`MAP_TAG`). A replaced or changed resource
  exists already and is not checked. A plan that fails it is kept and shown (`summary.failed`), but `approve` is a 409
  and the apply gate refuses it (`failedChecks`), approved or not: the job fixes the code and plans again.
- **Shown.** `GET /api/infra-plans` and the job's own `GET /job/infra-plans/:id` carry the summary; the job's `POST`
  answer says it, and says when the plan failed. Infra changes shows each plan's words and level, its callouts, its blast
  radius and its checks, a failed plan in red with no Approve, and **Show the plan**, the raw text, read when opened.
  `infra.plan_recorded` carries `summary { words, level, risks, failed }`.
- A plan kept before this has no summary, and is shown and gated as before.

**Why the job sends the JSON.** The hopper runs no terraform, and the text form of `terraform show` is meant for people:
its tags and its actions are not stable to read. The JSON form is terraform's own stable contract.

**Residual risk, stated.** The summary is read from the JSON the job sends, not from the saved plan file: a job could send
JSON that does not match its file. The wrapper on write boxes (a next part) runs `terraform show -json` of the saved file
itself. The MAP tag value is one constant: a second value earns a setting.

**Not built here (the next parts of #870).** Notifications to environment watchers; approval by risk (a low-risk uat plan
approved by its requester or automatically; the rest by the owner through the blast-radius gate); the timeline of
applies and drift, and the nightly drift plan; the terraform wrapper on write boxes; Argo CD syncs through the gate; the
check of a plan's `read` against the job's mints.

Tests: `test/domain/infra-plan-summary.test.ts` (the changes of terraform JSON, a helm diff and an Argo CD diff; the
words, the callouts, the level; the MAP tag check on new resources only), `test/domain/infra-plans.test.ts` (a failed
plan refused, approved or not), `test/integration/infra-plans.test.ts` (the summary kept, listed and on the timeline; a
plan without the MAP tag kept and listed, its approval a 409, its apply refused and STS not asked; a terraform plan with
no JSON a 400), `test/ui/infra-plans.test.ts` (the failed state, the explainer).

## Out-of-band changes (issue #871, part 1, 2026-10-12)

Follow-on to issue #870 (no apply without a plan). Goal: **track** infrastructure changes that did not come through IaC or
GitOps. Generic by the issue's rule: the hopper never classifies an action and keeps no per-action rule.

- **The rule** (`judge`, `src/domain/out-of-band.ts`, pure). A write is **out of band** unless a **controller identity**
  or a **plan-bound apply credential** made it. Drift is out of band by itself: a GitOps app out of sync (`gitops`), a
  non-empty `terraform plan` on unchanged code (`terraform-plan`). An audit-log write (`cloudtrail`, `kube-audit`) is
  judged by its principal only: in band when it matches a controller identity, or is the principal of a credential the
  vault minted for an approved plan and the write fell inside that credential's life; out of band otherwise, whatever
  the action.
- **Plan-bound apply credentials.** `vault.minted` now names `principal`: who the credential writes as, as an audit log
  names it (`mintPrincipal`): an AWS session `arn:<partition>:sts::<account>:assumed-role/<role>/<session name>` (the
  role's path dropped, as CloudTrail drops it), a Kubernetes token `system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<service account>`,
  an EKS token its role's session. A `vault.minted` with a `plan` and a `principal` is a plan-bound apply credential from
  its event's time to its `expiresAt`; the rule reads them from the event log (two hours before the earliest signal).
- **Controller identities**: the principals whose writes are GitOps's (an Argo CD or Flux controller's service account,
  an Atlantis role), one user's list (`infra_controllers`), a trailing `*` naming a group; `*` alone is refused, since
  then nothing is out of band. Set by an admin on Infra changes, or `POST /ui/api/out-of-band`
  `{ action: "controllers", identities }`; `infra.controllers_changed`.
- **Signals come from a job's read-only check**: `POST /job/infra-signals`, with its proxy token, JSON `{ signals }`, 1
  to 500 each time. A signal: `source`, `key` (its own id: CloudTrail's `eventID`, the audit log's `auditID`; for
  drift, what drifted), `target` (what changed), `what` (the action in the source's words), `who` (the principal;
  required for an audit-log signal), `at`, and `detail` (the record, the diff, the plan text; at most 64 KiB). The check
  keeps only writes; it runs with the read credentials jobs get by default. A signal that is not whole refuses the whole
  report (400, saying which and why). The answer counts what was recorded, what was in band and why, and what was
  reported before.
- **An out-of-band change is a record of its own** (`OutOfBandChange`; tenant migration 47, `infra_out_of_band`), never
  changed once kept: the signal, the job whose check reported it, and when. Reported again, it is not kept twice: an
  audit-log write once ever (by its source and key), drift once while it is not marked; drift found again after its
  mark is a new change.
- **Never silent.** Each one is `infra.out_of_band_recorded` on the reporting job's timeline: the Grok Bot routine sends
  it (body adds `change`, `signal`, `target`, `what`, `who`, `happenedAt`, and `infraUrl`, the Infra page, when the UI's
  URL is known), and webhook subscribers get it as any event.
- **A person marks it** on Infra (`#infra`, "The Infra page"), panel **Out-of-band changes** (every change, newest first, with who, what,
  when, the signal and its detail), or `POST /ui/api/out-of-band` `{ action: "mark", change, mark, reason? }` (admin):
  `adopted` (brought back into git), `reverted`, or `accepted` with a reason. The mark is a row of its own
  (`infra_out_of_band_marks`), once (a second is a 409); `infra.out_of_band_marked`. Tracking only: the hopper reverts
  nothing.

**The scheduled check** is part 3 below: a ready-made collector, run on a schedule outside the hopper.

**Part 2: an outside collector reports (2026-10-12).** A check that runs outside the hopper — a CI schedule, a cron job,
a small service beside the cluster — reports the same signals with an **API token**: `POST /ui/api/out-of-band/signals`,
JSON `{ signals }`, the same signal shape, limits and refusals as `POST /job/infra-signals`, least role operator. A grant
for it names the scope `out-of-band:signals` and nothing else ("Grants and refresh tokens"); the collector refreshes its
API token from the grant. Each signal is judged by the same rule. An out-of-band change it reports is kept with
`reporter` (the API token's label: the grant's; else the name of who signed in) in place of `job`; a change names one of
the two. Its `infra.out_of_band_recorded` names `reporter` and is on no job's timeline (no `jobId`); the notifiers send it
as any other; its mark (`infra.out_of_band_marked`) is on no job's timeline either. The panel says who reported each
change: the job, or the collector. The change is a JSON row, so no migration: a change kept before names its job.
So a scheduled check needs no schedule in the hopper: whatever runs it on a schedule reports here. Tests: the collector's report, its
scope refused without it, its mark, in `test/integration/out-of-band.test.ts`; who reported, in `test/ui/out-of-band.test.ts`.

**Part 3: the ready-made collector (2026-10-12).** `scripts/out-of-band-collector.ts`, run by Node with no install
beyond the repository: a read-only check that runs the tools it is given read credentials for, turns what they print into
signals, and reports them. It classifies no action; the hopper's rule judges each signal. The pure half is
`src/domain/out-of-band-collect.ts`:
- `--argo`: `kubectl get applications.argoproj.io -A -o json`; each application `OutOfSync` is drift (key
  `argocd:<namespace>/<name>`, detail its revision and its out-of-sync resources).
- `--flux`: `kubectl get` the Kustomizations and HelmReleases; each one whose `Ready` condition is not `True` is drift by
  its reason, and each suspended one is drift as `Suspended`: a suspended object no longer puts back what git says.
- `--terraform <dir>` (one or more): `terraform init`, then `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode -lock=false` in that
  directory, which the schedule checks out at the default branch. Exit code 2 is drift (`what` its `Plan:` line, detail the
  plan text, its end kept when it is too long); 0 is none; any other is a failed source.
- `--cloudtrail <region>` (one or more): `aws cloudtrail lookup-events` with `ReadOnly=false`, from the last run; each
  write by `userIdentity.arn` (else the user name), `what` `<service>:<event name>`.
- `--kube-audit <file>`: the audit log as JSON lines; each write (`create`, `update`, `patch`, `delete`,
  `deletecollection`) at `ResponseComplete` that went through (below 400), from the last run, by `user.username`. For a
  managed control plane, the schedule exports its audit log to the file first (EKS: CloudWatch Logs).
- **Where it reports.** In a hopper job (`HOPPER_TOKEN_FILE` set): `POST /job/infra-signals` on `HOPPER_URL`, with the
  job's proxy token. Else, as an outside collector: `POST /ui/api/out-of-band/signals`, with an API token from a grant
  with the scope `out-of-band:signals`. Its refresh token is in the **state file** (`--state`), or the first time in
  `HOPPER_REFRESH_TOKEN`; each run trades it at `POST /ui/auth/token/refresh` and writes the new one to the state file
  (mode 600) before anything else, since the sent one is spent. More than 500 signals go in more than one report.
- **Since its last run.** The state file keeps when the last whole run started; the audit logs are read from then (else
  `--since`, else the last 24 hours). A source that fails is said on stderr and the run exits 1; the other sources still
  report, and the run's place does not move, so the next run reads the failed one again. A signal reported twice is kept
  once, so an overlap costs nothing.
- **The schedule** is outside the hopper: cron, a systemd timer, a Kubernetes CronJob with the state file on a volume
  (`docs/deploy.md` "The out-of-band collector"). The hopper still has no schedule for jobs; a job that runs the script
  reports as the job.
- `--dry-run` prints the signals and sends nothing.

Tests: `test/domain/out-of-band-collect.test.ts` (each tool's output as signals, each one whole),
`test/scripts/out-of-band-collector.test.ts` (fake tools and a fake hopper: the refresh kept, the job's route, a failed
source, the place kept), and the collector against the real daemon with a real grant in `test/integration/out-of-band.test.ts`.

**Residual risk, stated.** The hopper judges what a check reports; a check that does not report a write leaves it
untracked. A plan-bound credential's principal is in band for its whole life, so a write it made that the plan did not
hold is not out of band here: issue #870's residual risk. A shared Kubernetes service account (`hopper-apply`) is in band
for every write in a plan-bound token's life, whichever box made it.

Tests: `test/domain/out-of-band.test.ts` (the rule, the signal, the marks, the principal of a mint, pure),
`test/integration/out-of-band.test.ts` (the real daemon, a joined box, STS and GitHub faked: drift and a console write
recorded, each an event; a controller's write and the write of the credential minted for an approved plan in band;
nothing recorded twice; marks once; refusals), `test/plugins/grokbot-intake.test.ts` (the notification),
`test/ui/out-of-band.test.ts`.

## The Infra page (issue #896, 2026-10-12)

Before: plans (issue #870) and out-of-band changes (issue #871) were two panels at the bottom of Vault, and each
showed nothing when its list was empty or its read failed. The feature was invisible until a job recorded a plan.

- **A top-level view, `#infra`** (`ui/src/views/infra.tsx`), in the navigation between Machines and Usage, on par with
  Jobs. Vault keeps one line that links to it. Three panels:
  - **Plans** (`infra-plans.tsx`): each plan, its state and who it waits for (by its risk: "Infra plans: approval by risk"), an
    agent's confirmation ask (issue #909), its summary, Approve, the auto-approve switch, its applies, and the raw plan on demand.
  - **Applies and drift** (`infraTimeline`, `ui/src/model/infra-plans.ts`, pure): one list, newest first, of plans recorded
    and approved, applies, drift (`gitops`, `terraform-plan`), out-of-band writes (`cloudtrail`, `kube-audit`) and marks.
  - **Out-of-band changes** (`out-of-band.tsx`), as before.
- **Always shown.** The page reads `GET /api/infra-plans` and `GET /api/out-of-band` once. Each panel shows a loading line,
  an error that says why with **Try again**, or an empty list that says how a job fills it (`POST /job/infra-plans`,
  `POST /job/infra-signals`). Nothing hides on an error.
- **Applies** (`PlanApply`, `src/domain/infra-plans.ts`; `InfraPlans.applies`, `src/infra-plans/service.ts`).
  `GET /api/infra-plans` adds `applies`: each `vault.minted` event that names one of the listed plans, since the oldest of
  them, newest first: `plan`, `at`, `operation`, `asset`, `job`, `expiresAt`, `renewal`. Read from the event log, so no
  new table and no migration. Never the credential.
- **API.** The four routes are under the OpenAPI tag `Infra` (they were under `Vault`). A UI session and an API token read
  and act the same way: approve is a box action, by the plan's risk.

- **Badge.** The nav entry counts the plans that wait for a person to approve them (issue #897) and the out-of-band
  changes no one marked (`changesUnmarked`, `ui/src/model/out-of-band.ts`), read again after each `infra.out_of_band_*` event.

**Not built here.** A plan detail route of its own; live updates over the event stream (the page reads on open and on Try again).

Tests: `test/ui/infra-plans.test.ts` (who a plan waits for, the apply line, the timeline's order and words, empty),
`test/integration/infra-plans.test.ts` (an apply against an approved plan listed with it, and no credential in the answer).
## Infra plans: approval by risk (issue #870, part 3, 2026-10-12)

Who approves a plan follows its risk. Before this, an admin approved every plan, whatever it changed.

- **The approver** (`approverOf`, `src/domain/infra-plans.ts`, pure), read from the plan's summary each time it is shown or
  approved, never kept:
  - `operator`: a low-risk plan (`summary.level` `low`) whose every environment named is `uat`. The person who runs the
    jobs (an operator) approves it, or an admin. With **auto-approve** on, the hopper approves it itself when the job
    records it.
  - `admin`: any other plan. Prod, IAM and identity, destroys and data make a plan `high`; an admin approves it, as the
    blast-radius gate's Let through is an admin's act, after a confirmation that says what the plan changes and why. A
    low-risk plan in another environment, in uat and another, or in none named is an admin's too: the issue names uat
    alone. So is a plan kept before summaries.
  - `nobody`: a plan that failed a check (the MAP tag).
  Each comes with `why` in words: `low risk, in uat only`, `high risk: destroys, IAM and identity, prod`, `low risk, but
  not in uat only: in dev`.
- **Approve** (`POST /ui/api/infra-plans`) takes an operator now; the service (`approveRefusal`) answers a 403 that says
  why when the plan's approver is an admin and the session's role is not. Still a box action. An API token whose role
  may approve a plan that is not low risk still approves nothing: a person confirms it (issue #909, "A person confirms
  what an agent asks"). A token whose role may not gets the 403, and no person is asked.
- **Auto-approve** (`InfraPlanSettings { autoApprove }`, the user's settings key `infraPlans`, off by default):
  `POST /ui/api/infra-plans/settings` (admin, a box action: it approves work), `infra.settings_changed { from, to, by }`.
  On, `record` approves a plan whose approver is `operator` in the same transaction: an approval row of its own
  (`by` "the hopper", `auto: true`) and `infra.plan_approved` with `auto`. Nothing is silent: the plan is on Infra
  and on the job's timeline like any other, and the job's answer says it was approved.
- **Shown.** `GET /api/infra-plans` carries each plan's `approver` and the `settings`; the job's `POST` and `GET` answers
  say who approves the plan and why. Infra says who each waiting plan waits for, offers Approve only to a role that
  may, asks an admin to confirm a high-risk plan, says when the hopper approved a plan itself, and has the auto-approve
  switch (an admin's). `infra.plan_approved` carries `level` and `auto`.

**Why uat alone.** The owner's rule names low-risk uat. A low-risk plan in dev or staging is likely as safe, but widening
the rule is the owner's call; a second environment earns a setting.

**Not built here (the next parts of #870).** Notifications to environment watchers for every plan and apply; the nightly
drift plan; the terraform wrapper on write boxes; Argo CD syncs through the gate; the
check of a plan's `read` against the job's mints.

Tests: `test/domain/infra-plans.test.ts` (the approver of each kind of plan, and the role each needs),
`test/integration/infra-plans.test.ts` (an operator's box token approves a low-risk uat plan and is refused a prod plan,
a 403, which an admin then approves; with auto-approve on, a low-risk uat plan is approved as it is kept, the event says
`auto`, and it mints; a prod plan still waits; an operator cannot turn auto-approve on), `test/ui/infra-plans.test.ts`
(the waiting words, the auto-approved words, whom Approve is offered to, the confirmation).

## Infra plans: environment watchers (issue #870, part 4, 2026-10-12)

Every plan, approval and apply reaches the people who watch its environment. Before this, a plan and its apply were on
Infra and on the job's timeline, and a webhook subscriber got the events, but no notifier sent them: a person who did not
open Infra did not learn of a plan.

- **The environment watchers** (`InfraWatchers`, `src/domain/infra-watchers.ts`, pure; the user's settings key
  `infraWatchers`): for each environment a plan summary names (`prod`, `uat`, `staging`, `dev`, `qa`), and for every plan
  (`*`), names as the notifier's receiver knows them: a handle, a team, a channel. An admin names them on Infra, or
  `POST /ui/api/infra-plans/watchers { watchers }` (the whole list; one line, no comma, at most 50 an environment; kept
  trimmed, each name once, an environment with no name dropped; 400 for an environment the hopper does not know).
  `infra.watchers_changed { from, to, by }`. `GET /api/infra-plans` carries `watchers`. Not a box action: it approves no
  work.
- **A plan's watchers** (`watchersOf`): the watchers of `*`, then of each environment the plan names, each once. A plan
  that names no environment, or was kept before summaries, reaches the watchers of `*` only.
- **The notification** (`planNotice`, read through the notifier feed's `infraPlan(id)` at each send, so it names the
  watchers as they are then). The Grok Bot routine sends:
  - `infra.plan_recorded`: each plan a job records, a failed one too;
  - `infra.plan_approved`: each approval, a person's (`approvedBy`) or the hopper's (`auto`);
  - `infra.plan_applied`: each `vault.minted` that names a plan, which is an apply; not its renewal, which is the same
    apply going on, and not a read, which names no plan.
  Each body carries the plan (`plan`, `tool`, `asset`, `target`, `repo`, `ref`, `commit`, `pullRequest`), its `words`,
  `level`, `risks`, `environments`, `blastRadius` and `failed`, its `approver` (who and why), `watchers`, and `infraUrl`;
  an apply adds `operation` and `expiresAt`. Never the plan's text or file, the credential, or the box.
- Webhook subscribers get the same events as before (`infra.plan_recorded`, `infra.plan_approved`, `vault.minted`); the
  watchers are not in them.

**Why names, not addresses.** The hopper's notifier is one receiver (the Grok Bot routine) that already tells people; the
hopper keeps no address book and sends no mail. It says whom to tell, and the receiver tells them. A notifier that
delivers to people itself would read the same names.

**Why a separate settings key.** The auto-approve record stays `{ autoApprove }`, so a build before this, which writes that
record whole, does not drop the watchers.

**Not built here (the next parts of #870).** The nightly drift plan; the terraform wrapper on write boxes; Argo CD syncs
through the gate; the check of a plan's `read` against the job's mints.

Tests: `test/domain/infra-watchers.test.ts` (a plan's watchers, the list's checks, the notice and what it leaves out),
`test/plugins/grokbot-infra-plans.test.ts` (the three posts, each with its watchers; no renewal, no read),
`test/integration/infra-plans.test.ts` (an admin names the watchers and an operator cannot; through the real daemon, a
plan recorded, approved and applied is posted three times, each naming its watchers, never the credential or the plan's
text), `test/ui/infra-plans.test.ts` (the watchers as a person types them).

## Infra plans: the apply wrapper on write boxes (issue #870, part 5, 2026-10-12)

The issue asks that terraform apply only the saved plan file, and that a plan hold the read credential it was made with.
Before this, the apply gate bound a credential to a plan, but a box with that credential ran any `terraform apply` it
liked: of the saved file, of a fresh plan, or with `-target` or `-var`. And a plan's `read` was kept as the job said it.

- **The apply wrapper** (`TERRAFORM_APPLY_WRAPPER`, `src/sandbox/terraform-wrapper.ts`). Every tools image with terraform
  that is not read-only — a write box's — puts a `terraform` first on `PATH`, in `/opt/hopper-tools/apply-wrapper`, in
  front of the real binary in `/opt/hopper-tools/bin` (`$HOPPER_TOOLS`). A read-only image keeps the read-only wrapper
  ("A read-only infra box"); an image with no terraform gets neither.
  - `terraform apply` needs `HOPPER_PLAN`, the id the hopper answered when it recorded the plan. The wrapper fetches the
    plan's saved file from the hopper, with the job's proxy token (`GET /job/infra-plans/:id?file=1`, the route that
    already served it), and runs the real binary's `apply` with that file, then removes it. A plan file the caller names
    must be that file, by its SHA-256; it is applied in its place. No `HOPPER_PLAN`, an id the hopper does not know, a
    plan with no saved file, a job with no way to the hopper, or another file: refused, saying why, and the real binary
    does not run. In a need box (issue #1007, "Need steps"), which holds no proxy token, the hopper put the plan's saved
    file there, `HOPPER_PLAN_FILE`: the wrapper applies that file and fetches nothing; one it cannot read is refused.
  - An apply takes only the flags that leave the saved plan as it is: `-auto-approve`, `-input`, `-no-color`,
    `-compact-warnings`, `-json`, `-lock`, `-lock-timeout`, `-parallelism`. Any other flag (`-destroy`, `-target`,
    `-replace`, `-var`, `-var-file`, `-refresh-only`, `-state`, …) is refused: the job plans again with what it needs.
  - Each other command that writes infrastructure or state with no plan is refused: `destroy` (a destroy is a plan too:
    `terraform plan -destroy -out`), `import`, `refresh`, `taint`, `untaint`, `force-unlock`, `state rm`, `mv`, `push`
    and `replace-provider`, `workspace delete`. The rest (`init`, `plan`, `show`, `state pull`, `workspace select`, …)
    goes to the real binary as given. `TF_CLI_ARGS*` are cleared, so no flag slips past it.
  - Each refusal says `refused by the apply wrapper`. It is written into the image in base64 by one `RUN`, as the
    read-only wrapper is; the image's tag hashes the Containerfile, so a write box's image is built again once.
- **A plan's read credential** (`readRefusal`, `readProfileOf`, `src/domain/infra-plans.ts`, pure). A plan that names
  `read` is kept only when the vault minted that job a read credential of that profile (`vault.minted`, operation `read`,
  since the job was made): else a 400 that names what the vault did mint it. A plan that names none is kept as before: a
  job may plan with a vault secret.

**Why fetch the file, not trust the box's copy.** The plan the hopper keeps is the one a person approved and the notifiers
sent. The box's copy is the job's to change; fetched, the bytes applied are the bytes recorded.

**Why the vault stays the boundary.** The wrapper is one layer in the box, which the job controls: it can call
`$HOPPER_TOOLS/terraform` past it. The real binary gets a write credential only through the apply gate, for an approved,
current plan; the wrapper binds the command to the saved plan of that gate.

**The nightly drift plan** is the out-of-band collector (issue #871, "Out-of-band changes" part 3): `--terraform <dir>`
runs `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode` against live state, on a schedule outside the hopper (a nightly cron job, a
Kubernetes CronJob: `docs/deploy.md` "The out-of-band collector"), and a non-empty plan on unchanged code is drift, kept,
sent to the notifiers and shown on Infra. The hopper has no schedule for jobs, so it adds none here.

**Residual risk, stated.** The plan's `HOPPER_PLAN` and the plan the AWS profile's `--plan` names are both the job's to
set; the apply gate checks the credential's plan, the wrapper the file's. A job that calls the real binary past the
wrapper, with a credential minted for an approved plan, can still apply what its role allows for that credential's life:
part 1's residual risk. The summary is still read from the JSON the job sends, not made from the saved file.

**Not built here.** Routing Argo CD syncs through the same gate: the issue's next step after drift, issue #959.

Tests: `test/sandbox/terraform-apply-wrapper.test.ts` (a real `sh` and `curl`, a fake real binary and a fake hopper: an
apply with no plan refused; the saved file fetched with the job's token and applied, and removed; another file, an
unknown plan, a refused flag and each other write refused, the real binary not run), `test/sandbox/tools.test.ts` (a write
image puts the wrapper first on PATH; a read-only image and one with no terraform do not), `test/domain/infra-plans.test.ts`
(the read check), `test/integration/infra-plans.test.ts` (the real daemon: a plan naming a read the job was not minted is
a 400, and kept once the job was minted it).

## Infra plans: Argo CD syncs through the plan gate (issue #959, 2026-10-17)

Follow-up of issue #870. Before this, the apply gate held a terraform or helm apply, but an Argo CD auto-sync did not ask
the hopper: it applied what git said, and showed only as drift on Infra. The vault minted nothing for an `argocd-app`.

The issue gave two paths. **Taken: turn off auto-sync for a gated app, and sync it with a plan-bound `sync`
credential.** The other path — keep auto-sync and gate the merge to the branch Argo CD watches — needs the hopper to
write a status or a rule to GitHub ("GitHub text is neutral": the hopper writes only labels), and a merge on GitHub by a
person would still skip it.

- **A gated app** is an Argo CD Application with no automated sync (`spec.syncPolicy.automated` absent), labelled
  `io.hopper.plan-gate=true` (`ARGO_PLAN_GATE_LABEL`), whose sync only the service account `hopper-sync` in the
  namespace `argocd` may start (`docs/deploy.md` "Argo CD syncs through the plan gate"). The hopper changes no cluster:
  the operator sets this up.
- **A sync is minted only through the apply gate** (`mintTarget`, `src/domain/minting.ts`). `$HOPPER_SECRET kube sync
  argocd-app/<cluster>/<app> --plan <id>` mints a token of `hopper-sync` in `argocd` (`ARGOCD_NAMESPACE`) of that
  cluster, from the cluster's minting credential, after Access and the gate, as any other change: the plan is kept, of
  that app, not stale, not failed, approved, and made at the commit its branch is at now. Any other ask mints nothing and
  the cluster is not asked. `vault.minted` names the plan and the principal
  `system:serviceaccount:argocd:hopper-sync`, so the sync is an apply on Infra and a plan-bound write for the out-of-band
  rule.
- **An `argocd-app` takes sync only**, and names its cluster (`<cluster>/<app>`); `read`, `write` and `apply` are refused:
  read or change what it deploys through its cluster or namespace. Reads of an Argo CD app stay as they were (no read
  token for checks or need steps).
- **A plan for an `argocd-app` is a `gitops` plan** (`planInputProblem`): the `argocd app diff` its sync applies. A
  terraform or helm plan of one is a 400.
- **A gated app that syncs by itself is drift.** The collector's `--argo` (`argoSignals`, `src/domain/out-of-band-collect.ts`)
  reports each Application with the label and an automated sync policy: `what` `AutoSyncOnGatedApp`, key
  `argocd:<namespace>/<name>:auto-sync`. It is kept, sent to the notifiers and shown on Infra like any out-of-band change.

**Why a credential, not a sync by the hopper.** The vault is already the boundary for every change ("Infra plans: no apply
without a plan"); a sync is one more operation behind it, with no new route and no Argo CD credential in the hopper.

**Residual risk, stated.** As for any plan-bound credential, the `hopper-sync` token can, for its 10 minutes, sync what
its Role allows, at any revision: the gate binds the credential to the plan, not the sync to the plan's commit. A Role
limited to the gated app (`resourceNames`) keeps it to that app. A person or tool that Argo CD's own RBAC lets sync, or
someone who turns automated sync on again, skips the hopper: the collector reports the second as drift, and the first as
an out-of-band write when the Kubernetes audit log names a principal that is no controller identity. A sync from Argo CD's
UI or CLI writes as `argocd-server`: keep it out of the controller identities, so it is reported.

Tests: `test/domain/infra-plans.test.ts` (the sync target, sync only, the cluster named, a gitops plan, the gate with no
plan and with another app's plan), `test/domain/out-of-band-collect.test.ts` (a gated app with automated sync reported, a
gated one without and an ungated one not), `test/integration/infra-plans-argocd.test.ts` (the real daemon, a joined box, the
Kubernetes API and GitHub faked: a sync with no plan, an unapproved plan, another app's plan and a moved head mints
nothing and the cluster is not asked — the negative test of the issue's "Done when"; a terraform plan of the app is a
400; a current approved GitOps plan mints a `hopper-sync` token in `argocd`, the audit naming the plan).

## Infra applies off: changes through CI only (issue #1722, 2026-10-17)

Some installs apply infrastructure only in the infrastructure repository's CI, behind a GitHub environment approval. Their
sandboxes need fast read access to AWS and Kubernetes, and must never apply. Before this, the hopper always had a gated
apply path: an approved, current plan let the vault mint a write, sync or apply credential (no read deny policy for AWS,
a `hopper-<operation>` token for Kubernetes), and a need or box step with `--plan-id` ran the apply.

**Infra applies** is an instance setting, on by default (`getInfraApplies`, instance settings key `infraApplies`). The
hopper's admin turns it on or off on Infra (`POST /ui/api/infra-applies` `{ on }`, behind the instance guard); every
signed-in person reads it (`GET /api/infra-applies`). A change is `infra.applies_changed` (`on`, `by`), an instance event.
It is read at each ask, so a change applies at once.

Off:

- **The vault mints only reads** (`appliesRefusal`, `src/domain/infra-plans.ts`). A job's mint (`src/vault/mint.ts`) and a
  need step's mint (`src/vault/need-mint.ts`) refuse every operation but `read`, on any asset — an `aws-role`, a `cluster`,
  a `namespace`, an `argocd-app` sync —, plan or not. The refusal comes before Access and the apply gate, so no profile
  waits at the first-time gate for a change that cannot be minted. It is `vault.mint_refused`, and it says that the change
  goes through CI.
- **No step applies** (`APPLY_STEP_OFF`, `src/sandbox/need-steps.ts`). A need or box step with a plan, or with a need but
  read, is refused at its ask with a 409 and `step.refused`; no need box starts. A box step with no plan runs, minted its
  template's reads only, as before.
- **Read templates are unchanged.** Read sessions keep `ReadOnlyAccess` and the deny policy; read-only checks and mint
  tests mint reads only, as before.
- **Plans are still kept** and approved: a job can still record its plan for a person to read. Nothing can apply it while
  the setting is off; a credential minted before keeps its expiry (at most 15 minutes).

**Why an instance setting, not a user setting.** The policy is the operator's for the whole install: one user's toggle
could not keep another user's jobs from applying. **Why on by default.** An install that applies through the hopper keeps
working after the update; an install that wants CI only turns it off once.

Tests: `test/domain/infra-plans.test.ts` (the refusal for write, sync and apply; a read and the setting on let through),
`test/sandbox/need-steps.test.ts` (a step with a plan, one with a change need and a box step with a plan are refused and
no box starts; a read box step runs), `test/integration/infra-applies.test.ts` (the real daemon and a joined box: on by
default; off, a current approved plan mints nothing, STS is not asked and the refusal names CI; a read still mints; on
again, the apply mints; a bad body is 400).

## Git efficiency (issue #858 part 1, 2026-10-12)

The git half of issue #822. Before: a job in a work tree that was not its repository got a full `git clone` of it (in
`<work tree>/<name>`, or `.hopper-scratch/repos/<owner>/<name>`), and each job start ran a `git fetch` of every ref, with no
`--prune` and no filter. Nothing counted git fetches, and the GitHub API had lifetime counts only. Part 1 does steps 0 to 2
of the issue; steps 3 and 4 are later parts.

**GitHub traffic per sync pass** (step 0, `src/github-limiter/traffic.ts`). Measured first: each sync pass of a GitHub source
logs one line, `hopper: GitHub traffic of sync pass <source>: REST <n> (<route> <n>, …), GraphQL <n> (<read> <n>, …), git
fetches <n> (<owner/name> <n>, …; by job <job id's first 8> <n>, …)`.
- The shared limiter's hook counts every call it lets go (a deferred call is not made, so not counted): a REST call by method
  and Octokit's route template (`GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{issue_number}`), so one route is one count whatever the
  repository; a page link by its path without the query. A GraphQL call by the `GitHubApi` read or write that made it
  (`passReads` runs each in `traffic.read`), else its operation name, else its first two fields (`repository.issue`). A batched
  GraphQL request (`graphql-batch.ts`) counts once, under the read that scheduled it first.
- The git proxy counts each fetch that goes to GitHub, for its repository and its job: git asks for the refs once per fetch or
  clone (`GET info/refs?service=git-upload-pack`), so that ask is the fetch. A push is not a fetch. The fetch at a job's start
  goes through the proxy too, so it is counted.
- Which pass a call counts for is an `AsyncLocalStorage` context, as for the pass reads: two sources' passes at once count each
  its own. A call outside any pass (a job's git fetch, a job's own GitHub request, a GitHub watch) is counted "between passes",
  and the next pass that ends adds it to its line, once. A failed pass logs its line too.
- Counts only, in memory, logged and forgotten: nothing is kept, no event, no UI.

**The repository mirror** (step 1, `src/executors/herdr/job-worktree.ts`). One bare, blobless clone of each repository per
work tree: `<work tree>/.hopper-scratch/repos/<owner>/<name>.git` (`mirrorOf`), for a work tree that is no repository and for
one that is another repository's top alike. Made by `git clone --bare --filter=blob:none`; its branches are then moved from
`refs/heads/*` to `refs/remotes/origin/*`, `remote.origin.fetch` set to `+refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*`, and
`refs/remotes/origin/HEAD` to the default branch. So a job's worktree of it (`git worktree add --detach … origin/<default>`)
has the remote's branches where a clone has them: a branch the job pushes is `refs/remotes/origin/<branch>` in the mirror,
and the reap (`--not --remotes`) reads it as pushed. Blobs come on demand, when a worktree checks a file out. An extra job
adds only its worktree. The mirror's `origin` must be the job's repository; another is refused (`unmade`, "is not a mirror
of"). Cloned into `<mirror>.hopper-clone-<pid>` and moved in, so two jobs cloning at once leave one. The outcome is
`hopper-job-worktree-mirror` (replacing `checkout` and `other`), and `PaneState.checkout` names the mirror, which the
footer names as what the worktree is of. The old checkouts are no longer used; nothing removes them.

**Targeted fetch** (step 2). A job start that makes a worktree fetches the default branch only, pruned:
`git fetch --quiet --prune origin <default branch>` (the branch from `refs/remotes/origin/HEAD`), with `--filter=blob:none` in
a mirror. A repository that knows no default branch fetches as it is set up. The job's own branch is not fetched at the start:
it has none yet, and a run again finds its worktree and fetches nothing.

**Job rules.** The `[hopper job worktree]` line adds: fetch and push through the worktree's origin only; never clone the
repository again and never add a remote of your own, such as an ssh one. A clone over the job's own ssh remote went around
the hopper and left full clones behind.

**Not changed.** With job worktrees off (the print agents), a work tree that is no repository still gets the full checkout
`<work tree>/<name>`, and the job runs beside it: there is no worktree to make of a mirror. A work tree that is the job's own
repository is used as it is; only its fetch is targeted now.

**Left for later parts.** Step 3, one fetch per repository per sync pass (the daemon runs no git yet; a mirror on the
daemon's side, the broker answering fetches from it), with a job start skipping its fetch when the pass already fetched;
step 4, conflicts and mergeability from `git merge-tree --write-tree` and `git merge-base --is-ancestor` in place of GraphQL
`mergeable`. Both change only what the counts above show is hot. Part 2 below does them.

Tests: `test/github-limiter/traffic.test.ts` (through the real `makeRequest` and limiter against a fake GitHub: the line per
pass, routes per template, GraphQL per read, between passes once, two passes at once, a failed pass),
`test/sources/github-pass-reads.test.ts` (a read asked once is counted once, under its name),
`test/integration/git-proxy.test.ts` "counts each fetch of a job" (real git through the real proxy), `test/herdr/job-worktree.test.ts`
and `job-worktree-other-repository.test.ts` (real git, the origin served over a `file://` URL with blob filters allowed: the
mirror bare and blobless with its branches under `refs/remotes/origin`, a later job fetching the default branch only, an extra
job adding only its worktree, a pushed branch reaped as pushed, a mirror of another repository refused, worktrees off as
before), `test/herdr/executor-job-worktree.test.ts` (the mirror saved and named in the prompt with the new rule).

## Git efficiency, part 2 (issue #858, 2026-10-12)

Steps 3 and 4 of the issue. Before: whether a pull request had merge conflicts came only from GitHub's GraphQL `mergeable`,
which GitHub computes later: a pull request it had not computed yet read as mergeable, and a merge of it was tried and
refused. Each job start on a machine ran its own fetch, also when another start there had fetched a moment before.

**The hopper's mirror** (`src/git-mirror/mirrors.ts`). One bare, blobless git repository per job repository per user:
`<user's work dir>/git-mirrors/<owner>/<name>.git`. Per user, so no user's answer comes from objects fetched with another
user's credential. Made by `git init --bare` as a partial clone of `origin` (`extensions.partialClone`,
`remote.origin.partialclonefilter blob:none`), in `<path>.hopper-init-<pid>` and then moved in. Scratch only: a fetch makes
it again; nothing in it is the user's state.
- **One fetch per repository per sync pass.** The first question of a pass about a repository fetches it, and every later
  one in the pass waits on that fetch: `git fetch --quiet --prune --no-tags --filter=blob:none origin
  +refs/heads/<base>:refs/remotes/origin/<base> +refs/pull/*/head:refs/remotes/origin/pull/*`. `<base>` is the base of the
  pull request asked about first, in practice the default branch. `refs/pull/*/head` gives every pull request's head,
  a fork's too, with no API call to list them; a closed one's head never moves, so a later fetch moves only what changed.
  Which pass is the traffic count's pass id (`GitHubTraffic.passId`). The fetch is counted, `by hopper` in the pass line.
- **The credential.** The source's own: an installation token of the app, or the connected account's token
  (`GitHubApi.gitRemote`, each adapter's). Given to git in its environment as an `http.extraHeader`
  (`GIT_CONFIG_COUNT`), never on a command line, never logged. The remote is GitHub's web origin of the adapter's API base.
- **Conflicts from git.** `git merge-tree --write-tree refs/remotes/origin/<base> <head>`: exit 0 clean, 1 conflicts. A
  blob that git needs for a file both sides changed comes on demand from `origin`; a merge where only one side changed a
  file reads none.
- **Git cannot say**, and GitHub's answer stays: outside a sync pass; a fetch that failed (said once in the log, `hopper:
  git mirror of <repo>: …`, never the token); a pull request on another base than the one fetched; a head that is not the
  one the pass fetched (GraphQL `headRefOid`), so a push after the fetch is never answered from an old head; git failing.

**Git answers** (`src/sources/github/git-answers.ts`). A decorator of the `GitHubApi` port, under the pass reads
(`passReads(gitAnswers(adapter, mirrors))`), so a pass shares git's answer as it shares GitHub's: each open pull request
that `openClosingPullRequests`, `referencingPullRequests`, `pullRequest` and `openPullRequests` tell gets `conflicting` from
the mirror. The done-check (`completion.ts`), PR tending (`follow.ts`, `tending-queue.ts`) and the Pull requests list all
read through them, so all three take git's answer with no change of their own. The pull request reads ask GraphQL for
`headRefOid` and `baseRefName` too (`closer.ts`), fields of reads made anyway. `mergeable` stays in those reads as the
fallback; no call is made for it, then or before: it rides on reads the pass makes for drafts, checks and states.

**One fetch per pass at a job start** (`src/executors/herdr/job-worktree.ts` `passFetches`). A job start that fetched its
work tree's repository, on its machine, in the newest sync pass leaves the next start there nothing to fetch: the job
worktree command gets `$6` 0, and the worktree starts at what that fetch got. Keyed by machine, work tree and repository;
one per process, so every lane shares it. Before the first pass every start fetches. A mirror just cloned is not fetched
again either.

**Not done, and why.**
- **The broker answering fetches from the mirror.** A job's fetch is of its own machine's repository mirror, which a start
  fetches once per pass already; the hopper's mirror is on the daemon's machine. Answering git's smart HTTP from it means
  serving `upload-pack` in the daemon, for fetches the counts do not show as hot. Not built until they do.
- **Ancestry from `git merge-base --is-ancestor`.** No part of the hopper asks GitHub whether one commit is an ancestor of
  another, so there is nothing to replace.

Tests: `test/git-mirror/mirrors.test.ts` (real git, the origin over `file://` with its pull request heads at
`refs/pull/<n>/head`: clean and conflicting from merge-tree, the mirror bare and blobless, one fetch per pass and one more
in the next, nothing outside a pass, a head that moved, another base, a failed fetch said without the token),
`test/sources/github-git-answers.test.ts` (the port's four reads through the real pass reads take git's conflicts, the
repository fetched once in the pass; GitHub's answer outside a pass and with no git), `test/herdr/job-worktree.test.ts`
(a later start in the pass fetches nothing; the tracker by machine, work tree and repository).

## Needs you: one home per decision (issue #897, part 1, 2026-10-12)

Owner report: decisions that wait on a person lived in odd corners — request cards inside each source's card in Sources;
credential requests, vault grants and template approvals stacked at the bottom of Vault — and several panels
rendered nothing when empty, so a person could not tell the feature was there.

**As built:**
- **One home each.** Every decision that waits on a person has one top-level page, where it is acted on. A buried copy
  is removed or becomes a link to that page. Settings, Sources and the vault keep configuration.
- **Needs you.** `#needs-you`, the nav entry after the Dashboard (`ui/src/views/needs-you.tsx`): a row per kind — Intake, Access
  requests, Questions, Proposals, Research, Logins, Failures, the pre-sort — with its count, its high-priority count
  (#535) and a link to its home (`needsYouRows`, `ui/src/model/needs-you.ts`; `useNeedsYou`, `ui/src/store/needs-you.ts`).
  Its nav badge is the sum. Parked jobs have no row: they wait to be picked up, not for a decision; Parked keeps its
  quiet badge. It acts on nothing itself.
- **Intake.** `#intake` (it was Not taken, `#not-taken`, which still opens it): per source, every open labelled issue
  that waits on an intake decision, grouped by why, with Assign all; the request cards' one home. Since issue #1035 an
  issue that passed intake (taken, partly done, its pull request waits for review) is job progress, on Jobs: Intake lists
  none of them, only counts them in one line that links to Jobs, and says *Nothing waiting for intake* when none waits. A
  request declined there is no row either: one line counts them. Sources keeps each source's sync, the intake
  migration and the repos outside the job repositories, and links to Intake with its counts; it lists no issue and offers
  no Approve.
- **Access requests.** `#access-requests` (since issue #2374 the tab `#approvals/access-requests` of Approvals; `ui/src/views/access-requests.tsx`): Asked for (credential requests), Vault
  grants, and Template approvals (`template-approvals.tsx`: Approve, and Approve `<profile>` for a high-radius profile),
  plus a pointer to Users & access → API tokens for box tokens, and Bastions (issue #2146, "Bastions": each bastion of a job
  that runs now, with Stop). A template waits (`templateWaits`, `ui/src/model/vault.ts`) when
  it was never approved or a new image, secret or profile waits. A template a job asked for (`askedBy`) counts in the
  badge and the Needs you row while its job has not ended (issue #2196), and a high-priority job's template or sandbox run
  marks them (`accessRequestsHigh`) and comes first in its panel. Since issue #2197 both are one **run card** ("One
  approval per sandbox run"). Vault keeps Revoke, Check again, Edit and
  Remove, and links a waiting template here. The texts the hopper gives a job or a box for an approval or a grant name
  Access requests.
- **One vault read.** `useVault` (`ui/src/store/vault.ts`) keeps one copy of `GET /api/vault`, read when first used and
  again after each `vault.*` or `template.*` event (`rereadsVault`; issue #2196: a job's template request records only
  `template.saved`); the nav, Needs you, Access requests and Vault share it, and an edit's
  answer replaces it. A read that fails is no count; Access requests says why and still renders its panels.
- **Always rendered.** Needs you, Intake and each panel of Access requests render with nothing in them, and say what will
  show there.
- **API parity.** Every count is a read the UI makes with the same scopes — `/api/sources`, `/api/vault`,
  `/api/questions`, `/api/proposals`, `/api/research`, `/api/logins`, `/api/failures`, `/api/queue` — and every action is
  the `POST /ui/api/*` route the page uses (`help/needs-you.md`).

**Left for later parts:** a Needs you row for the plans that wait on the Infra page (issue #896), conflicted pull requests and machine joins
in Needs you, a global yolo indicator, and the duplicates of the question, decider and auto-park controls in Settings.

## Needs you, part 2: plans, conflicts, and yolo mode's one switch (issue #897, 2026-10-12)

**As built:**
- **Two more rows.** Needs you counts the Infra plans that wait for a person to approve them (`plansWaiting`, `ui/src/model/infra-plans.ts`:
  not approved, no failed check, not stale) and the open pull requests with merge conflicts (`conflictedPullRequests`,
  `ui/src/model/pull-requests.ts`). The Infra nav entry is badged with the first, Pull requests with the second (red), and
  the Pull requests header says how many conflict.
- **Shared reads.** `ui/src/store/polled.ts` keeps one copy each of `GET /api/pull-requests`, `GET /api/infra-plans` and
  `GET /api/yolo-mode` for the nav, Needs you and the header: read when first shown, every 30 seconds while shown, and again
  after a `job.pull_request_*` or `yolo_mode.*` event (a plan is recorded with no event). A failed read keeps the last answer.
  A page that reads or saves one itself (Pull requests, Settings → Yolo mode) puts its answer there.
- **Yolo mode in the header.** On every screen: `yolo off`, `yolo on`, or `yolo on: N of M repos` (`yoloIndicator`,
  `ui/src/model/yolo-mode.ts`), the summary as its title, a link to Settings → Yolo mode. An answer without the settings
  shows nothing, never off.
- **One switch.** Settings → Yolo mode is yolo mode's one switch. The per-repository switch on Pull requests is removed;
  each group keeps its yolo badge and links to Settings. The Queue cards keep their read-only badges.
- **No machine joins row.** A join code adds a machine at once: nothing waits for a decision. A machine whose box template
  waits for approval is counted in Access requests.

**Left for later parts:** the duplicates of the question, decider and auto-park controls in Settings, and Settings → Your
reports and Question history, if they stay actionable.

## Needs you, part 3: Settings keeps configuration only (issue #897, 2026-10-12)

**As built:**
- **Decider picks on Decisions.** The newest picks, each with Override, left Settings → Decider for the Decisions page, in
  a panel that always renders (`DeciderPicks`, `ui/src/views/minor-decisions.tsx`). Settings → Decider keeps the decision
  points, the TypeSafe API key, and a link to Decisions. Both read `GET /api/minor-decisions`; no route changed.
- **Question history on Questions.** It holds Correct, so it left Settings for a section of Questions:
  `#questions/history`, a tab beside the open questions. `#questions` alone still holds only the open questions (#151).
- **Your reports is its own view** (`#reports`; since issue #2374 the user menu links to it, with no nav entry). It holds no decision, but it is no configuration either.
- **Old links.** `#settings/history` and `#settings/reports` are replaced by their new hashes (`LEFT`,
  `ui/src/views/settings.tsx`).
- **No duplicates found for auto-park or the issue thread.** Auto-park and the issue thread are configuration, set only in
  Settings; Parked and Questions show a job's state (`ThreadState`), not their settings. The phase-shift settings on
  Questions and the failures settings on Failures are configuration with one home each, so they stay.

## Direct jobs (issue #901, part 1, 2026-10-12)

Requirement: customer support and account work (the first use: a locked-out customer's one-time-password lookup and fix)
runs through the hopper with no GitHub issue behind it. Customer details do not belong on GitHub.

**A direct job** is a submission a person makes straight to the hopper: a `title`, a `brief` (what to do), routing
`labels` (`sme:identity`), `authorizations` (what the submitter authorizes it to do or reach, each in their words), an
optional `repo` (`owner/name`, the one repository its work may open a pull request on), an optional `executor` (default
`herdr-claude`, the GitHub source's default too) and `priority` (default 50). It is kept as a record in the user's schema
(tenant migration 49, `direct_jobs`, the body as JSON), with `submittedBy` (the person and the way: `ui`, `api`, `cli`)
and `submittedAt`.

**Its job comes from a job source.** The `direct` job source (`src/direct-jobs/`) is the core's own, beside the plugin
sources: one per user, always on, named and of kind `direct`. Not a plugin: it holds no outside connection to configure,
and a plugin would need the user's store in its context. `POST /ui/api/direct-jobs` keeps the record, appends
`direct_job.submitted` and calls the source host's `ingest` with the item, in one transaction: so the job is queued from
the source `direct` (key `direct:<id>`), through the same queue gate, routing rules, lane caps, blast radius, vault, vault
grants and infra plan rules (#870) as any job. The routing rules match its labels and the source name `direct`, so a rule
sends `sme:identity` work to the seat or the sandbox box it names. The source's `discover` answers nothing (its items come
only through the route); `check` signals nothing; `report` keeps what was reported on the job and sends it nowhere;
`rerun` answers the same submission, so Run again runs it again.

**Trusted origin.** Its item is of a trusted origin: a person submitted it, through the UI session, the operator CLI, or a
**box token** — the route is a box action (`BOX_ACTIONS`, kind `start a job`), so an API token that is no box token is
refused (403), and a box token is one a person minted from a UI session (issue #881). Least role: operator.

**Private.** The job's prompt starts with the private line (`PRIVATE_LINE`): its brief and results stay in the hopper;
write none of them to GitHub or anywhere else; open a pull request only when the brief asks for a change to `repo`, and
then in neutral terms. Then the brief, then the context block: the labels, the authorizations ("do nothing that needs an
authorization not on this list: ask instead"), who submitted it and when, the repository or none, and what done means
(the job's last report is its result). Its environment has `HOPPER_DIRECT_JOB` and, with a repository, `HOPPER_REPO`. A
job with no repository has no repository the git proxy pushes to. `direct_job.submitted` carries the id, who, the way,
the labels, the authorizations and the repository — never the title or the brief.

**Reading back.** `GET /api/direct-jobs` (newest first) and `GET /api/direct-jobs/:id` answer the record and its newest
job: `status`, `result`, `error`, `finishedAt`, and its open `questions` (`id`, `text`, `tier`, `askedAt`). A requester
answers a question with `POST /ui/api/questions/:id/answer`, as any question. The notifiers tell of its questions and its
end as of any job's. The operator CLI: `hopper job submit --title … (--brief … | --brief-file …) [--label …]...
[--authorize …]... [--repo …] [--executor …] [--priority …]` and `hopper job direct [<id>]`.

**Residual risk, stated.** `job.queued` carries the job's spec, and so its prompt — the brief —, as for every job: a
webhook subscription to `job.queued` delivers it to the subscriber. The authorizations are told to the job and recorded;
the one that makes a vault grant is part 3, below.

**In the UI (part 2).** The view Direct jobs (`#direct-jobs`; since issues #2375 and #2374 the Run a job tab of Ask hopper, `#ask/direct-jobs`, in the Work nav group; `ui/src/views/direct-jobs.tsx`,
`ui/src/model/direct-jobs.ts`) has the submit form, for an operator or admin only: title, brief, labels (split at commas),
authorizations (one per line), repository and priority. It sends `POST /ui/api/direct-jobs` through the UI session, so the
record says `via: ui`. Below it, every direct job from `GET /api/direct-jobs`, read when shown and every 15 s: its state
(its job's status, or how many questions wait), who submitted it and the way, its labels and authorizations, its open
questions with a link to Questions, where a person answers them, its result and its error, and a link to its job view.
A viewer reads the list and gets no form. Nothing the view sends goes to GitHub.

**The vault authorization (part 3).** The authorization `vault` (`VAULT_AUTHORIZATION`) is the submitter's **vault
grant** ("Vault grants") for the direct job's item, `direct:<id>`. The route fixes the id first, and Access decides the
grant for that item as for Grant on Vault: OpenFGA `vault_grant#can_grant` for the person signed in, the user
whose jobs these are as `owner`. Refused: 403; OpenFGA not asked: 503. Either way nothing is kept: no record, no
`direct_job.submitted`, no job. Allowed: the submit's one transaction also keeps the grant (`by`: the submitter, `job`: its
first job) and appends `vault.granted { job, key, by }`, so the audit names who authorized the vault, as for a person's
Grant. Run again keeps it (the grant is the item's); Revoke on Vault takes it back. The template's approved
scope still bounds what the job gets, and the job's box still asks through the vault's checks: the grant widens nothing.
Its prompt says `vault: granted by the submitter`, or `vault: not granted`. Every other authorization stays words told to
the job and recorded: the hopper has no grant to make of them. Why one reserved word, and no field of its own: a vault
grant is per item, never per secret ("Vault grants", residual risk), so the submitter's choice is yes or no, and the
authorizations list is where the submitter already says what the job may reach.

**The submitter by name (part 4).** Every Grok Bot routine notice about a direct job's job — its question at the human,
its end (`job.finished` with the result, `job.failed` with the error), a login it waits on, an artifact it made, a plan of
an infrastructure change — carries `directJob` (the id) and `submitter` (the person who submitted it: the job's source
`author`, the record's `submittedBy.person`), so the receiver tells that person, and an agent reads the result back with
`GET /api/direct-jobs/:id`. A job of any other source carries neither. Why the notifier, and no channel of the hopper's
own: the hopper holds no address of a person (no mail, no chat id), and a notifier is already where the hopper tells
someone outside; the receiver maps the name to its own channel. In the hopper, the submitter reads the job back in Direct
jobs, as before. Residual risk, stated: as for every job, the notice carries the title (`issueTitle`) and, at the end,
the result; a person who configures the routine trusts its receiver with them, as with `job.queued` above.

## Direct queries (issue #2184, parts 1 and 2, 2026-10-19)

Requirement: a caller (the first one: Grok Bot) asks the hopper an off-the-cuff question — "where does the otel collector
run?" — with no GitHub issue. A job that only looks answers it, with the same seats, sandboxes, vault and approval rules as
any job, and the hopper sends the answer back to a webhook of the caller's.

**A direct query is a direct job with a `query`** (`DirectQuery`, `src/domain/direct-jobs.ts`): the record, the `direct`
job source, the queue gate, the routing rules, the lane caps, the reads and Run again are the direct job's ("Direct
jobs"). What a query adds:

- **The request.** `POST /ui/api/direct-queries { requestId, question, callback?, mode?, repos?, clusters?, labels?,
  executor?, priority? }` (operator; a box action, kind `start a job`, so an API token must be a box token). Behind the
  hopper's normal sign-in: from outside only through the public URL or remote access while an admin has it on.
  - `requestId`: the caller's own id. The query's id is its hash (`directQueryId`, `query-<32 hex>`), so the same request id
    again answers the query kept, `replayed: true`, and makes no record, event or job; with another question or callback,
    409. A retry of a request whose answer was lost is safe.
  - `question`: the brief. The title is its first line, at most 120 characters.
  - `callback`: the name of an active **webhook subscription** (400 when none is named so). See "The callback" below.
  - `mode`: `look`, the default. `change` is refused (422): a change goes through a direct job or an issue.
  - `repos`, `clusters`: where to look first. Told to the job as hints; they allow nothing.
  - `labels`: routing labels beside `direct:query` (`DIRECT_QUERY_LABEL`), which every query's job has, so a routing rule
    sends queries to the seat or the sandbox box it names.
- **Look only.** The job's prompt starts with `QUERY_LINE` (`src/direct-jobs/item.ts`): the question and the answer are
  private; look only; change no code, infrastructure or secret; push nothing, open no pull request, file no issue, write
  no comment; ask the vault and the sandbox only for reads; no port-forward, proxy or tunnel; when the answer needs a change,
  end failed and say what a person must file. The rules are enforced where the hopper can enforce them, not only told:
  - the job's environment has `HOPPER_DIRECT_QUERY` (`DIRECT_QUERY_ENV`); `isDirectQuery` reads it from the job's spec;
  - the GitHub proxy refuses every op that is no read (`isRead`) for such a job, 403 with `LOOK_ONLY`
    (`checkRequest`, `ProxyAsker.lookOnly`), recorded as `github_proxy.refused`;
  - the git proxy refuses every push, at the ref advertisement already (`LOOK_ONLY`);
  - the record has no `authorizations`, so no vault grant is made at submit, and no `repo`.
- **Where it stands** (`directQueryState`, from its newest job): `accepted` (no job at work yet), `running`, `waiting` (a
  question or its own wait: it comes back through Questions, and the Grok Bot notifier names the direct job, as for any
  direct job; a question that reaches a person goes to the callback too, below), `answered`, `failed` (also a job turned
  away at the queue gate), `cancelled`.
- **Reading back.** `GET /api/direct-queries` (newest first) and `GET /api/direct-queries/:requestId`: the direct job's view
  with `query` and `state`; the answer is `job.result`, the evidence the job's `artifacts`. A caller polls this. To cancel,
  it cancels the job, `POST /ui/api/jobs/:id/cancel`, as any job.
- **Where the answer and evidence are kept.** In the hopper only: the record (`direct_jobs`), the job, its timeline and its
  artifacts (`OUTPUTS_LINE` asks for them). Nothing goes to GitHub. A person can promote a finished query to GitHub as any
  direct job ("Promote to GitHub").
- **Its UI home** (part 2): the Direct queries view (`#direct-queries`, `ui/src/views/direct-queries.tsx`; since issues #2375 and #2374 the Ask
  a question tab of Ask hopper, `#ask/direct-queries`, beside Run a job), not in Settings. It lists each query, newest first: where it stands, who asked it and the way,
  its callback, its hints, its open questions (a link to Questions), its answer, its error and its evidence (the job's
  artifacts). An operator asks a question there (a request id the page makes, `ui-<32 hex>`, from
  `crypto.getRandomValues`: a LAN page over plain HTTP has no `randomUUID`), and cancels a query whose job is not at an
  end. The Direct jobs view leaves direct queries out (`onlyDirectJobs`): each lives in one place.

**The callback.** The events of a query: `direct_query.accepted` (in the submit's transaction, never the question),
`direct_query.answered` (`answer`, the job's result; `artifacts`, links that need a hopper sign-in; `url`),
`direct_query.failed` (`error`), `direct_query.cancelled` and `direct_query.question_asked` (part 2: `questionId`, `question`,
`answerUrl`), each with `id`, `requestId` and `callback`. The ends are
appended by the `direct` source's report, once per job and end (`queryEnded`). A question is appended when it reaches the
human stage, once per question, in the transaction of its `question.escalated_to_human` (the question service's
`onToHuman`, `DirectJobs.questionAsked`); a question a level answers never goes out. The caller answers it with
`POST /ui/api/questions/:id/answer`, as a person does in Questions: a box action, so its API token is a box token, as for the ask. The webhook dispatcher delivers an event
whose `callback` names a subscription to that subscription too, whatever events it lists (`matches`,
`src/webhooks/dispatcher.ts`). So the callback is a webhook delivery: signed with the subscription's own signing secret,
kept sealed in the vault (`x-hopper-signature`, "Webhooks"), at least once, deduped by `x-hopper-delivery`, retried with
backoff, kept across a restart, through the outbound guard and into the send log ("Outbound sends").

**Decisions:**
- **The callback names a webhook subscription, not a URL.** A URL per request would let any API token holder make the
  hopper post to a host of its choice — an outbound destination nobody approved, and a way out for the answers. A
  subscription is a person's, made through the UI session, with its secret in the vault and its sends guarded. A caller
  that needs another URL asks a person to add a subscription.
- **A webhook delivery, not a saga of its own.** A delivery is already a durable record with a key, attempts, a backoff and
  a claim that two hosts share ("Sagas: work that survives a stop" asks no more of a single POST). A second outbox for
  one POST would be one more to keep.
- **A direct job, not a record of its own.** The record, its job source, its reads and its promotion are the direct job's;
  a query adds a field to its JSON body, so no migration, and the build before reads the record as a direct job.
- **`change` is refused, not turned into an issue.** Filing an issue for an agent would make a job of a request nobody
  trusted ("Trusted origin"); the caller, or a person, submits a direct job or files the issue.

**Residual risk, stated.** A webhook subscription that lists `direct_query.answered` or `*` gets every query's answer, as one
that lists `job.finished` gets every result. The proxies refuse a query's writes on GitHub; the vault and the sandbox
refuse writes only as for any job: a write template waits for a person's grant, and the standing read grant gives reads
only. A person who grants a query's job a write template widens it.

**Not done yet (later parts):** the Direct queries view, a top-level home in the UI (list, state, answer, evidence);
a question at the human sent to the callback too.

**Verification:** `test/integration/direct-queries.test.ts` (a box-token caller asks, a look-only job answers, the callback
gets `accepted` and `answered`, signed, with no GitHub call; the same request id replayed and a conflict; a failed query's
callback; `change`, an unknown callback and a plain API token refused, nothing kept), `test/direct-jobs/direct-query.test.ts`
(the prompt, the marker, the id, the state, the GitHub proxy's and the git proxy's refusals).

## Direct jobs: its pull request (issue #1068, 2026-10-16)

Requirement: a direct job that opens a pull request on its repository gets the same care as a job of an issue: the
hopper shows it in Pull requests, tends it (rebase, fix checks), and merges it in yolo mode. Before, the `direct` source
had no `JobSource.follow`, and a person handled the pull request on GitHub.

- **Which pull request.** The one the job opened on its repository through the hopper's GitHub proxy: the newest
  `github_proxy.done` of op `pr.create` on the job's timeline whose `repo` is the direct job's (`openedPullRequest`,
  `src/domain/direct-jobs.ts`). A tend job opens none: it follows the pull request it was handed (`tendOf`). The `direct`
  source's report of a job that ended done keeps it, `pullRequest` and `follow: open`, as a GitHub source's report does.
  A job that opened none follows nothing. Why the proxy's record, not a branch push the git proxy recorded: a push names
  a branch, not a pull request, and the job opens its pull request through the proxy in any case — no job holds a GitHub
  token (issue #652).
- **Whose connection.** The user's own connected GitHub account, the one the job's proxy acted with (issue #1380):
  `createDirectPullRequests` (`src/sources/compose.ts`) builds the follow, the merge gate (`mergesOnReady`), the tend
  note (`tendStarted`) and the failed checks' logs (`checkLogs`) over it, with the user's yolo mode, landing branches and
  change rules (`pullRequestSettings`, `src/users/source-context.ts`). The `direct` source takes them as a port
  (`DirectPullRequests`): `src/direct-jobs/` knows no GitHub. While no account is connected, a follow throws and is
  asked again at a later sync, and nothing is merged.
- **The follow** (`followDirectPullRequest`, `src/sources/github/direct-follow.ts`). It reads the pull request only.
  Merged or closed on GitHub: it ends there. Open: what is seen of it is kept, it is moved to the landing branch or closed
  as superseded (issue #1143), and the hopper merges it once ready when its change kind's gate allows — yolo mode on for its
  repository, or a kind merged with no person (issue #1076). A direct job has no issue, so the merge closes nothing, and no
  issue is read, labelled or commented on.
- **Tending.** The sync loop's after done is the same as for any source (`src/sources/after-done.ts`): a pull request seen
  with merge conflicts or failing checks runs its item again with the tend brief (`JobSource.rerun`, the same submission
  again), and the tend job pushes to the same branch.
- **In Pull requests.** A direct job's card has no `issue`; it has `directJob`, the link to its direct job view, shown as
  "direct job". It has no Merge now, Close PR or Send back for rework: those go through a GitHub source's outbox (issue
  #1238), which the `direct` source has not. A person does those on GitHub.

**Verification:** `test/sources/github-direct-follow.test.ts` (open and kept, merged by yolo mode, failing checks kept,
merged or closed by a person, nothing followed), `test/direct-jobs/pull-request.test.ts` (the opened pull request kept to
follow, none for another repository, a tend job's handed pull request, no follower), `test/sources/pull-request-list.test.ts`
(a direct job's card), `test/ui/pull-requests-view.test.ts` (its link, and no Merge now or Close PR).

## Checkpoints and resume elsewhere (issue #921, 2026-10-12)

Split from #919. When a machine drops, the job's agent session and the work it did not push were lost with it, and a
parked job could resume only on the machine it was parked on. Now the hopper copies both off the machine while the job
runs, and a parked job with such a copy can resume on any machine.

- **The checkpoint.** A job at work (`running`, `waiting_answer`, `waiting_on`) whose executor has `checkpoint` —
  herdr-claude, for a job with an agent session and a job worktree of its own — is checkpointed every ten minutes
  (`CHECKPOINT_EVERY_MS`, a pass each minute, one at a time; a machine that cannot be reached is asked again at the next
  interval, not each pass), and once more when it is parked, after `Executor.park` ended its agent, so the session is
  whole (`releaseParked`). One more at a **missed heartbeat** of its machine (issue #1569, "The lost-machine move"), at
  most once a minute. No setting: the interval is fixed.
- **Read on the machine, never through the pane.** `MachineShell.checkpoint(jobId, worktree, session)` runs the fixed
  script of `src/client/checkpoint.ts` through the machine's own connection: this machine, ssh, or a client target's
  `POST /checkpoint` (a client older than it answers 404: no checkpoint, as for a missing `/reach`). The worktree must be
  the job's own — `.worktrees/<name>/<job id>` or in its scratch dir, or, for a job that started before issue #1188 and
  still runs, its place in the layout before (`.hopper-scratch/<job id>/…`, `workspace/worktrees/<name>-<job id>`, issue
  #1353) — and the session id plain, or it is refused. A refusal or a failure on the machine is said as the machine said
  it, never as a machine not reached. The script only reads: an index of its own
  (`GIT_INDEX_FILE`, so the job's index is never locked; `GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0`; no fetch, no prompt) takes the work tree
  as it is, untracked files too, a `node_modules` link to shared dependencies left out. The **base** is the job's branch
  as pushed when HEAD holds it, else where HEAD left the default branch, else HEAD: always a commit the remote has. It
  prints the branch, the base, HEAD, the commits after the base (50 at most), the patch from the base to that tree
  (`git diff --binary`) and the agent session's file (`<config>/projects/*/<session>.jsonl`, the config `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`
  or `~/.claude`), gzip and base64. More than 10 MiB compressed is no checkpoint (`too large`): the output stays under the
  16 MiB a script may print.
- **Scrubbed, then kept.** The hopper unpacks each part and masks secrets before it keeps anything
  (`src/secrets/mask.ts`): in the session log, every string of each JSON line, so each line stays JSON its agent reads;
  in the patch, only the lines it adds — a context or removed line is the base's, and masking it would keep the patch from
  applying. `maskSecrets`: GitHub tokens, 32-byte keys (which covers a job's proxy token and the hopper's own), private
  key blocks, AWS access key ids, Anthropic and OpenAI keys, Slack tokens. And by value (issue #1957) each vault secret the
  vault delivered to the job — the user's own and the shared ones its delivery events (`vault.delivered`,
  `vault.step_delivered`) name, read now as a delivery reads them (`Vault.deliveredTo`, `src/vault/delivered.ts`; in the
  vault container, the wire op `delivered-to`) —, as `[vault secret, masked]`: a vault secret has no pattern. The patch is read as bytes (`latin1`), so a file
  in any encoding comes back as it was. The latest checkpoint is kept, compressed, in the user's schema
  (`job_checkpoints`, tenant migration 48: a table only, the build before runs on it); what it is — when, where, the
  branch, base, HEAD, the commits not pushed, its size, whether it holds the session — is `job.checkpoint`, and
  `job.checkpointed` says one was taken. A checkpoint the same as the last one kept — the same branch, base, HEAD, commits,
  machine, patch and session (issue #1975: a job that waits changes nothing) — is not kept again and records no event; the
  take answers the one kept. A checkpoint goes a week after its job ended (`CHECKPOINT_KEEP_MS`).
- **Resume elsewhere.** `POST /ui/api/jobs/:id/requeue` `{elsewhere: true}` (least role `operator`, as Pick up), for a
  parked job whose checkpoint holds its agent session (`elsewhereRefusal`, else 409). Its question, proposal or research
  report must be answered first (409): the claim resumes the agent with the answer, never to wait on it again elsewhere.
  It is queued with the answer pending, `resumeOn` cleared — a pin of its spec (a person's, a routing rule's) stays —,
  `parked.elsewhere: { at, checkpointAt, from }` set and `job.unparked { to: queued, elsewhere: true }`. This relaxes the rule
  above that a parked job resumes only on its machine; a plain Pick up still does.
- **The claim.** `Executor.resume` with `job.parked.elsewhere` set (herdr-claude's `relocate`): on the machine the job got, a new
  pane in that machine's work tree for it, a new job worktree of its repository as for any start, then — before shared
  dependencies are linked — the restore command (`restoreCommand`), typed into the pane's shell, which has the job's way
  to the hopper (a machine that runs its jobs without the hopper's proxy cannot restore one: the job fails, saying so). With
