  no way to the hopper in that pane (issue #2316: `HOPPER_URL` not set, or its token file not readable after a wait of a few
  seconds), the restore prints `hopper: the job has no way to the hopper: <what is missing>`, and the job leaves that machine
  by the no-way move below (issue #2355; a new pane on the same machine got none either). When it cannot move, it fails
  with that line, the known cause `no-way-to-hopper` (transient, retry), never a hand-off with no known cause. It gets the checkpoint's parts from the hopper (`GET /job/checkpoint/patch` and `/session`, with the
  job's proxy token), checks out the base on the job's branch (fetched through the hopper when it is not there), applies
  the patch as uncommitted changes, and puts the session file where Claude finds it for that directory
  (`projects/<the directory, each character not a letter or digit a dash>`). A worktree that holds changes already is the
  job's own work there (it came back to a machine it ran on) and is kept as it is (`kept`). Then `claude --resume
  <session>`, and the agent is sent `elsewhereBrief` (`src/engine/park.ts`): it moved, from which checkpoint, its new work
  tree, the commits not pushed then — uncommitted changes now, to commit again —, that work after the checkpoint is lost,
  then the answer. A restore that fails fails the job, with what the shell said. The next outcome clears it with `parked`.
  **A patch that does not apply whole** (issue #2428: a job failed with `the patch did not apply`) does not fail the job:
  the restore applies it file by file (`partly`), each file it cannot apply keeps the base's content and is said on a line
  `hopper: left out <file>`, and the whole patch is kept in the worktree's git dir (`hopper-checkpoint.patch`, the list
  in `hopper-checkpoint.patch.left-out`), where `git add` never takes it. The job's progress names the files; the agent
  is told first (`restoredInPartNote`, `src/client/checkpoint.ts`) which files are not in its work tree and where the
  patch is, so it makes those changes again.
- **The no-way move** (issue #2355, `src/engine/no-way-move.ts`). A job picked up to resume elsewhere found no `HOPPER_URL`
  in its pane on a lane pod, and each new pane there had none either: it ended failed, "claude did not start in 3
  attempts", while a fresh start of its item ran on the same machine. Nothing of the job runs on that machine before its
  restore, so it now goes back to the queue — its answer, agent session and checkpoint kept, `job.requeued` with
  `no way to the hopper there` in its reason — and that machine is held for ten minutes as the reach check holds one
  (`reach-holds.ts`, its address problem says why). The cases: the restore's no-way line (the executor's failure says
  `noWayToHopper`), a reach check that finds the machine out of reach, and a machine that gives the job no way to the
  hopper at all (`placeCredentials`: no URL its jobs reach the hopper at there, or no shell; before, the pane opened with no
  `HOPPER_URL` and no word of why). The pane's screen goes on the job's timeline as progress, the evidence of what that
  machine lacked. A job that resumes elsewhere holds no pane on any machine, so the decider holds it off a machine a person
  drained and one with an address problem, as a new job (`opensPane`, `src/decider/assign.ts`); a job that resumes in its
  own pane still returns there. After three such moves (`MAX_NO_WAY_MOVES`) it fails as before.
  **The remote out of reach** (issue #2639). A restore during a network outage could not fetch its checkpoint's base, said
  `the checkpoint's base … is not on the remote`, and failed; the failure assessor ran its item again as a new job, so
  the work after the last push, the session and the job's approvals were lost. The restore now asks the remote
  (`git ls-remote origin HEAD`) when the base is not fetched: when the remote does not answer, it prints
  `hopper: the remote is out of reach: …` (`RESTORE_REMOTE_OUT_OF_REACH`, the executor's failure says `remoteOutOfReach`),
  and the job goes back to the queue as above — `the remote out of reach there` in its reason, counted apart from the
  no-way moves, three at most — and that machine is held for ten minutes, so the same checkpoint is restored after the
  hold, on that machine or another. A base the remote answers without is not on it: the job fails as before.
- **The route.** `GET /job/checkpoint/:part` (`src/http/job-checkpoint.ts`) serves only the job's own checkpoint, only
  while it runs resuming elsewhere: 401 a token that is no running job's, 409 a job not resuming elsewhere now, 404 a part
  it does not hold. It changes nothing and records nothing.
- **UI.** The Parked row says when its last checkpoint was taken, and offers **Resume elsewhere**, confirmed (it says from
  which checkpoint, the commits not pushed, and that later work is lost); disabled while its question waits on an answer.
  The job view shows the checkpoint: when, where, its size, the commits not pushed.
- **What it does not do.** A job whose machine dropped while it ran is not parked by itself; a person parks it (the park
  takes no new checkpoint when its machine cannot be reached: the last one stands) and resumes it elsewhere. A failed job
  does not resume elsewhere. What the job left on the old machine stays there until the sweep finds its job ended.

## The token ledger (issue #2302, 2026-10-21)

Owner request: the hopper read each Claude account's session and weekly usage, but not which work used the tokens. Now it
keeps what each job's agent spent, read from the agent session's own log, and never from its terminal.

- **Where it reads.** The session log a checkpoint copies (`<config>/projects/*/<session>.jsonl`, "Checkpoints and resume
  elsewhere") has a `usage` block on each assistant message: input, output, cache-read and cache-write tokens (and the part
  written to the one-hour cache), with the model. That is the data ccusage reads. `sessionTokenUse`
  (`src/domain/token-usage.ts`, pure) counts each message once — a message is written again as it streams, so the last line
  of each message id and request id wins —, never a `<synthetic>` one, and sums them per model.
- **When.** At each checkpoint: the scrub worker (`checkpoint-scrub.ts`) unpacks the session anyway, and counts it before it
  scrubs it. And once more as a run ends (`Checkpoints.tokens`, the job run's `end` step, before its outcome is recorded):
  the same read on the machine, count only — nothing is scrubbed or kept but the counts —, so the last turns are in. A lost
  machine is not asked. A job that resumes elsewhere carries its session file, so the next read is the whole session again.
- **What it keeps.** `job_token_use` (tenant migration 89, `src/store/token-ledger.ts`): one row per job, agent session and
  model — the counts, the assistant messages (`turns`), the first and last counted message, when it was read, the machine
  and lane it was read on, and the **last account** of that machine's Claude then (the label only). A session read again
  replaces its rows: the log only grows. Counts and metadata only: no text of the session, as the acceptance asks.
- **Estimated cost.** `estimatedCostUsd`: the model's list price per million tokens (input, output, cache read), a cache
  write 1.25 × input (2 × to the one-hour cache). A model the list does not know has no estimate: its share counts nothing,
  and the total says `costKnown: false`.
- **Reads.** `GET /api/jobs/:id/tokens` (`JobTokenView`): a job's totals, per model, its sessions, machines and accounts.
  `GET /api/usage/tokens` (`by` job, issue, repo, machine, lane, account, model or day; `job`, `repo`, `since`): the user's
  ledger summed per group, the costliest first, with the top spenders. `hopper usage tokens [--repo|--since|--by]` and
  `hopper usage tokens --job <id>` read them. The job view shows a **Tokens** panel.
- **Tokens over time** (part 2). `split` (one of the same groups) gives each group `parts`: its rows summed per that second
  group (`tokenRollup(…, split)`), which sum to it. The Dashboard's **Tokens over time** panel, beside the usage graph
  (`ui/src/views/dashboard/token-history.tsx`, chart `ui/src/charts/token-days.tsx`, model `tokenDays` in
  `ui/src/model/token-ledger.ts`), reads `by=day&split=repo` or `split=account` (the dashboard layout's `tokenSplit`) for the
  last 30 UTC days and draws one stacked bar per day: every token (input, output, cache read, cache write), the five biggest
  stacks of the range in their own colour and the rest as `other`, so each day still sums to the ledger. Its header line is
  the ledger's total for the same days, so the graph reconciles with the job ledger. A session counts on the day of its last
  counted message, as `by=day` does: the ledger keeps a session's totals, not each message's time. `hopper usage tokens
  --split <group>` reads the same.
- **The token budget** (part 3). The user's `TokenBudgetSettings` (`src/domain/token-budget.ts`, pure): `jobTokens` (every
  token, as the views count them) and `jobCostUsd` (the estimated cost), 0 for no cap, both off by default. An admin sets it
  (Settings → Token budget, `POST /ui/api/token-budget`, `token_budget.settings_changed`, `hopper usage budget set`);
  `GET /api/token-budget` and `hopper usage budget` read it. After a checkpoint keeps a running job's use, the **budget
  pause** (`src/engine/token-budget.ts`) sums the job's ledger and asks `budgetReached`; over a cap, the job is marked
  `budgetPaused` (`{ at, tokens, costUsd, why }`) and parked by its run — here, or relayed to the hopper that runs it — as the
  Park button parks it: lane freed, pane and agent ended, work tree and agent session kept, its checkpoint taken. The park
  records the mark's why (`job.parked` `auto`, `why`), so Parked shows it. Needs you's **Budgets** row
  (`budgetPausedLines`, `ui/src/model/token-ledger.ts`) lists each such job with why, linked to Parked. A person's pick up
  clears the mark and sets `budgetFrom`: what the job had spent then; its budget then counts from there, so each go-on gives
  a whole budget again. The job is never killed. The check runs only at checkpoints (every 10 minutes, `CHECKPOINT_EVERY_MS`),
  so a job may go over its cap by what it spends between two. No schema change: both marks are in the job's JSON, which a
  build before this ignores.
- **Waste signals** (part 4). The same read of the session log counts the **failed test runs**: a shell command (`Bash`
  tool use) that runs a test suite (vitest, jest, pytest, `npm test` and the like) whose tool result is an error, on the model
  that ran it. Only the count is kept (`failed_tests`, tenant migration 90), never the command or its output. `tokenWaste`
  (`src/domain/token-waste.ts`, pure, thresholds in `WASTE`) flags a job's **waste signals**: `no_progress` — 150 turns or
  more with no push through the hopper (`github_proxy.done` or `gitlab_proxy.done`, `git.push`) and no commit in its last
  checkpoint; `failing_tests` — 5 failed test runs or more; `resume_loop` — 5 claims or more (`attempts`: its start, then
  each resume or start again); `cache_churn` — 2M cache-write tokens or more that are a quarter or more of what went through
  the cache. `GET /api/jobs/:id/tokens` answers them as `waste`, with why; the job view's Tokens panel lists them.
  `GET /api/usage/tokens` answers `waste`: the jobs of the range with a signal, the costliest first, at most twenty; the
  Dashboard's Tokens over time lists the first three, each linked to its job. Signals only: nothing pauses or stops a job for
  one.
- **Tokens per merged pull request** (part 4), the efficiency number. `GET /api/usage/tokens` answers `perMerged`: the pull
  requests merged in the range (`job.pull_request_merged`, each pull request once, of the `job` or `repo` filter), and every
  token and the estimated cost the range holds divided by them. The range is `since`, else the ledger's first counted
  message, so merges from before the ledger do not count. Every job's spend counts, a failed one's too: it is the cost of
  what was merged. The Dashboard's Tokens over time shows it for its 30 days.
- **Day budgets** (part 5), an input of admission. `TokenBudgetSettings` also has `dayTokens` and `dayCostUsd` (the most all
  the user's jobs may spend in one UTC day) and `repoDayTokens` and `repoDayCostUsd` (the most the jobs of each repository may
  spend in one UTC day, the same cap for each repository), 0 for no cap, off by default; a setting stored before them reads
  them off (`tokenBudgetOf`), so no record changes. A day counts as the ledger's `day` group counts it: the rows whose
  session's last counted message is on that UTC day (`daySpendOf`), so a held job and the Dashboard's tokens over time agree.
  A job's repository is its item's (`source.repo`), as the `repo` group's. In each Decision, while a day cap is on and a job
  waits, the engine reads the day's ledger (`budgetHeldOf`, `src/engine/token-budget.ts`) and names each waiting job a
  reached cap covers in the Decision's `budgetHeld` input, with why (`dayBudgetHold`); the decider holds it (`job.held`,
  `holdReason`) as it holds a job for its sandboxes or its stamp, after the origin, stamp, text and queue-gate checks. The
  hold covers a new job and a job that goes on — after a question, a pick up or a preemption —, as the budget counts what is
  spent, not what is new. Its words name the cap and the day, not the spend, so a held job is held once, not again at each
  checkpoint. A running job runs on: its own cap still pauses it. The hold ends by itself on the next UTC day, or when an
  admin raises or turns off the cap (the next Decision reads it). With every day cap off, no Decision reads the ledger.
- **Subagents** (part 6). Claude Code writes each subagent's messages to a log of its own, beside the session's:
  `<config>/projects/<dir>/<session>/subagents/agent-<id>.jsonl`, not into the session's file. The checkpoint script
  (`src/client/checkpoint.ts`) now also prints them, one after the other, gzip, as `subagents`; the scrub worker counts them
  with the session (`scrubParts`), and `sessionTokenUse` counts a message both hold once (by message and request id). They
  are counted only: no checkpoint keeps them, nothing scrubs them, and a resume elsewhere does not need them. They do not
  count against the checkpoint's size: when the session and the patch fit and the subagents do not, the checkpoint leaves
  them out, and their tokens are not counted. A client release before this one prints no `subagents`, so it counts as before.
- **Print-mode Claude** (part 6). A `claude` print-mode job ("Print-mode agent executors") keeps no `agentSession`, so no
  checkpoint reads its log. Each turn's JSON result says what the turn spent: `modelUsage`, per model, its subagents' too.
  The `claude` dialect reads it (`Dialect.usage`, `printTurnTokenUse` in `src/domain/token-usage.ts`), whatever the turn
  answered, and the executor gives it to the run's `tokenUse` (`ExecutionContext.tokenUse`, `src/domain/ports.ts`), by the
  turn's session id. The engine adds it to what the ledger holds of that session (`keepTokenUse(…, turn)`,
  `withTurnUse`), since a result counts its own turn only; the session's first and last counted message are when its turns
  started and ended. The result gives no turns per model: `num_turns` goes to the model that wrote most. The one-hour
  cache write is the result's `usage.cache_creation`, given only to a turn of one model. The budget pause does not park a
  print-mode job, which has no park; the day budgets count its spend as any other.
- **What it does not do**: the other print-mode CLIs (cursor-agent, codex, opencode, omp) are not read: their answers name
  no Claude model with a list price, and the issue asks for Claude's.

Verification of part 3: `test/domain/token-budget.test.ts` (the caps, the words, counted from a go-on),
`test/integration/token-budget.test.ts` (the real daemon over the fake herdr: the setting and its event; a running job that
reaches its budget at a checkpoint is parked with why, its session kept; picked up, it runs on and is paused again only by

## Stack resources (issue #947, 2026-10-12)

Owner request: the hopper showed resource use per machine (issue #560), but nothing of its own database or the other
containers it runs or adds on. Read every container's use directly from the container runtime, and Postgres from
Postgres; follow the existing pattern (JSON over the authenticated REST API, a service label on each reading); one
Resources view; in core, not a sidecar.

**What the existing pattern is.** There is no Prometheus endpoint: the machine resources are JSON (`GET /api/machines/history`,
the `resources` reading on each machine) from `/proc` and cgroup v2. In a container install, "this machine" is the
hopper's own cgroup only. So this part adds one JSON read in the same style, labelled by service, and no exporter.

**The containers** (`src/stack-resources/containers.ts`, the **container meter**). Through the runtime socket sandbox boxes
start through (`HOPPER_PODMAN_SOCKET`, else `HOPPER_DOCKER_SOCKET`; `HOPPER_SANDBOX_RUNTIME=docker` picks Docker's): Podman and
Docker both serve the Docker-compatible API, so one reader serves both, over the shared socket call
(`src/sandbox/socket-http.ts`). Which containers: those of the hopper's own compose project — the
`com.docker.compose.project` label of the container whose id starts with the hopper's host name, else `hopper`, compose.yaml's
`name` — labelled by `com.docker.compose.service`, and each box whose `io.hopper.box` label is this hopper's instance id,
labelled by its container name. Per container: the list's state; inspect's state, health, start time, restart count, CPU
quota (`NanoCpus`, or `CpuQuota`/`CpuPeriod`), memory limit (`HostConfig.Memory`; 0 is none — the runtime's stats then
say the computer's memory, which is no limit) and named volumes; for a running one, one-shot stats (`stream=false`):
CPU, memory less `inactive_file` (cgroup v2; `total_inactive_file` on v1), network bytes summed over its networks, and
block I/O. **CPU** is cores busy between two reads of the meter (its own clock); at a first read, the runtime's own
earlier reading when it gives one (Docker's `precpu_stats`), else none. **Disk use** (`/system/df`: each container's
writable layer, each volume's size) counts every layer and volume, and took over a minute on a runtime with many images:
it is read at most every 10 minutes, in the background, one at a time, and a read waits for it 2 seconds at most, else uses
the last one or none. A runtime that does not answer, or refuses the list, is a `problem`, not an error.

**Postgres** (`src/store/database-stats.ts`, the store's `databaseStats`): over the instance store's connection, read-only
queries of Postgres's own views — client connections (all, active) against `max_connections`, `pg_database_size`, the
cache hit rate (`blks_hit / (blks_hit + blks_read)` of `pg_stat_database`, since the statistics were reset), lock requests
not granted, transactions open over 5 minutes and the oldest open one, and statement latency from `pg_stat_statements`
(calls and mean time, this database's; the view found by its extension's schema). compose.yaml loads it
(`shared_preload_libraries`) and makes it in `public` once Postgres takes connections, apart from the password step, so it
never holds the stack's health back. Not installed, or installed but not loaded: `statements` says why.

**OpenFGA** (`src/stack-resources/openfga.ts`, the **OpenFGA meter**; part 2 of the issue). OpenFGA serves its own metrics
in the Prometheus text format, on by default, at `:2112/metrics`; the hopper reads them at the host of `HOPPER_OPENFGA_URL`
on that port (no setting of its own: compose's `openfga` serves it on the compose network, and the port is OpenFGA's
default). From `grpc_server_handled_total` of `openfga.v1.OpenFGAService`, method `Check`: the checks, and the failed ones
(any code but `OK`; OpenFGA's own validation errors show as `Code(2000)`, and count). From OpenFGA's histogram
`openfga_request_duration_ms` (method `check`, every label set summed): the mean check time, as OpenFGA measures it (whole
ms per check, so a fast check reads 0 and the mean is below 1). Both count since OpenFGA started, as pg_stat_statements
counts since its reset. A line reader of its own, not a library: it reads two counters, and the one npm parser of the format
has had no release since 2019. It waits 2 seconds; no OpenFGA, an error status or no answer is the part's `problem`.

**The read** (`GET /api/resources`, `StackResources`): `containers` (the readings, or `problem`: no socket, not reached),
`postgres` (the reading, or `problem`), `openfga` (the reading, or `problem`), `solr` (the reading, or `problem`, each with
`pending` while search is set up; part 5 below), `at`. Read when asked, nothing kept, `no-store`. An instance read
(`assertInstanceRead`): the hopper's admin, or loopback without a session. A part that fails says why and the rest is
read.

**UI.** Resources (`#resources`; since issue #2374 the tab `#usage/resources` of Usage, in Fleet; `ui/src/views/resources.tsx`): a row per container of the stack
and, apart, per sandbox box — service, state and health, uptime, restarts, image; CPU (against its quota), memory against
its limit with a bar, network, disk read and written and its layer, volumes with their size —, Postgres's readings, and
OpenFGA's: the mean check time and the share of checks that failed. It
reads when it opens and every 10 seconds while the page is shown (CPU is the use since the read before).

### Stack resources over time (part 3 of the issue)

The machine resources keep a machine sample a minute (issue #560); the stack resources now do the same, for the whole
hopper rather than per user, so the Resources page shows each part's use over the last day, week or month.

**What is kept.** Only what reads as a share, so the usage graph draws it unchanged on its 0–100% axis: per running
container its **CPU** (cores busy, of its CPU quota, else of the cores it sees — the runtime stats' `online_cpus`, now on the
container reading as `cores`) and its **memory** (in use, of its limit, else of the most it may use — the stats'
`memory_stats.limit`, the computer's memory when it has no limit, now `memMaxBytes`); Postgres's **connections** (of
`max_connections`, service `postgres`); and OpenFGA's **failed checks** (the share of its checks since the record before
that failed, service `openfga`; fewer checks than before is a restart, and gives nothing). Latency, sizes and byte counts
are not shares and are not kept: the page reads them now.

**Recording.** The **stack recorder** (`src/stack-resources/history.ts`) reads `GET /api/resources`'s read every minute, on
the usage recorder's loop (`createRecordLoop`), and keeps a **stack sample** per service and metric in `stack_samples`
(instance schema, migration 38; key: service, metric, time). A part that cannot be read, or a container that does not run,
adds nothing: the graph shows a gap. Every hour, samples older than 30 days (`STACK_HISTORY_RETENTION_DAYS`) are pruned:
there is no instance setting for the history retention (the usage history's is each user's), and a sample a minute per
service and metric adds up — about 15 lines for a full stack, 650 000 rows in 30 days.

**The graph** (`GET /api/resources/history`, `StackHistory`): the machine resource graph's query and step
(`resourceGraphRange`, `src/http/machine-history.ts`), per service, metric and step the peak, and the gaps by the same rule
(`src/store/stack-history.ts`). The same instance read as `GET /api/resources`. On the Resources page, *Stack resources over
time* (`ui/src/model/stack-history.ts`): a line per service and metric, a colour per service, a dash per metric; a sandbox
box's lines are hidden until shown, since boxes come and go. It reads again once a minute; no SSE event, as nothing else waits on it.

### Sandbox boxes on client targets (part 4 of the issue)

A sandbox box the hopper started on a client target (issue #708) runs in that machine's own Podman (else Docker), which the
hopper reaches only through the machine's client: the remote runtime. The **remote box meter**
(`src/stack-resources/remote.ts`) reads them for the stack resources.

**Which machines.** Each machine a sandbox record names that is not `local`, once per user and machine; no record on a
client target, no machine is read. The machine's relay is the sandbox module's own (`sandboxClientsOf`).

**How.** The container meter itself (`containers.ts`), with the machine's name and its runtime's API prefix (the Podman or
Docker adapter's), its calls carried down the machine's link (`relayCall`, `src/sandbox/remote.ts`). Libpod's list, inspect
and per-container stats answer in the Docker-compatible shapes the meter reads (checked live against rootless Podman 5).
Only this hopper's boxes there (`io.hopper.box` its instance id); no compose project, since none on that machine is the
hopper's. No disk use: the client carries no `/system/df`, which counts every image and volume on the machine. A meter
is kept per user, machine and runtime kind, so CPU is the use since the read before; a machine that holds no box any more
forgets it.

**The client's check** (`src/client/runtime.ts`). One more call: `GET <prefix>/containers/<id>/stats`, only on a container the
hopper labelled as its box, and only with the query `stream=false` and nothing else. A stream would hold the link's call
open until its time out. A client of a release before this one refuses it (403): the boxes then show their state, uptime
and limits, and no CPU or memory, until the hopper loads its client release there (never while a job runs).

**The read.** `GET /api/resources` has `remoteBoxes`: per machine, by name, its box readings (`machine` set, `service`
`<machine>/<container name>`, as two machines may each have a box of one name), or `problem` (no such client target now, no
runtime there, no answer). The stack recorder keeps their CPU and memory as for a box beside the hopper. On the Resources
page they show under *Sandbox boxes*, after the boxes beside the hopper, each with *on <machine>*; a machine that cannot be
read says why there.

A container target is not a box and has none: it is a container a person runs, reached only through the docker socket
proxy, which lets through ping, inspect and exec, never stats. So the stack resources do not read it.

### Solr (part 5 of the issue)

Solr is the search index's (issue #945, "Search"). The **Solr meter** (`src/stack-resources/solr.ts`) reads it for the stack
resources, from Solr's own metrics API: `GET /solr/admin/metrics` on the Solr of the core `HOPPER_SOLR_URL` names (compose:
`http://solr:8983/solr/hopper`, so `http://solr:8983/solr/admin/metrics`), JSON, four `key`s of the core's registry
(`solr.core.<core>:…`). No setting of its own, and no credential: the hopper reaches Solr on the `search` network it shares
with it alone.

- **Query latency**: `QUERY./select.requestTimes`, the core's `/select` handler: every search, type-ahead and count the
  hopper sends. `count` is the queries since the core was loaded; `mean_ms` and `p95_ms` are Solr's own timer, whose
  reservoir weighs the last minutes most, so they say how Solr answers now, not since it started. No time before the first
  query.
- **Failed queries**: `QUERY./select.errors` `count`, since the core was loaded.
- **The index**: `SEARCHER.searcher.numDocs` (documents a search sees now) and `INDEX.sizeInBytes` (the index on disk).
- **Documents waiting to be indexed** (`pending`): not Solr's. They are every user's pending index updates (`search_pending`,
  and the jobs an event named since the last pass), the sum of each user's `search.status().pending`. They grow while Solr is
  down, so they are given with Solr's `problem` too. With no search set up (no `HOPPER_SOLR_URL`), Solr's part is only the
  `problem`, and nothing waits.

A JSON API, so no parser: the metrics API has given these names since Solr 7, and compose runs 9.11 (checked live). It waits
2 seconds; an error status, no answer, or a core Solr does not hold is the part's `problem`. Latency, sizes and counts are not
shares, so the stack recorder keeps none of them: the page reads them now. On the Resources page, the *Solr* panel: the mean
and 95th percentile query time over the queries, the failed queries and their share, the documents and the index size, and
the documents waiting; Solr not read says why, above what waits.

Tests: `test/adapters/container-meter.test.ts` (the project and the boxes chosen, CPU between reads and the runtime's own,
memory less the cache against its limit, network and disk summed, the disk use's sizes and its failure, a stopped
container, a hopper not in a container, a runtime that does not answer), `test/adapters/openfga-meter.test.ts` (checks, failed checks and the
mean time from OpenFGA v1.22.0's text, other methods and the health check left out, no check yet, the metrics URL, an error
status, no answer), `test/integration/stack-resources.test.ts` (the
meter's readings and the real Postgres's, no socket, a meter that throws, no pg_stat_statements, OpenFGA's reading, no
OpenFGA, an OpenFGA meter that fails, Solr's reading with the documents waiting, no Solr, Solr down with a document waiting),
`test/adapters/solr-meter.test.ts` (a real Solr after documents are written and searched; the numbers from Solr 9.11's
answer, no query yet, the metrics URL, a core Solr does not hold, an error status, no answer),
`test/integration/instance-admin.test.ts` (an instance read), `test/scripts/compose.test.ts` (pg_stat_statements loaded),
`test/ui/resources-view.test.ts` (the rows, Postgres, Solr, what cannot be read, the graph's lines),
`test/integration/stack-history.test.ts` (a record's shares, OpenFGA's failed checks between records and after a restart,
a box on a client target, the peak per step and the gaps, the retention), `test/ui/stack-history.test.ts` (the lines),
`test/adapters/remote-box-meter.test.ts` (through the real client: only this hopper's boxes there, by machine, CPU between
reads, a machine read once, no client target or no runtime, a client that refuses the stats), `test/client/runtime.test.ts`
(a box's one-shot stats carried; another container's, or a stream, refused). Live: the meter against this computer's
rootless Podman and its hopper stack (every service, a CPU-bound container read at one core, its limits); the Postgres
reading against `postgres:17-alpine` with pg_stat_statements loaded; the OpenFGA metric names against `openfga/openfga:v1.22.0`
(checks allowed, denied and refused) and its endpoint read from inside the hopper's container on the compose network; the
remote box meter through the client's end against rootless Podman 5 (a labelled box at a 0.5-core quota read at 0.50 cores,
its memory against its 256 MiB limit).

## Search (issue #945, parts 1 to 4, 2026-10-12)

Owner direction: Solr in the hopper stack now, and search built on it from the start, not keyword search first.

**The container.** compose.yaml runs `solr` (`docker.io/library/solr`, slim), required like Postgres and OpenFGA, one core
in standalone mode (not SolrCloud): `solr-precreate hopper` makes the core `hopper` from Solr's default config at its first
start, on the volume `solr`. On no host port, and on a network of its own, `search` (`hopper_search`), that it shares with
the hopper alone: no box and no other service reaches it, so Solr holds no credential and the hopper keeps none for it
(nothing in `.env`, nothing in the vault). The hopper does not wait for it (`depends_on` names Postgres only). The hopper
reads `HOPPER_SOLR_URL` (compose: `http://solr:8983/solr/hopper`); unset, search answers `not-configured` and nothing is
marked. The stack check (issue #697) names a missing `solr` and what it turns off.

**The schema is the hopper's.** `ensureSchema` (`src/search/solr.ts`) puts the hopper's fields and the field type
`hopper_prefix` (words cut into their first 1–20 characters, for type-ahead) into the core through Solr's Schema API at
the first pass of each start, and turns off Solr's own field guessing (`update.autoCreateFields=false`): a document with
a field the schema lacks is refused. So the schema ships in the hopper's image, and a new build adds what it needs to the
core it finds. Why no Node client for Solr: none has a steady release history, and the five calls this needs are plain
HTTP; `fetch` over Solr's JSON API (recorded per the library rule in the repository law).

**Postgres is the source of truth.** The index is a copy: each document is built from the database again whenever it is
written, so a lost `solr` volume loses nothing. Every document carries the hopper's instance id and the user id
(`instance`, `user`); every read filters on both, so two hoppers, or two users, never see each other's documents.

**What part 1 indexes: jobs.** One document per job (`jobDocument`, `src/search/document.ts`): `title` (its item's, a
direct job's, its goal, else its prompt's first line), `brief` (a direct job's brief, else its prompt, at most 32,000
characters), `status`, `labels`, `repo`, `source`, `requester` (the issue's author, the direct job's submitter, else
`spec.submittedBy`), `machine` and `lane`, `result` (and the pull request when it finished partly done), `questions` (each
question with its answer), `failure` (its error), `verdict` (the failure assessor's decision, summary and reasons), and
`created`, `updated`, `finished`. A direct job's document is `private`.

**Part 3: artifacts and infra plans.** `type` `artifact` (`artifactDocument`): its `title`, `brief` (its summary and its
latest revision's note), `repo` (its issue's, else its job's), `job`, `created`, `updated` (its latest revision), and
`content`, its text where that is cheap: a text kind (markdown, text, CSV, JSON, HTML, SVG) of at most 1 MiB, HTML and
SVG as their words (scripts, styles and comments out, each tag a space, entities decoded: an HTML deck's slide text). An
image, a PDF or a file is indexed by its metadata alone. No HTML library: none in the dependencies does this, and search
needs the words, not a parse; Solr escapes what it answers. `type` `infra-plan` (`planDocument`): `title` `<target>
(<tool> plan)`, `brief` (its summary in plain words, each risk's words, its blast radius, each check that failed),
`status` (`approved` once approved, `failed` when a check failed, else `recorded`; stale is a matter of the clock, not of
the index), `repo`, `job`, `updated` (its approval's time). **The plan's own text is never indexed**: it can hold resource
values a summary leaves out. An artifact or plan of a direct job is `private`, as the job is. A hit's `url` is its view:
`#job/<id>`, `#artifacts/<id>`, or `#infra` for a plan (it has no view of its own); the Search view links each the same way,
with the type named beside the title and an artifact's matched text as a snippet.

**Part 4: linked issues and pull requests, and intake items.** Their documents come from the **issue graph** ("The issue
graph"): every open labelled issue a GitHub source lists is read into it, taken or not — the intake items —, with the issues
and pull requests linked to it. `type` `issue` (`issueDocument`), one per issue node, `ref` its URL: `title` (its title, else
`<repo>#<number>` for an issue read only as a link), `status` its state on GitHub (`open`, `closed`), `brief` its approved
text (the item snapshot's title and body), `links` (each edge in words: `closed by o/r#9`, `references`, `sub-issue of`,
`blocked by`, `in project <title>`, each from both ends), `job` (the job whose source key is the URL), with its labels and
requester, and `intake`: what intake did with it when a job source lists it now (`taken: job <status>`, or `not taken:
<reason>`), and that source as `source`. The intake outcome is the source's own list of the last sync, read when the
document is built: Postgres keeps the graph and the snapshots, the source the outcome, so a lost index loses nothing a
sync does not give again. `type` `pull-request` (`pullRequestDocument`), one per pull request node: `title` `<repo>#<number>`
(the graph has no title of a pull request), `status` (`open`, `closed`, `merged`), `links` (the issues it closes or
mentions, with their titles: a pull request is found by its issue's words), `job` the job of an issue it closes. Neither is
private. A time GitHub did not give (a pull request, a linked issue never read itself) is the newest read of an issue it is
linked to. A hit's `url` and link is its job's view, `#job/<id>`, else the item itself on GitHub (the UI opens only an
`https://` URL, in a new tab); the Search view names the type, and shows the matched links (`Linked`) and intake
(`Intake`) as snippets.

**Never indexed:** every text is masked first
(`maskSecrets`, `src/secrets/mask.ts`: GitHub tokens, 32-byte keys, private keys, cloud and API keys), and the vault, the
system secrets, connected accounts, sign-in and webhook secrets are never read to build a document.

**Index updates: pending index updates.** A user's search subscribes to its event log: each event that names a job puts
the job in memory, an `artifact.*` event its artifact (and a merge's target, `into`), an `infra.plan_*` event its plan
(`keysOf`, `src/search/index.ts`; keys `artifact:<id>`, `infra-plan:<id>`), a `source.*` intake event or `item.snapshot_recorded`
each issue it names (`issue:<url>`), and each read of the issue graph a source keeps every issue and pull request it gave
(`graphKeys`; `issue:<url>`, `pull-request:<url>`; the source context names them to the user's search, `changed`); a job
written brings along its issue and the pull requests that close it, which name the job and its status (`itemsOfJob`), and the pass (every 2 s) marks those jobs in `search_pending` (tenant migration 50: `key` `job:<id>`,
`version`, `marked_at`; a table only, the build before runs on it), then takes the oldest marks (100 per write, 10 writes
per pass), builds each document again and writes it (`commitWithin` 1 s); a job no longer in the store is removed from the
index (a removed artifact too). A mark is cleared only at the version taken, so a document marked again during the
write is written again. Solr not
reached or refusing: nothing is cleared, search is **degraded** with Solr's own words, and the pass waits longer each time
(2 s doubled, up to a minute). Stop marks what is still in memory, so the next start writes it.

**Backfill.** At the first pass that reaches Solr, a user with no document in the core (a new core, a lost volume, an
install from before) has every job, artifact, infra plan, and issue and pull request node of the issue graph marked (`markAll`). **Reindex** (`POST /ui/api/search/reindex`, least role
operator) marks them again when a person asks; the pass then writes them in the background. `GET /api/search/status`
says `backfill: { at, done }`: done once nothing it marked is pending.

**The API** (`src/http/search.ts`; the UI, the operator CLI and an agent with an API token use the same routes: the CoS
reads search as any agent does, with an API token of a grant whose scopes cover `/api/search` — the `read-only` preset's
`*:read` does —, and no route of its own).
`GET /api/search?q=&type=&status=&label=&repo=&from=&to=&limit=&offset=`: edismax over the text fields (title weighted
highest), every word required, best match first, then the newest; `type`, `status` and `repo` any of the values given
(comma-separated or repeated), each `label` given required, `from`/`to` on the time it was made. The answer: `state`,
`why`, `total`, the page of `hits` — `type`, `ref`, `title`, `status`, `labels`, `repo`, `created`, `updated`, `url` (its
job view, `#job/<id>`) and `highlights` (Solr's unified highlighter, HTML-encoded, `<mark>` around each match) — and
`facets` (`type`, `status`, `labels`, `repo`). `GET /api/search/suggest?q=&limit=`: titles whose words start with what
was typed. Neither is cached.

**Every hit is checked against OpenFGA.** The access model has `search_hit` (`owner: [user]`, `reader: [user, user:*]`,
`can_view: owner or reader`). For each hit of the page, and each suggestion, Access asks `search_hit#can_view` for the
person who asks, telling for that check only the user whose work it is as `owner` and, unless the hit is private, every
user as `reader`. A direct job's hit is private: its owner sees it, no one else. A model the hopper wrote and nobody edited
is upgraded to the default with `search_hit`; an edited one that lacks it hides every hit and says so. OpenFGA not set
up or not reached: every hit is hidden, and search is `degraded` with why (fail closed). **Residual risk, stated:**
`total` and `facets` count the documents Solr matched before Access decided each hit; today a request reads only its own
user's documents (tenancy), so the viewer is always the owner and nothing is counted that they cannot see.

**When Solr is down** search answers `degraded` and why, the hits empty; every other route works as before, and the
updates wait in `search_pending` until Solr takes them.

**In the UI and the operator CLI** (part 2). The **command palette** (issue #2661, "The command palette" below; it replaced
the header's search box) asks `GET /api/search/suggest` 150 ms after a person stops typing (two characters at least) and
lists the titles with its other entries; its last entry opens the **Search view** on the words. The Search view
(`#search/<search>`, `ui/src/views/search.tsx`) keeps the whole search in the hash — `q`, each `type`,
`status`, `label` and `repo` picked, `offset` — URL-encoded as one part (`ui/src/model/search.ts`), so a link and the back
button work. It reads `GET /api/search` (20 a page): the total, each hit with a link to its job view (`#job/<id>`, not the
answer's `url`, which may name the public URL), its title and at most two snippets (asked, result, question, failure,
verdict, in that order) with the matched words marked, its status, repository, labels and when it changed; and the facets
(status, labels, repository, type), each value with its count, which filters when picked and stops when picked again (a
picked value stays shown with 0 when nothing matches it). Highlights are **never put into the page as HTML**: they are read
as text, only `<mark>` and `</mark>` taken as tags and Solr's entities decoded, so a job's own markup shows as text. Search
degraded or not set up: the view says so with why, and no hits. **`hopper search`** (`src/cli-operator-search.ts`) is the
same routes for a script: `hopper search <words>… [--type|--status|--label|--repo <v>]… [--from|--to <ISO time>]
[--limit|--offset <n>]`, `--suggest <words>`, `--index` (the index's state), `--reindex` (operator); it prints the answer as
JSON, and a bad filter is the daemon's 400.

Solr's readings are on the Resources page ("Stack resources", Solr, issue #947).

Tests: `test/search/document.test.ts` (the fields, masked secrets, a direct job private; part 3: an artifact's metadata and
text, an HTML deck's words, no text of an image, an artifact of a direct job private, a plan's summary and status and
never its text; part 4: an issue's title, state, approved text, links, job and intake, a linked issue not read itself, a pull
request's state, links and job), `test/search/keys.test.ts` (part 4: the keys an intake event and a read of the issue graph
mark, and where an issue's or a pull request's hit links), `test/adapters/solr-index.test.ts`
(a real Solr: the schema put in twice, an unknown field refused, words, highlights escaped, facets, every filter,
suggest, two hoppers and two users apart, Solr not reached), `test/integration/search.test.ts` (a real Solr and the
daemon: a job found by its words after its events, private direct jobs, no secret indexed, degraded while Solr is down
and caught up after, the backfill and Reindex, Access not asked, and `hopper search`; part 3: an artifact found by its text and a plan by its
summary with their links and the type facet, a removed artifact gone, Reindex marking artifacts too; part 4: an issue and a
pull request found by their words with their job's link, an intake item by why it was not taken and written again after an
intake event, and an agent's API token searching on the same routes), `test/ui/search.test.ts` (part 2:
the highlight read as text, the search in the hash, the Search view's hits, facets and degraded state; part 3: each type's link and the text snippet; part 4: an issue's and a pull request's link, never other than
`https://`, and the links and intake snippets), `test/authz/model.test.ts`, `test/update/drift.test.ts`
and `test/scripts/compose.test.ts` (the `solr` service). The Solr tests use `HOPPER_TEST_SOLR_URL` when it names a core,
else start Solr in a container (`test/support/solr.ts`).

## The command palette (issue #2661, 2026-10-23)

Owner direction: replace the header's search box with one global command palette, so everything in the hopper is a few
keys away.

**Opens.** Cmd-K or Ctrl-K on every screen, or the header's button (`data-slot="palette-button"`, every width; an icon on
a phone, so the navigation drawer no longer lists Search). `ui/src/app/command-palette.tsx`, on **cmdk** (the library
shadcn's Command component wraps: fuzzy match, groups, the keyboard and the listbox roles, over Radix's dialog, which the
UI already ships). Arrows move, Enter picks, Escape closes; Backspace in an empty input goes back from a job's actions.

**What it finds**, grouped in this order (`PALETTE_GROUPS`, `ui/src/model/command-palette.ts`, pure):

- **Pages**: every view of the navigation, each merged page's other tabs (`Jobs: Queue order`), Your reports and Search.
- **Commands**: from the **scope registry** (`GET /api/scopes`, "Grants and refresh tokens" The scope registry): every
  route that changes something (a `POST` route's own scope, not a body's action) whose least role the person's role
  allows. Its words are the route's summary. So a new route is a new command with no edit to the palette, and a viewer sees
  none. A command on no one job opens the page where it is done: its area's page (`queue:order` → `#jobs/queue`), else a
  Settings section of its area's name (`yolo-mode:edit` → `#settings/yolo-mode`), else its section's page; the palette
  never sends a command's request itself, since most need input that page asks for.
- **Jobs, issues, pull requests, artifacts, infra plans**: the jobs the page already holds (the queue's, matched at once),
  and the search index's suggestions (`GET /api/search/suggest`): the hopper's own copy in Solr, never a GitHub call per
  key. A job the page holds is not listed twice.
- **Questions** and **machines**: from the store.
- **Vault**: secrets, shared secrets, system secrets and templates **by name only** (`vaultEntries` reads `name` and
  nothing else, never a value, a scope or the last characters), from the vault view the page already reads.
- **Settings**: each Settings section (`SETTINGS_SECTIONS`).

**A job's actions.** A job picked shows Open the job, then each job action of the registry (`POST /ui/api/jobs/:id/<act>`)
the role allows. Approve, End wait, Re-queue, Lift quarantine, Approve trust, Dismiss and Cancel send their request with no
body (Cancel asks Enter once more); Run again goes through the give-back (`store/give-back.ts`), as its button does; any
other action, and one added later, opens the job, where it is done. The daemon still decides each request: the palette
only hides what the role cannot do.

**Recents.** With no words typed, the last eight picks come first (`localStorage`, per browser: a convenience, so storage
that cannot be read or holds junk gives none).

**Why cmdk and not code of our own**: it is the established React command menu (shadcn's), steady releases, and its
dependencies are Radix packages the UI already has; writing the fuzzy match, the list's keyboard and its ARIA ourselves
would be ours to keep. Tests: `test/ui/command-palette.test.ts` (the commands from the registry, the role filter, a new
permission shown with no edit, the pages commands open, the vault by names only, recents, and the palette on the page:
Ctrl-K, every page, a job found and its actions, Cancel's second Enter).

## Promote to GitHub (issue #946, 2026-10-12)

Follow-up to #901. Direct jobs are not only account fixes: they are diagnostics, artifacts, diagrams and presentations.
Their outputs are **artifacts** of the job, kept private in the hopper and shown with the direct job. A person may
**promote** a finished direct job to GitHub. Nothing is posted without a preview the person edits and confirms.

- **Non-code outputs.** The direct job's prompt has an outputs line (`OUTPUTS_LINE`, `src/direct-jobs/item.ts`): put what
  you make for a person to see — a diagnostic, a diagram, a presentation, a report — as artifacts of this job
  (`sh "$HOPPER_ARTIFACT" put`); they stay private; make no public link. `GET /api/direct-jobs[/:id]` answers the job's
  `artifacts` (`id`, `title`, `summary`, `kind`, `revision`, `url`), and the Direct jobs view lists them with links to
  Artifacts.
- **The offer.** A direct job whose job finished and that has no live promotion is offered (`offer`, `promotionOffer`):
  `asked` when its submitter ticked **Offer to promote it to GitHub when done** (`promoteWhenDone` on the submission; the
  CLI's `--promote-when-done`), `suggested` when its job made an artifact. An offered row is pinned at the top of Direct
  jobs. The offer posts nothing.
- **The preview.** `POST /ui/api/direct-jobs/:id/promotion/preview { repo?, target?, includeRequester? }` (operator; only
  once its job finished or failed, else 409; with the person's own GitHub connection, else 409). The repository is the one
  asked, else the live promotion's, else the direct job's. It answers: the repository's `visibility` (read from GitHub), the
  `target` (`issue`, or `comment` on issue `number`), the `title`, the `body` — the brief, then `### Results` and the job's
  result (text, or JSON; at most 8000 characters) — with secrets and personal data masked (`cleanText`), the routing
  `labels` without the hopper's own (`carriedLabels`: `hopper`, `hopper:*`, which on GitHub could start a job), the job's
  `artifacts`, the `footer` as it would be posted, the live promotion it would `update`, the scan's `findings` and the
  `notes` (a public repository; links need a hopper sign-in; what is left out — logs, credentials, the authorizations, the
  audit trail —; a revoke unpublishes nothing). It changes nothing.
- **What is posted.** The body the person confirmed, then the footer (`promotionFooter`): `### Artifacts`, each chosen
  artifact as a link to `<public URL>/#artifacts/<id>` with its summary and revision; `From the hopper:
  <public URL>/#direct-jobs/<id>`, which needs a hopper sign-in; `Promoted by <their GitHub login>.`; and `Requested by
  <the submitter>.` only with `includeRequester`. Links are made only on the hopper's public URL (`HOPPER_PUBLIC_URL`, or
  the remote access URL while it is on): a LAN address is a machine detail. Without one, things are named by id. An
  artifact is linked, never attached: GitHub's API takes no attachment, and a private artifact stays behind the hopper's
  sign-in. A small text artifact the person ticks is committed instead (part 2, below).
- **The scan** (`src/promotions/scan.ts`). Before posting, the title and the whole text are scanned: a secret (GitHub
  tokens, 32-byte keys, private keys, AWS, Anthropic, OpenAI and Slack keys — `maskSecrets`) is always refused (422);
  personal data (email addresses, phone numbers in international form, IP addresses, private host names, home
  directories) is refused on a public repository, and on another unless the person ticks `allowPersonalData` (422). A
  public repository needs `confirmPublic` (409). Customer data the patterns cannot find is the person's to check: the
  preview says so.
- **The post.** `POST /ui/api/direct-jobs/:id/promotion { repo, target, title, body, labels, artifacts, includeRequester?,
  confirmPublic?, allowPersonalData? }` (operator), with the **promoting person's** own GitHub connection
  (`githubProxy.promotions()`), never the job's: jobs hold no GitHub token. A new issue gets the labels and no assignee,
  so it starts no job. A comment goes on the issue picked (409 when it is not there). An artifact not of the job is 400;
  GitHub's refusal is 502.
- **Made again.** One promotion is live per direct job. Promoting again edits what it posted — the issue's title and body
  (its labels added), or the comment — and records the artifact revisions linked now. Another repository or target while
  one is live is 409: revoke first.
- **Stale.** The view's `promotion.stale` lists the artifacts linked whose revision is newer now; the row shows **stale**
  and offers **Promote again**.
- **Revoke.** `POST /ui/api/direct-jobs/:id/promotion/revoke` ends the live promotion in the hopper (`revokedAt`,
  `revokedBy`). It unpublishes nothing: GitHub keeps the issue or the comment. The confirm step says so. A later promotion
  posts anew.
- **Record and events.** `direct_job_promotions` (tenant migration 51, a table only: the build before runs on it): the
  repository, kind, number, URL, the comment's id, the artifact revisions linked, who promoted it and when, the revoke.
  Never the text: GitHub has it. `direct_job.promoted` (`id`, `repo`, `kind`, `number`, `url`, `by`, `artifacts`, `update`;
  on the job's timeline) and `direct_job.promotion_revoked` — never the text.
- **UI.** On a direct job's row (`ui/src/views/direct-job-batch-wait.tsx`, `ui/src/model/promotions.ts`): the offer, the
  promotion with its link, **stale** and **Revoke** (confirmed), and **Promote to GitHub** (operator or admin): the
  repository and the target, **Name the requester**, then **Preview**; the preview's title, text, labels and artifact
  ticks are editable, the footer and the notes are shown, and **Confirm and post** waits for **Post to this public
  repository** on a public one.

**Part 2: committed artifacts and the job view (2026-10-12).** The issue asks that small artifacts be "attached or
committed to a branch", big or private ones linked. GitHub's API takes no attachment, so a small artifact is committed.

- **What may be committed** (`commitRefusal`, `src/domain/promotions.ts`). A text artifact (`TEXT_KINDS`: HTML, SVG, CSV,
  Markdown, JSON, text) of at most 256 KiB (`COMMIT_MAX_BYTES`). The hopper scans only text, so an image, a PDF or another
  file is linked only; so is a bigger one. The preview's `artifacts[].commit` says where each would go
  (`{ branch, path }`) or why it is linked only (`{ no }`).
- **Only when the person ticks it.** The post takes `commit`: the ids of linked artifacts to commit (an id not in
  `artifacts`, or one `commitRefusal` refuses, is 400). Nothing is committed by default. Each one's file name and content
  are scanned as the text is (`scanText`, `postRefusal`): a secret is 422; personal data is 422 on a public repository,
  and on another without `allowPersonalData`. The public repository's confirm covers the commit too.
- **Where.** The promotion's own branch `hopper-promotion/<direct job id>` (`promotionBranch`), made from the default
  branch's head when it is not there, never the default branch itself; the path `hopper-promotions/<direct job
  id>/<artifact id>-<file name>` (`promotionPath`). With the person's own connection (`PromotionGitHub.branch`,
  `putFile`: the git refs and contents APIs), never a job's. The commit message is neutral: `Promote <file name>, revision
  <n>, from the hopper` (`commitMessage`). The commits are made after every check passed and before the issue or comment
  is posted; the footer then links each committed artifact to its file on GitHub, `(revision <n>, committed to branch
  …)`. The preview's footer cannot know the ticks, so it shows every artifact as a hopper link.
- **Made again.** Promoting again updates each ticked file in place (its `sha` read first), a new commit on the same
  branch. The record keeps, per artifact, `committed` (`branch`, `path`, `url`) in the promotion's JSON (no migration:
  the build before reads the row and leaves the field out). A revoke leaves the branch and its files: the preview's notes
  say so. `direct_job.promoted` is unchanged (version 1): it counts the linked artifacts, never the text.
- **Promote from the job view** (issue #935). A job whose source is `direct` (`directJobOf`, `ui/src/model/promotions.ts`)
  shows, under its facts on `#job/<id>`, its direct job's title with a link to Direct jobs and the same promotion part
  (`JobPromotion`, `ui/src/views/direct-job-batch-wait.tsx`, reading `GET /api/direct-jobs/:id`): the offer, the
  promotion, **Revoke** and **Promote to GitHub**. A job from anything else reads no direct job.

Tests: `test/promotions/promotion.test.ts` (what may be committed, the branch and path, the footer's lines),
`test/integration/direct-job-promotions.test.ts` (a commit to the branch with the person's token, updated when promoted
again; a binary, an unlinked, a personal-data and a secret artifact refused; the fake GitHub's branches and files are
`test/support/fake-contents.ts`), `test/ui/promotions.test.ts`, `test/ui/direct-jobs-view.test.ts` (the commit tick) and
`test/ui/job-view-promotion.test.ts` (the job view).

## PR tending without lanes, part 1 (issue #967, 2026-10-12)

Pull requests with merge conflicts and passing checks waited for hours: each tend is a job, the jobs compete for lanes, and
the Claude usage cap held the hopper to two lanes. A card said "the hopper tends it next" while nothing happened.

This part:

- **The base merge** ("Tending a waiting pull request", "The base merge"): a simple conflict — the base merged with no
  conflict, or only lines both sides added to a Markdown file — is merged and pushed by the hopper itself, in its mirror,
  with no job and no lane. Only a real conflict becomes a tend job.
- **The card says why.** A tend job queued or held says why it waits to start (its lane cap or hold). A tend the source
  refused says why, in place of "tends it next".

Left for later parts of issue #967, by the issue's ask: tending started by GitHub's events, not only by each sync; merged
and closed pull requests reconciled at once; a lane kept for rework jobs, so a real conflict never waits behind feature
work; migration numbers given out at merge time, so two pull requests cannot claim the same number (a migration renumbered
by the base merge); and a pull request blocked by another named on its card.

Verified: the base merge against real git (`test/git-mirror/base-merge.test.ts`: an origin over `file://` with blob filters,
as GitHub serves one), and the tending queue with the in-memory GitHub (`test/integration/base-merge.test.ts`).

## PR tending without lanes, part 2: tend jobs elbow in (issue #967, 2026-10-12)

A real conflict still needs a tend job, and a tend job waited for a free lane behind feature work: the usage cap held the
hopper to two lanes. Now tending's job (`spec.tend`, set when `SourceHost.rerun` is by `tending`) elbows in past a machine's
lane cap as a specialty job does ("Specialty jobs elbow in"): only when it fits nowhere inside the caps, within the
machine's `elbowIns` (shared with specialty jobs), never at a usage hard limit or under resource pressure. Its lane drains
first, so the machine is back at its cap when it ends. The lanes panel marks it `elbow-in · over the cap`.

Not taken: a lane kept empty for tend jobs. With the cap at two lanes, one kept lane halves the feature work, and it stands
idle while nothing needs tending. An elbow-in costs a lane only while a tend job runs.

Left for later parts of issue #967: tending started by GitHub's events, not only by each sync; merged and closed pull
requests reconciled at once; migration numbers given out at merge time; a pull request blocked by another one named on its
card.

Tested: the decider (`test/decider/elbow-in.test.ts`), the tend job's flag over the real daemon
(`test/integration/pull-request-tending.test.ts`, `test/integration/github-rerun.test.ts`) and the lanes panel
(`test/ui/board.test.ts`).

## PR tending without lanes, part 3: migration numbers at merge time (issue #967, 2026-10-12)

Two pull requests that each added a migration both claimed the next number (#957 and #963 both took tenant migration 50).
The migration lists are positional: a migration's version is its place in the list. Both pull requests appended at the
same place, so the second to merge had a real conflict, and a tend job had to wait for a lane to resolve it.

Now:

- **Additions files** (`src/git-mirror/mirrors.ts`, `additionsFiles`). A repository marks a file `hopper-merge=additions` in
  its `.gitattributes`. The base merge reads the attribute from the base branch as fetched (`git check-attr --source`), never
  from the pull request, so a pull request cannot mark its own files. In a marked file, a conflict where both sides only
  added lines is resolved as in a Markdown file: both additions kept, the base branch's first. A changed or removed line is
  still a real conflict. git's own merge ignores the attribute: it is not `merge=union`, which also keeps both sides of a
  changed line.
- **The hopper's migration lists are additions files.** The newest migrations of each track moved to a file of their own,
  each entry on its own line: `src/store/migrations-recent.ts` (instance, 37 on) and
  `src/store/tenant-migrations-recent.ts` (tenant, 48 on). `.gitattributes` marks both. When two pull requests each append
  a migration, the base merge keeps both, the base branch's first: the pull request merged second takes the next number,
  with no job and no lane. The number in a migration's comment is the one its author saw; the place in the list is its
  version. A test that names a migration's version by number fails its checks after such a renumber, and a `fix_checks`
  tend job corrects it.

Left for later parts of issue #967: tending started by GitHub's events, not only by each sync; merged and closed pull
requests reconciled at once; a pull request blocked by another one named on its card.

Tested: the base merge of an additions file against real git (`test/git-mirror/base-merge-additions.test.ts`: both
additions kept, the base branch's first; a changed line is a real conflict; a file only the pull request marks is not
resolved), and the repository's own marks (`test/store/migration-lists.test.ts`).

## PR tending without lanes, part 4: a sync on GitHub's events (issue #967, 2026-10-12)

Replaced by issue #985's in-motion cycle ("The in-motion cycle", 2026-10-13): the sync watch and the event feeds below are
gone; a sync at once after a merge or close stays. Kept here as the record of what was.

A pull request's status changed only at a sync, and tending ran only then: a pull request merged on GitHub stayed on the
list until the next sync, and each merge left the other pull requests to wait a full poll interval for their base merge.

Now:

- **The sync watch** (`src/sources/sync-watch.ts`). Every `WATCH_MS` (15 seconds) between syncs, the sync loop asks each
  source that can say (`JobSource.moved`) whether a pull request or a branch moved in the repositories whose pull requests
  its jobs follow (`follow: open`) or tend (`follow: tended`). Moved: a sync of that source at once, so a merged or closed
  pull request is reconciled, and a moved base branch is tended, in seconds. A source that syncs now, is removed, or follows
  nothing is not asked. One ask per source at a time. A failed ask starts no sync: it is logged once when it changes, and
  the next tick asks again. The sync timer still runs.
- **GitHub's event feed** (`src/sources/github/moved.ts`, `GitHubApi.repoEvents`). The GitHub source reads the first page
  of each repository's feed (`GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/events`). A `PullRequestEvent` (opened, closed, merged, reopened) or
  a `PushEvent` newer than the newest event the last ask saw is a move; any other event is not. The first ask of a
  repository only learns its newest event, and this is kept in memory: a restart starts afresh, and its first sync reads
  everything. A move in one repository is a move even when the read of another failed; with no move, a failed read throws.
  The read is a GET, so the shared rate limiter asks it conditionally (ETag): an unchanged feed is a 304, which costs no call
  of the rate limit. The hopper still takes no inbound webhooks: it pulls.
- **A sync again after a merge or close.** A `job.pull_request_merged` or `job.pull_request_closed` recorded while its source
  syncs makes the next sync of that source run at once (`Slot.again`), not after the poll interval. Recorded between syncs
  (a person's Merge now or Close PR), it starts a sync at once. So after the hopper's own merge, the next sync sees the new
  base and starts the base merges of the others. A sync that merges nothing waits for the timer: this never loops.

Residual: GitHub's event feed lags its events, from about half a minute to some minutes when GitHub is busy. A move it shows
late is one the sync timer may see first. A pull request's checks finishing is not in the feed; that is still seen at the
next sync.

Not taken: GitHub's webhooks. They need a public URL that GitHub can reach, and the hopper pulls by design ("Remote access":
it takes no inbound webhooks).

With parts 1 to 4, the issue's ask is met: a simple conflict is merged in the hopper's mirror with no job and no lane (part
1); a real conflict's tend job elbows in past the lane cap (part 2); migration numbers are given out at merge time (part 3);
each card says why it waits, and names the pull request that holds it (part 1 and issue #939, `heldBehind`); and tending
starts on GitHub's events and at once after a merge (this part).

Tested: the sync loop with a scripted source (`test/sources/sync-moved.test.ts`: a move starts a sync before the timer, only
followed and tended repositories are asked, a failed ask is no sync, a merge syncs again at once and a sync with no merge
waits), and the GitHub source over the fake GitHub's feeds (`test/sources/github-moved.test.ts`: the first ask learns, an
opened, merged and closed pull request and a push are moves, other events are not, a failed read does not hide a move
elsewhere).

## Failed checks' logs (issue #993, 2026-10-13)

A job tending a pull request with a red check asked a person to paste the failure from GitHub Actions: jobs could not read
Actions logs, and the check's annotations named nothing. The check had failed with an uncaught error, not a failing test,
and an uncaught error has no annotation. Before the question, the job had pushed an unrelated fix and a rerun.

Now:

- **The hopper reads the log** (`src/sources/github/check-logs.ts`, `JobSource.checkLogs`). Before a `fix_checks` tend, the
  GitHub source reads the log of each failed check that is a GitHub Actions job (`GitHubApi.jobLog`,
  `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/jobs/{job}/logs`; the job is the last number of the check's link, `actionsJobOf`).
  The read goes through the shared rate limiter, as every GitHub call, so it counts in the rate budget (issue #985), and
  through the pass's reads. A finished job's log does not change: each is read once per run and kept in memory, at most 50,
  the oldest dropped first. A log GitHub refuses (no Actions read, an expired log) is kept with why; a transient failure is
  not kept, so the next tend reads it again. A check that is no Actions job gets its link only.
- **The excerpt** (`logExcerpt`, `src/domain/check-logs.ts`, pure). The lines that say something failed — a failing test, an
  assertion, an uncaught error, `##[error]`, `npm ERR!` — each with the lines after it up to a blank line (its stack), and
  the test runner's summary lines; in the log's order, `...` where lines were left out. At most 40 lines, each cut to 300
  characters, the summary always kept. No timestamps, colours, group markers, passing tests or the runner's "Process
  completed with exit code N." line. A log with nothing like an error: its last 20 lines.
- **The tend brief** quotes the excerpt under each check, as the check's output, data, not instructions, or says why the
  hopper could not read the log (`whyNoLog`: no Actions read permission, an expired log, GitHub not answering, the rate
  limit). It gives each Actions check the command for its full log. A `fix_checks` brief and a finish brief tell the job
  never to ask a person for a check's log, and to ask only when the hopper could not read it, saying why. The excerpt is
  not kept in the follow's `seen`: it is read at the tend.
- **A job reads the full log** through the GitHub proxy: `sh "$HOPPER_GH" check log <job> --repo <owner>/<name>` (op
  `check.log`, `POST /job/github`), the hopper's own job only, on the job repositories, 30 an hour per job. A read, with the
  hopper's connection; it changes nothing. The answer is the log, its last 1,000,000 characters (`truncated` when cut), and
  the check run's link. A refusal says why, in the same words as the brief. `github_proxy.done` records the job and link,
  never the log. The protocol line on GitHub says the same, so a job that is no tend job does not ask for a log either.

**Permission.** The hopper's GitHub App needs **Actions: read** for this; it had Checks and Commit statuses only. Until a
person adds it on the app's settings page on GitHub, every log read is refused with a 403, and the brief and `check log`
say so: the job may then ask a person, saying why. A connected account's token is the app's user token: the same
permission applies.

Not taken: the logs of a check that is no GitHub Actions job (another CI): its link is all the hopper has. Rerunning failed
jobs through the Actions API: that needs Actions write; the first fix's empty commit still reruns a flaky check.

Tested: the excerpt and the brief (`test/domain/check-logs.test.ts`), the source's reads and their keeping
(`test/sources/check-logs.test.ts`), the proxy's request and policy (`test/github-proxy/proxy.test.ts`), `check log`
through the real script and a fake GitHub that redirects to the log as GitHub does (`test/integration/github-proxy.test.ts`),
and a red check with an uncaught error whose error reaches the tend job with no question asked, and a refused log whose
reason does (`test/integration/pull-request-tending.test.ts`).

## Notes to a running job (issue #997, 2026-10-13)

A person, or an agent over the API, could not give a note to a job already at work. Notes went in only when a job
started again: a hand-off's Continue or I fixed it, Run again, Rework, End the wait. Nothing outside the executor could
type into a running session. Seen live: a job waiting on AWS access could not be given the instance's details; the only
way was to wait and run it again.

- **The note** (`src/domain/job-notes.ts`, `JobNote`): its `text` (agent text, Markdown, at most 4000 characters), who
  sent it (`by`: the session's person, never written to GitHub) and how (`via`: `ui`, `api`, `cli`), `at`, and its `state`:
  `queued`, `delivered` (`delivery` `start` | `turn` | `resume`, `deliveredAt`) or `carried` (`carriedTo`). Kept on the job,
  `job.notes`, oldest first, in its JSON: it outlives a restart. No schema change.
- **Sent** (`POST /ui/api/jobs/:id/notes { text }`, least role `operator`, a box action: it changes work on a machine).
  `src/engine/notes.ts` `recordNote`: a job that may still run takes one — queued, held, claimed, running, on a question, on
  its own wait, parked, or failed as the newest job of its item (a later run carries it); else 409. `job.note_added { noteId,
  text, person, via }`. `GET /api/jobs/:id/notes` lists them. A note ends no wait and lifts no hold: the job gets it when it
  goes on.
- **Delivered** where the job's session reads text, never mid-turn and never over a dialog. The run's context carries
  `notes` (`ExecutionContext.notes`, `runNotes`): `waiting()` reads the store, `take(how)` marks the queued notes delivered
  in one tx (`job.note_delivered { noteIds, delivery }`) and answers the text (`notesText`: a fixed head line, the notes, a
  fixed last line, no person named). herdr-claude takes them:
  - **at a turn boundary** (`delivery: 'turn'`): the monitor (`watchTurn`) asks `notesWaiting` only when Claude is ready and
    its turn is over — it ended (not a lost send), or the watch waits for Claude to work by itself (after the nudges
    stopped) — and the turn did not end on a question, a proposal, a research report or a login. The executor sends the
    notes as the next turn (`send`: `readyFor`, the turn anchor, the lost-send retry) and watches it, under the same
    timeout. The turn's own outcome is dropped: a `HOPPER_DONE`, `HOPPER_FAILED` or `HOPPER_WAITING` before the note is
    said again after it, if it still holds. Background work does not hold a note back: Claude is ready at its input box.
  - **in its task** as it starts (`start`), before the protocol footer;
  - **after the answer** it resumes with (`resume`), when the answer goes in as text. An answer that picks a dialog's
    option, or answers a dialog before the job's text, goes alone; the notes follow at the next turn boundary.
  A print-mode agent (cursor-agent) takes them as it starts or resumes: it has no turn boundary the hopper types into.
  Another executor leaves them queued.
- **Waiting jobs.** On a question, its own wait (#483), a hold, parked (#501), waiting for a template or sandbox approval
  (#991, #992): the notes stay queued and go in when it goes on — with the answer, the end of the wait, the pick up, or as
  its first turn ends after Claude went on by itself.
- **Carried** (`carryNotes`, from `ingest` in `source-host.ts`): a new job of the item — Run again, the assessor's rerun,
  Rework, a hand-off's I fixed it, Retry — takes the earlier job's queued notes, queued on it with `carriedFrom`; on the
  earlier job they are `carried`, `carriedTo` the new job. `job.note_carried { noteIds, nextJobId }`. Continue resumes the
  same job: its notes stay on it and go in with its brief.
- **UI.** The job view (`#job/<id>`) lists the notes under the job's facts (`ui/src/views/job-notes.tsx`): who sent each,
  how, when, and its state in plain words; **Add note** for an operator while the job takes notes. The three events are
  in the job's timeline (`event-line.tsx`).
- **Residual risk.** A note is typed into the job's agent session as the person wrote it: it is the person's instruction,
  with the same weight as an answer. The box action gate keeps it from an API token that is no box token.
- **Not built.** A note on the Dashboard rows and the operator CLI (the route takes it); a note that ends a wait.

## A box start holds nothing else (issue #1002, 2026-10-13)

Seen on a hopper in a container on WSL: a person approved a sandbox run, and the whole hopper stopped answering — the
UI, other approvals, other jobs — while the box started. The approve route did not wait for the start, and every call
of the start is asynchronous (the runtime's socket, `src/sandbox/socket-http.ts`). But the start's first part ran
inside the approval's request, the start had no time limit of its own, and nothing told what held the event loop.

- **The start runs after the approval, never in it** (`createSandboxRequests`, `src/sandbox/requests.ts`). Approve
  records `vault.sandbox_approved`, sets the request `starting`, and answers. The start begins on the next turn of the
  event loop (`setImmediate`), so no part of it runs in the request. The same for skip sandbox approval.
- **A time limit on each start** (`START_MS`, 20 minutes: an image pull and a build may take long, each with its own
  limit in the runtime adapter). A start that has not ended by then fails the request with the reason (`the box did not
  start in 20 min`), `vault.sandbox_failed`, which ends the job's wait (`src/skills/waits.ts`). What the start does after
  is not the request's: a box that comes up late runs to its time limit, as a box of a request no longer at work does.
  Each start has its own limit; one that hangs holds no other start, approval or job.
- **The event loop watchdog** (`watchEventLoop`, `src/http/event-loop.ts`). A timer every 500 ms; one that runs more
  than 2 s late is a stall. It is logged — `hopper: the event loop stalled for 3.1 s; requests in flight: POST
  /ui/api/sandbox-requests` — with the routes of the requests in flight while it lasted (route patterns, never URLs: no
  id or token reaches the log). `/api/health` answers the last stall for 10 minutes (`eventLoopStall`: `at`, `ms`,
  `during`), and the top bar shows a **stalled** badge with them.
- **What it cannot say.** The stack of the code that held the loop: once the loop is free, that code has ended. (Issue
  #1383 reads it while the loop is held, from a worker thread: "Reading the held event loop".) The routes name the handler; a stall with none in flight was a
  timer or the engine. The store's calls block the loop by design (`src/store/db.ts`, up to 30 s each), so a slow
  database shows as a stall too.

Tests: `test/sandbox/requests.test.ts` (the approval answers before the start runs; a start that hangs fails at its
limit while another starts; a late start leaves the request failed), `test/http/event-loop.test.ts`,
`test/integration/sandbox-start-hangs.test.ts` (the real daemon: a start whose image pull never ends; the approval, the
health, the queue and the vault answer in under 500 ms; another request is declined and another job runs; the request
fails at its limit and the job is told).

## Jobs read beyond the job repositories (issue #1015, 2026-10-13)

Seen: a job could not clone a private repository of the person's organization to read one branch of it. It was no job
repository, so the git broker fetched it without credentials, and GitHub refused. The job repositories are an intake
filter: where jobs come from and where a job writes. They were also limiting what a job reads, which nobody asked for.

- **A git fetch goes with the job's user's connection, whatever the repository** (`createGitProxy`,
  `src/github-proxy/git-broker.ts`). A job clones and fetches any repository its user's GitHub connection sees. A fetch
  is `git-upload-pack`: it only reads. The token stays in the hopper; the job gets the repository, never the token.
- **A push is unchanged**: only to the job's own repository, when it is a job repository, or to the job's fork, under the
  ref check. A push to a repository the job only reads is refused before anything reaches GitHub.
- **The GitHub proxy's reads go anywhere too** (`checkRequest`, `src/github-proxy/policy.ts`). The hopper's own job may
  ask `issue.view`, `pr.view`, `repo.view` and `check.log` on any repository the hopper's connection sees. Every write —
  `issue.create`, `issue.comment`, `issue.close`, `pr.create`, `pr.ready`, `repo.fork` — stays on the job repositories
  (and the job's fork). Another user's job still only files an issue.
- **No narrower token is minted.** The issue suggested a scoped mint. The hopper never hands the token to the job, and a
  fetch cannot write, so a token limited to reads would guard nothing the broker does not already guard. A connected
  account's token is a user token, which GitHub does not scope per repository; a GitHub App installation token can be,
