  but only for the repositories the app is installed on, which would refuse the case this issue is about.
- **Residual risk, said plainly.** A job now reads every repository its user sees, private ones included. What it reads
  it may put in what it writes: its own repository, its pull request, an issue it files. That is the same reach as the
  person's own `gh` login, which a job had before issue #652; the trusted origin (issue #652) still decides which issues
  become jobs.

Tests: `test/integration/git-proxy.test.ts` (a private repository outside the job repositories clones with the user's
connection; a push there is refused and never reaches GitHub), `test/github-proxy/proxy.test.ts` (the own job's reads on
any repository; every write elsewhere refused; another user's job refused).

## Box steps (issue #1004, 2026-10-13)

Since issue #1349 ("Sandboxes are burned after each step"), a box step names a template, not a box, and runs as a need
step in a need box of its own; no box's helper asks the vault for the job. What follows is the model before it.

Seen on a hopper (issue #1004, the ask of issue #990): a job on a seat asked for a sandbox, the hopper started box B for
it, and the job failed: `$HOPPER_STEP` took only Windows hosts, and its commands did not reach B. Seats never hold infra
access; the minted credentials are only in the box. Owner direction (issue #990): the job asks the hopper, the hopper
gives it a sandbox step with minted, scoped credentials, and streams the result back to the job on its seat — no box
pinned by a person, no routing rule, no gate opened by hand. This answers issue #769's open question 1 with its option 2:
the job runs commands in the box through the hopper.

- **The ask.** `sh "$HOPPER_STEP" box BOX (--command TEXT | --script FILE) [--input PATH]... [--output PATH]...
  [--timeout S] [--into DIR]`: `POST /job/step?box=…`, the same route, script and result fetch as a Windows sandbox step,
  with the job's proxy token. The command is POSIX sh; `--script FILE` goes with the inputs as `.hopper-step/script.sh`.
  `hosts` lists the job's boxes after the Windows hosts, `box NAME  template T`. Its help is the `box-step` skill.
- **Which box.** Only a box the job's own sandbox request started (`state: running`, still there): `StepBoxes.of`,
  `src/users/sandbox-requests.ts`. That request's approval — a person's, or a toggle's, each an event — is the approval
  of the job's use of the box. Another box, or one of another job: 404, `step.refused`. Only a box beside the hopper,
  as every box a job's request starts is; a box on another machine is a `problem`: its runtime's relay answers each call
  whole, and a step's output streams.
- **The run** (`runBoxStep`, `src/sandbox/box-step.ts`), through the container runtime's own API beside the hopper
  (`exec` and `copyIn` on the `ContainerRuntime` port; `src/sandbox/exec.ts`: libpod's and Docker's exec, start attached
  with no terminal, the framed stream split into stdout and stderr, the exit code from the exec session; the archive
  `PUT` with `copyUIDGID=true`). Never a pane. The command runs as the box's own user, with the box's sandbox flags. In
  order: (1) the box makes `$HOME/.hopper-step/<step id>` (700) and `$HOME/work`, on its home volume, the only place it
  writes; (2) the step's command and the job's proxy token are copied into the scratch dir, the inputs into the work dir;
  (3) the command runs in the work dir under `sh`, with `HOPPER_TOKEN_FILE` naming the token and `HOPPER_SECRET` the
  box's vault helper (the path its client named in `/release`); (4) the outputs come back on the stdout of `tar -cf -`,
  one that is not there said in the log; (5) the scratch dir goes, the token with it, whatever came before. The work
  dir stays: the next step finds its files. A stop (the timeout, or the job gone) reads the command's process tree from
  `/proc`, then sends TERM, then KILL.
- **The vault.** A box's vault ask passes `boxAsk` (`src/vault/box.ts`) when the job runs on the box, **or** when a box
  step of that job runs in that box now (`WindowsSteps.onBox`, given to the vault as `stepsOn`). Every other check stays:
  the job at work, its proxy token, the box's template and launch scope, the job's **vault grant** (a first ask without
  one is refused and opens a grant ask that names the box), Access for each mint, and the apply gate for each operation
  but read. When the step ends, the same ask from the box is refused again: `the job does not run on <box>`.
- **What it records.** `step.started`, `step.finished` and `step.refused` carry `box` in place of `host`. Never the
  step's output. A box step takes no `--secret`: its credentials come from the box's helper, so none reaches the seat.
- **The sandbox answer** (issue #1009) tells a job not on the box to run each command there as a box step, and that
  `$HOPPER_SECRET` in the step is the vault's helper.

**Residual risk, stated.** For the length of a step, the job's proxy token is a file in the box's scratch dir, owned
by the box's user, and the box's helper asks the vault as that job: a process in the box that reads it can ask for what
the job may get on that box, as a job on the box could, until the step ends and the file goes. The token is honoured
only while the job is at work. A process the step started in the background and that left the tree before the stop
runs on until the box ends.

**Not built.** A box step on a box on another machine (a streamed relay through the client); more than one step at a time
in one box; stdin to a step.

Tests: `test/sandbox/box-step.test.ts` (the runtime double runs each command on this machine: the work dir, the token
file and the helper, the log, the exit code, nothing left in the box; inputs and outputs; an output not there; a stop
kills the tree and the scratch still goes; a runtime with no exec), `test/adapters/runtime-exec.test.ts` (the exec and
archive calls of both APIs, against the API double; a remote runtime has neither), `test/vault/box-ask.test.ts`,
`test/windows-steps/domain.test.ts`, `test/integration/box-steps.test.ts` (the real daemon, the real `hopper-skill` and
`hopper-step` and the box's real client: under YOLO a seat job asks for a sandbox and runs a step in its box with inputs
and outputs; another box or a `--secret` refused; in a step, the box's helper asks for the job and stops at its vault
grant, and outside a step the same ask is refused).

## Sandboxes are fresh and leave nothing (issue #1371, part 1, 2026-10-15)

Owner direction: every sandbox a job or a step gets is fresh, made from a clean base, and destroyed with all its state
on any outcome; nothing is reused across jobs; and cleanup acts only on resources labelled as sandbox resources, never
on host Podman or the hopper stack. Issue #1349 makes a sandbox one step and burns it after; this part adds the two
guards below. What is left is listed in the issue's pull request.

- **A fresh home or no sandbox.** A need box (`need-box.ts`) and a check box (`check.ts`) start only on a home volume
  they made: when `createVolume` answers that a volume of that name is there already — an earlier box's, or anyone's —,
  the step or check does not run (`staleHome`, `src/sandbox/owned.ts`), and that volume is left as it is: the step
  removes only what it made. The names already hold a random part, so this is a guard, not a path a step takes.
- **Only sandbox resources are stopped or removed.** A **sandbox label** (`owned.ts`) is `io.hopper.box`,
  `io.hopper.need` or `io.hopper.check` on a container or volume, and on Kubernetes the runtime's own `POD_LABEL` on its
  pods (`true`) and claims (`claim`). The Podman and Docker adapters, over their socket, inspect a container before each
  `stop` and `remove` and a volume before each `removeVolume`, and refuse one with no sandbox label ("the hopper leaves
  the box …: it carries no sandbox label"); one already gone is no error, as before. The Kubernetes runtime reads the pod
  or claim first (`KubeApi.readClaim`, new) and refuses the hopper's own pod, its Postgres's claim, or any other. The
  check is in the adapters, not in the callers, so a wrong id in any caller (the reconcile pass, a sweep, a step's
  cleanup) never reaches a stack container. Through a machine's relay the adapters do not check: the machine's client
  holds the same line at its end (`src/client/runtime.ts`), so the relay carries no extra call.
- **Residual risk.** The hopper still holds the runtime's socket (#603): the label check stops a mistake in the hopper,
  not a compromise of its process. A volume or container from before labels, with none, is no longer removed by the
  hopper; it shows as a cleanup problem and a person removes it.

Tests: `test/sandbox/fresh-sandbox.test.ts` (a check box on a home that is there does not run and leaves it; on a fresh home
it runs and leaves nothing), `test/sandbox/need-box.test.ts` (the same for a need box; a later step of the same template
does not see a marker file an earlier one wrote), `test/adapters/podman-runtime.test.ts`,
`test/adapters/docker-runtime.test.ts` and `test/sandbox/kubernetes.test.ts` (a stack container, a volume or claim of
someone else's, the hopper's own pod: refused, nothing deleted).

**Part 2 (2026-10-15): leaked homes are swept.** Before, a home volume whose remove failed, or one a hopper that stopped
mid-step left with no box, stayed for good: the sweeps listed only containers or pods.

- **The runtimes list volumes by label.** `ContainerRuntime.listVolumes(labels)` (optional, as `listImages`) answers the
  volumes that carry every label, by the name `removeVolume` takes. Podman (`GET /volumes/json`) and Docker
  (`GET /volumes`) answer it over their socket only; through a machine's relay there is none, so a client target's
  leaked home is not swept yet. The Kubernetes runtime lists its own claims (`POD_LABEL=claim`, `KubeApi.listClaims`,
  new) and answers each by the hopper's name for it, kept on the claim as the `io.hopper.name` annotation; a claim made
  before the annotation answers its Kubernetes name.
- **The sweeps remove a home no box holds** (`sweepHomes`, `owned.ts`). The check pass's sweep (`check.ts`, with its
  `holds`) and the need box sweep (`service.ts`, with `stepping`) remove the boxes no run holds, as before, then each
  home volume of the same label and this instance (`<box name>-home`) whose box no run holds. A step or check holds its
  name before it makes its home, so a home that is being made is never swept. A volume with no sandbox label, or another
  hopper's, is never listed; the adapters' own label check still stands behind each remove.
- **The chart's Role reads and lists claims.** Part 1 reads a claim before it removes it (`readClaim`), and part 2 lists
  them; the sandbox Role (`deploy/helm/hopper/templates/sandbox.yaml`, `docs/deploy.md`) now has `get` and `list` on
  `persistentvolumeclaims`. Without `get`, a claim's remove was refused in a real cluster and the claim stayed.

Tests: `test/sandbox/leaked-homes.test.ts` (each sweep removes this hopper's homes that no run holds; a stack volume, one
with no label and another hopper's stay; the home of a step or check that runs now stays), `listVolumes` cases in
`test/adapters/podman-runtime.test.ts`, `test/adapters/docker-runtime.test.ts` and `test/sandbox/kubernetes.test.ts`, and
the Role in `test/scripts/helm-chart-sandbox.test.ts`.

**Part 3 (2026-10-15): need boxes and the home sweep on a client target.** A need step runs where a check runs
(`places.forCheck`): beside the hopper, else on a client target of the user's. Before, the machine's client
(`src/client/runtime.ts`) took only `hopper-sandbox-*` and `hopper-check-*`, so a need box there was refused; and a
runtime through a machine's relay had no `listVolumes`, so the check pass's home sweep did nothing there.

- **A need box runs on a client target.** The client takes a need box as it takes a check box: the `io.hopper.need`
  label, a `hopper-need-<name>` name, its script once as `sh -c`, its end awaited and its output read. A sandbox box is
  still never waited on or read.
- **The volumes of a label are listed through the relay.** The client carries Podman's `GET /volumes/json` and Docker's
  `GET /volumes`, read-only, so `listVolumes` is now on every runtime (the port's call is no longer optional) and
  `sweepHomes` sweeps a client target's leaked check homes when the check pass sweeps it.
- **The client removes only a labelled volume.** Before a `DELETE` of a volume, the client reads it and refuses one with
  no sandbox label ("the volume … carries no sandbox label"), as the adapters do over their socket (part 1). A home's
  name alone is no proof the hopper made it; one already gone answers 404, as before.
- **Left.** The need box sweep (`sweepSteps`, `service.ts`) still runs only beside the hopper: a need box a client
  target leaked stays there until a later step on that machine. Issue #1349 (#1368) rewrites that sweep and its ledger;
  the sweep of client targets goes with it. (Done by #1349 part 3: "Sandboxes are burned after each step".)

Tests: `test/client/runtime.test.ts` (a need box carried under its own label and name, with a wrong name refused; the
volumes of a label listed; a volume with a home's name and no sandbox label not removed), `test/adapters/remote-runtime.test.ts`
(a need box's life through a machine's client, and its leaked home listed and swept there), and the `listVolumes` cases in
`test/adapters/podman-runtime.test.ts` and `test/adapters/docker-runtime.test.ts`, now through a relay too.

**Part 4 (2026-10-15): the acceptance checks on a real runtime.** Parts 1 to 3 were shown against doubles. This part shows
them where the runtime is real, and changes no code of the hopper.

- **On Kubernetes, the kind check runs need boxes** (`scripts/kind-sandbox-check.ts`, after `scripts/kind-check.ts
  --keep`, `.github/workflows/kind.yml`). On the cluster the kind check kept, with sandbox boxes on, need boxes run
  through this checkout's Kubernetes runtime as the hopper's own service account, so the chart's sandbox Role is all
  they get. Each box ends one way: it succeeds, fails, times out or is cancelled. After each, no pod, claim or secret
  with its need label stays. A later box of the same template sees neither the home's marker file nor the work
  directory's, and two boxes at once see nothing of each other. The runtime refuses to remove the hopper's own pod and
  each claim of the release, and the release's pods are the same at the end. The workflow runs when the chart, either
  check or the Kubernetes runtime changes.
- **On Podman, a job's own runtime leaves nothing** (`test/client/job-runtime-podman.test.ts`). With a real podman, in
  a stand-in for the user's runtime dir: a volume, a network and a container that a job makes carry its job label, and
  after its reap there is no storage, runtime dir or network config of the job's. A runtime set up again for a job of
  the same id lists no volume, network, container or image. Where a real podman does not work, the test is skipped.

**Part 5 (2026-10-15): kill the hopper and start it again, on Kubernetes.** The acceptance asks that a sandbox a hopper
that stopped left is gone after its next start. The reconcile pass and the sweeps were shown with doubles
(`test/sandbox/leaked-homes.test.ts`, `test/sandbox/reconcile*.test.ts`); this part shows it in a real cluster, and
changes no code of the hopper.

- **The sandbox check kills the hopper** (`crashAndRestart`, `scripts/kind-sandbox-check.ts`, its last step). It reads
  the hopper's instance id from its database (`settings`, `instanceId`), scales the hopper's deployment to 0 and
  deletes its pod with no grace. While the hopper is down, it makes a need box of that instance and its home claim,
  through the hopper's service account, as a step the hopper started and never ended leaves them. Then it scales the
  deployment to 1, waits for its rollout, and no pod, claim or secret with the box's need label may stay.
- **Only the restarted hopper can have removed it.** The box is made after the hopper's pod is gone, so the running
  hopper's sweep (every 10 s) never saw it.
- **No job is marked here.** No check has a job (a job needs a GitHub sign-in). A run that a stopped hopper left ends as
  `swept` in the sandbox runs ledger of #1368; its own outcome is part of the ledger work below.

Tests: `test/scripts/kind-sandbox-check.test.ts` (with a fake kubectl and the runtime double: the hopper is stopped
before the box is made; a hopper that leaves the box fails the check; an instance id that cannot be read stops the
check before the hopper is stopped). The kind workflow runs the step itself.

**Part 6 (2026-10-16): each way a run ends has its own outcome.** The ledger of #1349 had `succeeded`, `failed` and
`swept`: a step past its time limit, one the job stopped waiting for, and one a stopped hopper left all read as
`failed` or `swept`. The need box sweep on client targets went in with #1349 ("Sandboxes are burned after each step").

- **Timed out.** The need box (`need-box.ts`) holds the step's time limit with its own timer, not only through the
  runtime's `wait` (now given the limit and 5 s more): a wait that hangs past the limit still ends the step. The box is
  stopped, then removed with its home as before, and the result says `stopped: 'timed-out'`.
- **Cancelled.** A step the job stopped waiting for (its signal aborted, before or after the box started) says
  `stopped: 'cancelled'`. `outcomeOf` (`src/domain/sandbox-runs.ts`) takes `stopped` first.
- **Interrupted.** At start (`Sandboxes.start`, before the first pass), no step runs yet, so each run with no end was
  left by a hopper that stopped mid-step: it ends as `interrupted`, with its job in the log line. The sweep that follows
  burns its box and home and notes the burn, as before. `swept` stays for a run whose box the sweep burned while this
  hopper ran.
- No migration: the outcome is a field of the run's JSON body, and the older outcomes keep their meaning.

Tests: `test/sandbox/need-box.test.ts` (a step past its limit is stopped and removed as timed out; one the job stops
waiting for, as cancelled), `test/sandbox/sandbox-runs.test.ts` (the ledger's `timed-out` and `cancelled` runs, burned;
at start, a run a stopped hopper left ends as `interrupted` and its box and home are gone).

**Part 7 (2026-10-16): a sandbox's credentials end with it** (decision #1394). The acceptance asks that a credential
issued to a sandbox no longer works once that sandbox is destroyed. Before, a Kubernetes TokenRequest token was bound to
nothing and worked to its expiry (10 minutes), and an AWS session to its own (15 minutes).

- **Kubernetes: each token is bound to a Secret of its own** (`src/vault/bindings.ts`, a **mint binding**). For a need
  box (`need-mint.ts`) and a check box (`checks.ts`), the vault names a Secret (`hopper-mint-<uuid>`) in the mint target
  (`bindTo`). The minter (`minter.ts`) makes it, empty and labelled `io.hopper.mint`, in the service account's namespace,
  then asks for the token with `boundObjectRef` to it. When the cluster refuses the token, the Secret is deleted at once.
  The mint's event records the binding (`bound` on `vault.minted` and `vault.check_minted`), and the vault holds it for
  the sandbox. Since issue #1628 the vault holds and records it (`vault.binding_named`) before the minter runs.
- **The sandbox's end deletes it.** A need step releases its sandbox's bindings (`releaseMints`) after its box is burned,
  whatever the outcome — it succeeded, failed, timed out, was cancelled, or its run threw —, and also when a later mint
  of the step is refused or the job drops the step before it runs. The check pass releases a check box's bindings after
  the box is removed. The minter deletes each Secret (a 404 is no error), the API server refuses the token within its token cache time (10 s by default, seen by the cloud acceptance test, issue #1956), and
  `vault.unbound` records it. Through the vault's own container (#586), the delete crosses as the op `unbind`: only that
  container holds the minting credential.
- **Reconcile.** An unbind that fails (the cluster is not reachable) is logged and waits. The reconcile pass
  (`reconcilePass`, each user's runtime) runs at start and every 5 minutes. It reads the last 7 days of mint events and
  unbinds each binding that no sandbox holds now and no `vault.unbound` ended: one a hopper that stopped mid-step left,
  or one whose unbind failed. A binding of a need box that another live hopper on the same database runs is that
  hopper's (issue #1954, "The crash harness" part 7): its step's `need-step` saga is leased to that hopper, so the pass
  leaves it; once that lease ended, the binding is left behind and the pass unbinds it.
- **The minting credential needs more rights.** Its identity needs `create` and `delete` on `secrets` in each namespace
  where it mints (`docs/deploy.md` "Minting short-lived credentials"). Without them, a sandbox's mint fails and says so.
  It is no fallback to an unbound token, because that token would outlive its sandbox. Only `create` and `delete`: the
  hopper names each Secret it made, so it needs no `list` or `get`.
- **Residual risk: AWS and EKS keep their floor.** STS cannot end one session by itself. The way to do it is a deny
  policy on `aws:TokenIssueTime` for the role, which needs `iam:PutRolePolicy` and also ends the sessions of other
  sandboxes that still run. The owner chose not to do that (#1394). So an AWS session minted for a sandbox works for up
  to 15 minutes after the sandbox is destroyed, and an EKS token (signed with such a session) for up to 14. Both stay at
  their minimum: `AWS_SESSION_SECONDS` (900, STS's floor) and `EKS_TOKEN_SECONDS` (840).
- A box job's mint on a machine (`mint.ts`, `createMinting`) and a person's mint test are no sandbox: they bind nothing.

Tests: `test/vault/bound-tokens.test.ts` (against a Kubernetes API double: the token is bound to a labelled Secret, works
until the Secret is deleted and is refused at once after; a token the cluster refuses leaves no Secret),
`test/vault/mint-bindings.test.ts` (a release unbinds each of its sandbox's bindings and records it; a failed unbind
never rejects and the reconcile pass unbinds it; after a restart, the pass unbinds each binding no unbound event ended and
leaves the bindings of sandboxes that run now; a need step's Kubernetes token is bound, an AWS session is not), and
`test/sandbox/need-steps.test.ts` (a step that succeeds, fails, times out, is cancelled or throws, a step whose later
mint is refused, and one the job drops all release their bindings).

## Kubernetes sandboxes, end to end on kind (issue #1422, 2026-10-15)

Owner direction: a CI suite on a kind cluster, installed by the Helm chart alone, proves that the hopper on Kubernetes
starts sandboxes on demand, burns each after its step, keeps them apart, holds them to their limits, and leaves nothing
when it restarts. It asserts behaviour and order only; no timing budget runs on GitHub Actions.

- **The chart caps each box** (`sandbox.limits.cpus`, `sandbox.limits.memoryMb` → `HOPPER_KUBERNETES_BOX_CPUS`,
  `HOPPER_KUBERNETES_BOX_MEMORY_MB`, `src/sandbox/settings.ts`). The Kubernetes runtime gives a box no more than that
  (`most`, `src/sandbox/kubernetes.ts`); a box that asks for less keeps what it asks. Before, a need box always asked
  for 4 CPUs and 8 GiB as its requests, and the sandbox check had to wrap the runtime to ask for less. Unset, nothing
  changes.
- **A box killed for its memory says so.** When its pod's container ended `OOMKilled`, the runtime's `logs` ends with
  one line that says so and names the limit, so the step's log reads why it ended with exit 137.
- **The kind check restarts the hopper** with `kubectl rollout restart` after its pod delete, and asks its health and
  master key again (`scripts/kind-check.ts`, issue #1406).
- **The sandbox check adds three cases** (`scripts/kind-sandbox-cases.ts`, run by `scripts/kind-sandbox-check.ts`
  before the kill and restart of #1371): the limits, as the box's cgroup holds them, and a box over its memory killed
  and reported; isolation, a box that reaches the hopper and not another box, a Service of the release, its node or the API server, with
  no service account token and its credential only in its file; and many at once, dozens of need steps through the
  sandbox module (`createSandboxes`, as the hopper runs them), more than the nodes have room for, so some wait for
  the scheduler, each with its own output, then nothing left, no open run in the ledger, no problem, no box a lane pod
  or with a client's link. A box's CPU and memory limits are its requests too, so "queued, not failed" is the
  scheduler's: a pod with no room is pending until room comes, within the 15 minutes `start` waits.
- **The node and the API server too.** On kind a box reaches neither its node nor the API server on it: kind's network
  plugin holds a pod off its node, and the check asserts it. Not every plugin does ("Egress" in docs/deploy.md), so
  `--node-reach` makes those two probes said, not asserted, on such a cluster.
- **What is not asserted.** The hopper's memory
  before and after the burst is printed, never asserted: load numbers run locally. The steps run through the sandbox
  module in the check's own process, not through a job of the hopper: a job needs a GitHub sign-in, which no check has.
- **The workflow runs on every sandbox change**: `src/sandbox/**`, `src/domain/sandboxes.ts`,
  `src/domain/sandbox-runs.ts`, the chart and both check files (`.github/workflows/kind.yml`).

Tests: `test/sandbox/kubernetes.test.ts` (a box capped by the chart's limits; an OOMKilled box's log),
`test/sandbox/runtime-select.test.ts` (the variables), `test/scripts/helm-chart-sandbox.test.ts` (the chart sets them
only when given), `test/scripts/kind-check.test.ts` (the rollout restart, in order; another key after it fails; the
workflow's paths) and `test/scripts/kind-sandbox-check.test.ts` (the pure steps of the new cases: the limits read from
the hopper's env, the room on the nodes, a pod queued, each probe read, isolation). The kind workflow runs the cases.

## Approve several at once (issue #1018, 2026-10-13)

Seen: a person approved several waiting items, and the UI showed them all as in progress, but they went through one at
a time. Approve all listed sent the template, waited for its answer, then sent each profile, and stopped at the first
that failed. And there was no way to approve several cards in one action. The routes were not the cause: each answers
once the decision is recorded, and a box starts in the background (issue #1002).

- **One home for an approval on Access requests** (`ui/src/store/access-approvals.ts`). A template card's Approve (or
  Approve all listed), a sandbox run card's Approve, and Approve selected all call `approveItems`. Each item is a card:
  a template (`templateItem`: the edits `allListed` names, `ui/src/model/vault.ts`) or a run (`runItem`). Every item's
  posts go out at once (`Promise.allSettled`), never one after another: an item waits only for its own answers, and a
  failure on one stops no other. Each item keeps its own state — `pending`, `approved`, or `failed` with why — which its
  card shows (`Approving…`, `Approved`, `Not approved: <why>`). An item still pending is not sent again.
- **Approve selected.** An admin ticks the cards (a checkbox on each template and run card that waits), or **Select all
  waiting**, then **Approve selected (N)** in one confirm. The bar counts the last batch: `3 approved`, or `2 approved,
  1 failed`. Each answer is the vault's view, kept through `viewAnswer` (issue #1019), so answers that come back in any
  order leave no stale view.
  A template saved again is a new item (its key has `savedAt`), with no state of the last one; leaving Access requests
  forgets the items that ended and the selection.
- **No new route.** Each approval is the same `POST /ui/api/vault` or `POST /ui/api/sandbox-requests` as before, with
  the same role, box action and events: an API client approves several by sending several, the same way. The browser
  sends them over its own connections; each answers in milliseconds, so 20 go through in about a second.

Tests: `test/ui/sandbox-runs-view.test.ts` (Approve all listed sends both while neither has answered; Approve selected
sends every approval while none has answered, each card shows its progress then its result; a refusal on one leaves the
others approved and says why), `test/sandbox/requests.test.ts` (20 runs approved at once each answer at once, and their
boxes start side by side).

## Need steps (issue #1007, 2026-10-13)

Owner rules (issue #1007, rolling up #990, #998, #1003, #1004, #1006): no seat holds an AWS, Kubernetes, terraform or
vault credential; no routing rule or machine pin sends infra work to a box; no person starts a box by hand for a job. A
job on any seat that needs an account or a cluster asks the hopper while it runs; the hopper runs that one step in a
sandbox with credentials minted for it, and gives the output back. The job goes on on its seat. Before it, a job's
`sandbox` ask started a box that joined as a machine, and the job could not reach it (#1004, #1009): job 89486b46 failed
with "this seat job cannot run commands in it".

Two kinds of sandbox step, one way in (`hopper-step`, `HOPPER_STEP`, `/job/step`, the job's proxy token):

| | Windows sandbox step | Need step |
|---|---|---|
| asked as | `sh "$HOPPER_STEP" run HOST …` | `sh "$HOPPER_STEP" need NEEDS --why … …` |
| runs | on a **Windows host** a person set up, over ssh, PowerShell | in a **need box**: a one-shot container of a ready template that covers the needs, `sh` |
| credentials | vault secrets the host gives, by name, after the job's vault grant | each need's **minted credential**, for the step only, after Access and the apply gate |
| skill text | `windows-step` | `need-step` |

Both give the output to the job as it comes, then answer the exit code and the outputs (`GET /job/step/:id`), keep the
result an hour, and record `step.started`, `step.finished`, `step.refused` on the job's timeline. Since issue #1568 a need
or box step is kept in the database and run by a saga, and the job reads its log and result by polling ("Need steps
kept as sagas"); a Windows step still streams in its request (#1611). "Windows sandbox steps"
above holds the Windows half; this section the Linux half.

- **The ask.** `POST /job/step?needs=&why=&plan=&planId=&command=&timeout=&output=…`, the inputs as a tar body (at most
  32 MiB since issue #1568, kept in the database until the step runs: they are copied into the box; a need box on a machine of the user's takes 64 KiB, see below). NEEDS as a template request writes them, `<operation>/<kind>/<asset>`.
  A need the vault mints nothing for (only `aws-role`, `cluster` and `namespace` are minted) is a 400 before any template
  is made. `--secret` is refused: a step gets what its needs name, never a vault secret by name.
- **The template** (`coveringTemplate`, `src/sandbox/need-steps.ts`). A template of the user's that is ready — approved, its
  image the approved one, every profile approved, its read-only check passed when it takes one — and that declares every
  need. More needs are fine: the step is minted only what it named, so a wider template gives it nothing more. The one
  with the fewest profiles wins. None: the route asks for the template through the skill waits as `sandbox-template`
  asks (`TEMPLATE_SKILL`, with `why` and `plan`), so it is made once and never twice (`asked-<hash>` of the needs, and
  issue #998's reuse), approved only by the read policy, the auto-approve policy, a remembered write approval, skip
  template approval or a person, and checked before its first step when it is read-only. While it waits the answer is
  202 `waiting: …`, and the wait opens a watch that ends the job's own wait (`HOPPER_WAITING`) when it is ready (issue
  #998). `ready=1` asks only that, and runs no step.
- **hopper-step waits by itself.** `need` asks with `ready=1` first; on 202 it says the reason once and asks again every
  10 s (`HOPPER_STEP_POLL_S`), for `--wait` seconds (default 1800). Ready, it runs the step: one approval of a write need
  and the step goes on with no other action. When `--wait` runs out first, it tells the job to end its turn with
  `HOPPER_WAITING`; the watch wakes it, and it runs the same command again.
- **The mints** (`mintForNeedStep`, `src/vault/need-mint.ts`; with the vault in a container, minted where the minting
  credential is, as a check box's). Per need, before the inputs are taken: the job at work; Access asked as a live job
  of the template (`decideCheckMint`, the need box as the check), so only a profile approved for the template is minted;
  for an operation but read, the apply gate (issue #870) — an approved, current infra plan, `--plan-id`; the minting
  credential for the account or cluster; the job still at work. `vault.minted` with the need box as its `machine` and the
  job, or `vault.mint_refused`; never a credential. A refusal is a 403 that names the need and why.
- **The need box** (`runNeedBox`, `src/sandbox/need-box.ts`, through the sandbox module's `needStep`: beside the hopper, else
  on a client target of the user's with a runtime, as a check runs). The template's image with its tools, under the
  sandbox flags, the step label `io.hopper.need` (the reconcile pass leaves it; the check pass's sweep removes one no step
  holds), `NEED_BOX_SCRIPT` as its one-shot script. The credentials, the command and the outputs come in its environment,
  never in the script. The step's files — the inputs and, for `--plan-id`, the plan's saved file — are copied in once the
  box runs, as the box's user (the runtime's archive call, as a box step's): the plan file under `$HOME/.hopper-need`,
  the inputs extracted into `$HOME/work`, then a mark that all are there, which the script waits for. A runtime with no
  copy (one on a machine of the user's, through its client) takes them in the environment as a tar in base64, at most
  64 KiB together; more is a problem before any box is made. The script writes the AWS profiles (`[<account>-<role>]`, the first `AWS_PROFILE`)
  and the kubeconfig (a context per cluster or namespace, the first current) under the box's home with umask 077, takes
  them out of the environment, and runs the command in `$HOME/work` with `sh -c`. One AWS role
  is also the AWS CLI's own variables. After the command it prints the outputs as a tar in base64 between two marks,
  which the job's log never shows (`shownSoFar`, `splitOutput`), with the tar's **outputs sha256** as the box made it
  (issue #2288). A runtime's log once lost one line of the base64: 57 bytes gone mid-file, the tar's NUL padding at the
  end of the file, the same length. So the hopper computes the sha256 of the tar it decoded and compares the two: on a
  difference it reads the box's log once more (the box is still there, and a read changes nothing), and when they still
  differ, or the box gave none (its image has no `sha256sum`), the step ends with a problem and no outputs. The digest is
  kept with the step's result (`outputsSha256`, in `step.finished`), sent in `x-hopper-step-outputs-sha256`, and
  `hopper-step` checks it again on the job's machine before it unpacks the tar. The digest is of the tar, not of each
  file: the tar holds every output file whole, so one digest covers each byte of each file, and the hopper needs no tar
  parser. **The outputs' limit** (issue #2406): their tar holds at most 16 MiB (`NEED_BOX_OUTPUTS_MAX_BYTES`). Over it,
  the box sends none of it, only its size (`HOPPER-STEP-TOO-BIG`), and the step's problem names the size and the limit:
  all or none, as a part of the outputs is not what the job asked for. A one-shot box beside the hopper or on a Podman
  host keeps its log in a file (`k8s-file` on Podman, `json-file` on Docker; `libpodCreateBody`, `dockerCreateBody`):
  journald, Podman's default on a systemd host, kept less than 1 MB of a 2 MB output, so outputs over about 1 MB never
  came back. A box on a machine of the user's keeps its runtime's log setting (its client takes none); a log cut short
  there names how much of the outputs came. The box's output is read every second and streamed with
  each credential's value masked (`maskSecrets`); the exit code is the command's; a timeout or the job's request gone
  stops the box. The box and its home volume are removed after it, whatever came before.
- **`terraform apply` in a need box.** A step with `--plan-id` gets, after its write credential is minted through the apply
  gate, the plan's id as `HOPPER_PLAN` and the plan's saved file, as the hopper keeps it, as `HOPPER_PLAN_FILE`
  (`planFile`, from the user's infra plans). The apply wrapper in the box applies that file ("Infra plans: the apply
  wrapper on write boxes"): the need box holds no proxy token, so it cannot fetch it. A plan with no saved file gives the
  box its id only, and the wrapper refuses the apply, saying why.
- **What the job learns.** `need-step` in the skill catalog, its full help `NEED_STEP_HELP`; and the `sandbox`
  answer for a job not on the box names `hopper-step need` (issue #1009's text changed).

**Decided here.** The step runs one command, not the rest of the job: the job's work tree, agent and GitHub stay on its
seat. A superset template is used for a step but never for a `sandbox` box: the box is given every profile of its
template, the step only its needs. The need box is the check box's mechanism, not a sandbox box: it joins no hopper, so
no lane, join code or reconcile record is made for it, and nothing outlives the step.

**Also in this change.** A job's FAILED reason is read whole: every line after the marker, at most 4000 characters
(`failedReason`, `src/executors/herdr/screen.ts`); before, it was cut after its first line, often at a colon. A job picked
up with a question 5 h old waits the full auto-park timeout again (`test/integration/auto-park.test.ts`): the pick up
already restarted the timer (issue #692); the path that re-parked jobs, a question on the issue thread, was fixed in
issue #1006's own change.

**Not built.** A step's output on the job stream (the response carries it). The HTTP server that hung on an approval
(#1003) was fixed in its own change. A need box on a machine of the user's takes at most 64 KiB of files: its client
relays no copy.

Tests: `test/sandbox/need-box.test.ts` (the real script under `sh`: inputs of 300 KiB and the plan file copied in, the
environment small; a runtime with no copy takes 64 KiB and refuses more), `test/sandbox/need-steps.test.ts` (a step with
an approved plan gives its box the saved file and the id), `test/sandbox/terraform-apply-wrapper.test.ts` (in a need box
the wrapper applies `HOPPER_PLAN_FILE` and fetches nothing), `test/integration/need-steps.test.ts`.

**Residual risk, stated.** A step's command runs with its credentials: it can print them, and the mask is a guard
against an accident, not a boundary. The credential lives for its mint's time (an AWS session 15 minutes, a token 10)
and holds what its role or service account allows. A template a person approved for one job's needs now serves any
job of the user's whose needs it declares; the step is still minted only what it names, after Access.

Tests: `test/sandbox/step.test.ts` (the box's environment; the real script under `sh`: credentials into files and out of
the environment, inputs, output, exit code, outputs back, the box gone; a stop; the template a step takes),
`test/integration/need-steps.test.ts` (the real daemon and `hopper-step`, OpenFGA and the container runtime as doubles,
STS faked: a read in the policy after the check, with no person, and again with no second template; a person's wider
template minted only the need; a write that waits, one approval, then the apply gate; a need the vault mints nothing
for), `test/integration/job-sandboxes.test.ts` (the answer names `hopper-step need`), `test/herdr/screen.test.ts`
(the whole FAILED reason), `test/integration/auto-park.test.ts` (a question 5 h old), `test/domain/job-bom.test.ts`.

## The work-item ledger (issue #1067, 2026-10-13)

The problem: no one place said where a work item stands. Each view derived its own answer from `jobs.status`, the
failures store, a job's follow JSON, the issue graph's nodes or the event log, so the views did not agree (the Jobs
graph said 0 failed, Failures said 136). The ledger is the one answer. This is its first part: the ledger, its reducer,
its rebuild and its read. The views move onto it in the next parts, and each one's own derivation is deleted then.

**A work item** is one item of a source, by its source key (an issue's URL; a direct job's own key), whichever of its
jobs works it. **The ledger** (`work_items`, tenant migration 55) has one row per work item: its `state`, `state_since`,
its job (the newest), its pull request, the version, and the whole item as JSON (`src/domain/work-items.ts`
`WorkItem`): the state the events alone say (`eventState`), the pull request's state, the issue's state and why it
closed, what it waits on in plain words (`waitingOn`), the job whose failure it is (`failedJobId`) and the jobs whose
work was kept, not pushed (`keptWork`).

**Only the reducer writes it.** `applyEvent(item, event, key, job)` is pure. The event log (`src/store/events.ts`)
runs it inside the transaction that appends each event the ledger reads (`LEDGER_EVENT_TYPES`), so an event and its
item's move commit or roll back together, and two daemons on one database cannot fork the state. A read of the issue
graph (`IssueGraphRepository.record`) gives each item what GitHub said of its issue and its pull request
(`applyRead`), in the read's transaction. `stateOf` settles the two: while a job or a person acts on the item
(`waiting_for_approval`, `queued`, `working`, `needs_you`, `waiting_outside`) the events win; after that a merged
pull request is done, and an issue closed as completed is done, as not planned or a duplicate dropped. A read of the
issue older than the item's newest event says nothing new. A new job of the item (`job.queued`) takes it over and
clears what GitHub said before. An older job's end moves nothing; an older job's merge does (a tend hands a pull
request to a newer job). A job's own run status stays on the job: the item's lifecycle is only the ledger's.

**The states.** `waiting_for_approval` (a request card), `queued`, `working` (its own background command too),
`needs_you` (a question, a proposal or a research report escalated to a person — issue #1174: `waitingOn` `a proposal`,
`a research report` —, a hand-off, a parked job), `waiting_outside` (a named outside wait),
`pr_open` (a finished job's pull request, on its way to the merge: there is no "ready for review"), `partly_done`
(a part merged, the next part runs), `done`, `failed` (the newest attempt failed, nothing replaced it, nobody dismissed
it: the only failure any count may count) and `dropped` (dismissed, declined, cancelled, rejected, a pull request
closed without a merge, an issue closed as not planned). "Superseded" is no state: a newer job moves the item.

**Rebuild.** `rebuildWorkItems` replays every event the ledger reads, in order, with each job's item, kind and
followed pull request from the `jobs` table, then the issue graph's issue and pull request nodes, through the same
reducer, in place of the rows there are. Tenant migration 55 runs it, so the ledger is right after the deploy with no
hand edits and no GitHub call. `hopper ledger rebuild [--user <id>]` runs it again. `work_items_applied` keeps the
newest event the ledger saw; a store opened with an event the ledger reads appended after it — by the build before,
on a store moved to an older update channel — is rebuilt at open. A test checks that the rebuild gives the rows the
live writes gave.

**The read.** `GET /api/work-items`: `counts`, every state with how many items are in it (`GROUP BY state`), and the
items, filtered by `state`. Read-only, like every `/api/` read.

**Part 2: the views read the ledger (2026-10-13).** Every count of a failure is the ledger's now, so the Jobs graph,
Failures, the dashboard and the queue agree with `SELECT state, count(*) FROM work_items`:

- **Failures' counts** (`countsOf`): `failed`, the items in `failed`, and `needsPerson`, the items in `needs_you` on a
  hand-off (`HANDOFF_WAIT`). The `status: ['failed'], unassessed` count is gone from the view; the assessor still uses
  it to find its own backlog.
- **Work not pushed** (`keptWorkLeft`, `keptWorkShown`): from the items' `keptWork`, not the event scan. An item done,
  or its issue closed, lists none; while a newer job works the item or its pull request is open, only that job's own.
  The Failures section's count (`GET /api/sections`) reads the same list.
- **Locked entries** (`isLocked`): a failed job whose failure is its item's (`isFailureOf`). No "newest and not
  dismissed" rule of its own.
- **The queue** (`GET /api/queue`) answers `items`, the ledger's counts. The dashboard's Failed card shows
  `items.failed` — work items failed now — not the failed jobs of the last 24 hours.
- **The Jobs graph** (`GET /api/jobs/graph`) reads each job's item: `stageInItem` settles a failed or cancelled job's
  stage and a part's, and an issue node is at its item's state (`ITEM_STAGE`). `job-rollup.ts` keeps only the pull
  request rollup; its superseded staging and the issue-closed rule are deleted. An open pull request's words name what
  it waits on: "PR open: checks running", "fixing checks", "has merge conflicts", "draft", "waiting for the merge".
  "Ready for review" is gone from the graph, the list and the stage filter ("PR open").

**In flight (issue #1113, 2026-10-14).** An item is **in flight** (`isInFlight`, `src/domain/work-items.ts`) while it
is `working`, or `pr_open` with its pull request wait `checks_running`, `fixing_checks` or `merge` (issue #1164: no
longer one the follow has not seen yet). A draft or merge conflicts wait on a fix, not on the run. The ledger
counts them (`inFlight()`: the rows in `working` and `pr_open`, through the same rule), and `GET /api/queue` answers
`inFlight`. The header shows that count on every screen, a link to `#jobs/in-flight`: the Jobs view with its in-flight
filter on, the job nodes the graph marks `inFlight` — each the item's own job, its item in flight. The badge has no
poll of its own: the store reads the queue after each event on the stream, as it does for every other count.

**One count, one breakdown (issue #1164, 2026-10-14).** The badge read the ledger and the dashboard's Running card
counted the jobs `claimed` or `running`, so they disagreed: the badge counted pull requests with no job, and a pull
request whose wait the follow never read stayed in it for good. Now `inFlightOf` gives each item one part
(`inFlightPartOf`): `running` (`working`, no wait), `ownCommand` (`working` on its own command wait: it holds its lane,
so it counts; any other own wait is `waiting_outside` and holds no lane), `pullRequests` (`pr_open`, its wait
`checks_running`, `fixing_checks` or `merge`). A pull request whose wait was never read is not in flight: an item the
follow lost cannot inflate the count, and its first look puts it in. `GET /api/queue` answers
`inFlight: { total, running, ownCommand, pullRequests }`; the badge shows `total` with the parts as its title, and the
dashboard's **In flight** card (in place of Running) shows the same `total` and the same parts in the same words
(`ui/src/model/in-flight.ts`). The Jobs view's filter reads the same rule. Neither recounts the job list.

**Header badges (issue #1181, 2026-10-15).** The header shows the KPI cards the user picks in the Dashboard's Customize
as **header badges**: In flight, Lanes, Waiting, On a question, Finished, Failed (`HEADER_BADGES`,
`src/domain/header-badges.ts`). Each badge shows its card's own total: the cards and the badges read one selector
(`useKpis`, `cardTotals` in `ui/src/model/header-badges.ts`), so a badge and its card cannot disagree. The default is one
**Lanes** badge: the lanes holding a job, busy and draining — the Lanes card's number, not the ledger's in flight, which
also counts pull requests. The choice is the user's own, a viewer's too: `GET /api/header-badges`,
`POST /ui/api/header-badges` (role viewer), kept in the user's settings (`headerBadges`), not in the browser as the
dashboard layout is. The In flight badge, when chosen, is the issue #1113 badge, its link and title unchanged.

**The Lanes card (issue #1181).** Its number is the lanes holding a job, busy and draining: a draining lane still runs
its job. Its cap is the machines' **effective** lane caps — the decider's, usage pacing included (`GET /api/usage`
`machines[].cap`); the machine's lanes when no reading names it or it is offline. Under the number: the lanes open, then
the lanes still unopened under the cap, or the idle lanes past it, and `N over the cap` when lanes holding a job pass
it — never a 0 that hides them. The decider never starts a job past the cap for an ordinary job: a draining lane counts
in `occupied` until it closes (`test/decider/draining-cap.test.ts`). Lanes pass the cap only by an elbow-in, critical
priority's one lane, or a reattach with no lane idle ("Answered in the pane"); each drains first.

**Part 3: what GitHub says is ledger input (2026-10-14).** Before it, the ledger heard of GitHub only through the
issue graph's reads and the follow's merge or close, so an item whose issue closed while its pull request waited, or
after its job failed, stayed `pr_open` or `failed` until the next read happened to see it.

- **The pull request wait** (`PullRequestWait`, `pullRequestWaitOf`): what an open pull request waits on first —
  `draft`, `conflicts`, `fixing_checks`, `checks_running`, `merge` —, from what the follow saw of it. The follow
  (`src/sources/after-done.ts`) records `job.pull_request_seen` when it differs from the item's `pullRequestWait` for
  that pull request — also at a follow that found nothing new, so an install that saw its pull requests before this
  part records each once. The item keeps it and says it in `waitingOn` ("its checks to pass", "a fix of its failed
  checks", "the merge"); a merge, a close or a new job clears it. The Jobs graph's words read the same rule
  (`src/domain/job-words.ts`): one answer to "what does this pull request wait on".
- **An issue closed or reopened** is an event of its own: `work_item.issue_closed` (`reason`) and
  `work_item.issue_reopened`, keyed by the item's source key, `via` a GitHub delivery ("GitHub deliveries") or the
  fallback read. The reducer folds it as a read of the issue (`applyRead`): an item no job or person acts on is done
  when closed as completed, dropped when not planned; reopened, it stands where its events put it. One rule makes the
  event for both (`issueChangeEvent`), and none when the ledger holds that state already.
- **The fallback read** (`src/work-items/fallback-read.ts`, one per user, in the user's runtime): every 5 minutes it
  picks up to 50 items no job or person acts on and not done (`FALLBACK_READ_STATES`: `pr_open`, `partly_done`,
  `failed`, `dropped`; issue #1105: a part merged or a dropped item may close as completed too), of a GitHub issue, with
  no news for 30 minutes — no event moved them and it did not read them — (`fallbackReadPick`). Its first read, a minute
  after the start, reads every such item, quiet or not and past the limit: the rows the ledger holds are reconciled with
  GitHub at each start (issue #1105; a migration cannot read GitHub). It reads their issues in one GraphQL call through the component
  watchers' `states` (the user's own connection, the shared rate limiter, a reconcile call), and records each close or
  reopen. A pull request's merge stays the follow's, which already polls the pull requests in motion. With no GitHub
  connection it reads nothing and logs why. When it read each item lives in memory. The ledger-vs-GitHub watcher still
  reports drift: the fallback read is how the ledger catches up, the watcher how a missed path is found.
- Rebuild replays the new events as any other: no migration. `GET /api/work-items` answers `pullRequestWait`.

**Part 4: Intake, Needs you and the sync read the ledger (2026-10-14).** Before it, the Intake badge and Needs you's
Intake row counted the request cards of each source's last sync, and the sync asked GitHub on its own whether a failed
job's issue was closed as complete: two more answers beside the ledger's.

- **A request card names its source** (`requestSource`, from `source.request_opened`). A sync that listed every
  repository of an item (none in its repository errors) and no longer offers a card the ledger has waiting for approval
  — its issue closed, its label or assignee gone, of a trusted origin now — records `source.request_withdrawn`
  (`withdrawRequests`, `src/sources/github/origin.ts`): the item is dropped. Offered again, the card opens again: "opened"
  is opened with this text since its last withdraw. So `waiting_for_approval` holds only the cards Intake offers now.
- **The Intake badge and Needs you's Intake row** count the request cards the Intake page shows under Needs approval
  (`requestsWaiting`, by the page's own rule `intakeGroups`; issue #1193), not the ledger's `waiting_for_approval`: the
  ledger lags a card the source lists (a reopened card, issue #1126, showed on the page with no badge). One rule for each
  nav badge and its page: a badge counts what its page shows waiting, from the same data, and changes when the page does.
  Infra's page shares its reads with the badge and Needs you (`setPolled`), so an approve or a mark there changes them at
  once.
- **Closed as complete** (issue #350) is the ledger's rule (`issueClosedAsComplete`, "A failed job whose issue is closed
  as complete is finished"): the source's read is only ledger input. `JobSource.closedAsComplete` is gone; a source answers
  `issueState(job)`, open or closed and why.
- **Tenant migration 57** rebuilds the ledger, so the cards waiting before it name their source.

Questions, proposals, research reports, logins, access requests, infra plans and the pre-sort are no work items: Needs
you's other rows keep their own sources. The Failures row already reads the ledger (part 2).

**Done when, as the issue says it:** one `work_items` table and reducer, which every count of a work item reads (parts 1
to 4); the rebuild runs on deploy (migrations 55, 57); no "Ready for review" (part 2): an open pull request says what it
waits on (part 3). #1036, #994, #1057, #1064 and #1065 are closed already.

## The item lifecycle (issue #1891, 2026-10-18)

The problem: what happens to an issue after its job ends was not durable. A job's end with no ready pull request still
put `hopper:pr-ready` on its issue and left its item in PR open with no pull request, so the item waited on nothing and
Intake said its pull request waited for review (seen live: an issue whose every pull request was a part). An event after
a job's end could move its item back to queued, and nothing moved it again (seen live: nine items queued in the ledger
whose jobs had all finished). Nothing owned an item in that phase and nothing gave it a deadline.

This is milestone 1, part 1: the promise of each state, a state that needs a reference, and a timed reconciler that
corrects the ledger. The item saga in the `sagas` table, the label mirror through the GitHub outbox, the second look for a
merged pull request that only mentions the issue, Run again and Won't do on a pull request closed without a merge twice,
and the writes held while a sign-in has ended are the next parts.

- **Each state's promise** (`src/domain/item-lifecycle.ts`, pure). Every **work item state** not ended has an **owner**
  — `scheduler`, `lane_worker`, `github_observer`, `assessor`, `reconciler` or `person` —, how often it is checked, and
  for PR open a **deadline**, an hour from `state_since` (from the item's last move since issue #1892 part 18; issue #1231's rule; part 7 gives the other states no person holds
  one). `done` and `dropped` have none. Each kind
  of move names its owner too (`transitionOwner`). The ledger keeps the owner, the next check and the deadline of each
  row as columns (`owner`, `next_check_at`, `deadline`; tenant migration 82, which also rebuilds the ledger; a rebuild
  adds the columns when the table has none, so `hopper ledger rebuild` writes them too).
- **`blocked`, a new work item state.** The item broke its state's promise and waits on a person; `blockedCause` says
  why: `no_pr` (its job ended done naming no pull request) or `stale` (in PR open past its deadline with no open pull
  request a job follows). Not active: a read of its issue's close settles it as done or dropped, and a new job of the item
  takes it over. The job graph shows its issue as `waiting`.
- **PR open needs a pull request** (`hasReference`). The reducer never writes `pr_open` with no pull request named: such
  a move blocks the item as `no_pr`. The first look at its pull request (`job.pull_request_seen`) or its follow
  (`job.pull_request_followed`) puts it in PR open again. So the migration's rebuild blocks every item left in PR open
  with no pull request.
- **No `hopper:pr-ready` with no pull request** (`src/sources/github/report.ts` `finished`). The report names the newest
  ready pull request that closes the issue, references it or is on a branch named for it; else the newest open one of
  those in any state of review; else the job's own open one those miss (issue #2510, `ownOpenPullRequestOf` in
  `completion.ts`): one in another repository that mentions the issue, opened or pushed to by the job (issue #2004), else
  the newest one the job opened through the hopper (`github_proxy.done` of `pr.create`) that is still open, whatever its
  text or branch says, so a base-branch update by someone else or a closing keyword only in its title does not unlink it;
  else the newest open part, with `hopper:partly-done`. None open: `hopper:blocked` (a new
  end label, which keeps the issue out of Intake as the others do and comes off with Run again), and the follow looks
  again at each sync. One it finds open swaps `hopper:blocked` for `hopper:pr-ready` (or `hopper:partly-done`); the follow's
  end takes `hopper:blocked` off with the other waiting labels.
- **The item reconciler** (`src/work-items/reconcile.ts`). Every 5 minutes, under the sweep lease `item-reconcile` (one host
  of those on one database), it takes the items whose next check is due (`WorkItemLedger.due`, at most 200) and asks
  `correctionOf`. An item queued or working whose job — the item's newest — ended, or one blocked as `no_pr` whose finished
  job's report has named a pull request since, is folded again from that job's end event; an item in PR open past its
  deadline is blocked (`no_pr` or `stale`). Each correction is one `work_item.reconciled` event, which the reducer applies
  only while the item is still in the state it names (`from`): a second pass, or a second host, changes nothing. A
  change newer than two minutes is left for the events in flight. An item that keeps its promise is checked again later
  (`WorkItemLedger.checked`). It reads only the database: no GitHub call.
- **Failures.** The stuck cause `pr_open_stale` lists the blocked items (`blockedStuck`): a `no_pr` item only after ten
  minutes, as its report names its pull request a moment after the job's end.

**Part 3: a pull request closed without a merge, and a merged mention.**
- **`pr_closed`, a new blocked cause.** A pull request closed without a merge on GitHub — not a person's Close PR, not
  the hopper's close as superseded — moves an item no job acts on to `blocked` (`pr_closed`), not to `dropped`. The item
  counts its closes in a row (`closedWithoutMerge`); a merge ends the row, a new job does not. A person's Close PR still
  drops the item.
- **Run again once, by itself.** The item reconciler's correction `run_again` (`runsAgainBySelf`): an item blocked as
  `pr_closed` on the first close in a row, within a day of it, whose newest job ended, runs again — Run again on that
  job, `by: "reconciler"` on `job.rerun`, with a brief that names the closed pull request and asks the new job to learn
  why. It is no event of its own: the new job's `job.queued` moves the item, and Run again takes `hopper:pr-closed` off.
  The reconciler starts one run again per item at a time; a refused one is logged and tried again at the next check. A
  close older than a day — one the rebuild of tenant migration 83 finds — runs nothing by itself.
- **A second close waits on a person.** The item stays `blocked` (`pr_closed`) and Failures lists it under
  `pr_open_stale`, where Run again on its job takes it back through the GitHub outbox (a give-back row, issue #1238), with
  no label to edit on GitHub. An item the reconciler runs again is not listed.
- **A merged mention ends the wait for a pull request** (`mergedPartOf`, `src/sources/github/follow.ts`). A job that
  ended naming no pull request, with none open, takes a pull request of its issue's repository that mentions the issue
  and merged since the job began — its own part first — and ends as a merged part (`mention: true` in its source state).
  So an item blocked as `no_pr` because a pull request of several issues only mentioned it moves on: `partly_done`, or
  done when every declared part is done; `hopper:blocked` comes off.
- **Tenant migration 83** rebuilds the ledger, so an item whose pull request GitHub closed, with its issue still open, is
  blocked as `pr_closed` and listed in Failures.
- **Not in this part:** the item saga in the `sagas` table, the label mirror (`labelsFor`) with label drift counted,
  Won't do on a blocked item, deadlines for the states other than PR open, and one notice when an item is blocked.

**Part 4: labels mirror the database.**
- **`labelsFor`** (`src/sources/github/item-labels.ts`, pure): the end labels a work item's state wants on its issue. An
  item a job works (queued, working, waiting outside) carries none; PR open carries `hopper:pr-ready`, or
  `hopper:partly-done` for a part; blocked carries `hopper:blocked`, or `hopper:pr-closed` when its pull request was
  closed without a merge. The other states are not judged: their labels depend on more than the state (a hand-off, a
  failure, a part merged).
- **The label mirror** (`src/sources/github/label-mirror.ts`). At each discover, each listed issue's end labels are
  compared with its item (`labelDrift`). It reads only what the discover listed and the ledger: no call of its own, no
  new poll. An item that moved in the last two minutes, or with outbox rows not sent, is not judged: its move's own writes
  are on their way. A **label drift** is logged once and counted (`hopper.work_items.label_drift`, by state and whether
  it is corrected), until it changes or ends.
- **A blocked item's labels are corrected.** Its drift becomes GitHub outbox rows (act `mirror`, tagged with its state
  and cause), coalesced into one remove call and one add call, so `hopper:pr-ready` comes off an item the item reconciler
  blocked (the #465 case) and `hopper:blocked` goes on, or `hopper:pr-closed` after a second close. The send makes its
  repository due, so the next discover lists the new labels; the act once sent adds no row before that.
- **Not in this part:** a correction of the other states' drift (only counted), rows written in the transaction of each
  state change, the item saga in the `sagas` table, Won't do on a blocked item, deadlines for the states other than PR
  open, and one notice when an item is blocked.

**Part 5: Won't do and Run again on a blocked item, in Intake.**
- **Won't do** (intake action `wont_do`). Discover offers it on an issue its labels keep out as blocked (`hopper:blocked`
  or `hopper:pr-closed`); the act goes through only when the ledger holds the item `blocked`, as the database is the
  truth, else it is refused with the state the ledger has. It records `work_item.dropped` at once (with the job source,
  the item's newest job, the blocked cause and who pressed it), and the reducer drops a blocked item, only a blocked
  one, so a second press changes nothing. Its GitHub change is outbox rows kept in the same transaction, coalesced into
  one remove call — the end labels and the claim the last listing showed — and one add call, `hopper:rejected`, so no
  hopper takes the issue again and no one edits `hopper:pr-closed` on GitHub. Labels only: no comment, and the issue
  stays open. A second press before the next listing adds no row. Run again on its job later takes `hopper:rejected` off
  as it takes any end label off.
- **Run again on the same row.** The row of a blocked item names its newest job (`liveIntake`), and offers Run again on
  it, the job's own give-back (a row of the GitHub outbox, issue #1238).
- **Failures** points there: the stuck cause `pr_open_stale` says to press Run again or Won't do on the item's row in
  Intake. It keeps no per-item buttons of its own, as no other stuck cause does.
- **Not in this part:** the item saga in the `sagas` table, rows written in the transaction of each state change, a
  correction of the other states' label drift, deadlines for the states other than PR open, and one notice when an item
  is blocked.

**Part 6: one notice when an item is blocked.**
- **The item reconciler asks a person once** (correction `ask`). A blocked item that is stuck work for a person
  (`blockedStuck`: Failures lists it under `pr_open_stale`) and that no one was asked about yet gets one
  `work_item.person_asked` event, with its cause, its newest job and the pull request it names. So a `no_pr` item is asked
  about only after ten minutes, and an item the reconciler runs again by itself is not asked about.
- **Once per block.** The event marks the item (`personAsked`), and its state stays. A second pass, or a second host,
  asks nothing more. The mark goes when the item leaves `blocked` or is blocked for another cause, so the next block asks
  again.
- **A notifier sends it on.** The Grok Bot routine posts `work_item.person_asked` with the cause in plain words
  ("Grok Bot routine webhook").
- **Not in this part:** the item saga in the `sagas` table, rows written in the transaction of each state change, a
  correction of the other states' label drift, and deadlines for the states other than PR open.

**Part 7: deadlines for the states other than PR open.**
- **Each state no person holds has a deadline** (`checkOf`), from `state_since`: queued, working and waiting outside an
  hour, partly done a day, PR open an hour as before. A state a person holds has none: waiting for approval (a request card
  waits as long as a person likes), needs you, blocked, and failed (Failures lists it for a person already).
- **Past it with no move, the item is blocked as `stale`** (`correctionOf`), and then asked about once (part 6). A state a
  job holds (`JOB_HELD`: queued, working, waiting outside) is stale only when no job of the item is found — none named, or
  the one it names is gone. A live job's lane and its own wait have their own deadlines, so an item a job holds is never
  stale while the job is there; an ended one is folded again from its end, as before (now also from waiting outside).
- **A partly done item a day on with no job for its next part is stale.** Its merged part is history: the block lets go of
  it (`pullRequest`), so `stateOf` does not read the part's merge as the whole item's.
- The deadline column of a row is written at the row's next change, or by `hopper ledger rebuild`. The reconciler does not
  read the column: it works the deadline out from `state_since`, so no migration is needed.
- **Not in this part:** the item saga in the `sagas` table, rows written in the transaction of each state change, and a
  correction of the other states' label drift.

**Part 8: a block's labels in the block's transaction, and no second copy of the item.**
- **The reconciler's block writes its labels** (`blockLabels`, `src/sources/github/item-labels.ts`; `rowsOf`,
  `src/work-items/reconcile.ts`). A block of an item whose newest job is a GitHub job keeps its issue's label change as
  GitHub outbox rows (act `mirror`, tag `blocked:<cause>`, as the label mirror tags its own) in the transaction of its
  `work_item.reconciled` event: the end labels of the state it leaves come off (PR open's `hopper:pr-ready` and
  `hopper:partly-done`, partly done's `hopper:partly-done`), and the blocked label goes on. The rows coalesce into one
  remove call and one add call, and the job's source sends them within `OUTBOX_EVERY_MS`, not at the next discover. A
  remove of a label the issue does not carry changes nothing (GitHub's 404 is ignored), so the rows need no read of the
  labels. When the rows cannot be kept, the block is not kept either, and the next pass tries both again. A block of an
  item with no GitHub job (an approved request card that never got a job) writes none: no job names its source, and the
  label mirror corrects its labels at the next discover, as in part 4.
- **The other moves write their labels as before.** A job's end, the follow of its pull request and a person's act change
  GitHub's labels themselves, or through the outbox (Won't do, Run again), and the ledger then folds what they did. The
  reconciler is the one owner that moves an item in the database with no GitHub act: so it is the one that needs rows of
  its own.
- **The item's saga is its event stream, with `work_items` its projection; no `sagas` row.** The `sagas` table is the
  instance's, and its coordinator drives steps in order; a work item is a user's, moved by its events in the user's
  schema, in the event's own transaction. A second copy of each item in the instance's table could not be written in that
  transaction, and two copies of one state are the drift this issue is about. What the issue asks of the saga is in the
  ledger already: one row per issue (key: its URL), a pure transition table and its invariants (`item-lifecycle.ts`,
  `work-items.ts`), an owner, a next check and a deadline per row, one host at a time (the sweep lease), and a replay
  (`hopper ledger rebuild`).
- **Not in milestone 1:** a correction of the other states' label drift. It is logged and counted (part 4); the issue
  names its correction as the follow-up, done in issue #1933 ("The label mirror corrects every judged state").

**Verification:** `test/domain/item-lifecycle.test.ts` (owners, deadlines, the corrections), `test/domain/work-items.test.ts`
(PR open never with no pull request; the reconciled event, once), `test/work-items/reconcile.test.ts` (queued after its job
finished folded again once, a rebuild replays it; a job's end with no pull request blocked, then in PR open when its report
names one; PR open past its deadline blocked as stale; two hosts on one database, only the lease holder acts),
`test/store/tenant-migration-82.test.ts`, `test/sources/github-report.test.ts` (blocked with none open; a draft named).
Part 3: `test/work-items/reconcile.test.ts` (closed once, run again once and no second while it runs; closed twice, a
person decides), `test/store/tenant-migration-83.test.ts`, `test/sources/github-follow-merged-part.test.ts` (a merged
mention ends the follow as a part; one merged before the job began does not).
Part 4: `test/sources/github-item-labels.test.ts` (each state's labels, the drift), `test/sources/github-label-mirror.test.ts`
(the #465 case corrected in one coalesced change, once; a second close; another state's drift logged once and not
corrected; an item that moved a moment ago not judged).
Part 5: `test/domain/work-items-wont-do.test.ts` (a blocked item dropped, a person's move; once), `test/sources/github-wont-do.test.ts`
(offered on a blocked issue, dropped at once and its labels in one coalesced change; a second press adds nothing; refused
when the ledger does not hold the item blocked), `test/sources/intake-live.test.ts`, `test/ui/intake-wont-do.test.ts`.
Part 6: `test/domain/work-items-person-asked.test.ts` (asked once; forgotten on a move out of blocked or a new cause),
`test/domain/item-lifecycle.test.ts` (asked only about stuck work, once), `test/work-items/reconcile.test.ts` (a stale item
and a second close asked about once), `test/plugins/grokbot-intake.test.ts` (the post).
Part 7: `test/domain/item-lifecycle.test.ts` (each state's deadline; stale only with no job of the item found; partly done a
day on; a state a person holds never), `test/work-items/reconcile.test.ts` (an approved request card with no job blocked as
stale, asked once, a new job takes it over; a live queued job never; partly done a day on, not read as done).
Part 8: `test/sources/github-item-labels.test.ts` (`blockLabels` of each state), `test/work-items/reconcile-labels.test.ts`
(a block's rows kept with it, coalesced into one remove and one add, once; no block when its rows cannot be kept; no rows
with no GitHub job).

### The label mirror corrects every judged state (issue #1933, 2026-10-18)

Follow-up of milestone 1. Before it, the label mirror corrected only a blocked item's drift. Each other judged state's drift
was only logged and counted.

- **Every judged state's drift is corrected.** An item a job works (queued, working, waiting outside) loses each end label
  on its issue. An item in PR open loses each end label but its waiting label. The correction is the one path of part 4:
  GitHub outbox rows (act `mirror`, tag `<state>:<cause>`), coalesced into one remove call and one add call, once. An item
  that moved in the last two minutes, or that has outbox rows not sent, is not judged. The reconciler of #1892 builds on
  this path; it adds no second one.
- **PR open with no waiting label gets one.** `labelsFor` names the label to add: `hopper:partly-done` when the item's
  pull request is a part, else `hopper:pr-ready`. Either one on the issue is no drift. The ledger does not hold that a pull
  request is a part; the item's job does (`partlyDone`, or `part` in its source state), so the intake gives the mirror
  `partOpen(key)`. `labelDrift` has no `missing` flag now: a drift always names the label to add.
- **Corrections are counted apart.** `hopper.work_items.label_corrections` counts each correction queued, by source and
  state. `hopper.work_items.label_drift` still counts each drift once, and its `corrected` attribute says whether the
  mirror queued its correction (false: the same act went through and the next discover still lists the drift).

**Verification:** `test/sources/github-item-labels.test.ts` (PR open's label to add, of a part or not),
`test/sources/github-label-mirror.test.ts` (a drift of each judged state one coalesced change, once; PR open with no
waiting label; an item with outbox rows not sent not judged).

### Intake reads the ledger; a label edited by hand is a person's event (issue #1892 part 1, 2026-10-21)

Milestone 2, part 1. Before it, Intake took an item's reason from the end labels on its issue (`labelReason`), so a stale
label showed a state the ledger did not hold, and a label a person took off was read back as state.

- **Intake reads the ledger.** For an item in a state the label mirror judges (`labelsFor`: queued, working, waiting
  outside, PR open, blocked), the end-label reason is the ledger's (`ledgerReason`, `src/sources/github/discover.ts`): PR
  open says its pull request (or its part) waits for review; blocked names its cause (no pull request, past its deadline,
  pull request closed), with Won't do; a job at work gives no end-label reason. The end labels on the issue do not count
  for such an item: the mirror corrects them. The labels still decide for an issue the hopper does not know, and for the
  states the mirror does not judge yet (failed until part 3, done, dropped, partly done, needs you, waiting for approval). The
  backburner and an address to another hopper always count: they are a person's labels, not a mirror of state.
- **A label taken off by hand is a person's event.** Before the discover judges Intake, the label mirror compares each
  listed issue's labels with what it saw at its last discover (`edits`). The end label the item's state wants
  (`labelTakenOff`, `src/sources/github/item-labels.ts`), seen then and gone now, is `work_item.label_edited` with `means:
  run_again`, when the item did not move since the label was seen (and not in the last two minutes) and no outbox row of
  its own is unsent. The ledger keeps the ask on the item (`runAgainAsked`), and its state stays. Intake gives that item
  no end-label reason, so the discover runs it again as it runs any ended item. The mirror does not put the label back.
  The new job's `job.queued` moves the item, and any move forgets the ask. Removing `hopper:pr-closed` or `hopper:blocked`
  from a blocked item, or `hopper:pr-ready` / `hopper:partly-done` from an item in PR open, is a Run again. A swap of PR
  open's two waiting labels is no edit.
- **A missing label is never read back as state.** A label not on the issue when the mirror first sees it is no edit: the
  mirror puts it back, and the item stays where the ledger has it. What the mirror saw is kept in memory. After a start,
  the source gives the mirror the labels of the listing cache (`github_listed_items`, "Repository listings") before its
  first discover lists again (`start`), as seen when that listing was read (its `fetched_at`). So an edit made while the
  hopper was stopped is a label edit too, when the item did not move since that listing. An issue the cache does not
  hold is first seen at that discover.
- **A give-back drops the mirror's unsent rows.** Run again and Rework move the item, so the source drops the label
  mirror's outbox rows for that issue that are not sent yet (`dropMirror`, `dropLabelRows` since part 14, `src/sources/github/outbox.ts`): they were for
  the state the item left. Without it, a hopper killed between the reconciler's give-back and the new job left the next
  hopper's mirror to put `hopper:pr-closed` back (it is missing at its first sight), and that row went out after the
  reconciler's second give-back took the label off (the crash tests' `give-back:rerun-by-reconciler:after-give`). A row
  queued after the drop is kept off too: while a give-back runs, and for the reconciler's grace after it, the mirror does
  not judge the item (`busy`, `src/sources/github/label-mirror.ts`); the new job's `job.queued` moves it meanwhile. A
  give-back that made no job is judged again after the grace, and its label put back.
- **The report tells the ledger of a close it finds.** A job that ends on an issue already closed puts `hopper:done` on it
  (`report.ts`), and now also records `work_item.issue_closed` (`via: read`) when the ledger does not hold the close. Before,
  the ledger blocked such an item for want of a pull request until the fallback read came, and Intake (now reading the
  ledger) offered Won't do on a reopened issue in place of its reopened card.
- **A block that a close as completed hid is history at a reopen.** A reopen of the issue moves a blocked item whose issue
  closed as completed to done (`applyRead`), so the reopen is judged as a done item's (a reopened card, issue #1126). After
  a close as not planned, the block stays.
