  reads it. Its labels change nothing that the hopper does.
- **An item dropped by a request card that its source withdrew.** The source withdraws a card when it no longer offers the
  issue (`withdrawRequests`, "The work-item ledger"): its issue closed, or its label or assignee gone, so neither Intake nor
  the mirror reads it. A card a person withdrew by an end label they put on (part 7) is listed, and that label is theirs: the
  labels decide Intake's reason, as part 7 says.

**Decision.** **Not judged, and not built.** A rule for these cases would guess what the issue carries, and a wrong guess
writes a label that a person did not ask for. The labels of an item the hopper does not judge count only as the labels of an
item it does not know (`labelReason`), as milestone 2 asked.

**Verification:** `test/sources/github-label-not-judged.test.ts` (each case: `labelsFor` and `ledgerReason` give no answer,
whatever the facts).

### No pull request found is no resting state (issue #2693, 2026-10-23)

A job exists to make its pull request, so "no pull request was found" must not be where an item stops. Two cases showed it:
a job opened its pull request with "Closes #N", and the item sat blocked with `hopper:blocked` until a later read named it;
and a job ended on a proposal a person rejected, and its item sat blocked for days, with no one to follow it.

- **A job's end names the pull request it opened** (`src/store/work-items.ts` `withOpened`). At a `job.finished` whose
  report named no pull request yet, the ledger takes the newest pull request the job opened through the hopper before that
  end (`github_proxy.done` of op `pr.create`, from its own record). So the item is in PR open at once, whatever GitHub's
  search, its links or the time of the report say. A rebuild reads the same: only a `pr.create` before the end counts.
- **No `hopper:blocked` for want of a pull request** (`labelsFor`). A `no_pr` block wants no end label: the label mirror
  takes `hopper:blocked` off, a report that finds none open puts no label on, and the reconciler's block writes none.
  `hopper:blocked` stays only for a `stale` block. Intake gives the item the reason `NO_PR` ("the hopper looks for one, then
  runs it again"), with Won't do. A done item whose report found no pull request (`doneReported: 'no_pr'`) wants no label,
  and keeps out as done but open (`DONE_OPEN`), not taken again.
- **It runs again by itself** (`runsAgainForPullRequest`, `src/domain/item-lifecycle.ts`). The ledger counts its ends in a
  row with no pull request (`noPullRequestEnds`; a pull request to wait on, a merge or a done end ends the row; the
  reconciler's replay of the same end is no second end). Ten minutes after such an end (`BLOCKED_NO_PR_MS`), with no pull
  request named since, the item reconciler runs it again: Run again on its finished job, `by: reconciler`, with a brief
  that says the earlier job ended with no pull request (`noPullRequestBrief`). Up to `NO_PR_RUNS_AGAIN` (2) times in a row;
  past that, a person is asked once (`work_item.person_asked`) and Failures lists it. An item blocked so before the count
  was kept counts as one end.
- **A decision is no end** (`src/engine/reviews.ts`). A job of an issue (its source names a repository and a number) whose
  proposal or research report a person rejects goes back to the issue's work: queued again in its session, in the work
  phase, told the outcome and the notes, and asked to open its pull request, ask a question first, or close the issue when
  it needs no change. A job of no issue still ends with the rejection as its result (issue #1659). An accepted one goes on as
  before: to its next section, to its follow-ons, or on with its work.
- **`hopper:needs-decision`** (`src/sources/github/labels.ts`), a new end label. An item whose job waits on a person's
  decision — a question, a proposal or a research report (`DECISION_WAITS`) — wants it, so its issue says it waits on that
  decision and not on a pull request. A job parked by itself at a person (auto-park, issue #2335) keeps waiting on the
  decision in the ledger, not on a pick-up. Every other state takes the label off. Taken off by hand, it asks for nothing
  (no label edit).

**Verification:** `test/store/work-items.test.ts` (a job's end names the pull request it opened through the hopper),
`test/sources/github-no-pr-label.test.ts`, `test/domain/item-no-pr-run-again.test.ts`,
`test/work-items/reconcile-no-pr.test.ts` (runs again, then asks a person once),
`test/integration/proposal-reject-issue.test.ts` (a rejected proposal of an issue's job goes back to its work),
`test/sources/github-needs-decision-label.test.ts`.

## One start at a time per repository mirror (issue #1075, 2026-10-13)

The issue asks for one shared object cache per repository per machine, so a job checks out from a local copy instead of
cloning. Issue #858 built most of it: the **repository mirror** (one bare, blobless clone per repository per work tree,
"Git efficiency"), a job worktree made of it, and one fetch per repository per sync pass. What was missing is safety
for concurrent jobs: two starts on one machine could fetch into the same mirror at once, add worktrees at once, and git's
automatic gc ran detached, beside whatever the next start did.

**As built** (`src/executors/herdr/job-worktree.ts`):
- **The start lock** (`JOB_WORKTREE_LOCK`, `hopper-start.lock`). A directory in the git common dir of the repository a job
  worktree is made of: the repository mirror, or the work tree's own repository. A start that makes a worktree takes it
  around its fetch and its worktree add, and lets it go after, also when git fails or the shell is stopped (a trap). So
  starts on one machine use one repository one at a time. A start whose worktree is there already (a run again) takes no
  lock and waits on nothing.
- **Why a directory.** `mkdir` is made or refused at once on every machine the job worktree command runs on; `flock` is
  not on every one (macOS has none). The holder writes its pid in it.
- **A lock whose holder ended** (its pid no longer runs), or one held for more than 300 seconds, is moved aside and taken
  over, and the start says so on its stderr (`hopper: took over the start lock <path>`). The start's own wait for the
  outcome is 10 minutes, so a start that waits the whole time still finishes.
- **Git's gc in the foreground.** Every git command under the lock runs with `gc.autoDetach=false` and
  `maintenance.autoDetach=false`, which `-c` passes on to the fetches a blobless checkout makes. Git's automatic gc and
  maintenance then run inside the lock, never beside another start's fetch or worktree add. `git worktree prune` before
  each add removes the entries of worktrees the reap removed.
- **A later start in the same sync pass** (`$6` 0, it fetches nothing) waits on the lock too, so it makes its worktree of
  what the first start's fetch got, not of what was there before it.

**Done when, as the issue says it:**
- A new job on a warm machine fetches only what changed on the default branch, or nothing in the same pass (issue #858).
- Concurrent jobs on one machine share the mirror without corrupting it: this section.
- The repo-query API is its own issue.

**Not done, and why.**
- **A fetch on push webhooks.** The hopper pulls. It takes only GitHub's `issues` deliveries, for intake (issue #1079,
  "GitHub deliveries"), not `push`. The fetch at a start, once per sync pass, is its pull.
- **Mounting the mirror read-only into job containers.** A job worktree writes to the common dir (its index, its commits,
  blobs fetched on demand), so a read-only mount cannot hold a job's worktree. Not built until a box needs one.
- **A lock around the job's own git.** A job's commits, fetches and pushes in its worktree are outside the lock; git's own
  ref and index locks cover them, and git keeps unreferenced objects for two weeks before a gc removes them.

**Residual risk, stated.** Two starts that find the same ended holder at the same moment can both take the lock. Then they
run at once, as every start did before; git's own locks still keep the repository sound.

Tests: `test/herdr/job-worktree-lock.test.ts` (real git and sh: a start waits while a live process holds the lock, then
makes its worktree and lets the lock go; a lock whose holder ended is taken over and said; six concurrent starts each get
a worktree at the remote's newest commit, and `git fsck` passes; a work tree that is the job's repository locks the same
way; a worktree there already is entered whatever holds the lock).

## Repo queries: jobs ask the hopper, not GitHub (issue #1074, 2026-10-13)

Owner requirement: a job reads GitHub through the hopper, never directly — a pull request's state, its diff, its
commits and its checks, an issue and its comments —, so jobs spend less of the rate limit, do not read again what the
hopper already read, and see the work as the work-item ledger (issue #1067) sees it. After issue #652 a job holds no
GitHub token, so its only reads were the proxy's `issue.view`, `pr.view`, `repo.view` and `check.log`, each one REST
call; a job that wanted a diff or its checks had no way but to ask a person or guess.

**The repo queries** (`src/github-proxy/policy.ts` `READS`, `api.ts`). Four reads more, each a `hopper-gh` command and an
op of `POST /job/github`, on any repository the connection sees (as every read, issue #1015), on the job's fork too;
the hopper's own job only, rate-limited as `pr.view` (120 an hour per job, 600 per machine):

| command | op | GitHub calls on a miss | answer beside `number` and `url` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pr diff N` | `pr.diff` | `GET …/pulls/N/files`, every page | `files` (file, status, additions, deletions, `from` when renamed); `diff`, each file's patch as `git diff` writes it, at most `MAX_DIFF_CHARS` (200 000; then `truncated`) |
| `pr commits N` | `pr.commits` | `GET …/pulls/N/commits`, every page | `commits` (sha, message, author, date) |
| `pr checks N` | `pr.checks` | the pull request, `GET …/commits/<head>/check-runs` (every page) and `…/status` | `state`, `merged`, `head`, `headSha`, `checks` (id — the `check log` job —, name, status, conclusion, url), `statuses` |
| `issue comments N` | `issue.comments` | `GET …/issues/N/comments`, every page | `comments` (id, author, createdAt, body, url): an issue's, or a pull request's conversation |
| `pr reviews N` | `pr.reviews` | `GET …/pulls/N/reviews`, every page (issue #1072 part 3) | `reviews` (id, author, state, body, submittedAt, url), `decision` (`approved`, `changes_requested`, `none`) |
| `run list [--branch B] [--event E]` | `run.list` | `GET …/actions/runs?branch=B&event=E`, one page of `RUN_LIST_MAX` (50), the newest (issue #2318) | no `number`; `url` (the repository's Actions page), `total` (how many runs match), `runs` (id, name, event, branch, headSha, status, conclusion, runNumber, runAttempt, createdAt, url) |
| `run view RUN` | `run.view` | `GET …/actions/runs/RUN` and `…/actions/runs/RUN/jobs`, every page (issue #2318) | the run's fields as in `run list`; `jobs` (id — the `check log` job —, name, status, conclusion, startedAt, completedAt, url), the latest attempt's |

`run list` and `run view` (issue #2318, `src/github-proxy/runs.ts`) read a run that no pull request names: a branch's
push runs, a release job's result. `pr checks` reads only a pull request's head commit. The cache key of `run list` also
names its branch and its event, so two lists of one repository are two answers. A run is never final: it is read again
once its answer is 30 s old.

The diff is built from the files' patches, not asked as `application/vnd.github.diff`: one JSON route, the file list
with it, and the same cap GitHub puts on patches (a file with none says so).

**The repo-query cache** (`src/github-proxy/repo-query.ts`, in the broker). Every read — the four above and `issue.view`,
`pr.view`, `repo.view`, `check.log` — is a **repo query**. After the token, the shape, the asker, the connection and the
rate limit (steps 1–5 of "GitHub through the hopper"), the broker looks for a kept answer under the query's key (op,
repository in lower case, number):
- kept less than `REPO_QUERY_FRESH_MS` (30 s) ago: answered from the cache, no GitHub call;
- a read of a pull request that is merged — its own answer said `merged: true`, or the job's user's work-item ledger
  says its pull request is merged and the answer was read at or after the ledger item's `stateSince` — : answered from
  the cache for as long as it is kept. A read from before the merge is what was there before it, so it is read again
  once;
- else GitHub, through the shared rate limiter, whose ETag (`If-None-Match`, issue #436) makes an unchanged answer a 304
  that GitHub does not charge; the answer is kept.

The cache is one per hopper, shared by every job: the reads all go through the one connection. It keeps at most
`REPO_QUERY_ENTRIES` (500) answers and `REPO_QUERY_CHARS` (20 000 000 characters of JSON), the oldest pushed out first;
an answer larger than that is not kept. A job's own write through the proxy (`issue.comment`, `issue.close`, `pr.ready`)
drops every answer about that issue or pull request, so the job reads what it wrote. In memory: a restart reads each
query once again. A connection that is gone answers 503 as before: nothing is served from the cache without one.

**Each answer says where it came from**: `source` (`github` or `cache`; `hopper` for `pr status`, issue #1072) and `readAt`, when GitHub was read for it.
Where the job's user's ledger holds the item — the issue by its key, a pull request by `byPullRequest` (its newest item)
— the answer also carries `ledger`: the item's `key`, `state`, `since` and, as known, `pullRequestState`, `issueState`
and `issueReason`. So a job sees GitHub's answer and the hopper's word on the work side by side. `github_proxy.done` of a
read records `source`: how many of a job's reads went to GitHub is a count of its own timeline.

**No direct reads.** The job rules' GitHub line (`GITHUB_PROXY_LINE`) names the new reads and says: "Read GitHub only
through the hopper: never curl api.github.com or a github.com page." `hopper-gh`'s help says the same, and how fresh an
answer is. A job has no token to read with (issue #652), and git goes through the hopper; the line closes the
unauthenticated way (public repositories answer without a token).

**Measured** (`test/github-proxy/repo-query.test.ts`). A job that, for 10 minutes, reads its pull request and its checks
every 10 seconds and its diff, its commits and its issue's comments every 2 minutes, its pull request merged at 5
minutes: **135** GitHub calls with no cache (every read a call, as before), **35** with it — checks and the pull request
11 each (every 30 s until the merge, then none), diff and commits 4 each, the comments 5. Two jobs that read the same
pull request share the answers. In the daemon (`test/integration/github-proxy.test.ts`): the second read of each of the
four new queries within 30 seconds reaches GitHub not at all, and a comment the job posts makes the next read of the
comments GitHub's.

**Declined, against the issue's text** (decisions recorded 2026-10-13). "Kept fresh by webhooks": the hopper takes no
inbound webhooks and pulls by design (issue #985 "Webhooks: not part of issue #985", "Remote access"); the cache is kept
fresh by its 30 s window, the ledger's merged state, the job's own writes and the free 304s. "Batched GraphQL only for
actively moving PRs": the in-motion cycle (issue #985 part 3) already reads the followed pull requests so; a job's
query reads REST, which the ETags make free when nothing changed. Answering `pr.view` and `pr.checks` from the in-motion
cycle's batch (`seen`) would spare more calls, but its rollup alone does not name the checks a job asks for; it is the
next step if the counts on Settings → GitHub rate limit (`job` kind) still show jobs' reads high.

| dir | owns | must not import |
|-----|------|-----------------|
| `src/github-proxy/repo-query.ts` | the repo-query cache: the key, when a kept answer answers, the bounds, what a write drops (pure but for the clock) | as `src/github-proxy/` |

Tests: `test/github-proxy/repo-query.test.ts` (the key, fresh and final answers, the ledger's merge before and after a
read, the bounds, a write's drop, who may ask, the broker's `source` and `ledger`, the measurement, no connection),
`test/integration/github-proxy.test.ts` (the four queries through the real daemon and `hopper-gh`, GitHub read once
each, the ledger's word, a write's drop), `test/store/work-items.test.ts` (`byPullRequest`).

## Component watchers (issue #1077, 2026-10-13)

The problem: drift between the hopper's state and reality — stale job states, wrong failure counts, stuck pull
requests — was found by people, late. The answer: a dedicated watcher per component, as in "Redesigning source
control" (Anthropic engineering). Each **component watcher** checks one component on its own interval against its
source of truth and reports **drift**: where the two disagree.

**The runner** (`src/component-watchers/service.ts`). One per user, in the user's runtime, beside the GitHub watches;
it starts and stops with it. Each watcher checks at start, then every `intervalMs`, one check at a time. A check
answers the drift by **kind**. A kind new since the check before is one `drift.found { watcher, kind, items }`; one gone
is one `drift.cleared { watcher, kind }`. A failed check keeps the drift as it was, stores why (`error`, logged once per
new problem) and records nothing. The drift lives in memory: a restart checks again at once, and a drift still there is
found again.

**The first watcher: ledger vs GitHub** (`src/component-watchers/ledger-github.ts`, every 15 minutes). It reads the
work-item ledger ("The work-item ledger") and compares each item no job or person acts on with GitHub. The sample
(`ledgerGitHubSample`, pure): the items in `pr_open`, `failed` and `partly_done` first, then the `done` and `dropped`
ones of the last 7 days, newest first, at most 100, each item's issue and its pull request. The read: one GraphQL call
per 50 URLs (`resource(url:)`, each URL a variable), with the user's own GitHub connection through `makeRequest`, so the
shared rate limiter paces it; it counts as a `reconcile` call. A URL GitHub does not answer for is no drift. The kinds
(`ledgerGitHubDrift`, pure), the first that fits each item:

- `failed_but_finished`: the ledger says `failed`; GitHub says its pull request merged, or its issue closed as
  completed. A wrong failure count.
- `pr_open_but_ended`: the ledger says `pr_open`; GitHub says its pull request merged or closed, or its issue closed. A
  stuck pull request.
- `pull_request_state`: the pull request state the ledger holds is not GitHub's (`abandoned` reads as closed).
- `issue_state`: the issue state the ledger holds is not GitHub's.

A close or a merge on GitHub newer than the grace (10 minutes) is no drift yet: the hopper's own follow may not have
seen it. An item a job or a person acts on is never drift: the events win while they last.

**The watchers of the hopper's own records** (`src/component-watchers/store-watchers.ts`, each every 5 minutes; the
comparisons `src/domain/drift-jobs.ts`, pure). The job record is their source of truth: the ledger is folded from a
job's events, and a Decision opens and frees a lane for a job. Each check reads the store in one synchronous pass, so no
event lands between its reads. A job or an item that changed in the last 5 minutes (the grace) is no drift yet. They
need no GitHub connection; only their drift issues do.

- **Ledger vs jobs** (`ledger-jobs`). It reads each item in an active state with the job it names, and each job not
  over with its item, when the item names that job. The kinds:
  - `active_but_job_ended`: the ledger says a job or a person acts on the item; its job ended, or there is no such job. A
    stale job state. A hand-off on that failed job (`needs_you`, `failedJobId` the job) is no drift.
  - `ended_but_job_active`: the ledger says the item ended (`pr_open`, `partly_done`, `done`, `failed`, `dropped`); its
    job is not over. The ledger missed a start.
  - `state_differs`: an active state the job's status does not give. `queued` and `held` give `queued`; `claimed` and
    `running` give `working`; `waiting_answer` gives `working` or `needs_you`; `parked` gives `needs_you`; `waiting_on`
    gives `waiting_outside` or `working`. An `operator_led` job is worked by hand: not checked.
- **Lanes vs jobs** (`lanes-jobs`). It reads every lane, and the jobs that are `claimed` or `running` or that a lane
  names. The kinds:
  - `lane_busy_job_not_running`: a busy or draining lane whose job is not `claimed` or `running`, or names no job. A
    stuck lane.
  - `job_running_no_lane`: a `claimed` or `running` job no busy or draining lane runs. A job idle while it runs.
- **Intake vs jobs** (`intake-jobs`; the comparison `src/domain/drift-intake.ts`, pure). Items that wait with no action.
  It reads each job source's status as the source sync keeps it (`statuses()`): the intake of its last sync, its sync
  times. The truth is the job records and the source's own timer. The kinds:
  - `taken_no_job`: the last sync took the item (no reason), and no job has its key. A sync makes the job of each item
    it takes in the same pass, so a taken item with no job waits for nothing. Read only once that sync ended more than the
    grace ago.
  - `sync_overdue`: no sync runs, and the source's next sync time is more than the grace past. Its timer stopped: no new
    item is taken.
  - `sync_stuck`: a sync runs, and the source's last sync ended more than 2 hours ago (`SYNC_STUCK_MS`). No new item is
    taken until it ends.

  A source that fails its syncs is not drift here: the source sync tells the owner of it already (`source.stalled`), and
  the cause is mostly outside the hopper. An item of these kinds is an issue's URL or a source's name, hashed in the issue
  as every item is.

**The cleanup: cleanup vs ended jobs** (`cleanup-jobs`, issue #2715; `src/component-watchers/store-watchers.ts`, every 5
minutes; the comparison `src/domain/drift-cleanup.ts`, pure). A thing an ended job left on a machine is a hopper bug, not
a person's chore. It reads the resource ledger's cleanup leftovers ("The resource ledger", `cleanupLeftoversOf`): each
ended job whose entry still failed once the grace period after its end passed is one item, its key the job's id, in one
kind per cause the reap named — `cleanup_mount`, `cleanup_process`, `cleanup_userns`, `cleanup_permission`,
`cleanup_cause_unknown` (no cause: an older client, or a failure before issue #2715), `cleanup_reap_failed` (the reap
did not run to its end). An entry whose machine is offline, or that no executor reaches, is no drift: the machine shows
it, and bringing a machine online is the one act a person has. No path and no machine goes in an item.

**The integration branch: default branches vs checks** (`branch-checks`; `src/component-watchers/branch-stack.ts`, every
15 minutes; the comparison `src/domain/drift-branches.ts`, pure). The hopper merges jobs into each job repository's
default branch, so a red one fails every job after it. The watcher reads the head commit of each job repository's
default branch (the user's job repositories, Sources) and its checks' rollup (`statusCheckRollup`), one GraphQL call per
50 repositories (`repository(owner:, name:)`, each owner and name a variable), with the user's own connection through
`makeRequest`, a `reconcile` call. A repository GitHub does not answer for, or a head with no checks, is no drift: a
repository with no checks is "Repositories with no checks". The kinds:

- `checks_failing`: the head's checks failed or errored, and it was committed more than the grace (15 minutes) ago: a
  re-run in the grace may still turn it green.
- `checks_stuck`: the head's checks are pending or expected, and it was committed more than 2 hours ago
  (`BRANCH_STUCK_MS`).

Each item is the repository, hashed in the issue as every item is; it says `default branch head` and the checks' state.

**The database and the stack: stack health** (`stack-health`; `src/component-watchers/branch-stack.ts`, every 5
minutes; the comparison `src/domain/drift-stack.ts`, pure). It reads the stack resources ("Stack resources") against what
a healthy stack is. The kinds:

- `service_down`: a container of the hopper's compose stack does not run, or runs `unhealthy`. A sandbox box is a job's,
  not the stack's: not read.
- `part_unreadable`: the containers, Postgres, OpenFGA or Solr do not answer. A part the hopper is not given (no runtime
  socket, no `HOPPER_OPENFGA_URL`, no `HOPPER_SOLR_URL`) is no drift. The item never says why a part does not answer: the
  why can name a host or a path.
- `database_strain`: Postgres holds 90% or more of its connection limit (`CONNECTIONS_HIGH`), or a transaction is open
  longer than 5 minutes (`LONG_TRANSACTION_S`).

The stack starts and restarts with the hopper, and the runner checks at start: so the watcher answers an item only once
two checks in a row found it. The stack is the instance's, not a user's: only the oldest user's runtime has this
watcher, so one drift issue tells it, and `GET /api/component-watchers` lists it (`instance: true`) only for the hopper's
admin, as `GET /api/resources`. Not **stack drift** ("Stack drift"), which compares the stack with its compose file.

Each drift item says what the component says (`says`) and what its source of truth says (`truth`); the drift issue's
table names the two columns after its watcher (`ledger` and `GitHub`, `ledger` and `job record`, `lane` and `job
record`, `intake` and `job record or sync timer`, `branch` and `checks`, `stack` and `healthy stack`). An item of `lanes-jobs` is a lane id or a job id, hashed in the issue as every item is.

**The drift issue.** With the user's setting on (`fileIssues`), each kind of drift is one issue on the hopper's own
repository (`REPORT_REPO`), through the user's own GitHub connection, as a bug report is ("Report a bug"): labelled
`user-report`, no assignee, so it never starts a job. Its body ends with its **drift key** (`Drift key:
<watcher>/<kind>`). Before it files, the runner looks for the open issue with that key in its body (`GET
/search/issues`, then the line itself), so a restart or a second hopper updates the issue it finds instead of filing
again. While the drift lasts, the issue's body is edited (`PATCH`) when what it lists changed; once it is gone, the
body says no item is in it now. A person closes it. Each write is one event: `drift.issue_filed` or
`drift.issue_updated { watcher, kind, number, url }`. A write that fails is stored (`issueError`) and tried again at
the next check. The text names no item, repository or person: an item's repository may be private, so each item is the
first 12 hex digits of the SHA-256 of its key, with what the ledger and GitHub say and since when; Settings → Component
watchers lists the items by key.

**The setting.** `fileIssues`, default off: the user's (`componentWatchers` in the user's settings), an admin's,
Settings → Component watchers (`POST /ui/api/component-watchers`), `component_watchers.settings_changed`. Off, a drift
is an event and a line in the panel only: a hopper filing on another repository with a person's account is that
person's choice. It applies at the next check.

**API.** `GET /api/component-watchers`: the setting, and each watcher with its last check and the drift it found now,
each item by key; an instance watcher only for the hopper's admin.

## GitHub deliveries (issue #1079, 2026-10-14)

A new issue, labelled and assigned, took up to the intake sync interval to show in Intake: on 2026-10-14 five issues filed
at 01:19 showed at 01:25. Intake reads the listing cache and lists a repository again only every `intakeSyncMinutes`
(default 15, "Repository listings"); nothing told the hopper that an issue changed. Owner decision on the issue: add
GitHub's webhook; most hoppers get no delivery without a relay, and that is accepted. This amends the earlier sign-offs that
the hopper takes no inbound webhooks (issues #967, #985).

**As built:**
- **The route** (`src/http/github-deliveries.ts`): `POST /github/webhook`, off `/api/`, behind the Host guard like every route,
  never with a session. GitHub signs each delivery's body with the **GitHub webhook secret** (HMAC-SHA256,
  `X-Hub-Signature-256`). The check is node:crypto's HMAC and `timingSafeEqual`: a library for it carries more than the few
  lines it replaces. Only JSON (415 else, saying to set the content type). No secret: 404, nothing taken. No signature or a
  wrong one: 401, counted and said on the page, nothing done. A delivery id (`X-GitHub-Delivery`) taken before is taken
  once (200): the last 500 ids are kept in memory.
- **What it takes:** `issues` deliveries whose action can change intake — opened, edited, labeled, unlabeled, assigned,
  unassigned, closed, reopened (`deliveryTarget`, `src/domain/github-deliveries.ts`). `ping` 200; any other event 202,
  counted as not read. `pull_request`, `check_suite` and `push` come later, as the work-item ledger needs them (#1067).
- **What it does** (the hopper still pulls): for each user, `SourceRegistry.repoChanged(repo)` asks each running source
  whether the repository is one of its job repositories, as its last discover scanned them (`JobSource.repoChanged`). Each
  that says yes marks the repository due in its listing (`IntakeListing.markDue`) and syncs once `DELIVERY_SYNC_MS` (2 s)
  after the first delivery of a burst — GitHub sends opened, labeled and assigned together. That sync is a timed one: it
  lists only the repositories due, so the one named, and reads its new issues as any discover does. No other GitHub read is
  made. The delivery is a `source.delivery_received` in that user's log, with the sources that took it; none for a
  repository no source of the user takes. It changes no job, question, webhook or setting.
- **The work-item ledger** (issue #1067, part 3): a delivery that closed or reopened an issue that is one of a user's work
  items is also a `work_item.issue_closed` (with GitHub's `state_reason`) or `work_item.issue_reopened` in that user's log,
  which moves the item in the event's transaction; none when the ledger holds that state already. That is a read model
  moving, not a job, a question, a webhook or a setting.
- **The timed listing stays** as the fallback for a delivery that never comes. A listing a delivery made resets that
  repository's interval, so timed listings per hour do not rise.
- **The secret** is a system secret of the instance's vault (`github-webhook-secret`, kind `github-webhook`), the whole
  hopper's: the hopper's admin makes it on **Settings → GitHub webhook** (`POST /ui/api/github-deliveries`, `make`): 32
  random bytes, hex, answered once (`generatedSecret`); a second make rotates it, and the old one is refused from then.
  `remove` takes it away, so nothing is taken. Never kept in a vault backend: it is the whole hopper's. `GET
  /api/github-deliveries` shows the path, the events, the secret's metadata, what came in since the start, and the last
  refusal's reason; instance admin only.
- **How GitHub reaches the hopper.** Most hoppers are on loopback or a LAN. A relay on a computer that reaches the hopper
  sends the deliveries on: the page shows the payload URL (this page's origin and `/github/webhook`) and a GitHub CLI
  command for one (`gh webhook forward --repo=OWNER/NAME --events=issues --url=… --secret=…`). A hopper behind a reverse
  proxy at its public URL takes them from GitHub direct. The remote access tunnel lets only the API paths through
  ("Remote access"), so not these: through it, use a relay too. The relay must send the hopper's Host (the Host guard).
- **Why not the hopper's app's webhook.** The connected-account sources go through the hopper's app, one GitHub App for
  every hopper ("Sign in with GitHub"): an app has one webhook URL, so it cannot reach each hopper. A repository webhook,
  or the admin's own `github-app` source's webhook, pointed at a relay or the public URL, does.

**Residual risk, stated.** `/github/webhook` is reachable by anyone who reaches the hopper. Without the secret a request
does nothing but count as refused; with it, the most a delivery does is a sync of the repository it names, which a
person's Sync now does too. A replay of a signed delivery with a new id starts one more sync; the debounce keeps it to one
per source every 2 s.

Tests: `test/sources/github-repo-changed.test.ts` (the repository named is listed at the next timed sync, only it; a
repository not the source's is not; case; app mode), `test/sources/sync-repo-changed.test.ts` (one due sync per burst,
after `DELIVERY_SYNC_MS`; a source that takes none does not sync), `test/integration/github-deliveries.test.ts` (the real
server and database: no secret, 404; a wrong or missing signature, 401 and nothing done; a signed delivery syncs its source
and is recorded; a redelivery is taken once; another repository, `ping` and `push` record nothing; rotate and remove; only
the admin makes the secret), `test/ui/github-deliveries.test.ts`.

## Change reads (issue #1125, 2026-10-14)

A new issue, labelled and assigned in a job repository, did not reach Intake for hours on 2026-10-14; the `github-app`
source's sync passes asked GitHub nothing (`REST 0, GraphQL 0`). Two causes, both in `src/sources/github/listing.ts`:
- **Nothing noticed a change between listings.** Intake lists a repository again only every **intake sync interval**
  ("Repository listings"); a **GitHub delivery** ("GitHub deliveries") makes it due sooner, but most hoppers run locally
  and get none.
- **A failed repository stayed failed while another source listed it.** The **listing cache** is the user's, one row per
  repository, shared by the user's GitHub sources. A repository was due again once its last listing *or* its last failed
  ask was older than the interval, the newer of the two. While the `github-account` source listed it every interval, a
  repository the `github-app` source failed to list was never due for the app: it said the old error, and its issues were
  never in the app's intake.

Owner decision on the issue: a GitHub webhook is an optional accelerator, off by default. The default path is the hopper's
own reads, made cheap: conditional requests (a `304` costs no call), `since=`, a modest interval, feeding what a delivery
feeds.

**As built:**
- **The change read** (`GitHubApi.issuesChangedSince`, both adapters; `src/sources/github/app/rest.ts`):
  `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues?state=all&sort=updated&direction=desc&per_page=100&since=<t>`, where `t` is the listing's
  `since` (GitHub's clock, never the hopper's): the newest `updatedAt` of an issue its listing held when read, then the newest
  issue change each change read answered. The same `t` is the same URL, so
  the shared rate limiter's ETag cache makes it a conditional request: while nothing changed, GitHub answers `304`, which
  costs no call. An **intake call** (it waits at the intake reserve) that never waits: a call that would wait is not made
  (`deferAfterMs: 0`).
- **When:** in a timed sync (`discover({ due: true })`, every `pollSeconds`, default 60), for each job repository that is not
  due, has a listing, and did not fail; at most once a minute a repository (`CHANGE_READ_EVERY_MS`), however often the
  source syncs. A sync a person asked for lists every repository and makes none.
- **What it does** (`readChanges`): it makes the repository due, as a delivery does, when it names an open issue with the
  source's label that the listing does not hold, a listed issue now closed or without the label, or a full page (more may
  have changed). A listed issue changed otherwise — its title, body, comments, labels or assignees, the hopper's own label
  writes too — has its row read in place (title, labels, assignees, `updatedAt`), so its **listed reads** go to GitHub
  again and no new listing is made. Pull requests are the listing's and the in-motion cycle's: a change read skips them.
  A change read that fails (a rate limit, a network error) changes nothing; the timed listing stays.
- **A failed repository** is due again an interval after this source asked, whatever another source's listing keeps fresh.
  It is not change-read.
- **Intake says why** (`ui/src/views/intake.tsx`, `intakeTrouble`): a paused source has its panel, with why it lists
  nothing (`Not listing issues: …`); a source whose last sync failed says so, with its error; each job repository its last
  sync could not list is named with what GitHub said (`repoErrors`). Before, a paused source had no panel and the
  repository errors showed nowhere.
- **Cost:** one REST call a repository a minute, almost all `304` (free); GitHub charges one for each credential (an
  installation token lasts an hour; the ETag cache is per credential) and one more when an issue changed. A GraphQL listing
  only when GitHub says the repository has a change intake must take. At 60 repositories for an hour,
  `test/integration/github-budget.test.ts` holds it: the charged change reads are 60 for each installation token and the
  changed repositories' few. The pass line counts the change reads (`REST`), so a source that is not paused and has a job
  repository shows them at least once a minute.

**Where a change read starts (issue #1276, 2026-10-15).** New labelled issues did not reach intake until the next listing,
up to the intake sync interval later. `t` was the newest `updatedAt` of the listing's rows, and a **listed read** of one issue
(a job, a follow or a discover reads its in-flight issues every pass) set that issue's row to its current `updatedAt`. The
hopper's own labels and comments change those issues all the time, so `t` jumped past issues no change read had seen, and
GitHub never answered them. Now the cursor is its own column, `github_listings.since` (tenant migration 63): a listing sets it
to the newest issue change it holds, a change read moves it to the newest issue change it answered, and nothing else moves
it — a read of one issue proves nothing of the others. A pull request's change moves no `since`, as a change read skips
pull requests, so its `304` stays. A listing the build before kept has no `since`: its rows' newest stands in until the
next listing. Test: `test/sources/github-change-read.test.ts`.

**Not here:** closes and reopens of a work item's issue move the work-item ledger through a delivery or the ledger's
fallback read (issue #1067 part 3); a close or reopen a change read sees makes the repository due, and intake drops or
lists the issue, but it records no ledger event (issues #1105, #1126).

## Landing batches (issue #1073, 2026-10-14)

**The problem.** Job pull requests merged straight into `dev`, each gated on the full test suite. That was slow: every
pull request waited for about 4 minutes of shards, jobs stalled behind the same failures, and `dev` was still never
tested as a whole — two pull requests with green checks could break each other (the merge gate only stops merge
conflicts, "PR tending without lanes").

**The branch model.** `main` (the **landing branch**) → `dev` (the **tested branch**) → `beta` → `stable`. A
job's pull request merges into `main` after the fast checks only: the gates (typecheck, lint, the UI build,
What's new) and the test files its change affects (`.github/workflows/pr.yml` job `affected`, `vitest run --changed
HEAD^1`, in the full suite's ten shards, issue #1104; issue #1038). The full suite runs on `main`'s tip as a **batch run**, and a green batch run moves
`dev` by the whole batch in one merge. `dev` → `beta` → `stable` stays as it is (`scripts/promote.sh`). `main` is
no update channel: no hopper follows it.

**The landing branch is a setting, not the default branch** (issue #1142). Each repository's settings name it
(`landing`, `main` when left out, so a setting saved before it reads `main`). The runner never reads GitHub's default
branch. Before, it did, and a repository whose default branch was still its tested branch ran no batch at all: every pass
stopped on that `problem`, so merges into `main` piled up and `dev` never moved, with no check run on `main`'s tip.
Other parts of the hopper still read the default branch for a pull request's base — a job's work tree, `hopper-gh pr
create` with no `--base`, the tending queue's rebase —, so a job may open its pull request into the tested branch. The
runner moves each such job pull request to the landing branch at its next pass ("Job pull requests move to the landing
branch" below), so it lands there all the same. A landing branch that is the tested branch runs no batch and says so
(`problem`). Since `main` is a branch no job pushes to (`RELEASE_BRANCHES`), a job pushes its own branch and opens its
pull request into `main`.

**What a pass costs when nothing is new.** The runner reads the landing branch's tip (`GET …/git/ref/heads/<landing>`)
and the compare of the tested branch with that tip. Both go through the shared rate limiter, which sends the ETag of the
last answer (`If-None-Match`): an unchanged tip and an unchanged tested branch answer 304, which GitHub does not charge.
No webhook is needed: a GitHub delivery is optional. The last tip tested is an event (`landing_batch.promoted` or
`.failed`, "The state" below), so the same tip never runs twice, after a restart too.

**The settings** (`landingBatches`, the user's, `POST /ui/api/landing-batches`, an admin's, Settings → Landing
batches): per repository (`owner/repo`, lowercased), `landing` (the landing branch, default `main`), `tested` (the tested branch), `everyMerges` (N, default 5) and
`everyMinutes` (the timer, default 60). Read at each pass, so a change applies with no restart
(`landing_batches.changed`).

**When a batch run starts** (`batchDue`, pure). The runner (`src/landing-batches/runner.ts`) passes once at start and
every 2 minutes, for each repository the settings name. It reads the landing branch's tip and compares the tested
branch with it (`GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/compare/{tested}...{tip}`): the commits ahead, and the pull requests among
them, from their merge commits (`Merge pull request #N …`). No run while one is at work. **Skip when nothing is
new:** no run when the landing branch has nothing the tested branch lacks, or when its tip is the last tip a batch run
tested (a red batch with no merge since) — whatever the timer or N say, so an idle period starts no full suite and
promotes nothing. Else a run starts with no batch run before, after `everyMerges` merges, or `everyMinutes` after the
last batch run started.

**A batch run.** A branch `hopper-batch/<tip, 12 characters>` made at the tip (by sha, so the tip tested is the tip
compared), and a pull request of it into the tested branch, neutral text that lists the pull requests in the batch.
`pr / test` runs on it with the full suite, as on every pull request into `dev`. No job pushes to a batch run's branch
(`checkPush`): what its checks test is what the hopper merges. `landing_batch.started` records the tip, the branch, the
pull request and the merges. Each pass then reads the pull request and its check runs on the tip (`batchChecks`,
pure):

- every check completed and none failed: **green**. The hopper merges the pull request with a merge commit, only while
  its head is still the tip (`sha`), and removes the branch: `landing_batch.promoted`. `dev`'s head is then the merge
  of a pull request whose checks passed, which is what a hopper on the `dev` channel updates to ("What a hopper updates
  to").
- a check failed (or was cancelled or timed out), no check in 30 minutes, merge conflicts with the tested branch, or
  its branch moved: **red**. The hopper closes the pull request and removes the branch: `landing_batch.failed` with the
  reason and the checks (`checkRuns`: with their ids). The tested branch does not move, and the same tip does not run
  again. When checks failed, a bisect within the batch starts ("A red batch" below); with merge conflicts, a back-merge
  ("Merge conflicts: the back-merge" below).
- a person merged it first: `landing_batch.promoted` with no merge commit; closed without a merge: failed.

**Job pull requests move to the landing branch.** Each pass, an open pull request of one of the user's jobs whose base
is the tested branch is moved to the landing branch (`PATCH …/pulls/{n}` `base`, `landing_batch.retargeted`), so the
pull requests jobs opened before the switch land there too. A pull request that is no job's is left as it is, and so is
the hopper's own (a batch run, a bisect, a back-merge: its branch starts `hopper-batch/`), even when a job named it
(issue #1311): its head is a landing branch tip, so GitHub refuses the move. A move GitHub refuses skips only that pull
request: the others move and the batch run goes on, and the refusal is logged once, not on every pass.

**The state.** Every step is an event (`landing_batch.started`, `.promoted`, `.failed`, `.retargeted`, `.stuck`,
`.restarted`, `landing_batches.changed`); the state of each repository — the batch run at work, the last tip tested and the last tip
promoted, when the last run started, how it ended — is reduced from them (`landingBatchStates`, pure). The last tested
tip and the last promoted commit are therefore events, not a table. `GET /api/landing-batches` answers the settings and
each configured repository's state with what the last pass found (`why` no run started, or the `problem`); Settings →
Landing batches shows it.

**A stuck landing pass, and how it is recovered** (issue #1333). The problem: the landing pass stopped on a 422 when it
moved its own batch pull request (#1311). The fix merged into `main`, but the running hopper updates from `dev`, and
`dev` moves only through the landing pass: the stuck pass held back its own fix, and `main` was 172 commits ahead of
`dev`. The batch run was green the whole time; the pass never reached its merge. A person closed it on GitHub by hand.
Now:

- **One step's error never stops the others.** A pass of a repository is steps (`passRepo`): the move of job pull
  requests to the landing branch, the batch run at work (read, merged on green, ended on red), the bisect, the culprit's
  revert, the back-merge, the start of a batch run. A step that throws is a problem of the pass, and the next step still
  runs; a move or a comment GitHub refuses never holds a green batch run back. The pass's `problem` lists each step that
  failed, with its error.
- **A pass that fails the same way again is surfaced.** The runner keeps, in memory, the run of passes that ended with
  the same `problem`. At `LANDING_BATCH_STUCK_PASSES` (3, about 6 minutes) the pass is **stuck**:
  `landing_batch.stuck { repo, error, since, passes }`, once per run of failures, and the repository's view has `stuck`
  while it lasts. Needs you's **Landing** row lists each stuck repository with its error, and links to Settings →
  Landing batches, which shows it too. A changed error is logged once, not on every pass. A pass with no problem ends the
  run; a restart of the hopper finds it again after 3 passes.
- **Restart batch is the way out, with no hand edit on GitHub.** `POST /ui/api/landing-batches/restart { repo }`, an
  admin's, on Settings → Landing batches while a batch run or a bisect is at work, or the pass is stuck. It records
  `landing_batch.restarted { repo, tip, by, closed }` at once and answers (issue #1194): the event ends the batch run and
  the bisect at work in the state, and the next batch run starts at once (`restarted`, `batchDue`), at the landing
  branch's tip, the same tip too. After the answer, and after the pass in flight, the runner closes their pull requests,
  removes their branches and passes. A close or a removal GitHub refuses is logged and the restart goes on: a removed
  branch closes its pull request all the same. A culprit's revert or a back-merge that waits still holds the next batch
  run: each has its own way out (a person reverts or merges by hand). Not a box action: it starts no job and merges
  nothing itself; the new batch run's merge is the runner's, on green, as for any batch run.
- **Not built.** An automatic restart after N refusals on the batch pull request: a stuck pass now goes to a person, with
  the error. Once the step isolation above is in, a refusal on one step no longer stops the merge of a green batch, so
  the case that needed it is gone.

**A stop between a GitHub call and its record** (issue #1589). Each step was a GitHub write, then its event. A hopper
that stopped between them lost the record of what GitHub did: the next pass opened a pull request again (GitHub refused
it with 422, and the repository was stuck), read a batch run it had closed as "closed without a merge" (its failed checks
lost, no bisect), opened a second revert, filed a second issue, or left `stable` moved with the canary still running.
Now the record comes first, or the write is found before it is made again:

- **A batch run is recorded due** (`landing_batch.due`: the tip, the branch, the merges, the issues its text closes, why)
  before its branch and pull request. A pass that finds a due batch run with no `landing_batch.started` starts that one,
  not a new one at a newer tip.
- **A pull request is opened once** (`openOnce`, `src/landing-batches/once.ts`): when GitHub refuses it, the open pull
  request from the same head branch into the same base is the one. This is the batch run's, the bisect run's and the
  back-merge's; their branches are named by a sha, so the branch is the key. Making a branch that is there moves it to
  the sha (`createBranch`), so a back-merge's merge is made again on a branch a stopped pass left.
- **An end is recorded before its close.** `landing_batch.failed` (with the bisect's start or the culprit, whose points
  are read first) and `landing_batch.bisect_tested` come before the removal of the run's branch and the close of its pull
  request; `landing_batch.restarted` lists the ones it ends. The state keeps these pull requests (`closedRuns`), and each
  pass closes the ones still open among the open pull requests into the tested branch it reads anyway. The branch goes
  first (issue #1954 part 8): GitHub closes a pull request whose branch is removed, so a stop between the two leaves
  neither. The other way, a stop after the close left the branch of a closed pull request, which no pass reads again. Merge conflicts
  record the back-merge due with the failure (`conflicts`), and a pass starts a due back-merge.
- **A revert and an issue are found first.** Before GitHub's revert of the culprit, the open pull request into the
  landing branch with the revert's title; before a fix issue, a back-merge issue or a canary issue, the open issue with
  its title and the hopper label changed since the culprit, the failure or the hold (`findIssue`: the issues list, which
  shows a new issue at once, not the search).
- **`stable` already at the candidate** while the canary runs records `landing_batch.canary_promoted`: a pass moved it
  and stopped, or a maintainer did.

No outbox: each write's intent is an event the state already reads, or the step's own state (a culprit with no revert, a
held canary with no issue). A merge needs nothing: the next pass reads the pull request merged.

**A red batch** (part 2, `src/landing-batches/red.ts`, the rules `src/domain/landing-bisect.ts`, pure). Only failing
checks say that the batch itself fails; a red batch for no check in time waits for the next merge as before, and one with
merge conflicts gets a back-merge (below). A **cut-off check** (issue #2086) is no failing check: GitHub cancelled it,
or it passed its time limit (`cancelled`, `timed_out`; a test shard at the job's limit), so the run says nothing of the
tests. The check to require fails with it, so one cut-off check makes the whole run cut off (`batchChecks` kind
`cut-off`), whatever else failed. A cut-off batch run is recorded failed with `cutOff`, closed, and starts no bisect;
the next pass runs the same tip again (`batchDue`, "batch run #N was cut off"), at most `BATCH_RERUNS` (2) times in a
row. Then the tip waits for a new merge, as a tip tested already: a cut-off check never bisects, never makes a culprit,
never reverts and never files a fix issue, because CI timing on a shared runner is no behaviour of the code. A cut-off
bisect run is `unknown` with `cutOff`: its point runs again, at most `BATCH_RERUNS` times, and only then the bisect
ends with no culprit. A run with a failed test and a cut-off check runs again too: the run after it, with no cut-off
check, bisects as before. When checks failed:

1. **The batch's points.** The hopper compares the tested branch with the failed tip and walks the landing branch's
   first-parent line back from the tip (`batchPoints`): each point is the merge of one pull request (its number from
   `Merge pull request #N …`) or a direct commit, oldest first. The tip is known to fail, the tested branch to pass.
   One point: it is the **culprit** at once. More: `landing_batch.bisect_started` with the points and the failed checks.
2. **The bisect** (`bisectNext`), one step a pass. A **bisect run** tests the point in the middle of the good and the
   bad end: a branch `hopper-batch/bisect-<sha, 12 characters>` at it (under the batch prefix, so no job pushes to it)
   and a pull request of it into the tested branch, so the full suite runs on that point as on a batch run
   (`landing_batch.bisect_run`). The hopper reads its checks as a batch run's; when they end it closes the pull request
   and removes the branch, never merging it: `landing_batch.bisect_tested`, `good` (the good end moves to it) or `bad`
   (the bad end moves to it, with the checks that failed there). A run with no verdict (no check in time, merge
   conflicts, its branch moved, closed by a person) is `unknown` and ends the bisect with no culprit: the batch waits
   for the next merge. A batch of N points takes at most ⌈log₂ N⌉ bisect runs. With one point left between the ends,
   the bad end is the **culprit**: `landing_batch.culprit`, with its pull request, the checks that failed at it and
   the bisect's results.
3. **The revert.** The culprit's pull request — the one its merge names, else the merged pull request GitHub gives for
   the commit (`GET …/commits/{sha}/pulls`, so a squash merge counts too) — is reverted through GitHub's own revert
   (GraphQL `revertPullRequest`): a pull request into the landing branch, neutral text (`revertText`),
   `landing_batch.revert_opened`. Each pass then merges it (a merge commit, only at its head) until GitHub lets it —
   branch protection may want its checks first —: `landing_batch.reverted`. A direct commit, a refused revert, or a
   revert closed without a merge is `landing_batch.revert_failed` with the reason: a person reverts it by hand.
4. **The fix issue.** Once, through the user's own connection: an issue on the repository with the hopper label,
   assigned to the user's connected account, so Intake takes it like any other work (`landing_batch.fix_filed`). Its
   text (`fixIssueText`) names the culprit's pull request and the issue its body closes or is part of, the revert (or
   why there is none), each failing check with the last 60 lines of its log (GitHub Actions' job log, masked:
   `logTail`), and the bisect's results. It names no person.
5. **The rest promoted.** While the bisect is at work, or the revert of a pull request waits, no batch run starts
   (`batchDue`). Once the revert merged, the next batch run starts at once (`revertedSinceRun`), whatever N or the timer
   say: the landing branch with the culprit reverted, so a green run moves the rest of the batch to the tested branch.
   A second culprit in it is found the same way.

**Cost.** One full run per batch. A red batch costs a run, plus at most ⌈log₂ N⌉ bisect runs and one run again after
the revert.

**The landing stage of a work item** (part 3, `src/domain/work-item-landing.ts`, pure). The ledger ("The work-item
ledger") reads the `landing_batch.*` events too. So the row of each work item whose job's pull request merged into the
landing branch says where that pull request stands on its way to the tested branch: its `landing` stage, beside its
state (which stays `done`, as the merge made it). A landing event names a repository and pull requests by number — a
batch's `merges`, a bisect's `points`, a culprit, a revert's `culpritPullRequest` — or the tip of their batch. The store
folds it into each item of that repository with a merged pull request (`applyLanding`), in the transaction that appends
it, and a rebuild replays it the same way. The stages:

| Stage | Set by | Means |
|---|---|---|
| `waiting` | `landing_batch.pending`; a red batch run, a bisect with no verdict, or a culprit that is another | merged into the landing branch; waits for a batch run |
| `batch_run` | `landing_batch.started` naming it (`tip`, `batch`) | in the batch run at work |
| `bisecting` | `landing_batch.bisect_started` naming it | in a red batch that a bisect tests |
| `culprit` | `landing_batch.culprit`, or the `landing_batch.revert_opened` of its pull request (`revert`) | the first change of its batch that fails |
| `reverted` | `landing_batch.reverted` of its batch | reverted from the landing branch; `landing_batch.fix_filed` adds `fixIssue` |
| `promoted` | `landing_batch.promoted` of its batch run | on the tested branch |

A culprit or a reverted one stays so: later batches name its merge again (its revert is a commit of its own), and move
it no more. A new job of the item (`job.queued`) clears the stage, as it clears what GitHub said.

**`landing_batch.pending`.** The runner records the merges beyond the tested branch that wait for a batch run. It does so
at a pass that starts none (`batchDue` says no), and only when they differ from the last ones recorded
(`pendingChanged`; a batch run started clears them). So the ledger knows that a merge waits before a batch run carries
it, and an idle repository records nothing new. Tenant migration 56 rebuilds the ledger once, so the landing events
recorded before it set each item's stage.

**On the Pull requests view.** `GET /api/pull-requests` answers `landing` (`landingCards`): each item with a landing
stage that is not `promoted`, a `reverted` one for a week, the newest stage first. The view lists them under
**Landing**, each with its pull request, its stage in plain words, its fix issue and how long ago.

**Merge conflicts: the back-merge** (part 4, `src/landing-batches/back-merge.ts`, the state and text
`src/domain/landing-back-merge.ts`, pure). A job's pull request with merge conflicts against the landing branch is
tended as before ("PR tending without lanes"): its base is the landing branch. What tending cannot see is a conflict
between the two branches themselves: a batch run with merge conflicts says the tested branch has a change the landing
branch lacks (a fix pushed to it, a pull request merged into it by a person), and every later batch run would have the
same conflicts, so the tested branch would never move again. So, after `landing_batch.failed` for merge conflicts:

1. **The back-merge.** A branch `hopper-batch/back-merge-<tip, 12 characters>` at the failed tip (under the batch prefix,
   so no job pushes to it), and the tested branch merged into it by GitHub's own merge (`POST …/merges`). Merged: a
   pull request of it into the landing branch, neutral text (`backMergeBody`), `landing_batch.back_merge_opened`.
2. **Its merge.** Each pass merges it (a merge commit, only at its head) once GitHub lets it — branch protection may want
   the fast checks first —, and removes its branch: `landing_batch.back_merged`. While it is open no batch run starts;
   once merged, the next one starts at once (`backMergedSinceRun`), whatever N or the timer say. Closed without a merge:
   `landing_batch.back_merge_failed`, and the next merge starts a batch run as usual.
3. **A real conflict.** GitHub answers 409: it cannot merge the two. The branch is removed, `landing_batch.back_merge_failed`
   with `conflict: true`, and one issue is filed through the user's own connection — the hopper label, assigned to their
   connected account, so Intake takes it (`landing_batch.back_merge_issue_filed`). Its text (`backMergeIssueText`) says
   which batch run had the conflicts and what to do: a branch of the landing branch, the tested branch merged into it, each
   conflict resolved, a pull request into the landing branch. While that issue stands — until a back-merge or a batch run
   is promoted — a later batch run with the same conflicts files none. GitHub answers 204 (nothing to merge: the landing
   branch has the tested branch already, so GitHub's `mergeable` was stale): `back_merge_failed`, no issue.

Not taken: the base merge of the hopper's mirror ("The base merge"), which also resolves additions files. It works on a
pull request inside a source's sync pass, with that pass's fetch; the batch runner has neither, and a back-merge is rare.
A conflict in an additions file therefore files the issue, and a job resolves it.

## Issues fixed on the landing branch (issue #1175, 2026-10-14)

**The problem.** A job's pull request merges into the landing branch (`main`), but GitHub closes an issue from a closing
keyword only on a merge into the default branch (the tested branch, `dev`), and a batch run's pull request carried no
closing keyword. So the issue stayed open after its fix merged. The follow put `hopper:done` on it, and the next sync took
an open issue with `hopper:done` whose job ended for a reopened one: a **reopened card** asked for approval again, and an
approval ran a second job on work already done. A culprit's revert, meanwhile, left its item `done`.

**Waits on its batch** (`awaitsBatch`, `src/domain/work-item-landing.ts`, pure). An item waits on its batch while it is
`done` by a merged pull request of a repository with landing batches, and its landing stage is `waiting`, `batch_run` or
`bisecting` — or it has none yet and it is done for at most an hour (`LANDING_UNSEEN_MS`): the runner names a merge within
one pass, so an older merge with no stage predates the batches, and a reopen of its issue is a person's. Its ledger state
stays `done`. A sync (`awaitingBatch`, `src/sources/github/origin.ts`) says such an issue is "done: merged into the landing
branch; its batch run closes the issue", in the pull request waiting group, with no action: no reopened card, so no
approval and no job. The source asks through `IntakeContext.awaitsBatch`, which the user's store answers from the ledger
and the landing batch settings.

**The batch run closes the issues.** A batch run's pull request text (`batchBody`) ends with `Closes <ref>` for each issue
its job pull requests close (`batchClosingIssues`): of the batch's merges, the ledger's `done` items with a merged pull
request — not a part (`partly_done`), not a culprit or reverted one (`failed`, below) — whose issue is not closed, `#N` in
the batch's repository, `owner/name#N` in another, in the order of the merges. Its merge into the tested branch is a merge
into the default branch, so GitHub closes them, as it would close the issue of a pull request merged there: the hopper
itself closes no issue. A red batch run is closed, not merged, and closes nothing. The bisect's runs are never merged.

**A culprit is not done** (`stateOf`, `src/domain/work-items.ts`). An item whose landing stage is `culprit` or `reverted`
(`isLandingUndone`) is `failed`, whatever its issue says, until a new job takes it over (`job.queued` clears the stage):
its change is off the landing branch. Its row names its fix issue (`landing.fixIssue`), and Pull requests → Landing lists
it. The ledger settles the state at each landing event (`applyLandingEvent`). Its issue is open (the batch that carried it
was red, so nothing closed it), and its item waits on no batch, so the next sync offers it as a reopened card: a person
runs it again, or lets the fix issue's job do the work. Tenant migration 59 rebuilds the ledger, so a culprit recorded
before it is failed too.

Not taken: the hopper closing each issue itself after a promotion. That is a GitHub write of the hopper's own, and the
rule is that the merge closes an issue, never the hopper ("GitHub text is neutral" in `AGENTS.md`). An issue closed
before this change whose fix was reverted (the old path) is not reopened: its fix issue carries the work. Issue #1232
takes it for the one case the batch run's text misses (below).

## A promoted item is done (issue #1232, 2026-10-15)

**The problem.** An item of three parts: its first part merged into the landing branch and was promoted with its batch.
Its last pull request ("Closes #N") merged later, and at once Intake offered the issue as a reopened card, waiting for
approval. Its batch run carried no closing keyword for it (the item was not `done` any more), so the issue stayed open
after the promotion too, and the card stayed.

**Why #1175 missed it.** The ledger kept one landing stage per item. The first part's `promoted` stayed on the item when its
next pull request merged, so `awaitsBatch` read that pull request as promoted already, waiting on no batch. The next
`landing_batch.pending` did not move it either: `pending` moves only an item with no stage or one `waiting`.

**A landing stage is of one pull request.** `ItemLanding.pullRequest` names the pull request the stage is of; `applyLanding`
sets it at each event. `landingOf` gives the item's stage only when it is of the item's pull request (a stage folded before,
with no number, counts as the item's): `awaitsBatch`, `stateOf`, `batchClosingIssues` and the Landing list read it. A new
merge thus has no stage until a landing event names it, and waits on its batch like any other. Tenant migration 60
rebuilds the ledger, so every stage names its pull request.

**A promoted item whose issue is still open is closed** (`promotedOpen`, `src/domain/work-item-landing.ts`; `closePromoted`,
`src/sources/github/origin.ts`). At a sync, an open issue with `hopper:done` (the follow puts it on only for a merge that
did the whole item, or every declared part) whose item's pull request its batch run promoted, while the ledger does not
hold its issue closed, is closed by the hopper as completed, with no comment. The sync records the close
(`work_item.issue_closed`, `via: landing`) and lists the item as "done: promoted to the tested branch with its batch; the
issue is closed". It opens no reopened card, and a stale one is withdrawn (`source.request_withdrawn`), so the item reads
`done` again: a withdrawn card with a merged pull request settles to `done`, not `dropped`. A close that fails is said on
the item and asked again at the next sync, still with no card. The item's state may be `done` or `waiting_for_approval`
(the stale card): no person's reopen gives it a promoted stage of its own pull request, because a reopen after a close
ends the landing stage (`applyRead`), and an issue the ledger holds closed is never closed again. A reopen the hopper never
saw (no delivery, no read between the close and the reopen) is taken for an open issue once: the hopper closes it, records
it, and the next reopen is a reopened card.

**A part.** An item whose last merge was a part (`partly_done`) has no `hopper:done`: the next sync takes its next part as
before, and none of this applies.

## Waits on its batch, read from GitHub (issue #1337, 2026-10-15)

**The problem.** A job pull request merged into the landing branch (`main`) while the default branch is `dev`. GitHub
closes an issue only on a merge into the default branch, so the issue stayed open until the batch run's merge. In that
window the done-check said "no pull request closes or references it" (the issue's timeline showed no cross-reference of
the merge, and a job made after the merge did not count an older merge), and the job went to Needs a person. Intake offered
such issues again as requests, and their approval ran jobs that found nothing to do.

**Why #1175 and #1232 missed it.** Both read the work-item ledger (`awaitsBatch`, `promotedOpen`). The ledger knows the
merge only when the hopper saw it: a merge it missed, or an item a failed done-check left not `done`, waits on nothing.

**One rule, read from GitHub** (`waitsOnBatch`, `src/sources/github/batch-wait.ts`). An open issue of a
repository with a landing branch **waits on its batch** when an open batch run (`hopper-batch/…`) closes it in
its text, or a pull request merged into the landing branch that closes it (a closing keyword) is listed in an open batch
run's text, or merged after the newest open batch run was opened and within `BATCH_WAIT_MS` (three hours). An older
merge that no open batch run lists went out with an earlier batch run: the issue is open for another reason, as when a
person reopened it. The landing branch is read by `mergedPullRequestsInto` (the newest 50 merged pull requests into a
branch, one GraphQL read, shared in a sync pass), the open batch runs by `openPullRequests`.

- **The done-check** (`notComplete`): an open issue that waits on its batch is done; a merge into the landing branch
  at or after the job was created counts at any age. The batch run's merge closes the issue; nothing more is needed.
- **Intake** (`waitingOnBatch`): an issue with `hopper:done`, and an issue it would take with no job here or one that
  ended, is "done: merged into the landing branch; its batch run closes the issue", in the pull request waiting group with
  no action. No request card, no reopened card, no job.
- A read GitHub refuses leaves Intake as it was (said in the log); in the done-check it throws, and the check asks again.
- **The job graph** (`GET /api/jobs/graph`, part 2): an issue node that waits on its batch is `done`, with
  `awaitsBatch`, and says "Merged: waits on its batch run", whatever its job's end or its item. The route reads the issues
  Intake's last sync said so (`awaitingBatchKeys`, `src/sources/intake-live.ts`: the reason above, from GitHub or from the
  ledger) and the items of the graph's jobs the ledger has waiting (`awaitsBatch`); `awaitBatch` (`src/domain/job-rollup.ts`)
  marks only the issue nodes already in the graph. The graph makes no read of its own. Not taken: a job stage of its own
  for it; the job keeps its stage, as the ledger has its item.

## A job that waits on its batch (issue #1356, 2026-10-15)

**The problem.** A job's pull request ("Closes #N") merged into the landing branch while its job still acted on the item:
the job then waited, `waiting_on` its issue's close, for the batch run to reach the tested branch. The batch run carried no
closing keyword for it, because `batchClosingIssues` took only `done` items and the item read `waiting_outside`; and
`promotedOpen` skipped it for the same reason. The ledger may also not link the item to the pull request at all (a job's
pull request it never followed). Nothing closed the issue, so the job waited for ever.

**The batch run reads its pull requests' own text** (`closingReferences`, `src/domain/landing-batches.ts`; the runner's
`batchCloses`). As it starts, the runner reads each merged pull request of the batch and adds every issue its text closes
with one of GitHub's closing keywords (`close`, `fix`, `resolve` and their forms, before `#N`, `owner/name#N` or the
issue's URL) to the ledger's list, once each. "Part of #N" is no closing keyword, so a part closes nothing. A text that
cannot be read is logged, and the batch run starts with the rest. The batch run's merge into the tested branch then closes
them, as before: the hopper closes no issue itself here.

**A whole merge counts while its job still acts** (`mergedWhole`, `src/domain/work-item-landing.ts`). The ledger keeps
`wholeMerged` on an item when a merge is recorded as the whole item (`job.pull_request_merged`, not a `part`) while a job
acts on it; a new job (`job.queued`) clears it. `batchClosingIssues` and `promotedOpen` take such an item in `queued`,
`working`, `needs_you` or `waiting_outside` as they take a `done` one. Tenant migration 68 rebuilds the ledger.

**The waiting job sees the close.** The fallback read also reads items in `waiting_outside` (`FALLBACK_READ_STATES`),
so a close GitHub made with no delivery is recorded (`work_item.issue_closed`, `via: read`) and wakes a job that waits on
that issue (`settledBy`). A wait that starts on something the ledger holds settled already — its issue closed, its pull
request merged or closed (`settledAlready`, `src/domain/wait-on.ts`) — ends at once (`wait`, `src/engine/outcome.ts`), as
the event would have ended it: no event comes for it any more.

## A batch run is no member's pull request (issue #2132, 2026-10-19)

**The problem.** A batch run closed without a merge (red), and its members whose own pull requests had merged into the
landing branch got `hopper:pr-closed` and a blocked item (`pr_closed`). Intake then offered them again, and an approval
would redo merged work. Seen on many batches.

**Why.** A batch run's text closes the issues of its job pull requests ("Closes #N", issue #1175), and it targets the
default branch, so GitHub lists it among the issue's open closing pull requests. A job whose report found no open pull
request of its own (its pull request merged into the landing branch while it ran) was then answered the batch run, by the
report (`pullRequestOf`), by the follow's look for one (`openPullRequestOf`), or by reconciling (`unfollowedPullRequests`,
issue #763). The follow took the batch run's close for the item's pull request closed without a merge.

**A batch run is no issue's work** (`fromReleaseBranch`, `src/sources/github/completion.ts`). A pull request whose head
starts with `hopper-batch/` is read as a release branch's (issue #876): never an issue's open closing pull request
(`openClosingWork`, for the report, the follow, the done-check and the job's own pull requests), never a part or a merged
mention, and never adopted by reconciling. Only a person's or a job's pull request is followed for an item, so a red batch
run moves no member: it keeps its merged state (`done`, its pull request merged), and Intake says it waits on its batch
(`waitsOnBatch`, issue #1337) until a later batch run carries it to the tested branch. A member whose own pull request
closed without a merge is flagged `hopper:pr-closed` as before. A culprit is still `failed` (issue #1175).

**A merge that closes the issue is the whole item** (`mergedPartOf`, `src/sources/github/follow.ts`). When the follow
finds no open pull request, it takes the newest merged pull request since the job began. One whose text closes the issue
with a closing keyword now comes first and is followed as the whole item, so it ends `done` with `hopper:done`. Before, it
was followed as a part (a mention, issue #1891), and the issue was offered again for its next part.

Not taken: a state of its own for "merged, waits for its batch run". The ledger's `done` with `awaitsBatch`, the graph's
"Merged: waits on its batch run" and Intake's "done: merged into the landing branch; its batch run closes the issue"
already say it.

## Landing batches: the canary (issue #1073 part 5, 2026-10-14)

**The problem.** `stable` moved straight from `beta` to every stable install at once. A change that broke on a stable
install reached all of them before anyone could see it.

**The branch model.** `beta` → `canary` → `stable`. The **canary branch** holds the **stable candidate**: a maintainer
promotes a commit of `beta` to it (`scripts/promote.sh canary`; the first promotion makes the branch at `stable`'s head
and the candidate must contain `stable`). `canary` is no update channel, and no job pushes to it (`RELEASE_BRANCHES`).
Its image tag is `canary` (`.github/workflows/image.yml`).

**The canary subset.** A stable install takes stable releases early when its admin turns **Take stable releases early**
on (Settings → Version; `UpdateSettings.canary`, the instance setting `updateCanary`, key/value, no migration). Such an
install, on the stable channel, follows `canary`'s head while it is ahead of `stable` — `stable`'s head is its ancestor
and it is not `stable`'s head —, else `stable` (`src/update/updater.ts`). The target's ref is then `canary`: the build
installs from that branch, the release check checks that commit as any other, and an image install pulls the `canary`
tag. Turned off on a candidate, or once `stable` has it, the install goes back to `stable` (as a move between channels:
the target is `stable`'s head, though the install contains it). So the subset is each install's own choice, and the
maintainer's hopper needs no list of installs and no telemetry from them.

Not taken: a share of installs chosen by a hash. The share would have to reach every install, the hopper's own
repository has no place for it but a branch's content, and the canary's commit must be the candidate itself (a
fast-forward to `stable`). And a hopper that picks itself into a canary without its admin's word is a surprise.

**The health signal: bug reports.** Every install already has one way to report trouble: **Report a bug** ("Report a
bug"), filed on the hopper's repository labelled `user-report`, with the context `Hopper: <branch> at <12 characters
of the commit>`. A canary install's report therefore names `canary at <candidate>`. The batch runner asks GitHub for the
issues labelled `user-report` created since the window started whose text names the candidate's 12 characters
(`GET /search/issues`). One or more: the candidate is **held**. Not taken: a health report each install sends; it would
be a new outward channel from every install, with what it says about that machine.

**The canary window** (`canaryHours`, per repository in Settings → Landing batches, an admin's; absent: no canary step).
Each pass of the batch runner (`src/landing-batches/canary.ts`, the rules
`src/domain/landing-canary.ts`, pure) compares `stable` with `canary`:

1. Nothing new on `canary` beyond `stable`: nothing happens (an idle period records nothing).
2. A new candidate (its tip is not the newest one seen): `landing_batch.canary_started` with the tip and the window. The
   window counts from it.
3. The candidate at work: its bug reports. Some: `landing_batch.canary_held` with them, and once one issue through the
   user's own connection — the hopper label, assigned to their connected account, so Intake takes it
   (`landing_batch.canary_issue_filed`) —, its text fixed (`canaryIssueText`): the reports, and what to do. None, and
   the window passed: `stable` moves to the candidate as a fast-forward (`PATCH …/git/refs/heads/stable`, `force:
   false`), `landing_batch.canary_promoted`; the push starts the image build of `stable`, and every stable install is
   offered it. None, the window still open: it waits.
4. A held candidate stays held: a fix goes through `main` and up the channels as any change, and its promotion to
   `canary` is a new candidate with a new window. A maintainer who read the reports and finds them not about the
   candidate moves it by hand (`scripts/promote.sh stable`, from `canary` only).

The move of `stable` is a ref update with the user's own GitHub connection, so branch protection on `stable` must let
that account update it, as it lets the maintainer's push. The candidate is a merge commit of `dev` promoted up, so the
release check offers it on `stable` as it did on `canary` ("Updates only to a merged pull request with passing checks").
