**The state.** The events reduce to each repository's `canary` (`reduceCanary`): the tip, `running`, `held` (with the
reports, the reason and the issue) or `promoted`. `GET /api/landing-batches` answers it and what the last pass found of
the canary (`canary.why` or `canary.problem`); Settings → Landing batches shows a line for it.

## The shrink guard (issue #1096, 2026-10-14)

**The problem.** A tend job resolved a merge conflict by emptying `docs/design.md` (18,034 lines on `dev`, then 0) and
`docs/glossary.md` (781, then 0). The checks passed and the pull request had no merge conflicts, so yolo mode would
have merged it and removed both files from `dev`. A person saw it first. The checks cannot see it: a removed document
breaks no test.

**Where.** In the git proxy, before a push reaches GitHub (`src/github-proxy/git-broker.ts`). Every job's push goes
through it (issue #652), so the guard covers a tend job and any other job that rebases or merges its base branch, and a
refused push changes nothing on GitHub. Not taken: a check after the push, before the merge. The bad branch would be on
GitHub, a person could merge it, and the job would be finished already.

**What is judged.** Each ref update of a push to a branch that is there already (a new branch has no head before the
push), against the branch's **base**: the base branch of its open pull request, else the repository's landing branch
where it has landing batches, else its default branch (issue #1147). Not taken: the default branch always. With landing
batches the default branch (`dev`) is not where pull requests merge (`main`), so each change on `main` and not yet on
`dev` looked like the branch's own, and a file `main` shrank on purpose made the guard refuse every rebase onto `main`. A
read of the pull request that fails counts as none: the read does not hold up the push. A push to a job's fork compares
with the fork's own landing or default branch: its pull request is on the parent. The push's pack is indexed in a **quarantine** beside the user's mirror (`src/git-mirror/
push-lines.ts`): an object directory of its own, with the mirror's as an alternate, removed after. Nothing a job pushes
enters the mirror. The base branch and the branch's head before the push are fetched into the mirror first when it
lacks them (blobless, with the user's own connection). A push whose merge base with the base branch is the head's merge
base brings nothing of the base branch in: it is not judged. A job's own edits are its own business.

**The rule** (`src/domain/shrink-guard.ts`, pure). Each file the push or the branch changes is counted in lines at four
commits: where the branch's own change starts (its merge base before the push), its head before the push, the base branch
as the push brings it in (the merge base after), and the push. A file is refused when the push empties or removes it,
or takes more than the guard's percent of its lines,

- against the base branch as brought in, or
- against the branch's head before the push, when the base branch did not shrink it,

and the branch's own change (start → head) did not empty or shrink it so. A file the branch's own change shrank, but did
not empty or remove, is still refused (issue #1218) when the push empties or removes it and the base branch kept it, or
when the push takes more than the percent of the lines the branch kept and the base branch did not shrink it too. So a
pull request that removes or shrinks a file keeps doing so through a rebase, a file the base branch removed stays
removed, and small edits pass. A file the branch added, which is neither where its change starts nor on the base branch
as brought in, is the pull request's own and is not judged (issue #2225): a rebase may rename it, empty it or remove it.
A case: a pull request adds `docs/adrs/ADR-0019-….md`, the base branch takes ADR 19 for another decision, and the
rebase renames the pull request's ADR to 20. git counts each path on its own (`--no-renames`), so the old path went
from its lines to none, and the guard refused the push. A file both sides added at one path is still judged. A binary file
has no lines and is not judged. `git diff --numstat` against the empty tree counts the lines, with one batch fetch of the
blobs it needs.

**The refusal.** git's own: `ng <ref> <reason>` for each ref, so the job sees `! [remote rejected] … (the shrink guard
refused this push: it brings in dev and empties or shrinks files your pull request does not: docs/design.md (18034 lines
on dev, 0 after). Redo the resolution: keep the lines of both sides, then push again)`, at most 10 files named. The
refusal is `github_proxy.refused` on the job's timeline, with the files in `shrunk`. The job does the resolution again.

**Tending failed, not done.** A job whose last push the guard refused, and no push went through after, does not end done
whatever its source says (`guardedVerdict`): it fails with `not complete: tending failed: the shrink guard refused its
last push, which emptied or shrank docs/design.md, and no push went through after` (a tend job; another job's says the
same without "tending failed"). A failed tend job waits on a person, as any failed tend (issue #927), and its pull request
is not merged: the Pull requests card says `tend failed`, and the work-item ledger records the failure as it records any.

**The percent** (Settings → Shrink guard, an admin's; `GET /api/shrink-guard`, `POST /ui/api/shrink-guard`,
`shrink_guard.changed`): 50 by default, from 1 to 100. At 100 only a file emptied or removed is refused. Read at each
push, so a change applies to the next one.

**Git cannot say** (no credential, the base branch gone, git failing): the push goes on, as before the guard, and the
mirror logs why. The guard is a net for a resolution gone wrong, not a gate a broken mirror may close on every push.

**The hopper's own base merge** (issue #1218). Two merges of `main` into a pull request's branch emptied
`docs/design.md` (19,416 lines on `main`, then 0), and yolo mode merged them into `main`. Neither was a job's: the
hopper's base merge ("The base merge", issue #967) made and pushed them from its mirror, and the git proxy, where the
guard is, sees only a job's push. The cause: `git merge-file` exits with the number of conflicts, and above 127 when it
fails, with no merge printed. The base merge read any exit above 0 as conflicts, so a failure became an empty
resolution. Now an exit above 127, or a merge with no conflict marker, resolves nothing, and the conflict goes to a tend
job. And before the push, each file the base merge resolved is judged by the rule above, at the merge base, the pull
request's head, the base branch and the resolution, at the default percent: a resolution the guard refuses is not
pushed, the mirror logs the files, and the conflict goes to a tend job. Not taken: the user's own percent. The mirror
holds no settings, and a resolution that keeps both sides' added lines never loses half of a file.

**The container image's git** (issue #1624). Three more base merges emptied `docs/design.md`, and one of them also
`docs/glossary.md` and `docs/hopper-io-security.md`, after the fix above: the hopper that made them ran a build from
before it. The cause under both: the container image is Debian bookworm, and its git (2.39) has no
`git merge-file --object-id` (git 2.43) and no `git check-attr --source` (git 2.40). Each exits 129 with no output, so in
the container every base merge failed, and the build before issue #1218 read that as an empty resolution. With the fix
above the base merge pushed nothing and resolved no conflict at all. Now the base merge uses only what git 2.39 has: each
side of a file is read with `git cat-file blob` into a scratch file of its own in the mirrors' dir, and `git merge-file`
merges the three files; a side that is not UTF-8 is not resolved, as it would not be written back as it was. The base
branch's `.gitattributes` is read through a scratch index of its tree (`git read-tree`, then
`git check-attr --cached`). The tests run each base merge also with a git that refuses the two newer options. Not taken:
a newer git in the image only. A build on a host with an older git would fail the same way.


## Job worktrees in the workspace (issue #1103, 2026-10-14)

Superseded by "Job worktrees in `.worktrees`" (issue #1188): the paths below are the layout that issue replaced.

**The gap.** A job's worktree was in its scratch dir, `<work tree>/.hopper-scratch/<job id>/<name>`, made of a repository
mirror in the scratch dirs, `<work tree>/.hopper-scratch/repos/<owner>/<name>.git`. A work tree is often a checkout itself, so
each job left a copy of the repository nested inside the repository, its name repeated, and nobody asked for that layout.
The workflow repos the hopper runs in already tend their repositories in `<work tree>/workspace/<name>` and put task
worktrees in `<work tree>/workspace/worktrees/<repo>-<task>`.

**The change** (`src/executors/herdr/job-worktree.ts`, `src/client/reap.ts`, `src/engine/sweep.ts`):
- **Where.** Every job worktree is `<work tree>/workspace/worktrees/<name>-<job id>` (`jobWorktreeOf`): `<name>` is the
  job's repository's, or the work tree's own when the worktree is of the work tree. Never in the scratch dir. The scratch
  dir stays the job's temporary files and credentials.
- **Of what.** A work tree that is the top of the job's repository: of it, as before (`made`). Any other: of the
  repository's **checkout** in the workspace, `<work tree>/workspace/<name>` (`checkoutOf`), the one the workspace tends,
  used as it is, or cloned there the first time (outcome `checkout`, which replaces `mirror`). No mirror is made. The
  start's fetch moves only `refs/remotes/origin/*`, so a person's branch and files in that checkout stay as they are. Its
  `origin` must be the job's repository, else `unmade` ("is not a checkout of").
- **Git ignores it.** A `workspace` the hopper makes has a `.gitignore` of `*`; `workspace/worktrees` always has one. A
  work tree that is a repository shows neither as untracked.
- **The reap** takes the job's worktrees in the workspace with its scratch dir, by the same rule: removed when clean and
  pushed, kept and recorded as `job.work_kept` otherwise, removed whatever they hold on a discard. It finds them by the
  scratch dir's work tree and the job id.
- **The sweep** surveys `workspace/worktrees/*` too (`hopper-tree <age> <path>`). An ended job's worktree is reaped as its
  scratch dir is, by that dir's path, also when the dir is gone: no worktree outlives its job. A name whose job id the
  hopper does not know is never touched.
- **Leftovers.** The scratch dirs of ended jobs, with the worktrees an older release made in them, go as before: the
  sweep removes each clean and pushed one once `scratchMaxAgeHours` old, and keeps each with work not pushed, listed in
  Failures as work not pushed for a person to push or discard. A mirror an older release made goes at a reap in its work
  tree once no worktree is made of it. The checkpoint, shared dependencies and kept work read worktrees in both places
  while old ones are kept.

**Not changed.** The scratch dir, its temp link, credentials and shared dependencies (`.hopper-scratch/deps`). With job
worktrees off, the checkout is `<work tree>/workspace/<name>` (was `<work tree>/<name>`), and the job runs in the work
tree. Two repositories with one name in one work tree share `workspace/<name>`: the second is refused with why.

Tests: `test/herdr/job-worktree.test.ts`, `job-worktree-reap.test.ts`, `job-worktree-other-repository.test.ts`,
`job-worktree-lock.test.ts` (real git and sh), `test/client/reap.test.ts` (the survey's trees), `test/engine/sweep.test.ts`
(trees planned), `test/client/checkpoint.test.ts`, `test/domain/kept-work.test.ts`, `test/herdr/shared-deps.test.ts`.

### Hopper's own disk use (issue #1120, 2026-10-14)

One host held about 880 GB of hopper leftovers: job checkouts, unused images, orphaned volumes, exited job containers,
old database backups, update logs, and kept work whose records named folders a person had removed. Nothing removed them.
The issue asks that every resource the hopper makes is recorded with its owner and removed when the owner ends; that a
periodic reconcile removes orphans and old images, with a backup retention; that Machines shows the hopper's disk use per
host against a budget; and that kept-work records are reconciled against disk. It ships in parts.

**Part 1: kept work reconciled against disk** (`src/engine/sweep.ts` `goneKept`, pure; `src/client/reap.ts`).
- **The survey names its work trees.** For each work tree asked about whose `.worktrees` (issue #1188; or the layout before's scratch area) is there, it
  prints `hopper-root <path>` (`Survey.roots`). A work tree that is not there, or has no scratch area (an unmounted disk, a
  path not made yet), is not named, so nothing in it counts as gone.
- **Gone is resolved.** On each pass, kept work (`job.work_kept`, newest work event) of an ended job that ran on the
  machine swept, whose scratch dir is in a named work tree, and which the survey found neither as a scratch dir nor as a job
  worktree (`.worktrees/<name>/<job id>`, issue #1188), is recorded as `job.work_removed` with `gone` and the scratch dir. Nothing
  is removed: the folder is already gone. One log line each. The work-item ledger drops the job from its item's kept work,
  so Failures and its badge stop listing it.
- **Not resolved:** a parked or live job's (its work tree is its own while it may go on), another machine's, and any while
  the machine's client is older than this (it names no work tree).
- **Should it come back** (a disk mounted again), the sweep finds the scratch dir; once it is `scratchMaxAgeHours` old it
  reaps it with the reap's rule, and work not pushed is kept again as `job.work_kept`.

**Part 1: older images go with the update** (`scripts/update.sh` `prune`, docs/deploy.md "Update" step 7). Once every
check of the update passed, it removes each image labelled `org.opencontainers.image.title=hopper` but the one the hopper
runs and the one it ran before (read from the hopper's container before the stack stops), so a person can still go back.
`rmi` without force: an image a container uses, or with more than one name, stays. The update keeps one database backup
(`hopper-backup.dump`, replaced each time), so it adds no backups. The manual `image prune` command stays valid.

**Part 2: the hopper's disk use per machine, and the disk budget** (`src/domain/hopper-disk.ts`, pure; `src/engine/sweep.ts`;
`src/client/reap.ts`; Machines).
- **The survey measures it.** For each work tree it names (`hopper-root`), it prints `hopper-du <KiB> <path>` for its
  `.worktrees` (issue #1188; and for what the layout before left, while it is there), by `du -skx` (a link, such as a worktree's `node_modules`, counts as a link).
  Each measure is cut off at 20 s by `timeout`, so a slow disk never holds the survey (and so the sweep) up; one cut off
  says nothing, and a machine with no `timeout` (macOS by default) or a client older than this measures nothing.
- **The sweep keeps it.** Each machine's last measure (`Sweep.disk`), in the store since issue #2494 (part 7 below): a
  restart still shows it until the first pass, at startup, measures again. `GET /api/machines` carries it on each machine it measured as `hopperDisk` — each place, their
  sum, when, and the disk budget now —, and each Machines card says it, "over disk budget" when over.
- **The disk budget** (`diskBudget`, a user setting; none by default): `POST /ui/api/machines/disk-budget` (admin, `null`
  turns it off), `GET /api/machines/disk-budget`, the Disk budget panel on Machines. One budget for each machine.
- **Over it, the sweep frees what it may.** It plans with no age, so every ended job's scratch dir and job worktree is
  reaped at once, not after `scratchMaxAgeHours`; the reap's rule still keeps work not pushed, and a parked or live job's
  work is never touched. When a reap removed one, it surveys again for the measure.
- **Still over, a person is told**: `machine.disk_over_budget` (the use, the budget, each place), once while it stays over;
  `machine.disk_within_budget` once it is back within it. Webhooks take them. The budget turned off forgets who was told. Since
  issue #2494 (part 7 below), what the event log last told of each machine stands after a restart: a machine still over is
  not told again.

**Part 3: a job's containers and volumes** (`src/client/reap.ts` `JOB_LABEL`; `src/engine/sweep.ts`; `src/engine/cleanup.ts`).
The exited per-job database containers and the orphaned volumes came from jobs' own test runs: a job killed at its end
left its test container, and the test sweep removed a dead run's containers without their anonymous volumes.
- **The owner is a label.** A container or a volume labelled `hopper.job=<job id>` is that job's (a **job container**).
  The hopper's own tests label every container they start so when they run in a job (`HOPPER_JOB_ID`;
  `test/support/sweep.ts` `containerLabels`), and their sweep of a dead run's containers now removes their anonymous
  volumes too (`rm -f -v`).
- **The reap removes them at the job's end**, in each container runtime on the machine, and the engine records
  `job.containers_removed` with each one (the cleanup's reap, the sweep's, a discard's). Not with `keep` (a timed-out
  job's), nor at a client's isolation stop: the job may go on.
- **The sweep removes orphans**: the survey names each job with a job container there, and the sweep reaps an ended one
  at once, whatever its age. A job the hopper does not know, or one not ended (parked too), is never touched.
  `test/integration/sweep-orphans.test.ts` (issue #2498) checks both ends on this machine with the real reap and survey:
  at a job's end, finished or failed, its cleanup leaves no process, container or worktree of the job; after a restart,
  the sweep reclaims an ended job's tagged process, container and worktree; neither touches what is untagged or the
  tag of a job the hopper does not know.
- Each runtime call is cut off at 30 s by `timeout` where it is, and only ids a runtime gave are passed on, never one
  that starts with `-`. A machine with no runtime, or one whose runtime cannot be reached, removes and names none.

**Part 4: the leftover box builds** (`src/sandbox/leftover-builds.ts`, pure but for its one removal; `src/sandbox/images.ts`;
`src/sandbox/service.ts`). The images the boxes left were the hopper's own builds: each set of **box tools** on a base
image is a build `localhost/hopper-box-tools:<hash>`, and each build kept the images of its fetch stage, untagged. Nothing
removed either.
- **The fetch stage is labelled.** Its first instruction is `LABEL io.hopper.tools-stage="fetch"` (`TOOLS_STAGE_LABEL`),
  so every image a build keeps of that stage carries it. An untagged image is the hopper's only by that label; a tagged
  one only when each of its tags is in `localhost/hopper-box-tools`. An image of anyone else's is never taken. (The label
  changes the Containerfile, so each set of tools builds once more, under a new tag; the old builds are leftover.)
- **A leftover box build** is one of those that no container uses (any state), that no sandbox record names, and that
  was built more than 7 days ago (`LEFTOVER_BUILD_MS`): a box of the same tools within that time takes it unbuilt.
- **The reconcile pass removes them**, beside the hopper, at its first pass and then at most once an hour
  (`LEFTOVER_PASS_MS`), newest first, never forced: the runtime keeps one a container uses, or one that is the parent of
  another (it goes with its child, at once or at a later pass). One log line says how many it removed. No event: no job
  owns a box build.
- **The runtime port** gains `listImages` (every image, intermediate ones too: `GET /images/json?all=…`) and
  `removeImage` (`DELETE /images/<id>`, no query: gone or kept is false). Podman and Docker over their sockets, and the
  remote runtime through a client target's client (issue #1202, below).

**On client targets** (issue #1202: `src/client/runtime.ts`, `src/sandbox/remote.ts`, `src/sandbox/service.ts`). The
builds a box on a client target took stayed there: its client allowed no image call. It now allows two, each checked
on the machine, as a second line behind the hopper's own rule:
- **The image list** (`GET /images/json`, only with `all=true` for Podman or `all=1` for Docker, no filter): the client
  answers only the hopper's box builds in it — each tag a tools image's (`localhost/hopper-box-tools:<16 hex>`), or no
  tag and the fetch stage's label. The hopper learns nothing of the other images on the machine.
- **A remove** (`DELETE /images/<id>`): only by a full image id (64 hex, `sha256:` or not), with no query, so never
  forced; the client inspects the image first and refuses it unless its id is that id and it is a box build of the
  hopper's, as above. A name is refused: in Docker a remove by name only untags. An image someone tags between the
  inspect and the remove keeps that tag: the runtime refuses an unforced remove of an image with more than one name.
- **The reconcile pass** runs the same removal on each client target it reached at that pass (dialled in, its boxes
  listed), with the same rules: 7 days, no container there uses it, no sandbox record names it, never forced, at most
  once an hour. A target not dialled in keeps its builds until a later pass. A client of an older release refuses the
  calls; the pass logs that, and the builds stay until the client updates.
- **Residual risk.** A compromise of the hopper's process can remove, on a machine, an image of the hopper's box builds
  that no container uses; the hopper rebuilds it when a box needs it. It cannot remove or read anyone else's image.

**Part 5: the shared checkouts in the disk use** (`src/client/reap.ts` survey). A job worktree is made of its repository's
checkout in the workspace (`workspace/<name>`, cloned there once, issue #1103), and the checkout's git objects grow with
each fetch. The measure left it out, so a machine could be over its disk budget with nothing on Machines to say so.
- **The survey measures each one.** Each directory in a named work tree's workspace with a `.git` (a repository checkout;
  not a plain folder, not a link, not the layout before's `worktrees`) is a place of its own in `hopper-du`, beside the
  work tree's `.worktrees` and what the layout before left (issue #1188). A workflow repository's own clones in its workspace count too: the hopper's jobs use them as their
  checkouts when they name that repository.
- **One `du` per work tree.** The places of a work tree are measured by one `du -skx` call, cut off at 20 s, so more
  checkouts add no more 20 s waits to the survey (which has 60 s in all). `du` counts a file once across its arguments.
- **The shared dependencies** (`.worktrees/@deps`, issue #410, issue #1188) are in `.worktrees`, so the measure had them already;
  an entry no job worktree links to goes after the scratch age (`src/executors/herdr/shared-deps.ts`).
- **The sweep never removes a checkout**: jobs to come are made of it, and git's own automatic gc keeps its objects packed
  (each start fetches under the start lock with gc in the foreground, issue #1075). Over the budget, the checkouts are in
  `machine.disk_over_budget`'s `paths`, so a person sees why it stays over.

**Part 6: the caches and the container storage** (issue #2494, `src/client/reap.ts` survey, `src/domain/hopper-disk.ts`).
Seat homes grew to 20–30 GB each, mostly package caches (NuGet, Gradle, Go, npm) and container storage, and Machines
showed none of it. This part measures them; a cache policy and an image prune are later parts of issue #2494.
- **The survey measures the caches** in the home of the user it runs as, once per survey: each place of `CACHE_DIRS`
  (`~/.nuget/packages`, `~/.gradle/caches`, `~/.gradle/wrapper/dists`, `~/go/pkg/mod`, `~/.cache/go-build`, `~/.npm`,
  `~/.local/share/pnpm/store`, `~/.cache/yarn`, `~/.yarn/berry/cache`, `~/.cache/pip`) that is there and no link, by one
  `du -skx`, and `~/.cache` whole by a second, each cut off at 20 s: `hopper-cache <KiB> <path>`. Fixed places only, with
  no variable that could name another: nothing else of the home is read, `~/.claude` least of all. The hopper counts in
  `cache` only what the other kinds' places in `~/.cache` do not hold (`cacheUseOf`).
- **It measures the container storage**: each runtime there (`docker`, `podman`) answers `system df` (cut off at 20 s),
  `hopper-df|<runtime>|<type>|<size>|<reclaimable>`; the hopper reads `Images`, `Containers`, `Local Volumes` and
  `Build Cache` and their sizes in decimal units, and leaves any other type out.
- Neither runs where `timeout` is missing. The survey may now take 120 s (`SURVEY_TIMEOUT_MS`), on this machine, over ssh
  and through a client target's `/survey`; a client older than this measures neither.
- **Shown with the disk use.** `hopperDisk` on `GET /api/machines` carries them as `caches` (per kind, biggest first) and
  `storage`, and each Machines card says them (`caches`, `container storage`). They are not the hopper's own disk use:
  the disk budget does not count them, and the sweep removes none of them. Kept with the rest of the measure.

**Part 7: the measure in the store** (issue #2494, `src/store/disk-measures.ts`, tenant migration 94; `src/engine/sweep.ts`).
The measure lived in memory only, so a restart showed no disk use on Machines until the first pass, and a machine still
over its disk budget was told again.
- **One row per machine** (`machine_disk_measures`): its last measure (`DiskMeasure`: when, each place, and the caches and
  container storage as the survey said them), as JSON. Each pass that measured something replaces it. The disk budget
  is not in the row: each read applies the budget now, as before.
- **Read once.** The sweep reads every row at its first read (`Sweep.disk`, or its first pass), then keeps them in memory
  and writes each new measure through.
- **Told once across restarts.** The sweep reads, once, the newest `machine.disk_over_budget` or
  `machine.disk_within_budget` of each machine (`overBudgetTold`): a machine whose newest is over counts as told.
- A machine removed keeps its row; nothing reads it, as `GET /api/machines` lists only the machines there are.

**Part 8: the storage prune** (issue #2494, `src/client/prune.ts`, `src/domain/storage-prune.ts`, `src/engine/sweep-prune.ts`).
Container storage grew on seats with nothing to remove it: images no container used, exited containers, and the anonymous
volumes they left. Part 6 measures it; this part removes the old part of it, on a machine that asks for it.
- **Off by default.** A machine option, `pruneAfterDays` (whole days, 1–3650), turns it on for that machine. On a
  person's own machine, the images no container uses may be theirs, so no default prunes them.
- **The survey lists the exited containers** of each runtime there (`docker`, `podman`), each by its full id, when it
  stopped (`State.FinishedAt`, docker's RFC 3339 time or podman's Go time) and its label keys:
  `hopper-exited|<runtime>|<id>|<stopped at>|<label keys>` (`Survey.exited`).
- **The hopper chooses the containers** (`containersToPrune`, pure): stopped more than `pruneAfterDays` days ago, and with
  no label it keeps: `com.docker.compose.project` and `io.podman.compose.project` (the stack), `io.x-k8s.kind.cluster` (a kind
  node), `hopper.job` (a **job container**, which its job's reap removes) and any `io.hopper.` key (boxes, need and check
  boxes, which their own sweeps remove). A container with no stop time is never chosen.
- **The prune runs through the machine's own connection** (this machine, ssh, a client target's `/prune`), a fixed sh
  script, each runtime call cut off at 60 s, the whole in 300 s (`PRUNE_TIMEOUT_MS`). It checks each container again there:
  still exited and still with no label it keeps (the client takes only `<runtime>:<hex id>`). Then, in this order:
  - each chosen container, by `rm -v` (with its anonymous volumes; a named volume stays), its writable layer's size read first;
  - each volume no container uses (`dangling=true`) that is anonymous — a 64-hex name, and podman's `Anonymous`, or docker's
    `com.docker.volume.anonymous` label — with no label it keeps, by `volume rm`, its size read from its mount point where
    the hopper's user can read it. A seat's home or the stack's database is a named volume: never removed;
  - the images no container uses, built more than `pruneAfterDays` days ago, by the runtime's own
    `image prune -a -f --filter until=<hours>h --filter label!=org.opencontainers.image.title=hopper`, so the hopper's own
    images (the one it runs and the one before, part 1) stay; each one's size from the image list before the prune.
  - Nothing is forced: the runtime keeps a container that runs, a volume or an image a container uses.
- **When.** The sweep prunes last in a pass, once a day per machine (`PRUNE_EVERY_MS`), or once an hour while the machine's
  disk is low (`PRUNE_LOW_MS`). The time of the last prune is in memory: a restart prunes again at its first pass.
- **Recorded.** A prune that removed something is one `machine.storage_pruned` event: each item with its runtime, kind,
  id and size where the runtime said it, their sum (`bytes`) and the age. A prune that fails (a client older than this has
  no `/prune`) is logged once while it fails, and the pass goes on.
- **Residual risk.** On a machine with the option, an image a person pulled and does not use is removed after its age, and
  a person's container stopped that long goes with its writable layer. The runtime pulls an image again when a container
  needs it. Docker before 23 does not label its anonymous volumes: none of them is removed there.

**Part 9: the trim** (issue #2494, `src/client/trim.ts`, `src/domain/disk-trim.ts`, `src/engine/sweep-trim.ts`). A thin
disk (an EBS volume, a WSL distro's virtual disk) gets back a block the hopper freed only when the filesystem tells it, by
a discard. Nothing told it: the space the reaps and the prune freed stayed taken below the filesystem.
- **Off by default.** A machine option, `trimAboveGiB` (GiB, more than 0), turns it on for that machine.
- **What a pass freed.** The sweep adds up, per machine, what its passes there freed since the last trim: the bytes the
  storage prune said it removed (part 8), and the drop of the hopper's own disk use its reaps made. On a machine with the
  option, a pass whose reaps removed a scratch dir measures again after them (as one over its disk budget does) for that
  drop. A job that writes meanwhile hides some of it: the sum is at most what was freed.
- **The trim.** Once the sum reaches the option, the sweep runs a fixed sh script through the machine's own connection
  (this machine, ssh, a client target's `/trim`), with no argument: `fstrim -v` on the mount point of the filesystem the
  home is on (`df -P "$HOME"`), cut off at 240 s, the whole in 300 s (`TRIM_TIMEOUT_MS`). fstrim needs root. When it is
  refused and the user is not root, the script asks `sudo -n` (no password: it never waits on one) and runs fstrim by its
  full path. Then the sum starts again from nothing, whatever the outcome.
- **Recorded.** Each trim is one `machine.disk_trim_ran` event: the freed bytes that started it, the mount point, the
  outcome (`trimmed` with the bytes fstrim said, `refused`, `unsupported` — no fstrim, or no discard there —, `failed`)
  and what fstrim said when it did not trim. A trim that cannot run (a client older than this has no `/trim`) is logged
  once while it fails, and the pass goes on.
- **WSL: the compaction report.** In a WSL distro (`WSL_DISTRO_NAME`, or `microsoft` in `/proc/version`), the event says
  `hostCompaction`: the virtual disk file on the Windows drive shrinks only once it is compacted there, and the hopper
  cannot do that from inside. The event is the report that a compaction is worth it: it comes only after the option's
  bytes were freed. A person on the Windows host runs one of:
  - `wsl --manage <distro> --set-sparse true` once (WSL 2.0 or later): the virtual disk then gives back what a trim frees;
  - or, with the distro stopped (`wsl --shutdown`), `Optimize-VHD -Path <its ext4.vhdx> -Mode Full` (Hyper-V module), or
    `diskpart`'s `compact vdisk`.
- **Residual risk.** On a machine where the hopper's user has sudo with no password, the hopper runs `fstrim` as root, with
  its full path and the mount point only. fstrim on a busy filesystem slows its disk for a short time.

**Part 10: the cache caps** (issue #2494, `src/client/caches.ts`, `src/domain/cache-caps.ts`, `src/engine/sweep-caches.ts`).
The tools' caches in a machine's home (NuGet, Gradle, Go, npm, pnpm, Yarn, pip) grow with every job and nothing capped
them. The survey measures them since part 5; this part caps them.
- **Off by default.** A machine option per kind, `cacheCap<Kind>GiB` (`cacheCapNugetGiB`, `cacheCapGradleGiB`,
  `cacheCapGoGiB`, `cacheCapNpmGiB`, `cacheCapPnpmGiB`, `cacheCapYarnGiB`, `cacheCapPipGiB`), turns on that kind's cap.
  The rest of `~/.cache` has no cap: its contents are not known.
- **Which kinds.** Each kind whose places, as the pass's survey measured them, take more than its cap. While the
  machine's disk is low, each kind with a cap that holds anything, under its cap too: a low disk frees what it can.
- **Only while no job is there.** No clear while a job that has not ended (queued for the machine, claimed, running,
  waiting, parked, led by an operator) is on that machine, as the store says just before the clear, or while the pass's
  survey found a scope or a process of any job there (another hopper's too). Jobs never wait on it: the sweep tries again
  at a later pass. Once a machine's caches are cleared, not again for an hour.
- **The clear.** A fixed sh script through the machine's own connection (this machine, ssh, a client target's
  `/caches`), its arguments the kinds, each checked against the known ones on both sides. It empties a kind whole: it
  removes the kind's fixed places under the home (the survey's `CACHE_DIRS`), each only when it is a dir and no link, each
  removal cut off at 120 s. Go's module cache is made writable first (Go makes it read-only). For Gradle, the Gradle
  daemons of the machine's user are stopped first (`pkill`, issue #2489): they hold its caches open. Nothing else of the
  home is touched: never `~/.claude`, `~/.claude.json`, the rest of `~/.cache`, or a link and what it points at.
- **Recorded.** One `machine.caches_cleared` event per clear that removed something: each place removed, by its kind,
  with its size as the survey measured it, and the sum. The sum counts toward the trim (part 9). A clear that cannot run
  (a client older than this has no `/caches`) is logged once while it fails.
- **Why the whole kind, not the oldest entries.** A cache is a copy of what its tool fetches again. Emptying it costs one
  slower build, the next one; an eviction by age needs a size per entry, and each tool lays out its cache its own way.
  The tools' own commands (`go clean -modcache`, `npm cache clean`) were not used either: a non-login shell over ssh
  often has no tool on its PATH, and each does what the removal of its place does.
- **Residual risk.** A job that starts on the machine between the store's check and the end of the clear finds a cache
  emptied under it: its tool fetches again what it misses. The clear's own window is short, and the hour between clears
  keeps it rare.

**Part 11: the bytes of each job** (issue #2494, `src/client/reap.ts` `jobdu`, `src/domain/hopper-disk.ts` `jobDiskOf`).
The measure said what `.worktrees` takes as a whole, not which jobs take it.
- **The measure.** In the same survey, where `timeout` is, one more `du -skx` per work tree: each job's scratch dir
  (`.worktrees/@scratch/<job id>`) and each job worktree (`.worktrees/<name>/<job id>`) on its own, cut off at 20 s. No
  other `@` dir, no link, and no dir whose name is not a job id. The layout before issue #1188 is not measured by job.
- **Kept.** Each job's worktrees and scratch dir summed (`worktreeBytes`, `scratchBytes`, `bytes`), biggest first, the
  50 biggest only (`KEPT_JOB_DISKS`), so a machine with many jobs left keeps a short measure. They go in the measure the
  store keeps (part 7) and in `hopperDisk.jobs` on `GET /api/machines`. The budget counts `.worktrees` as before.
- **Shown.** The Machines card names the three biggest jobs, with their sizes, and how many more there are.
- **Cost.** The job dirs are read a second time in each pass, after the `.worktrees` measure, so their entries are in
  the page cache already.

**Part 12: the disk use over time, and the disk gauges** (issue #2494, `src/machines/history.ts` `sampleOf`,
`src/machines/disk-gauges.ts`). The measure showed only the last pass, and nothing outside the hopper read it.
- **A seat is a machine.** Each seat (a container or a VM with its own home, its own client or ssh target) is a machine of
  its own, and the sweep measures it on its own: its home's filesystem, the hopper's places in its work trees, each job
  there, its caches and its container storage. Seats on one host are a **host pool** (issue #2499); each still has its
  own measure. A lane is one job slot of a machine: its use is its job's (part 11).
- **Over time.** Each machine sample (the resource recorder, every minute) keeps, from the machine's last disk measure in
  the store, the hopper's own use (`hopper_disk`: its places summed, the bytes the budget counts) and the caches
  (`cache_disk`: each kind, a cache inside `~/.cache` counted once), tenant migration 97. A measure more than an hour old
  (`DISK_MEASURE_FRESH_MS`; the sweep measures every 10 minutes) adds neither. The store's row is read, not the sweep's
  memory, so a hopper that does not hold the sweep lease samples them too.
- **The graph.** `GET /api/machines/history` and `GET /api/machines/:id/history` draw two more lines per machine, each a
  share of the disk's total: `hopper` (the hopper's disk) and `caches`, beside `disk` (the disk used). On the Usage page
  they are hidden until shown.
- **The gauges** (src/telemetry/live.ts, "Telemetry: what runs now"): `hopper.disk.bytes` by `hopper.disk.kind` — `hopper`,
  each cache kind, and each kind of container storage (`images`, `containers`, `volumes`, `build-cache`) —, summed over the
  machines online with a measure at most an hour old; and `hopper.machines.disk` by `hopper.disk.state` (`ok`, `low`,
  `critical`), the machines online with a disk reading. The recorder shows the gauges the machines at each record.
- **No machine in a gauge.** The telemetry exports enums only, never a name or an id; a machine's id is a person's name for
  it, often a host name. So a gauge sums the machines, and each machine's figures stay on Machines and `GET /api/machines`.
  Seats of one host that share a filesystem are summed as they are: each one's own places, never the free space.

**Part 13: the disk defaults** (issue #2494, `src/domain/disk-defaults.ts`, `src/machines/disk-defaults.ts`
`withDiskDefaults`, `src/http/ui/disk-defaults.ts`). Each knob was a machine option only, so a fleet of machines needed
the same options on each one.
- **The setting.** One user setting, `diskDefaults` (`GET /api/machines/disk-defaults`, an admin's
  `POST /ui/api/machines/disk-defaults`, the Disk defaults panel on Machines): `diskLow` (the low and critical thresholds)
  and `sweep` (the sweep interval, the scratch age, the retention per job status, the storage prune's age, the trim
  threshold and the cache cap of each kind), in the shapes the machine snapshot uses. Each field has the bounds of the
  machine option of the same meaning. `null` clears it.
- **Applied.** The plugin host applies it to each machine as the machines are listed (every engine tick), so the decider,
  the sweep, the disk watch and `GET /api/machines` see the same machine. A field the machine's own options set wins; a
  field they leave out takes the default; a retention per status and a cap per cache kind each on its own. The disk is
  judged again by the thresholds that result. The machine's own thresholds are on its snapshot (`diskThresholds`) for this.
  A container target takes none: its disk is not read and the sweep does not treat it.
- **Cost.** The setting is read from the store at most once a second (`DISK_DEFAULTS_READ_MS`), not at each tick, so a
  change applies within a second with no restart.
- **No "off" for one machine.** A machine option absent means "the default", so a machine cannot turn off a default
  prune, trim or cache cap; its own value can only make it less strict (a longer age, a higher threshold or cap).

**Part 14: a machine's own disk budget, and the dry run** (issue #2494, `src/domain/sweep-dry-run.ts`,
`src/engine/sweep-dry-run.ts`). The disk budget was one value for every machine, and a person could not see what the
sweep would remove before it removed it.
- **A machine's own budget.** The machine option `diskBudgetGiB` (`sweep.budgetGiB`) is its disk budget, in place of the
  user's disk budget (`budgetOf`). With no budget of the user's, it still holds. `GET /api/machines` shows each machine's
  `hopperDisk.budgetBytes` and `over` by the budget it has. A seat is a machine (part 12), so this is the budget per seat too.
  The disk defaults do not carry a budget: the user's disk budget is already the one for every machine.
- **The dry run.** The machine option `sweepDryRun` (`sweep.dryRun`), or the disk defaults' dry run (a check box in the
  Disk defaults panel). On such a machine, a pass of the sweep reaps, prunes, clears and trims nothing. It records what
  it would remove as one `machine.sweep_dry_run` event: each scratch dir it would reap, with what the job takes there
  (part 11), the work kept before apart; the jobs whose processes and containers it would stop; the exited containers the
  prune would remove and what the runtimes say they could reclaim, at most; the cache places over their caps; and whether
  the trim would be due. Again only once that changes; after a restart, once more. The reap at a job's end keeps the
  scratch dir there (as a retention does), so the sweep lists it. A person's discard still runs, and the measure, the
  budget's events and the leftovers listing go on as before. `sweepDryRun: false` wins over a default dry run.

**Part 15: the record of each cleanup pass** (issue #2494, `src/engine/sweep-pass.ts`). Each part of the sweep recorded
its own event, but no one event said what one pass did on a machine.
- **One event for each real pass.** The sweep tallies what a pass did on a machine and records it as one
  `machine.sweep_passed` event: what it removed by kind — `scratch` (ended jobs' scratch dirs with their job worktrees),
  `job-storage` (the containers and volumes labelled with a job), `storage` (the storage prune), `caches` (the cache
  caps) —, each with its count and its bytes where they were measured (the reap's own measure, else the pass's survey,
  part 11; a job's containers and volumes have none); `freedBytes`, the sum; the work the reaps kept, with why
  (`dirty`, `stash`, `unpushed`), `again` when an earlier pass kept it too; the dirs the reaps could not remove; and
  the fstrim result (part 9).
- **Only with news.** A pass records the event when it removed something, kept work or could not remove a dir for the
  first time, or ran fstrim. A pass that only keeps the same work again records none, so a machine with old kept work
  does not record one every interval. A dry run records `machine.sweep_dry_run` in its place (part 14).
- **On any machine.** The pass runs through the machine's own connection, as every part does: an e2e test runs one on a
  client target, through its signed `/survey` and `/reap`.

The Grok Bot routine posts the disk budget's events (issue #1203, "Grok Bot routine webhook"). **Not the hopper's to
know:** a container a
job starts without the label (the job's own tooling outside the hopper's tests), and the fetch-stage images built before
part 4 (untagged and unlabelled: `podman image prune` once removes them). **Bounded already:** database backups and
update logs (the update keeps one backup, `hopper-backup.dump`, and one build log, each replaced).

**Verification:** `test/engine/sweep.test.ts` ("kept work whose folder is gone", "the hopper's own disk use"),
`test/client/survey-roots.test.ts` (the survey for real, its measure too), `test/scripts/update.test.ts` (the older images
removed, none on a failed update), `test/integration/disk-budget.test.ts` (the setting through the daemon),
`test/ui/hopper-disk.test.ts` (the card's text and the budget form). Part 3: `test/client/job-containers.test.ts` (the reap and the
survey for real, with a fake container runtime), `test/engine/sweep.test.ts` ("a job's containers and volumes"),
`test/integration/work-kept.test.ts` (the event at a job's end), `test/support-run.test.ts` (the tests' labels). Part 4:
`test/sandbox/leftover-builds.test.ts` (which builds are leftover, their removal, once an hour from the reconcile pass),
`test/adapters/runtime-images.test.ts` (the image calls of both runtimes), `test/sandbox/tools.test.ts` (the stage label). Part 5: `test/client/survey-roots.test.ts` (each checkout measured, not a plain folder or a link). Part 6: `test/client/survey-disk-use.test.ts` (the caches and the
container storage for real, with a fake runtime), `test/domain/hopper-disk.test.ts`, `test/ui/hopper-disk.test.ts`. Part 7:
`test/store/disk-measures.test.ts` (a row per machine, read back after a restart), `test/engine/sweep-disk-kept.test.ts`
(the measure written and shown after a restart; told once across a restart). Part 8: `test/client/storage-prune.test.ts`
(the survey's listing and the prune for real, with a fake runtime), `test/domain/storage-prune.test.ts`,
`test/engine/sweep-prune.test.ts`. Part 9: `test/client/disk-trim.test.ts` (the trim for real, with a fake fstrim and sudo),
`test/engine/sweep-trim.test.ts`. Part 10: `test/client/caches.test.ts` (the clear for real in a home made for the test,
with a fake pkill), `test/domain/cache-caps.test.ts`, `test/engine/sweep-caches.test.ts`. Part 11:
`test/client/survey-job-disk.test.ts` (the measure for real), `test/domain/job-disk.test.ts`, `test/engine/sweep-disk-kept.test.ts`. Part 12:
`test/machines/resource-sample.test.ts`, `test/integration/machine-history.test.ts` (the lines through the daemon),
`test/machines/disk-gauges.test.ts` (the points, and the gauges through an in-memory metric reader), `test/ui/machine-history.test.ts`. Part 13:
`test/machines/disk-defaults.test.ts`, `test/integration/disk-defaults.test.ts` (the setting through the daemon, and a machine with
it applied), `test/ui/hopper-disk.test.ts` (the form). Part 14: `test/domain/sweep-dry-run.test.ts`, `test/engine/sweep-dry-run.test.ts`
(nothing removed, the event once while it stays the same; a machine's own budget), `test/engine/cleanup-retention.test.ts` (the
scratch dir kept at a job's end), `test/plugins/sweep-options.test.ts`. Part 15: `test/engine/sweep-pass.test.ts`,
`test/integration/sweep-pass-remote.test.ts` (one pass on a client target, through the daemon: a clean job's dirs removed with

## Tool accounts (issue #1128, 2026-10-14, part 1)

Owner request: an operator with several Claude accounts on several machines cannot see which machine is signed in as which
account, and a signed-out Claude holds jobs with no way to fix it away from the desk. The issue asks for eight parts; this
part ships the inventory: the **tool accounts** (glossary), an Accounts view, `hopper accounts` and its route, and each
account's week windows (part 6). Expiry warnings, remote sign-in, remote herdr access, failover, infra-credential hygiene
and the API for those are follow-ups.

- **From the usage sources, no new read.** A usage source already reads its machine's tool and account (`claude-plan`:
  `claude auth status --json` beside `/usage`, every `intervalSeconds`, on the machine or through its client). The tool
  accounts group those accounts by service and identity (`toolAccountsOf`, `src/http/accounts.ts`, pure). An account
  names its machine in `detail.machine`; a source with no account read yet names no machine and is left out.
- **Sign-in.** `Account.signedOut` (new): the tool read that it is signed in as nobody (`claude-plan`: `loggedIn` not
  true). Such machines are one entry per service with no identity, so a signed-out machine is seen beside the accounts;
  a machine whose read failed (not dialled in, the command failed) is `unknown`, an entry of its own, with the reason.
  An account is `signed-in` when it has an identity.
- **Read at, last used.** `UsageSourceState` gains `accountReadAt` (each read that gave an account, with or without
  readings) and `executors` (the option, so the route knows which jobs are the tool's). Last used is the latest
  `startedAt` of a job on that machine (`machineOf`: its lane's) whose executor the source names, every job when it names
  none. No expiry: `claude auth status` gives none, so no expiry is shown; part 2 needs one.
- **Spend.** The week windows (`window` starting `week`) of the sources of the account's signed-in machines: the newest
  reading of each window, throttling ones first. Machines on one account read the same limit, so one reading is the
  account's. The session window is left out: it is not a spend limit.
- **Route.** `GET /api/tool-accounts` → `{ accounts: ToolAccount[] }`, a read as every `/api/` read (UI session, API
  token with its scope in State and usage, the API door). No token or id: the accounts carry what `parseAuthStatus`
  keeps (email, plan, organization, sign-in method).
- **CLI.** `hopper accounts` prints that answer (viewer).
- **UI.** Accounts is a view of its own (not under Settings), in the nav group Sources & machines since issue #1943, and since issue #2374 the tab `#machines/accounts` of Machines in Fleet: `ui/src/views/accounts.tsx`, model
  `ui/src/model/tool-accounts.ts`, read through the shared polled reads (`useToolAccounts`, every 30 s; a usage source
  emits no event). A card per account: its plan and organization, each machine with its sign-in, read and last-used
  times and why, and its week gauges. The nav badge counts the machines signed out.

Tests: `test/http/tool-accounts.test.ts` (the grouping), `test/integration/usage-accounts.test.ts` (the route and
`hopper accounts` against the fake claude, signed in and signed out), `test/ui/accounts-view.test.ts`.

## Tool sign-in (issue #1128, 2026-10-14, part 2)

Owner request, part 3 of the issue: a signed-out Claude on a machine holds jobs, and the only fix was its login command in a
terminal there. Now a person signs it in again from the hopper — the UI, a phone through remote access, the CLI or the API.

- **Who starts it.** The usage source that reads the tool on that machine (`UsageSource.signIn`, optional, in the port): it
  already knows how to run the tool there. `claude-plan` runs `claude auth login --claudeai [--email <email>]` on its machine the
  way it runs a read: this machine (in its probe dir), an ssh target (`sh -c ON_MACHINE`, ssh passes stdin), or a client target, whose client runs its own claude (`POST /sign-in`, `src/client/sign-in.ts`: `start`
  answers `{id, url}`, `paste` writes the code and answers how it ended, `cancel`; one at a time; the argv is the client's own,
  the request names only the account). A source that has it says `signIn: true` in its state; the tool accounts carry it per
  machine (`ToolAccountMachine.signIn`).
- **What runs.** Checked on the real CLI (2.1.292): with no TTY, `claude auth login` prints `visit: <URL>` and `Paste code here
  if prompted >`, reads the code from stdin, prints `Login failed: …` and exits 1 on a bad code, exits 0 when it signed in. The
  first https URL it prints is the sign-in URL; none in 30 s, or an end first, and the sign-in did not start (502, with the tool's
  last line). It is stopped 15 minutes after it started with no code, and 60 s after the code if it has not ended.
- **The login.** A login kind of its own, `paste_code` (`LOGIN_KINDS`): open the URL, sign in, paste the code the page shows.
  The sign-in service (`src/logins/sign-ins.ts`, per user) reports it on the machine with no job (`run` `sign-in`, not
  renewable, `expiresAt` the 15 minutes), so it shows in Logins and counts as a Needs-you item as any login. A job never reports
  a `paste_code` login: `loginReportOf` takes `device_code` only. A new sign-in on the same machine and tool cancels the one before.
- **The code.** `POST /ui/api/logins/:id/code {code}` (operator, a box action): one line of printable characters, written to the
  tool's stdin, never kept, logged or in an event; the tool's reason has the code taken out. The tool's end completes the login
  (`auth.completed`) and the source reads the account again at once, or fails it with the tool's last line (`auth.failed`).
- **The URL.** As every login's: `GET /api/logins` answers it only to a UI session of the user (operator or admin). The start's
  answer carries no URL. The URL itself grants nothing: the code comes from the person's own sign-in at the provider.
- **Its life.** The process on the machine lives in this daemon's memory: the sweep (every 5 s) stops a sign-in whose login ended
  (cancelled, dismissed; expired fails it), and fails an open sign-in login nothing runs (a restart: start it again).
- **One sign-in per machine, not one token for all.** The issue asks that the token be installed on every machine of the account.
  Each machine signs in on its own instead: a token copied between machines shares one refresh token, and the first refresh
  on one machine ends the others' sign-in. Signing in each machine is one more paste.
- **The job it held goes on** (part 5 of the issue's "what is left", 2026-10-14). A herdr job whose Claude has no credential asks
  a **not-signed-in question** (issue #533, its text starts with `NOT_SIGNED_IN`, now in `src/domain/questions.ts`; it names
  Accounts). When a tool sign-in completes, the sign-in service calls `onSignedIn` with the machine and the tool, and the
  composition root answers each open not-signed-in question raised on that machine (`src/questions/signed-out.ts`
  `answerSignedOut`, through `QuestionService.settleWith`): answer `SIGNED_IN_ANSWER`, by `sign-in` (a trail attempt of role
  `fixed`, its reason naming the login), at whatever stage the question is. At Claude's prompt the answer types nothing: the
  executor sends the job's text once Claude shows it is signed in, else asks again. Not answered: a question of Claude's login
  screen (`LOGIN_SCREEN_MARK`: an answer is typed into its options, and the login screen does not see a sign-in made beside
  it), another machine's, another tool's sign-in. `src/logins/` still knows no question: the callback is the seam.
- **Routes.** `POST /ui/api/tool-accounts/sign-in {source, email?}` (operator, a box action) → the `LoginView` without its URL;
  `POST /ui/api/logins/:id/code`. CLI: `hopper accounts sign-in <source> [--email]`, `hopper accounts sign-in-url <login>`,
  `hopper accounts code <login>` (the code on stdin). UI: Accounts → Sign in (an operator, on a machine whose source can), which
  goes to Logins, where the card opens the sign-in page and takes the code (`ui/src/components/sign-in-code.tsx`).

Tests: `test/questions/signed-out.test.ts`, `test/client/sign-in.test.ts` (the runner against the fake claude, the client's route, `POST /sign-in` on a real client),
`test/plugins/claude-plan.test.ts` (over ssh), `test/integration/usage-accounts.test.ts` (signed out → signed in through the
daemon, a wrong code, one per machine, no URL, a restart, the CLI), `test/ui/logins-view.test.ts`, `test/ui/accounts-view.test.ts`.

## Last account (issue #1269, 2026-10-15)

Owner request: a Claude sign-in (a job's device login, or a tool sign-in from Accounts) did not say who the machine was signed
in as before, so the person could not tell which account to sign in with. A login's `account` (issue #698) is only what the
tool shows on its login screen, and Claude's re-auth shows none.

- **Where it comes from.** The usage source that reads the tool on the machine: `claude-plan` already runs `claude auth status
  --json` there at each read (the CLI's own status command), and keeps the email and the organization (`parseAuthStatus`; ids
  and the token it prints are dropped). No other read of the machine and no config file: the source is the one place that runs
  the tool there.
- **What is kept.** `last_accounts` (tenant migration 65), one row per machine and service: `LastAccount` — the identity, the
  organization, `capturedAt` (when it was last read signed in as it). Only the label: no token, no id. The logins' sweep
  (`src/logins/last-accounts.ts`, at each engine tick) keeps what the sources read signed in, and writes only what changed. A
  signed-out read keeps the row: it is the last account, so it outlives the session ending, and a restart.
- **A completed sign-in.** Its source reads the account again at once (issue #1128); the next sweep keeps the new account.
- **Shown.** `LoginView.lastAccount` on a login of a tool whose account the hopper reads (`LAST_ACCOUNT_TOOLS`: `claude`; the
  tool's command, `claude auth login` → `claude`) on a machine: the `LastAccount`, or `null` when none was ever read there;
  absent on any other login. To every reader of the login, as `GET /api/tool-accounts` shows the same identity. The Logins card
  says "Last signed in as <identity> (<organization>) on <machine>", or "No previous account known for this machine
  (<machine>)". Not in an event, so no webhook or notifier carries the email.
- **Every Claude sign-in request shows it** (part 2). Two more places ask a person to sign Claude in, and both say the same
  line through one lookup (`lastAccountOf`, `src/domain/logins.ts`): a job's not-signed-in question (`NOT_SIGNED_IN`, issue
  #533; `QuestionView.lastAccount` for the machine that raised it, absent on any other question and on one with no machine),
  and a machine on Accounts that is not signed in (`ToolAccountMachine.lastAccount`; absent on a signed-in machine, which
  names its own account). The UI writes it once (`lastAccountText`, `ui/src/model/logins.ts`) for the Logins card, the
  question card and the Accounts machine.
- **Per machine, not per lane.** A usage source reads one machine's tool, and the lanes of a machine share its Claude config:
  the key is the machine and the service.

Tests: `test/integration/last-accounts.test.ts` (recorded, shown on a sign-in, on the signed-out machine and on a
not-signed-in question, updated by a completed sign-in, kept across a restart, none known, no token),
`test/http/tool-accounts.test.ts`, `test/ui/logins-view.test.ts`, `test/ui/question-machine.test.ts`,
`test/ui/accounts-view.test.ts`.

## The job's terminal (issue #1128, 2026-10-14, part 3)

Owner request, part 4 of the issue: open a machine's herdr session through the hopper as a web terminal attached to its panes,
view and type, over the hopper's own machine connection; Access decides it, and its sessions are events. This part ships it for
the panes the hopper's jobs run in: the **job's terminal** (glossary).

- **What it reaches.** A job's own pane, the one its executor holds (`PaneState` in its executor state). The executor port gains
  `paneScreen(job, lines)` and `typeInPane(job, {text} | {keys})` (`src/domain/terminal.ts`, optional, present together); the
  herdr-claude executor reads and writes the pane on the herdr it lives on, the same way it runs the job (`herdrOn`: this machine,
  an ssh target, or a client target through its client's signed `POST /herdr`). No new route on the client, no new port: what
  the hopper can do to a job's pane already goes this way. Panes no job holds are reached by the **machine's terminal**
  (below).
- **Which jobs.** `running`, `waiting_answer` and `waiting_on`: a job holds its pane at work and while it waits with it. Any other
  status, or an executor with no terminal (a print-mode agent, `command`), is 409. A machine that does not answer is 502.
- **Reads.** `POST /ui/api/jobs/:id/terminal/screen {lines?}` → `{ jobId, sessionId, screen, at }`: herdr's `recent` source, the
  last `lines` lines with the scrollback (200 by default, 2000 at most). A POST, because a read opens a terminal session. The UI
  reads it again every 1.5 s while the Terminal is open; nothing streams, and nothing runs while nobody looks.
- **Input.** `POST /ui/api/jobs/:id/terminal/input {text} | {keys}`: text written to the pane as it is (`herdr pane send-text`,
  at most 4000 characters), or keys pressed (`herdr pane send-keys`) from a fixed list of herdr key names (`TERMINAL_KEYS`:
  enter, esc, tab, backspace, the arrows, ctrl+c, ctrl+d). One of the two, else 400. A box action ("change work on a machine").
- **Who.** An operator (both routes), through a UI session or an API token whose scopes name the route (the Jobs section of the
  scope registry). Then Access: OpenFGA's `terminal#can_attach` (new type `terminal`, `owner: [user]`, `can_attach: owner`), the
  job's user told as its owner at each check. Fail closed, as every Access check: no OpenFGA, OpenFGA not reached, or a model that
  lacks the type (`terminalGaps`; an edited model must add it in Users & access → Access) is 403 with the reason. A job, a machine or a
  box never attaches: the routes are the UI's.
- **Audit.** A **terminal session** is one person's (and one way's: UI, API, CLI) on one job, kept in memory
  (`src/engine/terminal.ts`): it opens at their first read or input (`terminal.opened`, `sessionId`, `person`, `via`), and a new
  one opens after two minutes with neither. Each input is `terminal.typed` with the session, and `chars` (how many characters) or
  `keys` (the key names). The text is never in an event, a log or the store: a person may type a secret into a pane.
- **Residual risk.** Typing into a job's pane is acting as the agent's operator: it can approve a dialog or stop the job. It is
  the same power as answering its question or sending it a note, so it takes the same role, plus Access and a box token over the
  API. The screen may show what the agent printed, secrets included; only an operator who passes Access reads it, as one could
  in a terminal on the machine.

Not in this part: a person's own herdr panes and tabs on a machine (no job holds them), an interactive terminal emulator in the
page (the screen is text, read again; a terminal library is a dependency for a later part if polling proves too slow), and a CLI
command (the routes are there for an API token).

Tests: `test/integration/job-terminal.test.ts` (view and type through the daemon over the fake herdr, the session and its events
without the text, a job with no pane, a bad input, Access down), `test/ui/job-terminal-view.test.ts`, `test/authz/model.test.ts`.

## Infra credentials on machines (issue #1128, 2026-10-14, part 4)

Owner request, part 7 of the issue: a machine the hopper runs jobs on must hold no infra credentials, so the hopper flags the
infra credential folders (`.aws`, `.keycloak`, `.terraform.d`) a machine's home holds. These are the **infra credential folders**
(glossary; now **infra credentials**, a wider list, and they hold the machine: "Machine readiness" below, issue #1248)
(glossary).

- **Read with the probe, no new connection.** Each machine is read where its disk and resources are read already:
  this machine at every list (`infraCredentialsAt(homedir())`), an ssh target in its probe (`INFRA_CREDENTIALS_COMMAND`, one line
  that it ran, then `hopper-cred <name>` per folder its home holds), a client target in its client's `/release` answer
  (`infraCredentials`, checked against the list: `infraCredentialsOf`). One module, `src/client/infra-credentials.ts`, owns the
  list, the read and the checks; the client and the hopper share it. A container target is not read (no home of its own).
- **Names only.** A folder or a file of that name counts. Nothing in it is read, opened or listed. The snapshot carries the names
  (`MachineSnapshot.infraCredentials`): `[]` when none, absent when not read (a container target, a client older than this,
  offline). Only the last read counts: a folder removed is gone from the next probe.
- **Flag, never hold.** Machines shows the badge "infra credentials" and the names, and says to remove them on the machine;
  Accounts shows the names on the machine's row (`ToolAccountMachine.infraCredentials`). No job is held, and no machine is taken
  out of placement: the folders say something about the machine's setup, not about whether a job can run there. The decider does
  not read the field.
- **API.** `GET /api/machines` and `GET /api/tool-accounts` carry the field, as any read (UI session, API token with its scope).
- **The list is fixed.** The three folders the issue names. A setting can come when a second list is asked for.

Tests: `test/client/infra-credentials.test.ts` (the read, the ssh command, a client's answer), `test/adapters/infra-credentials.test.ts`
(this machine, an attached machine's probe, the ssh probe, a client's `/release`), `test/http/tool-accounts.test.ts`,
`test/ui/machine-infra-credentials.test.ts`, `test/ui/accounts-view.test.ts`.

## Machine readiness (issue #1248, 2026-10-15)

The case: an attached machine could not reach the hopper and was still offered work; it ran jobs as the host's own login
user, whose home held cloud and cluster credentials (AWS, kube). A job there could use them, which breaks #652's rule: a job
holds no owner credentials. Requirement: a machine takes jobs only as a credential-free job user that reaches the hopper;
until then it is **not ready** (glossary), takes no job, and says why on its Machines row and in Needs you. Issue #1467
below makes the credentials a warning by default, and a hold only in strict mode or after an admin's stop.

**Credentials hold the machine.** This reverses "Flag, never hold" above. The read is the same one, wider
(`src/client/infra-credentials.ts`, **infra credentials**): folders and files under the home — cloud CLI config (`.aws`,
`.azure`, `.config/gcloud`), `.kube`, `.keycloak`, `.terraform.d`, the GitHub CLI's `.config/gh/hosts.yml`,
`.git-credentials`, `.config/git/credentials`, `.netrc`, ssh private keys (`.ssh/id_rsa`, `id_ecdsa`, `id_ecdsa_sk`,
`id_ed25519`, `id_ed25519_sk`, `id_dsa`; public keys and `authorized_keys` are not credentials) —, a `git credential
helper` in the global git config, and token variables by name (`$AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `$AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`,
`$AWS_SESSION_TOKEN`, `$AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET`, `$ARM_CLIENT_SECRET`, `$GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS`, `$KUBECONFIG`,
`$GH_TOKEN`, `$GITHUB_TOKEN`, `$GITLAB_TOKEN`, `$VAULT_TOKEN`; set and not empty). The job user's context is read where
its jobs run: this machine, its home and the environment its jobs start with (`scrubbedEnv`); a client target, the client's
home and environment, which its herdr session and so its jobs inherit; an ssh target, the probe's own shell. No value is
read or printed: a variable is tested with `printenv` into a command substitution that is never echoed, a git config only
for a `helper =` line.

The decider's `credentialHolds` (`src/decider/assign.ts`) holds a machine with any that the credential check holds (#1467): a job is held with `no machine running
executor <x> is ready: <m> is not ready: its job user holds credentials a job could use (<names>). Run its jobs as a
dedicated user that holds none`, or `pinned machine <m> is not ready: …`, never failed there. Its order among the holds:
after the address hold, before herdr. A job resuming there returns to the pane it holds. The placement picks
(`src/engine/lane-calls.ts`) leave out such a machine and an off-network one too.

**A warning, not a gate, by default** (issue #1467, 2026-10-16). Holding every machine with credentials stopped all work on a
local single-user install, where the owner's own login is the only one there. So the credentials are a warning: the machine
stays ready and takes jobs, and its card says what its job user holds, with the guided fix folded under Reduce risk. The
decider holds it only when the **credential check** holds it (`credentialHeld`, `src/domain/machine-credentials.ts`): an admin
stopped it (Stop taking jobs), or **strict mode** is on (an admin's setting, `POST /ui/api/credential-check`, off by default,
for a shared or hosted hopper) and no admin acknowledged it. The engine gives the decider the ids it holds
(`DecisionInputs.credentialHeld`), the placement picks ask the same rule, and `GET /api/machines` carries `credentialHeld` per
machine, so the card's state is the decider's and they cannot disagree. Each machine has one row in
`machine_credential_acceptances` (issue #1459): an active row is a **credential acceptance** — Use anyway on a held machine, or
Acknowledge on a warning, which folds it — with the credentials it named; a row with `revoked_at` set is a stop. A credential
found later that the acknowledgement did not name raises the warning again; the machine keeps taking jobs. The rows from
#1459 keep their meaning: an accepted one takes jobs, a revoked one is held. The card shows one state: **Taking jobs** with
the one-line warning, Acknowledge and Stop taking jobs; **Taking jobs** acknowledged, the warning folded; or **Not taking
jobs** with why (strict mode, or an admin's stop), the fix steps first, and Use anyway. Needs you lists each held machine
and each warning no admin acknowledged. Tests: `test/decider/infra-credentials.test.ts` (the rule, held and not held),
`test/ui/machine-infra-credentials.test.ts` (each card state), `test/ui/machine-credential-card.test.ts` (each state rendered,
no contradicting text), `test/integration/machine-credential-acceptance.test.ts` (default, strict, stop, restart).

**Infrastructure tools stay off the machine** (issue #1502, 2026-10-17). A job that wrote terraform ran `terraform` on the
machine. terraform's version check then wrote `~/.terraform.d` with only `checkpoint_cache` and `checkpoint_signature`, and the
credential check flagged it. Three parts: every job's tools get `CHECKPOINT_DISABLE=1` (`JOB_TOOL_ENV`,
`src/executors/herdr/start.ts`; the herdr tab and the print agents, after the payload, so a payload cannot turn the version check
back on); the read counts a `.terraform.d` folder only when it holds more than those two files (a file of that name still
counts; the ssh probe applies the same rule); and one protocol line (`INFRA_TOOLS_LINE`, `src/job-rules/`) tells every job
to run terraform, aws, kubectl, helm and the like only in a sandbox the hopper starts for it, never on the machine itself.
Tests: `test/client/infra-credentials.test.ts`, `test/herdr/executor-dialog.test.ts`, `test/job-rules/infra-tools.test.ts`.

**Reach is the address hold.** An ssh target's probe already asks which of the hopper's addresses it reaches (#698); one
that reaches none has an address problem and takes no new job. A client target reaches the hopper through its door, at the
URL it dialled in at, which works while it is online; the reach check at each start (#695) stays. Not ready means either.

**Ready again with no restart.** Each probe reads afresh (30 s; this machine at every list): the probe after the
credentials are gone, or the job user is changed, drops the hold.

**Where a person sees it.** Machines: the badge "not ready", what the job user holds, and the guided fix (`jobUserFix`,
`ui/src/model/machines.ts`): the commands an admin runs there for a **dedicated job user** `hopper-job` — `useradd
--create-home`, `passwd --lock`, and for a client `loginctl enable-linger` so its user units run —, then how the machine
moves to it: a client target is added again as that user (Add machine, its line run under `sudo -iu hopper-job`) and the old
one removed; an ssh target gets the hopper's public key in that user's `authorized_keys` and its ssh target edited to
`hopper-job@<host>`. Its work tree is made under that user's home by the next probe. A credential a job needs comes from the
vault, through a grant. Needs you: the row Machines, one line per online machine not ready, with why. Accounts: the machine's
row says it is not ready.

**A WSL machine's address** (part 4). The seat of the case was a WSL distro on the computer whose WSL runs the hopper's
container. Its probe asked the public URL and the LAN names, and the first LAN name is the container's bare name, which only
the compose network resolves: an address problem, and no address named that it reaches. WSL distros on one computer share
one network, and the compose file publishes the hopper's port on loopback there, so such a machine reaches the hopper at
the **host link base** (#712), default `http://localhost:<port>`, the address Windows opens it at. So when the hopper runs
in WSL (`/proc/version` names Microsoft, read once at start), an ssh target's probe asks that address too
(`wslHopperUrl`, `addressCommand`, `src/machines/hopper-address.ts`): last, only when no other address answered, and only
when the machine's own `/proc/version` names Microsoft, so a machine on another computer never asks its own loopback. It is
verified as every address is: `GET /job/address` answers 204, else not reached. Reached, it is the machine's
`hopperUrl`, and the machine is ready. Not reached, the address problem names it: `a WSL machine on the computer that runs
the hopper reaches it at <url>, and this one did not (<why>)`, before what to set. A WSL machine on another computer
than the hopper's needs an address it reaches on the LAN (`HOPPER_PUBLIC_URL`, `HOPPER_LAN_NAMES`), as any machine
does. A client target needs none of this: it reaches the hopper at the URL it dialled in at.

Residual risk: a WSL machine on the hopper's computer that runs a second hopper on the same port reaches that one at
`localhost`, and `/job/address` does not say which hopper answered. The reach check (#695) takes any answer, so the jobs
there fail at their first ask of the hopper, with a 401: the proxy token is this hopper's.

**Not built yet.** The hopper does not run the guided fix itself (it needs root there; the admin runs it). It does not
check that the job user is used only for jobs: the read is what it can see.

Tests: `test/machines/hopper-address.test.ts` (a WSL machine asked the host link base, a machine not in WSL not asked it, the address named when not reached), `test/client/infra-credentials.test.ts` (the list, a home's and an environment's read, the ssh command never printing
a value, a client's answer), `test/decider/infra-credentials.test.ts` (held, pinned, resuming, ready again),
`test/adapters/infra-credentials.test.ts` (a machine not ready until its next probe finds none, then it takes the job),
`test/ui/machine-infra-credentials.test.ts` (the text, the guided fix, Needs you's lines), `test/ui/needs-you.test.ts`,
`test/ui/accounts-view.test.ts`.

## Pull request housekeeping (issue #1143 part 1, 2026-10-14)

**The problem.** Job pull requests sat with no signal on them. Three still had `dev` as their base after `main` became the
landing branch (issue #1073), and the batch runner moves only a pull request based on the tested branch. Others had
nothing left to land, and stayed open. The pull request itself never showed what the hopper did with it.

**What the follow does now** (`src/sources/github/follow.ts`), with no job and no lane, for an open pull request a job
follows, never on a person's act:

- **Retarget.** Its repository has landing batches, and its base is not their landing branch (the setting's `landing`,
  `main` when left out; never GitHub's default branch, issue #1142) and is no open pull request's head (a stack, issue
  #900, stays as it is): the hopper changes its base to the landing branch (`GitHubApi.retarget`, `PATCH …/pulls/{n}` with `base`). The follow returns `retargeted`,
  recorded as `job.pull_request_retargeted { pullRequest, from, to }`. It is not merged in the same follow: the next read
  sees its merge conflicts and checks against the new base, and tending goes on from there. The batch runner's own move
  from the tested branch stays: it runs for every job pull request of a repository with landing batches, followed or not.
- **Superseded.** Nothing is left to land, so it is closed without a merge (`job.pull_request_closed` with `superseded`,
  why):
  - its issue is closed as completed by the merge of another pull request: the item is done, `hopper:done`. A part
    ("Part of #N") is superseded this way too (issue #1433): its issue's close says the whole is done, so the part has
    nothing left to land. Before, an open part stayed open as a stale pull request, and a job waiting on it never woke.
  - the hopper's mirror says its base branch has every commit of it (`commits` empty, `git log base..head`): the item
    gets `hopper:pr-closed`, as any pull request closed without a merge, and waits for a person, who decides whether the
    issue is done.
- **What the pull request shows.** One fixed comment for each act (`src/sources/github/pr-notes.ts`): moved to the
  landing branch, closed as superseded, and a tend job started (`JobSource.tendStarted`, after `job.pull_request_tended`:
  "rebases this pull request", or "fixes the failing checks"). Neutral text: it names no person and no machine. A comment
  GitHub refuses is lost, never retried: the act it reports stands.

**The batch read** (issue #985): a follow reads GitHub, not the batch, when the base is off the landing branch or the
issue is closed, so housekeeping is never skipped for want of a read. A repository with no landing batches has no
landing branch: none of its pull requests is moved.

**The shrink guard** (issue #1096) covers every tend job already: their pushes go through the git proxy.

**Part 2: what no follow reaches.**

- **A pull request a job named, followed or not, leaves the tested branch.** The batch runner's move from the tested branch
  ("Landing batches") took only followed pull requests; one of an item whose newest job follows it no more (a failed tend,
  a rework, a job from before the follow) stayed on `dev`. Its list is now every job whose source state names a pull
  request not merged and not abandoned (`JobFilter.namesPullRequest`): the record of the pull requests jobs opened, which
  does not depend on the follow. The batch runner's move posts the same fixed note as the follow's
  (`LandingBatchGitHub.comment`, `retargetNote`).
- **A held rebase is tended within an hour** ("No hold lasts for ever", above).

**Part 3: a failed rebase, once its base moves.** A rebase tend job fails when it cannot keep the intent of both sides
("Conflicts a rebase sends to a person"). The base it failed against does not stay: the change it conflicted with can be
changed again, reverted from the landing branch (a red batch's culprit), or a person can land the other half. So the
hopper does not leave it to a person for ever:

- Each sync, before the tends, while the tended job's tend job is a `rebase` that ended failed and its end is reported,
  the source says the commit the pull request's base branch is at (`JobSource.baseTip`, `GitMirrors.baseTip`: `git
  rev-parse` of the base as this pass fetched it, no new fetch). The first commit is kept (`tended.baseAt`): the base when
