  large piece of CPU work the hopper did there on a timer. It runs in a worker thread now, one a checkpoint, which ends
  with it. The same scrub (`scrubParts`), so a checkpoint is what it was. A job's checkpoint read
  (`GET /job/checkpoint/*`), the transcript read and a git push's body unpack with zlib's thread pool, not `gunzipSync`.
- **A dial-in refused as stale is dialled again at once** (`src/client/server.ts`). A machine signs its dial-in when it
  sends it; a dial-in that waits in the socket's queue behind a stall is read when the stall ends, older than the 30 s
  window, and refused `stale`. The client's backoff had grown meanwhile (to 30 s). The client now dials again at the first
  backoff (1 s), signed fresh, after a stale refusal, once: a second stale refusal in a row is a clock that is wrong, not
  a stall, and backs off as any failure. The window is not widened: the hopper's side is unchanged. (Issue #1383 credits
  the time the loop was held: "Reading the held event loop".)
- **A session with no HOME** (`probeSsh`, `src/machines/attached.ts`). A WSL machine reached over ssh answered an empty
  home, and was offline with `its home is not an absolute path: ""`. The probe now takes the user's home from the user
  database (`getent passwd`) when HOME is empty, and uses it for the rest of its command (the work tree); the home comes on
  a line of its own (`hopper-home <path>`), so a line a shell's startup file prints is never taken for it. Still none:
  the reason says the session has no HOME and the user database names none.
- **Label writes that change nothing are not sent** (part 2, `relabel` in `src/sources/github/report.ts`). A sync pass
  of a `github-account` source made up to 84 label calls. They hold no loop (asynchronous), but each costs a GitHub call
  and its records. Most changed nothing: a remove is one `DELETE` a label, and the hopper removed every label it might
  have set — the claim and its holder, `hopper:failed`, and on Run again all six end labels —, so most answered 404; and
  the first label write to a repository made all eight hopper labels. Now, where the hopper holds the issue's labels as
  just read (a job's end, a follow's end, Run again, a stale claim's release), it removes only the labels the issue
  carries and adds only the ones it lacks; it makes only the label it adds, once per repository per process, and so does
  an add the GitHub outbox sends (issue #1238). Where it holds
  none (a failed, cancelled or rejected job's end), every write is sent as before: a read to save one `DELETE` costs as
  much as it saves. Not batched: GitHub has no call that adds and removes at once but the one that sets every label, and
  that would undo a person's label set between the read and the write.
- **A job list reads only the jobs that changed** (part 3, "Database": jobs are read by row version). Postgres's own
  stats on the hopper that stalled showed about one full read of `jobs` a second, about 15 MB each, all parsed on the
  event loop.
- **A job or failure filter parses no body** (part 4, "Database": a filter parses no body). The `followed`,
  `namesPullRequest`, `unassessed` and `undismissed` job filters and the `problemId` and `outcome` failure filters cast
  every row's body to JSON in Postgres, on every list, while the loop waited. They read generated columns now.
- **A sync reads its jobs a few times, not each job again and again** (part 5, `src/sources/after-done.ts`). Each sync of
  a source went through every job of that source, ended ones too, and read each one about eight times, a get each: when
  it caught up, to choose whom to follow, whether it was its item's newest job (a read by source key), whether it watched
  its base, and twice each to keep or drop a hold on its pull request. With about 740 jobs that was some 6,000 store
  calls a sync, each a round trip and a 20 KB body parsed, and the loop of holds made about 2,000 of them in a row with
  no `await`. Now a sync reads the jobs table in a few whole lists (ids and versions, bodies only of the rows that
  changed); the newest job of each item comes from that list; only a tended job watches its base; and only a job held
  now or held before has its hold kept or dropped. A get of a job that did not change sends no body ("Database").
  Every store call is counted by its statement (`slowStoreCalls.count`), so a test says how many a piece of work sends.
- **An idle hopper's store calls, measured** (part 6). With the test app's 50 ms tick and 40 ended jobs, an idle hopper
  sends about 30 small store calls a tick: about ten reads of `jobs` (ids and versions; no bodies), six `settings` rows
  by key, and three each of open `handoffs`, `questions` and `problems`. At the 2 s production tick that is about 15
  calls a second, none of them a stall. Before part 5 a sync added about eight reads of `jobs` for each job.
  `test/integration/idle-store-calls.test.ts` keeps the reads of `jobs` a tick bounded, whatever the job count.
- **Not done here.** No cache of `settings`, `handoffs` or `questions`: their reads are small rows by key or by status,
  and a cache would serve a value older than a write made past this process (the operator CLI). What a stall's log line
  names as holding the loop, on a build with these parts, is the next thing to move: no hopper has yet run the
  attribution through a stall.

**Verification:** `test/store/slow-calls.test.ts`, `test/http/event-loop.test.ts` (the store's part named, none said,
one raised a minute), `test/engine/checkpoint-scrub.test.ts` (the worker answers what the scrub in place does),
`test/client/stale-dial.test.ts` (the first backoff after a stale refusal, once), `test/adapters/ssh-machine.test.ts`
(a session with no HOME), `test/sources/github-label-writes.test.ts` (part 2: no label write that changes nothing),
`test/store/jobs-read.test.ts` (part 3: a list reads only the bodies that changed; part 5: nor does a get), `test/store/job-filter-columns.test.ts`
(part 4: a filter sends no JSON cast, and answers as before on rows from before the migration and from the build before),
`test/integration/sync-job-reads.test.ts` (part 5: a sync of a source with 40 ended jobs reads `jobs` fewer than 40
times; it read it 332 times before), `test/integration/idle-store-calls.test.ts` (part 6: an idle hopper with 40 ended
jobs reads `jobs` fewer than 20 times a tick; 971 times in 2 s before part 5, about 420 after).

## A job source not configured says so (issue #1243, 2026-10-15)

The problem: a `github-app` job source that was on with empty options (no `appId`, no `slug`, no private key) was paused
and silent. Each sync still ran a pass: it asked GitHub nothing and logged `REST 0, GraphQL 0`, which reads as a healthy
quiet source. The Sources view hid it ("an unset GitHub App is not shown", issue #254), so its intake was dead and nothing
said why.

- **A setup problem** (`JobSource.setupProblem`, `SetupProblem` in `src/domain/sources.ts`). The app source's names what of
  its identity is not set (`loadGitHubApp` now returns `missing`), or that the key is no key, and its help page
  (`github-app-setup`). It is read at each sync, as `paused` is.

  report, the sync loop runs no pass: no traffic line, no `lastOkAt`. Its status is `needs-setup` with `setupProblem`;
  `itemsSeen` 0, and the UI shows *not configured* in place of each count. With jobs of its own to report, the pass runs
  for them, as for a paused source, and the status stays `needs-setup` with the setup problem, never ok (issue #1351).
- **Said once.** The log says `hopper: source <name> not configured: <reason>` when the problem starts or changes, and
  `hopper: source <name> configured` once when it clears. No event: the status and Needs you carry it.
- **Asked for in place.** Sources shows the source as *needs setup*, with a setup card: what is missing, the steps (an
  app already installed, or `scripts/create-github-app.sh`; its id and slug in Plugins; its key in the runtime), and a
  link to the help page `help/github-app-setup.md`. Needs you has a **Setup** row (`#sources`), one line per source.
- **Clears by itself.** Config completed later (the key given to the runtime, the id and slug saved) clears it at the
  next sync, with no restart.
- Why not a failure-assessor **problem**: a problem groups failed jobs and holds new ones of its scope. A source with
  no config has no failed job, and must hold nothing else.
- Not done here (later parts of issue #1243): pick an app already installed from the list of apps the connected account
  can see. The private key in the vault: the next section.

## The GitHub App's private key in the vault (issue #1243 part 2, 2026-10-15)

The setup card told a person to give the app's private key to the runtime, as an environment variable or a mounted file.
That puts a credential the hopper alone uses in a file on the machine, beside every other process's view of it (see issue
#880, which moved remote access's credentials out of `.env` for the same reason). The key is now the hopper's own **system
secret**, kept as the TypeSafe API key is ("The TypeSafe API key in the vault's system scope").

- **Kept in the vault** (`src/sources/github/app/key.ts`, `createGitHubAppKey`): the user's system secret
  `github-app-private-key`, sealed under the master key. `set` checks first that the value is a private key in PEM form
  (real line breaks or `\n` escapes, `pemFromEnv`); a value that is not is not kept, and the error does not carry it.
  `remove` drops it. Access (`system_secret#can_change`) decides each change, the user or an admin.
- **A write-only field** on the app source's setup card in Sources posts the key once (`POST /ui/api/github-app-key`, least
  role operator); the field is cleared, and no route answers the key: `GET /api/github-app-key` says only whether one is
  kept, who set it and when. It is listed on Vault in the system scope, and may be kept in a vault backend, as
  the other values a person gives.
- **Read by the old name.** The app source and its detection read the key through the user's runtime secrets by
  `GITHUB_APP_KEY_VARIABLE` (`GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY`); the user's runtime (`src/users/github-app-key.ts`) answers that name
  from the vault, never from the environment. The source reads it at each sync, so a key saved clears the setup problem at
  the next one, with no restart. The `privateKeyEnv` option is gone: a stored one is dropped when the options are read.
- **Imported once.** A key the runtime still gives as `<secret prefix>GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY` is kept in the vault at the
  start that finds none kept, a backfill marks it, and it is never read again; the log and the key's view name the
  variable, so a person removes it. `scripts/create-github-app.sh` still writes the key to its secrets file; the next
  start imports it.
- The missing part's name on the setup problem is `private key`, not a variable's name.

**Verification:** `test/sources/github-app-key.test.ts` (kept, opened, removed, refused when no key, Access decides, the
import once, never in clear), `test/integration/github-app.test.ts` (the key saved through the route clears the setup
problem without a restart; a key in the environment at start is imported), `test/ui/source-app-key.test.ts` (the field
posts once and clears).

## Pick an installed GitHub App (issue #1243 part 3, 2026-10-15)

The setup card told a person to find an app's id and slug on GitHub and type them into Plugins → Job sources. The card now
lists the GitHub Apps already installed on the person's organizations, and one press sets the app on the source.

- **The list** (`src/sources/github/app/installed-apps.ts`, `listInstalledApps`): `GET /orgs/{org}/installations` with the
  person's own GitHub connection, through the shared rate limiter, for each organization the connection knows
  (`src/users/installed-apps.ts`): the accounts the **hopper's app** is installed on, as last read (issue #1250), and the owners
  of the job repositories; never the connected account's own login, which is no organization. Read only on the ask
  (`GET /api/github-apps`), nothing kept, not cached.
- **Refused, said.** GitHub lists an organization's apps only to an owner, and only when the token may read the
  organization's Administration. The shipped hopper's app does not ask for that permission, so an organization may be refused:
  `refused` names it with why, and the card says so. The person then sets the id and slug by hand. No new permission is
  asked of the hopper's app for this.
- **Use this app** sets `appId` and `slug` on the source as an edit of its options (`POST /ui/api/plugins`, an admin's), the
  other options kept. No new mutation route: the plugins edit is the one place a source's options change. The private key is
  still pasted on the card (part 2); an installation does not carry it.
- With no GitHub account connected, or its sign-in ended, the answer says so (`notConnected`) and GitHub is not asked.

**Verification:** `test/integration/github-app-installed-apps.test.ts` (the apps of each organization, one refused with why,
the own login not asked, no connection asks nothing), `test/ui/source-installed-apps.test.ts` (the list, the refused
organization, Use this app posts the options edit with the other options kept).

## What a wait waits on (issue #1245, 2026-10-15)

Fourteen jobs were seen in `waiting_on` with no record of what they waited for. Neither the UI nor an operator could tell
whether to act, and nothing could wake them when the thing came. A job's own wait now always names what it waits on, typed.

- **The dependency** (`WaitOn`, `src/domain/wait-on.ts`): a pull request (`number`, `repo` when not the job's own, and
  `about`: `checks`, `merge` or `review`), another job, an item (an issue), a person (a question id), a `sandbox` or
  `template` approval, a vault grant, its own command, or an outside event (`what`). It is `wait.on` on the job and `on` on
  `job.waiting`.
- **Named by the job.** `WAIT_LINE` asks for an `on:` line after `HOPPER_WAITING`: `pr 12 merge`, `o/r#12 checks`,
  `job <id>`, `issue 45`, `question <id>`, `sandbox approval`, `template approval`, `infra plan <id>` (issue #2205),
  `vault grant`, `own command`, `outside: <what>`. `waitFields` reads it beside `for:` and `until:`. With no `on:` line, `waitOnOf` reads it from `for:` and
  `until:` (own command as `namesOwnCommand`; a pull request; an approval; a grant); what reads as none of them is an outside
  event with the `for:` text. So a wait is never recorded without one. A pull request or an issue number written with no
  owner (`PR #95`, `issue 4`) is in the repository the same text names, in a link or in words (`in owner/name`,
  `repository owner/name`): the first one after the number, else the last before it; only when the text names none is it the
  job's own (issue #2090: a wait on another repository's pull request was ended by the job repository's pull request with
  the same number). A field line the terminal wrapped goes on with that field in `waitFields`, so the `on:` line after a
  long `for:` line still reads (issue #2090).
- **Never without one.** The job repository refuses to write a job that enters `waiting_on` with no `wait.on`
  (`waitEntryProblem`, `src/store/jobs.ts`): the one place every write goes through. A job already on a wait keeps it.
- **Woken on the event, never a poll.** The engine hears each event and asks `settledBy` (`src/domain/wait-on.ts`) what it
  settles; each job on its own wait on that (`waitsFor`) is woken by the hopper (`wakeOn`, `src/engine/wait.ts`),
  `job.wait_ended { by: hopper, note }`, and told so in its pane:

  | Waits on | Woken by | Note |
  |---|---|---|
  | a pull request | `job.pull_request_merged`, `job.pull_request_closed`: its number, in `repo` or the job's own repository; whatever it waited for about it is over. `job.waited_pull_request_ended` too (issue #1433, below) | `<url> was merged` |
  | a job | `job.finished`, `job.failed`, `job.cancelled` of that job | `job <id> finished` |
  | an item | `work_item.issue_closed`: its issue, in `repo` or the job's own repository | `<url> was closed` |
  | a question | `question.answered`, `question.closed`, `question.dismissed`, `question.expired` | `question <id> was answered` |
  | a vault grant | `vault.granted`, `vault.grant_denied` for this job | `a vault grant was given` |
  | an infra plan (issue #2205) | `infra.plan_approved` of that plan; `infra.plan_rejected` of it (issue #2368) | `infra plan <id> was approved by <who>`; `infra plan <id> was rejected by <who>: <note>. …` |

  An approval is not woken here: a job asks for one through a skill request, whose watch ends its wait with the answer when
  it is ready (issue #998, `src/skills/waits.ts`), the box started, not only the template approved. A wake on the approval
  event would end the wait before that answer, and the answer would then find no wait to end. Checks keep `pr wait`
  (issue #1072). Its own command and an outside event are woken as before: by the job's own poll or a person; since issue #1508 also by
  the items an outside wait names ("Watched items"), and by the loss of the pane a poll ran in. Issue #1210
  carries the waits on hopper state a job polls for.
- **A wake a stop lost (issue #1571).** `wakeOn` runs in memory after its event commits. A stop between the two left the
  job `waiting_on` with nothing to wake it. So the engine reads the settling events again (`createMissedWakes`,
  `src/engine/wait.ts`; the types `SETTLING_EVENT_TYPES`, `src/domain/wait-on.ts`): at start, every one since the oldest
  wait began; on each tick, only the events since the tick before. Each job on its own wait that an event since its wait
  began settles is woken as above, with the same note. A job woken in memory already is no longer `waiting_on`, so it is
  not woken twice.
- **A pull request no follow holds (issue #1433).** Only a followed pull request records `job.pull_request_merged` or
  `job.pull_request_closed`. One whose follow ended (a tend took it, a newer job of its item), a stray a person closed, or
  one of no job ends with no event, so a job waiting on it stayed parked. Now each sync of a source reads the pull requests
  its jobs on their own wait name (`waitedPullRequests`, `src/domain/wait-on.ts`; `JobSource.endedPullRequests`, one REST
  read each, `src/sources/github/follow.ts`; `src/sources/waited-pull-requests.ts`). Each one merged or closed without a
  merge records `job.waited_pull_request_ended { pullRequest, state }` on each job waiting on it, and the engine wakes them
  on that event, as above. So a parked job wakes within one sync after its pull request closes. A read that fails is
  logged and asked again at the next sync. A direct job (issue #1721) is read so by the `direct` source: no GitHub source
  lists it, so the direct source answers `endedPullRequests` and `endedWatched` with the user's own GitHub connection
  (`createDirectPullRequests`, `src/sources/compose.ts`); with no account connected, none ended.
  Verified by `test/integration/waited-pull-request.test.ts` (closed or merged, the job wakes at the next sync),
  `test/sources/github-waited-pull-requests.test.ts` and `test/domain/wait-on.test.ts`.
- **Legacy waits.** A `waiting_on` job from before, with no `wait.on` and not on its own command, is **stuck work** of cause
  `wait_unnamed`, "Jobs waiting on nothing recorded". Its bulk action **Resume all** ends each wait, as a person does, with a
  note: go on, or end the turn with `HOPPER_WAITING` again and an `on:` line. That is its one tend pass.
- **UI.** Each says "waits on" the dependency, from one helper (`waitOnLinkOf`, `ui/src/model/board.ts`; `WaitsOnLink`,
  `ui/src/components/waits-on.tsx`): a link to the pull request or issue on GitHub, the job, or the question; "nothing
  recorded" for a legacy wait. The Queue view's own-wait rows, with the row's "for <since>". The job view: a "waits on" fact
  with how long it has waited, and its header ("Where it stands") says `Waiting on PR #12 to merge`. The job graph: a job
  node on its own wait carries `waitOn` and its words say it (`Waiting on …`, `Waiting on nothing recorded`); its details
  link it, beside "in stage", the time since the wait began.
- **Persisted state.** No migration: `wait.on` is optional in the job's JSON, and a wait without it is read as a legacy
  wait. A build before this one ignores `wait.on`.
- **Verification (part 2).** `test/domain/wait-on.test.ts` (each event wakes only the jobs waiting on what it settles; an
  approval wakes nothing), `test/integration/job-wait.test.ts` (a job waiting on another job goes on when that job ends),
  `test/domain/job-graph.test.ts` (the node's `waitOn` and words), `test/ui/jobs-view.test.ts` (the node's words and its
  details' link), `test/ui/board.test.ts` (`waitOnLinkOf`), `test/integration/skill-wait-wakes-job.test.ts` (an approval
  still ends the wait with the skill's answer).

## Watched items (issue #1508, 2026-10-16)

Jobs stayed `waiting_on` after what they waited for had happened: an issue of another repository closed ("until
identity#199 closes"), two issues closed, a workflow run completed after its deployment was rejected. Each was a wait on an
outside event, or on an item the work-item ledger does not hold, so no event came. Jobs that waited on a background poll in
their own pane waited for ever once a host restart killed the pane, and one failed with `pane lost` when it was woken.

- **What a wait watches** (`watchedOf`, `src/domain/watched-items.ts`). A wait on an item, and a wait on an outside event (or
  one with nothing recorded) whose `for:`, `until:` or `what` text names items: `owner/name#N`, `name#N` (a repository of
  the job's owner), `issue N` or `item N` (the job's own repository), a link to an issue or a pull request; a workflow run
  as `<repo> run N`, `workflow run N` (the job's own repository) or a link to `actions/runs/N`, its id five digits or more.
  The job's own issue is left out: its close ends the job (issue #1460).
- **The owner a wait writes is kept** (issue #2066). A wait on `outside: octo/hopper#2042` whose `for:` said `hopper#2042`
  watched `<the job's owner>/hopper#2042` too, which did not exist, and so ended at once. A `name#N` or `<repo> run N`
  with no owner is the job's owner's only when the text does not name that same name and number with its owner: then
  it is the one the text names.
- **Read at each sync** (`src/sources/watched-ends.ts`, `JobSource.endedWatched`; GitHub: `src/sources/github/watched.ts`).
  Each item is read by its number, the pull request first and then the issue, and a run through Actions
  (`GitHubApi.workflowRun`, `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runs/{run_id}`, Actions read). An issue closed, a pull
  request merged or closed, a run `completed` is ended. Once every item a wait names ended, though before the wait began
  (but not for a wait on an outside event, issue #2219 below), `job.waited_items_ended { items }` is recorded and the engine wakes the job on it (`settledBy` gives `watched`, for that job
  only), `job.wait_ended { by: hopper, note }`. A read that fails is logged and asked again at the next sync.
- **An item that does not exist** (issue #1691). A wait named `ledger#330`, a repository that does not exist, and was read
  again at every sync for a day, though every other item it named had closed. GitHub's answer that the repository, item or
  run does not exist (404, 410, GraphQL's "Could not resolve to …") is permanent, not a failed read: the item is
  `not_found`. A job one of whose items is `not_found` is woken at once, whatever its other items, with
  `job.waited_items_ended { items }` of those items only; its note says each cannot be read — GitHub answers a repository
  the hopper's connection has no access to as one that does not exist (issue #2066) —, so the job checks the owner and name
  and rewrites its wait. A refusal (403) or a rate limit is still a failed read.
- **No wake loop.** A job woken so that waits again on the very same items is not woken for them again: the sync keeps, in
  memory, the items each job was last woken for. After a restart such a job is woken once more.
- **What ended before an outside wait began** (issue #2219, 2026-10-20). Reported from a real run: a wait `on: outside:
  gated: …` whose text named a pull request closed before the wait began ended at once with "was closed", twice in a row.
  That close was what the job knew, not the event it waited for. Now each end carries when it happened, when the source
  says (`WatchedEnd.at`: an issue's `closedAt`, a pull request's `mergedAt`, else its `closedAt`, which the pull request read
  by its number now asks GraphQL for). An item a wait on an outside event (or one with nothing recorded) names that ended
  before the wait's `since` is left out of that wait (`endedBeforeWait`, `src/domain/watched-items.ts`), at the sync
  (`src/sources/watched-ends.ts`) and at the wait check (`items_ended`, `src/engine/wait-checks.ts`): the wait ends once
  every other item ended, and a wait whose items all ended before it began is not ended by them (its check says "ended
  before the wait began"). A wait on an item or a pull request still ends on one that ended before it (issue #1356), an
  item that does not exist is still said at once (issue #1691), and a run has no end time, so it ends the wait as before.
  Tests: `test/domain/watched-items.test.ts`, `test/integration/watched-items.test.ts`.
- **A deployment decision** wakes when its run completes: a rejection completes the run; an approval wakes the job when the
  run ends. A run that waits for its approval is not ended.
- **A wait its pane carries** (`paneCarriesWait`): on its own command, on an outside event that names nothing watched (the
  background poll of the wait line), or a legacy wait. On every tick (`src/engine/pane-answers.ts` `wakeLost`) such a job is
  asked `paneLost` (herdr-claude: no pane state, its agent or pane gone, or restored by herdr in another terminal). Lost:
  the hopper ends the wait, `job.wait_ended { by: hopper, note: "its pane was lost" }`, told to check what it waited for and
  start the poll again. So a job is woken after a daemon start and after a seat's restart alike. Before, a wait on its own
  command whose pane was gone was nudged, then flagged stuck: now it is woken. A wait the hopper watches (a pull request, an
  item, a job, a question, a grant, watched items) is left to that watch.
- **A stranded wait** (issue #1779). A wait the hopper watches is asked `paneLost` on the same tick too. Its agent session
  ended (Claude exited and the pane shows a bare shell, or the pane is gone): the wait is marked `strandedAt`, not ended,
  and the mark goes when its agent is seen again. Reported from a real run: two jobs waited on a template approval that
  could not come, their panes at a shell prompt; nothing showed it, and the only way out was cancel and run again. What it
  waits on still wakes it (its resume opens a new pane, below). Meanwhile it is stuck work, `stranded`, "Jobs on a wait
  whose agent session ended": **Wake all** ends each such wait as a person's End the wait. The Dashboard's wait row shows
  "stranded: its agent session ended". A person's end of a stranded wait tells the job that its session ended while it
  waited, so what it waited for may not have happened: check it, wait again, or ask for something that can happen. The
  operator CLI: `hopper failure stuck` lists the stuck causes, `hopper failure stuck <cause>` runs a cause's bulk action,
  and `hopper job end-wait <id> [--note <text>]` ends one job's wait; `hopper queue list` and `hopper job show` give a stranded
  wait's `strandedSince` (issue #1780's words for a wait). No event: the mark is on the wait, read by the views.
  Tests: `test/integration/job-wait-stranded.test.ts`, `test/domain/stuck.test.ts`, `test/ui/job-wait-view.test.ts`.
- **Resumed in a new pane.** A job resumed whose pane is gone (`resume`, herdr-claude) no longer fails `pane lost`: as for a
  pane herdr restored (issue #1465), what is left of the job is reaped, a new pane opens as at the start, Claude resumes the
  agent session, told `LOST_NOTE` and then its answer (`resumeLostPane`, `src/executors/herdr/restored.ts`). With no agent
  session recorded it still fails `pane lost`.
- **Cancel with a reason** is issue #1460's: `hopper job cancel <id> --reason <text>`, `POST /ui/api/jobs/:id/cancel`.
- **Persisted state.** No schema change: the watch is read from each wait's text, so waits recorded before this build are
  watched too.
- **Verification.** `test/domain/watched-items.test.ts` (what a wait watches, the wake, a wait its pane carries),
  `test/integration/watched-items.test.ts` (an issue closed before the wait, two issues, a workflow run, an item that does
  not exist; no second wake),
  `test/integration/job-wait.test.ts` (a lost pane wakes a wait on its own command and on a poll, and the job resumes in a
  new pane), `test/herdr/executor-herdr-lost.test.ts` (the resume and the probe).

## Lane pods (issue #1284, 2026-10-15)

Part of #1281 (hopper and every machine on Kubernetes). Owner request: a StatefulSet of **lane pods** (chart value
`replicas`) that register with the hopper by dialling out — one machine per pod, a stable name, a volume for the
work dir — in place of agent boxes reached over ssh. Ssh targets and agent boxes stay, outside a cluster.

**Built on the client target, not on the Kubernetes executor.** A lane pod is a client target ("Joining a machine"):
the sandbox box image, its hopper client dialling out to `GET /client/connect`. No sshd, no inbound port, no Service.
So this part needs nothing of #1283 (the pod-per-job executor): the two share no code.

**The lane pool key.** A join code joins one machine, once, for 10 minutes; a StatefulSet needs one credential for
every pod and every restart. The install makes a **lane pool key** — 64 hex, `openssl rand -hex 32`, a join code's
shape — and gives it to the hopper (`HOPPER_LANE_POOL_KEY`, or the file `HOPPER_LANE_POOL_KEY_FILE` names; read at each
join, a preshared key of the install's as `HOPPER_TUNNEL_KEY` is) and to the pods' join step (a Secret). `POST /client/join`
takes it as it takes a join code (`src/machines/lane-pool.ts`, constant time), and never spends it.

- A lane pod is a machine of the hopper's first user — the first person who signed in, the oldest user (by seq), whatever
  its id (issue #1767): the first GitHub user, or the operator CLI's local account (issue #1380). Before anyone has,
  the join is refused (409) and the join step tries again (every 10 s, part 2).
- It joins under its pod's name (`hopper-lanes-0`), with `pool: true` on its `client` instance. A key a machine
  holds joins as that machine, as before. **A pod that lost its volume** joins with a new key under its name: a lane
  pod of that name is the same machine, its key replaced and its other options kept (`applyMachineJoin`). A
  StatefulSet runs at most one pod of a name, so the old key is not in use. A machine of that name that is no lane
  pod is not taken: the pod is given `-2`.
- **Its join step runs at every start** (an init container): a pod keeps its link key in its volume, so the join
  answers the same machine, or adds it again after it was retired. Then the box's client dials in from its link.
- The key never reaches the container the jobs run in: only the init container mounts the Secret. A job that held it
  could join a machine of its own to the user's pool and be given that user's jobs.

**Leaving.** `POST /client/leave` (`src/http/client-link.ts`), signed with the client token over the user and the
machine key (label `hopper-leave`, `src/client/signature.ts`). From the first ask the machine is **leaving**
(`src/machines/links.ts`, in memory, until it dials in again): the decider places no new job on it
(`leavingHolds`, `src/decider/assign.ts`; a job resuming there with an answer still returns to its pane), and the
Machines view shows *leaving*. The answer: `{ jobs, retired }`, the jobs still on it (busy lanes, waiting panes).
- A client with `HOPPER_CLIENT_DRAIN` set (a lane pod) asks when it is told to stop, every 5 s, until no job is left
  or it is retired, then stops (`src/client/leave.ts`). The box's entrypoint now waits for its client before it stops
  herdr, whose panes the jobs run in. The pod's `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` is the most it waits; a job still on it
  then is a job on a machine that went away, as today.
- **A lane pod with no job left is retired** (`src/users/machine-leave.ts`): removed from the plugins config as a person
  removes a machine. Scaled down, the pool leaves no machine behind. Restarted, the pod's join step adds it again under
  its name: the same machine, with the machine defaults' lanes and executors. Any other machine is never removed by a
  leave: it only takes no new job until it dials in again.

**Part 2: the StatefulSet in the chart** (`deploy/helm/hopper/templates/lanes.yaml`, `docs/deploy.md` "Lane pods on
Kubernetes"). `lanes.replicas` (default 0) pods of the box image of the hopper's update channel (`box-claude` for
`latest` and `stable`, `box-claude-<channel>` for the others).
- The chart makes the lane pool key at the first install (the SHA-256 of 64 random characters: 64 hex) in the Secret
  `<release>-lane-pool`, kept at each upgrade (read back) and at an uninstall, as the runtime Secret is. The hopper's pod
  mounts it and reads it through `HOPPER_LANE_POOL_KEY_FILE`; in a lane pod only the init container `join` mounts it.
- The init container copies the image's home into the volume once, then joins under the pod's name
  (`metadata.name`) at the hopper's Service (`http://<release>:<port>`, a LAN name the chart already sets, from the pod
  network in `lanPeers`), again every 10 s until it is let in. A refusal before anyone signed in is no crash loop.
- One volume per pod (`volumeClaimTemplates` `home`, `lanes.size`): the link key, the agent's sign-in, the work trees.
  `persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy` `whenScaled: Delete`: a pod scaled away was retired, so its volume goes too.
- `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` is `lanes.drainSeconds` (3600); the lane container has `HOPPER_CLIENT_DRAIN`.
- No Service selects the pods, and the NetworkPolicy `<release>-lanes` lets nothing reach them (`ingress: []`). The
  NetworkPolicies of Postgres, OpenFGA and Solr do not name them, so a lane pod reaches none of them.
- The chart is not yet merged (#1282): part 2 is built on its branch, and lands it with it.

**Not done here:** a run of the acceptance on a cluster (1 → 3 → 1, a pod restart, a scale-down while a job runs): no
CI runner has a cluster. `docs/deploy.md` "Lane pods on Kubernetes" has the steps.

**Verification:** `test/integration/lane-pool.test.ts` (three pods join with one key; a restart with and without its
volume is the same machine; a wrong key, no pool, no user yet refused; a pod leaving with no job retired, then joining
again; another machine leaving stays, leaving until it dials in; a forged leave refused), `test/users/machine-leave.test.ts`,
`test/decider/leaving.test.ts`, `test/client/leave.test.ts`, `test/scripts/box-entrypoint.test.ts` (the client stopped
before herdr).

## Host-only parts in a cluster (issue #1289, 2026-10-15)

**Problem.** A **cluster install** runs the hopper and its **lane pods** as pods. A pod has no WSL, no systemd and no
container runtime socket. Parts written for a host read the host anyway: the resource meter read a node's WSL kernel as
WSL and a pod with no cgroup limit as the whole node; the client and the sandbox view asked for a Podman socket and
`systemctl --user`; remote access asked for `podman compose up -d`; the Machines view offered `podman network connect`.

**Decision.** One check, `inCluster` (`src/client/cluster.ts`): `KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST`, which Kubernetes gives every
container of a pod (the same check as the update's, `src/update/cluster.ts`, which now uses it). In the client
directory, so the client runs it as a plain file. Where it holds:

| Part | On a host | In a pod |
|---|---|---|
| Resource meter (`src/client/resources.ts`) | cgroup limits, else the host's `/proc/meminfo` and CPUs; WSL from `/proc/version` | never WSL, Windows never asked; always `container`, so the memory alert does not watch it; the cgroup's limits, else `HOPPER_POD_CPU_LIMIT` (millicores) and `HOPPER_POD_MEMORY_LIMIT` (bytes) |
| Windows link (`src/client/windows-link.ts`) | tested in WSL, dialling on loopback | never tested |
| `hopper windows-link report` | reported | refused: no Windows host is beside a pod |
| Client runtime `which` (`src/client/runtime.ts`) | no socket: run `systemctl --user enable --now podman.socket` | no socket: the hopper starts no sandbox box in a pod. A socket given is used |
| Sandbox view and launch beside the hopper (`src/sandbox/service.ts`) | no socket: give `HOPPER_PODMAN_SOCKET` | `NO_RUNTIME_IN_CLUSTER`: the hopper starts no box beside itself there |
| Host link `wsl` (`GET /api/host-link`) | from `/proc/version` | false |
| Network fix (`podman network connect`) | shown for an ssh target named by its container | none |
| Remote access status (`src/http/remote-access.ts`, `tunnelServiceProblem`) | no service: the compose stack runs them; gone: `podman compose up -d` | no service: reach it through the chart's Ingress; gone: check that it runs in the cluster |

The chart gives the hopper and each lane its own limits through the Downward API (`hopper.podLimits`,
`resourceFieldRef` `limits.cpu` divisor `1m`, `limits.memory` divisor `1`). With no limit set, Kubernetes gives the
node's allocatable: a pod with no limit may use the node. With cgroup v2 a limit is also the cgroup's, which the meter
reads first, with the cgroup's own use.

**Left as they are, and why.**
- The reap and the survey (`src/client/reap.ts`) call `systemctl` only where it exists (`command -v systemctl`), and
  find a job's processes by its environment where it does not. Nothing is reported.
- The herdr the hopper owns (`src/machines/herdr-owned.ts`) restarts `hopper-herdr.service` only where its unit file is.
  It is for ssh targets; a lane pod is a client target.
- The ssh probe (`src/machines/resources.ts` `RESOURCES_COMMAND`) reads an ssh target, which is never a pod of this
  install. The vault (`src/vault/service.ts`) reads nothing of the host.
- `systemd/*.service` are units for a host install; the chart installs none.
- Sandbox boxes in the cluster are issue #1281 part 5.

**Verification:** `test/client/cluster.test.ts`, `test/client/resources.test.ts` (a pod's cgroup limits; the Downward API
limits against the cgroup's use; a pod on a WSL node), `test/client/windows-link.test.ts`, `test/client/runtime.test.ts`,
`test/sandbox/cluster.test.ts`, `test/http/cluster-gates.test.ts`, `test/integration/host-link-base.test.ts`,
`test/scripts/helm-chart-lanes.test.ts`. `test/support/isolate.ts` unsets `KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST`, so a test run in a
lane pod reads as a host.

## Each job its own container runtime (issue #1295, 2026-10-15)

**What happened.** A job ran `podman system reset --force` on the host. It had moved `HOME` and `XDG_DATA_HOME` to a
temp dir, but not `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, so the reset wiped the user's rootless runtime dir. Podman then refreshed as after a
reboot: every container of the hopper stack showed as exited, the rootless network went, and the live hopper stopped
answering while its processes ran on untracked. The kind clusters and testcontainers of other jobs ran on the host's
podman socket too, beside the stack. A job's shell was the user's shell: every container runtime the user had was the
job's.

**As built** (`src/client/job-runtime.ts`, used by `src/executors/herdr/start.ts`, `src/executors/print-agent.ts` and
`src/client/reap.ts`):

- **The job's runtime.** In the job's scope, before Claude starts, the pane's shell runs a fixed setup script. Where the
  machine has podman and the user a runtime dir (`XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, else `/run/user/<uid>`), the job gets its own:
  - runtime dir `<the user's runtime dir>/hopper-runtime-<job id>`, mode 700 — never the user's runtime dir itself;
  - storage `<scratch dir>/containers/storage` (graphroot), its run state in the runtime dir (runroot, `tmp_dir`):
    `<scratch dir>/containers/storage.conf` in place of the user's (`CONTAINERS_STORAGE_CONF`), and
    `containers.conf` read over theirs (`CONTAINERS_CONF_OVERRIDE`);
  - socket `<runtime dir>/podman/podman.sock`, a `podman system service --time=0` started in the job's scope, so the
    reap's scope stop ends it. `DOCKER_HOST` names it, for the docker CLI and testcontainers; `KIND_EXPERIMENTAL_PROVIDER`
    is `podman`, so kind runs its cluster inside the job's runtime.
  - The user's bus and systemd's private socket are hard links in the runtime dir (the same tmpfs): podman's rootless
    network namespace has a `/run` of its own with only the runtime dir in it, and aardvark-dns (a network with DNS, as
    kind makes) reaches systemd only through them. The job reached both before; nothing is added.
  These are written to `<scratch dir>/containers/env.sh`, which the shell sources; `CONTAINER_HOST`,
  `CONTAINER_CONNECTION` and `DOCKER_CONTEXT` are unset. A print-agent turn sources the same, with no socket: nothing of a
  turn outlives it.
- **No runtime here.** A machine with no podman, or no runtime dir the user can write: `DOCKER_HOST` names
  `<scratch dir>/containers/no-container-runtime.sock`, which is not there. The host's docker socket is closed to the job
  all the same (`hopper-runtime-none`); a job that needs containers there has none.
- **The guards.** `<scratch dir>/containers/bin/podman` and `…/docker`, first on the job's PATH. Each sources `env.sh`
  again, so a job that changed HOME, `XDG_*`, DOCKER_HOST or a context gets its own runtime all the same, then runs the
  real command of its name further on PATH. Refused, exit 126: `podman system reset|migrate|renumber` (after any global
  options), and a global option that names another runtime or its storage (`podman --url|--connection|-c|--remote|-r|
  --root|--runroot|--tmpdir|--imagestore|--volumepath|--network-config-dir|--config`, `docker -H|--host|-c|--context|
  --config`), and an argument anywhere that names the user's runtime dir (`podman`, `containers`, `libpod`,
  `docker.sock` in it), the user's storage (`.local/share/containers`) or a host socket (`/run/docker.sock`,
  `/run/podman/podman.sock`): a job never mounts or dials the host's runtime through its own. A job's own runtime holds
  only its own containers, so `podman rm|stop` of anything not its own has nothing to find, and the hopper stack's
  containers, volumes and network are not in it.
- **Health checks.** podman runs a container's health check from a systemd timer it makes with `systemd-run`, found on
  PATH. The timer's podman has the user manager's environment, so it took the user's runtime dir, joined the user's own
  user namespace and never found the job's container: testcontainers (Postgres waits on its health check) waited until it
  timed out. `<scratch dir>/containers/bin/systemd-run`, first on the job's PATH, adds the job's runtime variables
  (`--setenv`, from `env.sh`) to podman's `healthcheck run` timers and passes every other call to the real `systemd-run`
  as it was.
- **The reap** (step 2 of "The reap"). Unless it keeps (`keep`: a timed-out job may go on), it finds the runtime dir by
  the job id in the user's runtime dir, and the scratch dir as given, else as the runtime dir names it — only ever a
  `…/.worktrees/@scratch/<job id>`. It writes the config again (a job that changed it cannot point the reset at another
  runtime), prints each container and volume as removed (`job.containers_removed`), runs `podman system reset --force`
  with `--root` and `--tmpdir` the job's (its runroot only in the config it wrote: Podman 4 refuses a `--runroot` longer
  than 50 characters, and the runtime dir's is), removes what of the storage is left through `podman unshare`, stops
  every process still started from the runtime dir (its environment's `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`: the pause process, network
  helpers), stops the health check timers of the containers it named and kills their scopes (what a reset that failed
  left in the user's systemd), and removes the runtime dir. The reap may take 180 s (`REAP_TIMEOUT_MS`): a kind cluster is slow to stop.
- **The survey** names each job whose runtime dir is still there as a job with a container left, so the sweep reaps an
  ended job's at once ("The sweep").
- **Labels.** Everything in a job's runtime is the job's, and its name carries the job id. The guards also put the
  `hopper.job=<job id>` label (issue #1120) on what a job makes by name — `run`, `create`, `container run|create`,
  `pod create`, `volume create`, `network create` —, the job id read from the scratch dir the guard is in. What a job
  makes through the socket (testcontainers) has no label added; it is in the job's runtime all the same.

**Residual risk.** The job is still the user's OS user. The guards stop a mistake made by name — the one that happened,
and what kind and testcontainers call —, not a job that runs `/usr/bin/podman` with the user's runtime named again, opens
the user's sockets by path, or signals the stack's processes. A boundary against that is a box ("Agent boxes",
"Sandboxing jobs: mechanisms compared"): a VM or another OS user. The job's image pulls are its own (no image store shared
with the user's), so each job pulls what it runs once.

**Not done here.** A job as another OS user, or in a VM: it differs in security and cost from what is built. A person
picked the sandbox below (Path 1 of the proposal) in its place. A test hopper's banner on the admin's page is
"Which hopper answers" below.

### The sandbox (issue #1295 part 3)

**Why.** The guards stop a mistake made by name. A job could still name the user's runtime dir again, open its sockets by
path, or signal the stack's processes. So Claude, and everything it runs, runs in bubblewrap, where the kernel hides them.

**As built** (`src/client/job-sandbox.ts`, used by `src/executors/herdr/start-isolation.ts`):

- **Where it starts.** After the job's container runtime, before Claude, the pane's shell runs the sandbox command. It
  makes a trial run of bubblewrap (`bwrap` with the namespaces below, `true`), writes the runner `<scratch dir>/sandbox/run`
  and the sandbox's `claude` `<scratch dir>/sandbox/bin/claude`, and puts that dir first on the shell's PATH. It prints
  `hopper-sandbox-on`. herdr starts `claude` from the pane's PATH (`agent start --kind claude`), so the sandbox's `claude`
  starts the real one (the next `claude` on PATH) through the runner. herdr sees Claude in the pane as before: its start,
  its prompt, its working and blocked states. Checked by hand with a separate herdr session.
- **No bubblewrap that runs** (none installed, or no user namespaces, as in an unprivileged container): `hopper-sandbox-none`,
  the sandbox's dir removed, and Claude starts as the user does, with the job's container runtime and its guards.
  `hopper-sandbox-failed` (its scripts could not be written) fails the job before Claude starts. No answer within 30000 ms
  is a start that timed out.
- **The runner** sources the job's `env.sh`, then runs its command in `bwrap` with its own PID and IPC namespaces
  (`--unshare-pid --unshare-ipc`, a new `/proc`, `--die-with-parent`), over the machine's root (`--dev-bind / /`):
  - the user's runtime dir and `/run/user/<uid>`: an empty tmpfs, but for the job's own runtime dir, bound at its path.
    In it, the user's bus (`bus`) is `/dev/null` and `systemd/` is an empty tmpfs: through them a job could start a
    process outside the sandbox (`systemd-run --user`). `DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS` is unset;
  - `/dev/shm`, the user's container storage (`$XDG_DATA_HOME/containers`, `~/.local/share/containers`, and the home's
    from the password database): an empty tmpfs;
  - `/run/docker.sock`: `/dev/null`; `/run/podman`: an empty tmpfs;
  - herdr's sockets (`~/.config/herdr/sessions` and the dir of `HERDR_SOCKET_PATH`): an empty tmpfs. Through them a job
    could type into a pane outside the sandbox;
  - `HOPPER_SANDBOXED=1`. A runner inside the sandbox runs its command as it is.
- **podman in the sandbox.** Rootless podman cannot start a runtime inside bubblewrap (`newuidmap`), so the job's socket
  stays outside, in the job's scope. In the sandbox, `CONTAINER_HOST` names the job's socket (`unix://<runtime
  dir>/podman/podman.sock`), so podman there is a remote client of it: the runner sets it, and `env.sh` sets it again
  while `HOPPER_SANDBOXED` is set (the guards source it). Outside the sandbox `env.sh` unsets it, as before. DOCKER_HOST
  names the same socket; `KIND_EXPERIMENTAL_PROVIDER` is still `podman`.

**Residual risk.**
- The podman service runs outside the sandbox, as the user. A container a job makes through its socket (testcontainers,
  the Docker API) can bind-mount a host path, such as the user's podman socket: the guards read only the CLI's arguments.
- The job is still the user's uid. Files in the home that are not masked can be read and written; Claude's own sign-in
  in `~/.claude` must be.
- The network is the host's: a job reaches the stack's ports on loopback. A network namespace of the job's own (pasta,
  only the hopper's port forwarded) is not built.
- The pane's terminal is shared (no `--new-session`, which would break Claude's terminal). On a kernel with
  `dev.tty.legacy_tiocsti` = 1, a job could push keys into the pane's shell outside the sandbox. Linux 6.2 and later
  default it to 0.
- A job that started a service with `env -u HOPPER_JOB_ID systemd-run --user …` to outlive it can no longer do that from
  the sandbox: the user's systemd is masked.

**Print-agent turns** (issue #1295 part 4, `src/executors/print-agent.ts` `isolatedTurn`). A print-mode agent (codex,
opencode, omp, Cursor's agent, Claude in print mode) runs in the same sandbox. The turn's scope runs `sh -c` of:
- the job's container runtime setup, as before;
- the sandbox setup (`sandboxCommand`, in a subshell: the turn uses the runner, not the sandbox's `claude`);
- the job's socket, `podman system service` through the job's guard, started in the scope. Its pid stays in the turn's
  shell, never in a file: the job can write its runtime dir, and the turn kills that pid from outside the sandbox;
- the agent through the runner (`<scratch dir>/sandbox/run env <the turn's variables> <the CLI> …`), then the socket
  stopped. The turn's exit code is the agent's. Nothing of a turn outlives it: in the sandbox's PID namespace, a process the
  agent left ends with the turn.

systemd 254 and later expand `$` in a scope's command, which would rewrite the script's own variables, so the turn's
`systemd-run` gets `--expand-environment=no` where it knows that option (a trial run first).

`hopper-sandbox-none` runs the agent as before, with the job's runtime and its guards. A runtime that wrote no `env.sh`, or
a sandbox that could not be set up, ends the turn with exit 125 and a line on stderr, so the job fails. The turn does not
wait for the socket: an agent's first podman call comes seconds after it starts. A turn killed from outside (a cancel, a
timeout) leaves its socket in its scope; the next turn stops that scope first, and the reap stops it at the job's end.

**Not done**: a network namespace of the job's own (pasta, only the hopper's port forwarded). The residual risk above
stands.

**Verification:** `test/client/job-sandbox.test.ts` (with the machine's bubblewrap, skipped where it cannot run; a
stand-in podman, claude and user runtime dir: the setup, herdr's `claude` running the real one in the sandbox with its
arguments, the user's runtime dir showing only the job's own, its bus masked, a wipe of the user's runtime dir and
container storage from the sandbox leaving them as they were whatever HOME and `XDG_*` say, herdr's sockets and the
storage not there, no host process seen, podman reaching the job's socket as a remote client, a reset still refused, a
nested runner, `/run/user/<uid>` empty, and none where there is no bubblewrap), `test/adapters/print-agent-executors.test.ts`
(each print-mode agent's turn in the sandbox with podman a client of the job's socket, that socket stopped when the turn
ends, a process the agent left gone with the turn), `test/herdr/executor-sandbox.test.ts`
(set up after the runtime, before Claude; none starts Claude as before; failed fails the job), and by hand with
stand-ins under the job's work tree: a stand-in user runtime dir with a real bus socket, a stand-in podman, the real
bubblewrap and the real Claude CLI (`claude --version` through the sandbox's `claude`). Not checked by hand: real podman
and kind through the job's socket from the sandbox.

**Verification:** `test/client/job-runtime.test.ts` (the setup, the guards, the reap and the survey for real, with a
stand-in podman and docker on PATH and a stand-in user runtime dir: a reset refused whatever HOME and `XDG_*` say, a flag
naming another runtime refused, an argument naming the host's runtime or a host socket refused, the job label on what a
job makes, podman's health check timers given the job's runtime, everything else run on the job's runtime, the reap resetting only the job's runtime with its
config written again, stopping what runs from it, and leaving the user's runtime dir as it was),
`test/herdr/executor-runtime.test.ts` (set up after the scope, before Claude; failed fails the job), and by hand on a
machine with podman 6: a job's network with DNS, a container listed by the job's docker and not by the user's podman, a
reset refused, a mount of the user's podman socket refused, the job label on a container, a health check passing, the
repository's own database tests (testcontainers, Postgres) passing on the job's runtime, and the reap leaving the stack's
containers as they were. kind was not run by hand: no kind on that machine.

## Which hopper answers (issue #1295, 2026-10-15)

**What happened.** A job installed a test hopper in its kind cluster. The test hopper made its own master key, and its
banner ("the master key is missing") reached the admin's page as if it were the real hopper's. The likely path: the job's
podman reset took the hopper stack down (the reset "Each job its own container runtime" stops), and the address of the
user's hopper, `127.0.0.1:4790`, was free; the test hopper took it (the chart's `kubectl port-forward svc/hopper 4790`,
or a port its kind cluster publishes). The page open on that address went on reading it, now from the test hopper, on
the same origin: with the user's session token sent along, and a session the test hopper did not know cleared.

**As built.**
- **The instance tag** (`src/http/instance-tag.ts`): every answer carries `x-hopper-instance`, 16 hex characters, a hash
  of the instance id (`settings.instanceId`), set on the raw response first thing, so a guard's refusal and the event
  stream have it too. The event stream's first event is the tag (`hopper.instance`, "SSE").
- **The page** (`ui/src/lib/instance.ts`): its hopper is the first tag it reads, else the tag this browser kept
  (`jh_instance` in localStorage), which the first tag it ever reads sets. An answer to `get`, `post`, the session read or
  a sign-in with another tag, or with none once the page knows its hopper, is another hopper's: dropped, with
  `OtherHopper`. From then on the page sends nothing more to that address — the session neither sent nor cleared — and
  takes nothing of it. The event stream takes no event before its tag once the page knows its hopper, and closes on
  another hopper's tag.
- **The notice** (`ui/src/app/other-hopper.tsx`, `HopperGate`): one card in place of the whole page — no view, no banner:
  which hopper the page talks to, which one answered, and that the page shows nothing of it. **Reload** reads the page
  again (the real hopper back: all is as before). **This is my hopper now** is for a hopper set up again (a new
  database, a new instance id): the kept tag and the session are forgotten, and the person signs in again.

**Residual risk.** The tag is no proof. A hopper a job changed can send the user's tag (it is on every answer), and a
page that loads from the other hopper runs that hopper's code. It stops the mistake that happened — a test hopper built
from this repository on the user's address —, not a job that means harm: that is the hard boundary of "Each job its own
container runtime". The first request after the switch still carries the session token to the other address; the page
stops at its answer.

**Verification:** `test/integration/instance-tag.test.ts` (the tag on every route, the page and a 404 alike, another
hopper's another, the stream's first event), `test/ui/other-hopper.test.ts` (an answer from another hopper dropped and
nothing more sent, the session kept; a fresh page knows its hopper from the browser; an answer with no tag; the master
key banner of a test hopper never shown, the notice in its place; This is my hopper now; the stream takes no event before
its tag and closes on another's).

## Polls of hopper state (issue #1210 part 2, 2026-10-15)

The problem: a tend job ran `sleep 60` in a loop and read another pull request's mergeability again and again, as its own
command. A second job ran `sleep 600` for an hour, waiting for the hopper to tend a pull request. Each read cost nothing,
but each job blocked work, and the UI said "its own command" where it waited on hopper state. Part 1 made such a tend job
hold nothing ("A tend job on its own command holds nothing"). This part gives the job the hopper's wait, and bounds the loop.

- **`pr wait --for mergeable`** (`waitRequest.for`, `src/github-proxy/policy.ts`; `prWaitOver`, `src/github-proxy/pr-status.ts`,
  pure). A wait on a pull request the hopper follows that ends when the hopper sees its `mergeable` other than it was when the
  wait opened (a mergeability not known yet is no change), or the pull request merged or closed. The watch keeps `for` and
  `from` in its body (`src/github-proxy/pr-waits.ts`), so a wait on its checks and one on its mergeability are two watches.
  It is answered again on the same events as a wait on checks: `job.pull_request_seen` fires when the follow's merge wait
  changes, as `conflicts` does. `--for checks` is the default, as before. The job rules' GitHub line and `hopper-gh`'s help say
  to use it, once.
- **A poll is flagged** (`src/github-proxy/polls.ts`, in memory). The same read (`op`, repository, number) of one job asked
  `POLL_READS` (3) times in `POLL_WINDOW_MS` (15 minutes) is a poll. It is still answered — a refusal would break a job that
  reads twice for a reason —, with `poll`, a note that names `pr wait` (or `HOPPER_WAITING` with `on:`), and the
  `github_proxy.done` event records `poll`, the count. A `pr wait` is never a poll.
- **The wait says what it polls.** When the job that polls is on a wait for its own command, the proxy tells the engine
  (`polled` → `Commands.pollSeen`, `recordPollSeen` in `src/engine/wait.ts`; `polledWait`, `src/domain/own-command.ts`, pure).
  The first time, its wait's `on` becomes what it polls (`polledOn`: `pr.checks` → the pull request's checks, another `pr.*`
  read → its merge, an `issue.*` read → the issue) and `polledAt` is set; `job.wait_polled { on }`. It stays `ownCommand`, so
  it still holds no tending queue, and shows as running: the Queue view's badge says "running: polls the hopper", and "waits
  on" names the pull request or issue. The ledger's `waitingOn` says `PR #8 to merge (it polls the hopper)`, not the job's
  `for:`. A merge or a close of what it polls now wakes it (`wakeOn`, issue #1245), as for any wait on it.
- **The cap.** On a poll an hour (`POLL_WAIT_CAP_MS`, as `MAX_HELD_MS`) or more after the wait began, the hopper ends it
  (`job.wait_ended`, by `hopper`): the job is told that its command only polls, what the hopper knows now (the last answer, as
  JSON), and to stop the poll and use `pr wait` or `HOPPER_WAITING`. No timer: the poll itself is the signal, so a command that
  stopped polling is left to the own-command nudge (issue #1037).
- **Not built.** A refusal of a poll; a poll that never reaches the hopper (a `sleep` loop on local state only) — the
  own-command liveness check stays the one guard there.
- **Persisted state.** No schema change: `polledAt` is optional in the job's `wait` JSON. A build before this one reads such a
  wait as any wait on its own command, with its `on` a pull request or an issue.

**Verification:** `test/github-proxy/pr-wait.test.ts` (`--for mergeable`: the watch opened though its checks ended, ended on
the next mergeability seen, the job's wait ended with it), `test/github-proxy/polls.test.ts` (the count, what a poll waits on,
the note, the engine told only for a wait on its own command, a `pr wait` no poll), `test/domain/own-command.test.ts`
(`polledWait`: typed once, still its own command, ended at the cap), `test/domain/work-items.test.ts` (the ledger's words),
`test/integration/job-wait.test.ts` (the engine types the wait, then ends it after an hour, and the job goes on).

## Moving a compose install onto a cluster (issue #1373, 2026-10-15)

**Problem.** The chart (#1282), the kubernetes executor (#1283), lane pods (#1284), the cluster update (#1285), sandbox pods
(#1286) and the cluster gates (#1289) run a hopper in a cluster. A person who runs the hopper with compose had no way to
get there with their data: no cluster on the host, no tool to move the database, and the master key had to be typed into
a Secret by hand.

**Decision.** One host script, `scripts/hopper-cluster.sh`, in every image (`hopper cluster script`), as `master-key.sh`
and `hopper-service.sh` are. The steps are in `docs/kubernetes.md`; here, why they are as they are.

- **k3s rootless, under a user unit.** One binary with its own containerd and image store in a folder of its own, so
  nothing of Podman changes. kind or k3d would run the cluster in Podman's own store: a container, an image and a volume
  beside the stack. The root steps it needs (cgroup delegation, subordinate ids) are said, never run.
- **Binaries checked against the checksums their release publishes.** They come from the same place, so this catches a
  broken download, not a release that was taken over. Pinned versions, which a person can change.
- **The data on a pipe**: `pg_dump` from compose's Postgres into `pg_restore` in the chart's, into a database made new.
  OpenFGA's store is the schema `openfga` of that database, so it moves with it; its migration runs again after.
  Solr's index is built again from the database, as when its volume is lost. Both sides must hold the same number of
  tables.
- **One writer at a time.** The release comes up with the hopper at 0 (`replicas`, a chart value for this) while the
  compose hopper runs; the compose hopper stops before the dump; the cluster hopper starts after it. The user service's
  port check is stopped first, or it would start the compose hopper again.
- **The master key never in a file or an argument.** It is read from the launch source — `HOPPER_MASTER_KEY`, the key
  sealed to the host, the compose hopper's launch environment, the terminal — and goes on a pipe into the Secret (no
  here-string: bash before 5.1 writes one to a file). Its fingerprint is worked out by `node` in the compose hopper, from
  stdin, so a compose image of any version can be moved; it must match the running hopper's before anything stops, and
  the cluster hopper's after it starts. With an outside store (`--external-secret-store`), the person puts the key there
  and the External Secrets Operator fills the Secret; the script writes nothing to the store.
- **The person's own Secret: the script never reads the key** (`--master-key-secret NAME`). The person makes the Secret
  in the namespace before the move; the script reads no launch source and never reads the Secret's value (only whether
  it has a `master-key`). Once the release is in, with the hopper at 0, a one-off pod of the release's image mounts that
  Secret as the chart does and prints only the key's short fingerprint (`kubectl run --rm`). A fingerprint that is not the
  running hopper's stops the move before the compose hopper stops. The outside store's Secret is checked the same way,
  so with either the script holds no key at any time. A pod, not `kubectl get secret` and a hash here: the key would
  then be in this script's memory, which is what this path exists to avoid.
- **Machines keep their lanes.** Their link keys are in the database. On a cluster bootstrap made, the Service is a
  `LoadBalancer` at compose's port, which k3s's load balancer takes on the host: a machine dials the address it joined.
  The names it dialled (compose's `HOPPER_LAN_NAMES`, the host's names, its tailnet name) go to the chart's `allowedHosts` (issue #1421).
- **The hopper's own launch settings** are carried in `extraEnv`: each variable the compose hopper was started with that
  its image does not set and compose's plumbing does not name. A secret one goes to a Secret of its own.
- **Rollback is compose again.** The cutover rolls back by itself when a step fails: the cluster hopper to 0, the
  compose stack started (through its user service when it has one). Nothing of compose is removed at any step: `stop`,
  never `rm` or `down`.

**Refused.** A compose install with the local KMS (profile `kms`): the keys of its data key are in the compose volume
`kms`, and the chart's local KMS starts with none. A `localhost/` image, unless the person names one the cluster pulls.

**Not built.** A move back from the cluster to compose; the job run of the acceptance in a check (it needs a GitHub
sign-in, which no check has).

**Verification:** `test/scripts/hopper-cluster.test.ts` (stubs for podman, kubectl, helm, systemctl and curl: the order
of the cutover, the key never in an argument or a file, the rollback, the refusals),
`test/scripts/helm-chart.test.ts` (`replicas`, `service.type`, `allowedHosts`, the chart in the image),
`test/scripts/kind-migrate-check.test.ts`, and `scripts/kind-migrate-check.ts` on kind.

## Reading the held event loop (issue #1383, 2026-10-15)

Seen after the parts of issue #1154: stalls of 57 s, 63 s and 129 s, each `no slow store call in it`. `/api/health` did
not answer from inside the container; OpenFGA and Solr calls timed out though both answered at once from another
process; a machine's link ended and its dial-ins were refused `stale`. The process held 2.5 GB resident. The watchdog
said what did not hold the loop, never what did.

- **A worker thread reads where the loop runs while it is held** (`src/http/event-loop-held.ts`,
  `event-loop-held-worker.ts`). The watchdog's tick writes a beat (ms since the epoch) into shared memory. The worker
  looks at it each second; when no beat came for 2 s (`HELD_SAMPLE_MS`, below the health port's 5 s `HELD_MS`, so the
  stalls of 2–4 s that came each minute name their code too, issue #2367), it opens the inspector on the main thread
  (`Session.connectToMainThread`), pauses it (`Debugger.pause`, which V8 takes as an interrupt, so a busy loop is
  paused where it runs, and a synchronous native call at the JavaScript that called it), reads the top 8 frames,
  and resumes it at once. At most four reads a held spell, 2 s apart. Each read is logged by the worker at once, on
  stderr, so the log says the loop is held while it is: `hopper: the event loop is held for 2.0 s now; it runs list
  (src/store/jobs.ts:88) ← …`. The watchdog names the reads with the stall when the loop is free (`held`: `afterMs`,
  `frames`), in its log line, in `/api/health`'s `eventLoopStall`, in `hopper.event_loop_stalled` (additive, still v1)
  and in the **stalled** badge's title.
- **A stall names the processes started in it** (issue #2367, `src/http/event-loop-processes.ts`). Each process the
  hopper starts holds the loop while it forks, longer the larger the hopper is (about 2 ms at 800 MiB resident here,
  more on WSL): the update check's thousands of git processes a minute were stalls of 2–4 s with almost no store time.
  Node names each child process it makes on the `child_process` diagnostics channel, so every caller is counted. The
  watchdog reads the totals at each tick, as it reads the store's; a stall's line adds `…; processes started in it: 41
  (git ×38, herdr ×3)` when any started, and `processes` (`count`, `programs`) is in `eventLoopStall` and
  `hopper.event_loop_stalled` (additive). A program is named by its file name only, never its path or its arguments.
  `spawnSync` makes no child process object and is not counted. A frame names its function and its file in the hopper's tree (`src/…`,
  `node_modules/…`, `node:…`), else the file name alone: never an absolute path. The debugger is on only for the read.
  No inspector port is opened: the session is in-process. A Node with no inspector starts with none, and says so.
- **A stall says the process's memory** (`memory`: `rssMb`, `heapMb`), and the watchdog logs each time the resident size
  grows past another GiB (`hopper: the process's resident memory grew past 2 GiB (2560 MiB)`), read each minute. A
  growth and a stall in the same log say whether the garbage collector held it (a read of "no JavaScript").
- **A machine's ask that waited behind a held loop is not stale** (`src/client/signature.ts` `fresh`,
  `src/http/client-link.ts`). A dial-in, a vault ask or a leave is signed when it is sent, and read only when the loop is
  free. The watchdog answers how long the loop was held since a moment (`heldSince`: the stalls of the last 10 minutes
  and the one still going on, which the request handler sees before the timer does). An ask signed at `ts` is fresh when
  its age is within 30 s plus that time, at most 5 minutes more (`HELD_CREDIT_MS`). An ask from more than 30 s in the
  future gets no credit. Its nonce is kept for the window and the credit (`createNonceCache(WINDOW_MS + HELD_CREDIT_MS)`),
  so an ask is still accepted once. The credit is only time the hopper itself could not read: it is never given for a
  loop that was free.
- **The event stream holds neither the loop nor the memory for a reader** (`src/http/sse.ts`, "SSE"). Each open UI tab
  holds a stream, and every event, delivery and sample is written to each. A write to a reader that does not read (a
  tab asleep, a link gone quiet before its socket closes) was kept in the hopper's memory, with no bound, as long as the
  stream stayed open: resident size that grows, and a heap the garbage collector takes longer and longer to go through.
  A reader 8 MiB behind (`BEHIND_BYTES`) now has its stream ended, logged (`hopper: ended an event stream whose reader
  fell … KiB behind`); its EventSource comes back with Last-Event-ID and is replayed from there. A replay read every page
  of the event log in one turn of the loop; it now reads one page a turn, the next once the reader took it, and live
  events wait until it ends, so none comes before an older one. A replay page is not held to the 8 MiB: it waits for the
  reader, so a slow one still gets the whole replay.
- **The waits heard their user's event log once more at each change** (`src/github-proxy/pr-waits.ts`,
  `src/skills/waits.ts`, part 3; the cause found). A `pr wait` watch and a skill request's watch are answered again
  when the user's event log says what they wait on may have changed, by one listener per user. The listener was kept
  once per `subscribe` function, but `user()` (`src/http/job-github.ts`, `src/http/job-skill.ts`) makes a new one at
  each call: every answer again added a listener, and every listener answers again at each change. So the listeners
  doubled with each pull request event (and each vault event): each event then ran that many answers again, each with
  its store reads of the open watches — thousands of fast store calls in one turn of the loop, longer at each event,
  and a listener set that grew with no bound. They are now kept by the event log itself (`events`, the user store's,
  the same object while the user's runtime runs): one listener each, however often they are answered again.
- **A response that never finishes is no longer in flight for good** (`src/http/event-loop.ts`). An event stream is
  hijacked, so when its reader goes, its response never finishes and Fastify runs no `onResponse`: the watchdog kept it
  as in flight, so every stall named `GET /api/events/stream` and `GET /job/stream`, and each such stream stayed in its
  map. A request now leaves it when its socket closes too.
- **Every store call counts in a stall** (`src/store/slow-calls.ts`, `src/http/event-loop.ts`, part 3). The stalls of
  57 s to 129 s said `no slow store call in it`, but only a call of 100 ms or more was kept: a stall of thousands of
  calls of 20 ms said the same. The store now totals the time and count of every call by statement, and the watchdog
  names the difference of the totals across a stall (`storeCallsBetween`), so `store` says the store's whole part,
  `SELECT jobs 41.0 s ×2050` included. The rest of the stall is the hopper's own code, or the garbage collector.
- **The health port answers while the loop is held** (`src/http/event-loop-held.ts`, `event-loop-held-worker.ts`, part
  4; `HOPPER_HEALTH_PORT`, the image sets 4791). `/api/health` on the daemon's port is served on the loop, so a held
  loop does not answer it, and a probe sees only a timeout. The held-loop thread, given a port, listens on `127.0.0.1` at
  it and answers `GET /api/health` (and `HEAD`) from the beat alone: `200 { ok: true, version, uptimeS }` while the beat
  is fresh, `503 { ok: false, version, uptimeS, eventLoopHeldMs }` once no beat came for 5 s (`HELD_MS`). Inside the
  container: `curl 127.0.0.1:4791/api/health`. It is a second listener, made as small as it can be: loopback only, never
  every interface, even with LAN peers; a loopback Host only (`127.0.0.1:<port>`, `localhost:<port>`, else 421), as the
  Host guard; one path (else 404) and GET only (else 405); the instance's version and uptime only, the same as the
  daemon's answer to a request with no user, never a user's state; it changes and records nothing, and reads no store.
  The image publishes no port for it. A port it cannot take is logged (`hopper: the health port cannot answer: …`) and
  the daemon starts without it. Unset (a host install): no health port. The image's `HEALTHCHECK` stays on the daemon's
  port: a held loop is not healthy, and the health port is there to say why, not to hide it.
- **The process reading** (`GET /api/process`, an instance read, `src/http/stack-resources.ts`; `reading` of
  `src/http/event-loop.ts`, part 4). The hopper's own memory now (`rssMb`, `heapUsedMb`, `heapTotalMb`, `externalMb`,
  `arrayBuffersMb`) and its event loop over the last minute: the delay of its timers (`monitorEventLoopDelay`, 20 ms
  resolution: `mean`, `p50`, `p99`, `max` in ms) and its use (`eventLoopUtilization`, 0..1). The minute going on is
  answered in place of the last one when it held the loop longer, so a stall shows at once. Memory growth and a slow
  loop show here before they are a stall, with no container runtime to ask (`podman stats`).
- **The heap-growth check** (`test/reliability/heap-growth.test.ts`, part 5). It runs locally, never as a pull request
  check: it takes minutes, and a heap bound is a reading of the machine. `HOPPER_HEAP_CHECK=1` runs it; the file is
  skipped without it. It drives one real hopper idle for 30 s, then busy: 3 rounds of warm-up and 12 measured rounds
  (`HOPPER_HEAP_CHECK_ROUNDS`, `HOPPER_HEAP_CHECK_IDLE_MS`), each a GitHub sync, an intake action the outbox sends, 10
  jobs to their end, 5 event-stream readers that come and go, and 5 checkpoints that fail (`git could not read the work
  tree`). It reads the heap used after a forced garbage collection (`gc`, exposed in the test process only) and checks
  it grows less than 8 MiB idle and 24 MiB busy after the warm-up. Each reading is logged (`heap check: …`). First run
  (2026-10-15): idle 139.2 → 140.8 MiB; busy 144.7 → 145.8 MiB over 12 rounds, with no growth trend. So none of the
  activity it drives holds memory with no bound. The same run stalled the loop for 3 to 9 s from about 150 jobs, each
  stall hundreds of `SELECT jobs` calls: issue #1411.
- **Not done here.** No other code is moved off the loop: the cause found (the waits, part 3) was in the loop's own work,
  not code that needs a thread. Left: the smaller collections with no bound (issue #1402) and the reads of `jobs` in a
  busy hopper (issue #1411).

**Verification:** `test/http/event-loop.test.ts` (a stall names the code the loop ran while held, from the real worker;
`heldSince`, a stall going on included; the memory line once per GiB; `frameOf` never an absolute path),
`test/client/signature.test.ts` (a dial-in, a vault ask and a leave credited the held time, at most 5 minutes; none from
the future; still once), `test/http/sse-held.test.ts` (a replay frees the loop between pages; a slow reader gets it whole,
a live event after it; a reader far behind is ended; one that reads is kept), `test/store/slow-calls.test.ts` and
`test/http/event-loop.test.ts` (the store's totals; a stall of many fast store calls names them with their count; a
stream its reader closed is no longer in flight), `test/github-proxy/pr-wait.test.ts` (the pull request and skill waits
hear a user's event log once, however often they are answered again), `test/http/event-loop.test.ts` part 4 (the health
port answers 200 while the beat is fresh and 503 with the held time while another process asks it with this one held; a
host that is not loopback 421, another path 404; no port, no listener; the process reading's memory and loop delay, and a
held loop in its `max`), `test/integration/config.test.ts` (`HOPPER_HEALTH_PORT`), `test/reliability/heap-growth.test.ts`
(part 5, local only: the heap of an idle and a busy hopper stays in a bound).

## Local accounts (issue #1380, part 1, 2026-10-15)

Issue #1380: return to a user model the hopper owns. Hopper owns its users — local accounts and any external SSO
(generic OIDC); users attach their own sources (GitHub by OAuth or a personal access token); the GitHub App no longer
required. Owner decisions on the issue: identity keyed by the verified email; external SSO trusted with JWKS checks; a
simple built-in realm of local users (email and password, or a passkey) when no SSO is set up, and the first-run admin;
a source's verified email must match the user's (a setting, on by default). The issue is an epic. This part is the
built-in realm: a hopper that runs with no GitHub and no identity provider, end to end, its first admin included.

Inputs, from `main` at `e48e2ec4`: issue #237 removed the password realm and its accounts (argon2 with them); issue #238
removed every bootstrap login, so a fresh hopper's only way in was GitHub's first sign-in (issue #239). OIDC (issue
#185) already discovers the issuer, checks the ID token's `iss`, `aud`, `exp` and `nonce` through openid-client, and
counts `email` only when `email_verified` is true. It did not check the signature: part 2 below.

**Decisions** (taken from the issue, none asked):
- **Not a realm of the sign-in config.** The accounts are rows of their own (`local_accounts`, instance migration 41),
  and their identities carry the reserved realm name `local-accounts` (the sign-in config refuses a realm of that name).
