  A new realm type would make the `sign-in` record one that an older build refuses to load — it stops the daemon — so a
  hopper moved to a steadier update channel would not start ("Update channels and promotion"). A table the build before
  never reads keeps that build running; it signs nobody in with it.
- **Keyed by email.** The subject is the email in lowercase; it is also the identity's `email` and `username`. A new
  account's first sign-in makes its user, as every identity's does ("Sign-in maps an identity to a user").
- **The account's own role.** Each account names its role; no role rule applies to it, and a super admin is a realm's.
  `roleIn` takes the accounts: a session of a removed account ends, and a role change applies to live sessions, at the
  change (`reconcile`).
- **The hash: scrypt from Node's crypto** (N=2^16, r=8, p=1, a 16-byte salt, `scrypt$N$r$p$salt$key`). The rule is an
  established library for a protocol or a hash; Node's crypto is OpenSSL's scrypt, and it adds no native dependency
  (argon2 needed one, and went with issue #237). An unknown email is checked against a hash of a random password, so it
  costs what a wrong password costs; both answer the same refusal.
- **The first admin from the operator CLI**: `hopper local-account add <email> [--role]`, the password on stdin. The CLI
  holds the database's credentials, the same trust as the daemon's environment, and it works the same on a container
  install and in a pod (`kubectl exec`). No sign-up page: on a public URL, whoever came first would be admin.
- **An admin runs the hopper, never another user's work** (issue #221). Once an account has signed in, an admin cannot set
  its password, nor add it again under the same email after removing it (its identity is still linked to that user):
  409. Its own user changes the password (`POST /ui/api/local-accounts/password`, the current one checked), which ends
  the account's other sessions and API tokens; a new password an admin sets on an account nobody signed in with ends its
  sessions too. Nobody removes, or lowers from admin, the account they signed in with from the UI.

**As built.**
- `src/auth/local-accounts.ts`: the hash and its check, the form realm, the identity, the role. `src/auth/index.ts`: the
  form realms are the local accounts first while there is one, then the LDAP realms; `password` (the form on the sign-in
  page) is on while either is.
- `src/store/local-accounts.ts` (`LocalAccountRepository`, `src/domain/local-accounts.ts`), migration 41.
- `src/http/local-accounts.ts` (the rules) and `src/http/ui/local-accounts.ts` (the routes): `GET /api/local-accounts`
  (an instance read, never a hash), `POST /ui/api/local-accounts` (the instance admin: `save`, `remove`), `POST
  /ui/api/local-accounts/password` (role viewer). `UiSessions.endIdentity` ends an identity's sessions but one.
- `src/cli-local-accounts.ts`: `hopper local-account list | add | password | remove`.
- UI: Settings → Sign-in → Local accounts (`ui/src/views/local-accounts.tsx`), and Your password for a session of a local
  account; the sign-in form asks for an email or username.

**Residual risk.** A password is as strong as its holder picks it (12 characters at least), and the form answers anyone
who reaches the UI, under the sign-in rate limit (20 a minute per client). There is no second factor yet.

**Left for later parts of issue #1380:** passkeys; OIDC's allowed email domains as their own setting (the role rules'
`emailDomains` do it now), the client secret only in the vault (it is a system secret since issue #657), and tests that
a token with a bad signature, a wrong `iss` or `aud`, or a key the provider removed is refused; identity keyed by email
in OpenFGA subjects, audit and attribution; GitHub as a source a user attaches (OAuth or a personal access token, in the
user's vault), with repositories picked per source, the acting identity shown per job, and the source-email match
setting; a source expiring marks only the source (not the session, issue #513); no GitHub App and no App private key
required; the migration of GitHub-signed-in users; Kubernetes and service-account tokens.

**Verification:** `test/auth/local-accounts.test.ts` (the hash, the realm, the role, the reserved name),
`test/integration/local-accounts.test.ts` (a realm-only hopper: the CLI's first admin signs in and is the instance admin;
the CLI's refusals; an admin adds an account that signs in as its own user; an admin never sets the password of an
account that signs in as another user; an account's own password change ends its other sessions; no lockout; the realm
name reserved), `test/ui/local-accounts-panel.test.ts`.

## OIDC: the ID token's signature against the issuer's keys (issue #1380, part 2, 2026-10-15)

The owner's requirements on issue #1380: hopper does discovery, verifies ID token signatures against the provider's
JWKS and handles key rotation, and checks `iss`, `aud`, `exp`, `nonce` and `email_verified`. Acceptance tests: a valid
token passes; a bad signature, a wrong `iss` or a wrong `aud` is refused; a rotated key is picked up without manual
action, and a removed key stops validating.

**What was missing.** openid-client v6 checks an ID token's claims, but not its signature when the token came straight
from the token endpoint over TLS (OIDC Core 3.1.3.7 allows that). The oidc realm never asked for more: a token endpoint
that answered a token signed by any key was believed.

**The change.** `src/auth/oidc.ts` gives discovery `client.enableNonRepudiationChecks`: openid-client then checks the
signature against the keys at the issuer's `jwks_uri`, and refuses a token signed with a shared secret (`HS*`), which
has no published key. A refusal names the claim or the key: openid-client's message plus the cause it wraps.

**Key rotation** is openid-client's JWKS cache (oauth4webapi): kept per discovered issuer for at most 300 seconds; a key
id it does not hold makes it read the JWKS again when its copy is at least 60 seconds old. So a new key is picked up at
the first token signed with it (one minute after the last read at most), and a removed key stops validating at the next
read (five minutes at most). These bounds are the library's constants; the hopper sets none.

**Decisions:**
- **The library's check, not one of our own.** jose (already used by the gateway realm) could verify the ID token a
  second time with a cache the hopper tunes. The library's check is one switch and no code to own.
- **Allowed email domains stay the role rules' `emailDomains`.** A new field in the `sign-in` record is one an older
  build refuses (its schema is strict): a hopper moved to a steadier update channel would stop. A realm whose rules
  match only on `emailDomains`, with no default role, lets in nobody else.

**Left for later parts of issue #1380:** as part 1 lists, but for the JWKS checks and key rotation: passkeys; identity
keyed by email in OpenFGA subjects, audit and attribution; GitHub as a source a user attaches, with its repositories,
the acting identity and the email match setting; a source's expiry marking only that source; no GitHub App; the
migration of GitHub-signed-in users; Kubernetes and service-account tokens.

**Verification:** `test/auth/oidc-id-token.test.ts` against `test/support/oidc-issuer.ts`, a loopback issuer whose keys
the test holds: a valid token; a token signed by a key the issuer does not publish (same key id); a wrong `iss`, `aud`,
`exp` or `nonce`; a rotated key read again after a minute; a removed key refused after five minutes, the new key
accepted; an unverified email left out.

## GitHub through the sign-in alone (issue #1377, 2026-10-15)

The problem: a hopper with a GitHub sign-in (the device code of the hopper's app), a token that renews and five job
repositories listed nothing. Intake showed `Not listing issues: no GitHub App configured`, Sources said `No GitHub
connection is configured`, and the `github-app` source said `needs setup: private key not set`. Two causes. The hopper had
two identities on GitHub: the user's sign-in, and an admin's own GitHub App with its private key (`github-app`). And the
plugins config of that hopper held no `github-account` instance, so no source read through the sign-in, while the Sources
card of the connection still showed the account and its repositories. A self-hosted hopper cannot be given an App private
key, so the second identity goes, not only its pause.

- **One identity.** The device-code sign-in is the hopper's app's user-to-server token. Every GitHub read and write —
  listing, intake, labels, comments, pull requests, checks, merges — uses it, through the connected account's source
  (`github-account`, `src/sources/compose.ts` `createAccountSource`). Jobs label, comment, push and open pull requests
  through the same token (the GitHub proxy and git through the hopper, unchanged).
- **Removed.** The `github-app` job-source plugin; the App adapter (`createAppAuth` JWT and installation tokens,
  `loadGitHubApp`, `@octokit/auth-app`); the vault's `github-app-private-key` system secret and `GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY`;
  the private-key setup card, `POST /ui/api/github-app-key`, `GET /api/github-app-key` and `GET /api/github-apps`; the
  help page `github-app-setup`; `scripts/create-github-app.*`; the source's app mode (`mode`, bot comments, installed
  repositories as the allowlist); and the setup problem of a source (`JobSource.setupProblem`, the `needs-setup` source
  state, Needs you's Setup row), which only the App source had. A plugin's detection keeps its own `needs-setup`.
  `src/sources/github/app/` is `src/sources/github/http/`: the REST and GraphQL calls the account's adapter makes.
- **Migration** (tenant migration 69, `src/store/migration-account-source.ts`). A plugins config whose job sources hold no
  `github-account` instance gets one. Each `github-app` instance leaves the config; the account's source takes its jobs and
  its source events (claims, request cards, intake), switched on where the app source was on and it was off; the
  work-item ledger is rebuilt from them, so a request card waits on a source that runs. The key's vault row goes. A config
  with no job sources section is left as it is: the built-in instances apply. The build before runs on the result.
- **A source that cannot be built shows.** Sources and Intake show the account's source with its error (state `error`,
  `lastError`) when the plugin host cannot build it, never leave it out.
- **The Sources summary reads the sign-in** (`ui/src/model/sources.ts`), never only whether a source status exists:
  signed in with repositories, issues are read through the connection; with none, it asks to choose them; with an
  expired token, to sign in again; with the source missing, switched off or unable to run, it says which. It never says
  `No GitHub connection is configured`.

**Verification:** `test/store/tenant-migration-69.test.ts` (a config with only `github-app` migrated: instance, jobs,
request cards and key; beside an account source; a config with none added; one left as it is), `test/sources/no-app-key.test.ts`
(no code names the key, its vault row, installation tokens, the setup route or the App source's states; no `github-app`
plugin; no `@octokit/auth-app`), `test/integration/github-writes.test.ts` and `test/integration/github-graphql-batch.test.ts`
(a daemon with only a sign-in and chosen repositories, its GitHub the node:http fake: it lists, takes, labels and posts on
the thread through the account's token), `test/integration/github-budget.test.ts` (the budget, through the account's
source), `test/ui/sources.test.ts` (the summary per state), `test/ui/intake-view.test.ts` (the account's source that
cannot run has its panel, with the error).

## A source that expires marks only the source (issue #1380, part 3, 2026-10-15)

Issue #1380: sessions are no longer tied to GitHub token expiry; a source expiring only marks that source as needing
re-auth. Acceptance test: a source token expiring does not log the user out; the source is marked as needing re-auth.
This replaces issue #513 ("A GitHub sign-in ends with its connection"), which ended every session of a user signed in
with GitHub when their GitHub connection ended.

**The change.**
- `src/http/ui/sessions.ts`: a session ends only by its own lengths, a realm change, a gateway's refusal or a logout. The
  `connectionEnded` hook and its check are gone; `src/http/index.ts` no longer gives it.
- The connection is marked as before: `connected_account.expired`, the account's state `expired` ("reconnect needed"),
  its job source paused with the reason. The header's **GitHub: reconnect needed** shows to everyone, signed in with
  GitHub or not, and the page no longer asks the daemon at once to go to sign-in.
- The Sources panel offers **Connect GitHub again** to everyone: on an ended connection, and on one GitHub gave no
  refresh token (issue #518). The device code connects the same user's GitHub again from the session it has.

**Decisions:**
- **`connection-ended` stays a reason of `ui_session.ended`.** Events recorded before this part carry it, and the event
  schema checks the events it reads; no new event carries it.
- **Signed in with GitHub, the panel still offers Sign out, not Stop working through GitHub** (issue #322). Taking the
  sign-in and the source apart in the panel belongs to the part that makes GitHub a source a user attaches.

**Left for later parts of issue #1380:** passkeys; identity keyed by email in OpenFGA subjects, audit and attribution;
GitHub as a source a user attaches (OAuth or a personal access token, in the user's vault), with its repositories, the
acting identity per job and the source-email match setting (checked again on refresh); no GitHub App required (no App
private key is required since issue #1377); the migration of GitHub-signed-in users; Kubernetes and service-account tokens.

**Verification:** `test/integration/source-expired-session.test.ts` (the real daemon and a fake GitHub on loopback: two
browsers signed in with GitHub, GitHub revokes the grant, both sessions live, no `ui_session.ended`, the account reads
`expired`; Connect GitHub again from the same session makes it `connected`; a renewal ends no session),
`test/ui/sources-view.test.ts` (signed in with GitHub, an ended connection keeps the session, the header asks to
reconnect, and the panel's Connect GitHub again shows the device code).

## Sandboxes are burned after each step (issue #1349, 2026-10-15)

Owner's model (issue #1349): a sandbox does one task and is then burned. A sandbox is **not** a registered machine and
has no lane, but the hopper tracks each one in a ledger. Seen on a hopper before it: the machines config held 13
`hopper-sandbox-*` client machines (one lane each) next to the real seats; boxes were up for hours, exited boxes were never
removed, and one was stuck in Created. A job's `sandbox` ask started a box that joined as a machine, and the job's box
steps (issue #1004) ran in that box between other jobs' work.

- **An approval starts nothing** (`src/sandbox/requests.ts`). A sandbox request's states are `waiting`, `approved`,
  `declined`; `starting`, `running` and `failed` are gone, and so are the background start and its time limit (issue
  #1002). `vault.sandbox_approved` is the last event of an approved request; `vault.sandbox_started` and
  `vault.sandbox_failed` stay in the event registry for the events kept from before. The `sandbox` answer (200) says the
  runs are approved, that a sandbox never runs the job and never joins as a machine, and how to run each command:
  `sh "$HOPPER_STEP" box <template>`.
- **A box step is a need step** (`NeedSteps.box`, `src/sandbox/need-steps.ts`; route `POST /job/step?box=`). The box it
  names is a template of one of the job's approved sandbox requests (`GET /job/step` lists them `box T  template T`).
  The template must be ready now (approved, image approved, no profile waiting, its read-only check passed). The step runs
  in a new **need box** of the template, minted `boxNeeds`: each of the template's profiles the vault mints for a step
  (an aws-role, a cluster, a namespace) that reads, and with `--plan-id` every one, through the apply gate as a need
  step's change is. A `--secret` is refused. Nothing is kept between steps: the job brings back with `--output` what its
  next step needs. The box step that ran in a long-lived box (`src/sandbox/box-step.ts`, the module's `step`), the
  Windows steps' box branch (`StepBoxes`, `onBox`) and the vault's `stepsOn` are removed: no box's helper asks for a job
  any more.
- **The sandbox runs ledger** (`SandboxRun`, `src/domain/sandbox-runs.ts`; instance migration 42, table `sandbox_runs`,
  `src/store/sandbox-runs.ts`). The sandbox module's `needStep` — the one way a need step or a box step runs — writes a
  run when the need box starts: user, job, step id, template, box, machine, start. When the step ends: end, outcome
  (`succeeded` for exit 0 with no problem, else `failed`), exit code, problem. Then it lists the runtime's need boxes;
  one still there is burned again, and once the box is gone, `destroyedAt`. `GET /api/sandboxes` answers the user's 50
  latest runs (`runs`).
- **The sweep** (the check pass, every 10 s, beside the hopper). Every need box of this hopper that no step holds is
  burned: stopped, removed, its home volume removed. Then every run beside the hopper not destroyed whose box is gone is
  marked destroyed, and one whose step never ended (a hopper that stopped mid-step) ends as `swept`. A step held here is
  one this process runs, or one another live hopper on the same database runs: its `need-step` saga's lease is that
  hopper's (issue #1954, "The crash harness" part 7, `SagaRepository.heldByOthers`), so its box, home and run are left
  to it. A box whose remove
  fails stays open in the ledger, and the next sweep tries again.
- **Registered sandboxes leave `machines`** (tenant migration 70, `src/store/migration-no-sandbox-machines.ts`). Each
  `client` machine whose `container` names a `hopper-sandbox-…` box is removed from the user's `plugins` record. At the
  next start the daemon closes the lanes of machines it does not know (recovery), and the burn pass burns their boxes,
  with their sandbox records (part 2, below). A job that ran on such a box is requeued or failed by the
  restart's recovery, as for any machine that went.

**Decided here.** A box step mints only the template's reads unless the step names an approved plan: a long-lived box
had every profile and the apply gate checked each change at its mint; a step names its plan up front, as a need step
does. The template name is the box a step names, as the step no longer has a container of its own until it runs.

**Part 2: no sandbox joins as a machine.** The person's test path that still started one is removed.

- **No launch.** Machines → Add machine adds a computer only (`ui/src/views/machine-join.tsx`); *A sandbox box*, its
  launch parameters and its `podman run` line are gone. `POST /ui/api/machines/sandbox`, its OpenAPI entry and its
  `BOX_ACTIONS` row, `hopper sandbox launch`, `launchBox` (`src/sandbox/launch.ts`), the reconcile pass
  (`src/sandbox/reconcile.ts`), the box's address (`address.ts`), the agent credential at launch, and the record cache
  (`records.ts`) are removed. `POST /ui/api/machines/join` takes `template` only: no `box` flags. A join code names no
  `container`, and the `client` machine plugin has no `container` option (tenant migration 70 removed every machine
  that had one).
- **The burn pass** (`src/sandbox/burn-launched.ts`, every 10 s and at start). Each box an older build launched — it
  carries `io.hopper.box` with this hopper's instance id — is stopped and removed with its home volume, beside the
  hopper and on each client target that holds a recorded box, through its client. The record goes once its box is gone.
  A box it cannot remove is a cleanup problem on Machines (`GET /api/sandboxes` `problems`) until a pass removes it; a
  client target that is away keeps its boxes and their records until it dials in. The check pass's sweep also removes
  the home volumes of those boxes. The `sandboxes` table stays, so the build before still runs on the store; the hopper
  writes no row to it.
- **The runtime port is smaller.** The start check (`startCheck`, the spec's `check`, the health check in the create
  bodies) and `exec` are removed: only a launched box used them. `copyIn` stays for need boxes (`copy-in.ts`).
- **A machine's client makes no sandbox box** (`src/client/runtime.ts`): it creates only check boxes and need boxes, and
  refuses a create with a health check or the `healthcheck` call. It still stops, inspects and removes a box an older
  hopper launched, so the burn pass reaches it.
- **The vault's launch scope is removed** (`LaunchScope`, `withLaunch`, `launchRefusal`, `launchedOf`): only a launched
  box had one. A machine joined as a template's instance gets what the template gives, as before.
- `GET /api/sandboxes` answers `runs` and `problems` only.

**Part 3: the sweeps reach client targets.** Before, the sweep and the burn pass looked beside the hopper, and the burn
pass also at a client target a sandbox record named: a need box a client target leaked stayed there, its run stayed open,
and a box an older build launched there with no record was never found.

- **Every client target dialled in** (`ClientTargets.allDialledIn`, `src/users/sandbox-boxes.ts`): each user's client
  targets whose link is up now. The burn pass looks on each of them and on each one a sandbox record names; the sweep on
  each of them and on each one an open sandbox run names.
- **The sweep on a client target** (`sweepPlaces`, `sweepSteps`, `src/sandbox/service.ts`) burns there, through its
  client, each need box of this hopper and of that target's user that no step holds, with its home, as beside the hopper.
  Each open run of that user on that target whose box is gone is marked destroyed; one whose step never ended ends as
  `swept`. It lists only that user's boxes (`io.hopper.user`): another user's client on the same runtime keeps theirs.
  The sweep of homes (`sweepHomes`) runs there too, for need boxes and for boxes an older build launched.
- **A target that is away** keeps its boxes, and its runs stay open, until it dials in again; the next sweep then burns
  them. A run on a client target that is removed for good is closed by part 5.

**Part 4: no time limit and no kept home on a template.** Before, a template's `ttlMinutes` and `keepHome` limits were
saved and shown, but no box read them: a sandbox does one step and is burned with its home.

- `TemplateLimits` (`src/domain/sandboxes.ts`) is `cpus` and `memoryMb` only. `save-template` refuses `ttlMinutes` and
  `keepHome` (400); `hopper template save` takes no `--ttl-minutes` or `--keep-home`; a template's form and its line in
  Vault show CPUs and memory only.
- Tenant migration 71 (`src/store/migration-template-limits.ts`) removes both from each stored template's limits, and
  the limits themselves when nothing is left. The build before reads both as absent.
- Tests: `test/store/tenant-migration-71.test.ts`, `test/ui/sandbox-launch.test.ts`, `test/ui/template-limits-view.test.ts`,
  `test/domain/template-limits.test.ts`.

**Part 5: a sandbox runs with its template's CPUs and memory; a run on a removed client target is closed.**

- **The template's limits are read.** Before, a need box and a check box ran with the hopper's defaults
  (`DEFAULT_LIMITS`), and a template's `cpus` and `memoryMb` were saved and shown but read by no box. Now both run with
  `boxLimits(t.limits)` (`src/sandbox/params.ts`): each the template's default, else the hopper's. A box step and a need
  step pass the template's limits to the need box (`NeedBox.template.limits`, `need-steps.ts`); the read-only check reads
  them from the template it checks (`check.ts`).
- **A run on a removed client target is closed** (`closeRemoved`, `src/sandbox/service.ts`, after each sweep). Each open
  run on a client target the user no longer has — removed from Machines, or its user gone — is closed:
  `destroyedAt` is the time of the close, and `machineRemoved: true` says that no runtime saw its box go. A step that
  never ended ends as `swept`. `ClientTargets.known(userId, machine)` (`src/users/sandbox-boxes.ts`) says whether the
  user has that client target now, dialled in or not; a target that is only away keeps its runs open, as before.
- **No migration.** `machineRemoved` is a new optional field of a `sandbox_runs` row's JSON body; the build before reads
  the row and ignores it. A template's stored `limits` keep their shape.
- Tests: `test/sandbox/template-box-limits.test.ts` (a need box and a check box with the template's limits, and with the
  hopper's defaults), `test/sandbox/need-steps.test.ts` (the template's limits reach the need box),
  `test/sandbox/sweep-remote.test.ts` (a run on a removed client target, and one of a machine the user never had, is
  closed), `test/store/sandbox-runs.test.ts` (`machineRemoved` kept).

**Decided here.** The jobs that waited for days on template checks or approvals of `asked-…` templates are not changed
by code. Those waits are a person's decision by design: a person approves or declines the template in Vault,
or runs its read-only check again (`hopper template check <name>`). The issue lists them as what was seen, not as what is
expected. With no sandbox as a machine, no such wait holds a machine's lane any more.

Tests: `test/sandbox/requests.test.ts` (an approval starts nothing), `test/sandbox/need-steps.test.ts` (a box step:
reads minted, changes with a plan, refusals), `test/sandbox/sandbox-runs.test.ts` (the ledger from start to destroy, a
failed step, a remove that failed and the next sweep, a box left by a hopper that stopped), `test/store/sandbox-runs.test.ts`,
`test/store/tenant-migration-70.test.ts`, `test/integration/box-steps.test.ts` (the real daemon, `hopper-skill` and
`hopper-step`: two steps, two sandboxes, none left, no machine, the ledger), `test/integration/job-sandboxes.test.ts`,
`test/integration/skill-wait-wakes-job.test.ts`. Part 2: `test/integration/launched-boxes.test.ts` (Add machine starts no box;
boxes launched before are burned, with their homes and records; a box it cannot burn is shown until it goes),
`test/integration/sandbox-remote.test.ts` (the burn on a client target, through its client; away, then dialled in; the
client makes no sandbox box), `test/client/runtime.test.ts`, `test/ui/template-limits-view.test.ts`. Part 3: `test/sandbox/sweep-remote.test.ts` (a need
box left on a client target burned with its home and its run swept; another user's box stays; away, then dialled in; a
launched box with no record burned), `test/integration/sandbox-remote.test.ts` (the same through a real client).

## The source email match (issue #1380, part 4, 2026-10-15)

Owner decision 4 on issue #1380: every source identity a user attaches must have a verified email equal to the user's
SSO or realm email; a GitHub source whose verified emails do not include it is refused with a clear message; the match is
checked again on token refresh; a setting, on by default, that an admin can turn off. Acceptance test: attaching a source
whose verified emails do not match is refused with a clear message; with the setting off, it is allowed.

**The check** (`src/connected-accounts/email-match.ts`, `service.ts`):
- **At the connect from Sources.** `POST /ui/api/connected-accounts` `connect` hands the service the email of the
  session's identity (`Identity.email`: only an address the realm vouches for). Once the device code is approved, the
  service reads who the token belongs to (`identity.ts` `whoIs`, now with `verifiedEmails`: every email `GET
  /user/emails` says is verified). None equal to the session's email (both trimmed, lowercase), or no emails shown: the
  account is not kept, its new grant is deleted at GitHub (best effort, as for a replaced grant, issue #514), and the
  status is `failed` with the reason. A match is kept on the account as `matchEmail`.
- **At each renewal.** The renewer, once the new pair is kept, asks the service (`afterRenewal`): an account with a
  `matchEmail`, while the setting is on, is read again; one that lost the email ends as an expired sign-in does
  (`end`: `ended`, `connected_account.expired`, its source paused, the owner told once), and the renewal throws, so no
  token is given. The session stays (part 3). GitHub not answering the read ends nothing: it is logged.
- **Not checked.** A sign-in with GitHub (`adopt`) and a held grant taken from Sources: the account is the person's own
  identity there. A session whose identity gave no email (no sign-in, a login code): nothing to match. An account kept
  before this change has no `matchEmail`, so its renewals do not check it until it is connected again.

**The setting** (`src/http/source-email-match.ts`, `src/http/ui/source-email-match.ts`): the instance's settings key
`sourceEmailMatch` (`on`/`off`; never set: on), read at each check, so a change applies at once. `GET
/api/source-email-match` (an instance read), `POST /ui/api/source-email-match` `{ on }` (the instance admin), each
change `source_email_match.changed`. UI: Settings → Sign-in → Source email match; Sources shows the email an account was
connected for.

**Decisions:**
- **Emails GitHub does not show refuse the connect.** The owner's rule needs a verified email; with none to read, the
  hopper cannot say it matches. The message says so and names the setting.
- **At a renewal, emails GitHub does not show end nothing.** `whoIs` cannot tell a refused email read from GitHub not
  answering it, and ending a working connection on a network fault would cost the person a reconnect.
- **The email checked again is the one kept at the connect,** not the email of a later session: the user model keeps no
  email of its own yet (identity keyed by email is a later part of issue #1380).
- **No migration.** `matchEmail` is a new optional field of the `connected_accounts` row's JSON body; the build before reads
  the row and ignores it.

**Left for later parts of issue #1380:** passkeys; identity keyed by email in OpenFGA subjects, audit and attribution;
GitHub by OAuth or a personal access token, with no GitHub App required; the acting identity shown per job; the migration
of GitHub-signed-in users to hopper users with GitHub attached as a source; Kubernetes and service-account tokens.

**Verification:** `test/connected-accounts/source-email-match.test.ts`: an account with the session's email connects and
keeps it; one without it, or whose emails GitHub does not show, is refused with the message and nothing is kept; with the
setting off it connects; a session with no email connects; a renewal ends an account that lost the email, keeps one that
has it, and checks nothing with the setting off or when GitHub does not answer; `whoIs` lists every verified email.
`test/integration/source-email-match.test.ts`: the setting's routes, its default, the instance admin's alone, and its event.

## Each job acts with its own user's GitHub, and the job page names it (issue #1380, part 5, 2026-10-15)

Issue #1380: jobs act on GitHub with the token of the source owner, and the UI shows which identity acts for each job.
Acceptance test: two users with separate sources each act only through their own sources; jobs act with the owning user's
token, and the acting identity is shown. Before this part, a job's git (issue #652) already used its own user's
connection, but the GitHub proxy (`POST /job/github`, issue #563) acted with the hopper's **oldest** user's connection
for every job, and another user's job could only file an issue.

**The change.**
- `src/github-proxy/broker.ts`: the broker asks `connection(userId)` for the job's own user's connection (`src/http/job-github.ts`:
  `tenants.user(id).githubProxy.connection`); `hopper()`, `own`, `forUser` and the copy of another user's event in the
  oldest user's log are removed. A job whose user has no connection, or whose sign-in ended, is refused (**503**, the
  connection's own reason) and nothing reaches GitHub: no other user's connection acts for it.
- `src/github-proxy/policy.ts`: there is no "another user's job" any more. Every job asks every operation, on its own
  user's job repositories and its fork, under the same checks; `OTHERS_MAY` and the `own` field of `ProxyAsker` are removed.
- **The acting identity.** Every `github_proxy.done`, `.refused` and `.failed` event (from the proxy and from git) carries
  `as`, the login of the connection that acts. Each answer the proxy gives from GitHub or its cache carries `as` too, so
  the job knows who acted. `hopper-gh help` says so.
- **The job page** (`ui/src/views/job.tsx`, `ui/src/model/acting-identity.ts`): the fact **GitHub as** is the login of
  the job's newest proxy or push event; before the job acted, its user's connected GitHub account
  (`GET /api/connected-accounts`), marked as not acted yet; with none, `Sources → Connect GitHub`.

**Decisions:**
- **No migration.** Events recorded before keep `own`, `forUser` and `job`; the event schema keeps them optional, and `as`
  is a new optional field. The build before ignores `as` (the daemon does not check event data when it reads).
- **The hopper's own records answer `pr status` with no `as`.** No GitHub identity acted for that answer.
- **The job page reads the connected account once** for the "not acted yet" case, not on each event. A job that acted
  shows the login its events name, which stays true when the account changes later.

**Left for later parts of issue #1380:** passkeys; identity keyed by email in OpenFGA subjects, audit and attribution;
GitHub by OAuth or a personal access token, with no GitHub App required; the migration of GitHub-signed-in users to hopper
users with GitHub attached as a source; Kubernetes and service-account tokens.

**Verification:** `test/github-proxy/proxy.test.ts` (two users: each job comments through its own user's connection, each
event and answer names it, no event in the other user's log; a user with no connection is refused and nothing is sent),
`test/integration/github-proxy.test.ts` (the real daemon and fake GitHub: a second user's job files and comments with that
user's token, never the first user's; a user with no connection is refused), `test/integration/git-proxy.test.ts` (a push
names `as`), `test/ui/acting-identity.test.ts` and `test/ui/job-acting-as-view.test.ts` (the job page's **GitHub as**).

## A personal access token (issue #1380, part 6, 2026-10-15)

Issue #1380: users attach their own sources, GitHub through OAuth or a personal access token, kept in the user's vault, and
the GitHub App is no longer required. Before this part, a GitHub source came only through the hopper's app: a sign-in with
GitHub, or a device code from Sources. An instance with no app (no client id) could not connect GitHub at all.

**The change.**
- **Connect with a token.** `POST /ui/api/connected-accounts` `{ action: 'connect-token', provider, token }` (admin of the
  user, as `connect`). `src/connected-accounts/token-connect.ts`: GitHub must take the token (`GET /user`), and the source
  email match applies as for a device code (the session's email). Then the token is kept as the connected account's access
  token, `grantedBy: 'token'`, `connectedBy: 'sources'`, with no refresh token and no expiry: a system secret in the user's
  vault (`connected-account.github.access-token`), sealed under the master key, as every connection's token. Without the
  master key nothing is kept. A refusal (GitHub refused the token, the email match, no key) answers `failed` with why, and a
  connection there was stays as it was.
- **No app.** The token path reads no client id. The status of a token's connection has no `installUrl` and no
  `configUrl`, and the UI names no app.
- **Its repositories.** Where the app is installed means nothing for a token. Its connection reads, in the same schedule and
  kept read (issue #1250), the repositories the token reaches: `GET /user/repos`, every page, one entry per owner
  (`identity.ts` `tokenRepositories`), `repositorySelection: 'selected'`. Sources lists them under **Repositories the token
  reaches**, and the person picks the job repositories from them as before. Intake reads the source's issues in them with
  the token.
- **Its end.** Nothing renews a token. A 401 ends the connection as any connection with no refresh token ends: it reads
  **expired**, its source pauses, the owner is told once, and the person stays signed in (part 3). Sources offers Connect
  again and the token field.
- **Never deleted at GitHub.** The token is the person's, not a grant of the app: a connect that replaces it, and a
  disconnect, delete nothing at GitHub (`replace` in `service.ts` skips a `token` connection). An app's grant that a token
  replaces is deleted as before.
- **Jobs.** A job's GitHub proxy and git ask the connection for its token as before (part 5): with a token connection, they
  act with the person's token, and **GitHub as** names its login.

**Decisions:**
- **A personal access token, not an OAuth App.** A token needs no registration and no client secret on the instance; an
  OAuth App would need both, and the device flow through the hopper's app already covers the OAuth case.
- **One connection per provider still.** A token replaces the connection there was, as a new device code does. Two GitHub
  sources for one user are not part of this change.
- **No migration.** `grantedBy: 'token'` is a new value in the JSON body of the `connected_accounts` row. The build before
  reads the row unchecked; on that build, a disconnect of a token connection asks GitHub to delete it through the app,
  which GitHub refuses, and the build only logs it.
- **No re-check of the email without a renewal.** The email match runs again at each renewal (part 4), and a token has
  none. A token keeps its `matchEmail`; the check at the next connect applies.
- **No expiry read.** GitHub says a fine-grained token's expiry only in a response header. A token that expired gets a
  401 and ends then, which says the same thing to the person.

**Left for later parts of issue #1380:** passkeys; identity keyed by email in OpenFGA subjects, audit and attribution;
more than one GitHub source per user, and sources from other forges; the migration of GitHub-signed-in users to hopper
users with GitHub attached as a source; Kubernetes and service-account tokens.

**Verification:** `test/connected-accounts/personal-access-token.test.ts` (a token connects with no app and is kept in the
vault, not the row; its repositories are read in place of the installations; a refused token, a refused email and no key
keep nothing and delete nothing at GitHub; a token is never deleted at GitHub when replaced or at a disconnect; a 401 ends
only the connection; GitHub's repository list, every page, grouped by owner) and `test/ui/personal-access-token-view.test.ts`
(the token field connects and is cleared; a token connection lists the repositories the token reaches, with no app link).

## The sandbox playground (issue #1410, 2026-10-15)

Owner direction: a hopper, on Kubernetes (kind and the Helm chart) or on Podman, is a playground where a person starts
many sandboxes at once. Before, the only direct path was Add machine → a sandbox box: one box per click, and each box
joined as a machine, against issue #1371 (a sandbox is no machine and takes no lane). Issue #1349 removed that path. And
nothing limited how many ran at once.

- **The playground** (`src/sandbox/playground.ts`). One create starts `count` **playground sandboxes**: the published box
  image of an agent, or the approved image of a template (its read-only check passed, its tools added as for a box), on
  the runtime the hopper selected, beside the hopper only. Each runs its image idle (`exec sleep infinity`, a one-shot
  container, never restarted), with the sandbox flags, on a fresh home made for it (`staleHome` refuses one that is there),
  with no secret, no join code and no start check. No join code is minted, so it never joins: it is no client target,
  takes no lane, gets no job, and `GET /api/machines` does not list it.
- **Limits** are the hopper's settings, and the chart's values (`sandbox.maxConcurrent`, `sandbox.maxPerUser`,
  `sandbox.defaults.*`, `sandbox.max.*`): `HOPPER_SANDBOX_MAX_CONCURRENT` (all users together, default 20),
  `HOPPER_SANDBOX_MAX_PER_USER` (default 10), and the default and most CPUs, memory and time limit of one
  (`HOPPER_SANDBOX_DEFAULT_*`, `HOPPER_SANDBOX_MAX_*`; defaults 1 CPU, 2048 MiB, 60 minutes; most 4, 8192, 1440). A
  default above its max stops the daemon at start. A size is the create's, else its template's default, else the
  hopper's (a template has no time limit since issue #1349: only the hopper's holds); over the hopper's max or the template's it is refused with 400, naming the limit. A count over the room the
  two counts leave starts what fits and answers `refused: { count, limit, setting, reason }`; none fits: 429 with
  `limit` and `setting`. The room is counted and taken in one synchronous step before any start, so two creates at once
  never pass a limit. A sandbox that failed holds no room.
- **Nothing is left, nothing is reused.** The playground keeps its sandboxes in memory only. A start that fails, or a
  destroy while one starts, removes what the start made (container, then home), and only then forgets it; a remove that
  fails keeps it `destroying`, with why, and the pass every 10 s tries again. The pass also destroys each sandbox past
  its time limit, and removes every container and volume with the playground label of this instance
  (`io.hopper.playground=<instance id>`, a **sandbox label**, so the adapters' own label check lets it go) that no
  sandbox in memory holds. At start the hopper runs the pass first: whatever a restart or a crash left goes then. On
  Kubernetes a sandbox is a pod and a claim; the runtime's one NetworkPolicy (`hopper-sandbox`) holds every sandbox pod
  and is shared, so it stays: deleting it while another box starts would leave that box a moment with no egress policy.
- **A quota for the sandbox pods only** (chart: `sandbox.quota.enabled`). A ResourceQuota is the namespace's, and the
  hopper's own pods are in the same namespace. So the chart makes a PriorityClass `<release>-sandbox` (value 0, never
  preempts), gives its name to the hopper (`HOPPER_KUBERNETES_PRIORITY_CLASS`), the Kubernetes runtime sets it on every
  sandbox pod (need and check boxes, playground sandboxes), and the ResourceQuota counts only pods of that
  class (`scopeSelector`): `pods`, `limits.cpu`, `limits.memory`. Every sandbox pod has CPU and memory limits, so the
  quota admits it. No LimitRange: it cannot be scoped, so it would also set limits on the hopper, Postgres, OpenFGA and
  Solr.
- **Routes.** `GET /api/sandbox-playground` (the user's sandboxes, how many run, the limits), `POST
  /ui/api/sandbox-playground` (admin, a box action: it starts containers), `POST /ui/api/sandbox-playground/destroy`
  (admin; `ids` or `all: true`, only the user's own). The UI: the **Sandbox playground** panel on Machines.

Residual risk: the playground starts containers on the hopper's runtime, as a job's box step does; a person with the admin
role can start up to the limits. A sandbox on Podman joins the hopper's network, as a need box does.

Tests: `test/sandbox/playground.test.ts` (50 with `maxConcurrent` 20 start 20 and refuse 30 naming the limit, destroy-all
leaves no pod or claim; the time limit; a restart removes what was left, and nothing else; the limits per user; sizes;
a failed start leaves nothing), `test/integration/sandbox-playground.test.ts` (over the API: 429 naming the limit; none is
in the machines list or its config; a restart), `test/scripts/helm-chart-sandbox.test.ts` (the
values and the quota), `test/integration/config.test.ts`, `test/sandbox/kubernetes.test.ts` (the PriorityClass),
`test/ui/sandbox-playground.test.ts`.

## Identity keyed by email (issue #1380, part 7, 2026-10-15)

Owner decision 1 on issue #1380: identity is keyed by the verified email throughout; usernames are display only. The
issue's migration: existing GitHub-signed-in users become hopper users with their GitHub attached as a source. Before this
part, a user was known only through its identity links (realm and subject): a person who signed in with GitHub and later
with a local account or SSO of the same email got a second, empty user, and their GitHub connection stayed with the first.

**The change.**
- **A user keeps its email.** `users.email` (instance migration 43), lowercase, unique among the users (`users_email`, on
  `lower(email)`). The migration gives a user a local account signed in as that account's email (its subject); every
  other user takes one at its next sign-in. `User.email`, `UserRepository.byEmail` and `setEmail`.
- **A sign-in is keyed by it** (`src/users/identities.ts` `userForIdentity`). Only `Identity.email` counts: an address the
  realm vouches for (OIDC with `email_verified`, or `trustUnverifiedEmail`; GitHub's primary verified email; LDAP, SAML
  and the gateway as their realm config names it; a local account's own email). A linked identity is its user, as before,
  and gives that user its email when it has none and no other user has it. An unlinked identity whose email a user is
  known by signs in as that user, and is linked to it. Else a new user, which keeps the email.
- **The migration of a GitHub-signed-in user.** Their next GitHub sign-in gives their user their primary verified email.
  A local account of that email (the operator CLI), or an SSO identity that vouches for it, then signs in as the same
  user: its work, and its GitHub connection, which part 3 already made a source that outlives every session. Nothing
  needs the hopper's app or a private key after that: the connection renews through the app's client id, or is a personal
  access token (part 6).
- **An admin never takes another user's email** (issue #221). Settings → Sign-in refuses a new local account of an email
  another user is known by, as it refuses one linked to another user (409, `src/http/local-accounts.ts`). The operator CLI
  does not: it holds the database's credentials.
- `GET /api/users` and Users & access → Users show each user's email.

**Decisions:**
- **Link at the sign-in, not in a migration.** The instance does not know a GitHub user's email until GitHub says it, and
  a migration cannot ask GitHub. The next sign-in reads it, with the check GitHub already did.
- **The first email wins.** A user's email is set once, by the first sign-in that vouches for one no other user has. A
  later identity with another email does not change it: an email that changes on each sign-in would move who is who.
- **Every realm's vouched email links.** The owner made external SSO trusted, and the admin chose each realm. A realm
  with `trustUnverifiedEmail` vouches for emails its provider did not verify: an admin turns that on only for a provider
  they trust to name people.
- **OpenFGA subjects, audit and attribution still name the user id** (OpenFGA subjects: replaced by part 9; audit and attribution: by part 10). The id is stable and every tuple and event names it;
  a user's email is now one lookup away. Keying those by email is a larger change with its own migration of tuples.
- **No migration of the old build.** `users.email` is a new column; the build before reads `SELECT *` and ignores it, and
  adds its users with none.

**Residual risk.** Whoever controls a realm that vouches for an email signs in as the user of that email. Before, such a
realm reached only users of its own identities.

**Left for later parts of issue #1380:** passkeys; OpenFGA subjects, audit and attribution keyed by email; more than one
GitHub source per user, and sources from other forges; Kubernetes (#1281) and service-account tokens (#909).

**Verification:** `test/users/identities.test.ts` (a linked identity gives its user its email, keeps the one it has, never
takes another user's; an unlinked identity with a user's email signs in as that user; else a new user with the email),
`test/store/migration-43.test.ts` (a local account's user takes its email; another user has none),
`test/integration/email-identity.test.ts` (a GitHub-signed-in user signs in with a local account of their email as the
same user, its GitHub connection still connected; a second OIDC subject of a verified email is the same user, an
unverified one is not; an admin is refused a local account of another user's email; `GET /api/users` names the email).

## Kubernetes and service-account tokens with no GitHub (issue #1380, part 8, 2026-10-15)

The issue's acceptance test: the hopper-owned user model works on the Kubernetes deployment (#1281) and with
service-account tokens (#909: grants with scopes). Parts 1 to 7 made sign-in work with no GitHub (local accounts, OIDC)
and made GitHub a source a person attaches. No check showed that either holds in a cluster, or that a person who signs
in without GitHub can give an agent a grant.

**What was found.** Nothing in the code needed a change. A grant (`POST /ui/api/api-tokens`, "Grants and refresh
tokens") is minted for the session's user and role, whatever realm signed them in. The operator CLI is in the image
(`/usr/local/bin/hopper`), and reads the database URL from the file the chart mounts (`HOPPER_DATABASE_URL_FILE`), so
`kubectl exec -i deploy/hopper -c hopper -- hopper local-account add <email>` adds the first admin in a pod. The kind
check's own comment said that a job run needs a GitHub sign-in: since part 6 it needs a GitHub source, after any
sign-in.

**The change: checks and docs.**
- `scripts/kind-check.ts` `withoutGitHub`: after the pod restarts, the operator CLI in the hopper's pod adds the first
  admin's local account, its random password on stdin. In the pod, on its loopback, that account signs in with its
  email and password (`POST /ui/auth/password`), must be admin through `local-accounts`, and mints a `read-only` grant.
  Its refresh token is traded at `POST /ui/auth/token/refresh`, and the new API token must read that person's grants
  (`GET /api/api-tokens`), the one just minted only. The kind check runs on the `dev` image, which holds parts 1 to 6.
- `test/integration/grants-without-github.test.ts`: a realm-only hopper's first admin (the CLI) mints a box grant from a
  preset; its tokens refresh, read, act within their scopes, and are refused outside them. A second local account's
  grant reaches only its own person's grants, is refused a role above its minter's and an admin read. A person signed
  in through OIDC mints a grant that reads as them.
- `docs/deploy.md` "On Kubernetes, with Helm": the first admin with no GitHub, and a grant for an agent;
  "Check the chart on kind": the new step, and that a job run needs a GitHub source, not a GitHub sign-in.

**Decisions:**
- **No bootstrap admin from the chart's values.** The CLI in the pod is the first-run admin, as on a container install:
  a password in Helm values stays in the release record in the namespace. The simplest path that meets the requirement.
- **The kind check signs in on the pod's loopback**, as its health check asks: from outside the pod the request is a LAN
  request, which needs allowed hosts set.

**Left for later parts of issue #1380:** passkeys; OpenFGA subjects, audit and attribution keyed by email; more than one
GitHub source per user, and sources from other forges.

**Verification:** `test/integration/grants-without-github.test.ts`; `test/scripts/kind-check.test.ts` (with fake
`kind`, `helm` and `kubectl`: the step's order, the password on stdin and in no argument, and each failure); the kind
check itself (`.github/workflows/kind.yml`, which runs on a change to `scripts/kind-check.ts`).

## OpenFGA subjects keyed by email (issue #1380, part 9, 2026-10-15)

Owner decision 1 on issue #1380: user records, OpenFGA subjects, audit and attribution use the verified email, never a
username. Part 7 gave each user its email. OpenFGA still named a person `user:<id>`, and a user's id is a slug of its name
(`User.id`): a username in every subject.

**What was found.** OpenFGA holds no state of its own here. Each push writes what the hopper's rows say and deletes the
rest ("Access: OpenFGA decides each mint"), and every check sends its tuple and contextual tuples at the time of the ask.
So a new way to name a person needs no migration of tuples: the next push moves them.

**The change.**
- **A person in OpenFGA is `user:<email>`** (`src/authz/objects.ts` `emailSubject`, `keyedByEmail`). OpenFGA takes no space,
  `:` or `#` in an id, so each is escaped (`encodeURIComponent`), and `%` too, so two emails never give one subject. `@`, `.`
  and `+` stay as they are.
- **Access keys tuples at the boundary** (`src/authz/service.ts`). The hopper still builds tuples by user id. Each push,
  each check and its contextual tuples, and the check of who is live are keyed by email just before they go to OpenFGA.
  `AccessOptions.emails` gives each user's email; `src/main.ts` reads it from the instance's users at each use. A user who
  takes an email at a sign-in is moved at the next ask: who is live, keyed, changed, so the push runs first.
- **A user with no email yet keeps `user:<id>`.** A GitHub-signed-in user from before part 7 has none until their next
  GitHub sign-in. An id holds no `@`, so it never names an email.
- **The access records name the email.** A decision's path, a check's reason (`user:<email> may …`), a mint's reason
  (`user <email> is not approved …`) and Users & access → Access's permission matrix name the email.

**Decisions:**
- **Key at the boundary, not in each object.** The objects that hold a user id (`job:<user>/<job>`, `machine:<user>/…`,
  `artifact:<user>/…` and the like) name the place the work is kept, not a person, and the user id is that place (the user
  schema, the work dir). Only `user:` subjects and objects are people. One mapping at the OpenFGA seam keeps every caller
  and every builder of tuples as it was.
- **No stored tuple changes.** The approvals Access keeps name templates and operation profiles, never a person.
- **The email escaped, not hashed.** An admin reads tuples in OpenFGA's own tools; an email reads as the person.
- **The user's id stays in the decision record's requester.** It names the user schema the job ran in; the reason and the
  path beside it name the email.

**Left for later parts of issue #1380:** audit and attribution keyed by email (the `by` of events and settings, now the
name the realm gave: a change must keep email addresses out of every text the hopper sends to GitHub); passkeys; more
than one GitHub source per user, and sources from other forges.

**Verification:** `test/authz/email-subjects.test.ts` (the tuples pushed name a user by its email, a user with none by
its id; a check asks as the email, the owner told by email; a user who takes an email is moved at the next ask; a
decision's path and reason, and the matrix, name the email; escaping); `test/authz/openfga-real.test.ts` (opt-in, a real
OpenFGA: a subject of an email, and of an escaped one, is stored and checked).

## Audit and attribution keyed by email (issue #1380, part 10, 2026-10-16)

Owner decision 1 on issue #1380: user records, OpenFGA subjects, audit and attribution use the verified email, never a
username. Part 7 gave each user its email; part 9 keyed OpenFGA by it. Who did an act was still recorded as the realm named
the person (`identityName`: name, username, email or subject, the first the realm gave): `Ada Lovelace` through one realm,
`ada` through another, for one user.

**The change.**
- **An act is recorded by the verified email of the session's user** (`src/http/ui/sessions.ts` `personOf`). Every `by`
  a UI session or an API token writes — settings changes, approvals, grants, artifacts, promotions, vault changes, the
  instance's own settings — and every acting person (`ActingPerson.person`: notes, hand-offs, failures, pull request acts,
  direct jobs, terminals) names it. `connectedOf` (`src/http/tenants.ts`) carries the user's email, read from the users
  when an act asks for it.
- **A user with no email yet keeps the name the realm gave.** A GitHub-signed-in user from before part 7 has none until
  their next GitHub sign-in; a realm that vouches for no email gives none.
- **The operator CLI keeps its own name** (`operator CLI`). Its session signs in no person, whichever user it acts for;
  a vault grant reads that name as the CLI's.
- **Text that leaves the hopper names a person without an email address** (`src/domain/users.ts` `nameWithoutEmail`: each
  address cut to its local part). A promotion's "Requested by" goes to GitHub. A direct job's "submitted by", a box
  template's "approved by" and an infra plan's "approved by" go to a job, which may write to GitHub. Every other `by` stays
  in the hopper: events, records and the UI.

**Decisions:**
- **No migration of events or records.** Events are the history: an act before this part stays recorded as the realm named
  the person then. Rewriting it would change what the audit says happened.
- **The local part, not a mask, where text leaves the hopper.** The person asked for the requester to be named; the local
  part names them, and holds no address. The publishing rule's other checks (the promotion's scan) still apply.
- **The email is read at each act, not kept in the session.** A user who takes an email at a sign-in is recorded by it at
  the next act, with no session to end.

**Residual risk.** The UI shows emails in timelines and settings history to everyone who reads that user's work. They
were already shown in Users & access → Users and Users & access → Access.

**Left for later parts of issue #1380:** passkeys; more than one GitHub source per user, and sources from other forges.

**Verification:** `test/http/attribution.test.ts` (the session user's email, else the realm's name; the operator CLI's own
name; an address cut to its local part), `test/promotions/promotion.test.ts` (a requester known by an email is named
without it), `test/direct-jobs/item.test.ts` (the job is told its submitter without an email), and
`test/integration/email-attribution.test.ts` (a setting changed by an OIDC user is recorded by their verified email; one
whose email the realm does not vouch for, by the name it gave).

## Passkeys for local accounts (issue #1380, part 11, 2026-10-16)

Owner decision 3 on issue #1380: local users sign in with an email and a password **or a passkey**. Part 1 built the
password. This part adds the passkey: a WebAuthn credential a local account adds, which then signs it in in place of its
password.

**The change.**
- **The WebAuthn checks are an established library's** (`@simplewebauthn/server`, its browser half
  `@simplewebauthn/browser` in the UI): the challenge, the origin, the RP ID hash, user presence and user verification,
  the attestation and the assertion's signature. `src/auth/passkeys.ts` keeps only the ceremonies and the rules around
  them. No hand-rolled WebAuthn code (AGENTS.md "Sign-in fails closed").
- **The relying party is the UI origin's host name.** The browser's Origin must be a UI origin (loopback, a LAN name, the
  public URL); its host name is the RP ID. A passkey keeps the host name it was added at (`rp_id`) and signs in there
  only: browsers bind a passkey to it anyway, and the check makes the rule the hopper's too. A passkey added at
  `localhost` does not sign in at the public URL; the person adds one there as well.
- **Each challenge is used once, by its own ceremony.** A registration's challenge is the session's (keyed by its
  token); a sign-in's is the `flow` id its options answered. Both are kept in memory for 5 minutes, at most 1000 at a
  time, and taken out at the first answer whether it holds or not. A restart drops them: the person starts again.
- **User verification is required and the credential is discoverable.** The passkey stands in for the password, so the
  device must prove the person (a PIN or a biometric), not only a touch. The sign-in asks for no email: the passkey names
  its account, and the hopper looks it up by its credential id.
- **What is kept**: `local_account_passkeys` (instance migration 44): the credential id, the account's email (a foreign
  key: removing the account removes its passkeys), the RP ID, the COSE public key, the signature counter, the
  transports, a name, when it was added and last used. No secret: a public key verifies, it cannot sign.
- **The role is the account's own, now.** A passkey sign-in is the account's sign-in: the identity `local-accounts` /
  the email, as the password's, so the same user, the same role, and every rule of part 1 (a removed account signs
  nobody in; a role change applies at once).
- **Routes.** `POST /ui/auth/passkey/options` and `POST /ui/auth/passkey` (the sign-in routes' rate limit, an exact UI
  Origin); `GET /api/local-accounts/passkeys`, `POST /ui/api/local-accounts/passkeys/options`,
  `POST /ui/api/local-accounts/passkeys` and `POST /ui/api/local-accounts/passkeys/remove` (a session of a local account,
  role viewer, its own passkeys only: 409 for a session of another realm). The session view's `signIn.passkeys` says
  whether any account has one: the landing page offers "Sign in with a passkey" then.
- **UI.** The landing page: "Sign in with a passkey" under the password form. Settings → Sign-in → Your passkeys: the
  session's passkeys (name, host name, added, last used), Add passkey with a name, and Remove. Settings → Sign-in →
  Local accounts shows each account's passkey count.

**Decisions:**
- **`@simplewebauthn/server`**: the WebAuthn library for Node with the longest release history and active upkeep; it
  needs no native code. Writing the checks here would mean owning CBOR, COSE and attestation parsing alone.
- **Attestation `none`.** The hopper trusts the person who signed in to add a passkey, not a device maker; an
  attestation check would refuse common authenticators and add nothing for a personal hopper.
- **Only the account's own session adds or removes its passkeys.** An admin never gets a way into another user's work
  (issue #221): an admin cannot add a passkey to another account. An admin who removes the account removes its passkeys.
- **A passkey is an addition, not a replacement.** The account keeps its password. A password change does not remove
  passkeys, and a passkey change ends no session.
- **The landing page offers a passkey only while one exists** (`signIn.passkeys`). It says one bit — some account has a
  passkey — to whoever reaches the landing page, the same reach as the password form.

**Residual risk.** The ceremonies are kept in memory: someone who reaches the sign-in routes can start up to the rate limit
(20 a minute per caller) of them; the cap of 1000 drops the oldest first, so a flood can make a person's own sign-in start
again. WebAuthn needs a secure context: a browser on plain HTTP at a LAN name offers no passkey (loopback and the HTTPS
public URL do).

**Left for later** (issue #1448): more than one GitHub source per user, and sources from other forges (GitLab).
The issue named them as later work.

**Verification:** `test/auth/passkeys.test.ts` (the relying party; the options; add, then sign in; the counter; a challenge
used once; another origin, another RP ID, no user verification or another challenge refused; another host name refused;
an unknown, removed, or removed account's passkey refused; a registration challenge is its session's, and a passkey is not
added twice) with a fake authenticator (`test/support/fake-authenticator.ts`, an EC P-256 key);
`test/integration/passkeys.test.ts` (a realm-only hopper end to end; another origin refused; an account's own passkeys
only; the account's removal removes them; a session of another realm adds none; the role now);
`test/ui/passkeys-panel.test.ts` (Settings and the landing page).

## Telemetry (issue #1486, part 1, 2026-10-16)

Issue #1486 asks for OpenTelemetry traces, metrics and logs across the hopper, so the data shows what to improve: slow
actions, stuck jobs, GitHub use, where failures come from. This part lays the base and the first signals.

**The change.**
- **The established SDK, from the usual launch environment.** `@opentelemetry/sdk-node` reads the `OTEL_*` variables:
  the exporters, the OTLP endpoint, protocol and headers, the sampler, the service name and resource attributes. No
  setting of the hopper's own, no file. `src/telemetry/sdk.ts` starts it once per process (`main()`), before the log mask
  covers stdout and stderr.
- **Off unless the launch names an exporter.** The SDK alone sends every signal to OTLP on localhost; a hopper with no
  collector must not try. `telemetryWanted`: on only with an OTLP endpoint (`OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` or a signal's
  own) or an exporter named for a signal other than `none`, and never with `OTEL_SDK_DISABLED=true`. Off, the API stays its
  no-op: each span, metric and log record costs next to nothing and goes nowhere.
- **The resource names no machine.** `service.name` `hopper` and `service.version`, then `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` and
  `OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES`; the host and process detectors are left out, so no host name, user or command line goes out
  unless the launch adds it.
- **Every request is a span** (`http.ts`, the first hook of the server): named by its route's template
  (`POST /ui/api/jobs/:id/approve`), never its URL, so no id, query or token in a path goes out, nor a header or a body.
  A caller's `traceparent` is its parent: a machine's call joins the trace that asked for it. The span is the active
  context in the handler (set again after the body is read), so its spans, GitHub calls and log lines are its children.
  An error records only its kind (`error.type`): a message may carry what the request carried. The latency is the
  semantic conventions' `http.server.request.duration` by method, route and status: a UI action's latency (approve,
  discard) is its route's.
- **A job is one trace** (`jobs.ts`), built from the user's event log as it appends: a root span `hopper.job`, and a
  **job span** for each part of the job's life — `queue` (queued to claimed or started), `run` (started to its end, a
  question or a wait), `question` (asked to answered, with each escalation an event on it), `wait`, `park`,
  `pull_request` (followed to merged, closed or abandoned). Each is timed by the events' own times. The root ends at
  the job's end; its pull request is followed after that, so that job span is a child of the ended root, in the same
  trace, while the hopper remembers the job (the last 2000 ended). Every other job or question event is an event on the
  root, or on its question's span. The attributes are picked by name — the job's id, executor, source, repository, issue
  and pull request number, lane, machine, outcome, and a question's target —: no event data, prompt, title, answer or
  error goes out. The spans live in memory: a restart starts a new trace at the next event of a job still open, and at
  most 2000 jobs are open at once (past that, the oldest is ended, marked `hopper.trace.evicted`). Built from events and
  not from the engine, a part of the hopper that appends an event is traced with no change of its own.
- **Metrics.** `hopper.job.span.duration` (by kind), `hopper.job.ended` (by outcome and executor), `hopper.job.events`
  (by type); `hopper.jobs` (live jobs by status) and `hopper.lanes` (lanes by state), read at each collection;
  `hopper.github.calls` (by route, status and cache use: a 304 answered from the cache is a hit),
  `hopper.github.call.duration` and `hopper.github.rate_limit.remaining` (by resource), from the shared rate limiter's
  hook, where each GitHub call is also a client span; `hopper.db.call.duration` by the statement's verb and table
  (`statementOf`, never its SQL or values); `process.memory.usage`, `nodejs.memory.heap.used`, `process.cpu.time`,
  `nodejs.eventloop.delay.max` and `.p99`.
- **Logs are bridged, not duplicated.** The hopper logs by writing lines to stdout and stderr, whoever writes them. Each
  write also goes out as a log record (`INFO` from stdout, `WARN` from stderr), with the trace and span it was written in.
  The bridge sits under the log mask (issue #685), so it gets the masked line. With `OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=console` it is not
  bridged: the console exporter's own lines would be exported again, without end.
- **A local viewer.** `compose.yaml` passes the `OTEL_*` variables through, and the optional profile `telemetry` runs
  Grafana's all-in-one OpenTelemetry image (a collector, Tempo, Prometheus, Loki and Grafana) on loopback
  (docs/deploy.md "Telemetry").

**Why an instrument is made again.** The API's tracer follows a provider set later; its meter does not: a meter taken
before the SDK starts stays a no-op for good. `instrument()` makes each instrument again when the meter provider changes,
so a module may hold one at its top.

**Left for the next parts** (the pull request lists them): the settings in the UI, Helm values, a built-in view of the
slowest actions, job span durations and GitHub use; trace context carried to machines, lane pods and boxes; spans for
sandbox create and teardown, work tree setup, tend, rebase, merge and deploy, the outbox and the sync; failure kinds,
assessor decisions, retries and escalation levels as metrics.

**Tests.** `test/telemetry/telemetry.test.ts`, with in-memory exporters and no timing asserted: when telemetry is on;
a job's span tree, its parent links, attributes and metrics; a request's span named by its route, the handler's span and
log record its children, its latency recorded; GitHub calls counted, a conditional hit as a hit, the calls left; the
process's and the queue's gauges; and no secret — a prompt, a title, a question, an answer, an error, a session, a bearer
token, a query, a body, a GitHub token, an id in a URL — in anything exported.

## A job pushes to another job repository (issue #1275, 2026-10-16)

**The problem.** A job's issue can sit in one repository while its change belongs in another: an orchestration
repository whose issues name the work, and the application repositories it stewards, where the code is. The git broker
let a job push only to its own repository (its source's), so such a job finished its code and tests, and could not
push, open its pull request, or finish. Its user could push to the other repository (`canPush`), and the job had no
other way: `repo fork` is for its own repository only.

**The change.** A job may push, open a pull request, and mark one ready on any of its user's **job repositories**, not
only its own: the job repositories already decide where a job writes (issue #1015, `checkRequest`), so a push follows
the same line. In the git broker (`createGitProxy`, step 3 of "Git through the hopper"), a push goes to the job's own
repository, to another job repository, or to the job's fork; on any of them only when its user can push there, with the
same ref check (`checkPush`: no default or release branch, no delete) and the shrink guard. A push to another job
repository its user cannot push to is refused before GitHub refuses it (`your user cannot push to <repo>`): the
contribution flow forks only the job's own repository. In the GitHub proxy (`checkRequest`), `pr.create` and `pr.ready`
are no longer held to the job's own repository; a pull request from the user's fork (`--head <login>:<branch>`) still
opens only on the job's own repository. The job's issue stays where it is: the pull request closes it by its full name
(`Closes OWNER/NAME#N`), which GitHub links as a closing reference when the pull request is on its repository's default
branch, so the completion check finds it among the issue's closing pull requests. `hopper-gh help` says so.

**Not changed.** A repository that is no job repository takes no push from a job but its own (issue #1131; changed by
issue #1806, "A job pushes wherever its user can push"). A fetch
reads any repository the user sees (issue #1015). A job without its own repository (a direct job) may push to the job
repositories too: it was refused all pushes before, with no reason the job repositories did not already settle.

**Decisions:**
- **The job repositories, not a list of stewarded repositories.** The hopper has no notion of which repository stewards
  which; the job repositories are the person's own choice of where the hopper works, and adding a repository there is
  how a person allows a job's push to it. A second list would be a second answer to the same question.
- **Any branch of the job's own work, not only a new one.** A job pushes its branch again after a review or a rebase
  (`--force-with-lease`), as on its own repository; refusing updates would leave it with a branch it cannot fix.

**Residual risk.** A job can now overwrite a branch other than the default or a release branch on any job repository
its user can push to, not only on its own repository. One bad issue, or one injected agent, still cannot change a
default or release branch, so `dev`, the published image and the hosts stay out of its reach; branch protection on
GitHub keeps the rest, as before ("Git through the hopper", residual risk). Yolo mode merges only the pull requests the
hopper follows, on the repositories where a person turned it on.

**Verification:** `test/integration/git-proxy.test.ts` ("pushes a branch to another of its user's job repositories,
forced too", "refuses a push to another job repository its user cannot push to", a repository the hopper does not work
on refused), `test/integration/github-proxy.test.ts` (a pull request on another job repository, marked ready; one
elsewhere refused), `test/github-proxy/proxy.test.ts` (`checkRequest`), `test/integration/contribution.test.ts`.

## Sandboxes before the start (issue #1471, 2026-10-16)

A direct job's brief said to work in a box of template `cluster-role-builder`. The job's only approved sandbox was of a
template its `--needs` made. It learned of the gap mid-run, when its box step was refused, and could not fix it: a
sandbox ask took only `--needs`. Several rounds of questions followed. Now the hopper finds the templates a job will need
before the job starts, and asks a person for them up front.

- **Named templates** (`namedTemplates`, `src/domain/sandboxes-before-start.ts`, pure). A template of the user's is
  named in a job's prompt when its whole name comes right after `template` or `box` (or `box of template`), quoted or
  not: `box cluster-role-builder`, ``template `cluster-role-builder` ``. A name that is only a word of the text is not
  named ("fix the web page" names no template `web`), and a name no template has is not named. Only the user's own
  templates are matched, so the check never guesses at a template that does not exist.
- **The ask** (`sandboxesHeld`, `src/users/sandbox-requests.ts`). At each Decision, the engine's gather step
  (`src/engine/decision-step.ts`, engine option `sandboxesHeld`) gives the waiting jobs to it. For each job that is
  accepted, of a judged origin and text, not resuming after a question, and with a prompt, it asks for the sandbox runs
  of every template the prompt names, with the purpose `BEFORE_START_PURPOSE`. A request is the one the job has when
  asked again: no second event, no second card. The approvals that skip a person — skip sandbox approval, the
  auto-approve policy, remembered write approvals — apply as to any sandbox request. The vault's view is read only when
  a waiting job may name a template.
- **The hold** (`sandboxesHold`, pure; the decider, `src/decider/index.ts`). A job is held `awaiting its sandboxes: …`
  while one of its requests waits for a person, or an approved one's template is not ready (`templateReady`: approved,
  its image approved, every profile approved, its read-only check passed). A declined request holds nothing: a person
  said no, and the job is told so when it asks. The hold comes after the queue gate and before every other judgement
  of a job not resuming: a person's approval of a router hold does not pass it. The decider stays pure: the reasons
  come in as the input `sandboxesHeld`.
- **One approval for all of them.** Every request of a job is on Access requests, panel **Sandbox runs**, at once,
  before the job starts: **Approve selected** (issue #1018) approves them in one action.
- **Requests live until the job ends.** A sandbox request was forgotten when its job was not at work. It is now kept
  while the job is queued, held, claimed or at work (`live`), so the approval given before the start is there when the
  job's box step asks. Requests are still kept in memory: after a restart, the next Decision asks again for a job that
  has not started.
- **A job may name a template** (`sh "$HOPPER_SKILL" sandbox --template NAME --why …`, `src/skills/broker.ts`). In place
  of `--needs`, not with it. The template stays as it is: the hopper makes and widens nothing. A template whose profiles
  change an asset takes `--plan`, as a `--needs` ask that changes one does. Approved, but the template not ready: 202,
  waiting. A template the user does not have: no. The refusal of a box step of a template the job has no approval of
  says how to ask for it by name.

**Tests.** `test/domain/sandboxes-before-start.test.ts` (named templates; the hold), `test/decider/sandboxes-before-start.test.ts`
(the decider holds; the queue gate first; never a job resuming), `test/users/sandboxes-held.test.ts` (asked once, all at
once; declined and skip sandbox approval do not hold; nothing asked for a job at the gate, not judged or resuming), and
`test/integration/job-sandboxes.test.ts` (a held job starts once a person approves its request; `--template`).

## A pane herdr restored (issue #1465, 2026-10-16)

**The problem.** Jobs failed right after their Claude session resumed: in the resumed session `HOPPER_GH`, `HOPPER_URL`,
the rest of the `HOPPER_*` variables and git's way to GitHub through the hopper (`GIT_CONFIG_*`) were unset, so git had no
credential and the job could not reach the hopper. The hopper did not resume those sessions. herdr did: its
`[session] resume_agents_on_restore` (on by default) restores every pane after a restart of its server and resumes each
supported agent into its own session. A restored pane keeps its pane id but gets a new terminal (`terminal_id`) and a new
shell, started with the server's environment, not the tab's: the variables the hopper gave with `herdr tab create --env`
are gone (seen with herdr 0.8.2: a tab created with `--env` loses the variable after `herdr server stop` and a new server).
The new shell is also outside the job's scope (the reap) and its sandbox (issue #1295), and never ran the job's start
steps.

**The change.** The hopper records the pane's terminal at its start (`PaneState.terminal`, from `tab create`'s
`root_pane.terminal_id`), and the agent session there too (`PaneState.agentSession`). `herdr agent get` already says the
agent's `terminal_id`, so each poll of the watch compares it at no extra call (`restoredByHerdr`,
`src/executors/herdr/restored.ts`). Another terminal is a **restored pane**: the watch ends with `paneRestored`, and the
executor stops that Claude and closes the pane as at a park (the reap without the scratch dir: worktree and session kept),
