- **A pull request's review** (`pr_review_ended`). A wait on `pr <N> review` is tested on its reviews, not only on its end.
  The job's source reads the pull request and its reviews (`JobSource.waitedReviews`; GitHub: `waitedReviews`,
  `src/sources/github/watched.ts`, through `GitHubApi.pullRequestReviews`, REST `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{n}/reviews`,
  a review not yet sent left out). `reviewOutcome` says: a review sent at or after the wait began, met, and the newest one
  says what (approved, asks for changes, comments, dismissed); none since, not met; the reviews not readable, not met;
  merged or closed, met; no pull request of that number, met (the job names the right one).
- **The job card** names the condition: "the hopper checks whether `<repo>#<N>` got a review".

**Decisions:**
- **Only a review after the wait began counts.** A review from before is the one the job read before it waited. A job that
  pushed a fix and waits for a new review is not woken at once by the old "changes requested", again and again.
- **Any review counts, a comment too.** The job reads it and decides. A wait that wants only an approval waits again.
- **The last output of an own command is not put in what the job is told.** The hopper wakes the job in its own pane, where
  the command's output already is, and the note tells it to read it. A pane that is lost has no output to give.

**Not built (later parts).** A model-based condition (only where no deterministic kind fits, with its reason); stalled
running jobs; the tailnet observation in the issue.

**Persisted state.** `pr_review_ended` is a new condition kind in the job's JSON, and no migration is needed. A build before
this one logs a check of that kind as failed at each pass and leaves the wait as it is; End the wait still ends it.

**Verification:** `test/domain/wait-checks.test.ts` (`reviewOutcome`, the condition and its key),
`test/engine/wait-checks.test.ts` (the real database: an old review does not end the wait, a new one does),
`test/sources/waited-checks.test.ts` (`waitedReviews`), `test/ui/board.test.ts` (the card).

### Part 4: what is left, closed (2026-10-17)

Part 3 left three items. Each is closed here by a decision. No code changes.

- **Stalled running jobs are re-checked already.** A running job with no progress is never left to a person by itself:
  - **The turn timeout.** Each turn of a job runs under its executor's timeout (herdr-claude: the payload's `timeoutMs`, an
    hour unless set, `src/executors/herdr/payload.ts`). The quiet watch after the nudges stopped (issue #491) runs under the
    same timeout (`startedAt` of the turn), so a Claude that sits quiet ends the turn as `timed out`.
  - **The timeout's assessment** (issue #630). The assessor reads the job's **liveness** (when its pane output last changed,
    whether it pushed, whether its pull request is open) and continues a job that still works, else retries it or hands it
    off by the rules. This is the scheduled re-check of a running job, once each turn timeout.
  - **The job lease** (issue #1662). A running job that no runner drives loses its lease at the next renewal
    (`renew` releases a lease of a job not in `driving`), and any hopper on the database takes it over (`takeOver`) as at a
    restart. A hopper that stops holds its jobs for `JOB_LEASE_MS` at most.
  - A second check beside these would only nudge the job again or time it out sooner. Each nudge costs the job a turn.
- **No model-based condition.** Every condition the issue names has a deterministic kind: a pull request (its end, checks or
  review), an issue, a workflow run, a job, a question, its own command, a time. An outside event that names nothing waits for
  the time the job names on its `check:` line (part 2), else its deadline, then the Failures view. A model call at each check
  costs money and gives a different answer on each run, and the hopper cannot test it.
- **The tailnet observation** in the issue (the API did not answer over the tailnet address, but answered on the host) is no
  part of the wait checks. It is the follow-up issue #1756.

**Verification:** read of `src/executors/herdr/executor.ts` (`watch`, the quiet watch's `startedAt`),
`src/executors/herdr/monitor.ts` (`timeoutMs`), `src/failures/chain.ts` (`livenessOf`), `src/engine/leases.ts` (`renew`),
`src/engine/recovery.ts` (`takeOver`). Their tests are those of issues #491, #630 and #1662.

### A pull request read that fails (issue #2210, 2026-10-20)

Report: a job waited on the checks of a pull request of another organization. The checks ended green, but the check said
only "the hopper cannot read <repo>#<n> now" and never ended the wait. `hopper-gh` read the same pull request (over REST).

- **The cause.** The source reads one pull request over GraphQL with each check run and its annotations
  (`PULL_REQUEST_QUERY`, issue #927). A FORBIDDEN error inside the rollup — on a check run, or on its annotations — was not
  the error on `statusCheckRollup` that issue #855 keeps the answer for, so the whole read threw. Now a FORBIDDEN error
  anywhere under `statusCheckRollup` keeps the answer (`checksForbidden`, `src/sources/github/closer.ts`): the parts GitHub
  gave hold, and the rollup's state still says the checks. A rollup GitHub refused whole stays `unknown`, and the checks
  fallback reads it over REST (issue #1244).
- **The error is said.** The sweeper kept no error: any failed read was "cannot read now". Now the check's result names it
  (`readPull`, `src/engine/wait-checks.ts`): `the hopper cannot read <repo>#<n> now: <GitHub's error>`, or `the job's source
  reads no pull request` when the job's source has no such read. The check is tried again, the time between doubling, as
  before; past its deadline it is overdue once and a stuck item for a person.
- **A direct job's waits.** The direct source (issue #901) now reads a pull request's checks and review too
  (`createDirectPullRequests`), with the user's own connection; unconnected, the read fails and says why.

## A labelled issue not assigned to the user is said (issue #1614, 2026-10-17)

Report: two issues were labelled `hopper` by a trusted author and assigned to nobody. No job started, and for 2 to 4
hours nothing said why: no log line, no problem, nothing on the issue. Assigning them started their jobs at the next sync.

The rule stays ("Intake by label and assignee", issue #387): an issue is taken only when it is assigned to the user's
connected account. Intake already listed such an issue under **Not assigned to you**, with Assign to me; but Intake's
badge and Needs you counted only the request cards, so nothing pointed a person at it. Now:

- **The log.** After each sync the sync loop logs each outcome in the `not-assigned` group once
  (`notAssignedTold`, `src/sources/sync-slots.ts`): `hopper: source <name> does not take <key>: <reason>. No job starts
  until it is assigned (Intake: Assign to me)`. A key taken or gone is forgotten, so it is logged again when it comes back,
  as `notRerun` (issue #1402). A paused source logs nothing new. Every source that sets the group says it: GitHub and GitLab.
- **The badge.** Intake's nav badge and Needs you's Intake row count the request cards and the issues not assigned to the
  user (`notAssignedWaiting`, `ui/src/model/intake.ts`); the badge's title names each.

Not done: a label or a comment on the issue. The hopper writes only its labels to an issue and posts no comments
(AGENTS.md "GitHub text is neutral"), and a new label for this would be one more write per unassigned issue, on every
repository, for a state the user can already see. Not a **Problem** either: a problem is a shared cause of failed jobs,
and no job failed. Taking an unassigned issue from a trusted author is the change issue #387 removed: assignment is how
two users of one repository each take only their own issues.

Tests: `test/sources/sync-not-assigned.test.ts` (logged once, again after taken and back),
`test/ui/intake-view.test.ts` (the badge, its title and the Needs you row count both kinds).

## Sweep leases: one host per sweep (issue #1627, 2026-10-17)

**The problem.** The sagas ("Sagas: work that survives a stop") make work of several steps safe on two hopper hosts on one
database. The sweeps and recoveries were not: each ran on every host, and some undid each other. Two dispatchers both posted
a due webhook delivery. Each host's tool sign-in sweep failed every open sign-in it did not run, so each failed the other's.
The outbound guard's dedupe keys were in memory, so a restart sent a send held before. The question timers, the machine
sweep, the failure assessor's sweep, the TL;DR sweep and the artifacts' retention sweep ran on each host. A client target
kept the jobs to stop when cut off in memory only, so a client restart while cut off forgot them.

**The sweep lease** (`SweepLease`, `src/domain/leases.ts`; the instance's `sweep_leases` table, migration 50,
`src/store/sweep-leases.ts`). The model is the saga lease: a row per sweep name with an owner and an until, on the
database's clock (issue #1954), so a host whose clock is off takes no lease another holds. A pass asks
`hold()` first: one statement takes the lease or renews it when no other owner holds it now, and the pass runs only while
this host holds it. `hold()` also says whether the host took it just now (`taken`): from another host that stopped, or at its
first ask. The host's **host leases** (`createHostLeases`, `src/sagas/leases.ts`) renew every lease the host holds every 10 s,
to 30 s on; the host releases them all when it stops. A host that stops without that renews nothing, so 30 s on its leases
end and another host takes each at its next pass. The owner is the saga coordinator's (`sagaOwner`). A part built with no
database of its own (a test) takes `soleLease()`: always held. The engine's passes ask their leases on each tick (issue
#1662), so a lease asks the database once a second at most (`LEASE_ASK_MS`): between asks its last answer stands. A
statement per pass on each tick held the event loop of a busy hopper. A held lease stays held by the renewal; a host that
does not hold one takes it at most a second after its holder released it.

The leases, each one per user (`<user id>/<name>`):

| Lease | What only its holder does | When it takes it from another host |
|---|---|---|
| `engine-sweep` | the machine sweep ("Work tree" → "The sweep") | sweeps every machine at once |
| `questions` | arms the human stage's timers, runs the question recovery and sweep; another host arms none and clears its own | runs the recovery: every open question armed again, its times kept |
| `failures` | the failure assessor's sweep | assesses the backlog and catches the hand-offs up, as at a start |
| `tldr` | the TL;DR sweep | — |
| `artifacts` | the retention sweep | — |
| `cleanups` | the cleanups a record says are owed (issue #1662) | does every one owed, as at a start |
| `auto-park` | auto-park (issue #1662) | — |
| `signed-out-move` | the signed-out move (issue #1662) | — |
| `busy-move` | the busy-machine move (issue #1977) | — |
| `checkpoints` | the checkpoint pass (issue #1662) | — |
| `pane-answers` | the read of each waiting job's pane (issue #1662) | — |
| `classifier` | the classifier's sweep (issue #1662) | — |
| `discovery` | each machine's discovery (issue #1662) | — |
| `missed-wakes` | the wakes a stop lost (issue #1662) | — |

A question with no timers and no fork is one the host before armed: the new holder arms it with its times kept. One whose
fork ended without a decision waits on a person again, as before (issue #570).

**The delivery claim.** A due webhook delivery is claimed before its POST (`claimDelivery`): its `next_attempt_at` moves on
past the attempt's time only while it is still due, in one `UPDATE`, so of two hosts that ask at once one gets it, and the
other leaves it. With no token from the outbound guard the delivery is due again at once, and no attempt is spent. A
delivery is made only on the host that recorded its event (the event feed is in memory), so its creation needs no claim.

**The outbound dedupe in the database** (the instance's `outbound_keys` table, `src/store/outbound-keys.ts`). A send's
dedupe key is kept as a SHA-256 of its destination URL and its key, until its dedupe window ends: the URL stays in memory.
The claim is one statement, so two hosts that ask the same key get one new. The rate buckets and the circuits stay each
process's: a limit per host only makes two hosts send at most twice the rate, never a send twice. A database error falls
back to this process's keys, with a line in the log.

**A sign-in is the host's that runs it.** A tool sign-in login names the host that runs it (`hostOwner`, its lease owner,
never answered by a route). A host's sweep fails an open sign-in login that nothing on it runs only when the login names
this host, names none (a login from the build before), or names a host whose host lease ended. A paste reaches the
sign-in only on the host that runs it: on another host it is answered as ended (open thread).

**The isolation file.** The client keeps the jobs the hopper named, and when it last heard the hopper, in `isolation.json`
in its client dir (mode 600): written when the jobs change, when it stops them, and with a hearing at most every 15 s. At its
start it reads the file, so a client restarted while cut off stops those jobs once its max isolation passed since the hopper
was last heard. A file whose last hearing is more than a day old is not read.

**Left as it was.** The engine's start recovery (`recovery.ts`) is not leased: it reattaches the jobs of this host's own
lanes, and a host that skips it would leave them; jobs on two hosts are the engine's own question. Event-driven work (the
failure assessor's assessment of a job that failed here, a delivery's creation) runs on the host whose event it is.

**Verification:** `test/integration/two-hosts.test.ts` (two hosts on one database: each delivery sent once; a sign-in host A
runs is not failed by host B, and is once A stopped; a dedupe key asked on one host is a duplicate on the other; a sweep
lease held by one host at a time, taken by the other once it stops), `test/client/isolation-file.test.ts` (a client
restarted while cut off stops the jobs named before; a file past its life is not read).

## Posted once (issue #1591, 2026-10-17)

Follow-up of #1524. **The problem.** Promote to GitHub (`src/promotions/service.ts` `promote`) made the issue or the
comment, then wrote the promotion's row and `direct_job.promoted`. Report a bug (`src/bug-reports/service.ts` `file`) added
its row only after GitHub answered, and the send later (`src/bug-reports/later.ts` `sendKept`) updated a kept row only after
the create. A stop, or a timeout where GitHub did make the issue, posted it again on the next try, and the hopper had no link
to the first.

**The change: the post key** (`src/domain/post-key.ts`, pure). The row is kept first, before GitHub is asked for a new issue
or comment, and its id is the **post key**: the text posted ends with it as a hidden line, `<!-- hopper post <key> -->`.
Before a create of a row that may already be on GitHub, the hopper looks for that key, from an hour before the row was kept
(`postKeySince`; GitHub's clock and the hopper's differ): the issues the account made (`GET /repos/{o}/{r}/issues`,
`creator`, `state=all`, `since`), or the comments on the issue (`GET …/issues/{n}/comments`, `since`). What it finds is
linked; only when it finds nothing is the issue or comment made. An edit has no key to look for: it is the same edit when
made twice.

- **Promote to GitHub.** A new issue or comment is kept as a **promotion send** (`direct_job_promotion_sends`, tenant
  migration 77, a table only: the build before runs on it and never reads it), with the repository, the target, the
  artifacts linked, who promoted it and when. GitHub's answer makes it the promotion, in one transaction
  (`PromotionRepository.sent`). A send a stop or a lost answer left is settled at the next promotion of the direct job, and
  at each start (`Promotions.recover`, from the user runtime's start; its stop waits for it): its key found, it becomes the
  promotion, with `direct_job.promoted`; the next promotion then edits it with the text the person confirmed now. Not
  found, the send goes. One promotion of a direct job at a time: a second while the first is on its way is 409.
- **Report a bug.** The report's row is kept `sending` with its body before GitHub is asked; GitHub's answer makes it
  `open`. A lost answer (no answer, 401, 403, 404, 429, 5xx) makes it `waiting`, as before. GitHub refusing the report
  itself (a 422) removes the row, as before nothing was kept. A row a stop left `sending` is `waiting` again at the next
  start (`ReportSender.start`). The send later looks for each kept report's key first (`findReport`): found, the report is
  linked, `bug_report.filed` with `later: true`; else it is sent. The look-up is by the account, not the label: GitHub drops
  the label of a person who may not triage. Your reports shows `sending` as Sending.

**Decisions:**
- **The key is the row's id.** It names nothing of a person or a machine, and it is on GitHub only as a hidden line.
- **A look-up reads the list, not search.** GitHub's search index lags behind a create; the list does not.
- **A look-up reads one page (100).** An issue or comment made within the hour before the row was kept is on it.

**Residual risk, stated.** A create still in flight after its timeout that GitHub finishes only after the look-up found
nothing posts a second one. File an issue (`src/issue-drafts/`) keeps no row before its create yet.

**Verification:** `test/integration/bug-reports-post-key.test.ts` (an issue made with its answer lost, sent later: one
issue, the report links it; a report a stop left `sending`: linked at the next start; a comment the same),
`test/integration/direct-job-promotions-post-key.test.ts` (an issue made with its answer lost, promoted again: one issue,
with the new text; a stop before the row: linked at the next start, one `direct_job.promoted`; a comment the same).

## Telemetry summary (issue #1486, part 2, 2026-10-16)

Issue #1486 asks for a built-in hopper view of the most useful numbers: the slowest actions, the job span durations and the
GitHub use. Part 1 exports them only to a collector the launch names; a hopper with none showed nothing.

**The change.**
- **Kept in the hopper's own process, telemetry on or off** (`src/telemetry/summary.ts`, `telemetrySummary`). The places
  that record the OpenTelemetry instruments feed it too: the request hook (`http.ts`), the job traces (`jobs.ts`, at the end
  of each job span) and the shared rate limiter's GitHub hook. So it shows what is exported, and it needs no collector.
- **What it keeps.** Per name, its count since the start and its last 200 samples (`TELEMETRY_SUMMARY_SAMPLES`), for the
  mean, the p95 (nearest rank) and the max. **Actions**: the requests that change something (not `GET`, `HEAD` or
  `OPTIONS`), by method and route template, the slowest p95 first, the top 10. **Job spans**: each kind that ended,
  timed by its events. **GitHub use**: by method and route template, the most called first, the top 10, each with its
  cache hits (a conditional request answered 304) and errors (no answer, or 400 or more), and the totals of all calls.
- **Names only.** A route's template, a job span's kind, a GitHub route's template: never a URL, an id, a value or a
  user. At most 500 names per list: the routes and job spans there are stay far under it.
- **One per process**, as the meter provider is. An action, a job span and a GitHub call are the process's, whichever
  user's they are, so the read is an instance read. In memory: a restart starts it again; nothing is stored.
- **`GET /api/telemetry`** (`src/http/stack-resources.ts`): the `TelemetrySummary`, `since` the process started and
  `exporting` when the launch's `OTEL_*` variables name an exporter. An instance read (403 for a session that is not the
  hopper's admin), not cached.
- **The Resources page** shows it last, as the Telemetry panel (`ui/src/components/telemetry-summary.tsx`): Slowest actions,
  Job spans and GitHub use, read again every 10 seconds while the page is open. A read the daemon refuses says why, and the
  rest of the page still shows. It says whether the numbers are also exported.

**Why not a metric reader.** The SDK's meter provider exists only while telemetry is on, and a second provider beside it
would double each instrument. A small keeper fed at the same places is less code than a second pipeline, and it is the
same numbers either way.

**Left for the next parts** (the pull request lists them): the telemetry settings in the UI; Helm values for a collector
and a viewer; trace context carried to machines, client targets, lane pods and boxes; spans for sandbox create and
teardown, work tree setup, tend, rebase, merge and deploy, the outbox and the sync; failure kinds, assessor decisions,
retries, escalation levels, sandbox spin-up time, CI gates, outbox batches and the DB pool as metrics.

**Tests.** `test/telemetry/summary.test.ts`: the keeper's order, top and samples; an action by its route template, a read
no action; each job span timed by its events; GitHub calls by route with a cache hit; no id, query or token kept — all with
telemetry off. `test/integration/stack-resources.test.ts` (the route through the real daemon) and
`test/integration/instance-admin.test.ts` (an instance read); `test/ui/resources-view.test.ts` (the panel, its empty and
refused states).

## Telemetry: how work goes (issue #1486, part 3, 2026-10-17)

Parts 1 and 2 traced jobs and requests and counted GitHub and store calls. The issue also asks for failures by kind,
assessor decisions, retries, escalations by level, dead letters, sandbox spin-up and the CI gate, and for Helm values for
a collector and a viewer.

**The change.**
- **The event log as metrics** (`src/telemetry/outcomes.ts`), one per user's runtime, beside its job traces. Each is read
  off an event the hopper already appends, so no part of it changes:
  - `hopper.job.assessed`, by `hopper.failure.class` (`transient`, `shared`, `job`), `hopper.assessor.decision` and
    `hopper.assessor.auto`: failures by kind, and what the assessor decided (`job.assessed`).
  - `hopper.job.retries`, by `hopper.retry.kind` — `requeued` (by the status it left) or `rerun` (by `user`, `assessor`,
    `tending`).
  - `hopper.question.escalations`, by `hopper.question.target`, the level reached; a re-notification is no new level.
  - `hopper.handoffs`, by `hopper.handoff.reason`: a failed job handed off to a person (Needs a person). The hopper has
    no dead-letter queue; this is where a job goes that nothing retries.
  - `hopper.sandbox.requests`, by `hopper.sandbox.outcome` (`started`, `failed`, `declined`), and
    `hopper.sandbox.spin_up.duration`, from the request's approval to its box started or failed: the time a person
    takes to approve is not the box's.
  - `hopper.landing_batch.ended`, by `hopper.landing_batch.outcome` (`promoted`, `failed`): the CI gate a batch run is.
  Each attribute is an enum, a level or a status, taken by name and only when it is a short word, else `other`: no
  reason, summary, signature, template or person goes out.
- **A sandbox request is a job span** (`jobs.ts`), `hopper.job.sandbox`, one per request: from `vault.sandbox_requested`
  to its box started, failed or declined, with its approval an event on it. So a job's trace shows how long it waited
  for its box, and why.
- **Helm values** (docs/deploy.md "Telemetry"): `telemetry.env` passes `OTEL_*` variables to the hopper as they are, and
  refuses any other name, so the block cannot set the hopper's own settings; `telemetry.envFromSecret` reads them from
  a Secret, for a header with a credential. `telemetry.viewer.enabled` adds the same all-in-one image as compose's
  `telemetry` profile, which the hopper exports to unless `telemetry.env` names another endpoint. Its NetworkPolicy lets
  only the hopper reach its OTLP port; Grafana is reached by `kubectl port-forward`.

**Left for the next parts** (the pull request lists them): the settings in the UI; trace context carried to machines,
lane pods and boxes; spans for work tree setup, tend, rebase, merge and deploy, the outbox flush and the sync with its
ETag fetches; concurrent sandboxes, the outbox's batch size and coalescing, and the store's pool.

**Tests.** `test/telemetry/outcomes.test.ts` (in-memory exporters, times from the events, no event text exported) and
`test/scripts/helm-chart-telemetry.test.ts` (what `helm template` renders).

## Telemetry: a job's trace on its machine (issue #1486, part 4, 2026-10-17)

Parts 1–3 traced a job from its events, in the hopper. The issue also asks that the work on machines, client targets and
lane pods carries the trace context from the server. A job's work runs there, outside the hopper's process, so its trace
stopped at the hopper.

**The change.**
- **A job's trace context** (`src/telemetry/jobs.ts`, `traceContext`): the variables its processes run with —
  `TRACEPARENT`, and `TRACESTATE` when there is one —, OpenTelemetry's environment carrier, made by the propagator the
  SDK uses (W3C trace context unless `OTEL_PROPAGATORS` names another). It names the job's open `run` job span, else its
  root span while the job is open. An ended job, a job not traced, and telemetry off give none: no variable is set.
- **Given with the job's variables** (`src/engine/runner.ts`, the engine port `traceContext`): the runner adds it to
  what `credentials` answers at each start, resume and turn. So it reaches every executor that asks for the job's
  variables: herdr on this machine, on an ssh target and on a client target, the print-mode agents, and the lane pods
  and job pods of the kubernetes executor. Each run is a new run span, so each start gets its own context.
- **The job's scripts send it back** (`TRACE_HEADER_SH`, `src/github-proxy/retry-after.ts`): `hopper-gh`, `hopper-skill`,
  `hopper-login` and `hopper-artifact` add a `traceparent` header from `TRACEPARENT`, only when the value is lowercase hex
  and dashes, as a W3C trace parent is: the variable cannot add a header. The request hook (`http.ts`) already takes a
  caller's `traceparent` as the parent, and the client door passes the header on. So a job's GitHub request through the
  hopper, and the GitHub calls it makes, are children of the job's run span.

No credential and no text goes in the context: a trace id, a span id and the sampled flag. A job is given no `OTEL_*`
variable: the hopper's exporter and its headers stay the hopper's. A tool in the job that reads `TRACEPARENT` and exports
on its own (set up on its machine) joins the trace.

**Left for the next parts** (the pull request lists them): the settings in the UI; git through the hopper and the
Windows step script with the header; a box's own processes; spans for work tree setup, tend, rebase, merge and deploy,
the outbox flush and the sync with its ETag fetches; concurrent sandboxes, the outbox's batch size and coalescing, and
the store's pool.

**Tests.** `test/telemetry/trace-context.test.ts` (in-memory exporter: the run span, the root, ended, off),
`test/github-proxy/trace-header.test.ts` (the real scripts against a stand-in: the header, and none for a bad value) and
`test/integration/job-trace-context.test.ts` (the real daemon: a job's `TRACEPARENT` is its run span, and its `hopper-gh`
request is a child of it).

## Telemetry: the outbox and the sync (issue #1486, part 5, 2026-10-17)

The issue asks for spans for the outbox flush and the sync with its ETag fetches, linked to the action that caused them,
and for the outbox's batch size and coalescing savings as metrics. A sync and an outbox send run on the sync loop's chain
and timers, after the request that asked for them answered. Under the context manager, the work inherited the context
of whoever started it: a sync after an intake action was a child of that request, long after the request ended, and a
timer's next sync was a child of the sync before it.

**The change.**
- **An outbox flush is a span** (`src/telemetry/sources.ts`, `traceOutboxFlush`; `src/sources/outbox-flush.ts`),
  `hopper.outbox.flush`: the root of a trace of its own, with `hopper.job.source`, `hopper.outbox.due` (the rows due)
  and `hopper.outbox.calls` (the calls planned after coalescing). It has a **cause link** to each action that asked for it
  in its batch window: the span active then, a person's request. The GitHub calls it makes are its children.
- **A sync is a span** (`traceSync`, `src/sources/sync.ts` `runSync`), `hopper.source.sync`: a root span with
  `hopper.job.source`, `hopper.sync.asked` (it reads everything again) and `hopper.sync.outcome` (`ok`, `error`). A sync
  asked for while one waits joins it, and so do its cause links. Its GitHub calls are its children, conditional reads
  answered from the cache (304) included, with `hopper.github.cache` `hit`. The sync after an outbox send is linked to the
  action that asked for the send. A sync is never linked to the sync before it (`causeNow` skips a sync span): that sync
  only set the timer.
- **Metrics**: `hopper.source.sync.duration` by source and outcome; `hopper.outbox.batch.size`, the rows due in each
  batch sent; `hopper.outbox.calls` by `hopper.outbox.result` (`sent`, `failed`); `hopper.outbox.rows.coalesced`, the rows
  sent with no call of their own (coalesced into another row's call, or cancelled by a later row).

The attributes are the source's name, counts and enums. A row's change, comment text, an error message and a key do not
go out. A failed sync records only its outcome.

**Why a root span and a link, not a child.** A flush or a sync can serve many actions (a burst of clicks in one batch, a
sync joined by many asks), and it runs after the request answered. A child of one request would hide the others, and
stretch that request's trace. A link is OpenTelemetry's way to say "caused by" across traces.

**Left for the next parts** (the pull request lists them): the settings in the UI; git through the hopper and the
Windows step script with the trace header; a box's own processes; spans for work tree setup, tend, rebase, merge and
deploy; concurrent sandboxes and the store's pool.

**Tests.** `test/telemetry/sources.test.ts` (in-memory exporters, a fake source in the real sync loop, no timing
asserted): an intake action's flush and the sync after it are root spans linked to the request, their GitHub calls their
children; a sync at start and one asked for with no span are linked to nothing; a failed sync is an error outcome with no
error text exported; a batch's rows, calls sent and failed, and rows coalesced are counted, with no row text exported.

## Lane pods of another release (issue #1454, 2026-10-16)

**Problem.** Lane pods (issue #1284, "Lane pods") joined only the hopper of their own Helm release: the chart set their
`HOPPER_URL` to the release's own Service, and made the lane pool key, which only a hopper started with
`HOPPER_LANE_POOL_KEY_FILE` read. A compose hopper, or any hopper outside the release, got no pod machines without
a new container. Since issue #1248 a host machine that holds user credentials is not ready, so pods that hold none are
the natural replacement.

**A key the hopper issues.** `POST /ui/api/machines/pool-key` (`issue`, `revoke`; an admin's, a box action) and the
operator CLI's `hopper pool-key [--revoke]` issue the session's user a **lane pool key**: 64 hex, a join code's shape,
answered once; only its SHA-256 is kept, in the instance table `lane_pool_keys` (instance migration 51), with its user
and when it was issued. One per user: a new key replaces the one before. `GET /api/machines/pool-key` says when it was
issued, never the key. `POST /client/join` takes it as it takes the install's key (`issuedLanePoolUser`,
`src/machines/lane-pool.ts`), after the install's key and before a join code: never spent, and the pod joins as a lane
pod (`pool: true`) of the key's user, under its pod's name. So it needs no restart: the join reads the table.
A revoked or replaced key joins no new pod; the machines that joined stay (a person removes them on Machines). A user
transfer or fold moves the key with the user's other rows.
- Why not the install's key in the UI: it is the install's, read from the runtime, and the hopper cannot change it. And
  a per-user key keeps a user's pods that user's machines, not always the first user's.
- Why one key per user, not a list: one runner-only release needs one key; a second is a replace away. A list earns its
  place with a second real caller.

**Runner-only chart mode.** `hopper.enabled=false` renders the lane pods' StatefulSet and their NetworkPolicy alone
(every other template is inside `if .Values.hopper.enabled`). `lanes.hopperUrl` names the hopper they join and dial in
at (`hopper.lanesHopperUrl`, `_helpers.tpl`: `http(s)://host:port`, no path); `lanes.existingSecret` the Secret with the
key under `key`, which the chart then does not make. Both are required with `hopper.enabled=false`: the render fails and
says which. With the hopper on, `lanes.existingSecret` is the key both the hopper and the pods read.

**Add machine → Pods on Kubernetes** (`ui/src/views/machine-pool.tsx`): makes or revokes the key, takes the URL the pods
reach the hopper at (the page's own, editable; a warning for a loopback URL), and shows the two commands
(`podRunnerCommands`, `ui/src/model/machines.ts`): the Secret, then the runner-only `helm install`.

**The hopper's guards are unchanged.** The pods reach the hopper as any client does: the Host guard (a LAN name or the
public URL) and the LAN peers decide. A job never sees the key: only the join init container mounts the Secret.

**Verification:** `test/integration/lane-pool-issued.test.ts` (a hopper with no install key issues one, a pod joins and is
online as a lane pod, a replaced or revoked key is refused, only the hash is kept), `test/scripts/helm-chart-runner.test.ts`
(the runner-only render, the refusals, the existing Secret with the hopper on), `test/ui/machines.test.ts`
(`podRunnerCommands`). `scripts/kind-check.ts` installs a runner-only release in its own namespace against the check's
hopper, by its URL, with a key from `hopper pool-key`, and checks the machine online and ready, no host path, no
credential and no hopper restart. **Not done in CI:** a compose hopper with a cluster, and a job on the pod: no runner has
both, and a job needs a job source. `docs/deploy.md` "Lane pods of another release" has the manual check.

## The infrastructure topology (issue #1781, parts 1 to 3, 2026-10-17)

Goal: show **which services exist** across the user's AWS accounts and Kubernetes clusters, and **what is linked to
what**, as one graph. A list of accounts or credentials is not enough. Read-only: nothing here writes to a cloud or a
cluster.

- **Topology sources.** A source is one AWS account in one region (`aws/<account>/<region>`) or one Kubernetes cluster
  (`kubernetes/<cluster>`, the cluster node's id: an EKS cluster's ARN, so it joins the cluster AWS reported). A
  read-only check reports one or more sources, each as a whole: `ok: true` with its `nodes` and `links`, or `ok: false`
  with the `error` that kept it from being read (`sourceReportProblem`, `src/domain/topology.ts`). A report that is not
  whole, or names a source twice, is refused whole (400, saying which and why): no half snapshot is kept.
- **Last good snapshot.** Each source is a row (`infra_topology_sources`, tenant migration 80): its last good snapshot
  with when it was read, and its last read. A good report replaces the snapshot; a failed one keeps it and says why
  (`afterReport`). So one account or cluster out of reach loses nothing of the rest of the graph, and its nodes stay with
  the time they were read.
- **One graph** (`joinGraph`, pure). The snapshots joined: a node two sources name is one node (the EKS cluster). A link
  names a node by its id (an ARN, `aws-account:<id>`, `k8s:<cluster>/<namespace>[/<kind>/<name>]`), or by an alias
  another source's node holds (`dns:<host>`: a load balancer, a database endpoint; `url:<queue URL>`). A link to an alias
  no node holds is dropped; a link to an id no source read gets a node of its own, **not seen**, when its id says what it
  is (an IAM role of another account, an account): so cross-account links show.
- **What AWS and Kubernetes answer, as nodes and links** (`src/domain/topology-discover.ts`, pure). The input is their
  answers as they give them: the AWS CLI's JSON (the SDK's shapes) and `kubectl get -o json`'s items, so a check outside
  the hopper and a discovery run inside it map the same way.
  - AWS (`awsTopology`): the account; VPCs; EKS clusters (`in` their VPC); load balancers and RDS databases (`in` their
    VPC, each with its DNS name as an alias); SQS queues (their ARN from the URL, the URL an alias); IAM roles, and each
    AWS principal of a role's trust policy `can-assume` it (an account root as the account).
  - Kubernetes (`kubeTopology`): namespaces `in` the cluster; deployments, services, ingresses and service accounts `in`
    their namespace; a service `selects` each deployment its selector matches; a deployment `runs-as` its service account
    and `uses` each AWS host name and queue URL its containers' environment names; a service or an ingress is behind
    (`routes-to` from) the load balancer whose host name its status names; an ingress `routes-to` its backend services;
    a service account `assumes` the IAM role its `eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn` annotation names (IRSA).
- **Who reports.** `POST /ui/api/topology/report`, JSON `{ sources }`, 1 to 100, each at most 20000 nodes and 50000
  links, least role operator; meant for an API token whose grant has the scope `topology:report` (area `topology`, in
  the Infra changes section of the scope registry). The reporter is the API token's label, else who signed in. Each report
  is `infra.topology_reported`: each source's key, `ok`, its counts or its error; never a node; on no job's timeline.
- **Topology** (`ui/src/views/topology.tsx`, its own page since issue #1943, "Topology: its own page"; pure model `ui/src/model/topology.ts`; the Globe view beside it, issue
  #1893, "The Topology globe"). The graph, drawn with d3's
  force layout (run to its end, so the same graph is drawn the same way), at most 400 nodes; filters by account, cluster,
  region and kind; a click on a node shows its id, where it is, its attrs, the sources that found it, its neighbours with
  the link in words, and the out-of-band changes whose target names it (its id, name, an alias or an attr, as `vpc-1`).
  Each source says what its snapshot holds and when it was read; a stale one says why. Every node is also listed by kind.
  `GET /api/topology` reads the graph; the page reads it once, with Try again on an error.
- **A job reads the topology** (issue #1905, `src/http/job-topology.ts`). A running job starts from the map, so it reads
  the graph `GET /api/topology` answers, at `GET /job/topology` with its proxy token (`Authorization: Bearer`), only
  while it is at work (running, waiting on an answer, waiting on something), else 401. `/api/` stays a person's read: a
  job's token is no UI session. A job learns the route from the `topology` skill (`src/skills/catalog.ts`), which reads
  it at `$HOPPER_URL`, never at `127.0.0.1` (on a seat, that is the seat's own loopback). The whole graph, as the person
  reads it: no slice, a job filters it. It changes nothing and records nothing; to read an account or a cluster now, a
  job asks for `aws-diagnostics` or `kube-diagnostics`.
- **Infra changes linked to nodes** (part 2, `entryNodes` and `nodeEntries`, `ui/src/model/topology.ts`, pure). Each entry of
  Applies and drift names what it **touched** (`subject`, `infraTimeline`): a plan, its approval and an apply their asset;
  drift and an out-of-band write (and its mark) their target. The nodes it touched: an `aws-account` its account node; an
  `aws-role` (`<account>/<role>`) its IAM role node and its account node, where the apply writes; a `cluster` the cluster
  node of that name; a `namespace` (`<cluster>/<namespace>`) that namespace node of that cluster; a target each node whose id,
  name, alias or attr it is, as before. An `argocd-app` or a `terraform-workspace` names no node. Each entry
  (`ui/src/views/infra-timeline.tsx`) lists up to three of its nodes; a click opens the node on the Topology page
  (`#topology/<node id>`, issue #1943). A node's details list every entry that touched it, newest first, at
  most 10: plans, approvals, applies, drift and out-of-band writes, not only the out-of-band changes. In the browser, from
  what the page reads already: no new route, nothing kept.

- **Topology discovery inside the hopper** (part 3, `src/infra-plans/topology-discovery.ts`, pure half
  `src/domain/topology-discovery.ts`). The hopper reads a user's topology itself, with the read credentials its vault mints:
  - **What it reads** (`discoveryTargets`): each account an `aws-account` minting credential mints for, in every region it
    has enabled (issue #1864), and the clusters `clustersToRead` names. A namespace's minting credential reads no whole
    cluster, so none is read for it.
  - **An account.** The vault mints a read session of the account's read role `hopper-read` (`aws-role/<account>/hopper-read`,
    the role cluster discovery signs in as) from the account's one minting credential (issue #1761), as for a mint test: the
    read profile, the read session policies, 900 s, the session named `hopper-topology-discovery` (`awsSessionName`). The
    reader (`TopologyReader`, a port; `src/infra-plans/topology-reader.ts` over the AWS SDK) lists the regions the account has
    enabled (EC2 `DescribeRegions`, as cluster discovery does, issue #1845; the credential's region alone when they cannot be
    listed) and asks, in each region (`regionsToRead`), EKS `ListClusters` and `DescribeCluster`, EC2 `DescribeVpcs`, ELBv2
    `DescribeLoadBalancers`, RDS `DescribeDBInstances` and SQS `ListQueues`; and in the credential's region only (the home
    region), the global lists too, IAM `ListRoles` and S3 `ListBuckets` (issue #1864); page by page, at most 20000 each: read
    calls only. Each region is a topology source of its own (`aws/<account>/<region>`). A region other than the home region
    that cannot be read is no source unless it held a snapshot before, so a region a policy denies adds no failed source.
    Each EKS cluster is a node in its account and region, `in` its VPC; each S3 bucket is a node (`arn:aws:s3:::<name>`) `in`
    its account, in the region S3 names. A credential that names an STS
    `Endpoint` (an AWS other than AWS's) is read at that endpoint for every service. A list the session may not read is left
    out; an account none of whose lists answer is reported failed, with the first error.
  - **A cluster** (`clustersToRead`): each cluster EKS listed in any region, by its ARN, then each cluster of its own minting
    credential or of a cluster override that no account listed, by its name; a cluster a cluster override names for EKS
    (`eksName`, in its `account` when it names one) by the override's name. Discovery decides the clusters, not the vault's
    entry names (issue #1864): a cluster no account listed and the vault mints no token for (a stale entry) is no source,
    unless it held a snapshot before; and a cluster source discovery reported that never held a snapshot and that a run did
    not report again is forgotten (`neverReadClusters`), so a stale entry cannot hide a real cluster. The vault mints a read token for `cluster/<name>` — its own minting credential, else found in the AWS
    accounts as `hopper-read`, the override applied (cluster discovery, issue #1766) — and the reader lists namespaces, deployments,
    services, ingresses and service accounts in every namespace (`@kubernetes/client-node`, 500 a page). A plain `http:` API
    server is taken (the client's `skipTLSVerify`, with no TLS to skip); an `https:` one's certificate is always checked.
  - **Reported as a check reports** (`report`, reporter `topology discovery`, `infra.topology_reported`), through the same
    mappers. A source that cannot be read is reported failed, so it keeps its last good snapshot and says why: the rest of the
    graph is read. An account the vault mints nothing for marks each of its kept sources failed (`accountUnread`); one never
    read has no source to mark, and its refusal is in its `vault.discovery_minted` event. A source past a report's limits is
    reported failed, saying so, never refused whole.
  - **Each mint** is `vault.discovery_minted` (`asset`, `credential`, `expiresAt`, or `reason`), on no job's timeline, never a
    key or a token. The minting credential never leaves the vault (`mintForDiscovery`, `src/vault/discovery-mint.ts`; in the
    vault's own container too, over its `mint` op); the hopper holds the minted session and token only while it reads.
  - **The saga** `topology-discovery` ("Sagas: work that survives a stop"): two steps, `aws` (the accounts; its output, the
    clusters to read) and `kubernetes` (the clusters). A stop between them goes on from `kubernetes`, on any hopper; a step
    done again reports again, which replaces the snapshot. Nothing to compensate: it writes nothing outside the hopper.
  - **On a schedule** (`createTopologyDiscoveries`, started with the sagas): every 30 minutes the hopper begins, for each user
    whose vault mints for an account or a cluster, the run of the 6-hour slot it is in (key `<user>/scheduled/<slot>`): one
    run per user and slot, whichever hopper of the instance begins it first.
  - **On demand**: **Discover now** on the Topology panel, `POST /ui/api/topology/discover` (operator, body `{}`; scope
    `topology:discover`), begins a run of its own (`<user>/asked/<id>`) and drives it to its end, then answers `state` and
    the graph. A stop meanwhile leaves the rest to the saga.

**Not built yet** (left for the next part of issue #1781):
- A ready-made topology collector script, as `scripts/out-of-band-collector.ts` is for signals.
- An account in more than its minting credential's one region: each credential reads its `Region` only.

**Decisions** (part 3):
- **Access is not asked for a discovery mint**, as for a mint test: no job and no template take part. What bounds it is the
  read profile — the read role `hopper-read`, the read session policies that deny every write, a cluster's read token — and
  the minting credential a person set. The schedule is the issue's ask; a person turns it off by clearing *Mints for*.
- **The hopper reads, not a box.** The reads are list and describe calls with a 15-minute session; a sandbox per run would
  add a container to start and tear down for no gain in reach. The `TopologyReader` port keeps them in one module.
- **The AWS SDK's clients**, one package per service (EC2, ELBv2, RDS, SQS, IAM beside EKS and STS), not the CLI: the
  hopper's image carries no AWS CLI, and the SDK's shapes are the CLI's JSON, which the mappers already read.
- **Each ask its own run.** Discover now begins a new saga each time; the button waits for its answer, so a person does not
  ask twice by mistake.

Tests: `test/domain/topology.test.ts` (the mappers, the join across AWS and Kubernetes, IRSA and trust across accounts,
a failed source keeps its snapshot, refusals), `test/integration/topology-discovery.test.ts` (part 3: the real daemon, database,
coordinator and minters, STS and the Kubernetes API on loopback, the reader at its seam: Discover now reads an account and
its cluster into one graph with the minted read session and token, each mint recorded with no key; an account the vault mints
nothing for and a cluster out of reach lose nothing of the rest), `test/domain/topology-discovery.test.ts` (the targets, the
clusters to read, the schedule: one run per user and slot), `test/infra-plans/topology-reader.test.ts` (each AWS list page by
page, read calls only; the Kubernetes lists page by page with the token, on loopback; a source none of whose lists answer),
`test/ui/topology-discover.test.ts` (Discover now), `test/integration/topology.test.ts` (the real daemon and database: an API
token reports a test account and a test cluster, the graph holds both and the links between them, a cluster out of reach
keeps its snapshot, the event, the scope and the refusals), `test/ui/topology.test.ts` (filters, neighbours, the nodes each
entry touched and the entries of a node, source words, the layout), `test/ui/infra-plans.test.ts` (each entry's subject),
`test/ui/topology-view.test.ts` (the panel draws, a click shows a node and the changes that touched it, a stale source, an
empty topology; the feed links an entry to its nodes and a click picks one).

## The Topology globe (issue #1893, 2026-10-18)

Follow-up to "The infrastructure topology": discovery reads every region (issue #1864), but nothing showed where the
nodes live. The Topology panel now has two views of the same graph, **Graph** (as before) and **Globe**. The globe is a
view, not a replacement, and reads only what the graph reads: no new route, no discovery, no cloud call.

- **The model** (`ui/src/model/topology-globe.ts`, pure). `REGION_PLACES`: each AWS region at the city or the area AWS
  names for it, in degrees. A node's region (`nodeRegion`): its own; else, for a Kubernetes object, its cluster's (an EKS
  cluster's region, from the whole graph, so a filter that leaves out the cluster leaves its objects where they live); else
  the region its ARN names. `globeOf` groups the nodes the filters leave per region, most first, with their counts by kind;
  makes one **arc** per pair of regions a topology link joins, with how many links; and lists each node with **no known
  place** apart, with why: no region (an account, an IAM role, a bucket S3 names no region for, a cluster of its own
  Kubernetes API) or a region the table does not know.
- **The view** (`ui/src/views/topology-globe.tsx`). The globe, then each region with its counts, the region picked with its
  nodes, and the nodes with no known place. A click on a region, on the globe or in the list, lists its nodes; a click on a
  node picks it, so the details are the graph's (`Details`, the page's selected node). The filters (account, cluster,
  region, kind) are the panel's, so both views show the same nodes. The globe draws any number of nodes: they are grouped,
  so the graph's limit of 400 does not apply.
- **The scene** (`ui/src/views/globe-scene.ts`, three.js, a chunk of its own loaded only when Globe is picked). A sphere,
  the land's outline (Natural Earth 1:110m, the `world-atlas` package, built into the UI: no map tile, no outside call, so it
  works offline), a marker per region (larger with more nodes; the region picked in the theme's warn colour) and an arc
  per pair of regions, lifted above the sphere. A person turns it by dragging and zooms with the wheel (three.js's
  `OrbitControls`); it draws only when the camera moves. The colours are the theme's CSS variables, read through a 1×1
  canvas so `oklch` colours work.
- **No WebGL.** Before Globe shows, `webglAvailable` asks a canvas for a `webgl2` or a `webgl` context. With none, or when
  the scene throws as it starts, the panel shows the graph and says why.

**Decisions:**
- **three.js, `world-atlas` and `topojson-client`**: established, maintained libraries for the scene, the land data and its
  decoding. The region table is our own: no maintained package maps AWS regions to places, and the table is short.
- **Regions, not nodes, on the globe.** All of a region's nodes are in one place, so one marker per region with its count
  reads better than a pile of points; its nodes are one click away.

Tests: `test/ui/topology-globe.test.ts` (region to coordinate, a node's region, the groups and counts, the arcs, the nodes
with no known place and why, a filter, the WebGL check), `test/ui/topology-globe-view.test.ts` (the panel in happy-dom
with the scene replaced at its module: the regions and arcs drawn, a click on a region and on a node, the filters shared
with the graph, the graph and why with no WebGL and when the scene cannot start).

## Topology: its own page (issue #1943, 2026-10-18)

Before: the topology and its globe were a panel at the bottom of Infra, and with no source the panel only said where to
set a credential. A primary view had no top-level home (issue #896), and the sidebar had three groups of one entry each.

- **A top-level view, `#topology`** (`ui/src/views/topology-page.tsx`), in the Infra nav group beside Infra. The panel
  (`topology.tsx`) is its content: graph and globe, filters, a node's details. It reads `GET /api/topology`, and
  `GET /api/infra-plans` and `GET /api/out-of-band` for the Infra changes a node's details list (`useLoad`, `NotYet`,
  `infra-load.tsx`, shared with Infra). `#topology/<node id>` (the id URI-encoded) picks that node.
- **Infra holds no copy.** One line links to Topology. Infra still reads the graph, only to name the nodes each Applies
  and drift entry touched; a click on one opens `#topology/<node id>`.
- **With no source, why and what to do** (`NoSources`, `topology-sources.tsx`). From the vault's view (`useVault`): it
  mints for no AWS account and no cluster, so there is nothing to read; or it mints for some (each named) and no read
  reported yet. Either way no read-only check reported a source. In place: **Add an AWS account** and **Add a cluster**
  open the vault's own form (`SetForm`, `vault.tsx`) with Mints for set to `aws-account/` or `cluster/` (an admin's; any
  other person reads where an admin adds one); **Discover now** once the vault mints for one (or when the vault's view
  cannot be read, so nothing hides). The report route for a read-only check is named too.
- **A failed read shows its error** (`ReadErrors`): each source whose last read failed, its name, when, and the error, in
  a box of its own above the graph. A graph with sources but no node says no source was read without an error.
- **Nav groups.** Infra (Infra, Topology); Sources & machines takes Accounts; Set up holds Skills and Settings. No group
  holds one entry only. Issue #2374 renamed them (Work, Fleet, Admin) and merged entries: "One canonical home per workflow". Group ids stay (`infra`, `sources-machines`, `settings`), so a collapsed group stays collapsed.

**Decisions:**
- **Topology in the Infra group**, not a group of its own: the two pages are about the same accounts and clusters, and a
  group of one entry is what the issue asks to remove.
- **Accounts beside Machines, Skills beside Settings**: Accounts says who each machine's agent tool is signed in as;
  Skills is configuration of what jobs get. The heading Settings over one entry Settings became Set up.
- **The vault's own form, opened in place**: no second form, so what is checked (the name, Mints for, an AWS account's
  JSON keys) is the vault's.

Tests: `test/ui/topology-page.test.ts` (the page in the whole app: the sidebar entry and no copy on Infra, the empty state
with and without a minting credential and the add form, a failed read's error, the graph and a linked node).

## Telemetry: what runs now (issue #1486, part 6, 2026-10-17)

The issue asks for the concurrent sandboxes and the store's pool as metrics, and parts 4 and 5 left git through the
hopper and the Windows step script without the job's trace header.

**The change.**
- **What runs now** (`src/telemetry/live.ts`): gauges read at each collection, from readers the parts that hold the
  things add (`liveReader`) and drop when they stop. Readers of one gauge are summed by their attributes. Started with
  the process's basics (`start.ts`), so telemetry off reads nothing.
  - `hopper.sandboxes`, by `hopper.sandbox.kind`, `hopper.sandbox.place` and `hopper.sandbox.state`: the need boxes of
    the steps that run now (`src/sandbox/service.ts`, kind `need`, state `running`, place `local` beside the hopper or
    `machine` on a client target), and the playground's sandboxes by their state (`src/sandbox/playground.ts`, kind
    `playground`, place `local`). Each is read from what the part keeps in memory, not from the runtime: a read costs no
    call.
  - `hopper.db.connections`: the stores open now (`src/store/db.ts`). The store has no pool: each open store holds one
    connection in the Postgres worker, and its calls block the process one at a time (design.md "Database"). So the
    count of open stores is the pool's size, and none is ever busy at a collection; how long each call blocked is part
    1's `hopper.db.call.duration`.
  Only enums: no box name, template, user, job or database URL goes out.
  - `hopper.disk.bytes` and `hopper.machines.disk` (issue #2494, "Hopper's own disk use" → "Part 12"): the machines' disk
    use by kind and the machines by their disk's state, from `src/machines/disk-gauges.ts`; no machine id.
- **A job's git carries its trace** (`src/github-proxy/git.ts` `jobGitConfig`): with the job's trace parent (the
  `TRACEPARENT` it runs with, `src/users/github-proxy.ts`), the job's git config adds `http.<hopper git route>.extraHeader`
  `traceparent: …`, for the GitHub and the GitLab route only. A fetch or push to any other URL sends no header. Only a
  value of lowercase hex and dashes is added, as for the scripts.
- **`hopper-step` sends it too** (`src/windows-steps/script.ts`): the same `trace_header` as the other scripts, on each
  request. So a Windows, box or need step's requests are children of the job's run span.

**Why readers and not an up-down counter.** An instrument is made again when the meter provider changes (part 1); an
up-down counter made again loses the adds before it, and a later close counts below zero. A reader answers what is there
at the collection, whichever provider asks.

**Left for the next parts** (the pull request lists them): the settings in the UI; a box's own processes; spans for
work tree setup, tend, rebase, merge and deploy.

**Tests.** `test/telemetry/live.test.ts` (in-memory metric reader, the container runtime double, the real database, no
timing asserted): a need box counts while its step runs and not after; the playground's sandboxes by state, none once
destroyed; each store connection open counted, and not once closed; no name or URL exported.
`test/github-proxy/git.test.ts` (real git reads the config: the header for the hopper's routes only, none for a bad
value), `test/github-proxy/trace-header.test.ts` (`hopper-step` against a stand-in) and
`test/integration/job-trace-context.test.ts` (the real daemon: the job's git config carries its run span).

## Telemetry: job steps (issue #1486, part 7, 2026-10-17)

The issue asks for spans for work tree setup, tend, rebase and merge in a job's trace. The job spans (part 1) are built
from events. These steps are work the hopper does for the job between events, and part 5 put them in the sync's trace,
apart from the job's.

**The change.**
- **A job step** (`src/telemetry/job-steps.ts` `traceJobStep`): a span `hopper.job.<step>` in the job's trace, a child of
  its run span, else its pull request span, else its root — an ended root too, while the hopper remembers the job
  (`jobStepParent`, `jobs.ts`). A pull request the job followed from its report has no pull request span, so its steps
  are children of the root. The span active when the step began (a sync, a request, the outbox) is a link: the step's
  GitHub calls are its children, in the job's trace. A job no trace holds gets its step as a child of the active span.
  Attributes: `hopper.job.id`, `hopper.job.step`, `hopper.job.step.outcome`, and enums of the step; an error records only
  its kind (`error.type`). The duration is `hopper.job.step.duration` by step and outcome. The telemetry summary keeps
  it with the job spans, so the Telemetry panel shows it.
- **The steps.**
  - `worktree` (`src/executors/herdr/start.ts`): the job worktree command in the pane, from typed to its outcome:
    `made`, `none`, `failed`, `timed_out`.
  - `follow` (`src/sources/after-done.ts`, `pull-request-acts.ts`): a follow of the job's pull request. The hopper's own
    merge (yolo mode) happens in it, and a person's Merge now or Close PR. `hopper.pull_request.act`: `none`, `merge`,
    `close`. Outcome: `merged_by_hopper`, `merged`, `closed`, `abandoned`, `checked`, `open`, `unchanged`.
  - `base_merge` (after-done.ts `mergedBase`): the base branch merged into the pull request in the hopper's mirror.
    Outcome: `pushed`, `conflicts`, `none`.
  - `tend` (after-done.ts `tendIfDue`): the job's item run again with the tend brief. `hopper.tend.step`: `rebase`,
    `fix_checks`. Outcome: `started`, or the refusal's reason. The rebase itself is the tend job's run, in that job's
    trace.
- **What made a job.** A job's root links to the span active at its first event: the request, the sync or the tend that
  made it. So a tend job's trace points to the tend in the trace of the job it tends.
- **A tend ends the pull request span** (`job.pull_request_tended`): the job follows it no more, and the tend job follows
  it in its own trace.

Only ids, enums and the step's name go out: no pull request URL, branch, file name, commit or error text.

**Why a child of the job and a link to the sync, not the reverse.** The issue asks for one trace per job with its
stages. A sync serves many jobs; a step serves one. The link keeps the way from the sync to its steps.

**Left for the next parts** (the pull request lists them): the settings in the UI; a box's own processes; deploy.

**Tests.** `test/telemetry/job-steps.test.ts` (in-memory exporters, no timing asserted): a step's parent, link,
attributes and metric; a step after the job's end; a tend that ends the pull request span and is linked from the new
job's root; a throw records only its kind; a job no trace holds; the herdr start's worktree step.
`test/integration/job-steps-trace.test.ts` (the real daemon, the fake GitHub): a base merge and the hopper's merge in the
job's trace, the base merge linked to its sync; a conflict the mirror cannot merge, tended, and the tend job linked to
the tend; no pull request URL or text exported.

## Telemetry settings (issue #1486, part 8, 2026-10-17)

The issue asks for an OTLP exporter configured through the hopper's settings and UI, and through the usual `OTEL_*`
launch environment. Parts 1 to 7 read only the launch's variables.

**The change.**
- **The telemetry setting** (`src/domain/telemetry-settings.ts`), the hopper's admin's, in Settings → Telemetry or
  through the API, never in a file: `on`, the OTLP `endpoint` (an http or https URL with no user, password, query or
  fragment; each signal goes to `<endpoint>/v1/<signal>`) and the `signals` (`traces`, `metrics`, `logs`). Kept in the
  instance's settings, key `telemetry` (`src/store/telemetry-settings.ts`); never set, it is off with every signal. A
  record of another shape reads as the default, so a build before this one and a build after it read the same store.
- **The launch wins.** When the launch's `OTEL_*` variables name an exporter (`telemetryWanted`, part 1), they configure
  telemetry for the life of the process, and the setting is only kept. Else the setting does.
- **It applies at once** (`src/telemetry/start.ts` `apply`): the SDK that runs is shut down — what it holds is flushed —
  and one is started from the setting, in order, one at a time. The SDK gets the setting's exporters, OTLP over HTTP and
  protobuf, for the signals it names and none other (`sdk.ts` `otlp`); the exporters still read the launch's other OTLP
  variables, such as `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS`. The daemon applies the kept setting at its start
  (`src/telemetry/settings.ts`). A start that fails leaves telemetry off and logs the error's kind.
- **Routes** (`src/http/ui/telemetry-settings.ts`): `GET /api/telemetry-settings`, the instance admin's read: the setting,
  `source` (`launch`, `settings` or `off`), `exporting` and `protocol`; `POST /ui/api/telemetry-settings`, role admin,
  the whole setting. A change is `telemetry.changed`, with the settings before and after and who changed it.
- **The Settings section** (`ui/src/views/telemetry-settings.tsx`): on or off, the endpoint, the signals, and a line that
  says where the config comes from now.

**Why no header in the setting.** A collector's header is usually its API key: a credential the hopper is given for an
outside service. Such a credential comes from the runtime ("Secrets"), so it stays `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS` at
launch, and the endpoint takes no user, password or query, where a credential could hide.

**Why one protocol.** OTLP over HTTP and protobuf is the OpenTelemetry default and every collector takes it. `http/json`
and `grpc` stay at launch (`OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL`), with the other exporters.

**What a change loses.** A span still open when the SDK changes belongs to the SDK that is shut down, and is not
exported. Each job's next span joins its trace again.

**Left for the next parts** (the pull request lists them): a box's own processes; deploy. Both are part 9, below.

**Tests.** `test/telemetry/settings-export.test.ts` (a stand-in collector on loopback, no timing asserted): off until the
setting turns it on, then spans and metrics reach the endpoint with the launch's headers, and off again flushes and
stops; only the signals named go out, under the endpoint's own path; the launch wins. `test/integration/telemetry-settings.test.ts`
(the real daemon and database): off by default; on exports the daemon's spans at once; the event; a bad setting is 400;
kept across a restart and applied at the start. `test/domain/telemetry-settings.test.ts` and
`test/ui/telemetry-settings.test.ts`: the endpoint's rules, the record, the UI's line.

## Telemetry: a box's own processes and deploys (issue #1486, part 9, 2026-10-17)

Part 8 left two stages of a job's trace: the work in a sandbox box, and the deploy. A box's processes ran with no trace
context: a need box gets its environment from the hopper, not from the job. A job's change reaches people through a
landing batch run (issue #1073), and no span showed it.

**The change.**
- **A need box's run is a job step** (`src/sandbox/service.ts` `needStep`; design.md "Telemetry: job steps"): the step
  `need_box`, a child of the job's run span. It covers each way a box runs: a need step, a box step and a container
  target's command. Outcome: the sandbox run's outcome (`succeeded`, `failed`, `timed-out`, `cancelled`).
  `hopper.sandbox.place`: `local` (beside the hopper) or `machine` (on a client target).
- **The box runs with the step's trace context** (`traceEnv`, `src/telemetry/jobs.ts`): `TRACEPARENT`, and `TRACESTATE`
  when there is one, in the box's environment, beside the step's own variables. The box's script keeps them, so the
  command and every process it starts see them. A tool in the box that reads `TRACEPARENT` and exports on its own joins
  the job's trace under the step. Telemetry off: no variable is set.
- **A landing batch run is a span** (`src/telemetry/deploys.ts`, `traceDeploys`, one per user's runtime beside the job
  traces): `hopper.landing_batch`, the root of a trace of its own, from `landing_batch.started` to `landing_batch.promoted`,
  `landing_batch.failed`, or `landing_batch.restarted`. Attributes: `hopper.repo`, the batch's `hopper.pull_request.number`,
  `hopper.landing_batch.merges` (how many pull requests) and `hopper.landing_batch.outcome` (`promoted`, `failed`,
  `restarted`). A daemon that stops ends an open one as `restarted`.
- **A job's deploy span** (`hopper.job.deploy`): for each pull request in the batch that a job of the user named, a span
  in that job's trace, a child of its pull request span, else its root, while the hopper remembers the job
  (`jobStepParent`). It lasts as long as the batch run, links to it, and ends with its outcome. The job is found by the
  pull request's repository and number, from the job's events.
- **Metric**: `hopper.landing_batch.duration` by outcome. The telemetry summary keeps it with the job spans as `deploy`.

Only ids, numbers and enums go out: no branch, commit, URL, check name or reason.

**Why a batch run is the deploy.** A job has no deploy step of its own: its pull request merges to `main`, and its change
reaches people when a batch run of `main` merges into `dev` (AGENTS.md "Changes reach people"). `beta`, `canary` and
`stable` move by `scripts/promote.sh` or the canary window, for many batches at a time: they are not in a job's trace.
A batch serves many jobs, so it has a trace of its own, and each job gets a span that links to it, as a job step links to
its sync.

**Not built.** Spans for `scripts/promote.sh` and the canary window. A box's own export: the hopper gives the box no
`OTEL_*` variable, as it gives a job none (part 4).

**Tests.** `test/telemetry/box-trace.test.ts` (in-memory exporter, the container runtime double, no timing asserted):
the step's parent, attributes and outcome; the box's `TRACEPARENT` names the step; none with telemetry off; no secret,
box name or template exported. `test/telemetry/deploys.test.ts`: the batch span and its attributes; a deploy span in each
job's trace, linked to it; failed and restarted; a batch of pull requests no job made; no branch, commit or URL exported.

## A job pushes wherever its user can push (issue #1806, part 1, 2026-10-17)

Decision of the owner on issue #1806, a follow-up of issue #1472 part 2. Before, a job pushed only to its own repository,
another of its user's job repositories, or its user's fork (issues #1131, #1275, #429). Kept work in a clone of any other
repository stayed for a person, and Push it was refused for it (issue #1470).

**The decision.** No hopper rule limits where a job pushes but its user's own write access on GitHub. When the user can
push to a repository, a job can push a branch there and open a pull request there. There is no allow list, no job
repository requirement and no setting for it. The only refusal is GitHub's own: the user has no write access.

**The change.**
- The git broker (`createGitProxy`, step 3 of "Git through the hopper") takes a push to any repository. It reads the
  repository as the user's connection sees it, and refuses the push when `canPush` is false (`your user cannot push to
  <repo>: GitHub gives its connection no write access there`; the job's own repository keeps its fork hint). The ref
  check (`checkPush`: a new branch of the job's own work, never the default branch, a release branch, a batch run's branch,
  a tag or a delete) and the shrink guard apply as on a job repository. Each push is a `github_proxy.done` (or `.refused`)
  event on the job's timeline, `op: git.push`, as before.
- The GitHub proxy (`checkRequest`) takes `pr.create` on any repository; GitHub refuses it when the user cannot open it.
  On a repository the hopper does not work on, a job marks ready, edits or closes only a pull request it opened, or its
  work item's (`PR_OWNED`, `ownsPullRequest`), and files, comments on and closes no issue.
- The account that acts on a repository that is no job repository is the account of the job's own repository (issue
  #1448), as for a fork.
- `hopper-gh help` and the kept work's push brief (`pushBrief`) say a job pushes to a new branch of any repository its
  user can push to.

**Not changed.** A fork's pull request (`--head <login>:<branch>`) opens only on the job's own repository, with
Contribution on. Issues and comments stay on the job repositories. The delivery job rule still sends a change another
repository needs as a required child issue.

**Left for later parts of issue #1806.** The opt-in yolo setting for a repository the hopper does not work on: today yolo
mode (issue #637) is set per job repository, and the hopper follows and merges only those pull requests. A push straight
to the target branch with yolo on is not taken: the ref check still refuses a default or release branch everywhere.

**Decisions:**
- **`pr.create` on any repository, not only where the job pushed.** A job opens a pull request from a branch; GitHub
  refuses one whose branch is not there or that the user cannot open. Tracking the job's own pushes per repository adds
  state for no new protection.
- **No issues on other repositories.** The owner's decision names pushes and pull requests. Filing an issue on a
  repository the hopper does not work on stays refused: such an issue is public text no person read first.
- **A push to the user's own fork with Contribution off is taken.** The user can push to it, and nothing else holds it.
  A pull request from that fork still needs Contribution on.

**Residual risk.** One bad issue, or one injected agent, can now push a branch to any repository its user can write to,
and open a pull request there, not only to the job repositories. It still cannot change a default or release branch,
and branch protection on GitHub keeps the rest. Every push and pull request is an event on the job's timeline.

**Verification:** `test/integration/git-proxy.test.ts` ("pushes a branch to a repository the hopper does not work on,
and opens a pull request there", "refuses a push to a repository its user cannot push to"),
`test/github-proxy/proxy.test.ts`, `test/github-proxy/contribution.test.ts`,
`test/integration/github-proxy.test.ts`, `test/integration/contribution.test.ts`, `test/domain/kept-work.test.ts`.

## Direct push (issue #1806, part 2, 2026-10-17)

The owner's decision on issue #1806 adds an opt-in yolo setting: when the user turns it on, the hopper may push straight
to the target branch, within the user's own GitHub rights; off by default; the UI says plainly what it allows; every push
is recorded. Part 1 ("A job pushes wherever its user can push") let a job push a branch to any repository its user can
push to, and kept the ref check: never a default or a release branch.

**The change.**
- **The setting.** `push` in the user's yolo mode settings (`YoloModeSettings.push`, `owner/repo` lowercased, sorted):
  the repositories where a job may push straight to the target branch. `directPushFor(settings, repo)`. Saved with yolo
  mode (`POST /ui/api/yolo-mode`, `push` whole, empty for none; `yolo_mode.changed` carries it), an admin's act, and shown
  in Settings → Yolo mode → Direct push, one repository a line, with a warning that says what it allows. Any repository,
  a job repository or not. Absent: none, so a store from before reads as off and the build before it still runs on it.
- **The target branch.** The repository's landing branch while it has landing batches (issue #1073), else its default
  branch as GitHub says. On this repository that is `main`, never `dev`: a direct push lands where a pull request would,
  and the batch runner still decides what reaches `dev`.
- **The ref check** (`checkPush`, `direct`): with direct push on, the target branch leaves the kept list. Every other
  release branch, a batch run's branch, a tag and a delete stay refused.
- **Only a fast-forward** (`createFastForward`, `src/git-mirror/push-lines.ts`): the git broker asks, for each ref update
  of the target branch that is there already, whether the push only adds commits on top of it. The user's mirror fetches
  the branch's head when it lacks it, indexes the push's pack in a quarantine, and runs `git merge-base --is-ancestor`.
  Not a fast-forward: refused (`a job pushes to <branch> only a fast-forward: …`). The hopper cannot check (no mirror, a
  fetch that fails): refused, never taken (`the hopper could not check …`). The shrink guard runs as on any push.
- **The record.** The push's `github_proxy.done` names the refs it moved on the target branch (`direct`), on the job's
  timeline; a refusal is a `github_proxy.refused` with its reason.
- `hopper-gh help` and the kept work's push brief say a push to the target branch is taken only with direct push on.

**Decisions:**
- **A setting of its own, not yolo mode's `on`.** Yolo mode is on for every job repository on many hoppers, this one
  included. Reading it as direct push would widen what a job may do on each of them without anyone turning it on. The
  decision asks for an opt-in, off by default: a repository is named, or nothing changes.
- **Per repository only, no switch for every repository.** A switch for all would reach every repository the user can
  write to, including ones nobody thought of. Naming each is one line more for a person.
- **Fast-forward only, and fail closed.** A push that rewrites the target branch would erase other people's commits, and
  GitHub allows it where the branch has no protection. Within the user's rights is a ceiling, not a reason to rewrite
  history. A check the hopper cannot make refuses: the job pushes a branch and opens a pull request, as without the setting.
- **The landing branch, not the default branch, on a repository with landing batches.** The default branch there is the
  tested branch: a push to it would skip the batch run that decides what reaches people.
- **No comment on the issue.** The decision says every push is recorded on the job and its issue. The job's timeline
  records it. A comment on GitHub is text the publishing rule keeps neutral, and the hopper posts none outside the listed
  exceptions; the work item links the job, and its timeline shows the push.

**Left for later parts of issue #1806.** Yolo mode on a repository the hopper does not work on (part 3, below). A push as
a durable work item (issue #1524 sagas).

**Residual risk.** On a repository a person named, one bad issue or one injected agent can add commits straight to its
target branch with no review, and whatever that branch triggers runs (a release, an image build, a deploy). It cannot
rewrite the branch, delete it, push a tag or reach any other release branch; branch protection on GitHub still applies.

**Verification:** `test/github-proxy/direct-push.test.ts` (off, a fast-forward, not one, not checked, the landing branch),
`test/github-proxy/git.test.ts` (`checkPush` with `direct`), `test/git-mirror/push-lines.test.ts` (fast-forward in real git),
`test/domain/direct-push.test.ts`, `test/ui/yolo-mode.test.ts`.

## Yolo mode on a repository the hopper does not work on (issue #1806, part 3, 2026-10-17)

The owner's decision on issue #1806: a job may push and open pull requests on any repository its user can push to, and
the opt-in yolo setting lets the hopper merge with no review, within the user's own GitHub rights, off by default, with
UI text that says plainly what it allows. Part 1 let a job open the pull request there. The hopper already follows a job's
pull request in its own repository (issue #1778, "A pull request in another repository"), under that repository's yolo
mode and change rule — and `yoloModeFor` fell back to `on` for any repository, so a hopper with yolo mode on for its job
repositories merged a job's pull request on any other repository too, and the change rule's `ready` kinds (docs, low-risk)
merged there with yolo mode off. Nobody turned that on for those repositories.

**The change.**
- **`on` covers the job repositories only** (`yoloModeFor(settings, repo, jobRepos)`, `src/domain/yolo-mode.ts`). A
  repository's own setting (`repos`) still wins everywhere. A GitHub repository (`owner/repo`) that is none of the user's
