  job repositories (`everyJobRepository`) has yolo mode on only when a person named it on. A GitLab project, asked by its
  URL, is never such a repository: a GitLab job works on its own project only.
- **No kind merges with no person there** (`mergeRuleFor`): on such a repository not named on, every kind's merge gate is
  `yolo`, so nothing merges and the card says `yolo off`. Named on, its change rule applies as on a job repository.
- **The follow, the direct jobs' follow, the repository checks and the Pull requests list** take both from the same two
  functions (`pullRequestSettings`, `src/users/source-context.ts`; `pullRequestList`).
- **Settings → Yolo mode**: a repository is added by name (`owner/repo`, **Add, on**), then saved as any per-repository
  setting (`POST /ui/api/yolo-mode` `repos`; `hopper yolo <owner/repo> on` too). A row that is no job repository says so,
  its default reads `Does not merge (not a job repository)`, and a note says the switch for every job repository does not
  reach it and what on allows (`OUTSIDE_YOLO_WARNING`).

**Decisions:**
- **A person names each repository, as for direct push.** `on` would otherwise reach every repository the user can write
  to; the decision asks for an opt-in, off by default.
- **The `ready` gates wait too.** A docs-only change on someone else's repository is still a change nobody reviewed; the
  change rule is the user's judgement of their own job repositories.
- **No migration.** The settings' shape does not change. A hopper that merged such a pull request by `on` alone now waits
  for a person, which is the safe side; the build before it still runs on the store.

**Left for a later part of issue #1806.** A push as a durable work item (issue #1524 sagas): part 4, "A push kept as a
saga" below.

**Residual risk.** On a repository a person named on, a job's pull request is merged with no review once it is ready, and
whatever that merge triggers runs. GitHub's branch protection and the user's own rights still apply.

**Verification:** `test/domain/outside-merge.test.ts`, `test/sources/pull-request-list.test.ts` ("a repository the hopper
does not work on"), `test/ui/yolo-mode.test.ts`.

## A push kept as a saga (issue #1806, part 4, 2026-10-17)

The owner's decision on issue #1806: every push is recorded on the job, and pushes are durable work items (issue #1524:
every call across a system boundary is a persisted record with an idempotency key, resumable on any host after a stop).
Before, the git broker recorded a push only after GitHub answered it (`github_proxy.done` or `.failed`). A hopper that
stopped while GitHub had the push recorded nothing: the push could be on GitHub with no event on the job's timeline.

**The change.**
- **The saga.** The git broker (`createGitProxy`, `pushes`) keeps each push it sends to GitHub as a `git-push` saga
  (`src/github-proxy/push-saga.ts`, `createGitPushes`), keyed `<job>/<request>`, after every check passed and before
  GitHub has the push. Its data: the repository, each ref update (`ref`, `old`, `new`), the `direct` refs, the job's
  machine, the acting login (`as`) and the repository whose account acts (`via`). A push the hopper refuses is no saga:
  it never reaches GitHub, and its refusal is recorded at once, as before.
- **Its one step, `settle`.** On the hopper that sends the push, the step waits until the broker recorded the push's
  event, then ends: one event, as before. The saga's lease is renewed meanwhile.
- **After a stop.** The next hopper (this one after its start, or another on the database) takes the saga when its lease
  ends. When the job's log holds an event of the request already (`GitUser.recorded`), it records nothing. Else it reads
  the refs on GitHub with the user's connection (git's ref advertisement, `info/refs?service=git-upload-pack`): the refs
  at their `new` commit are recorded as `github_proxy.done`, the others as `github_proxy.failed` (`the hopper stopped
  before GitHub answered the push, and GitHub does not have it: push again`). A read that fails is tried again with the
  saga's backoff.
- **Nothing is pushed again.** The pack lives only in the request. git's push is a compare-and-swap of each ref, and the
  job's git sends it again when its request failed; the saga only records what GitHub has.

**Decisions:**
- **The saga records, it does not push.** Keeping the pack to send it again would put up to 512 MB a push into the
  database, and push a change after the job's git was told that the push failed. The job's own retry is already
  idempotent: git compares each ref's old commit.
- **The broker still records in the request.** The event lands before the job's git reads the answer, as before, so a
  job, a test or a person sees it at once. The saga dedupes by the request id.
- **No new event field.** The resumed record has the same shape as the broker's; the event schemas do not change, and
  the build before this one runs on the store.

**Verification:** `test/github-proxy/push-saga.test.ts`, on the real database with two coordinators: a push GitHub
answers (the saga ends, one event); a hopper stopped while GitHub had the push, and GitHub took it (the next hopper
records it done) or did not (recorded failed); an event recorded before the stop is not recorded again.

## A machine's own usage limits (issue #1860, 2026-10-17)

**Problem.** Two machines can sign in to one Claude account: a Windows machine that takes only `hopper:windows`
work, and a Linux machine added to use the account's spare capacity. Each reads the same account, so their usage
readings say the same. Both scale their lane cap by the same usage limits. So in the soft band each drains only its
own lowest-priority lanes, and the secondary machine can spend the last of the budget that the primary's work needs.

Two shapes were offered: an `account` (or `usageGroup`) option that makes machines share one reading, with a
`usagePriority` per machine; or lower usage limits for the secondary machine. Built the second: the machines already
read the same numbers (each its own usage source of one account), so a shared reading adds nothing, and a
per-machine pair of limits is one option and no new grouping concept. It also serves a machine alone, which an
admin wants to keep below the user's limits.

**As built:**
- **`usageLimits`**, an optional option of every machine-source plugin (`local`, `ssh`, `container`, `client`,
  `kubernetes-cluster`): `{ "soft": <0..1>, "hard": <0..1> }`, soft below hard, else the config is refused. Not
  command-bearing. It reaches the decider on `MachineSnapshot.usageLimits`.
- **The decider (step 2).** `machinePolicy(m, policy)` (`src/decider/usage.ts`) puts the machine's own limits in
  place of the user's for that machine: its lane cap, its band, and its placement pressure. Other machines keep the
  user's limits. The machine's usage reason names them: `seat: 69% used, lane cap 0 of 4 (soft), its own usage
  limits 50% / 70%`.
- **Two machines on one account.** Give the secondary limits whose hard limit is at or below the primary's soft
  limit (e.g. 50% / 70% under the user's 70% / 95%): its lane cap reaches 0 before the primary loses a lane.
- **Lane tuning** reads the machine's own limits too.
- **`GET /api/usage`** answers `usageLimits` on that machine's lane effect. The Usage view's lane caps at the
  limits being edited keep such a machine's cap, and say `own limits`; its Lane effect bar marks its own limits.
- No stored state changes: the option is in the plugins config, absent on every config before it.

**Verification:** `test/decider/machine-usage-limits.test.ts` (the secondary's cap falls first and is 0 before the
primary loses a lane; a Decision starts on the primary only; without the option the user's limits apply);
`test/plugins/machine-targets.test.ts` and `test/plugins/host-sources.test.ts` (the option reaches the machine;
soft at or above hard refused); `test/ui/usage-limits-view.test.ts` (the cap does not follow the user's limits).

## The skill library (issue #1911, part 1, 2026-10-18)

**Problem.** A job of each kind of work — the work itself, research, a proposal — follows a skill. The skills lived in
the user's workflow repositories, and not every machine or box has those. The hopper must keep the skills itself, so a
job gets its skill on any machine, and a person must be able to choose the skill of each kind of work, or write one.

**As built (part 1).**
- **The skill library** (`src/skill-library/`, `src/domain/skill-library.ts`, pure). A **library skill** is a `SKILL.md`
  and the text files beside it. The **built-in library skills** — `work`, `research`, `proposal` — are the files of
  `src/skill-library/built-in/<name>/`, named by a content id over their files (`releaseOf`, as a run skill's): they ship
  with the hopper and are never edited or removed. The user's own are rows of `library_skill_versions` (tenant migration
  84), one per **library skill version**, never changed once kept. Limits: a name of lowercase letters, digits and dashes;
  at most 32 files, 4 path parts and 160 characters a path, 64 KiB a file (a credential file's limit on the machine),
  256 KiB in all; no `..`, no absolute path.
- **Routes** (`src/http/ui/skill-library.ts`, the OpenAPI tag `Skills`). `GET /api/skill-library`: every skill, the
  built-in ones first, with its newest version (no files), the **work skill settings**, the defaults and the kinds.
  `GET /api/skill-library/:name?version=`: one version with its files, and the skill's versions. `POST
  /ui/api/skill-library` with `action` `create` (refused when the name exists), `edit` (a new version; the same files keep
  none), `duplicate` (any skill's version, built-in or not, as a new skill) or `remove` (refused for a built-in one and while
  a setting names it). `POST /ui/api/work-skills`: `kinds` for every repository, `repos` per repository, `null` for the next
  setting down; each skill named must be in the library. Every change is an admin's, as the job rules are.
- **Permissions.** Each action is a scope of its own (`skill-library:edit.create`, `.edit`, `.duplicate`, `.remove`;
  `work-skills:edit`; `skill-library:read`), in the scope registry's new section **Skills**, so a grant's checkboxes list
  each one (issue #909). Access (OpenFGA) decides each API token's use as for every route.
- **Events.** `library_skill.saved` (name, version, seq, source, by — never the files), `library_skill.removed`,
  `work_skills.changed` (from, to, by), and `job.work_skill_chosen` on the job's timeline.
- **A job's work skill.** At a job's first start, `workSkillOf` reads its **kind of work** (`research`, `proposal`, else
  `code`, as its job cost kind) and the settings — its repository's, else the user's, else the built-in default — and
  records the choice as `job.work_skill_chosen` (kind, name, version, seq, `from`: `repo`, `user`, `default`). Each later
  start of the job reads that event and gets the same version, on whichever machine and hopper: an edit or a new setting
  reaches the next job, never a running one. A job whose kind of work changed chooses again. A version that is gone — a
  built-in one this build no longer has — gives the current choice, recorded again.
- **Delivery, for any agent CLI.** The work skill's files go into the job's **credentials dir** with the hopper's scripts
  (`jobProxy`, `src/users/github-proxy.ts`): `<scratch>/credentials/work-skill/<name>/<path>`, through the machine's own
  connection, mode 600, removed by the reap. `HOPPER_WORK_SKILL` names its `SKILL.md`. The job rules end with one line:
  `[hopper work skill] This job's skill for its kind of work (<kind>) is <name>, version <version>. When the variable
  HOPPER_WORK_SKILL is set, read the file it names before you start, …`. The line and the files reach every executor —
  herdr's pane and each print-mode agent — as the job rules and the credentials do. Nothing is written into the job's
  work tree, and nothing is read from a workflow repository.

**Decisions.**
- **The kinds are the job cost kinds** (`code`, `research`, `proposal`): one reading of a job's spec, not a second one.
- **The setting names a skill, not a version.** A job pins the version at its first start; pinning in the setting would
  make every edit a second step.
- **Per user and per repository, in the user's settings** (`workSkills`), as yolo mode's per-repository setting is; the more
  specific wins.
- **An admin's**, as the job rules and the repository job rules are: a skill is text every job of the user follows.
- **Text files only.** A binary asset is out of this part.

**Left for later parts.** The **Skills** page in the UI (a top-level view: list, source and version, create, edit,
duplicate, remove, and the choice per kind of work); import of a skill from a git repository (a workflow repository) and
its refresh, recorded; a skill that depends on another, delivered with it; the `orchestrate` skill, which issue #1909 bakes
into the hopper.

**Verification:** `test/domain/skill-library.test.ts` (the choice — repository, user, default —, a change of the settings,
a version's limits, the description, the delivery's paths); `test/integration/skill-library.test.ts` (on the real
database and HTTP edge: list, create, edit, duplicate, remove and their refusals and events; the settings and their
refusals; a job on a fresh machine with no workflow repository gets its skill's files, its variable and its line, by the
repository's setting, the user's and the default; an edit reaches the next job and leaves the earlier job's version; the
pinned version across starts after an edit and a new setting; each action's scope and role, and nothing changes with no
session).

## The Skills page (issue #1911, part 2, 2026-10-18)

Before: the skill library (part 1) was only in the API. A person could not see which skill each kind of work gets, or
write one, without a token.

- **A top-level view, `#skills`** (`ui/src/views/skills.tsx`), in the nav group Set up with Settings (issue #1943; it was a
  group of its own): the skill library's one home. It reads `GET /api/skill-library` once; each change answers the new view, which the page shows.
  Loading, an error that says why with **Try again**, or the panels.
- **Work skills.** One choice per kind of work (Code work, Research, Proposals) for every repository; its empty choice
  names the built-in default. Below it, **Per repository**: a row per repository with a choice of its own, a choice per kind
  whose empty choice says what the repository gets from the choice above, and **Add a repository** (`owner/name`). Each
  change is one `POST /ui/api/work-skills` with only that kind (`null` for the empty choice); the next job gets it.
- **Library** (`ui/src/views/skill-library.tsx`). Each skill: its name, where it came from (`built-in`, `written by …`, `a
  copy of <skill> <version>, by …`), its version's short id, how many versions it has, its description, and the settings
  that choose it. **Show files** reads `GET /api/skill-library/:name`. **Edit** (the user's own) opens the editor on its
  newest files; the name stays, and Save is an `edit`: a new version. **Duplicate** (any skill, a built-in one too) asks a
  new name and copies the version shown. **Remove** (the user's own) asks once; while a setting names the skill it is
  off, and the row says which settings name it. **New skill** opens the editor with a `SKILL.md` that names the skill.
- **The editor** holds a skill's files: a path and a text each, `SKILL.md` first, **Add a file**, remove one. It says what
  stops a save before Save (`draftProblem`, `ui/src/model/skills.ts`, pure: the name, an empty or a second path, a path
  that is no path in a skill, no `SKILL.md`), with the daemon's own checks copied; the daemon checks again.
- **The job shows its work skill.** `job.work_skill_chosen` on the job's timeline reads `<kind>: <skill> <version>
  (built-in | version <n>), by the repository's setting | your setting | the default` (`workSkillChosenLine`).
- `SkillLibraryView` moved to `src/domain/skill-library.ts`, so the UI takes its type from the domain, as with the other
  views.

**Decisions.**
- **A group of its own in the navigation**, not a section of Settings: the issue names the Skills page its own canonical
  home (issue #896), as the Infra page is. Since issue #1943 it is an entry of the nav group Set up, beside Settings, still its own view.
- **Each choice saves at once**, one kind per request, as yolo mode's per-repository switches do: there is no draft to lose
  and no version to conflict on, and the event names the one change.
- **Admins only**, as in part 1: the buttons and choices show only to a session that may change them; any person reads.

**Left for later parts.** Import of a skill from a git repository (a workflow repository) and its refresh, recorded; a
skill that depends on another, delivered with it; the `orchestrate` skill, which issue #1909 bakes into the hopper.

**Verification:** `test/ui/skills.test.ts` (pure: the source line, the choice per kind and which setting gives it, the
repository rows, the settings that name a skill, a draft's rows and problems, the timeline line);
`test/ui/skills-view.test.ts` (the whole app in happy-dom against a fake daemon: the nav entry; the list with source and
version; a choice for every repository and back to the default; a choice per repository and a new repository; create with
a second file; edit with the name fixed; duplicate of a built-in at the version shown; the files shown, and a skill a setting
names kept from removal with the reason).

## Importing a skill (issue #1911, part 3, 2026-10-18)

Before: a person wrote a library skill by hand or copied one. A skill that lives in a repository — a workflow repository's
`orchestrate`, for example — had to be copied file by file, and a change there did not reach the copy.

- **Import** (`POST /ui/api/skill-library`, `action: 'import'`; `importSkill`, `src/skill-library/import.ts`). A person
  names a GitHub repository (`repo`), the folder in it that holds the skill's `SKILL.md` (`path`; empty: the root), a `ref`
  to follow (a branch or tag; default `HEAD`, the default branch) and, optionally, a `name` (default: the folder's last
  part, else the repository's name, as a skill name, `importedName`). The hopper reads the folder with the user's own
  GitHub connection — the account of the repository (issue #1448) —, never a job's, and keeps its files as version 1 of a
  new skill of the user's. The version's source says where it came from: `{ kind: 'imported', repo, path, ref, commit }`,
  the commit read. Recorded as `library_skill.saved` with that source.
- **The read** (`createSkillSourceGitHub`, `src/skill-library/github.ts`): the ref's head commit
  (`GET …/commits/{ref}`), the trees down the folder's path one part at a time (a large repository's whole tree is never
  read), the folder's tree with `recursive=1`, then each file's blob. Before any file is read, `skillTreeFiles` (pure) refuses
  a folder with no `SKILL.md`, more than 32 files or a file over 64 KiB; then the version's own limits apply. A file that is
  no UTF-8 text is refused: a library skill holds text files only. A truncated tree is refused.
- **Refresh** (`action: 'refresh'`, `refreshSkill`). It reads the newest version's folder again at the ref it follows. When
  the files changed, it keeps a new version (`library_skill.saved`); either way it records `library_skill.refreshed` (repo,
  path, ref, the commit read, the version, `changed`, by). A skill a person edited since its import is not refreshed: its
  newest version is no import, and a refresh would drop the edit. Import the folder under another name instead.
- **Refusals.** 400: a folder path that leaves the repository or has strange parts, a folder that is no skill; 404: no such
  repository, ref or folder (GitHub's 404 or 422); 409: a name in use (a built-in one too), GitHub not connected, a
  built-in skill's refresh, a skill edited since its import; 502: GitHub failed.
- **Permissions.** `skill-library:edit.import` and `skill-library:edit.refresh`, an admin's, in the **Skills** section of
  the scope registry with the other actions.
- **The Skills page.** **Import** in the Library panel opens a form (repository, folder, ref, name). An imported skill's
  source reads `imported from <repo>/<path> at <ref> <commit>, by …`, and it has **Refresh**.

**Decisions.**
- **GitHub's API, not a clone.** The hopper reads only the folder, with the connection it already has, and keeps no clone
  on any machine: the skill moves with its jobs as every library skill does (issue #1524).
- **A ref, not a commit, is followed.** The import records the commit it read; a refresh reads the ref's head again. To pin
  a commit, name a tag.
- **A refresh is a person's act**, not a schedule: each new version is one a person asked for, and a running job never sees
  a change (it keeps the version of its first start).
- **An edited import is not refreshed.** The person's edit wins; refreshing over it would lose work silently.
- **Repositories beyond the job repositories.** A workflow repository is seldom a job repository; the account of the
  repository reads it when its install reaches it, else GitHub refuses and the hopper says so.

**Left for later parts.** A skill that depends on another, delivered with it; the `orchestrate` skill, which issue #1909
bakes into the hopper (it can then be a built-in library skill, or imported from a workflow repository with this part).

**Verification:** `test/domain/skill-import.test.ts` (the folder path, the tree's files and their refusals, the default
name); `test/integration/skill-import.test.ts` (on the real database and HTTP edge, against the fake GitHub: an import with
its source and event, read with the user's connection, under a name and a ref of its own; a job on a fresh machine gets the
imported files; a refresh with no change and one with a change, and their events; the refusals and no change with no
session); `test/integration/skill-library.test.ts` (the two new scopes); `test/ui/skills.test.ts` (the imported source
line); `test/ui/skills-view.test.ts` (Import and Refresh send their actions).

## Skills that require others, and the built-in orchestrate skill (issue #1911, part 4, 2026-10-18)

Before: a job got one library skill. A skill that leans on another one — a way of working that says "plan with the
orchestrate skill" — could not be sure the job had it, and the `orchestrate` skill was in no library.

- **`requires:`** (`skillRequires`, `src/domain/skill-library.ts`, pure). A `SKILL.md`'s front matter names the skills it
  requires: on its line, apart by commas, in brackets or not, or one `- name` a line below it. Each must be a skill name,
  at most 8 (`skillFilesProblem`, so create, edit, import and refresh refuse a bad one with 400). A name the library does not
  have is not refused when the skill is kept: a skill imported from a repository may require one that is imported later.
- **The choice** (`workSkillOf`, `src/skill-library/index.ts`). At a job's first start, after its work skill, the hopper
  takes each skill it requires, and theirs, breadth first, each once, at its newest version, at most
  `SKILL_MAX_REQUIRED` (8). `job.work_skill_chosen` now carries `requires` (each `name`, `version`, `seq`) and `missing`
  (a name the library has no skill of, or past the limit). Each later start gets the same versions; when one of them is
  gone, the job chooses again, as for the work skill itself. An older event with no `requires` keeps its choice.
- **Delivery.** Each required skill's files go into the job's credentials dir beside the work skill's, each in its own
  `work-skill/<name>/`. `HOPPER_WORK_SKILL` still names the work skill's `SKILL.md`. The `[hopper work skill]` line adds
  `It requires <name> (version <v>): read its SKILL.md in ../<name>/ …` for each one, and `The library has no skill <name>
  that it requires: go on without it.` for each missing one.
- **The built-in `orchestrate` skill** (`src/skill-library/built-in/orchestrate/SKILL.md`): plan a job of many steps as
  a task list with an acceptance test for each task, run independent tasks side by side, fan out a deliverable of its own
  as a required child issue, wait on it with `HOPPER_WAITING`, resume from the state that stays (branch, pull request,
  child issues), and finish by the job's done line. The built-in `work` skill requires it, so every code job gets it, on any
  machine, with no workflow repository. A person duplicates it to change it, or imports a workflow repository's own
  version under another name and names that in their skill's `requires:`.
- **The Skills page.** Each skill says which skills it requires, and marks one the library does not have
  (`requiresLine`, `ui/src/model/skills.ts`). The job's timeline line for `job.work_skill_chosen` adds `; with <name>
  <version>` and `; not in the library: <names>`.

**Decisions.**
- **Front matter, not a field of the version.** The skill's own text says what it requires, so an imported skill carries
  its requirements from its repository, and a copy carries them too. No migration: the versions kept are unchanged.
- **A missing required skill does not stop a job, and does not stop a save.** The job's line says it is missing, and the
  page says so before any job runs. Refusing the save would block an import whose required skill comes from a second import.
- **Removal is not refused** while another skill requires the removed one: only a setting holds a skill in place, as in
  part 1. The page then marks the requirement as not in the library.
- **The newest version of each required skill**, chosen at the job's first start and kept: the same rule as the work
  skill. A skill cannot pin the version of a skill it requires; a person who wants that duplicates the required skill under
  another name.
- **`orchestrate` is a library skill, not a second delivery path.** Issue #1909 (open) adds an `orchestrate` skill to the
  broker's catalog (`hopper-skill`). This part ships the library's own; #1909 can deliver the library's files and drop its
  copy, so one text exists (done in #1909 part 2: "Library skills through hopper-skill").

**Verification:** `test/domain/skill-library.test.ts` (`requires:` in its three forms, the refusals, the credentials of
several skills, the job's line); `test/integration/skill-library.test.ts` (the built-in list with `orchestrate`, and `work`
requiring it; a job on a fresh machine gets `orchestrate` beside `work`; a user's skill that requires a user's skill that
requires `orchestrate`, and one not in the library: the files, the event's `requires` and `missing`, the line; an edit of a
required skill reaches the next job and not a later start of this one); `test/ui/skills.test.ts` and
`test/ui/skills-view.test.ts` (the requires line, the timeline line).

## Conditional skills (issue #1924, parts 1 to 5, 2026-10-18)

**Problem.** A job that changed infrastructure code opened its pull request and ended done while most of its `terraform
plan` checks were red and one plan replaced a resource. The plan summary showed the delete, but nothing made the job read
it, and the done check trusted the job. A job must get the skills of what it works on, and the hopper must check the
skill's machine-checkable criteria itself before it takes the job as done.

**As built (part 1).**
- **Skill rules** (`src/domain/conditional-skills.ts`, pure). The work skill settings (issue #1911) keep `rules`: each a
  library skill and conditions — `repos`, `labels` (a label such as `iac` declares what the job is), `kinds` (its kind of
  work) —, one value of each condition named must match, and all conditions named together; at least one. `POST
  /ui/api/work-skills` takes `rules`, all of them in place of the ones before (`skillRuleProblem`; each skill named must be
  in the library), recorded in `work_skills.changed`. A skill a rule names cannot be removed. The rules are kept in the
  user's settings `workSkills`, an optional field: a store with none reads as before.
- **The choice** (`jobSkillsOf`, `src/skill-library/index.ts`). At a job's first start, when its work skill is chosen, each
  rule that matches its repository, its item's labels and its kind of work gives its skill's newest version, once each
  (the work skill itself never again), recorded as `job.conditional_skills_chosen`: name, version, `seq`, `why` (the
  conditions that matched) and `done` (its done criteria). Each later start reads that event and gets the same versions,
  on any machine; a rule changed later reaches the next job. A job that matched no rule records nothing.
- **Delivery.** The skills' files go into the job's credentials dir with the work skill's (`jobProxy`):
  `conditional-skill/<name>/<path>`, and an index, `conditional-skill/INDEX.md`, that lists each `SKILL.md`, why the job
  got it and what the hopper checks. `HOPPER_CONDITIONAL_SKILLS` names the index. The job rules end, after the work skill's
  line, with one `[hopper conditional skills]` line: each skill, its version and why, and the done criteria in plain words.
- **Done criteria.** A library skill may have a `done.json` beside its `SKILL.md`: `{ "criteria": [...] }`, checked when a
  version is kept (`doneFileProblem`). `checks-passed` (`checks`: a name, `*` any text): at least one check of the pull
  request's head commit — a check run or a commit status — matches, and each one that matches passed; a check still
  running is not passed. `plan-destroy` (`checks` optional, `max` 0 when absent): the `Plan: … N to destroy` lines (a
  replace counts there; `No changes.` is 0) in the output of those checks (title, summary and text) and in the pull
  request's comments written or edited since its head commit; none may be over `max`, and one must be there.
- **The done check** (`src/sources/github/done-criteria.ts`). When the GitHub done check finds the job done and the job
  got done criteria, the hopper reads the job's own open pull request that is ready for review (the newest): its head
  commit by its number, its checks with their output (`checkRuns`, `GET …/commits/{ref}/check-runs` and `…/status`), and
  its comments. A criterion not met keeps the job not done: `PR #N: done criteria of skill <name> not met: <each miss>`.
  An issue closed (merged, or closed as completed), or no open pull request of the job's own, is judged as before. A read
  that fails throws: not known is not done.
- **Rework.** The failure cause **Done criteria unmet** (before Not complete, whose text it shares) is `continue`: the job
  goes on in its own session and work tree (else a new job of its item), told what the done check found and to fix it on
  the same branch (`doneCriteriaBrief`). Each send-back counts against the retry limit (`criteriaFixes`); then the
  decision is a person's, and the job stays failed with the reason.
- **The built-in `iac` skill** (`src/skill-library/built-in/iac/`): wait for the plan checks after each push and read
  each root's plan; never apply; never add the MAP tag to a resource that exists; on a replace, find the attribute that
  forces it and keep its value or narrow `ignore_changes`. Its `done.json`: every check named `*plan*` passed, and no plan
  of them destroys or replaces a resource. A rule gives it to a job; no rule names it by default.
- **The job page.** `job.conditional_skills_chosen` on the job's timeline reads `conditional skills: <name> <version>
  (built-in | version <n>), by <why>; done when <criteria>` (`conditionalSkillsChosenLine`).

**Decisions.**
- **Rules are a setting, criteria are part of the skill.** Which jobs get a skill is the user's choice per repository and
  label, as the work skills are; what makes a job of that skill done is versioned with the skill's text, so a job is
  judged by the version it was given.
- **A declared kind is a label.** The issue names a declared job kind (`iac`, `gitops`); a label carries it, so no new
  field on a job or an issue is needed.
- **The criteria live in the event.** `job.conditional_skills_chosen` carries the criteria, so the done check reads the
  job's timeline only, and a removed skill still judges the jobs that got it.
- **Plan text from check output and comments.** A CI can put its plan summary in either. The rule reads both, and asks
  for at least one plan, so a summary that never comes is a miss, not a pass.

**As built (part 2).**
- **Paths.** A skill rule may name `paths`: globs of the files the change touches (`*.tf`: a glob with no slash matches a
  file name in any folder; `src/**`). They are not known at the start, so the rule gives its skill at the first start with
  why `paths <globs>`, and `job.conditional_skills_chosen` keeps the skill's `paths`. The done check reads the pull
  request's changed files (the hopper's mirror, `pullRequest`'s `files`) and checks that skill's done criteria only when
  one file matches (`pathsApply`). Files not known (no mirror) or not all named (`filesCut`): the criteria apply; not known
  is not a pass. Two rules give one skill: a rule with no paths makes it apply always; two with paths join their globs.
  The prompt line and the index say `when the change touches <globs>`.
- **Allowed deletes.** The issue may list the deletes it allows by resource address, after a line `Allowed deletes:`
  (a heading or bold too): the addresses on that line, in backticks or bare, and the `-`/`*` list right below it
  (`allowedDeletesIn`). The hopper reads them from the job's approved text, its item's snapshot (issue #662:
  `allowedDeletesOfJob`), never from the live issue, which an edit can change, and never from the job. For
  `plan-destroy`, each plan's resource lines before its `Plan:` line name the addresses it destroys or replaces
  (`# <address> will be destroyed`, `must be replaced`, `is tainted, so must be replaced`, a deposed object); a listed one
  does not count (`plansIn`). A summary with no resource lines names nothing, so each delete counts. The miss names the
  addresses the issue does not allow.

**Decisions (part 2).**
- **A paths rule delivers at the start, and judges at the end.** The job may touch the paths at any time, so it needs the
  skill's text before it starts; the hopper can only see the paths once the job pushed.
- **Not known applies the criteria.** With no mirror the changed files are not known: the done check applies the criteria
  rather than skip them, the same as a plan summary that never comes.
- **The allowed list is the approved text.** A list in the live issue or the pull request body could be written by anyone
  who can edit them, or by the job; the snapshot is the text a trusted person wrote or approved.

**As built (part 3).**
- **Yolo mode reads the done criteria** (`doneCriteriaHold`, `src/sources/github/done-criteria.ts`). Just before the
  hopper's own merge of a job's ready pull request (`waiting`, `src/sources/github/follow.ts`), it reads the job's done
  criteria again on that pull request now: its head commit's checks and their output, its comments since that commit, its
  changed files. A criterion not met, or not known (its checks cannot be read), holds the merge: the reason is kept as
  `mergeError` (`done criteria of skill <name> not met: …`), the Pull requests card says merge refused with it, and the next
  sync asks again. Met later, it merges. A person's Merge now is not held. The done check is the same as before.
- **`person-merges`**, a new done criterion (`paths` optional: relative globs). A pull request that changes a file its paths
  match (all, absent; files not known, or not all named, count) is merged by a person, never by yolo mode or a change kind's
  `ready` gate: `done criteria of skill <name>: a person merges a change to <paths>, not the hopper` (`mergeHolds`). It is no
  miss at the done check: the job is done once its pull request is ready.
- **The built-in `gitops-deploy` skill** (`src/skill-library/built-in/gitops-deploy/`): a production overlay change is a
  deploy on merge; the job never merges or applies, and starts the pull request body with a line `Deploys on merge:` that
  lists each production overlay it touches. Its `done.json`: `person-merges` for `**/overlays/production/**`,
  `**/overlays/prod/**` and `**/overlays/prd/**`. A rule gives it to a job; no rule names it by default.

**Decisions (part 3).**
- **The hold is a refused merge.** It is kept as `mergeError`, as GitHub's own refusal is, so the card, the tending queue
  and the next sync treat it the same: no new wait state, nothing new persisted.
- **Read again at each sync while held.** A plan comment can come after the checks end; a hold kept with no read could
  never lift. The cost is one checks read and one comments read per held pull request per sync.
- **The body flag is the skill's text, not a criterion.** The hopper does not read the pull request body at the done check,
  and the merge hold already keeps a person in front of the deploy; the line is for that person.
- **The name is `gitops-deploy`, not `gitops`.** A built-in skill wins over a user's own skill of the same name, and
  `gitops` is a likely name for one a user made already.

**As built (part 4).**
- **A part is checked too** (`partCriteriaMiss`, `src/sources/github/done-criteria.ts`). When the job's own open pull request
  that ships a part ("Part of #N", `partPullRequest`) is ready, the done check reads its done criteria as for one that closes
  the issue. One not met, or not known: the job is no part done; the miss is said in the same words (`PR #N: done criteria of
  skill …`), so the cause is **Done criteria unmet** and the job reworks. A merged part is not read again: yolo mode read the
  criteria before its own merge, or a person merged it.
- **GitLab merge requests** (`src/gitlab/done-criteria.ts`). The GitLab source takes the job's done criteria and allowed
  deletes as the GitHub source does. On the job's newest ready merge request that closes its issue: the checks are the jobs of
  its head pipeline (`GET …/pipelines/:id/jobs`; `success` passing, `failed` and `canceled` failing, `skipped` unknown, any
  other pending; no head pipeline, no check); a job's text is its log (`GET …/jobs/:id/trace`, its last 1,000,000
  characters), read only for a finished job a `plan-destroy` criterion names; the comments are its notes but GitLab's own
  lines, written or edited since its head commit (`GET …/repository/commits/:sha`); the changed files are its diffs' old and
  new paths (`GET …/merge_requests/:iid/diffs`; more than 2,000 diffs: not all named). A miss says `MR !N: done criteria of
  skill …`, which the cause **Done criteria unmet** reads as it reads `PR #N`. Yolo mode's merge (`followMergeRequest`) asks
  the same just before it merges: a criterion not met, or a `person-merges` that applies, is kept as `mergeError` and asked
  again at the next follow. An issue closed by a merged merge request, or a merge request merged since the job began, is
  judged as before.
- **A rule names a GitLab project in a subgroup.** A rule's `repos` take a path of two or more parts (`group/subgroup/name`),
  as a GitLab job's repository is its project's whole path.

**Decisions (part 4).**
- **A part meets the criteria before it ends partly done.** A part merges on its own, in yolo mode once its checks pass, and
  its plan applies like any other: a part that replaces a resource is the same hazard as a whole change that does.
- **Pipeline jobs are the checks, and their logs are the check output.** GitLab has no check run with a summary; the plan
  summary is in the job's log or in a note. Only the logs a plan criterion names are read, from their end, so a long log costs
  one bounded read.
- **The words are shared.** The GitLab miss and hold use the GitHub source's texts (`missText`, `holdText`), so the
  assessor, the brief and the Pull requests card read them the same way.

**As built (part 5).**
- **The Skills page edits the skill rules** (`ui/src/views/skill-rules.tsx`, its pure part in `ui/src/model/skills.ts`). A
  panel Skill rules, below Work skills, lists each rule in its order: its skill and its conditions as one line
  (`ruleLine`, now with `the change touches <globs>`). An admin adds a rule, edits one in its place, or removes one. The
  editor holds a library skill, the repositories, labels and paths as words split at commas and spaces, and a box per kind
  of work. It says what stops a save before Save (`ruleDraftProblem`, a copy of `skillRuleProblem`; the daemon checks again
  and has the last word). Each save sends every rule to `POST /ui/api/work-skills` (`rules`, in place of the ones before),
  as the daemon keeps them (`ruleOfDraft`: repositories lowercased, empty conditions dropped), and the page shows the view
  it answers. The next job gets the change; a running job keeps what it got.

**Decisions (part 5).**
- **Each save sends the whole list.** The route takes every rule in place of the ones before, so the page sends the list it
  shows with the one change. Nothing new on the daemon: no rule id, no route per rule.
- **Words in one field, split at commas and spaces.** A repository, a label and a glob hold no space, so one text field per
  condition is enough, and it reads as the rule line does.


**Verification:** `test/domain/conditional-skills.test.ts` (a rule's match and why, its problems, the settings' change,
done.json and its refusal, the plan's destroy counts, each miss, the prompt line, the delivery paths);
`test/sources/github-done-criteria.test.ts` (a plan that replaces a resource with every check green is not done, a plan
check still running or none, a plan in a comment since the head commit, no criteria and a closed issue as before);
`test/failures/done-criteria-unmet.test.ts` (the cause ahead of Not complete, the send-back under the retry limit and a
person at it, the chain's count, the Continue's brief); `test/integration/conditional-skills.test.ts` (on the real
database and HTTP edge: the rules and their refusals, a matching job's files, index, line and event, a job no rule
matches, the versions kept across a change of the rules); `test/ui/skills.test.ts` (the timeline line, a rule naming a
skill); part 2: `test/domain/conditional-skills.test.ts` (a paths rule's match, `pathsApply`, the destroyed
addresses, the allowed deletes, an allowed delete not counted), `test/sources/github-done-criteria.test.ts` (a paths skill
checked only when a changed file matches or the files are not known; an allowed delete), and
`test/integration/conditional-skills.test.ts` (a paths rule's skill and its paths kept; the allowed deletes from the
snapshot); part 3: `test/sources/github-yolo-done-criteria.test.ts` (a plan that replaces a resource holds yolo mode's
merge, met later it merges, a person-merges change held and one outside its paths merged, Merge now still merges, no
done-check miss), `test/domain/conditional-skills.test.ts` (`person-merges` in done.json, `mergeHolds`, the built-in
`gitops-deploy` skill), `test/ui/skills.test.ts` (its timeline line); part 4: `test/sources/github-done-criteria.test.ts` (a
part whose plan replaces a resource is not partly done, met it is, a merged part not read again), `test/gitlab/done-criteria.test.ts`
(over a fake GitLab: a plan job's log that replaces a resource with the pipeline green is not done and reworks, a plan job not
passed or none, a plan in a note since the head commit, a paths skill, a closed issue as before, yolo mode held and then
merged, a person-merges path held), `test/domain/conditional-skills.test.ts` (a rule naming a GitLab project in a subgroup).

## The crash harness (issue #1954, part 1, 2026-10-18)

**Why.** Every restart and saga test before stopped a hopper cleanly: its coordinator released its leases and each step
saw its abort. A crash does none of that. The harness proves the saga rules (#1524, #1662) for a process that ends with
SIGKILL, or whose database connection drops while a step's record commits.

**Kill points** (`src/sagas/kill-points.ts`). The coordinator passes one before each step's do or compensation starts
(its try already recorded) and one after it answered, before its record: `saga:<kind>:<step>:before-do`, `after-do`,
`before-compensate`, `after-compensate`. `killPoint(name)` ends the process with SIGKILL when the test run armed that name
(`HOPPER_TEST_KILL_POINT`, `<name>` or `<name>#<n>` for its nth pass) and only in a test run (`HOPPER_TEST_RUN`, which only
the test suite's setup sets, `test/support/run.ts`). A deploy sets neither, so each point is one environment read and goes
on. `killPointsOf(definition)` lists the points of a saga kind, in step order: what a test and the randomised run pick from.

**Hosts** (`test/crash/host.ts`, `test/crash/harness.ts`). Each hopper is a process of its own that runs the real
composition root (`startApp`, through `test/support/app.ts`'s seams) over the test's schema, with its own work dir and one
master key for all hosts of the test. The outside services are loopback fakes in the test process, so what they count
outlives the hopper that called them. A killed host holds its saga leases until they end; the test ends them at once
(`endLeases`), as their time would.

**A dropped connection** (`test/support/stalling-proxy.ts`). The hopper reaches Postgres through the proxy, which ends the
connection at the nth statement that holds a text: before Postgres reads it (the statement never ran), or once Postgres
answered it (it ran and committed, and the hopper never hears so). A saga's record is one statement, so it is all there
or not there.

**The randomised run** (`test/crash/random.test.ts`). Each seed picks a provider, whether the provider refuses the mint,
and a kill point (a compensation's when it refuses). `HOPPER_CRASH_SEEDS` seeds (default 2) from `HOPPER_CRASH_SEED`
(default from the clock); a failure names the seed and the kill point, so the same run is made again with that seed.

**Where it runs** (part 10, `.github/workflows/crash.yml`, `vitest.crash.config.ts`, `npm run test:crash`). Not in
`npm test`: each crash file runs for minutes, and with them the full suite's shards passed their 10-minute limit (issues
#2046, #2080). The crash workflow runs `test/crash/` in four shards nightly on the default branch, with ten seeds for each
randomised run; by hand, with the seeds and the first seed as inputs; and on a pull request that changes the sagas and
their kinds, the GitHub outbox and its writes, the item lifecycle, landing batches, the failure sweep, the database clock,
the stalling proxy or the crash tests. The secret canary workflow runs the `test/crash/secret-canary-*` files with this
config too.

**What part 1 covers: the remote access mint saga** (#1609). A kill at each kill point of each provider's mint, a kill
before and after its compensation, and a connection dropped before and after the record of a step commits: a second
hopper ends the saga, with one tunnel and one DNS record at Cloudflare (one credential and one domain at ngrok) and remote
access on, or, after a compensation, nothing at the provider and remote access off.

**What it found.** The mint's `record` step was not idempotent. A crash after it wrote the tunnel into the settings and
before the saga recorded the step left a try that threw ("the settings no longer ask for this tunnel"): the saga then
compensated, released the tunnel, and left remote access on with no tunnel. The step now finds the same tunnel kept and
goes on.

**Decisions.**
- **The host runs `startApp` through the test seams, not `node src/main.ts`.** The daemon's own entry has no seam for the
  outside services' URLs (the tunnel providers have none in the environment), and a test-only setting for each would be
  production surface. `startApp` is the composition root `main.ts` calls; only the seams differ.
- **Kill points sit in the coordinator only, for now.** The step boundaries of every saga kind come from one place. A
  GitHub call and its record inside a step, and an outbox send and its `sent` mark, are later parts.
- **The drop is at a statement, not mid-transaction.** A saga's record is one `UPDATE`, which Postgres commits alone, so
  "dropped mid-commit" is "dropped after Postgres answered it". A record of several statements needs a point inside its
  transaction: a later part.

**Part 2: two hosts racing one lease under a skewed clock** (2026-10-18). A host can take its clock from
`CRASH_CLOCK_SKEW_MS` (`test/crash/host.ts`: its `Date` that far ahead or behind, as a machine's clock that is off). The
first host holds the mint saga while a provider call hangs; the second host's clock is ahead by two leases, or the first's
is behind by two. **What it found:** each host timed a lease on its own clock. The second host read the first's live lease
as ended, took the saga and ran the step the first ran, then the whole mint. The sweep leases had the same fault. Now the
store times both leases on the database's clock (`src/store/db-clock.ts`: `clock_timestamp()` as text in the format of
`toISOString`, so the rows kept need no migration), and the repositories take a lease's length, not its end: `claim(id,
{ owner, ms })`, `hold(name, owner, ms)`, `renew(owner, ms)`, `live(name)`. Unit tests that moved a fake clock to end a
lease now end it in the database (`endLeases`).
**Decisions (part 2).**
- **The database's clock, not a bound on the skew.** The hosts on one database share one clock already; a bound on skew is
  a rule a machine's clock can break. A `nextAt` stays on the host's clock: it decides when a try is due, not who holds it.
- **Job leases and the wait-check leases are not in this part.** `job_leases` and `wait_check_leases` also compare a
  host's times; they are listed below.

**Part 3: the job leases and the wait-check leases under a skewed clock** (2026-10-18). **What it found:** the same fault
as part 2. A hopper whose clock was ahead read another hopper's live job lease as ended: it listed the job as unheld, took
its lease, and could take the job over; a person's act was no longer relayed to the hopper that drove it. A hopper whose
clock was behind wrote a lease end already past for the others. The wait-check leases did the same: a second hopper tested
a wait check the first was testing. Now both are timed on the database's clock (`src/store/db-clock.ts`), and the
repositories take a lease's length, not its end: `take(jobId, { owner, ms }, force)`, `renew(owner, ms)`, `unheld()`,
`heldByOthers(owner)`, `relay(jobId, act, owner)`; `claim(jobId, since, owner, ms)`, `holds(jobId, owner)`.
`createJobLeases` takes no clock. The rows kept have the same text format, so no migration is necessary.
**Decisions (part 3).**
- **The tests are in the process, not crash hosts.** A running job of a crash host is on a `job-run` saga, whose lease
  (part 2) decides who drives it; the takeover skips such a job. The job lease's own fault shows at the store, so its test
  is there (`test/store/job-leases.test.ts`), with each host's clock a faked `Date`. The wait-check test runs two wait
  sweepers with their own clocks on one database (`test/engine/wait-checks.test.ts`).

**Part 4: a job's push** (2026-10-19, "A push kept as a saga"). The git broker passes two kill points around its call to
GitHub: `proxy:git.push:before-send` (the `git-push` saga kept, nothing sent) and `proxy:git.push:after-send` (GitHub
answered, the broker recorded nothing). The test (`test/crash/push-kill.test.ts`, `test/crash/push-world.ts`) runs a job on
a first host whose real git pushes a new branch through it, to the fake GitHub's `git-http-backend` in the test process,
and kills the host at each of those points and at each boundary of the saga's `settle` step. A second host settles the
saga: it records the push once, `github_proxy.done` when GitHub holds the branch at the pushed commit, else
`github_proxy.failed`; the job's git then sends the push again to the second host, and GitHub holds the branch. The
randomised run on GitHub's writes (`test/crash/random-github.test.ts`) picks the push as a fourth family. **What it found:**
nothing; the saga and its read of GitHub's refs held at every point.
**Decisions (part 4).**
- **The broker's points take the proxy's names** (`proxyKillPoint('git.push', …)`): the push is one of the job's writes
  through the proxy, with the op its events already carry.
- **The test checks the event against GitHub, not against the point.** Where the saga's `before-do` kills the host, the
  push may or may not have reached GitHub yet; the test asserts the one event says what GitHub holds.

**Part 5: topology discovery** (2026-10-19, "The infrastructure topology"). The test (`test/crash/topology-kill.test.ts`,
`test/crash/topology-world.ts`) keeps a minting credential for an AWS account and one for its cluster on a first host, asks
for Discover now, and kills the host at each boundary of the `topology-discovery` saga's `aws` and `kubernetes` steps. STS
and the Kubernetes API are the loopback fakes of `test/support/fake-mint-apis.ts` in the test process; each host reads
with the crash reader (`test/crash/topology-reader.ts`, `CRASH_TOPOLOGY`). A second host ends the run: the person's run is
`done`, no run of discovery stays open, the graph holds the account and its cluster as one source each, read by
discovery, no Secret is left at the cluster, and neither host wrote a key. **What it found:** nothing; a step read again
reports the same sources again, which replace their snapshots.
**Decisions (part 5).**
- **The reader is in each host, not the test process.** It reads with what the vault minted and changes nothing outside;
  STS and the Kubernetes API, which the vault asks, are the fakes that outlive a host.
- **No exactly-once count of reads.** Discovery is read-only, with no compensation: a step done again reads again. The test
  asserts what it leaves (one source each, the run done), not how many reads it took.

**Part 6: a Windows step** (2026-10-19, "Windows sandbox steps"). The test (`test/crash/windows-kill.test.ts`,
`test/crash/windows-world.ts`) runs a job on a first host, adds a Windows host, and has the job ask for a step on
`/job/step`. It kills the host at each boundary of the `windows-step` saga's `run` and `sweep` steps, while the step runs on
the host (no kill point: a plain SIGKILL), and while it compensates a step the job stopped (`run`'s `before-compensate` and
`after-compensate`). Each host runs steps on the crash Windows host (`test/crash/windows-host.ts`, `CRASH_WINDOWS`), a
double at the `WindowsStepHost` seam that keeps each run and the host's scratch in files of the test's directory, so they
outlive a host. A second host ends the saga: the step ran on the host once, the host's scratch is swept, no step keeps a
host lease, the job's ask sent again is the same step, and the job reads one result: exit 0 after a kill at a step
boundary, `STEP_INTERRUPTED` after a kill while it ran, cancelled after a kill while it compensated. **What it found:**
nothing; the step's host lease and its kept result held at every point.
**Decisions (part 6).**
- **A double at the seam, not ssh with a fake binary.** The ssh host takes no binary from the environment, and a setting
  for one would be production surface. The ssh calls have their own test (`test/windows-steps/ssh-host.test.ts`).
- **The compensation of `sweep` is not in this part.** It runs only when the sweep fails past its tries; the job's stop
  reaches the compensation of `run` only.

**Part 7: a need step** (2026-10-19, "Need steps", "A need step kept as a saga"). The test (`test/crash/need-kill.test.ts`,
`test/crash/need-world.ts`) runs a job on a first host, keeps the minting credentials of an AWS account and a cluster, and
saves and approves a template that covers a read of each. The job asks for a need step on `/job/step`. The host is killed
at each boundary of the `need-step` saga's `run` and `release` steps, while the need box runs (a plain SIGKILL), and while
it compensates a step the job stopped (`run`'s `before-compensate` and `after-compensate`). Each host starts need boxes
through the real Podman adapter (`CRASH_PODMAN_SOCKET`, as `HOPPER_PODMAN_SOCKET`) on the libpod double
(`test/support/fake-libpod.ts`) in the test process, whose box runs on while its command says `hang`; STS and the
Kubernetes API are the loopback fakes. A second host ends the saga: the need box was made once at the most, no box or
home is left at the runtime, every Secret a minted token was bound to is deleted, the job's ask sent again is the same
step, and the job reads one result: exit 0 after a kill at a step boundary, `STEP_INTERRUPTED` after a kill while the box
ran, cancelled after a kill while it compensated. A last test starts the second host while the first host's box runs.
**What it found:** a hopper burned the need boxes of another live hopper on the same database. Its sandbox sweep, at its
start and every 10 s, burned each need box its own process did not run, and its reconcile pass of the sandboxes' tokens
deleted each Secret its own process did not hold. A second hopper that started, or that swept, while the first ran a step
stopped that step's box and ended its token. Now both leave a need box whose step's `need-step` saga another host holds on
the database's clock (`SagaRepository.heldByOthers`): the sandbox module takes those steps (`drivenElsewhere`) and names
their boxes (`elsewhere`), and the vault's reconcile pass takes the names. Once that lease ends (the host stopped), the next
sweep burns the box and the next pass unbinds its token.
**Decisions (part 7).**
- **The libpod double through the real adapter, not a seam.** The runtime is chosen from `HOPPER_PODMAN_SOCKET`, which a
  deploy sets too, so no test-only setting is added; and the boxes outlive a host because the double is in the test process.
- **The saga's lease says who runs a step, not the box's labels.** Two hoppers on one database share an instance id, so
  the box label cannot tell them apart. The `need-step` saga is leased to the host that runs the step, and renewed while it
  runs; a killed host renews nothing.
- **The release step and the reconcile pass.** A host that ends a step another host started holds none of its bindings,
  so its `release` step unbinds nothing; the reconcile pass does it once the other host's lease ended (at a start, else within 5 minutes). The
  test asserts what is left at the Kubernetes API, not which of the two deleted it.
- **The fake runtime API asks its handlers in order and stops at the first that answers** (`test/support/fake-runtime-api.ts`),
  as its comment said: a handler before the libpod double holds a box's wait (`after`) without the double ending the box.

**Part 8: landing batches** (2026-10-19, "Landing batches", "A stop between a GitHub call and its record"). The batch
runner's GitHub (`withKillPoints`, `src/landing-batches/once.ts`) passes a kill point once each write answered, before
the pass records its event: `landing:<write>:after-call`, for each of `createBranch`, `deleteBranch`, `openPullRequest`,
`merge`, `close`, `mergeInto`, `retarget`, `comment`, `revert`, `fileIssue` and `fastForward`. The test
(`test/crash/landing-kill-*.test.ts`, `test/crash/landing-world.ts`; a scenario's tests are split over files, so the
shards of the pull request check share them inside their 10 minutes) runs five scenarios of the in-process test of issue
#1589 on crash hosts: a red batch (batch run, bisect runs, culprit, revert, fix issue, the rest promoted), merge
conflicts (a back-merge, then the batch promoted), a real conflict (one issue), the canary held (one issue) and the
canary's window passed (`stable` moved). The landing batches' GitHub is a node:http fake in the test process
(`test/crash/landing-github.ts`, `CRASH_LANDING_URL`, the connected account's GitHub with no job source), so it holds
what a killed host made. A clean run of each scenario lists its writes, and the test kills the first host after each one
in turn (`landing:<write>:after-call#<n>`). A second host takes the passes on (a save of the same settings runs a pass)
to the end the clean run reaches: each pull request from one head once, one revert, one issue of each title, no pull
request left open and no branch `hopper-batch/…` left, and each step's event once. The randomised run on GitHub's writes
picks landing batches as a fifth family. **What it found:** a kill between a batch or bisect run's close and the removal
of its branch left the branch on GitHub for good: the next pass reads only the open pull requests. Now the branch is
removed first, then the pull request closed ("A stop between a GitHub call and its record").
**Decisions (part 8).**
- **A kill point after each write, in one place.** The runner's GitHub is wrapped once per pass, not each call site, so a
  write added later passes its point too. No point before a write: a kill there leaves only what a pass that never ran
  leaves.
- **A fake of the landing calls, not the source's fake GitHub.** The node:http fake GitHub of the job source has no refs,
  compare, merges or check runs. The landing fake answers only what `src/landing-batches/github.ts` asks, and the host
  runs no job source over it.
- **The branch first, not a sweep of old branches.** A sweep would need the branch of each ended run in the state, and a
  read of the repository's branches; the order needs neither.

**Part 9: the item lifecycle, and a drop inside a transaction** (2026-10-19, "The item lifecycle"). The item has no
`sagas` row (part 8 of #1891): its saga is its event stream, and the item reconciler is the owner that moves it with no act
of its own. The reconciler passes kill points (`itemKillPoint`, `src/work-items/reconcile.ts`): `item:block:inside-tx`
inside a block's transaction, with its `work_item.reconciled` event written and its label rows not; `item:<kind>:after-record`
once a correction's event is kept (`block`, `ask`, `replay`); and `item:run_again:before-call` and `after-call` around a
run again. The source's give-back passes `give-back:rerun-by-<by>:after-give` between the item given back and the new job
(`src/sources/rerun.ts`), as a person's Run again passes `give-back:rerun:after-give`. The test
(`test/crash/item-kill.test.ts`, `test/crash/item-world.ts`) seeds three items on the node:http fake GitHub: #1 in PR open
two hours with no pull request a job follows (blocked as stale), #3 blocked because its pull request was closed without a
merge the first time (run again once), #5 blocked as stale an hour ago with no one asked (asked once). A crash host's
reconciler checks every 300 ms (`CRASH_RECONCILE_MS`, the seam `itemReconcileEveryMs`), and the test makes each item's next
check due as its time would. A second host ends what is left: #1 blocked once, `hopper:pr-ready` off and `hopper:blocked` on
GitHub, each by one call; #5 asked about once; #3 one new job of its item and `hopper:pr-closed` off. A drop inside a
transaction of more than one statement (`test/crash/item-drop.test.ts`): the proxy ends the connection at the block's first
outbox row, before Postgres reads it or once it ran with the transaction open. Postgres rolls the transaction back: no
event, no move, no row; a second host blocks the item once. The randomised run on GitHub's writes picks the item reconciler
as a sixth family. The label mirror's own kill points are issue #1892 part 11 ("The label mirror under the crash
harness").
**What it found.**
- **A block wrote no label rows for a real job.** The reconciler kept a block's label rows only for a job of source kind
  `github`; a connected account's job is of kind `github-account`. So its issue kept `hopper:pr-ready` until the label
  mirror's next discover (an hour in a deploy's poll). Now every GitHub kind (`github`, `github-account`, `github-app`).
- **The label mirror put an end label back on an issue its discover ran again.** After a kill between the give-back and
  the new job, the next hopper's discover took the issue (no end label, assigned) as a new job, and its label mirror, in
  the same pass, judged the item still blocked and put `hopper:pr-closed` back. A person who takes the end label off on
  GitHub to run the item again got the same. Now the source passes the mirror no issue its discover takes as a new job.
**Decisions (part 9).**
- **After the give-back's kill, the new job is the source's sync's or the reconciler's.** Whichever of the next hopper's
  two comes first makes it; the other finds the item's newest job is no longer the ended one. When the discover takes the
  issue as a Run again from GitHub, no `job.rerun` by the reconciler is recorded and the new job gets no brief that names
  the closed pull request. The test asserts the one job; the brief is not carried over.
- **A block's own notice is not killed after its block.** The notice waits `RECONCILE_GRACE_MS` (two minutes) after the
  block, longer than a scenario, so #5 is blocked already when the test starts.
- **A kill before a run again's call delays it by one check** (5 minutes): the reconciler wrote the item's next check
  before the call. The test makes the check due, as its time would; the run again is not lost.
- **No drop at the block's COMMIT.** Every transaction ends with the same text, so the proxy cannot tell the block's; the
  kill point after the record is the commit's boundary.

**Left for later parts.** Kill
points between a GitHub call and its record (between an outbox send and its `sent` mark: issue #1959, below; a job's push: part 4); the nightly run of N seeds and
the run on pull requests that touch `src/sagas`, `src/sources/github/outbox*`, `src/work-items` or `src/landing-batches`
(a workflow file: a change to CI, which a job does not make from an issue's text).

**Verification:** `test/sagas/kill-points.test.ts` (a point ends the process with SIGKILL and says which, its nth pass, off
outside a test run and with none named, the points of a saga kind); `test/crash/mint-steps.test.ts` (each step boundary of
each provider); `test/crash/mint-compensation.test.ts` (each compensation boundary); `test/crash/db-drop.test.ts` (the
record of two steps, dropped before and after it commits); `test/crash/random.test.ts` (seeded picks); `test/crash/push-kill.test.ts` (part 4: a job's push at each kill point); `test/crash/topology-kill.test.ts` (part 5: topology discovery at each step boundary); `test/crash/windows-kill.test.ts` (part 6: a Windows step at each step boundary, while it runs and while it compensates); `test/crash/need-kill.test.ts` (part 7: a need step at each step boundary, while its box runs, while it compensates, and a second host while the box runs); `test/crash/landing-kill-*.test.ts` (part 8: landing batches killed after each GitHub write of five scenarios, and each scenario's clean run); `test/crash/item-kill.test.ts` (part 9: the item reconciler killed inside a block's transaction, after each correction and around a run again); `test/crash/item-drop.test.ts` (part 9: the block's connection dropped inside its transaction); `test/work-items/reconcile-labels.test.ts` and `test/sources/github-label-mirror.test.ts` (part 9: a connected account's job's block keeps its rows; an issue a discover takes as a new job is not judged); `test/store/sagas-held.test.ts` and `test/vault/mint-bindings.test.ts` (part 7: the sagas another host holds; the reconcile pass leaves their bindings); `test/crash/skewed-lease.test.ts` (part 2: the second host's clock ahead, the
first's behind); `test/integration/two-hosts.test.ts` (a sweep lease under a skewed clock); `test/store/job-leases.test.ts`
and `test/engine/wait-checks.test.ts` (part 3: a job lease and a wait-check lease, the second hopper's clock ahead, the
first's behind).

## The GitHub outbox under crashes and faults (issue #1959, part 1, 2026-10-18)

**Why.** Issue #1590 posted a comment once after a stop between its post and its row, in a unit test. Nothing proved the
outbox ("GitHub outbox") end to end: a process killed between a send and `sent` for each write kind, two hoppers on one
database, and GitHub's faults while the outbox drains.

**What it found.** Each hopper sent the same rows. A hopper at its start set every row left `sending` back to `pending`,
also a row another live hopper was sending, and sent it again: a comment held at GitHub was posted twice. Nothing else
kept two hoppers apart either: each read the rows due and marked them `sending` in two statements.

**The claim** (`claim`, `src/store/github-outbox.ts`; `OUTBOX_CLAIM_MS`, `src/domain/github-outbox.ts`). One `UPDATE`
takes the source's rows due — `pending` ones and `sending` ones whose claim ended — and makes them `sending` with the
claim's end as `next_at`. Postgres checks a row another send claimed meanwhile again and skips it, so of two hoppers one
gets each row. The send renews the claim of its rows before each call. The claim is 2 minutes: longer than a call's longest
wait at the rate limiter (60 s). A row a killed or stopped hopper left is sent again once its claim ends, by any hopper.
The start no longer resets rows (`recover` is gone). A clean stop releases what its send claimed and did not send
(`releaseOutbox`, at the sync loop's stop): the send makes no more calls, and those rows are due again at once, so a
restart sends them without waiting for the claim.

**Kill points** (`outboxKillPoint`, `src/sources/github/outbox.ts`): `outbox:<op>:before-send` before each coalesced call,
and `outbox:<op>:after-send` once GitHub answered it, before its rows are `sent` and their events recorded.

**The crash tests** (`test/crash/outbox-kill.test.ts`, `test/crash/outbox-world.ts`). A host runs the connected account's
job source over the node:http fake GitHub in the test process (`CRASH_GITHUB_URL`). A person declines a request card with
Close (`remove_labels`, `comment`, `close_not_planned`) and assigns another issue (`add_assignees`); a label mirror row
adds an end label (`add_labels`). The first host is killed at each kill point of each kind; once the claims end, a second
host sends what is left. GitHub then holds each effect once: the label off, one comment (posted once, found by its key
when GitHub took it before the kill), the close, the assignee, the label; each act's event is recorded once. Two live
hosts: a comment held at GitHub while the second host starts is posted once.

**The fault tests** (`test/integration/github-outbox-faults.test.ts`; the fake's `fail` with headers, `dropAfter` and
`hold`). A 5xx is tried again after its backoff, the item showing the next attempt and why. A 403 secondary rate limit
with `Retry-After` holds every call of the account until then (the fake hears nothing), and the rows drain with each write
once. A write GitHub applied whose answer never came (the connection cut) is sent again: the close and the assignment are
idempotent, the comment is found by its key. A row GitHub refused for good fails its item's later rows with it — nothing
after it is sent —, is listed with Retry, and the other item goes on; Retry sends the item's calls in order. While GitHub
holds the outbox's calls, a person's action answers at once (issue #1194).

**Decisions.**
- **A claim with an end, not an owner.** A host's identity is not in the user's schema, and a killed host never releases
  anything. The end time alone frees what a dead host held, as the saga lease does. The price: a restart after a crash
  sends what was in flight up to 2 minutes later. A clean stop releases its rows at once, the row of a call GitHub has not
  answered too, as before: if GitHub applies that call only after the next start read the issue's comments, its comment
  is posted twice. The window is the time a request a stopped process sent takes to reach GitHub.
- **The outbox's own write kinds only.** An issue edit, a pull request's edit, close or draft, an issue a job files and a
  sub-issue link are not outbox rows: a job asks for them through the GitHub proxy, or the source's report makes them.
  They are the next part.
- **The fake GitHub's faults sit in the fake** (`src/sources/github/http/fake-server.ts`), not in a proxy: the routes are
  matched there already, and a drop after the write needs the fake's own state.

**Left for later parts.** The GitHub proxy's writes under a kill (an issue a job files found by its key before it is
made again, a sub-issue link, an issue edit, a pull request's edit, close and draft); a person's Merge now, Close PR and
give-back rows under a kill (the sync loop's acts); a randomised run over the outbox's kill points.

**Verification:** `test/store/github-outbox.test.ts` (a claim takes each row once, a claim that ended is taken again, a
failed row never); `test/sources/github-outbox-comment-once.test.ts` (a comment left `sending` is sent once its claim
ends; two outboxes on one store); `test/crash/outbox-kill.test.ts`; `test/integration/github-outbox-faults.test.ts`.

## The GitHub proxy under crashes (issue #1959, part 2, 2026-10-18)

**Why.** Part 1 proved the GitHub outbox under kills and faults. A job's own writes go another way: through the GitHub proxy
("GitHub through the hopper"). The resend key (issue #1607) answers a request sent again from its `github_proxy.done`. A
hopper killed after GitHub made the issue or the comment, and before it recorded that event, left nothing to answer from:
the same request sent again to the next hopper made the issue or the comment a second time. The new crash test shows it on
the code before this change: an issue, a required child and a comment made twice.

**The change** (`src/github-proxy/resend.ts`, the broker). A write with a resend key (`issue.create`, `issue.comment`):
- is recorded `github_proxy.sending` (`op`, `repo`, `number`, `key`) before its call;
- ends with a **post key** (`src/domain/post-key.ts`, "Posted once"): `proxy-` and 24 hex characters of a hash of the resend
  key and its scope, the job's issue (a fan-out key is the issue's, issue #1909), else the job;
- sent again with a key that was sending before and has no answer recorded, is looked for on GitHub first
  (`ProxyApi.find`), from an hour before that first send: the issues the job's account made (`creator`, `state=all`), or
  the comments on the issue. Found, it is answered (`found: true` on the answer and on `github_proxy.done`), and a required
  child is linked as a sub-issue unless it is one already. Not found, it is made.

An edit, a close or a ready of a pull request has no key: it is the same change when made twice. A sub-issue link is
checked before it is made.

**Kill points** (`proxyKillPoint`): `proxy:<op>:before-send` before each write's call, `proxy:<op>:after-send` once GitHub
answered it, before `github_proxy.done` is recorded, and `proxy:issue.create:before-link` between a required child and its
sub-issue link.

**The crash tests** (`test/crash/proxy-kill.test.ts`, `test/crash/proxy-world.ts`). A host runs a job of issue #7 that
sleeps on the local machine (`CRASH_JOB`); the test asks the proxy as the job does, with its proxy token. For each write — a
follow-up issue, a required child, a comment, a pull request's edit, close and ready — and each kill point, the first host
is killed. The same request, with the same resend key, goes to a second host on the same database. GitHub then holds each
effect once: one issue, linked once, labelled and assigned as a routed child; one comment; the edit, the close, the ready;
and `github_proxy.done` is recorded once. The fake GitHub is `test/support/fake-forges.ts`, in the test process.

**The fault test** (`test/integration/proxy-resend.test.ts`). GitHub makes the issue or the comment and then answers 502;
the job sends the same `--key` again: it is found, made once.

**Decisions.**
- **An event, not a table.** The intent is one event on the job's timeline, as the answer is. The look-up reads the
  newest 1000 `github_proxy.sending` events, as the replay reads `github_proxy.done`.
- **A look-up only after a send with no answer.** A first send costs GitHub nothing more. Only a key seen sending before
  pays a list read.
- **The post key hashes the resend key.** A job may choose its key (`--key`); the hash keeps it, and the job's issue, off
  GitHub.

**Residual risk, stated.** As in "Posted once": a call GitHub finishes only after the look-up found nothing makes a second
one. A routed child whose assignee GitHub dropped, and whose second assign a kill stopped, is found unassigned.

**Left for later parts.** A person's Merge now, Close PR and give-back rows under a kill (the sync loop's acts); a pull
request a job opens (`pr.create`, no resend key: GitHub refuses a second one from the same head); a randomised run over
the outbox's and the proxy's kill points.

**Verification:** `test/crash/proxy-kill.test.ts` (13 scenarios; with the look-up turned off, the four after-send and
before-link cases of an issue and a comment fail); `test/integration/proxy-resend.test.ts`.

## A person's acts on a job under crashes (issue #1959, part 3, 2026-10-18)

**Why.** Parts 1 and 2 proved the GitHub outbox's intake acts and a job's writes through the GitHub proxy under kills. A
person's Merge now, Close PR and Run again are outbox rows too (issue #1238 parts 3 and 4), but the sync loop's own act
sends them (`OutboxActs`, `src/sources/pull-request-acts.ts`, `src/sources/rerun.ts`), and each makes more than one call.
Nothing proved them under a kill.

**What it found.**
- **Close PR killed after its close.** GitHub closed the pull request and the close was recorded, but the row was not
  `sent`. The next hopper sent the row again, found the job no longer following an open pull request, and failed the row
  (`job.pull_request_act_failed`, a Retry on Sources). Merge now had a guard for this since issue #1588; Close PR had none.
  Now a close row whose close is recorded is done, as a merge row whose merge is recorded is.
- **Merge now killed between the issue's close and its comment.** After the hopper's own merge of a pull request with no
  closing keyword, it closes the issue and then posts one comment (issue #677). A kill between the two left the issue closed
  as completed, so the merge found by its marker after the restart read the issue as closed by the merge and posted no
  comment. Now a merge found by its marker runs the close after it again (`closeAfterMerge`, `again`): the close is made
  again — it changes nothing on a closed issue —, and the comment only when the issue does not have it yet (read by its
  text, which names the pull request). A pull request whose closing keyword closed the issue is left as it is.

**Kill points.** The rows' own `outbox:pull_request|give_back:before-send|after-send`, and three inside the acts:
`follow:merge:after-call` (GitHub merged, nothing recorded; `src/sources/github/follow.ts`), `follow:merge:after-issue-close`
(the issue closed, its comment not posted; `src/sources/github/own-merge.ts`), and `give-back:rerun:after-give` (the source
gave the item back, no new job yet; `src/sources/rerun.ts`).

**The crash tests** (`test/crash/act-kill.test.ts`, `test/crash/act-world.ts`). A host runs the connected account's job source
over the node:http fake GitHub. Three jobs are kept in the admin's store, each finished or failed with its end reported:
one follows an open pull request that only mentions its issue (Merge now), one another open pull request (Close PR), one
failed with `hopper:failed` on its issue (Run again). For each act and each kill point the first host is killed; once the
claims end, a second host sends what is left. GitHub then holds each effect once: the pull request merged, the issue closed
