  over a WebSocket, so the upgrade answers NotFound and the probe is allowed, as it must be.
- **A box with no curl errs.** The upgrade then ends 127 with no Forbidden: the probe's outcome is `error`, never a refusal.
  The hopper's box images carry curl.

Tests (issue #2477): `test/sandbox/check-observe.test.ts` (a view role that may get `pods/exec` but not create it passes;
the get is an upgrade with the kubeconfig's server, the token not in argv), `test/support/fake-cloud-tools.ts` (`view-exec`,
a fake curl).
  Opening it is the cluster's RBAC change, a person's, not the hopper's.

Tests: `test/sandbox/check-observe.test.ts` (a credential the cluster does not take errs on both probes and the check
fails; one request Forbidden and the other errored is an error, not a refusal).

**A person's stop.** A bastion is kept in memory and ends by itself, but a person must be able to end one now: a job that
went wrong, a forward nobody needs any more.
- **The list.** `GET /api/vault` carries `bastions` (`Bastions.list`): each bastion of the user's jobs that starts or runs
  now, oldest first, as the job reads it (`BastionView`, `src/domain/bastions.ts`): its template, box, targets, state,
  start, TTL end and the tail of its output. Never a token. The UI reads the view again on `bastion.started` and
  `bastion.ended` (`rereadsVault`).
- **The stop.** `POST /ui/api/bastions/stop` (`job`, `src/http/ui/bastions.ts`) stops the job's bastion as the job's own
  `bastion stop` does: each relay connection closes, its tokens are released, its box is burned, and `bastion.ended` names
  the person (`by`). 404 when the job has none that runs. Answers the vault's view.
- **The panel.** Access requests → **Bastions** (`ui/src/views/bastions.tsx`): a card for each, with its job's link, its
  targets, when its TTL ends, and **Stop**.

**Decisions (the stop):**
- **A stop is a cancel, not a box action.** It starts nothing and changes no work on a machine, so an API token of the
  role may do it with no box token, as a job's cancel. Least role: operator, as a job's cancel.
- **In the vault's view, not a route of its own.** The bastions are what jobs on boxes hold now, beside the action grants
  live now, and Access requests already reads that one view. A bastion of a job of another user is not in it.
- **No confirm.** A stopped bastion leaves nothing, and the job asks again for a new one.

Tests (the stop): `test/sandbox/bastions.test.ts` (the list: the bastions that run, apart from what the caller changes,
and a stopped one leaves it), `test/integration/bastion.test.ts` (the real daemon: the vault's view lists the job's
bastion, never its token; a person's stop ends it, its box goes, `bastion.ended` names the person, a second stop is a
404), `test/ui/bastions-view.test.ts` (the panel, its Stop), `test/ui/needs-you.test.ts` (`rereadsVault`).

**The bastion read (part 6).** Grafana's API needs a token, and a relay command runs where the job runs, which gets no
vault secret. So the token goes into the bastion's box, and the hopper runs the read there for the job.
- **The bastion's secrets** (`sh "$HOPPER_SKILL" bastion … --secrets "<vault secret> ..."`, `Bastions.start`). Each must be
  one the template gives now (`gives`: in its scope and approved), else a 403 that names the template request to make. Each
  is read for the bastion's box through the vault's `forStep`, as a box step's secret (issue #1875): after the job's vault
  grant (none: a grant ask and a 403 that says so), `vault.step_delivered` with the box as its host. It goes into the box as
  a vault secret file, `$HOME/.hopper-need/secrets/read-<name>`, mode 600, holding the line `Authorization: Bearer <value>`;
  never in its environment, never to the job. The bastion's view and `bastion.started` name the secrets, never a value.
  Other secrets than the bastion that runs are a 409, as other targets are.
- **The read** (`sh "$HOPPER_SKILL" bastion read --targets T --path P [--secrets S] [--data JSON]`, `parseRead`,
  `Bastions.read`, `src/sandbox/bastion-read.ts`). A GET of the path, or, with `--data` (JSON, at most 64 KiB), a POST to
  Grafana's data source query (`/api/ds/query`) only. It is a relay connection (`Bastions.relay` with its own command):
  Access decides it (`bastion#can_relay`), it renews the TTL, and it is a `bastion.relayed`. The command (`readCommand`)
  is curl in the box to 127.0.0.1 at the target's port, with no proxy and a 30 s limit, its header read from the secret's
  file (`-H @file`, never on a command line), a POST's body on its stdin. Its output is the body and the HTTP status. The
  hopper answers the body when the status is 2xx; another status is a 502 with the target's words; an answer over 2 MiB is a
  413. Each read is a `bastion.read`: the target, method, path, status and size, or the problem, and how long it took;
  never the secret or the answer.
- **The skill** (`OBSERVABILITY_TEXT`): the secret named in the template request and at the bastion's start, then a search,
  a dashboard by uid, and a panel's query through `/api/ds/query`. The catalog line names Grafana.

**Decisions (part 6):**
- **The hopper runs the read in the box, not an HTTP proxy that adds the header.** The relay stays a byte pipe; a read is
  one command per request, as a relay connection is. curl is in the box image; the hopper adds no binary.
- **A GET, or a POST to `/api/ds/query` only.** Grafana's API changes things with POST, PUT and DELETE; its data source
  query is the one read that is a POST. Read-only past that is the token's own role (Viewer): the hopper does not parse
  Grafana's answers.
- **The vault's `forStep`, as a box step's secret.** The same grant, the same events, the same refusal of a minting
  credential, a system secret or a shared secret. The token is read once, at the bastion's start, and is not renewed.
- **A header file, not the bare value.** curl reads a header line from a file, so the token is never in an argument or in
  the box's environment. The relay's other commands do not read it.
- **The answer, not a file.** The job keeps it as its evidence (`> out/dashboards.json`), as it does a relay query's.

**Residual risk (part 6).** A job may read any GET path of a target its bastion forwards to, with the token: what the
Viewer role lets it read, it reads. A Viewer token can read the data sources' data through `/api/ds/query`.

Tests (part 6): `test/sandbox/bastion-read.test.ts` (the ask as the hopper reads it; the command under `sh` with this
machine's curl and a server on 127.0.0.1: the header from the file, a POST's body, the target's status, no curl),
`test/sandbox/bastion-reads.test.ts` (the secrets read for the box after the grant, as header files, never in its
environment; a secret the template does not give or the vault refuses; the read's command, its stdin, its noes, Access,
the event), `test/skills/bastion-skill.test.ts` (`--secrets` and `bastion read`), `test/skills/observability.test.ts`
(the Grafana asks parse as the hopper reads them).

## A comment ends the job's own wait (issue #2159, 2026-10-19)

**The problem.** A job on its own wait (waiting on a pull request to merge) did not see new comments on its issue. The owner
commented three times over three hours with a new blocker; nothing reached the job. It waited until a person ran End the wait.
Nothing watched the issue of a job on its own wait: the GitHub watch (issue #427) followed pointed jobs and jobs on a
question posted on the thread only, and no wait check reads comments.

- **Watched while it waits** (`src/github-watch/service.ts`, `waitWatchesOf` in `src/domain/comment-wake.ts`). A job on its
  own wait gets a GitHub watch on its issue, under the job's id (as a thread ask's), and one on its own pull request (the one
  its source follows), under `<job id>:pr`. `job.waiting` starts them, and its first poll is at once; a poll of a job no longer
  on its wait drops them. The poll is the watch's own (`GET …/issues/{n}` and its timeline, ETag 304s), on the user's interval
  (default a minute).
- **Which comment wakes it** (`wakingComment`). On `github_watch.changed` with comments added, for a job on its own wait,
  the sync loop reads the item's comments through the job source's thread (`src/sources/comment-wakes.ts`, on the job's report
  chain). The first comment the watch saw added, made at or after the wait began, by a trusted account — the user's connected
  account (the job's `source.assignee`) or a maintainer of the repository (`author_association` owner, member or collaborator),
  the rule of a thread ask's reply (`isTrustedReply`) —, not marked by the hopper, not empty, and not one a job posted through
  the GitHub proxy (`github_proxy.done` of `issue.comment`, by its link), ends the wait. A comment by anyone else wakes nothing.
- **Ended** (`SourceHost.wakeOnComment`, `recordCommentWake` in `src/engine/wait.ts`). In one tx, only while the job is on
  the same wait (`wait.since`): `job.wait_ended { by: hopper, note, comment: <its link> }`, queued again and pinned to its
  machine, as any wait the hopper ends. The job is told the comment's link and its text between `<<<hopper-untrusted-comment`
  and `hopper-untrusted-comment>>>` (cut at 4000 characters), as data, not instructions, and to wait again if its wait still
  holds.
- **UI.** The job view says "woken by a comment", with the comment's link, until the job waits again; the timeline line of
  `job.wait_ended` names the link.

**Decisions:**
- **Trusted is the thread ask's rule**, not intake trust (Access, `intake#can_start_jobs`). A comment that wakes a job
  starts no job and changes no text the job runs: it is a hint the job weighs as untrusted text. The same rule already lets a
  reply answer a job's question.
- **The GitHub watch, not the wait check.** The watch already polls an item on the user's interval with conditional
  requests, and records comment ids, authors and times, never their text. The text is read only when the watch saw a new
  comment.
- **Issue comments only.** A pull request's reviews and review comments wake nothing here: a wait on its review is tested
  as its reviews (issue #1694 part 3).

**Not built.** A comment made between the wait's start and the first poll of its watch, when the watch had no snapshot
before, is in that first snapshot and wakes nothing. A comment on a pull request the issue links but the job does not own.

**Persisted state.** No schema change: the watches are rows of `github_watches` (tenant migration 44), and `comment` is an
optional field of `job.wait_ended`. A build before this one ignores both.

**Verification:** `test/domain/comment-wake.test.ts`, `test/integration/comment-wake.test.ts` (the real daemon over the
fake herdr: a job on its own wait on a pull request; a stranger's comment on its issue wakes nothing; the owner's comment
wakes it within one poll, told the comment as untrusted text).

## One approval per sandbox run (issue #2197, part 1, 2026-10-19)

Seen on a hopper: an urgent job asked for a write step during a production outage. Its template waited for a person
on Access requests, Template approvals, apart from Sandbox runs, and the person looked for a run to approve for about 15
minutes. For one-off work, approving the template and approving its run are one decision.

- **The run card** (`runCards`, `src/domain/run-cards.ts`, pure; `GET /api/vault` `runs`). One card per job and template
  that waits for a person: the job's waiting **sandbox request**; an ask of the job that waits on a template for a
  person — `sandbox`, `sandbox-template`, a **need step**, and a named `--template` whose template waits
  (`SandboxRequests.waited`, kept in memory with the job's `--why` and `--plan` while the job lives); and a waiting
  template a live job asked for (`askedBy`). It names the job, why it asks, its plan (with each change's undo, as
  issue #1001 asks of a write), when it asked, and what waits: the template, the run, or both. A run a person declined is
  no card. A waiting template no live job waits on is no card: nothing runs when it is approved.
- **One approval** (`POST /ui/api/sandbox-requests` `approve-run`, `job` and `template`; `hopper sandbox approve-run`).
  The daemon approves the template as it is when any of it waits (`approveTemplate`: its image, tools, egress hosts, vault
  secrets and read profiles), each write, sync or apply profile it lists (`approveProfile`, remembered as a person's
  approval is, "Fewer sandbox approvals, part 2"), and the job's waiting run. The job's wait ends on these events as
  before, and its step goes on with no other approval. An API token's `approve-run` of a card that lists a write, sync or
  apply profile is asked of a person (202), as its `approve-profile` is (issue #909). A delegate approver (issue #1138)
  may decide a card as it may a template or a run.
- **One decline** (`decline-run`, `job`, `template`, `reason`). It declines the job's waiting run, or, when the job did not
  ask for its run yet, a run made declined now (`vault.sandbox_declined`), so the job's ask that waits on the template is
  told no (`sandboxWaits` answers the declined run, and the broker answers 403). A person's deny at gate 2, as `decline`.
- **No template card for a job's template** (`ui/src/views/sandbox-approvals.tsx`, `template-approvals.tsx`). Access
  requests shows Sandbox runs first, one card each, with the access the run needs — profiles in plain words, vault
  secrets, egress hosts, the image and its tools —, the template's blast radius, and Approve and Decline. Template
  approvals keeps only a template a person saved (no `askedBy`) that no run card holds. Approve selected selects run
  cards and those template cards.
- **The badge.** The Access requests badge, and its row in Needs you, count each run card once and a person's own
  waiting templates, so a job that waits on a write template raises the badge by one. A run card of a high-priority job
  (issue #535) comes first and marks the badge as a high-priority question does. Issue #2196 raises the badge for a job
  waiting on a template; that wait is now a run card, counted in the same row.

**Migration.** No stored format changes: the template's `askedBy`, `purpose` and `plan` are kept already, so a template
that waited before this build, of a job still live, is a run card at once. An approved template keeps working as before.

**Decided here.** The template stays the hopper's cache of the access, by the same name (`asked-<hash>`), so the same
needs find it again, and an approval still covers a later ask of the same needs. A run card is keyed by job and template,
not by request: a need step and a template request make no sandbox request, and keying by the request would leave their
waits with no card. The decline lowers the job's trust as a sandbox request's decline does.

**Not built (left for later parts).** An "allow again" choice on the card: today an approval of a card keeps the
template approved for every later job with the same needs, as before, and a person's write approval is remembered for
the time limit. An approval for this job only needs a template approval that names its job, read by the need step's
covering template and the template reuse.

**Part 2: a notice per new run card (2026-10-19).** The badge alone did not reach a person who was not looking at the
UI. Each new run card is one event, `vault.run_card_opened` (`template`, `waits`, `purpose`), on the job's timeline,
appended by `SandboxRequests` (`src/sandbox/requests.ts`) where the card first appears: a sandbox request that waits for
a person (after the approvers; when Jev reads it, only once Jev holds it), or an ask that waits on a template for a
person (`waited`, when the template waits for a person, not only for its read-only check). Once per job and template
while the hopper runs; a restart forgets which cards were sent, so a job that asks again after a restart sends its card
again. A waiting template a job asked for before a restart (`askedBy`) is a card with no new notice. The notifiers send
the event: the Grok Bot routine as `vault.run_card_opened`, with the job's priority and `high`, so the receiver ranks a
high-priority job's card first, and the Access requests link ("Grok Bot routine webhook"). Tests:
`test/sandbox/run-card-notices.test.ts`, `test/plugins/grokbot-run-cards.test.ts`, and `test/integration/need-steps.test.ts`
(a write need's one notice, on the real daemon).

**Part 3: allow again (2026-10-20).** Before, a run card's approval approved its template for every later job with the
same needs, and remembered each write for the time limit: one approval for one job was a standing approval for all.
The issue asks for a run's approval by default, and a choice to allow it again.

- **For this job only, by default.** `approve-run` with no `allowAgain` approves the template for the card's job's runs
  only: the template's approval names it (`approval.jobs`, `approvalJobs` in `src/domain/vault.ts`), and `vault.approved`
  carries `jobs`. No write approval is remembered. Another job that asks for the same access finds the template waiting
  for a person (`approvalCovers`): its ask is a run card of its own, and one approval adds that job to `jobs`.
- **Allow again** (`allowAgain: true`; the card's **Allow again** switch; `hopper sandbox approve-run --allow-again`):
  the approval is for every job, as before part 3, and each write, sync or apply approval is remembered.
- **Where the job is read.** Each place that decides whether a job's step may use a template reads the job:
  `templateReady(t, jobId)` (a box step, the broker's named sandbox, the sandboxes before the start), `coveringTemplate`
  (a need step), the template request's reuse and its waits (`waitsOf`, `approvedFor`), the sandbox request's approval
  by the person who approved the template (`approverOf`), and the run cards (`waitsForPerson`, `approvalsOf`).
- **No approval is taken away.** An approval for one job of a template already approved for every job, with the same
  image, tools, egress hosts and secrets, stays for every job: a card for one job never narrows what others had.

**Migration.** `approval.jobs` is a new optional field of the template's JSON body: no schema change. An approval kept
before has no `jobs`, so it covers every job, as it did: nothing that works today stops. A build before this one reads
an approval with `jobs` as one for every job: on a downgrade, a run approved for one job is approved for all, as before
part 3. Waiting templates were turned into run cards in part 1.

**Not built.** A box a person attached as a machine to a template (issue #602) takes jobs by `approvalWait`, which does
not read `jobs`: a template a job asked for has no such box. An approval for "the same kind of step" apart from the same
needs: the template is keyed by its needs, so the same needs are the same kind of step.

Tests: `test/domain/run-card-allow-again.test.ts` (the pure rules), `test/integration/need-steps.test.ts` (the real daemon:
a card's approval names its job and remembers nothing; with allow again it is for every job and remembered),
`test/ui/sandbox-runs-view.test.ts` (the switch and its post), `test/cli/sandbox-runs.test.ts` (`--allow-again`).

**Residual risk, stated.** One click now approves the template's image, egress hosts, vault secrets and every write the
card lists. The confirm says each of them, and the card lists them before the click. Each approval is still its own
event (`vault.approved`, `template.profile_approved`, `vault.sandbox_approved`) that names the person.

Tests: `test/domain/run-cards.test.ts`, `test/sandbox/requests.test.ts` (the kept asks; a decline before the run is
asked), `test/integration/need-steps.test.ts` (the real daemon and the real `hopper-step`: a write need makes exactly one
run card and no template card; one `approve-run` and the step runs in a need box with no other approval; a declined card
tells the step no), `test/ui/sandbox-runs-view.test.ts` (the cards, one post each; a person's own template card),
`test/ui/needs-you.test.ts` (the count, high-priority first), `test/cli/sandbox-runs.test.ts`.

**Approvals a rerun keeps (issue #2639 part 2, 2026-10-23).** Seen on a hopper: a critical job's restore failed during a
network outage, and the assessor ran it again as a new job. The rerun asked for the same template, and a person approved
its sandbox runs a second time, although the item, the template and the access were the same. A rerun (`Job.rerunOf`: the
assessor's, a person's Run again, or the source's offer of the item again) now keeps what a person approved for the job it
runs again:

- **A template approved for a job's runs only** (`approval.jobs`, part 3) covers the jobs that run it again. The vault's
  view widens the list (`withReruns`, `src/domain/vault.ts`) with each job's reruns (`laterRuns`,
  `src/domain/rerun-chain.ts`: from the item's newest job back along `rerunOf`), so every reader of `approvalCovers` — the
  run cards, the sandbox requests, the template request, the start hold — sees it. The stored template does not change.
- **A run a person approved** (a sandbox request approved by a person, or by an approval that names one) carries too: the
  rerun's request of the same template is approved at once, `by` `the approval of job <id>, which it runs again`
  (`carriedApprovalBy`). The requests are in memory, so the person's approvals of jobs that ended are kept for this, the
  newest 500 (`KEPT`, `src/sandbox/requests.ts`). The rerun's trust stamp must still let a run go with no person (issue
  #655 parts 7, 8 and 16): below `approved`, under a brake that asks a person, or outside its stamp, it waits as before.
- **A vault grant** needed nothing: it is kept for the item (`grantKeyOf`), so every job of the item has it.

A decline is not carried: the rerun asks, and a person decides again. Nothing else carries — a fork or a follow-on is
another item's job. The chain is walked 20 jobs at most (`RERUN_DEPTH`).

**Decided here.** Every rerun keeps the approvals, not only the assessor's: a vault grant was already kept for the item
across Run again, and a person who runs an item again expects the same access. A restart forgets the kept run approvals
as it forgets the requests; the template's approval for the job stays, so a rerun then gets one card for its run only
when the run itself needs a person.

Verification: `test/domain/rerun-chain.test.ts` (both ways along the chain, other items, the depth, a loop; the widened
approval), `test/sandbox/requests.test.ts` (a carried run, to a second rerun too; no decline carried; a job not a rerun
waits; a rerun below the trust waits), `test/integration/need-steps.test.ts` (real daemon: a run card approved for one job,
the job cancelled and its item offered again, and the rerun's write step runs with no card).

**The card carries the vault grant (issue #2639 part 3, 2026-10-23).** Seen on a hopper: a critical job needed a run
card's approval for a template, and then, once its step asked for the template's secret, a vault grant on a card of its
own, 6 minutes later. For one job and one template these are one decision.

- **On the card** (`runCards`, `granted`): a run card carries the job's vault grant (`vaultGrant: true`) when its template
  gives the vault — a vault secret or a profile the vault mints for — and the job's item has no grant yet. The card lists
  it (Vault grant) and its confirm says it. A grant ask of the same job and template is on the card, not in `grantAsks`
  (`looseGrantAsks`).
- **One approval.** `approve-run` of such a card grants the job's item the vault (`grant`, `vault.granted`, by the
  person), before the template and the run are approved, so the job's first ask of the vault finds it. Access decides
  first, as on Grant (`vault_grant#can_grant`, 403; 503 when it cannot be asked): a refusal changes nothing. An API token's
  card that waits for a person's confirm (issue #909) grants nothing until then.
- **What it widens.** Nothing beyond Grant: the grant is kept for the item, as every vault grant is, and the template's
  approved scope still bounds what the job gets ("Vault grants"). A person who wants the run with no grant declines the
  card, or approves the run and revokes the grant on Vault.

**Migration.** None: no stored format changes. `vaultGrant` is a new optional field of the vault's view.

Tests: `test/domain/run-card-vault-grant.test.ts`, `test/integration/run-card-vault-grant.test.ts` (the real daemon: one
`approve-run` approves the template and the run and grants the vault), `test/ui/sandbox-runs-view.test.ts`.

## A job waits on an infra plan (issue #2205, 2026-10-19)

Before: a job that waited on a person's approval of an infra plan could only say so as an outside event. The hopper did
not know the wait was on a plan: nothing linked the job to the plan, nothing woke the job on the approval, and nothing
checked that the plan was recorded at all. A job once waited on a production plan that no person could find on Infra, in
Needs you or in the CLI, and the change was made by hand.

- **A wait kind of its own** (`WaitOn` `{ kind: 'plan', planId }`, `src/domain/wait-on.ts`). The job writes
  `on: infra plan <id>`; the job rules list it with the other kinds (`WAIT_LINE`). A plan id after the word `plan` reads as
  this kind anywhere in the `on:` line, also in an outside event (`outside: gated: admin approval of infra plan <id>`), and
  in `for:` and `until:` when there is no `on:` line. A sandbox's plan (issue #1001) has no id, so it never reads as one.
- **Woken on the approval.** `infra.plan_approved` of that plan settles it (`settledBy`, `SETTLING_EVENT_TYPES`): the job
  is told `infra plan <id> was approved by <who>`, from the UI, the CLI or auto-approve alike.
- **Checked as it starts** (`planWaitEnd`, pure; `src/engine/outcome.ts`). The plan is read from the job's user's store,
  where Infra and Needs you read it. Approved already: the wait ends at once, as the approval would end it. Not recorded,
  stale, or failed its checks: no person can see or approve it, so the wait ends at once and the job is told why and what
  to do (record the plan with `POST /job/infra-plans`, or plan again). A job never waits on something nobody acts on.
- **The job is told where it shows.** `POST /job/infra-plans` answers a plan that waits with where it shows (Needs you,
  under Infra plans, and `#infra/<id>`) and the wait line to write; the apply gate's refusal of an unapproved plan says the
  same.
- **One place the owner sees.** Needs you's Infra plans row, its count and the badge already counted the plans that wait
  (issue #897). It now names each one (`planWaitingLines`, `ui/src/model/infra-plans.ts`): its short id, its summary, its
  risk, and who approves it; and it marks the badge for a plan a high-priority job recorded (`plansHigh`), as Access
  requests marks a high-priority job's run card (issue #2197). The shared read of `GET /api/infra-plans` is read again on
  each `infra.plan_*` event, so a recorded plan shows at once, not at the next 30-second read.
- **One click from the job.** A job's wait on a plan links to `#infra/<id>` (`waitOnLinkOf`, `ui/src/model/board.ts`):
  Infra marks that plan and scrolls to it, with its Approve; a plan not recorded is said so on the page.
- **The CLI** (`src/cli-operator-infra.ts`): `hopper infra plans` lists the plans that wait (`--all`: every plan, with its
  state), each with its summary, its risk and who approves it; `hopper infra approve <id>` approves one by its id or the
  short id the views show, through `POST /ui/api/infra-plans`, so the daemon checks the role by the plan's risk as for a click.

**Why no second mechanism.** The plans keep their one home, Infra, and Needs you keeps one row for them, as issue #2196
did for templates. No new table, route or migration: the wait is a field of the job, and the approval is the event it
already was.

**Not built here.** A plan that goes stale while a job waits on it does not end the wait: the job is woken only by the
approval, a person, or its own poll. The plans of other users are not shown to an admin: each user's Infra lists that
user's own plans, as before.

## Rejecting an infra plan (issue #2368, 2026-10-21)

Before: a plan had one decision, Approve. A plan a person decided against waited until it went stale, an hour after it was
made, and an admin could still approve it meanwhile. The job that waited on it waited for that hour, then planned again.

- **Reject, with a note.** `POST /ui/api/infra-plans` takes `action: 'reject'`, `plan` and `note` (1 to 1000 characters,
  `REJECTION_NOTE_MAX`); Infra shows Reject beside Approve on a plan that waits, with a field for the note and a confirm;
  `hopper infra reject <plan> --note <why>` does the same by its id or short id. Any operator or admin rejects any plan:
  a rejection takes a power away, so its risk needs no higher role. The route stays a box action, as it was for Approve.
- **A row of its own, terminal** (`infra_plan_rejections`, tenant migration 91; `PlanRejection`: `plan`, `by`, `at`,
  `note`). The plan itself does not change, as with an approval. `infra.plan_rejected` (`by`, `note`) goes on the
  timeline of the job that recorded the plan, and Applies and drift shows it.
- **Never approved after.** `approve` reads the rejection in its own transaction and answers 409 with who rejected the
  plan and the note; a reject reads the approval the same way, so one plan has at most one of the two. A plan approved
  already is not rejected (409): its apply may be under way. The apply gate refuses a rejected plan before anything else.
- **The job goes on at once.** `infra.plan_rejected` settles a wait on that plan (`settledBy`): the job is told
  `infra plan <id> was rejected by <who>: <note>. It is never approved: change course, or plan again and record a new
  plan`. A job that starts to wait on a plan rejected already is told the same at once (`planWaitEnd`).
- **The state.** Rejected comes before every other state (`planState`, the CLI's `stateOf`): a rejected plan waits for
  nobody, Needs you does not count it, and it is offered no Approve and no Reject.

**Not built here.** A job withdraws no plan of its own: a person rejects it, and the job, told so, records a new one. The
notifiers do not send `infra.plan_rejected`; webhook subscribers get it as any event.

Tests: `test/domain/wait-on-plan.test.ts` (the kind read from each way a job writes it, its wake, and how it ends as it
starts), `test/ui/infra-plan-needs-you.test.ts` (the count, the lines, the high mark, the link),
`test/integration/infra-plan-wait.test.ts` (the real daemon and CLI: a job waits on a production plan written as a gated
outside event; Infra and `hopper infra plans` list it; `hopper infra approve` or Approve on Infra wakes the job; a plan not
recorded ends the wait at once and tells the job why).

## The critical job tracker (issue #2203, parts 1 and 2, 2026-10-19)

Owner report, during a production outage: a critical job's template approval had no badge (issue #2196), and a question
the operator did not see cost minutes. What a critical job waits on must be in front of the person on every page.

**As built:**
- **Critical job.** A job whose live priority is at or above the **critical priority** (`HOPPER_CRITICAL_PRIORITY`,
  default 100; 0: off) — the same threshold the decider uses for one lane over the cap (issue #373). `GET /api/queue`
  answers it as `criticalPriority` (`src/engine/queries.ts`), so the UI and the decider name the same jobs.
- **The widget.** `ui/src/app/critical-tracker.tsx`, mounted by the shell above every view (`ui/src/app/app.tsx`), sticky
  under the header: it stays through navigation, and a reload shows it again from the store. It renders nothing while no
  critical job is tracked. The model is pure (`ui/src/model/critical-jobs.ts`); the rows come from the store
  (`ui/src/store/critical-jobs.ts`) and live on SSE as every view: the widget reads nothing of its own but a job's
  parts list when its timeline opens.
- **Each job.** Its title and issue, its status, its lane and the sandboxes it runs on (its approved sandbox requests), its
  current step in plain words and how long it has been in it (`currentStep`: what it waits on, why it is held, else its
  newest event as the event log says it), and its last four actions.
- **Waits, acted on in place.** Each wait that is a person's (`waitsOf`) is read from its one home and acted on there:
  a question, a run card, a vault grant ask, a credential request, an open proposal or research report, an open hand-off,
  a pending login, a changed item text, a hold for a person, the blast-radius gate, its own wait (Continue: `end-wait`).
  A quick act is a button that posts the route its page posts; any other opens the card of its home under the wait —
  `QuestionCard`, the run card, `ItemCard`, `HandoffRow`, `LoginCard`, `RequestItem`, `TextChangeCard`, exported from
  their views for this. So there is no copy: acting in the widget or on its page clears both, and Needs you counts it
  once (issue #897). The queue gate and an origin not judged stay links (`Accept in Queue`, `Approve in Intake`): they
  have no action of one job.
- **Attention.** A job with a wait is marked red with a pulsing dot, and the widget's border turns red. With browser
  notifications allowed (the widget's Notify me), each new wait notifies once per page load (`waitKey`).
- **Ended jobs.** An ended critical job stays until a person dismisses it; the dismissal is kept per browser with the
  dismissed notices (`critical:<job id>`, `ui/src/model/dismissed.ts`). A job that has not ended has no Dismiss.

**Decided here.** "Critical" is the critical priority, not a new threshold: the glossary already names it, and a second
number would make two kinds of critical. The widget is sticky in the page, not a floating box: it covers no content and
no toast, and it fits a phone's width. The ended-job dismissal is per browser, as the other notices are: it is a view
setting, not a decision.

Tests: `test/ui/critical-jobs.test.ts` (the model), `test/ui/critical-tracker.test.ts` (the whole app in happy-dom: on
every page and after a reload, live from the stream, each wait's action by its home's route, the dismissal after a
reload), `test/integration/high-priority.test.ts` (the queue answers the critical priority, and 0 when it is off).

### Part 2: the critical flag (2026-10-20)

- **The flag.** `critical: true` on the job (`src/domain/types.ts`; the job's body is JSON, so no migration). A job with
  it is a critical job whatever its priority, also while the critical priority is 0 (`isCriticalJob`,
  `ui/src/model/critical-jobs.ts`).
- **The route.** `POST /ui/api/jobs/:id/critical` with `{ critical: boolean }`, least role operator, the API's too
  (`jobs:critical`). The engine (`src/engine/critical-flag.ts`) sets or clears it in one transaction with
  `job.critical_flag_changed` (`critical`, `person`, `via`). 409 when it marks a job that ended; a clear is taken on any
  job. The same flag again records nothing.
- **The toggle.** The job view's **critical** row (`ui/src/views/job-critical.tsx`) says whether the job is critical and
  why — the flag first, else its priority —, with **Mark critical** (a job that has not ended) or **Clear critical flag**.

**Decided here.** The flag changes only what the tracker shows. The lane over the cap stays a rule of the critical
priority (help/lanes.md: "a rule of the priority, not a label"), so a person's flag spends no usage past the caps. The
flag is a mark on one job: a new job of the same item (run again, rework, a fork) does not take it. No box token: the
flag starts nothing.

Tests: `test/integration/critical-flag.test.ts` (set and clear through the real daemon, with who acted; the same flag
again, an ended job, an unknown job, no session, a bad body), `test/ui/critical-jobs.test.ts` (a flagged job is
tracked), `test/ui/job-critical-view.test.ts` (the job view's row and its buttons).

## Action grants (issue #2206, part 1, 2026-10-19)

Seen on a hopper: during a production outage a job was told to scale a managed node group. No role the vault mints for
could call `eks:UpdateNodegroupConfig`, so the job handed the command back to a person, who ran it by hand, and
production went out of step with the infrastructure code.

**Mechanism decided here.** A session policy only narrows what a role may do: the hopper cannot give a session an action
its role does not allow, and it never changes IAM (the hopper never changes the cluster or the account's identities). So
an operator makes one wide role per account, the **action role** `hopper-action` (`ACTION_ROLE`, `src/domain/minting.ts`),
and the hopper mints it only narrowed to the actions a person granted. `docs/deploy.md` "The action role" says how to make it.

- **The ask.** A need step names each action its one change on an aws-role needs: `sh "$HOPPER_STEP" need
  "apply/aws-role/<account>/hopper-action" --action "eks:UpdateNodegroupConfig=<ARN>" --plan-id <id> …` (at most 10;
  `actionsOf`: an IAM action with no wildcard, an ARN in the role's account or of no account). `actionNeed`: the actions
  go to the step's only write, sync or apply need on an aws-role; a change on the action role with no `--action` is
  refused. Each action no live grant covers is a `vault.action_asked` once per job and scope, and the route answers 202
  `waiting: a person grants <action> on <resource> as aws-role <role>`; `hopper-step` asks again by itself, as for a
  template that waits, and a job that ends its turn waits `on: vault grant`, which `vault.action_granted` and
  `vault.action_declined` settle (`settledBy`). The ask is read from the event log (`actionAsks`, `src/vault/action-grants.ts`:
  of a job at work, not declined, not covered now), so a restart keeps it and no state is kept in memory.
- **Infra applies off** (issue #1722): the route refuses the step with `APPLY_STEP_OFF` before any ask, so no action
  grant is asked for a change that cannot be minted.
- **The grant.** On Access requests, panel **AWS actions** (`ui/src/views/action-grants.tsx`): each ask names the
  action, the resource, the role, the job and why, with **Grant** and **Decline**; it counts in the Access requests badge
  and the Needs you row, and marks the badge for a high-priority job, as a run card does. `POST /ui/api/sandbox-requests`
  `grant-action` / `decline-action` (`job`, `grant`: `role`, `action`, `resource`), admin and a box action, as the route
  is. Only a waiting ask is decided (404 else). A grant is kept in the user's settings (`actionGrants`, no migration:
  absent reads as none) and covers a later ask of the same role, action and resource — the one-approval carry-over of
  issue #1001 — until the time limit of remembered write approvals (`rememberWritesHours`, `liveGrants`). `revokeAction`
  on `POST /ui/api/sandbox-approvals` revokes it (`vault.action_revoked`). The vault's view answers `actionAsks` and
  `actionGrants`.
- **The mint** (`mintTarget` with the actions, `src/vault/need-mint.ts`). The step keeps its actions (`NeedStep.actions`,
  in its JSON body: no migration), and its narrowed need is minted with `ReadOnlyAccess` and an inline session policy that
  allows each granted action on its resource and denies assuming any other role (`actionSession`, at most the 2048
  characters STS takes). Each grant is read again at each mint, so a revoke or the time limit bites at the next one. The
  rest is unchanged: Access and the template's approval, the apply gate (a current approved plan, issue #870), and
  `vault.minted`, which now names `actions`.
- **The record.** The apply is in the Infra changes feed as every plan-bound apply is (`GET /api/infra-plans`
  `applies`, issue #896), with the granted actions (`PlanApply.actions`); the out-of-band rule (issue #871) reads the
  minted principal as a plan-bound apply credential, as before.

**Decided here.** An API token or a delegate approver cannot grant or decline an action (403): granting a wide role's
action is a person's act, as the confirmation asks of issue #909 make an API token's write approval. The grant is per role,
action and resource, not per job, so an outage's second step needs no second click; its end is the remembered-write time
limit, so an admin who sets it to 1 hour has a person decide almost each time.

**The action check (part 2, 2026-10-20).** A missing permission shows when the job asks for its template, not partway
through its work. `sh "$HOPPER_SKILL" sandbox-template --needs "apply/aws-role/<account>/<role>" --actions
"<service:Action>=<ARN> ..."` names the actions the change does (`ASKED` keeps `actions`, so a watch asks again with
them). Before the template is made, `checkTemplateActions` (`src/vault/template-actions.ts`) gives each action a verdict
(`actionChecks`, `src/domain/action-check.ts`, pure):

- **ready** — the role allows it (IAM's policy simulation), and on the action role a person granted it;
- **waits** (`grant`) — on the action role, no live grant covers it: it is asked of a person now (`askActions`, the same
  `vault.action_asked`), so the grant waits on Access requests beside the template;
- **cannot** (`role-denies`) — the role does not allow it. No grant helps, as a session policy only narrows. The request
  is refused (409) before a template is made, with the need to ask for in its place (the action role, `--action`), or,
  on the action role itself, the operator's change to make;
- **cannot** (`no-role`, issue #2387) — the role does not exist in its account (IAM `GetRole` answers `NoSuchEntity`).
  No session of it can be minted, so the request is refused (409) the same way, before a template is made and before a
  grant is asked; the line names the role's ARN and, for the action role, that an operator makes it;
- **not checked** (`unchecked`) — IAM could not simulate it; the line says why, and nothing is refused for it.

The simulation is the port `ActionSimulator`: `iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy` (`src/vault/action-simulation.ts`,
@aws-sdk/client-iam) of the role's ARN, one call per action on its resource, after one `iam:GetRole` of the role (issue
#2387: a role the account does not have is `no-role`, and a `GetRole` IAM refuses for another reason goes on to the
simulation, as `ReadOnlyAccess` holds `iam:GetRole` but a narrower read role may not), with a read session of the account's read
role `hopper-read`, minted as topology discovery mints one (`mintForDiscovery`: no job or template takes part, so Access
is not asked, and `vault.discovery_minted` records it). It reads the role's own policies: a service control policy or a
resource policy can still refuse the call when it runs. A need step with `--action` and no template yet passes its actions
to the template request, so the template and the grant wait for a person in the same visit, not one after the other.
`--actions` on `sandbox` is refused: a box step's change is not narrowed to granted actions. With infra applies off, the
check refuses as the step does, and asks for nothing.

**Part 3: the action on the run card (2026-10-20).** In part 2 the template and the grant waited in the same visit, but
on two cards: the job's run card and an ask under AWS actions. A person approved one and still waited on the other.

- **On the card** (`runCards`, `actionAsks`, `src/domain/run-cards.ts`). A job's ask for an AWS action is on the job's
  run card when the card's template changes that aws-role (a write, sync or apply profile of `<account>/<role>`), as
  `actions` (the role, the action, the resource and the job's words). The vault's view lists it there only:
  `actionAsks` holds the asks no run card holds (`looseAsks`), so the badge counts the card once. An ask of a job with no
  run card (its template is approved) stays under AWS actions, as in part 1.
- **One approval** (`approve-run`). It grants each action on the card first (`vault.action_granted`, as `grant-action`),
  then approves the template, its profiles and the run as before, so the step that wakes on the template's approval
  finds its grant. **One decline** (`decline-run`) declines each action too (`vault.action_declined`, with the reason).
- **A person's act.** An API token or a delegate approver may decide no card with an action (403), as it may not
  `grant-action`. The confirm says what the approval also grants.
- **The operator CLI** (`src/cli-operator-actions.ts`): `hopper sandbox actions` (the asks, those on run cards first,
  and the grants), `grant-action <job> <account>/<role> <service:Action>=<ARN>`, `decline-action … [--reason <text>]` and
  `revoke-action <account>/<role> <service:Action>=<ARN>`. Each is the UI's own post.
- **The deploy guide** has the action role in Terraform beside the `aws iam` commands.

**Decided here.** A grant from a card is the same standing grant as `grant-action`: it covers later asks of the same
scope until the time limit of remembered write approvals, with or without Allow again. The issue's intake asked for that
carry-over (issue #1001), and a grant is kept by scope, not by job. Allow again still decides only the template.

**Migration.** None: the asks are read from the event log, and `actions` is a new field of the view only.

**Residual risk, stated.** The action role is wide in IAM; only the hopper's minting narrows it. A person who holds the
minting credential can assume it unnarrowed, as with any role it can assume. A resource ARN with a wildcard (`nodegroup/<cluster>/<group>/*`)
is granted as written: the card shows it whole before the click.

Tests: `test/domain/action-grants.test.ts` (the actions read, the need they go to, a grant's cover and time limit, the
session policy and its size, the action role never minted wider), `test/integration/action-grants.test.ts` (the real
daemon and the real `hopper-step`: an action outside the role asked once and shown on Access requests; one grant and the
step runs in its need box, STS asked for the action role with `ReadOnlyAccess` and the action on its resource; `vault.minted`
names the plan and the action; the apply in the Infra changes feed; the same action again at once; a decline tells the step
no; infra applies off asks nothing; a bare change on the action role refused), `test/ui/action-grants-view.test.ts`,
`test/ui/needs-you.test.ts` (the count), `test/ui/infra-plans.test.ts` (the apply's words), `test/domain/wait-on.test.ts`
(the wake), `test/domain/action-check.test.ts` (the verdicts and their words), `test/vault/action-simulation.test.ts`
(one simulation per action, of the role, with the read session; a refusal says why), and in
`test/integration/action-grants.test.ts` the action check (IAM answered on loopback beside STS: an action the role does
not allow refuses the template request before a template is made; on the action role the grant is asked at once; a need
step with no template asks for both in one visit, and runs once both are approved). Part 3: `test/domain/run-cards.test.ts`
(an ask on the card of its job and role; the others stay loose), `test/integration/action-grants.test.ts` (one
`approve-run` approves the template and grants the action, the step runs and its apply is in the feed; an API token may
not; one `decline-run` declines the action too), `test/ui/sandbox-runs-view.test.ts` (the action on the card and in its
confirm), `test/cli/sandbox-actions.test.ts`.

**No plan for a granted action (issue #2370, 2026-10-21).** Seen on a hopper: a run card for a node-group scale
(`eks:UpdateNodegroupConfig`) was approved, and the step was still refused: the mint asked for an approved infra plan, and
a plan is terraform, helm or gitops only. No plan of those tools records one AWS CLI call, so the card could never apply,
and the job parked on a recheck that could not clear. A person ran the command by hand.

- **The grant approves the change.** A need step's change narrowed to granted actions (`--action`, each covered by a live
  grant at the mint) is minted with no `--plan-id` (`src/vault/need-mint.ts`): the person granted exactly that action on
  that resource for that role, which is what a plan's approval says of a plan. The step's `--plan` text names the exact
  call and its undo, and the run card shows it before the click.
- **A plan named is still checked.** With `--plan-id`, the plan gate runs as before (a current, approved plan of the asset).
- **The refusal says the other way.** A change on an aws-role with no plan is refused as before, and the words now say
  to ask on the action role with `--action` and no plan (`applyRefusal`).
- **The record.** `vault.minted` names the actions and no plan. The Infra changes feed lists plan-bound applies only, so
  this apply is not there; it is on the job's timeline (`vault.action_granted`, `vault.minted`). The out-of-band rule
  (issue #871) reads only a plan-bound credential as in band, so its write shows as out of band: it is, until the
  infrastructure code is changed to match.

**Decided here.** No `aws` plan type. A plan is a saved file a tool applies and the hopper checks against the code; an
AWS CLI call has neither, and the action grant already holds its scope (one action, one resource, one role). A box step
and a change with no `--action` still need a plan.

**Migration.** None: no stored shape changes.

Tests: `test/integration/action-grants.test.ts` (a node-group scale card with no plan goes from one `approve-run` to
applied, `vault.minted` naming the action and no plan; a plan the step names is still checked).

## Unhealthy lanes (issue #2234, 2026-10-20)

**What happened.** The hopper's sandbox box `hopper-sandbox-claude` failed every job it took for two hours, 11 of 11,
each with `claude did not start in 3 attempts: pane … never set up the job's container runtime within 60000 ms`. The
failure assessor classed each as a start race and reran it, and each rerun went to the same lane again.

**The cause.** A box starts herdr from its entrypoint with no `SHELL` in its environment, so herdr's panes run `sh`, which
in the box image (Debian bookworm) is dash. Dash has no line editor: it reads what the terminal hands on, and a terminal
in canonical mode keeps at most 4095 characters of a line (Linux's `N_TTY_BUF_SIZE` less the newline). The runtime
command (issue #1295) was one line of 5.9 KB, its guards written into it. Dash got a cut line with an open quote, sat at
its continuation prompt, and printed no outcome: the 60 s wait passed every time. A machine whose panes run bash or zsh
reads the line through its line editor and never met the limit. Reproduced with herdr and a shell with no line editor:
the line ends at a `>` prompt; the same line in bash prints `hopper-runtime-own`.

**The fix.** `TERMINAL_LINE_MAX` (`src/executors/herdr/client.ts`) is the longest command typed into a pane. The runtime
is set up in two steps (`guardsCommand`, then `setupCommand`, `src/client/job-runtime.ts`), the second typed once the
first printed its outcome, so the terminal never holds both. The fake herdr's shell runs nothing longer than a terminal
line, so a command that grows too long fails a test instead of a lane.

**Unhealthy lanes** (`src/engine/lane-health.ts`, `src/decider/lane-health.ts`). A lane whose last 3 starts failed with
the same start error — its lane's fault (`isLaneFault`), the same first 120 characters of its normalised text (the pane's
screen after them differs from job to job) — is unhealthy for 30 minutes. Its machine carries it (`unhealthyLanes`, kept
in memory as reach holds are), and the Decision counts the machine as one lane fewer for each lane out that holds no
job, places no new job on it, and numbers a new lane there past it; the machine's idle reason names it. Machines shows a
badge, the lane, its failed starts, when it is tried again and its last error. `lane.unhealthy` records each time a lane
goes out. When the 30 minutes pass, one job is placed there: a start that fails the same way puts the lane out again at
once, one that gets under way (or fails for its own reason) makes it healthy. A person's cancel counts neither way.

**A rerun avoids the lane.** For a waiting rerun of a job that failed for its lane's fault, the Decision's inputs name
that lane (`avoidLanes`). The job goes to another machine when one may take it — a start failure is most often the
machine's, as here —, else to another idle or new lane of that machine, and to that lane only when there is no other: it
is a preference, never a hold.

**Verification.** `test/client/job-runtime.test.ts` (each step fits a line, the steps run for real),
`test/herdr/executor-runtime.test.ts` (every typed command fits, the guards before the setup),
`test/engine/lane-health.test.ts`, `test/decider/unhealthy-lanes.test.ts`, `test/ui/machine-unhealthy-lanes.test.ts`.

## The sandbox host (issue #2272, 2026-10-21)

**The gap.** A sandbox (a need or box step, a bastion, the read-only check, the warm pass) started beside the hopper when it
had a runtime, else on the first of the user's client targets dialled in with one. A person could not say where sandboxes
run: a step could land on a worker seat that runs coding lanes, and so the credentials minted for it reached that seat. A
dedicated machine for sandboxes was not possible to point at.

**The change, part 1** (`src/domain/sandbox-host.ts`; `src/engine/sandbox-host.ts`; `src/store/machine-drain-settings.ts`;
`src/sandbox/runtime.ts` `createPlacements` `where`; `src/sandbox/service.ts` `hostOffline`; `src/sandbox/need-steps.ts`
`hostWait`; `src/http/ui/sandbox-host.ts`; `src/cli-operator-machine.ts`; Machines, `ui/src/views/machine-sandbox-host.tsx`):
- **The sandbox host** (glossary) is a user's setting: the machines the user's sandboxes start on, first first, at most 5.
  `local` is the runtime beside the hopper; any other is a machine the hopper knows that runs **no coding lane** (its lanes are
  0), so no minted credential reaches a worker seat. A machine with lanes is refused: set its lanes to 0 first.
- **Placement.** While it is set, every sandbox starts only on the first machine of it whose runtime answers now (a client
  target dialled in with a rootless runtime, or the runtime beside the hopper): never on another machine and never beside the
  hopper when `local` is not named. None online: the sandbox does not start, and the reason is `sandbox host <name> is
  offline` (`sandbox hosts <a>, <b> are offline` for a list). Not set: sandboxes start where they did before.
- **A step waits.** A need or box step looks at the sandbox host before it mints anything: while it is offline, the step waits
  (every 10 s), and its log says once `hopper: sandbox host <name> is offline: the step waits for it, and never starts on
  another machine`. Once the host is back, it mints and runs. Its saga holds its lease meanwhile; a hopper that stops leaves the
  step to wait again on any host. A step whose job stops meanwhile ends cancelled, with nothing minted. A read-only check
  finds no place, and waits for its next pass; a bastion that cannot start says why.
- **A change** is read at each sandbox: no restart, no redeploy. A sandbox that runs already ends where it started; the next one
  starts on the new host. Kept in the user's settings (`sandboxHost`: the machines, who, the way, when), so a restart keeps it.
- **Set** by an admin: `POST /ui/api/machines/sandbox-host {hosts}` (`[]` clears it), the Machines card's Use as sandbox host
  (adds it last) and Stop as sandbox host, and `hopper machine sandbox-host [<machine>...|--clear]` (no machine: print it).
  Each change records `machine.sandbox_host_set` with the list before and after, who and the way; one that changes nothing
  records nothing. Not a box action: it starts and stops no work.
- **Shown.** `GET /api/machines` carries `sandboxHost` (the list) and marks each machine of it with its place. The card has a
  *sandbox host* badge, its place, and how many sandboxes run there now (its sandbox runs not ended).

**Not changed.** Sandbox network rules: no API-server proxy, no port-forward RBAC, no new port or tunnel. A box step's vault
secrets still go only into a need box beside the hopper (`NO_SECRET_COPY`).

**Left for the next parts** (path 2 of the proposal): a **Podman host** record reached over the hopper's own ssh key and
pinned host key by `podman system dial-stdio` — part 2, "Podman hosts" below —; the host's CPU and memory and its totals on
Machines; and on Kubernetes `local:<node>`, a box pod pinned by `nodeSelector`.

Tests: `test/domain/sandbox-host.test.ts` (which machines can be the host), `test/sandbox/sandbox-host.test.ts` (placement, no
fallback, offline, a change mid-run), `test/sandbox/need-step-host-wait.test.ts` (the wait), `test/integration/sandbox-host.test.ts`
(the route, the event, a restart, the CLI), `test/ui/machine-sandbox-host.test.ts` (the card).

### Podman hosts (issue #2272 part 2, 2026-10-21)

**The gap.** The sandbox host could name only `local` or a machine of the user's with no lanes, and a machine needs the
hopper client. A dedicated VM for sandboxes needed a hopper client on it, and a box step with vault secrets still ran only
beside the hopper (`NO_SECRET_COPY`).

**The change** (`src/domain/podman-hosts.ts`; `src/sandbox/podman-hosts.ts`; `src/sandbox/podman-host.ts`;
`src/sandbox/socket-http.ts` `RuntimeSocket`; `src/sandbox/runtime.ts` `PodmanHosts`; `src/http/ui/podman-hosts.ts`;
`src/cli-operator-podman-host.ts`; Settings → Podman hosts, `ui/src/views/podman-hosts.tsx`):
- **A Podman host** (glossary) is a Linux computer with rootless Podman (4 or later) that a person set up for sandboxes. It is
  kept in the user's config record `podman-hosts`: a name (never `local`), an ssh destination (`[user@]host`), its pinned host
  key, and the most CPUs and memory (MiB) a box gets there. Not a machine: no hopper client, lane or job runs there. The record
  is read at each sandbox, so an edit needs no restart.
- **Added** with its host key confirmed, as a Windows host is: Settings → Podman hosts reads the key the host presents
  (`POST /ui/api/machines/host-key`), shows its fingerprint, and pins it on Pin this key and save; `hopper machine podman-host
  add <name> <user@host>` prints the key and its fingerprint and adds nothing, and the same command with `--host-key '<key>'`
  pins it. `POST /ui/api/podman-hosts` takes the whole list against the version read (admin, a box action: it says where
  work runs). `GET /api/podman-hosts` reads it; `hopper machine podman-host list|remove` too.
- **Used** once the sandbox host names it (`hopper machine sandbox-host <name>`, or Use as sandbox host on its row). A name
  that is both a machine and a Podman host is refused. Placement is part 1's: the first host of the list whose runtime
  answers, never another, none online `sandbox host <name> is offline`.
- **The transport.** Each call of the Podman adapter (`podman.ts`, unchanged in its calls) goes over a stream that `ssh` opens
  in place of the socket: `ssh … -- <host> podman system dial-stdio`, its stdin and stdout the host's Podman API. The ssh
  connection is the one every ssh target gets ("Target authentication"): the hopper's own key, public-key authentication
  only, the hardened options, nothing forwarded, and the pinned key only, written to `<workdir>/<user>/ssh/podman/<name>.known_hosts`.
  One connection is shared per host (ControlMaster, 60 s). node:http drives the stream as it drives a unix socket, so the
  copy into a box (`copy-in.ts`) and a command in a box (`box-pipe.ts`) go over it too.
- **The host's key line.** The account's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` gives the hopper's key one forced command:
  `command="podman system dial-stdio",no-pty,no-port-forwarding,no-agent-forwarding,no-X11-forwarding <public key>`
  (`AUTHORIZED_KEYS_OPTIONS`; the section shows the line whole). The key then runs no shell and forwards nothing.
- **Health** is ssh plus libpod `/info`: the adapter's own `problem()` — ssh that fails says why (`ssh to <name> failed
  (exit 255): …`), and a rootful Podman is refused as it is beside the hopper.
- **Vault secrets.** A place now says whether it takes a step's vault secrets (`Placed.secrets`): beside the hopper and on a
  Podman host, by a copy into the box's file system over the same stream — never in its environment, never to a process of
  the hopper's on the host —; on a machine of the user's, still refused (`NO_SECRET_COPY`).
- **A dropped wait.** A step's wait can last its whole time limit over one ssh stream. When the stream drops (not a refusal of
  Podman's), the runtime looks the box up again by its id after 5 s and waits again, until the time limit; a box that is gone
  ends the step with why. The box is made once, by its name, so nothing runs twice. A hopper that stops mid-step leaves the
  step to its saga as before: the run ends `interrupted`, the sweep burns the box on the host by its labels.
- **The most a box gets** there is the host's `cpus` and `memoryMb`, as a Kubernetes box gets the chart's.
- **The sweep** looks on a Podman host that an open sandbox run names, as on a client target, and burns a need box a step
  left there; a run on a Podman host the user removed is closed in the ledger, as on a removed machine.

**Not changed.** Sandbox network rules. A box there joins the host's network (`host`), as on a client target; the egress proxy
of a read-only box is only beside the hopper. Part 3 below removes the leftover box builds on a Podman host.

**Security.** One new exposure: the hopper's ssh key can drive the host's rootless Podman — the same trust a Windows host
gets. The forced command limits the key to dial-stdio. Only key authentication to a pinned host key is used.

Tests: `test/domain/podman-hosts.test.ts` (the record), `test/domain/sandbox-host.test.ts` (the sandbox host names one),
`test/sandbox/podman-host.test.ts` (ssh dial-stdio against a libpod double: health, ssh failing, a box with secrets, the
limits, a dropped wait), `test/sandbox/sandbox-host-podman.test.ts` (placement, secrets, offline, the sweep),
`test/integration/podman-hosts.test.ts` (route, sandbox host, CLI), `test/cli/podman-host.test.ts`, `test/ui/podman-hosts.test.ts`.

### Podman hosts on Machines (issue #2272 part 3, 2026-10-21)

**The gap.** A Podman host showed only in Settings. To size it from real numbers, a person needs to see on Machines which
host is the sandbox host, how many sandboxes run there and how much CPU and memory it uses; and the box builds that
sandboxes leave there filled its disk.

**The change** (`src/sandbox/podman-host-status.ts`; `src/sandbox/podman.ts` `podmanInfo`; `src/stack-resources/remote.ts`;
`src/users/sandbox-boxes.ts` `podmanHostsInUse`; `src/sandbox/service.ts`; `ui/src/views/machine-podman-hosts.tsx`):
- **Status.** `GET /api/podman-hosts/status` reads each Podman host now, one libpod `/info` over its ssh stream (at most 10 s):
  the same health as the sandbox module's (`podmanInfo`, which `problem()` now uses too), and the computer's CPUs, the share
  of CPU time busy (`host.cpuUtilization`), and its memory in use and in all (`memTotal`, `memFree`). Read when asked, never
  kept. A host that does not answer has its reason and no numbers.
- **Machines** shows a *Podman hosts* section, below the machines, while the user has one: each host's *sandbox host* badge
  and its place, how many sandboxes run there now (its open sandbox runs, as a machine's card counts them), its CPU and
  memory, or `sandbox host <name> is offline: <why>`. It reads again every 15 s.
- **Each box's use.** The remote box meter (Stack resources) reads the boxes on each Podman host in use — one the sandbox
  host names, or one an open sandbox run names — with the container meter over the host's ssh stream, labelled
  `<host>/<box>`, as on a client target.
- **Leftover box builds.** The reconcile pass removes them on each Podman host in use too, at most once in
  `LEFTOVER_PASS_MS`, never forced, as beside the hopper and on a client target: only an image with the hopper's tag or
  stage label.

**Not changed.** No new credential, route that changes anything, or call outside the forced command: `/info`, the container
list, its stats and the image calls go over the same dial-stdio stream.

Tests: `test/sandbox/podman-host-status.test.ts` (online, not reached, rootful), `test/adapters/remote-box-meter.test.ts` (a
Podman host's boxes over its stream), `test/sandbox/leftover-builds.test.ts` (the builds on a Podman host in use, not on
one not in use), `test/integration/podman-hosts.test.ts` (the status route), `test/ui/machine-podman-hosts.test.ts` (the
section).

## Exit at start (issue #2432, 2026-10-22)

**What happened.** On one seat, new jobs failed about a minute after their start with `claude exited:` and the last lines
of the pane: the setup commands (the job worktree, shared dependencies, Claude's config kept), the `claude … --session-id`
line, then only Claude's resume hint. Jobs on the same seat that ran in a session already open went on and finished. The
failure assessor matched no known cause, so each failed job went to a person.

**What the hopper could not see.** The failure text was the pane's last 20 lines. Claude Code draws its screen and takes
it away when it exits, so what was left was mostly the setup, and Claude's exit code was never read. The cause on the
seat is not found from these records: the change below makes the next such failure say what Claude said and how it
stopped.

**The change** (`src/executors/herdr/exited.ts`; `monitor.ts`, `startup.ts`; `src/failures/causes.ts`;
`src/reliability/fault.ts`):
- **The exit code.** When Claude's agent is gone from its pane, the hopper reads the screen, then types
  `printf 'hopper-claude-exit-%s\n' "$?"` at the shell prompt Claude left, and reads the code back (5 s at most). Every
  pane is a POSIX shell (issue #367), so `$?` is Claude's status: in the job's sandbox too, as bubblewrap exits with its
  command's status. A code above 128 also names the signal. A pane that is gone or does not answer gives
  `exit code unknown`.
- **What Claude printed.** The text is the lines after Claude's own command line (the one with `--session-id`), its
  shell prompt after them left out; the pane is Claude's terminal, so its stderr is there too. With no such line on
  screen, the last 20 lines, as before.
- **Exit at start** (glossary). Claude gone during startup is `claude exited at startup (…)`. Claude gone in the task's
  turn (its anchor is the protocol footer, which only a new session is sent) before the watch saw any line of output is
  `claude exited at the start of a new session, before any output (…)`. Any other exit is `claude exited (…)`.
- **The known cause Resource limit** (`resource-limit`, issue #2498): an exit after OOM kills in the job's scope is
  never an exit at start or a sign-in, whatever Claude printed ("Job limits and resource-limit failures").
- **The known cause Exited at start** (`exited-at-start`): transient, retry, after Login expired, Disk full, Machine
  offline and Herdr outdated, so a text Claude printed that names one of those keeps that cause. It is a **lane fault**:
  the rerun avoids the lane — another machine when one may take it, else another lane ("Unhealthy lanes", issue #2234) —
  and 3 such starts in a row on one lane put it out for 30 minutes. No second hold mechanism: the seat's health is the
  lane health that issue #2234 made, which the stall work of issue #2427 also leaves as it is. The same failure on the
  item's run before still stops it for a person (issue #1461): a rerun on another seat that exits the same way is not a
  seat's fault.

**Verification.** `test/herdr/exit-at-start.test.ts`: the exit code read and its command's echo not taken as one; the text
after the command line; an exit in the task's turn with nothing shown is an exit at start, with its code and signal, and
one after output is not; the cause, the lane fault, the assessor's retry, and the rerun's avoided lane.

## The resource ledger (issue #2504, part 1, 2026-10-22)

Requirement (issue #2504): a job that ends leaves nothing behind. Each thing the hopper makes for a job is recorded when it
is made, a durable cleanup reaps each one on its own machine, work not pushed is kept and flagged, a reconciler reaps what
no live job holds, and each job shows its cleanup status. The cleanup itself exists already: the **reap** at the job's end,
its **cleanup record** (issue #1570) and **deferred cleanup** (issue #371), and the **sweep** (issue #410). What was
missing is the record of what each job has: the reap and the sweep find a job's things by path and job id only, and no
one can ask "what does this job still hold, and why".

**Part 1: the ledger.** The `job_resource_ledger` table (tenant migration 92, `src/store/resource-ledger.ts`, pure rules in
`src/domain/resource-ledger.ts`), one **ledger entry** per job, kind and locator:

| Kind | Locator | Recorded from |
|---|---|---|
| `scratch_dir` | `<work tree>/.worktrees/@scratch/<job id>` | the executor's saved state, its `cwd` |
| `job_worktree` | its path | the saved state's `jobWorktree` |
| `job_scope` | `hopper-job-<job id>.scope` | the saved state's `scope` |

- **When it is recorded.** Each `saveState` of a job's executor writes the job's state and its ledger entries in one
  transaction (`recordLedger`, `src/engine/resource-ledger.ts`), on the machine the job runs on. An entry already there is
  left as it is, so a later save changes nothing. An executor that saves none of these fields records nothing.
- **How it is closed.** Each reap that ends — the cleanup at the job's end (`src/engine/cleanup.ts`), the sweep's reaps and
  a discard (`src/engine/sweep.ts`) — closes the job's entries as it says (`reapClosures`): a dir it names as still there is
  `failed`, with that path as the reason; with work kept, the scratch dir and the job worktree are `kept` together, as the
  reap keeps them; else each is `reaped`. A scope is always `reaped`. A reap that did not look at the scratch dir (the
  sweep stops only a scope or processes) closes only the scope. A `kept` entry a later reap removes becomes `reaped`, and so
  does a `failed` one (part 2); a `reaped` entry is not judged again. A reap that could not reach the machine closes nothing: the entries
  stay `live` until a reap goes through.
- **Cleanup status** (`cleanupStatusOf`). `none` with no entry; `in_use` while the job has not ended; `pending` while its
  cleanup is deferred or an entry is still `live`; `in_progress` while its cleanup record is owed; then `failed` if an
  entry failed, `kept_work` if one is kept, else `done`.
- **Shown.** The job's parts list (`GET /api/jobs/:id/bom`, the job page) has, in the machines group, a part `cleanup` with
  the cleanup status and how many entries are closed, and one part per entry with its locator and state. An entry is a
  record, but one whose removal failed counts as `failed`.

**Verification.** `test/domain/resource-ledger.test.ts` (the entries from a state, the closures, the status);
`test/engine/sweep-ledger.test.ts` (the sweep closes entries: kept work later removed, a dir left, a scope-only reap);
`test/integration/resource-ledger.test.ts` (a job that ends cancelled, finished or failed has every entry reaped; work kept;
a removal that failed; the parts list).

### Part 2: cleanup leftovers (2026-10-22)

A failed removal or a cleanup that never reached its machine stayed in the ledger with nothing to say so: the job's page
showed it only to a person who opened that job. The issue asks that a leftover found after a grace period is never silently
ignored.

- **Cleanup leftover** (`cleanupLeftoversOf`, `src/domain/resource-ledger.ts`, pure). An ended job's entries still `live`
  or `failed` once `CLEANUP_GRACE_MINUTES` (60) passed after its end (`finishedAt`, else `updatedAt`). A job that has not
  ended, and a job the store does not know, is no leftover here. The store reads the candidates in one query
  (`ResourceLedgerRepository.open`: every entry `live` or `failed`).
- **A failed entry is judged again.** A later reap that removed a `failed` entry's dir — the sweep reaps an ended job's
  scratch dir again at each pass while it is there — closes it `reaped`; one that still leaves it keeps it `failed`, with
  the new reason when it changed. Only a `reaped` entry is final. So a leftover ends when a reap removes it.
- **The leftover check** (`src/engine/cleanup-leftovers.ts`). With each sweep pass, only on the host that holds the sweep
  lease, before the sweep: each leftover is recorded once per job as `job.cleanup_leftover` (its end, the grace period, and
  each entry: machine, kind, locator, state, reason) and logged. A job already told — in memory, or by its event after a
  restart — is not told again. A check that fails is logged and throws nothing.
- **Failures.** None since issue #2684: a cleanup leftover is the cleanup worker's, which tries again at each sweep pass,
  and Machines counts it (part 3). The stuck cause `cleanup_leftover` is gone.

**Left for later parts** of issue #2504: containers, volumes, processes, agent sessions, herdr panes and build daemons as
entries; the cleanup as a persisted work item per entry with backoff, on each machine's own transport, and container storage
that only a `podman unshare` removes; the reconciler that compares each machine with the live jobs, also for a job outside
the job-list window and what was left before the ledger — and that closes an entry whose thing is no longer there (removed
by hand), which today stays a leftover; leftover counts and bytes on Machines.

**Verification (part 2).** `test/domain/resource-ledger.test.ts` (`cleanupLeftoversOf`; a failed entry reaped later);
`test/engine/cleanup-leftovers.test.ts` (told once, also after a restart; a check
that fails); `test/integration/resource-ledger.test.ts` (real database: Failures lists the job after the grace period, and
not after a reap removes the entry).

### Part 3: the reconciler closes what is gone; Machines counts leftovers (2026-10-22)

An entry whose thing a person removed by hand (or a cleanup outside the hopper) stayed `live` or `failed` for ever: no reap
looks for a dir that is not there, so the job stayed a cleanup leftover. And Machines did not show which machine holds them.

- **The reconciler** (`goneClosures`, `src/domain/resource-ledger.ts`, pure; `closeGone`, `src/engine/resource-ledger.ts`).
  With each sweep of a machine, after its survey and before its reaps, each open entry (`live` or `failed`) on that machine
  of an ended job whose thing the survey no longer found is closed `reaped`, with the reason `not found on the machine`:
  a scratch dir only in a work tree the survey looked in (`Survey.roots`); a job worktree only when the survey lists job
  worktrees (`Survey.trees`; a client older than that lists none, so none is judged); a scope that no longer runs. A job
  that has not ended, a job the store does not know and another machine's entry are not judged. It removes nothing: what
  the survey still finds, the sweep's reaps remove as before. It reads the ledger, not the job list, so a job outside the
  job-list window is judged too.
- **Kept work that is gone** (issue #1120's `goneKept`, `job.work_removed` with `gone`) now also closes the job's entries
  `reaped`.
- **Machines** (`GET /api/machines`, `cleanupLeftovers`): each machine's cleanup leftovers, counted — jobs, entries, and how
  many entries failed —, absent when none. The card shows them as a fact and a warning badge.

**Left for later parts** of issue #2504: containers, volumes, processes, agent sessions, herdr panes and build daemons as
entries; the cleanup as a persisted work item per entry with backoff, on each machine's own transport, and container storage
that only a `podman unshare` removes; the reconciler for things the ledger does not name (a scratch dir of a job the hopper
does not know, what was left before the ledger) and for machines no longer known; leftover bytes on Machines (the survey
measures no size per job dir).

**Verification (part 3).** `test/domain/resource-ledger.test.ts` (`goneClosures`, `machineLeftoversOf`);
`test/engine/sweep-ledger.test.ts` (an entry removed by hand is reaped; kept work gone); `test/ui/hopper-disk.test.ts` (the
card's text); `test/integration/resource-ledger.test.ts` (real database: `GET /api/machines` counts the leftover on its
machine after the grace period).

### Part 4: the job's container runtime as an entry (2026-10-22)

The containers, volumes and storage a job makes in its own container runtime (issue #1295) were not in the ledger. They are
the largest part of what a job leaves, and the storage can hold files of the job's user namespace that a plain `rm` cannot
remove. The reap already resets that runtime (`podman system reset`, then `podman unshare rm` of its storage); the ledger
did not say so.

- **The entry.** Kind `container_runtime`, locator `<scratch dir>/containers`: the runtime's dir, with its storage, its
  config and its guards. The herdr executor saves it in the job's state (`containerRuntime`) once the runtime is set up
  (`src/executors/herdr/start-isolation.ts`), and the next `saveState` records it as the other entries. A machine with no
  podman gives the job no runtime and no entry.
- **Closed.** As the scratch dir's entries (`reapClosures`), but work kept does not keep it: the reap resets the runtime
  whatever the scratch dir holds. A dir in it the reap names as still there (`left`) fails it, with that path. A reap that
  did not look at the scratch dir does not judge it.
- **Gone.** The reconciler closes it `reaped` when its scratch dir is gone from a work tree the survey looked in
  (`goneClosures`).
- Shown in the parts list as "Container runtime on <machine>", and in `job.cleanup_leftover` as any other entry.

**Left for later parts** of issue #2504: processes, agent sessions, herdr panes and build daemons as entries; the cleanup as
a persisted work item per entry with backoff, on each machine's own transport; the reconciler for things the ledger does
not name and for machines no longer known; leftover bytes on Machines.

**Verification (part 4).** `test/domain/resource-ledger.test.ts` (the entry from a state; closed with work kept; failed
while its storage stays; gone with its scratch dir); `test/herdr/executor-runtime.test.ts` (saved once set up, none with no
podman); `test/engine/sweep-ledger.test.ts` (the sweep closes it with the scratch dir, not with a scope-only reap).

### Part 5: entries kept for a retention (2026-10-22)

With a retention set for the status a job ended in (issue #2494, `retainHours`), and for a timed-out job (`liveness`), the
reap at the job's end keeps its scratch dir and job worktrees for the sweep. That reap said nothing kept, so the ledger
closed those entries `reaped` while they stayed on the machine. And had it left them open, the leftover check would have
told a leftover 60 minutes after the end, long before the retention ends.

- **Until when** (`retainedUntilOf`, `src/domain/retention.ts`, pure). The job's end (`finishedAt`, else now) plus the hours
  its machine keeps the status; a timed-out job's, plus the sweep's scratch age (`scratchMaxAgeHours`, absent 24). None: the
  reap keeps nothing for a time.
- **The cleanup at the end** (`src/engine/cleanup.ts`). Such a reap closes the scope only, as a reap that did not look at the
  scratch dir. Each other entry still `live` or `failed` (`retainedEntriesOf`) gets `retainedUntil` (tenant migration 95,
