  column `retained_until`; `ResourceLedgerRepository.retain`, which does not change a closed entry). The sweep's reap once
  the retention is over closes them as before; the column stays as the record.
- **Leftovers.** An entry with `retainedUntil` is a cleanup leftover only `CLEANUP_GRACE_MINUTES` after the later of the
  job's end and its `retainedUntil` (`cleanupLeftoversOf`); the job's other entries are judged from its end as before.
- **Cleanup status** `retained` ("Cleanup: work kept for its retention") while every `live` entry has `retainedUntil` and
  none failed; each such entry's part says "kept until <time>".

**Left for later parts** of issue #2504: processes, agent sessions, herdr panes and build daemons as entries; the cleanup as
a persisted work item per entry with backoff, on each machine's own transport; the reconciler for things the ledger does
not name and for machines no longer known; leftover bytes on Machines.

**Verification (part 5).** `test/domain/retention.test.ts` (`retainedUntilOf`); `test/domain/resource-ledger.test.ts`
(`retainedEntriesOf`, the leftover after the retention, the status and the part); `test/engine/cleanup-retention.test.ts`
(the cleanup keeps the scratch dir's entry open with its retention, and closes the scope); `test/integration/resource-ledger.test.ts`
(real database: `retain` kept, and kept on a later close).

### Part 6: the reconciler records what the ledger does not name (2026-10-23)

What a job left before the ledger existed, and what a reap never recorded, had no entry: the sweep still removed it by its
age, but a removal that failed was no **cleanup leftover**, so it was silently left. The issue asks that the reconciler
reap what no live job holds, whether the ledger names it or not, also for a job outside the job-list window.

- **The records** (`unledgeredEntriesOf`, `src/domain/resource-ledger.ts`, pure; `reconcileLedger`,
  `src/engine/resource-ledger.ts`). With each sweep of a machine, after its survey and the closures of part 3, and before
  its reaps: each scratch dir, job worktree (either layout) and running scope the survey found there of an ended job the
  store knows, which no entry on that machine names (`ResourceLedgerRepository.onMachine`), is recorded `live` on that
  machine, made now. The sweep's reaps then close it as any other entry.
- **Kept until the sweep's reap.** A recorded scratch dir or job worktree gets `retainedUntil` (`ResourceLedgerRepository.record`
  now takes it) set to when the sweep reaps it (`sweepReapAtOf`, `src/domain/retention.ts`, pure, as `retentionOver`
  judges it): the dir's birth plus the scratch age, or with a retention for the status, the job's end plus it. So a
  dir younger than that is no leftover; one whose reap fails or never comes is one 60 minutes after that time. A scope has
  none: the sweep stops it in the same pass.
- **Not recorded.** A thing of a job that has not ended (it records its own), and of a job the store does not know — another
  hopper's, a test's —, which the sweep never touches. A key the ledger has, in any state, is left as it is.
- **The job list.** The sweep looks up a job id not in its newest 2000 jobs in the store, so a job outside the window is
  reaped, and recorded, as any other.

**Left for later parts** of issue #2504: processes, agent sessions, herdr panes and build daemons as entries; the cleanup as
a persisted work item per entry with backoff, on each machine's own transport; entries on machines no longer known;
leftover bytes on Machines; the work trees the sweep looks in come from the newest jobs' saved state, so a work tree only
an older job used is not surveyed.

**Verification (part 6).** `test/domain/retention.test.ts` (`sweepReapAtOf`); `test/domain/resource-ledger.test.ts`
(`unledgeredEntriesOf`: what is recorded, and what is not); `test/engine/sweep-ledger.test.ts` (a recorded dir whose reap
failed is `failed`, its scope `reaped`; a job the hopper does not know is neither recorded nor reaped; an entry the ledger
names is left as it is); `test/integration/resource-ledger.test.ts` (real database: `record` with `retainedUntil`, never
over an entry there, and `onMachine`).

### Part 7: the sweep looks in the work trees the ledger names (2026-10-23)

The sweep surveyed only the work trees that the newest jobs' saved state names (their `cwd`). An entry in a work tree that
only an older job used was never surveyed again: the reconciler could not close it as gone, and the sweep's reaps never
found it. So it stayed a **cleanup leftover** for good, also after the thing was removed.

- **The roots** (`ledgerRootsOf`, `src/domain/resource-ledger.ts`, pure; `sweptRoots`, `src/engine/resource-ledger.ts`).
  On each machine, the sweep surveys the work trees the job list names, plus the work tree of each open entry (`live` or
  `failed`) on that machine: a scratch dir's and a container runtime's (its scratch dir's) work tree, and a job worktree's,
  in either layout. A scope has none. Another machine's entries add nothing here.
- **What follows.** The survey of that work tree lets the reconciler close what is gone (part 3), record what the ledger does
  not name (part 6), and lets the sweep's reaps remove what is old, as in any other work tree. A work tree with no
  `.worktrees` is not in the survey's `roots`, so nothing in it is closed as gone.

**Left for later parts** of issue #2504: processes, agent sessions, herdr panes and build daemons as entries; the cleanup as
a persisted work item per entry with backoff, on each machine's own transport; entries on machines no longer known;
leftover bytes on Machines; a `kept` entry in a work tree no job in the job list used is not surveyed.

**Verification (part 7).** `test/domain/resource-ledger.test.ts` (`ledgerRootsOf`: each kind, once, sorted; closed entries,
scopes and another machine's add nothing); `test/engine/sweep-ledger.test.ts` (the sweep surveys a work tree only an open
entry names, and closes that entry when its dir is gone).

### Part 8: kept work in the reconciler (2026-10-23)

A `kept` entry (work not pushed) was not in the work trees the sweep surveys (part 7 took only `live` and `failed`), and the
reconciler judged only `live` and `failed` entries. Kept work of a job in the job list was closed when gone (`goneKept`), but
kept work of an older job stayed `kept` for good, also after a person removed it.

- **The roots** (`ledgerRootsOf`, `sweptRoots`). The sweep surveys the work tree of each entry on the machine that is not
  `reaped`: `live`, `failed` or `kept`. The sweep reads them with `onMachine`, as the reconciler already does.
- **The closures** (`goneClosures`, `closeGone`). A `kept` entry of an ended job whose scratch dir or job worktree the
  survey no longer found is closed `reaped`, with the reason "not found on the machine". A `kept` entry still there stays
  `kept`: the reconciler removes nothing, and the reap keeps work not pushed as before.

**Left for later parts** of issue #2504: processes, agent sessions, herdr panes and build daemons as entries; the cleanup as
a persisted work item per entry with backoff, on each machine's own transport; entries on machines no longer known;
leftover bytes on Machines.

**Verification (part 8).** `test/domain/resource-ledger.test.ts` (`ledgerRootsOf` names a kept entry's work tree;
`goneClosures` reaps a kept entry that is gone, keeps one still there, and never judges a reaped one again);
`test/engine/sweep-ledger.test.ts` (the sweep surveys the work tree of kept work no job in the job list used, and closes the
entry once its dir is gone).

### Part 9: a job's processes and containers as entries (2026-10-23)

The ledger named a job's dirs and its scope, but not its processes or the containers and volumes labelled with its id. The
survey already finds both (`processes`: a process carrying `HOPPER_JOB_ID=<job id>`; `containers`: a container or a volume
with the label `hopper.job=<job id>`, issue #1120), and the sweep reaps an ended job that still has one. The ledger did not
record them, so a process or a container that stayed was no cleanup leftover.

- **The kinds** (`src/domain/resource-ledger.ts`). `job_processes`, locator `HOPPER_JOB_ID=<job id>`
  (`processesLocatorOf`), and `job_containers`, locator `hopper.job=<job id>` (`containersLocatorOf`; the label is `JOB_LABEL`
  in `src/client/job-runtime.ts`). Neither has a work tree. No migration: the kind column is text.
- **Recorded** by the reconciler (`unledgeredEntriesOf`), from the survey, for an ended job the store knows: each job with a
  process there, and each job with a container or a volume there. A live job's are in use and not recorded; a job the store
  does not know is never recorded. The executor does not record them at the start: the hopper does not make them itself.
- **Closed by a reap** (`reapClosures`). The reap always stops the processes, as it does the scope, so `job_processes` is
  closed `reaped` by every reap, and a retention does not keep it (`retainedEntriesOf`). The reap removes the containers
  unless it keeps the scratch dir (a timed-out job's): `job_containers` is closed `reaped` by a reap that looked at the
  scratch dir, kept work or not; after any other reap it stays open until the survey says.
- **Closed gone** (`goneClosures`). `job_processes` once the survey finds no process of the job; `job_containers` once the
  survey lists containers and names none of the job's (a client older than issue #1120 lists none, so it judges none).
- **Left as before.** The leftover check (part 2), Machines (part 3) and the parts list read these entries as any other.

**Left for later parts** of issue #2504: agent sessions, herdr panes and build daemons as entries; the cleanup as a
persisted work item per entry with backoff, on each machine's own transport; entries on machines no longer known; leftover
bytes on Machines.

**Verification (part 9).** `test/domain/resource-ledger-kinds.test.ts` (the locators match the reap's variable and label;
`reapClosures`, `retainedEntriesOf`, `goneClosures`, `unledgeredEntriesOf` and `ledgerRootsOf` for both kinds);
`test/engine/sweep-ledger.test.ts` (the sweep records an ended job's processes and containers, its reap closes the processes,
and the next survey that finds no container closes the containers).

### Part 10: the bytes of the cleanup leftovers on Machines (2026-10-23)

Machines counted the cleanup leftovers on each machine (part 3), but not what they hold on disk. The sweep already measures
what each job there takes (issue #2494: `jobs`, each job's `worktreeBytes` and `scratchBytes`, the 50 biggest).

- **The bytes** (`machineLeftoversOf` in `src/domain/resource-ledger.ts`, given the machine's `hopperDisk.jobs`). For each job
  with a leftover there: its `scratchBytes` when a leftover entry is its scratch dir or its container runtime (the runtime is in
  the scratch dir), its `worktreeBytes` when one is a job worktree; each part once. A scope, processes or containers hold no
  bytes the measure names. `bytes` is absent when the measure names none of those jobs.
- **Not measured.** `unmeasured` counts the jobs with a leftover on disk that the measure does not name: the measure keeps
  the biggest jobs only, and a machine may have none yet. So the bytes are at least what the leftovers hold, never more but
  for a dir removed after the last measure, which the next survey closes gone (part 3).
- **On the card** (`cleanupLeftoversText`): after the counts, `<size> on disk`, and `<n> jobs not measured` when there are some.

**Left for later parts** of issue #2504: agent sessions, herdr panes and build daemons as entries; the cleanup as a
persisted work item per entry with backoff, on each machine's own transport; entries on machines no longer known.

**Verification (part 10).** `test/domain/resource-ledger-bytes.test.ts` (the sum per entry kind, each part once; the jobs not
measured; no bytes without a measure); `test/ui/hopper-disk.test.ts` (the card's text).

### Part 11: the agent session as an entry (2026-10-23)

The issue asks that a job's agent (Claude) sessions are in the ledger, so that none stays live once the job ended (issue
#2335 ends a parked or waiting job's session). The executor already reports the session its agent runs in once the agent is
up (`agentSession`, issue #501); the ledger did not record it.

- **The kind** `agent_session`, locator the session id (`agentSessionEntryOf`, `src/domain/resource-ledger.ts`). Recorded in
  the same transaction as the job's `agentSession`, on the machine the job runs on (`recordAgentSession`,
  `src/engine/resource-ledger.ts`, from `src/engine/job-run.ts`). A fresh session at a re-queue is a second entry; the
  same session resumed is the same entry.
- **Closed by a reap** (`reapClosures`). The agent runs in the job's scope and carries `HOPPER_JOB_ID`, so the reap stops it
  as it stops the processes: every reap closes it `reaped`, also one that did not look at the scratch dir, and a retention
  does not keep it (`retainedEntriesOf`).
- **Closed gone** (`goneClosures`) once the survey finds neither a process nor a scope of the job on its machine.
- **Not recorded by the reconciler.** The survey lists no agent session, so `unledgeredEntriesOf` records none.
- **Only the running session.** The session's own data (Claude's transcript) is not this entry: a checkpoint and a resume
  elsewhere read it (issue #921). The reap does with it what it did before.

**Left for later parts** of issue #2504: herdr panes and build daemons as entries; the cleanup as a persisted work item per
entry with backoff, on each machine's own transport; entries on machines no longer known.

**Verification (part 11).** `test/domain/resource-ledger-kinds.test.ts` (the entry; `reapClosures`, `retainedEntriesOf`,
`goneClosures`, `ledgerRootsOf`, `unledgeredEntriesOf`); `test/integration/resource-ledger.test.ts` (real database: the
session the executor reports is recorded, reaped by the cleanup at the end also with work kept, and on the parts list).

### Part 12: entries on a retired machine (2026-10-23)

An entry on a machine that left the hopper — a lane pod or a job pod that ended, a sandbox box, an ssh target a person
removed — stayed `live` or `failed` for good: no sweep surveys a machine that is not listed, so no reap or reconciler ever
judged it, and the job stayed a cleanup leftover on Failures with nothing a person could do about it.

- **Retired.** A machine is retired as issue #919 says (glossary "Retired machine"): no machine source lists it, and the
  plugins config does not name it. A machine still configured is not retired, also when it is offline or its instance did
  not build. While the plugins config has an error, no machine is retired and nothing is judged.
- **When.** The leftover check, with each sweep pass, first tells each cleanup leftover as before (`job.cleanup_leftover`,
  after the grace period). Then each told entry on a retired machine (`retiredClosures`, `src/domain/resource-ledger.ts`,
  pure; `src/engine/cleanup-leftovers.ts`) is closed in the new state `retired`, with the reason "its machine <id> is
  retired: it is no longer configured, so no reap reaches it", and logged. So the leftover is told once, never silently
  ignored, and then leaves Failures and the leftover counts; the entry stays as the record.
- **Not final.** As `kept` and `failed`, a `retired` entry is judged again by a reap and by the reconciler on a machine of
  that name, should one come back: it becomes `reaped` (or `failed`, `kept`) as the reap says.
- **Cleanup status** `machine_retired` ("Cleanup: its machine is retired, so what it holds there was not removed"), after
  `failed` and the live states, before `kept_work`. The entry's part says "not removed: its machine is retired", with the
  reason.
- Persisted state: the `state` column is text, so no migration. A build before this one reads a `retired` entry as closed.

**Left for later parts** of issue #2504: herdr panes as entries; the cleanup as a persisted work item per entry with
backoff, on each machine's own transport.

**Verification (part 12).** `test/domain/resource-ledger-retired.test.ts` (`retiredClosures`: a machine neither listed nor
configured, one configured but not listed, a plugins config with an error; a `retired` entry is no leftover, is judged
again by `reapClosures` and `goneClosures`; the cleanup status and the parts); `test/engine/cleanup-leftovers.test.ts` (the
check tells the leftover, then closes it retired; nothing on a listed or configured machine, nor with a config error);
`test/integration/resource-ledger.test.ts` (real database: a `retired` entry is kept, is not open, is not on Failures, shows
on the parts list, and a later reap closes it `reaped`).

### Part 13: the herdr pane as an entry (2026-10-23)

The issue asks that no herdr pane of a job stays once the job ended (issue #2335 ends a parked or waiting job's pane). The
executor already saves the pane the job works in (`paneId`); the ledger did not record it, so a pane the cleanup could not
close was no cleanup leftover.

- **The kind** `herdr_pane`, locator the pane id, on the machine the job runs on. Recorded from the executor's saved state, as
  the other entries (`ledgerEntriesOf`). A job that goes on in a new pane (a restart, a resume, a move) records the new pane
  as a second entry.
- **Closed only by the cleanup at the job's end** (`paneClosures`, `src/domain/resource-ledger.ts`, pure; `closeLedger` in
  `src/engine/resource-ledger.ts`, from `src/engine/cleanup.ts`). The pane is closed by the job's executor, never by a reap
  of the machine, so no reap closes this entry (`reapClosures` leaves it out), and a retention does not keep it.
  - The executor's own cleanup went through: each of the job's pane entries is `reaped`. The executor closed the pane it
    works in, or found it gone; each pane the job worked in before was closed when the job left it (a park, a restart in a
    new pane, the end of a pane left on another machine, issue #1569).
  - Only the reap through the machine went through (issue #2490): `failed`, with the reason "the cleanup did not reach its
    herdr, so the pane may still be open". It is a cleanup leftover after the grace period. When the machine is retired,
    part 12 closes it.
  - The cleanup is deferred: the entry stays `live`. A person who marks the deferred cleanup done (they closed it by hand)
    closes it `reaped`, with the reason "a person marked the cleanup done: closed by hand".
- **Not judged by the reconciler.** The survey lists no pane, so `goneClosures` and `unledgeredEntriesOf` do not judge one, and
  a pane has no work tree (`ledgerRootsOf`).
- Shown in the parts list as "Herdr pane on <machine>", and in `job.cleanup_leftover` as any other entry. No migration: the
  kind column is text. A build before this one reads the entry as any other.

**Left for later parts** of issue #2504: the cleanup as a persisted work item per entry with backoff, on each machine's own
transport (today the cleanup record, its deferral and the sweep's passes retry the job's cleanup as a whole). Part 14 does it.

**Verification (part 13).** `test/domain/resource-ledger-panes.test.ts` (the entry from a state; no reap closes it; the
closures of `paneClosures`; no retention; the reconciler does not judge it; the parts list); `test/engine/cleanup-panes.test.ts`
(reaped through the executor, failed through the machine, live while deferred and reaped when a person marks it cleaned up);
`test/integration/resource-ledger.test.ts` (real database: the pane the executor saves is recorded, and the cleanup at the
end reaps it in each end state).

### Part 14: the maids — a cleanup item per entry, with backoff (2026-10-23)

Before this part, the cleanup record, its deferral and the sweep's passes retried a job's cleanup as a whole: an entry the
cleanup at the job's end left `failed` (a dir it could not remove, a machine it reached only through another route) waited
for the sweep's reap a day later, and a deferral was tried again on every tick.

- **A cleanup item** is a ledger entry still `live` or `failed` of an ended job whose own cleanup is over (no `cleanupDue`,
  no `cleanupDeferred`: that cleanup judges the entries first), past its retention (`retainedUntil`) and its next attempt
  (`maidWorkOf`, `src/domain/maids.ts`, pure). Never a herdr pane: only the job's executor closes one (part 13). A job the
  store does not know is not judged.
- **The maids** (`createMaids`, `src/engine/maids.ts`) run with each sweep check, on the sweep lease's holder, once the
  sweep's pass ends, never beside it: two reaps of one job's dirs at once would race, and the pass would not record what it
  freed. One pass at a time; a sweep check while the pass and the maids run waits for them. For each job and machine with an item due, one reap there through the machine's own
  shell (this machine, ssh, a client target: the first executor there that gives one, as the sweep), given the job's scratch
  dir as its entries name it (`maidScratchOf`: the scratch dir, the container runtime's dir, or the job worktree's work tree).
  The reap is the one the job's cleanup and the sweep use: it stops the scope and the processes, removes the job's
  containers and volumes and its own container runtime through podman (`podman system reset`, then `podman unshare rm` of what is left of its root-owned storage), then the
  scratch dir and the job's worktrees, unless they hold work not pushed.
- **As the reap says** (`reapClosures`): each entry it removed is `reaped`; one it kept for work not pushed is `kept`, with
  `job.work_kept`, and never tried again (the kept-work guard). An entry it did not close — still there, or not looked at
  because no entry names the scratch dir — is an **attempt**: `failed` with why, one attempt more, tried again after a
  backoff (`repo.tried`). So is each item when the reap fails (`the reap on <machine> failed: <error>`), the machine is
  offline, or no executor reaches it.
- **Backoff** (`maidRetryMs`): 1 minute after the first attempt, doubled after each one, 1 hour at most. It goes on while
  the entry is open: the leftover check tells it once the grace period passed (part 2), and part 12 closes it once its
  machine is retired.
- **Durable.** The attempts and the next attempt are on the entry (tenant migration 98: `attempts INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT
  0`, `next_attempt_at TEXT`), so a hopper that stops between attempts goes on from them at its next start. **No double
  free**: the reap removes only what is still there and a missing dir is no error, and a `reaped` entry is never judged
  again (`close` leaves it).
- **Not on a dry run** (issue #2494): the maids skip a machine whose sweep is on a dry run, as the sweep removes nothing
  there. A machine no source lists is skipped too: the leftover check tells it, and part 12 closes it.
- The entry's part in the parts list adds "the maids tried it <n> times, next at <time>" while it is open. A build before this
  one runs on the migrated store: it names its columns when it writes, and reads no new column.

**Verification (part 14).** `test/domain/maids.test.ts` (which entries are due, by job and machine; a job not ended, its own
cleanup due or deferred, a closed entry, a herdr pane, a retention and a next attempt not due are left; the backoff; the
scratch dir from each kind); `test/engine/maids.test.ts` (real database: a transport failure, then a new hopper on the same
database after the backoff completes the cleanup, and a later pass reaps nothing; an entry still left is tried again with a
longer wait; work not pushed is kept and flagged and never tried again; an offline machine is an attempt; a dry run and a
job whose own cleanup is due are left).

## Push requirements (issue #2555, 2026-10-22)

**The problem.** Jobs pushed without the repository's CI gates run first. In one repository, 8 of 9 red pull request runs
passed the whole test job (12–15 minutes) and then failed only the changed-files coverage gate, by 2–7 lines or branches.
Each miss cost about 47 billed minutes and one more CI round. The gate's own command runs in a minute on the job's machine.

**The rule.** A **push requirement** is a rule a repository keeps in its **requirements file**, `.hopper/requirements.yaml`:
an `id`, a **requirement condition** (`when`), the checks to run, and their pass criteria (`src/domain/push-requirements.ts`,
pure).

```yaml
requirements:
  - id: kotlin-coverage
    when: { paths: ["src/**/*.kt"] }
    checks:
      - name: changed-files coverage
        run: ./gradlew koverVerify
        thresholds: { changedLines: { min: 80 }, changedBranches: { min: 70 } }
  - id: migrations
    when: { any: [{ paths: ["**/*.sql"] }, { paths: ["**/migrations/**"] }] }
    checks: [{ name: migration tests, run: ./gradlew migrationTest }]
  - id: workflows
    when: { workflows: true }
    checks: [{ name: actionlint, run: actionlint }]
```

- **Conditions.** `paths` (globs of the files the commit changes against where it leaves its base; a glob with no slash
  matches a file name in any folder, as a skill rule's), `fileTypes`, `repos`, `branches`, `bases` (globs), `kinds` (the
  job's kind of work), `labels` (its item's), `dependencies` (a dependency manifest or lock file changed), `workflows` (a
  file in `.github/workflows/` changed), combined with `all`, `any` and `not`, nested. No `when`: it always applies. Each
  condition says in words why it holds or not; a requirement that does not apply is **skipped** with that reason (no
  changed files match `**/*.sql`).
- **Checks.** A shell command (`sh -c`), at the top of the work tree, with `env` if it names one. It passes when it exits 0
  and each of its thresholds holds on what it measured: it prints a line `hopper-measure <name>=<number>`, and gets each
  bound as `HOPPER_MIN_<name>` and `HOPPER_MAX_<name>`. A threshold it measured nothing for fails, saying which line it
  must print. So the pass criteria are the CI gate's own, by the same command. `ci` names the CI check it stands for
  (part 5, below). A failed check whose output holds V8's `JavaScript heap out of memory` says so on its own line (issue
  #2721): the heap limit its node had — the last `--max-old-space-size` on the command, else in its `NODE_OPTIONS`, else
  Node's default where the client runs — and the command, so a heap too small is not read as a failing test.
- **Levels.** The hopper's default, the repository's file, a folder's `.hopper/requirements.yaml` (**path-scoped**: its
  requirements apply only when the commit changes a file in that folder, and their checks run in it), the job's override.
  A requirement of the same id at a higher level replaces a lower one whole, its thresholds too, stricter or looser
  (`effectiveRequirements`). A deeper folder's replaces a shallower one's.
- **A file that cannot be read** (not YAML, an unknown condition, an id twice) is said with its path, and no evaluation of
  the commit is made: its push stays refused until the file is fixed.

**The evaluation.** `hopper-requirements` (`src/github-proxy/requirements-script.ts`), kept in the job's credentials dir
as `hopper-relay` is — a POSIX sh line that runs a Node module with no dependency, the job's token in a header — runs in
the job's work tree: `sh "$HOPPER_REQUIREMENTS" check`.

1. It reads the commit checked out (HEAD, on a branch; changes not committed are refused: an evaluation is of a commit),
   and the repository from `origin`.
2. It asks the hopper the branch's base (`POST /job/requirements`, `op: base`): the base the git proxy judges the push
   against, as the shrink guard's — the open pull request's base, else the landing branch, else the default branch
   (`baseBranchOf`). `--base` names one.
3. It fetches the base, and lists the files the commit changes from their merge base (`git diff --no-renames`). It reads
   each requirements file of the base's tip and of the commit; the commit's file replaces the base's at the same path
   (issue #2712: a branch made before its repository kept a requirements file still meets it).
4. The hopper plans (`op: plan`): which requirements apply, with the job's kind of work and labels, and why each other one
   is skipped.
5. It runs each check of each requirement that applies, here, on the job's machine, and keeps the output here.
6. The hopper judges the runs (`op: record`) and records `push_requirements.evaluated` on the job's timeline: the repository,
   branch, base and commit; each requirement `passed`, `failed` or `skipped` with its reason, each check's command, exit
   code, thresholds and measured values, and a failed one's `problem`. Never a check's output: it can hold anything.
7. It prints each requirement, and for a failed check the last 200 lines of its output, and exits 1 when one failed.

`sh "$HOPPER_REQUIREMENTS" dry-run` does steps 1–4 and prints what applies, with the commands and thresholds, and what is
skipped and why; it runs and records nothing. `--json` prints the hopper's answer.

Not taken: the hopper runs the checks. The hopper's machine has no work tree of the job's and none of its toolchain; the
job's machine has both, and its sandbox already holds what the job runs. Not taken: the hopper evaluates the conditions
in the client. One copy of the rules, in the domain, tested once; the client only gathers and runs.

**The gate** (`src/users/push-requirements.ts`, the git broker's `pushRequirements`). In the git proxy, after the shrink
guard, each branch a job's push moves to a commit is judged: the job's newest evaluation of that commit in that
repository passed, the push goes on; it failed, the push is refused with the requirements that failed. With no
evaluation of the commit, the commit's tree and the base's tip are read in the user's mirror, the commit in the push's
quarantine (`src/git-mirror/push-requirements-at.ts`): no requirements file in either, the push goes on, as before; one, the push is refused,
as git's own refusal: `octo/tools has push requirements, and 4f1c2a9e8b7d has no passing evaluation: run sh
"$HOPPER_REQUIREMENTS" check in the work tree at that commit, fix what fails, and push again`. With no requirements file,
the **default push requirements** (below) are planned against the files the commit changes from where it leaves the base,
read in the same quarantine (`git merge-base`, `git diff --name-only --no-renames`, as the client lists them), with the
job's kind of work and labels: one applies, the push is refused the same way, naming it (`the hopper's default push
requirements apply to 4f1c2a9e8b7d (workflows), …`); none applies, the push goes on with no evaluation. A new commit (an
amend, a rebase) needs a new evaluation. Git cannot say (no credential, git failing): the push goes on, as with the shrink guard —
a net, not a gate a broken mirror may close on every push. But when the base's tip holds a requirements file and only the
pushed commit cannot be read, the push is refused as for one that holds it (issue #2712). A branch deleted is not judged.
A refusal of a failed evaluation names each failed requirement with why: `kotlin-coverage (changed-files coverage: it
exited 2)`.

**A gate that cannot run where the job runs** (issue #2712, 2026-10-24). Seen: a repository added a coverage gate to its
requirements file, and for a day its jobs' branches that changed the files it names still reached GitHub and failed that
gate in CI. Those branches were made before the file was on the base, so their commits held no requirements file: the
client found no requirement, and the gate read none in the commit. Its command, run on a job machine with no JDK and no
container runtime, exits 2. What holds now:
- The base's requirements hold for every branch that merges into it (step 3 above, and the gate).
- Any exit but 0 fails a check: 1, 2, 127 alike (`judgeEvaluation`). A failed check is never a pass or a skip, and the push
  of its commit is refused with its exit code; the client prints the last 200 lines of its output.
- A check that needs what the job's machine lacks runs where it is: its `run` can be a box step,
  `sh "$HOPPER_STEP" box <template> --script <file>`, with the files it reads as `--input` ("Box steps"), whose exit code is the step's. The client passes the
  job's environment to each check, so `HOPPER_STEP` is there. Not taken: the hopper picks a box for a requirement by
  itself. The repository knows its toolchain, and a box needs the template's approval; the file names it once.

**Trust.** The job runs its checks and reports their exit codes: a job that lies passes its own gate. The gate is for a
job that works as asked, to catch in a minute what CI catches in fifteen; CI still runs every gate on the pull request.

**The default push requirements** (part 2, `pushRequirementDefaults`, a user setting; none by default). An admin edits them
on Settings → Push requirements (`ui/src/views/push-requirements.tsx`): the same shape as a requirements file, as JSON, as
every setting of the hopper is (no YAML in its own config); `GET /api/push-requirements`, `POST /ui/api/push-requirements`
(admin; refused with the file's own reasons when it cannot be read), recorded as `push_requirements.defaults_changed` (the
ids before and after, and who) when they change. `POST /job/requirements` puts them below the commit's own
(`effectiveRequirements`, level `default`), so a repository's requirement of the same id replaces one whole, a stricter or a
looser threshold alike. Read at each evaluation and each push: a change applies without a restart. Not taken: a push with
no evaluation refused whenever defaults are set. A default that never applies to a repository would then cost every job
of it a run of `check` before each push; the gate plans the defaults itself, as the route does, and asks only where one
applies.

**The job's push requirements** (part 3, level `job`). A direct job's submitter sets them with the submission:
`pushRequirements` on `POST /ui/api/direct-jobs` (a list, as a requirements file's `requirements`; refused 400 with the
file's own reason, and nothing kept), `hopper job submit --push-requirements <file>` (a file in the shape of
`.hopper/requirements.yaml`, read before the call), or the JSON field of the Run a job form. They are kept on the direct
job's record (`pushRequirementOverride`), so Run again keeps them; `direct_job.submitted` records their ids only, as the
defaults' event does. `POST /job/requirements` puts them above every other level, and the gate plans them with the
defaults when the commit holds no requirements file: one applies, the push is refused, naming `the job's own push
requirements`. The job's prompt names them and the command to run. A job of an issue has none: an issue's text is not a
person's setting, and a requirement from it could loosen a repository's gate. Not taken: a field on the job's spec. The
record already holds what the submitter chose, and a re-run reads it again.

**The push requirements summary** (part 4, `src/domain/push-requirements-summary.ts`, pure). The evaluation of a pull
request's pushed commit, as a section of its body between two hidden lines (`<!-- hopper push requirements -->`): passed
or failed, the commit and its base, and a table — each requirement, its level and status (a skipped one's reason, a failed
check's problem), each check's name, command, thresholds and measured values. A pipe or a backtick in a cell does not break
the table; a cell is cut at 300 characters and the table at 50 rows, so the body stays under GitHub's limit. Never a
check's output, as the event.
- **At `pr create`.** The proxy adds it to the job's text, before the post key line, from the job's evaluation of the
  commit its newest push moved the head branch to (`github_proxy.done`, op `git.push`, its `heads`). That commit has no
  evaluation (no requirement applied, or none was run): nothing is added. The job's act, as the rest of its text.
- **After each push.** The git broker tells the user's side when GitHub took a push (`pushed`, never awaited). For each
  branch it moved to a commit the job evaluated, the hopper reads the branch's open pull request and replaces the section
  in its body, or adds it, with the user's connection of the repository, and records `push_requirements.summarized`
  (`repo`, `number`, `head`). Only a pull request the job may edit (`ownsPullRequest`, as for `pr edit`): a person's pull
  request on that branch stays as it is. The rest of the body is not changed. A body the job edits with no section gets it
  back at its next evaluated push. GitHub refusing it is logged; the push stands.
- The text names no person and no machine: the requirement ids, levels, commands, thresholds and measures are the
  repository's file, the admin's defaults or the submitter's, masked for tokens as all proxy text. AGENTS.md "GitHub text
  is neutral" lists the exception.

Not taken: a comment on the pull request. One per push buries the conversation; one edited in place is the same as a
section of the body, but a person sees it only when they scroll. Not taken: a check run or a commit status. A check run
needs an installation token, and the hopper acts with its user's connection; a status holds 140 characters, not the
commands and measures.

**The push requirement metrics** (part 5, `src/domain/push-requirement-metrics.ts`, pure). A check that stands for a CI
check says so: `ci: { checks: ["coverage*"], minutes: 47 }` — globs of the CI check names (any case), and the billed
minutes of a CI run that fails on it (optional). The evaluation carries `ci` with each check, so the record says it.
- **A CI run caught.** A commit whose newest evaluation failed on a check with `ci`: the gate kept it off CI. Its billed
  minutes saved are the most its failed checks name; one that names none is **unpriced**. A commit that failed, then
  passed with no change (a flake) is not counted: its CI run would have passed too.
- **A CI miss.** The follow reads a job's open pull request with failed checks, and keeps its head commit with them
  (`failedHead`). When the job evaluated that commit in that repository, and a failed CI check matches `ci.checks` of a
  check of a requirement that applied (passed or failed, never skipped), the hopper records `push_requirements.ci_missed`
  (`repo`, `pullRequest`, `head`, the CI `checks`, the `requirements`, `minutes`), once for each pull request and head
  (`src/sources/ci-missed.ts`). No evaluation of the head (a push no requirement applied to, or a commit another job
  pushed): no miss is known, and none is recorded.
- **The report.** `GET /api/push-requirements/metrics?days=30` (1–365) counts, of the events since then, `caught`,
  `minutesSaved`, `unpriced`, `missed` and `minutesMissed`, in all and for each repository. Settings → Push requirements
  shows them in one line.

Not taken: billed minutes read from GitHub. The hopper reads checks with the user's connection, and the billing of a
run (its runner, its rounding, a self-hosted runner that bills nothing) is not in a check run; the repository knows its
cost and writes it once, by its gate. Not taken: a miss judged by the check's name alone. A CI check and a local check
of different names stand for the same gate only when the file says so.

**Verification.** `test/domain/push-requirements.test.ts` (the file read and refused; every condition and `all`, `any`,
`not` nested, table-driven over paths, branch and base, labels and kind of work; the skip reasons; the levels, with a
stricter and a looser threshold; a path-scoped requirement; the plan; the judgement: two requirements, one failing; a
threshold missed, a measure not printed, checks not run); `test/integration/push-requirements.test.ts` (a real hopper, a
fake GitHub's git, the real client: the dry run lists exactly the plan and records nothing; a push with no evaluation is
refused and nothing changes on GitHub; a check under its threshold fails with its output, and the push is still refused;
after the fix the evaluation passes, is recorded with its command, thresholds and measured values, and the push goes
through; changes not committed are refused; a repository with no requirements file takes a push with no evaluation; part
2: the defaults are an admin's setting, refused when they cannot be read and recorded when they change; a repository with
no requirements file gets them, so a push one applies to is refused until its evaluation passes, at level `default`; a
push they all skip goes on with no evaluation; a repository's requirement of the same id replaces a default with its
looser threshold; part 3: a direct job's own requirement replaces the repository's, with a looser and a stricter
threshold, at level `job`; it applies at the push in a repository with no requirements file; a submission whose
requirements cannot be read is refused and nothing is kept); `test/ui/push-requirements.test.ts` (the panel's summary
and the check of the JSON it sends); `test/ui/direct-jobs.test.ts`, `test/cli/direct-submit.test.ts`,
`test/direct-jobs/item.test.ts` (the form's field, the CLI's file, the prompt line); part 4:
`test/domain/push-requirements-summary.test.ts` (the section's text: status, command, thresholds, measured values, a
skipped one's reason, a failed check's problem, a pipe and a backtick; the body: added at the end, before the post key
line, replaced in place) and `test/integration/push-requirements-summary.test.ts` (the job's `pr create` holds the
summary of its pushed commit; after its next evaluated push the hopper replaces it and records it; a person's pull request
on a branch the job pushed is not changed); part 5: `test/domain/push-requirement-metrics.test.ts` (`ci` read and
refused, carried into the evaluation; a miss only for a requirement that applied and a matching check; a commit caught by
its newest evaluation, a flake not counted, an unpriced one; each miss once, each repository apart) and
`test/integration/push-requirement-metrics.test.ts` (a real hopper, the fake GitHub: a job's pull request whose head the
job evaluated fails CI on a mirrored check, and the miss is recorded once over two syncs; the route reports it with the
run caught; a failed check no requirement stands for records nothing; `days=0` is refused).

## Delivery forecasts (issue #2554 part 1, 2026-10-22)

Owner requirement: for an urgent fix, one answer to "when is it in production?", and which part of that wait is a
person's. The hopper said only "job running", "PR checks pending" and "dev CI running".

Part 1 is the pure core, in `src/domain/`. Nothing reads it yet: the history, the ledger, the API, the CLI and the UI
are the next parts (below).

- **Delivery steps** (`delivery-steps.ts`): `queued` → `coding` → `pr_checks` → `landing` → `landing_checks` →
  `promotion_set` → `test_gate` → `production`. For the hopper's own repository, `landing` is the merge onto `main` and
  `landing_checks` the batch run into `dev` ("Landing batches"). A **step estimate** is the nearest-rank p50 and p90 of
  the step's measured durations, with the sample size; under `MIN_SAMPLES` (5) it is `low` and has no number, so no
  forecast is made up.
- **Promotion sets** (`promotion-sets.ts`): a **promotion set schedule** names weekly cutoffs as local times in the
  owner's time zone. A change whose landing checks end strictly before a cutoff is in that cutoff's set; at the cutoff or
  after it, in the next one. Set N is the Nth cutoff after the epoch. The test gate ends `testGateAfterMinutes` after the
  cutoff, production `productionAfterMinutes` after that. The local time comes from `Intl` (`zoned-time.ts`, shared with
  the claude-plan usage parser): Node 24, which CI runs, has no `Temporal`.
- **The forecast** (`deliveryForecast`): each path chains the steps from the current one; a step starts when the one
  before it ends, the p50 and the p90 chains apart, and the current step ends no earlier than now. A measured step takes
  its estimate; a scheduled step its cutoff or minutes, so the p90 chain can land in a later set than the p50 chain
  (`set`, `setP90`). A step with a `low` estimate is `unknown`, and so is each step after it: no time is given. The
  time left at p50 is split: a person's wait at a **delivery gate** (`humanMs`), the wait for a cutoff (`scheduleMs`)
  and the rest (`machineMs`).
- **Expedite**: the expedited path is computed beside the normal one. With `expedite: out_of_cadence` the
  `promotion_set` step ends at once (`outOfCadence`); with `none` the two paths are the same. It is never later.
- **Slipping**: the current step past its p90 end (a scheduled step: its scheduled end) is slipping, with a **blocker**
  from a fixed set: the change's own, else the step's default; at a delivery gate always `human_gate`. Since the current
  step ends no earlier than now, the later steps move with the clock.
- **A delivery gate** is a step a person ends, with its owner: the forecast of a change at one has
  `wait: { kind: human_gate, owner, since }`.
- **Delivery ledger and accuracy** (`forecast-accuracy.ts`): one row per step with the predicted and the actual start
  and end; `forecastAccuracy` is the mean absolute error of the predicted ends per step and per repository.

**Decisions.** Scheduled steps take their times from the schedule, not from history: the set's times are the commitment.
A merge exactly at a cutoff goes to the next set. The p90 chain sums each step's p90, an upper bound that does not
assume the steps are independent.

**Left for the next parts.** The step durations measured from the events (`job.*`, the pull request checks,
`landing_batch.*`) per repository; the promotion set schedule as a setting per repository, with the gate owners; the
expedite flag on a job, an issue or a pull request; the delivery ledger kept in the database, written when a forecast is
made and as each step ends; `GET /api/delivery-forecast` and `hopper forecast` for a job, an issue, a pull request and a
promotion set; times shown in the owner's time zone in the UI; accuracy over time.

**Verification.** `test/domain/delivery-steps.test.ts`, `test/domain/promotion-sets.test.ts` (just before, at and after a
cutoff, across a day and the end of daylight saving time), `test/domain/delivery-forecast.test.ts` (shape, order,
`low` history, expedite, slipping, the gate wait, the same output twice), `test/domain/forecast-accuracy.test.ts` (a
change run end to end, its ledger and the error per step and per repository).

**Part 2 (2026-10-23): the measured steps and the read.** `src/domain/delivery-history.ts` reads a **delivery track**
for each job from its events: `queued` from `job.queued` to the first `job.started`, `coding` to the first
`job.finished`, `pr_checks` to `job.pull_request_merged`, `landing` the merge itself (no time), `landing_checks` from
the merge to the `landing_batch.promoted` of the first batch run whose `landing_batch.started` `merges` names the pull
request (from `pr.create` through the hopper, `job.pull_request_followed` or the merge). After that the change is in
`promotion_set`. `stepHistory` gives each step's durations from the ended steps of a repository's tracks.
`GET /api/delivery-forecast?job=|issue=|pr=` (`src/http/delivery-forecast.ts`) and `hopper forecast --job|--issue|--pr`
answer the forecast of that change, from the tracks of the last 30 days (`HISTORY_DAYS`). With no promotion set schedule
yet, the forecast's `schedule` is absent and the scheduled steps are `unknown`; there are no delivery gates and no
expedite. A failed, cancelled or rejected job with no merge carries no change: 409.

Decisions: no event ends a pull request's checks, so `pr_checks` holds the checks and the wait for the merge, and
`landing` takes no time. A job's own ended steps count as history when they are in the window.

Left: the promotion set schedule setting per repository with the gate owners; the expedite flag; the delivery ledger in
the database; a promotion set lookup; the UI in the owner's time zone; accuracy over time.

Verification: `test/domain/delivery-history.test.ts` (each step from its events, the batch run's merges, the history per
repository), `test/integration/delivery-forecast.test.ts` (the shape of the answer for a job, an issue and a pull request,
the order of the ends, 400, 404, 409), `test/cli/forecast.test.ts`.

**Part 3 (2026-10-23): the delivery settings and the promotion set lookup.** The **delivery settings**
(`src/domain/delivery-settings.ts`, the settings key `deliverySettings`) hold per repository (`owner/repo`, lowercased)
its promotion set `schedule` and its delivery `gates` (each step a person ends, with its `owner`). An admin edits them
in Settings → Delivery, as one JSON object (`GET /api/delivery-settings`, `POST /ui/api/delivery-settings`, each
repository whole or `null`, `delivery_settings.changed`); the daemon checks the time zone with `Intl`, the cutoffs, the
minutes and the gate steps. `GET /api/delivery-forecast` reads them at each request: the scheduled steps get their times
and sets, and the gates their owners. `scheduledPlace` (`delivery-forecast.ts`) moves a change through the scheduled
steps by the clock: a step with no gate ends at its scheduled end; a step with a gate holds the change until a person
ends it, so the change shows `wait` with the owner and, past the step's end, `slipping` with `human_gate`. Past the end
of production with no gate, the change is delivered: `deliveredAt` and no `forecast`. `?set=N&repo=owner/name` (and
`hopper forecast --set N --repo owner/name`) answers that promotion set (`promotionSetNumbered`, at most `MAX_SET`): its
cutoff, test gate and production times, when it opened, its own step from its opening, and the changes of the window in
it (their landing checks ended before its cutoff) or `expected` in it by their p50 path.

Decisions: the hopper sees no sign-off of a gate yet, so a gated step holds the change until a later part records the
person's act; an ungated scheduled step is taken to end on time, because the schedule is the commitment. A change is in
a set from the end of its landing checks, as part 1 says; before that, its set is its p50 path's. The settings are
edited as JSON in the UI, with no form per field: one maintainer, and the daemon checks each value.

Left: a person's act that ends a delivery gate (and the events of the test gate and production); the expedite flag on a
job, an issue or a pull request; the delivery ledger in the database; the times in the owner's time zone in the UI;
accuracy over time.

Verification: `test/domain/delivery-schedule.test.ts` (a set by its number, the scheduled place with and without a
gate, delivered, the settings patch), `test/integration/delivery-settings.test.ts` (save and read back through the
daemon, the event, 400 and 403, scheduled times and the gate's owner in a forecast, a held change waiting and slipping,
a delivered change, a set by its number with its change, 400 and 404), `test/ui/delivery-settings.test.ts`,
`test/cli/forecast.test.ts`.

**Part 4 (2026-10-23): the expedite flag.** A person flags one change as expedited, or not: `POST
/ui/api/delivery-expedite` (operator) names exactly one of `job`, `issue` (`owner/name#N`, lowercased) or `pr`, and
`expedite` on or off; `hopper forecast --job|--issue|--pr … --expedite on|off`. Each change of a flag records
`delivery_expedite.changed`; the same flag again on that target records nothing. `expediteOf`
(`src/domain/delivery-expedite.ts`) reads a track's flag: the newest flag that names its job, its issue or its pull
request, so a flag on an issue covers each job of it, and an off on the job overrides an older on of its issue. `GET
/api/delivery-forecast` reads every flag (not bound to the window) at each request: an expedited change has `expedited`
`{ by, at }` and `forecast.expedited`, the path part 1 computes beside the normal one (with the schedule's `expedite:
out_of_cadence`, the `promotion_set` step ends at once; never later than the normal path); a promotion set lists it with
`expedited: true`.

Decisions: the flag changes the forecast only — no job's priority, no queue and no promotion. The hopper promotes
nothing itself, so it shows the fastest path the schedule allows and leaves the promotion to the person; a priority lane
for its job is the job's priority, which a person already sets. The change's place stays the normal schedule's until
the events of the test gate and production are recorded. The route does not check that a job id names a job: a flag is
a mark that a later job can match, and a wrong one changes no forecast.

Left: a person's act that ends a delivery gate (and the events of the test gate and production); the delivery ledger in
the database; the times in the owner's time zone in the UI; accuracy over time.

Verification: `test/domain/delivery-expedite.test.ts` (each target, the newest flag, another change's flag),
`test/integration/delivery-expedite.test.ts` (the expedited path beside the normal one, out of cadence and never later,
the set lookup, once only, off through another target, 400 and 403), `test/cli/forecast.test.ts`.

**Part 5 (2026-10-23): a person clears a delivery gate.** A **gate clearance** is the person's act that ends a delivery
gate — the test gate's sign-off, a production approval — for one promotion set of a repository: `POST
/ui/api/delivery-gate` (operator) names `repo`, `set` and the gated `step` (`promotion_set`, `test_gate` or
`production`), recorded as `delivery_gate.cleared`; `hopper forecast --set N --repo owner/name --clear <step>`. The first
clearance of a gate counts: the same again records nothing and answers the first. 404: no promotion set schedule or no
such set; 409: the step has no delivery gate. `gateClearancesOf` (`src/domain/delivery-gates.ts`) reads them for one set;
`scheduledPlace` takes them: a cleared gate ends its step at the clearance, not before the step starts, so the change
goes on to the next step from then, and a cleared production gate delivers it (`deliveredAt`). `GET
/api/delivery-forecast` reads every clearance at each request (not bound to the window), for the set a change is in (from
the end of its landing checks) and for a promotion set looked up by its number.

Decisions: a clearance names a promotion set, not one change, because a set goes through the test gate and to production
as one; a change expedited out of cadence keeps its normal set's place, as part 4 says. The clearance is the event of the
test gate and of production: the hopper records the act and promotes nothing, and an ungated scheduled step still ends on
time. The operator role clears a gate, and the clearance records who: the gate's `owner` is a name in the settings, not a
user the daemon can check. A clearance before the step starts ends the step when it starts, so a person may sign off
early. The forecast's path still shows a later gated step with its scheduled time and owner until the change reaches it.
A clearance cannot be taken back: a later part can add that if it is needed.

Left: the delivery ledger in the database; the times in the owner's time zone in the UI, with the gate clearance there;
accuracy over time.

Verification: `test/domain/delivery-gates.test.ts` (the first clearance per step, another repository or set, a clearance
ending its step, before the step starts, before the cutoff, production delivered, an ungated step),
`test/integration/delivery-gates.test.ts` (a cleared test gate moves a change and its set to production, a cleared
production gate delivers it, once only, 400, 403, 404 and 409), `test/cli/forecast.test.ts`.

**Part 6 (2026-10-23): the delivery ledger kept.** The **ledger pass** (`src/engine/delivery-ledger.ts`, its own pass lease
`delivery-ledger`) runs every 10 minutes (`DELIVERY_LEDGER_EVERY_MS`), the first one interval after the start. It reads
the delivery tracks of the last 30 days, forecasts each change as `GET /api/delivery-forecast` does (the shared reads moved
to `src/engine/delivery-reads.ts`), and writes the **delivery ledger** (`delivery_ledger`, tenant migration 99,
`src/store/delivery-ledger.ts`): one row per change (`job:<id>`) and step. A row keeps the first prediction that gave the
step a time (`predictedStart`, `predictedEnd` at p50, `predictedAt`); a later forecast never replaces it. The actual start
and end are the newest the pass sees: the measured steps from the track, the scheduled steps from `scheduledActuals`
(`src/domain/delivery-forecast.ts`: an ungated step ends at its scheduled end, a gated one at its gate clearance; the step
the change is in has no end). `scheduledPlace` is now the last of those. `GET /api/delivery-ledger?job=|repo=` and
`hopper forecast --ledger [--job|--repo]` answer the rows and `forecastAccuracy` of them.
Issue #2638: the pass offers every row of the window, but the store writes only a row that is new, gets its first
prediction, or gets a new actual time; it reads the kept rows once to compare. With ~7k rows, a full upsert held the event
loop 2-4 s every 10 minutes; an unchanged ledger now costs that one read and no write.

Decisions: the first prediction is kept, because the accuracy must measure what the hopper told a person, not a forecast
moved by the clock; a step the first forecast could not time takes the first one that could. The ledger is written by a
pass, not by the forecast read: a read changes nothing, and a change nobody asked about still gets a prediction. The
interval bounds the error of an actual time the pass did not see in time: none, since the actual times come from the events
and the schedule, not from the pass's clock. A change delivered before its first pass has actual times only, and is not
counted. The pass reads the window once per pass, as one forecast read does. Only the normal path is kept; the expedited
path is not.

Left: the times in the owner's time zone in the UI, with the gate clearance there; accuracy over time.

Verification: `test/domain/delivery-ledger.test.ts` (scheduled actuals, ungated, gated before and after its clearance, no
schedule, agreement with `scheduledPlace`), `test/integration/delivery-ledger.test.ts` (a change run end to end has a
predicted and an actual time for every step and the accuracy report its error; a later pass keeps the first prediction;
400), `test/cli/forecast.test.ts`.

**Part 7 (2026-10-23): the delivery view and the accuracy over time.** Settings → Delivery shows, above the delivery
settings (`ui/src/views/delivery-forecasts.tsx`, its pure part `ui/src/model/delivery-forecast.ts`): for each repository
with a promotion set schedule, its **open promotion set** — the one a change that ends its landing checks now goes in,
`GET /api/delivery-forecast?repo=owner/name` with no `set` (`hopper forecast --repo`) — and the two sets before it, each
with its cutoff, test gate and production times, its step, the person a gate waits on and since when, a slip, the time
left split into a person's wait, the wait for a cutoff and machine time, its changes, and a button per gated step left
that clears it (`POST /ui/api/delivery-gate`, operator); a change looked up by its job id, `owner/name#N` or pull
request URL, with the same parts and its expedited path; and the forecast's error over time. Every time is on the
owner's wall clock: the time zone of the repository's promotion set schedule (`zonedTime`, by `Intl`), else the
browser's, named beside the times. `GET /api/delivery-ledger` answers `overTime` too (`accuracyOverTime`,
`src/domain/forecast-accuracy.ts`): the mean absolute error of the predicted ends per `period` (`day`, or `week` from
its Monday, the default) of the actual end and per step, in `timeZone` (default: the schedule's of the repository the
rows are of, else UTC); `hopper forecast --ledger --period day|week --time-zone <zone>`. The answers' types moved to
`src/domain/` (`DeliveryForecastView`, `PromotionSetForecastView` in `delivery-forecast.ts`, `DeliveryLedgerView` in
`forecast-accuracy.ts`), so the UI reads them as types.

Decisions: the view is in Settings → Delivery, beside the schedule it depends on, not a page of its own (the nav has no
room for one more home). A job's page does not show its forecast: each forecast reads the 30-day window, too much for
every job page a person opens; the lookup reads it on request. A period is placed by the actual end, the time the error
is known. With no `timeZone` and rows of more than one repository, the error over time is in UTC.

Left: none; part 7 closes issue #2554.

Verification: `test/domain/forecast-accuracy.test.ts` (per day in a time zone, per week from its Monday, the same rows
twice), `test/integration/delivery-ledger.test.ts` (`overTime` per day, a named zone, the default period, 400 for a bad
period or zone), `test/integration/delivery-settings.test.ts` (the open set, 404 with no schedule),
`test/cli/forecast.test.ts`, `test/ui/delivery-forecast.test.ts` (times across the end of daylight saving time, durations,
the time zone, the query, the rows, the gates to clear).

## Database reads (issue #2231, part 1, 2026-10-23)

**The problem.** A job that needs rows of a database had no way to read them inside the rules: the vault mints for an
AWS role, a cluster or a namespace only, a read-only box's egress reaches AWS and the cluster API servers only, and a
read profile maps to view access, which has no `pods/exec` or `pods/portforward`. Jobs worked around it (exec in a read
profile, port-forward RBAC, hand-run SQL). The issue asks for a per-step, read-only database read: a login minted for
the step, short-lived, audited, approved as other profiles are, and no new cluster opening.

- **The asset** (`src/domain/access.ts`). `database` joins the asset kinds, named `<cluster>/<namespace>/<database>`, and
  takes `read` only (`profileProblem`). Its read is **high radius** (`highRadius`): it reads rows of data a person may not
  want a job to see, so only its own approval approves it. The read policy never holds it (`inReadPolicy`,
  `readPolicyProblem` refuses a database entry), and a template request with a database need is approved by a person
  only, whatever the policies and toggles say (`automaticApprover`), as a vault secret or an egress host is.
- **The minting credential** (`src/domain/database-read.ts`, `MINTS_FOR_KINDS`). A vault secret that mints for
  `database/<name>`: one JSON value — `engine` (`postgres`), `host`, `port`, `database`, `user`, `password`, `sslmode`
  (`verify-full` by default), `ca`, and `schemas`, the schemas a database read role may SELECT from. The login needs `CREATEROLE`,
  and CONNECT, USAGE and SELECT with the grant option on what jobs may read; nothing else (help/vault.md).
- **The database read role** (`src/vault/postgres-reads.ts`, the `DatabaseReader` seam). For each read the minting login makes a
  role `hopper_read_<16 hex>`: `LOGIN NOINHERIT`, `CONNECTION LIMIT 2`, `VALID UNTIL` 15 minutes on, its password a
  SCRAM verifier made in the hopper (the clear password never reaches the server or its log), `default_transaction_read_only
  = on`, `statement_timeout` 60 s, `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` 30 s, CONNECT on the database, USAGE and SELECT on
  the named schemas. The minting login grants itself the role (a subset of its own privileges), so it may end the role's
  sessions and take its grants back. Before any use it checks what the role could change — a table, a sequence, a schema
  or the database, through the role's grants or `PUBLIC`'s —, and drops it when it could change anything.
- **The read.** The hopper connects as the role and runs the job's one statement as a cursor in a `BEGIN READ ONLY`
  transaction, over the extended protocol: a cursor is a query's only, and the extended protocol takes one statement. It
  fetches 1000 rows at a time and answers CSV with a header (NULL empty, an empty string quoted), each value as Postgres
  sends it. More than 100000 rows or 16 MiB is refused, never cut. Then `ROLLBACK`, and the role is dropped: `NOLOGIN`, its
  sessions ended, `DROP OWNED`, `DROP ROLE`.
- **Access and the run** (`src/vault/database-reads.ts`, `src/skills/database-skill.ts`). `sh "$HOPPER_SKILL" database read
  --template T --database D --sql S`: the template must name `read/database/D`; while a person has not approved that
  read, or the job's sandbox runs of the template, the ask waits (202), as a bastion's does. Then Access decides the read
  for the template (`decideCheckMint`, the read as the check) at each read, and a deny mints nothing.
- **The audit.** `database.role_minted` (job, read, template, database, minting credential, role, decision, expiry),
  `database.read` (the same, the SQL, rows, bytes or the problem, ms), `database.role_dropped` (`read-ended` or
  `expired`), `database.read_refused`. No password, no connection string, no row.
- **The backstop.** `VALID UNTIL` ends a role's logins at its TTL. The reconcile pass (`reconcileMints`, at start and
  every 5 minutes) drops each read role whose `VALID UNTIL` passed, in each database a minting credential mints for: a
  hopper that stopped mid-read leaves its role at most that long.

**Decisions (part 1):**
- **The hopper runs the read, not a box.** The issue let the read run in a box, with the credential delivered as aws and
  kube credentials are. The hopper must reach the database itself to mint the role; running the read there too means the
  role's password never leaves the hopper, the row and byte cap is the hopper's own (Postgres has none for a role), the
  statement is one SELECT by construction, and a box gets no database egress at all — tinyproxy's CONNECT allowlist does
  not carry a Postgres client without a tunnel helper in every image.
- **Schemas are the minting credential's, not the profile's.** An operation profile is an operation on an asset; the
  schemas a database read role may read are set once by the person who sets the minting credential up.
- **No renewal.** A read is one statement under 60 s; its role lives 15 minutes and is dropped at its end. Each read mints
  again, after Access.
- **The answer through the skill route, never the job stream.** A read that waited is asked again with no SQL (the skill
  waits keep no `sql`): its answer says the read may run, so no row is kept in the job stream's results.
- **Postgres first.** The issue named SQL Server as the highest priority. Postgres went first because the repository's
  tests run on a real Postgres already, so every requirement (writes refused, other schemas and databases refused, the
  drop, the TTL) is checked against the real engine; the seam takes a second engine.

**Part 2: SQL Server** (`src/vault/sqlserver-reads.ts`, `mssql` on tedious; `readerByEngine` picks the reader by the
credential's `engine`, `sqlserver`, port 1433 by default).
- **Tables as well as schemas.** The credential takes `tables` (`<schema>.<table>`) beside `schemas`, at least one of the
  two, on both engines: the CRM read joins two tables of a schema that holds many more. On SQL Server the minting login
  needs the grant option on each such table itself; the schema's does not let it grant one table.
- **The read role** is a SQL login and its user in the credential's database, `hopper_read_<16 hex>` both: SQL Server
  has no role that logs in. A contained user would need a contained database. The login's password goes as a SQL Server
  2012 hash (`PASSWORD = 0x0200… HASHED`, SHA-512 of the UTF-16LE password and a 4-byte salt), so the clear password
  never reaches the server or its log; no password policy (a hash cannot be checked), its default database the
  credential's. The user gets `SELECT ON SCHEMA::` or `ON OBJECT::` for what the credential names.
- **The check.** SQL Server has no read-only transaction and no role setting for one, so nothing stops a write but what
  the login may do. The hopper connects as the new login and asks `fn_my_permissions` (server and database) and
  `HAS_PERMS_BY_NAME` for each table, view, procedure and schema it can see: a permission that changes something (a
  write, ALTER, CREATE, CONTROL, EXECUTE, IMPERSONATE, …), a table or view it could write or alter, a procedure it could
  run (one granted to `public` may write for it by ownership chaining), or a schema it could alter. Any of them, and the
  login is dropped and the read fails. Running the check as the login needs no IMPERSONATE for the minting login.
- **The read** runs in a transaction the hopper rolls back, streamed, rows counted against the same caps; more than one
  result set, or none, fails. One statement is not checked by construction as on Postgres (a batch may hold more); the
  check above is what keeps a second statement from changing anything. Values are text: a date as ISO 8601 UTC, `bit`
  1 or 0, binary `0x…`; tedious reads `decimal` as a JavaScript number (the help says to CAST it).
- **The end.** `ALTER LOGIN … DISABLE`, `KILL` each session the minting login can see (with `VIEW SERVER STATE` and
  `ALTER ANY CONNECTION`), `DROP USER`, `DROP LOGIN`. Without those two permissions a held session keeps the login, the
  drop fails and the sweep tries again: an outcome the help names, as the permissions are optional.
- **The backstop.** No `VALID UNTIL`: the sweep drops each read login whose `create_date` is older than the TTL (the
  server's own clock) and each read user in the database whose login is gone or old. A login left while the hopper is
  stopped stays until it starts again; only the hopper had its password.

**Part 3: the vault in a container of its own** (issue #586). Access decides each read in the hopper, as for a mint. Only
the read Access allowed crosses: the op `database-read` (`src/vault/wire.ts`) carries the job, the template, the database,
the SQL, the read's id and Access's decision. The vault container opens the minting credential, mints the database read
role, runs the read and drops the role (`readAllowed`, `src/vault/database-reads.ts`), and answers the rows and its events,
which the hopper appends. A minting credential kept in a vault backend is read in the hopper, as for a mint. A vault
container out of reach answers 503, recorded as `database.read_refused`. The sweep crosses too (`database-sweep`, at each
reconcile pass). So the vault container, not the hopper, needs the route to the database. Tests:
`test/integration/database-read.test.ts` runs the read with the vault in the hopper and in its own container, and the
sweep through the container; `test/vault/database-reads.test.ts` hands a read Access allowed to another vault.

**What is left (later parts).** The live proof on the target clusters, after a person has set up the minting
credentials and the route below.

**The route to an in-cluster database (owner decision, 2026-10-24).** The hopper must open a TCP connection to the
database to mint and to read. A database inside a cluster has no route from where the hopper runs. Four ways were put to
the owner: `pods/portforward` for the observe role and a bastion's forward; an internal load balancer or a NodePort; a
NetworkPolicy and a hopper part in the cluster; a read replica or an export outside the cluster. The decision: **a person
runs `kubectl port-forward` to the database and a relay to it, and the hopper ships no tool for either.** The minting
credential's `host` and `port` name the relay's end, which the hopper (or the vault container) reaches. The same holds for
the SQL Server behind a private load balancer: a person's relay from a network that routes to it.
- **Why no tool.** A forward the hopper starts needs an RBAC change for the observe role (`pods/portforward`), which the
  issue's stop rule forbids, and a hopper part that holds it open. A person's own forward uses the person's own cluster
  access, is opened only while the person keeps it, and makes no change to the cluster, its RBAC or its network.
- **What stays the same.** The database read role, Access, the audit and the sweep work as before: the relay carries
  only the TCP stream. No box reaches the database, and no credential goes to the relay.
- **The trade-off the person takes.** A forward reaches the pod's ports, and the relay's end is open to whoever reaches
  it: bind it to loopback, or to an address only the hopper reaches. TLS through a relay: the server's certificate names
  the database's own host name, not the relay's, so `verify-full` fails on an address. Give the hopper's machine a host
  name the certificate names that resolves to the relay (a hosts entry), or use `require` only on a path the person trusts.
- **When the forward or the relay is down**, the mint fails with the connection's error and is recorded as
  `database.read_refused`; a read role left in the database stays until its `VALID UNTIL` (on SQL Server, until the sweep
  reaches it again).

Tests (part 1): `test/vault/database-read-domain.test.ts` (the asset, high radius, the read policy, the credential, the
CSV), `test/vault/postgres-reads.test.ts` (a real Postgres: the role's attributes and settings, every write refused also
with the read-only default off and in `BEGIN READ WRITE`, another schema and another database refused, the PUBLIC
check, the cap, the drop ends a session, the sweep, a credential of tables), `test/vault/sqlserver-reads.test.ts` (part 2,
a real SQL Server: the login and user, every write refused also in a transaction of its own, another schema, table and
database refused, a write permission or a procedure through `public` refused at the mint, the hash, one result set, the
cap, the drop ends a session, the sweep by age and of orphan users), `test/vault/database-reads.test.ts` (Access, the events, no
password in an event or an answer, the drop after a failed read), `test/skills/database-skill.test.ts`,
`test/integration/database-read.test.ts` (through the real hopper, `hopper-skill` and Postgres: the wait for a person,
the CSV, a write refused, every role gone, no password in an answer or an event).

## The sweep and a job whose agent still runs (issue #2707, 2026-10-24)

**Problem.** The sweep stopped the agent of a job that still worked, and the failure read as the agent's own exit
(`claude exited (exit code 143, signal 15)`). The Failures view then grouped such jobs as a Recurring problem and held them.
Two ways led there:
- An answered question or an ended wait queues the job again with its answer pending (`pendingAnswer`). Its pane stays
  open, and its agent waits there for the answer that its next claim types in. The sweep took `queued` and `held` as not
  live, so it stopped that agent.
- A pass reads the jobs once, before it surveys each machine. A job that started after that read was still `queued` to
  the pass, so the sweep stopped what it had just started.

**Decision.**
- A job whose processes may run (`processesMayRun`, `src/engine/sweep.ts`) is a live job, or a job queued or held with an
  answer pending. A parked job has no pane: what runs of it is still stopped.
- Before each reap, the sweep reads the job again from the store. When its processes may run now, the sweep reaps
  nothing of it.
- When the sweep stops the processes of a job that has not ended, it records `job.processes_stopped { machineId, status }`
  and logs the status it read.
- A failure whose text says that the agent exited, with a `job.processes_stopped` and no `job.failed` of the job after it,
  names the sweep: `the hopper's sweep stopped its processes on <machine> while it was <status>: <the agent's exit>`
  (`sweptError`, `src/engine/outcome.ts`). That is the built-in cause **Stopped by the sweep** (`swept`,
  `src/failures/causes.ts`): transient, retry. So it is never a Recurring problem, it holds no other job, and the failure
  card names the sweep's reason.

**Residual risk.** The read before the reap and the start of a job are not one transaction: a job claimed during the reap's
round trip can still lose its processes. Its failure then names the sweep and runs again.

**Verification:** `test/engine/sweep-live.test.ts` (a job with an answer pending is not reaped, a parked one is; a job
started after the pass read the jobs is not reaped; the event and the log line; the failure text and its cause).

## Step schedules (issue #2716, 2026-10-24)

**The problem.** A box step ran only from a job: a job asked, the hopper ran one command in a need box of the job's
approved template. A task that must run each day on its own — the phrase-drill database backup, which must not depend on
one workstation, or the scheduled read-only infra check that issue #871 leaves for later — had nothing that ran it.

**A step schedule** (`StepSchedule`, `src/domain/step-schedules.ts`) is a person's: a name, a template, a repository, a
folder of it (`input`) and a script in that folder, a daily time in UTC (`HH:MM`), and a timeout. The hopper runs
`sh ./<script>` in a new need box of the template at each due time, with no job and no agent. The folder is read at the
repository's default branch when the run starts, with the user's own GitHub connection (the account of the repository,
`src/step-schedules/github.ts`: the default branch, its head commit, the trees down to the folder, the folder's tree,
each blob, at most 1000 files and 32 MiB), and put in the box's work directory at its repository paths, as
`hopper-step box --input <path> --script <path>/<script>` puts a job's inputs. The tar keeps a path over 100 bytes in the
ustar prefix (`tarNameParts`, `src/sandbox/socket-http.ts`).

- **Saved** (`POST /ui/api/step-schedules` `save`, `hopper schedule save`; operator, a box action). The template must be
  there, and must hold no profile the vault mints (an AWS role, a cluster or a namespace): a scheduled run gets no minted
  credential (409, `NO_MINT_ON_SCHEDULE`; not built). A due time before the save never runs.
- **When it runs** (`dueNow`). Each 30 s each hopper looks at the user's schedules. The newest due time at or before now,
  after the save, is due unless a run of it is there. A hopper that was down across several due times runs the newest
  once when it starts; the older ones are not run.
- **Once, and one at a time.** A run is claimed in the user's database before anything runs (`scheduled_runs`, tenant
  migration 100): a unique index on the schedule and due time of due runs, and one on the schedule of the runs not ended.
  So two hoppers on one database claim it once between them, and **run now** (`run`, `hopper schedule run`) is refused
  (409) while a run of the schedule has not ended. A claim no saga took within a minute (a hopper that stopped between
  the two) ends `interrupted`, so the schedule is not held for good.
- **The `scheduled-run` saga** (`src/step-schedules/saga.ts`), one per run, begun at the claim, runs it on whichever host
  holds it. A run whose need box started in the sandbox runs ledger before a stop is **not run again**: it ends
  `interrupted` with `STEP_INTERRUPTED`, as a need step does (issue #1568), because the script may have had its effect.
  The need box's sweep leaves a box another live hopper's `scheduled-run` saga holds, as it leaves a need step's.
- **The run.** The template must be ready, as for a job's box step (`templateWait`): an approval for some jobs only does
  not cover a schedule. Its vault secrets — what the template gives, but a shared secret and its agent credential — go in
  only when a person granted the schedule the vault: read for that run only through the vault's step delivery (the ask
  names the `schedule` in place of a job: no job need be at work), copied into the box as files, never in its
  environment, each value masked in the kept output. Then the sandbox module's `needStep` runs the box, as a box step's
